FTL or Faster Then Light is a indie kick started game by Subset Games, In which you play as a space ship captain tasked with getting the secret plans of how to defeat the Death Star sorry I mean Enemy Mother Ship to the rest of you fleet while being cased by the rebel fleet. The game  is different as all of the systems and events are randomly generated so no one with have the same experience though life is hard in this galaxy with permadeath and may a foe you will die may times by this part of the experience and increases the replay ability of this game which you could get through in about thirty minutes.
The game is played for a top down real time strategy view with you being able to pause at anytime to assign tasks to your crew as you mange your shields, engines, weapons, oxygen, airlocks and many other systems. Other then the combat their will be may choices you have to make from spending your hard fought scrap on repairing your ship, getting better shields or that cool new Perseus missile launcher. As well as dialog choices similar to a choose your own adventurer story with the all powerful Blue opinions in may  cases if you have a type of crew, weapons or module.
The game features 7 unique races with the plain humans, the mechanical Engi who are good at repairing, the violent Mantis who like nothing more than to rip you limb for limb, the Rockmen who laugh off fire, the powerful Zoltan with the ability to add more power to your systems, the ancient crystal the ancestors of the rock men and the traitorous slugs with their telepathic abilities.
The music by Ben Prunty is split into two distinct styles the peaceful and calming low key music when you drifting in space and readying your ship for the next jump into the unknown, Contrasting the fast paced, heart pumping battle music which adds so much stress and tension to the intense battle management.
Overall FTL is a great unique indie title with brilliant design and hours of fun to be had here.

Some time ago I was reviewing GTA 3 and said it's still a classy and enjoyable product, even by todays standards. Well, I wasn't lying, but I know that the industry have made a huge leap forward since the times of the GTA 3 release. Honestly saying, even the GTA V is not an absolute king of the day at moment. It's just a one great game from the row. But, it's a progress which is really much obliged for everything to the GTA 3, Vice City and San Andreas games. Those titles are like cornerstones of the great skyscraper of the gaming industry and the milestones for its progress altogether.
Oh, anyway, let's cut short to the game already, yeah?
The top selling points of the Vice city are - the spirit of 80's, with music, cars and everything, and the cunning story, with the main character who's not just some random guy like Claude from GTA 3 or people before him. Those things are good and touching even now. Jeez, I love the 80's! And I love the Vice City game!
Yeah, by the time it was released, there was some more things to talk about. Like the weather visual effects, addition of bikes, and some more things - all of them was mind-blowing then, but seems standard issue now. Even the furious missions like "the Demo man", where you need to blow things with RC models, while using quite the challenging controls and time limits to do so - now seems as usual stuff as well. I bet many drone operators in the US who are using the real deal Predators somewhere in the Afghanistan, have started with the GTA RC missions...
But, if you're now wandering, if the GTA Vice City is still an option to play, and what's for, I'll answer you: Yes, for it's the blast from the past, with the whole set of things we're love 80s for. And yeah, it's quite playable, after you tune yourself with controls a bit.
So, my mark is 8.5/10, and I recommend the game for everyone.

The short version: Tough being more then 10 years old, Half-Life 2 is still a legendary game that is a blast to play, with a gripping story that'll intriuge the interested to learn more about it and it's world (like me, wich lead to me spending hours on the Half-Life Wiki), with awesome sound and music, some of the best characters you'll ever see and facial animations that would make some companies even today jealous. If you want to see why everyone loves this game or why everyone is shouting "HAL-LIFE 3 CONFIRMED" then get this game! It has fast-paced action, with a great weapon variety and besides that all the Gravity Gun!
My recomandation: If you want to see a well made classic shooter, get it! NOW!
Half-Life 2, the Half-Life 2. The sequel to a game that changed the face of gaming and defined the genre of the first person shooters. And you know what? Half-Life 2 surpassed Half-Life 1.
Let's get to the basics:
The gamplay of HL2 is that of a more classic shooter, as the Playermovement is extremely fast, even if sprint is limited, you can run trough the battlefield like a champion. This means that strafing, flanking and other tactics that require movement, are all possible. You're not some slow moving sloth-soldier who can only run for 3 Seconds and regenerates his health. No, you're  Gordon Freeman.
The shooting aspect is very well done and requires you too really get close to the enemy. This results, obviously, in close-quarters combat, as neither the enemies, nor you, can really hit anything in the distance. This comes from the fact that the weapons that your going to use the most frequently, loose effectivnes in distance. The SMG, has a wide spread and it's single bullets don't do much damage, wich requires you too really get close to get as many of them as possible into the enemy. This also goes for the AR2, wich has even worse spread. For the shotgun it's pretty obvious, aswell as for explosive weapons and the Gravitygun. Your options for distance fighting are either the crossbow or the magnum, but both have very limited ammo and if your facing 10 or more enemies in the field, without some way of getting more ammo, your going to run out of it quickly.
So the basic shooting gameplay is quick and close, with different tactics that can be applied to different enemies. Out of all this the Gravgun is going to make the most difference as it's your only experimental weapon this time, different to Half-Life 1 where you had three powerfull experimental/special weapons. But the Gravgun makes up for this by being one of the funniest ways to kill things.
Besides the gameplay, I also have to say that this game aged really well. It's hard to describe, but it's something about the artstyle or the texturework, that makes HL2 look reasonable, even in this day and age.  But if your looking to buy this game now, Graphics shouldn't be your priority.
The Story, while very well written, with fleshed out characters that have great voice acting (atleast in the english dub) and that show very pretty facial animations. But it can be a bit hard to follow or not immediatly be understood by a new player, as HL2 is more often than not "show don't tell". Often you'll gain significant information about the backstory, world information or information in general about the world of Half-Life by looking for it yourself (tough, a visit in the Wiki can also help). Some might see this as a negative, but for me, this is something positive. By not force feeding the player the story, this game can easily be played by powergamers that don't care about the story and just want to progress (tough, the game is still going to lock you in a room with a staged cutscene, where the NPCS play out the story and the Player can either embrace it and Roleplay as Gordon Freeman or just hop around on the Furniture). As Playerfriendly as this kind of storytelling can be, I have to admit, it's still a shame how much of it is so hard to find and find out about....but one can see this also as a way to flesh the games world out. Indeed HL2 is filled with details that are not in full display or need some work to be found (you wouldn't believe how many players I have seen who do not understand that the humanoid Combine Units are all humans who have been indoctrinated or persuaded to serve the Combine).
The sound, as usual, is also very well made with weapons that have some punch to them and a soundtrack that fits perfectly in the dystopian science-fiction world an creates the right atmesphere in the right moment.
Overall, I have to say Half-Life 2 is a legendary game that earns it's hype and let's you understand, why Half-Life Fans are waiting so desperatly for Half-Life 3

Half-Life 2 is a first-person shooter game developed and published by Valve Software (Corporation) and is a sequel to the extremely popular and revolutionary 1998 game
. Half-Life 2 was originally released back in 2004 and was then boasting the newly developed, highly flexible and powerful Source Engine, it then became an instant classic by making good use of new technology, excellent storytelling, gameplay mechanics and an unrivaled online experience. Alongside its predecessor, both games left a lasting impression, particularly on the FPS genre, as an industry standard for future FPS games to come.
Half-Life 2 puts the player once more behind the thick-framed bulletproof glasses of Gordon Freeman, an MIT Graduate of Theoretical Physics with an uncanny ability to wield military hardware and the person indirectly responsible for opening a portal to an alien world and exposing Earth to an invasion that is to be known as the 'Black Mesa Incident'. Half-Life 2 is set 20 years after the events of Half-Life 1 and the world is now under the full control of the 'Combine', an interdimensional empire that is currently harvesting the natural resources of Earth including the human race which is now close to extinction.
+ Graphics and artstyle that looks just as good as it is now (2015), as it was eleven years ago (2004).
+ Excellent sequel with an excellent story that expands the Half-Life Universe
+ Excellent memorable supporting characters such as Alyx Vance
+ Great sound quality, facial animation, and voice acting adds to the immersive experience
+ Excellent enemy AI
+ Great level and environment designs but...(see CON #1)
+ Fun gunplay and gameplay mechanics
+ Good selection of weapons and equipment with very creative special abilities (Gravity Gun)
+ Atmospheric with excellent use of lighting, sound effects and environment design
+ Challenging difficulties
+ Expanded levels that give some room for exploration, but doesn't destroy the narrative storytelling
+ Lengthy game time
+ Very affordable price (though I highly recommend the Half-Life Complete pack)
+ Multiplayer is still active as far as I can tell
+ Tons of available mods that expand player experience
- Driving section may be a little too long but it does offer a few 'stops' where the player can stretch his leg muscles and trigger finger.
- The Squad Support AI is down right suicidal with no command to tell them to stay in place for more than 15 seconds before they follow you again.
- Rag-doll physics engine can be unrealistically (albeit hilariously) glitchy
- No Steam Workshop Support for the multitude of MODS that are available.
Much like its predecessor, Half-Life 2 is a
of a game and is a MUST BUY and MUST OWN for any fan of the first person genre because how else can you describe a game that is almost 11 years old, yet, can still retain all the fun and excitement of a recently released title.
If you decide to purchase and try this game, I do recommend you purchase
so you may also avail of the two Episodes that was subsequently released.
Half-Life 2's use of the amazing Source engine reflects on the fact that this game's graphics, despite showing some age, still manages not only to look good, but also to look authentic and atmospheric with its excellent use of sound and music that makes the environment feel alive. Graphics aside, the gameplay has survived for even after a decade and has still not lost its charm. The enemy AI provides an imposing challenge while gunplay and the creative weapons creates one of the most fun and immersive experience you can get on a first-person shooter. Storywise, the Half-Life universe can be considered as one of the most beautifully crafted worlds in gaming history. Half-Life 2 fully emphasizes this point with its amazing and memorable supporting characters that can establish a connection with the player on an emotional level. To recap, Half-Life 2 is the game that once again redefined how modern first-person shooters will be made in the future and remains as the benchmark for good single player FPS gaming experience.

A friend of mine recently told me to buy this game and to play co-op with him, but I took a look at the gameplay and thought it wasn't the kind of game that I would enjoy. I also thought having characters so small on the screen would prove annoying and disorienting. I was ready to dismiss the game entirely despite the "overwhelmingly positive" rating. But my friend insisted, assuring me it was well worth the ten dollars and I wouldn't regret it. So I got it.
My friend wasn't lying.
The "small characters" concern I had actually feels natural within this game. It's a super fun rogue-like platformer, like if you took Binding of Isaac, gave him a gun, and changed the camera angle from being overhead telling him to go crazy murdering creatures. Tons of cool power ups that you can stack are available throughout the levels, and if you unlock the sniper you can one-shot a lot of enemies, and they balance this out by making you reload after every shot to prevent it from being OP (though it's still badass as it is!) Single player or with a couple friends, this game is a good time. I do recommend it.

Shadowverse does a number of things very well.  Classes are diverse.  The evolve mechanic adds strategic depth.  It's rare to run out of cards to play.
In addition, Shadowverse is extremely generous to new players.  Everyone begins with ~40 packs in tickets and gold, and ~10 arena runs.  For some, this might be a sufficient reason to try it out.
However, Shadowverse suffers from the same faults as so many other online CCGs.
All the inexpensive, competitive decks are aggro.  Control and midrange require numerous legendaries else play at a disadvantage.  Most players recognize this, so the low-level ladder is an exercise in repetition.
The ladder is a grind.  Until B-rank -- which would take 70 straight wins to reach -- rating gain is such that one will climb even with a 33% winrate.  This isn't matchmaking system - it's a progression mechanic.   The vast number of games required to gain ranks futher incentives fast, uninteractive decks.
Shadowverse is intended to be a fast game.  Creature card damage is high in comparison to players' health and most decks play some sort of direct damage.  This leads to a tempo heavy, "remove-or-die" style of play because every deck carries the threat of 5+ out-of-hand damage.
Finally, once the free stuff dries up, progression becomes a slow, slow grind.   It may take months to build a new deck from scratch (unless, of course, it's aggro).
With a fleshed out collection and competent opponents, Shadowverse looks to be a deep game.  It's just such a chore to get there.
---
11/2 Edit:  The arena mode, Take Two, is pretty fun.  Also, an answer to common responses:
Yes, this game is more generous than many other F2P CCGs.   A marginally less bad model does not equate a good one.  Card games don't need to be P2W - see Netrunner.
Yes, you can win in D-B ranks with whatever deck you want.  No, that does not mean you're playing a competitive deck.
Shadowverse is not a bad game.  I just don't recommend it.

Let me start off by saying; I love Dead Space. Both as a game and a series, the lore alone in this game is facinating and worth playing the trilogy.
But I cannot, as a fan of this game and the now disbanded developers, recommend the Steam/PC version of this game in any way. It has so many issues with it that really take away from the fun.
#1 You 100% need to install a mouse acceleration fix if you plan to play with M+KB, mouse acceleration is on by default and it's awful. You can find this in the guides but it's pretty much 100% mandatory.
#2 You have to tweak your Nvidia settings specifically for this game if you want to play it safely with as few bugs as possible, Cap your FPS at 60, turn off V-sync in-game and have Nvidia turn it on itself. First chapter you'll get stuck unable to pass an invisible door when you run into your first killable enemy.
#3 Never ♥♥♥♥ing use Continue Game when loading your save. This is a weird one, and you'll hate yourself if you do so on accident. Continue game defaults your games difficulty to Medium. So if you are playing on Easy the enemies get a bit harder, and if you are playing on Hard or Impossible, the enemies become a joke. There is no way to fix your file without hex editing.
This is just some of the garbage I've run into in almost 8 hours of play. It's still Dead Space, the gameplay, sound, music, story, etc are all solid. But this port is so ♥♥♥♥ing bad I can't recommend it at all. Maybe the Origin version is better but I doubt it.

I quite enjoyed Biohazard Revelations 2.  I ended up getting the worst possible ending though, which surprises me because I shot a lot of zombies in the face.  On the last chapter I'm pretty sure I got 90% of those buggers right in the dome.  But alas that wasn't enough and has nothing to do with how to achieve the good ending.  But I digress...
I'll be blunt here.  I love Resident Evil, but I haven't honestly truly enjoyed one of them as much as Revelations 2 since Resident Evil Code Veronica on the PS2.  I didn't like what Capcom did with the series after that, making it into an action game.  Biohazard 2 pulls the series back into a more survival horror type experience.  The pace is slower and the environment is genuinely creepy.  Granted there are decent amounts of run and gunning, but it's not constant like Resident Evil 4 or 5 or 6.  The game is pretty tense at times, and ammo is always in short supply.  There are some pretty creative monsters too, like the invisible flying ones.  The partner dynamics are solid.  You always have a partner with you in Revelations 2 and you have to switch back and forth between them all the time in order to accomplish certain tasks.  It makes the puzzles more involved, and ultimately more rewarding.  All the aspects of a solid game are accounted for, good story, great graphics, good sound, good stuff all around.  Nothing about the game bugged me, and that's saying a lot.  So I have to recommend this game, especially if you liked the older style Resident Evil games, but even if you just like horror and/or shooting.
Also, I really enjoyed playing as some of my favorite Resident Evil characters from back in the good old days of the original 2 games.  They even make some good references to those times in Revelations, and there's even a little bit of a mansion area in the final chapter.  It's even styled just like the mansion in the very first game!  That was a nice surprise for me.  Takes a guy back...
Cheers, and Happy Easter!

Here we are. Almost a decade later after the first Dead Space was released. I can still vividly remember the first time setting my eyes on the USG Ishimura. I had such little knowledge about the pure, adrenaline, pulse pounding experience I was about to get. Neither did engineer Isaac and his crew. After crash landing on the starship and trying to investigate what seems to be an abandoned ship at this point, Isaac and his crew are ambushed by grotesque monsters with long sharp limbs ready to rip them apart. Isaac gets separated from the others - all alone to defend himself. Now he must try to find a way off of this ship. This is where the real nightmare begins.
Dead Space is truly a classic horror game, easily one of my all time favorites! We are talking about a game with incredible atmosphere and disturbing imagery that will leave you wanting more after it's over. With such a enthralling sci-fi story behind it, packed with tense and very violent combat, Dead Space was more than just another horror game brought to the table. It redefined survival horror! An excellent start to a great franchise.
One of the most unique features in the game is the combat. The combat here separates it from any typical action game, because the means of killing enemies (necromorphs) is to dismember their body. It puts a cool tactical spin on how you engage these monsters. You won't be looking to use the biggest machine gun, instead you will use the sharpest tool at your disposal. If it cuts flesh, you can kill them...in a very gory fashion!
Now, there are a couple of issues with Dead Space, specifically the PC version, which keeps it from being a perfect ten game. There are numerous bugs in the game that you pretty much have to fix by yourself, if you plan on playing it with a keyboard and mouse. Some graphic settings are missing and/or are dated and just don't look as good today. You pretty much have to adjust some of them through your video card or use SweetFX for better visual appeal. Some of the game physics are just down right awful.
With the end of Visceral Games, I think it's important that we take a moment and appreciate this outstanding and terrific game that has done so much for the genre - never will we forget the scary moments Dead Space offered us. Never forget those who helped create this universe. I won't.
Here we are. Thank you, Visceral Games!

Absolutely a return to form for Capcom and the RE series.  This game has nearly everything survival horror fans like, though it's certainly not perfect.  My thoughts:
+Excellent graphics and motion capture.  Environments are detailed but not cluttered, and the setting (an abandoned island) hearkens back to RE: CV, one of the best in the series IMO.
+Voice acting is surprisingly strong!  Believe it or not, this crew has just the right blend of fun and drama with the dialog, and Capcom isn't afraid to poke fun at its own series, either.  Standout voiceover work for Claire Redfield, in particular.
+Enemy design is fresh, but evokes a bit of the past as well.  Enemies require a bit of tactics to handle and can vary their strategies, too.  First episode could have used a solid boss fight, though.
+Teamwork between characters is real, and actually relevant.  Compared to RE:6, this game actually makes having multiple characters relevant and fun.
There's a few problems, too:
-Story is pretty vague in this intro.  Leaves a lot of questions but not necessarily in a good way . . .
-Weapon feedback (hitting and firing) is a little iffy.  Stabbing enemies either makes them freak out or does precisely nothing.
-A bit of jittering and framerate issues, but nothing as bad as release week!
All in all, for the price this is an amazing deal and I'm incredibly psyched for episode 2.  DON'T LET US DOWN, CAPCOM!!!

I got this game because I was bored and wanted a mindless title to pass the time. I was quite surprised with my gameplay experience.
If you like Solitaire-style card games, faery themes, and raising dragons, then you might enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are decent - the amount of detail in the cards are very simple. The music and sounds are okay - they do add to the mystical/relaxing vibe emitted by the game - but I quickly muted the music in favor of my own.
Controls are super simple and only involve mouse clicking. There is no tutorial, but tips are always provided when a new element is introduced. The learning curve is mostly non-existent to minimal depending on your knowledge of card games involving a standard deck of 52.
Gameplay consists of you trying to clear a randomized arrangement of cards before running out of cards in your deck (Solitaire-style format). You start by drawing a card, and must click on cards in the play area to interact with your active card. Unlike Solitaire, you can click on cards exactly one value higher or lower than your active card. For example, you start a level and draw a 5 - you can now click on any 4's or 6's in the play area (note that you cannot click on 5's). Chaining combos are important in this game because it will allow you to build up your score meter faster, resulting in more money awarded and a better end score. Your end score fills up a "global" meter that is shown at the end of every level (or hand). After 9 hands, you must have accumulated enough points to free a captured faery. There is always one level objective that lasts for all 9 hands (ex: achieve a 8-chain combo), and completing this will boost your score and money.
New mechanics are added as you progress through the game to keep things challenging. One includes a vine stack that cannot be accessed until you clear a separate stack of cards that has a flower at the end. Another common one is an ice stack of cards that can only be used if you first click a "fire" card, which is usually located beneath many other cards.
Money is used to buy upgrades in the Faereland in the form of buildings. These upgrades will give you things like an extra undo (you start with only 1 and can get up to a maximum of 3) and a count of how many cards are left in your deck. Sometimes, resources will also drop when you clear a stack of cards - these are used to hatch and evolve your dragons. Yes, dragons.
After playing for a while, you will eventually find a dragon egg (there are a large number of dragon variants). You can hatch them once you've accumulated enough resources (there are 3 kinds). Your dragon will start as a baby, and you can select one active dragon at a time - your active dragon will gain experience whenever you win a hand. Once your dragon receives enough experience, it will evolve and have some lore you can read.
Besides the standard story mode, there is a challenge mode and the ability to replay previous levels.
Overall, the game plays well for a Solitaire-based game with extra elements to keep it from running dry. If you are interested in this style of gameplay, then give it a try. I try not to mention price if I feel it is unnecessary, but I got this game when it was discounted at 95% ($0.54 CAD) and sincerely think that this is not worth the full price at all ($10.99 CAD). The content is just far too shallow to warrant that price, when countless other titles exist for the same, if not lower price.
Recommend!

Shadowverse does a number of things very well.  Classes are diverse.  The evolve mechanic adds strategic depth.  It's rare to run out of cards to play.
In addition, Shadowverse is extremely generous to new players.  Everyone begins with ~40 packs in tickets and gold, and ~10 arena runs.  For some, this might be a sufficient reason to try it out.
However, Shadowverse suffers from the same faults as so many other online CCGs.
All the inexpensive, competitive decks are aggro.  Control and midrange require numerous legendaries else play at a disadvantage.  Most players recognize this, so the low-level ladder is an exercise in repetition.
The ladder is a grind.  Until B-rank -- which would take 70 straight wins to reach -- rating gain is such that one will climb even with a 33% winrate.  This isn't matchmaking system - it's a progression mechanic.   The vast number of games required to gain ranks futher incentives fast, uninteractive decks.
Shadowverse is intended to be a fast game.  Creature card damage is high in comparison to players' health and most decks play some sort of direct damage.  This leads to a tempo heavy, "remove-or-die" style of play because every deck carries the threat of 5+ out-of-hand damage.
Finally, once the free stuff dries up, progression becomes a slow, slow grind.   It may take months to build a new deck from scratch (unless, of course, it's aggro).
With a fleshed out collection and competent opponents, Shadowverse looks to be a deep game.  It's just such a chore to get there.
---
11/2 Edit:  The arena mode, Take Two, is pretty fun.  Also, an answer to common responses:
Yes, this game is more generous than many other F2P CCGs.   A marginally less bad model does not equate a good one.  Card games don't need to be P2W - see Netrunner.
Yes, you can win in D-B ranks with whatever deck you want.  No, that does not mean you're playing a competitive deck.
Shadowverse is not a bad game.  I just don't recommend it.

Here we are. Almost a decade later after the first Dead Space was released. I can still vividly remember the first time setting my eyes on the USG Ishimura. I had such little knowledge about the pure, adrenaline, pulse pounding experience I was about to get. Neither did engineer Isaac and his crew. After crash landing on the starship and trying to investigate what seems to be an abandoned ship at this point, Isaac and his crew are ambushed by grotesque monsters with long sharp limbs ready to rip them apart. Isaac gets separated from the others - all alone to defend himself. Now he must try to find a way off of this ship. This is where the real nightmare begins.
Dead Space is truly a classic horror game, easily one of my all time favorites! We are talking about a game with incredible atmosphere and disturbing imagery that will leave you wanting more after it's over. With such a enthralling sci-fi story behind it, packed with tense and very violent combat, Dead Space was more than just another horror game brought to the table. It redefined survival horror! An excellent start to a great franchise.
One of the most unique features in the game is the combat. The combat here separates it from any typical action game, because the means of killing enemies (necromorphs) is to dismember their body. It puts a cool tactical spin on how you engage these monsters. You won't be looking to use the biggest machine gun, instead you will use the sharpest tool at your disposal. If it cuts flesh, you can kill them...in a very gory fashion!
Now, there are a couple of issues with Dead Space, specifically the PC version, which keeps it from being a perfect ten game. There are numerous bugs in the game that you pretty much have to fix by yourself, if you plan on playing it with a keyboard and mouse. Some graphic settings are missing and/or are dated and just don't look as good today. You pretty much have to adjust some of them through your video card or use SweetFX for better visual appeal. Some of the game physics are just down right awful.
With the end of Visceral Games, I think it's important that we take a moment and appreciate this outstanding and terrific game that has done so much for the genre - never will we forget the scary moments Dead Space offered us. Never forget those who helped create this universe. I won't.
Here we are. Thank you, Visceral Games!

The game picks up on the Revelations timeline, right after the events of Rev 1. Except you get to play as new characters and you don't know anything about Rev1 characters. From what I could gather, REV1 and REV2 events occur sometime after RE5.
Each Episodes are split into two chapters. As for the story, you start up as Claire Redfield and Moira Burton teaming up and trying to figure out why you got abducted to a strange new place that has gone terribly wrong... like usual!
On the second chapter of each episodes, you play as Barry Burton teaming up with Natalia, a child that has some hidden secret! The neat twist here is that events with Barry and Natalia occurs six months AFTER those of Claire and Moira.
So without saying too much, here's a rundown of the pros and cons.
+Gloomy and tense atmosphere/setting on an isolated island. Other areas of the game reminiscent of past RE games like a mansion level (RE1) and sewers (RE4).
+Interesting characters and story.
+Took a while but you can play in CO-OP now since it wasn't properly functionnal on the early days of the release.
+Raid Mode offers replayability, if that is your soft of thing... but, it is a huge grindfest if you seek to unlock everything.
+The Struggle and Little Miss "EXTRA" Episodes adds some more backstory.
-Game was filled with an unoptimized mess. Required lots of fine tuning by Capcom and that is why I've waiting about two weeks to play this game as it is intended.
-Uneven pacing between episodes, especially at the begining (EP 1 Ch 1) and the last episode that seems and feels rushed. There are moments of filler and "being dragged" until you get to the Episode's finish line.
-Game seems meant to be played at Easy/Normal for the first playthrough and then, you could play the Hard mode. It takes a long time to unlock the skills and gather weapons, ammo, items, etc. Basically, highly advised to start the game at Easy or Normal... I did a Normal playthrough and many times, I lacked ammo to kill enemies.
-Poor partner A.I. makes you feeling like a babysitter and switching back and forth from the two characters. At least, you don't have to keep healing the partner like RE5/RE6.
-For those who really care, many achievements are bugged and won't pop.
Not bad, not excellent either. It is a good average game that can entertain you for a few hours. Took me a good 16h since I wanted to take my time and explore what and when I could. I'd still advise anyone wanting to get this game to have previous knowledge of RE games since you could feel lost here and there.
I recommend Biohazard Revelations 2 mainly to RE/BH fans. For newcomers, you better do your homework and get accustomed to the story of past RE events. It is not really mandatory since REV2 has its own set story, apart from the franchise.

I was new to the Shadowrun universe before playing this game, and I have to say that I love the setting. If you don't know, imagine a cocktail of two parts Blade Runner, one part the Matrix, one part Native American shamanic magic, and two parts Dungeons and Dragons. Shake and serve with a garnish of film noir.
But this is a game, so let's talk about gameplay. Unfortunately this isn't a very good game. Basically, there are two gameplay modes:
In this mode you walk around and talk to people. However, it doesn't seem to make a lot of difference which dialogue option you pick so really it lacks the immersiveness of (for example) Mass Effect and just feels like an exercise in speed reading. This mode also includes endless fetch quests dressed up with thin narrative excuses. This feels like a linear game masquerading as open-world.
You'd think that the huge variety of characters in Shadowrun (you can be an elven hacker, a human shaman or a samurai troll, to name a few) would open up a variety of exciting combat styles. Unfortunately this isn't the case. Whichever character you play, the most successful strategy is ususally "get behind cover and take shots at them", unless you're a melee character in which case it's "walk right up to them and attack them". The AI is pretty dumb and won't try to prevent your melee characters from getting in close - they'd much rather take potshots at the party member who is hiding behind a barrel 20 meters away than the troll who is currently slashing them up with a katana.
There's no concept of stealth in this game. You can move your characters right up behind unaware guards and it won't give them any combat advantage. They won't even get 100% hit chance with their weapons at point blank range!
It's easy to get lost. Erm, did nobody remember to bring a map of the hospital (or warehouse) we're raiding this week? The maps tend to be pretty linear but sometimes it's not obvious where you have to go and you have to spend time looking around. If you're stuck in turn-based combat movement, exploration takes
. I probably spend half the time on combat missions actually fighting, and the other half walking around trying to find a door.
The inventory/encumberment system is needlessly restrictive and makes no sense. The drones shouldn't even take up inventory space, because they follow you around. A pistol weighs less than a rifle and takes up less space (that's why people use 'em!) but the game doesn't really care.
It's pretty buggy overall. Often, I'll be stuck in combat movement during what is clearly supposed to be a 'story' bit (i.e. when I'm trying to restock at my hideout). This is annoying as hell because movement takes 3-4 times as long. Sometimes I won't be able to move at all from my current tile. The solution to this is to quicksave and quickload, this usually fixes the problem. But with a professionally-made game (this ain't Dwarf Fortress) it shouldn't be happening at all.
Really love that kind of RPG. Feeling nostalgic and having a lot of fun with lots of clishees and puns. Great game!

FTL, from Subset Games and a Kickstarter project, is a space flight simulator with roguelike elements such as randomly generated levels, self-improvements and permadeath. You can upgrade your ship, gain new crew members, buy new weapons, and fight various battle across the cosmos. If you like the idea of a longer version of The Binding of Isaac, this game is perfect (you can save upon exit, but never reload a save, just adding to the fun).
FTL is a game which any sci-fi enthusiast will appreciate. You are in control of a federation ship which is fleeing from a rebel fleet in an attempt to give an intercepted data packet to the remnants of the federation fleet. So you’re basically the Empire in Star Wars, but where the rebels are evil and the Empire are good.

A definite improvement over the first Revelations game, which was itself a definite improvement over the likes of Resident Evil 6...so at least the series is heading in a positive direction.  We're still not back to the glory days of Resident Evils 1-4 and Code Veronica, though - try The Evil Within instead if you want something THAT good! - but this is probably the best Resident Evil game since number 4 (yes, THAT long ago).
It's certainly nice to see the horror taking precedence over the action again, and the character-swapping mechanics are possibly the most successfully realised in a Res Evil game, period (i.e. MORE than just a cheap gimmick).  And, wait for it...STEALTH in a Res Evil game, for the first time ever if I'm not mistaken!  Nice.  Add in some frankly amazing graphics, probably the best characterisation and dialogue in the history of the franchise, and some nice little in-jokes for the long-term fans ("NOW who's the master of unlocking?"), and yeah, it's pretty hard to complain about this one.  Keep it up, Capcom...

Wall of text incoming! 8-)
I got the game + Season Pass during the Halloween sale for ~17€ and I kinda wish I payed twice the amount, because the game is such a blast to play and has LOTS of great content!
The game is full of details and you can see that the developers once again poured all their hearts into this one.
Everything is once again bigger and better. And the Batmobile is a BEAST of a machine! :D
The plentiful AR challenges give you a chance to prove your abilities after finishing the main game, if you're into this sort of thing.
The DLC Episodes are really short but still quite good. The exception is A Matter of Family, which is much longer and really well done. Maybe except for Batgirl's abilities, which are rather disappointing...
Season of Infamy: Most Wanted Expansion, which were interwoven into the main story/the city, are also excellent and reintroduce a couple of great villains.
It's a real pity and a big stain that the game had such a rough start on PC at the beginning... That's why I got the game more than a year later and wanted to give Warner Brothers as little money as possible - as sort of a punishment.
That being said it works very well now - if you disable the Gameworks fog and smoke setting, which drains performance during Batmobile chases and some other scenes, even if you have a second graphics card to offload the physics calculations.
I played the game at 2560x1600 with everything maxed out except for fog & smoke for my main playthrough and it worked and looked great almost all of the time. I also turned off chromatic aberration, not because of performance (makes no difference) but because I think it's a lame effect if used all the time.
The game overall works even better than Arkham City, because there is no microstuttering when looking around the city - it's very smooth with the occasional hitch when a lot of stuff is loading.
It's a bit of a letdown that it doesn't support SLi because then I could probably turn interactive smoke on, or even downscale from 4K, which would probably improve the visuals even further, making the okayish Antialiasing superfluous. :-/
What often doesn't work all that well is the Level of Detail - there are many really ugly textures visible in the distance, especially when zooming in, where there should be better ones instead. This can sometimes break the immersion...
Overall if you enjoyed the previous Arkham games you should feel right at home and enjoy yourself a lot! :)

This is probably one of the hardest modern strategy games out there. I had trouble with it when I first started playing it in easy mode, while most games a generally start on the hard or hardest difficulty and roll through it. This game requires you to be very careful and think about every move you make on the battlefield. Getting a favorable engagement is key because a simple misposition can end in a sqaud member death, and unlike other video games they actually die not just "not unconcious" from a stream of bullets. You actually grow attached to your most powerful squad members and every victory is incredibly rewarding. I recomend saving a bunch when you first start playing until you get the feel of the game just so you don't mess up to badly. Now a lot of the complaints go with "The orginal  X-com is much better/harder". Most older strategy games had a ton of micromanaging that for some people just becomes tedious while others consider it depth. This reboot focuses on strategy in the battlefield rather than paying for every bullet you fire. There is still plenty of customization but it is something that does not require hours of your time to worry about and you become more focued on the upcoming battle.

It's been a while since I've played a good tile-based strategy game let alone a great one like FF: Tactics, so I was fairly reluctant to try out XCOM at first. A friend had been telling me to get it for a while, and I did.
TL;DR I enjoyed the game immensely. Wholly recommend.
The story is not much to talk about. Aliens attack the Earth and it's your job as commander to stop them with your squads.
The gameplay, however, is fantastic. It is flexible in terms of strategy and it seems the missions are all somewhat randomly generated so if you reload the game, the mission will always have different combat parameters (though the objective is still the same). Having only played the normal mode, I can say that the aliens are fairly balanced: favoring to focus your troops to pick them off, instead of the mindless AI we see today in other games. The combat system itself is refreshing with it's special over-the-shoulder view of the "pawn" acting - complete with killcam! That's not to say jetpacks, rappels, robots, and hazards in the environment are all there at your and your enemy's disposal.
Before and after a mission, you'll be spending time at your homebase. This underground facility features the ability to build structures however you want. Labs, workshops, foundries, generators, alien cages, and so on are all available options. I was pleasantly surprised that every aspect introduced in the game at the start is important. Capturing aliens not only progresses your game but allows you to explore whole new avenues of tech to help your troops. Armors, troops, and planes can be researched and built, but upgrading them can be a viable option, too. There are more aspects, but you get the gist. Taking that into consideration, the each player's game can be slightly unique as not everyone will want to upgrade or build the same projects. And to me at least, that's a good thing!
In the midst of all this good stuff are some fairly minor issues I take with the game. Some cut scenes are repeated throughout the game with different context and the weapons themselves are fairly limited in capacity. The biggest issue I take with the game though is that character customization is.......basic. Sure you can customize faces and names, but you can't customize the character class when you hire them nor can you customize what country they are from. hell, gender is can't even be switched. Makes for creating your dream team difficult. But again, not a big deal really.
Overall though, I highly recommend this game to strategy lovers.

Packs can be a bit dissapointing but cygames throws so many at you anyway it's hard not to log back in (btw it takes a while to fill out a collection, I am warning you now). The gameplay is fastpaced and satisfying, focusing almost exclusively on tempo but without it feeling like a onesided beating when you brick or something like that due to the evolve mechanic... The evolve mechanic activates on 4 or 5 mana depending on who started first and allows you to beef up 1 unit and allow it to attack another follower (minion ect) the turn it's played, quite a few have special abilities for that mechanic that get really annoying when used well. I am not saying it solves everything and allows you to pull games out of a shitheap but it certainly makes it more forgiving and easier to deal with good curves and dominate when ahead (but overextending will get you punished and all that).
It can be tough to like the game at first, as one of it's biggest features is the grind... The art and animations all suck you in quite well and the novelty keeps you coming back again and again at least for just a few games, but initially you don't really notice it and the whole experience can become a little bland (gameplay is fun, but the depth can be lacking somewhat if you don't have many cards). Although you drown in a mountain of packs when you begin I imagine this is to give you an initial rush so you keep hunting for those very generous early rewards and going off that high to lengthen it into a longer hobby. Again I should mention that sometimes packrates are not that great (hs should still take a few notes),  this is mostly only a concern because the disenchant to crafting ratio has a huge disparency and even if you net a legendary it is almost never worth disenchanting (except you actually have to to get a complete deck, afterwards it's just a case of "♥♥♥♥ it, it will take way too long to craft the rest of this class").
Another thing to note is this game is only rewarding if you are f2p, 3 packs for 10 USD? No ♥♥♥♥ing thank you, sure you can buy the prebuilt decks for good value but it's still very expensive and half of the rares and legendaries are not very strong in the meta anyway. Become a decent player and invest in take two (aka arena) and if you go 4-1 consistently (with an occasional 5-0 or 3-2) you can really snag some fat rewards over time (there is no 3 strikes, rather your playthrough is recorded over 5 games and your score is counted at the end, like a tournament). You do not get gold passively playing either (I don't really need to explain the purpose of gold...) so i'd be careful in how you invest your time, if you like to collect, however there are plenty of interesting ways to aquire gold:
- Story mode has many assorted rewards in solo play, mostly it's vials and gold (vials being dust, spirit, any random crafting material name ever) and you get gold in increments of 30 usually but sometimes its much more.
- Quests ofc lol which are the same quests as you get anywhere. Play some factions in ranked, evolve stuff, kill stuff. You can get from 10 to 50 gold from up to 3 quests and can replace 1 a day (faction quests always suck man). There is also a static quest of linking shadowverse to another device you own, for 3 standard packs.
- Score rewards... these are basically rewards for how far you climb in one season, gold can be pretty rare here but you get card sleeves and sometimes take two tickets.
- Achievements! Yes these exist too, and they actually mean something! Well not really but they are sometimes a really nice static mine of resources, giving gold and other things upon completion (rank up rewards of 100 gold are found here)
- AI matches are suprisingly a lucrative feature in this game, you can beat ai elite level 1 and 2 for about 300 gold per faction (it might be 400 but it has been so long since I beat elite 1) with 7 factions. It helps
- Event rewards sometimes happen with ridiculous amounts of stuff to earn in the mix, one time you had to win 20 unique  private games for 2k gold. These happen about once every month.
- Take two grants you 130 gold for going 4-1 (it is 150 for a ticket but you can get them for free quite often) and 250 for going 5-0, it's not that much for anything else but you get 1 pack (sometimes 2 for 5-0) for playing take two.
- Guess what? They even have log in bonuses that actually get pretty big, all of it gold or packs (with a take two ticket to spice up the deal)
Now I have spoken alot about the collection grind, what about the gameplay? To be frank, there isn't much to say... The gameplay is cheap fun that just seems to not get boring, it is fast and easy to understand. Anyone can be decent with a bit of thinking and honestly it is kept stupidly simple so you can just play. It normally just feels like a absurdly satisfying counting game when trading for value (or SMOrcing, because this is a game that caters for EVERY ♥♥♥♥ing playstyle so you can be THAT guy). Play lots of♥♥♥♥♥♥at once on curve and just have enough gas to end the game where you can (this is not an endorsed strategy, try at your own risk).
I haven't really said much praise of this game for a positive raiting, but that's because I like it that I choose to point out all the shortcomings. Yeah I could sing it's praises but then that gives you the reader an unrealistic expectation of the game and I don't want that, give it a chance I say, knowing exactly what you are about to do. Play 200 hours while only scratching the surface, spend $16 and realize you got ripped off but not give a♥♥♥♥♥♥anyway. Open 30 packs and get 6 legendaries and go think that is really cool. Love the art and end up playing a deck just for the aesthetics, even if you know most of it gets outsourced. Love every edge and bump that makes it a little sore, because it is so damn fun you just learn to love it anyway.
I can't say this game actually has alot going for it, but it doesn't need to because it is not supposed to. It is not a masterpiece, it is just very addictive and I don't mind... I like it because it doesn't try to be something it can't be. Enjoy, see you in a couple months when you come back to the real world :).

I think Shadowrun is a fantastic RPG, one that is a thinker, and is a rewarding experience.
I've never played the original, but was lead to Shadowrun after greatly enjoying the new XCOM. The adventures feature a decent amount of text, never feeling like too much, and the stories you unfold really grab you and demand you keep pursuing them to the end.
Controlling your characters is straightforward, with a wide array of attacks and special abilities available. The levelling-up system is smooth and offers plenty of customization options to create unique characters. There's a multitude of races with differing specialties too, available in both new character creation and as playable characters throughout the game.
The other great thing is the ability to create new characters and stories via the Steam Workshop. Players from all over the world have contributed to a massive stockpile of supplementary material, all available for free download.
Shadowrun Returns is an immersive and challenging game that supports its enthusiastic community. I definitely recommend this game to any Steam user.

Go here, go there, do this, do that...follow the "storyline...." Ho-hum. Snooze-fest. They could have given us an open world, a dynamic world where everything continued on without you, but your actions had consequences. Instead, a boring by-the-numbers game was made instead.
If it was any more boring, it would a Will Smith movie...if it sucked any worse, it would be any Star Wars movie.
The only redeeming factor is the character advancement. Even that doesn't really stand out.
The game is extremely linear. You MUST follow the plotline/storyline, read a LOT and then they insert a little shoot-em-up that's sound in its turn-by-turn mechanics, but boring as hell. In fact, that pretty much sums it up: boring as hell.
It needs a complete revamp. Lose the set piece maps, give it a random city generator, dynamic NPCs who have their own lives that proceed without you but can be used for your play, either as friend or foe or just a source for more stuff. Give it vehicles, give it co-op and let the players make their own stories in a world that reacts to their actions and is never the same, play after play.
This game? You're better off with renting a movie or three from Red Box or Hulu: you'll get more enjoyment and not feel robbed of what could have been.

Dead Space released in 2008 to very high praises. The PC version nets an 86 Metacritic score, and an 8.0 user rating. As someone who likes horror games, I'm not sure why it took me so long to try it, given its high score and general atmosphere. I decided to try it out since it's close to Halloween 2017, and EA just announced the closure of Visceral studios. After playing the first 2 chapters of this game I have to say...how did this ever turn into a franchise? Let me elaborate;
Dead Space does a few things right - but for the things it does right in the beginning of the game, it very quickly loses all that goodwill. There is an introduction in-game cutscene but it's nice and short. It gives you some basic info and gives our character a reason to be there. The action starts quickly, and the tension immediately follows. This is imperative for horror games - they need to give you a reason to be scared. If the game doesn't show you WHY you should be scared it's failing. The game gives you upgrades pretty quickly (stasis, magnet thing) and a few gimmicky ways to use them. I didn't see any puzzles to use these actions but again, I could only force myself to play for 2 chapters. The inventory management doesn't pause the game which is nice. The monster dismemberment technique was new when Dead Space came out, and I think it does it pretty well. Honestly I think it probably pushed game developers to start thinking more about destructable environments too, which is obvisouly a good thing.
As I said though, this game fails to deliver in the long term. At the outset the game sounds like it's amazing...the atmosphere looks cool, and it has some new and cool gameplay features. Once you learn how to use the plasma cutter you start to realize that you're on a super-linear fetching game with some occasional shooting. Due to the nature of the dismemberment mechanic, each enemy has to have long appendages, and therefore has the same weakness. The point I'm driving at here is that the enemies are all so similar and that makes the game boring. The enemies pop up in reall predictable places and even when they're charging at you just aren't scary. I don't know if it's the "enemy music" or sound effects, but they just come charging at you and you know you have to shoot off their legs/arms. They're not tough. They're not scary. They show up in predictable places. They suck.
As you wander around the ship, you have your CO telling you where to go and what to do. A tram takes you to these different locations and after you complete a task, you get back in the tram for the next section's fetch quest. I can see how this can be a lucritive idea. It gives some scale to the ship since each area is fairly large...but it seems really silly in action. Essentially the game boils down to "Go here, get this, but OH WAIT this room looks like it'll have...oh yup enemies. Wonder how I have to kill them...? Oh look, you only have to shoot their legs off BIG SURPRISE....Ok I got the thing. Time to get back in the tram and do it again"
I feel like I should like this game more. Horror...check. SciFi...check. Sadly, it's also Boring...check.

TL;DR: Shadowverse is an impressive game, and probably the best candidate so far to be in actual competition with Hearthstone. It has interesting mechanics and is reasonably polished. The story mode is cool, even though it's unfinished. I have no idea about the "meta" but that's something that will change over time anyway. Overall, recommend any fan of CCGs to give it a shot.
Unlike all of the other Hearthstone-inspired games coming out, this game actually has an interesting setting. The characters are cool, and the cards are cool. This may not be important to everyone, but it's definitely important to some people, and it's important to me. I can't stand the thought of playing a game like Elder Scrolls Legends with its super generic western RPG setting with the same stuff we've seen thousands of times. This is the main reason I gave this game a shot in the first place.
The game borrows heavily from Hearthstone, which is fine. Instead of Hero Powers to balance out RNG, we have Evolve, which is a much more powerful mechanic, although I find it a little boring. Amulets (basically like Enchantments from MTG) are a welcome addition, and the ones that count down by 1 each turn are cool. However, I find being limited to 5 minions on the board to be a little too restricting. I have a feeling this was a decision made in consideration of mobile, but it can't really be changed at this point without significantly changing the balance of the game. What I do like about it is that it allows for some more powerful effects, like "Fanfare: Give +1/+1 to all followers." without potentially snowballing if you have a huge board.
The artwork is quite good, and HiDPI compatible. The boards are cool, but they make the actual game very difficult to look at. There needs to be much more contrast between what is in play and the background. This is probably my #1 complaint about the game. The visual design of the Hearthstone interface is much more suited for the type of game this is.
Please add an option to switch between Japanese and English voice acting. I'm sure the English cast is talented, but it just never sounds natural for people to read these scripts translated from Japanese. Speaking of which, I used the unofficial method to change to the Japanese audio, and I gotta say, the translation is pretty weird in some places. The text doesn't match what is being said at all, and the changes don't seem to make sense. It's not stuff people wouldn't understand or anything like that.

In truth, this is a very comfortable and welcoming addition to the RE franchise.
While embracing it's survival horror roots it brings fresh mechanics to the table as well.
Do you hate co-op in survival horror games? I personally do.
This game not only competently and seamlessely let's you switch between two characters at any time mid-play - it deeply encourages it. I too recommend this style of play as you get more out of the game. Each character comes with their own strengths and weaknesses. In example, Claire can carry firearms where as Moira can only wield a flashlight to blind enemies, a crowbar to use with powerful finishing blows and sub-weapons. This breathes fresh air in how to approach each fight. New to the franchise is also the ability to stealth kill with your knife. This gives a type of satisfaction you never thought possible. Online co-op is also available.
Online co-op is also available for Raid Mode, which made it's debut in Revelations. This, whether you want to acknowledge it or not, is the other 50% of content this game has in store. With a vast variety of levels, weapons, mods and a high lvl cap, this mode will have you plugging hours upon hours into it.
While crafting in RE is nothing new, REV2 does a good job at bringing new items to the table. Not only do you need to worry about your health depleting, you'll need to worry about losing blood and becoming blinded. You can now gather the supplies to craft Tourniquets to stop your character from bleeding out when they get those deep wounds as well as the supplies to craft Disinfectant when you get blinded by the enemy's fluid discharges. New sub-weapons such as Fire Bombs, Decoy Bottles, Exploding Bottles and Smokescreen Bottles  are craftable and come in handy against the new threats. Be careful though, because your item menu is in real-time.
Alot of new infected make their appearances in this game and I was very impressed with the direction they decided to take it. Finally embracing it's influences shamelessly you will definitely get a slight feeling that the characters might have just escaped from Silent Hill. I personally had a few flashbacks of playing The Suffering back in the day while encountering a few enemies. Don't let this shoo you off, for the influence is lovingly presented with RE's signature style. They all feel very comfortable and are solid entries within the family of infected. I will not list the new enemy types because experiencing them is half the excitement.
I HIGHLY recommend this title to RE fans and survival horror fans everywhere.

In terms of soundtrack, this game has Chipzel on the board, and even after resetting the game probably a million times, the music never drove me insane, it's that good. I can happily listen to Focus and Otis on repeat for many many hours on end. Courtesy is still good, but it's a bit more toned down, which suits the stage, but it's not as good for random listening, in my opinion, as Otis or Focus.

Surviving for more than 5 seconds during one of the first 20 times you play will seem like the most accomplished you've done all week. But it won't be good enough. Oh no, next ypou'll go for 10 seconds, then 20, 45, then you hit 60. Guess what, you've unlocked a new difficulty. Psssshh, now that you've got the hang of it, beating this next one will be super simple right? No, your wrong. Why would you think that? Nope instead, this new level will pummel like that first day you started playing. But after days of trying, you'll finally conquer it, only to be greeted with a new and more challenging difficulty. Then one day, months from when you started playing, you'll finally get there. The last difficulty. You've been trying this difficulty out for a while. In fact, right now, you're only 10 seconds away from victory. 9 Seconds, it's so tantalisingly close. 8, just hang in there. 7, the sweat on your fingers is impeading your ability to win. 6, don't think about the time or you'll lose focus. 5, don't think about anything except that sweet sweet victory. 4, your riding these waves of victory like an ♥♥♥♥♥♥ on a hot summer's day. 3, the game is watching your O face. 2, GAME OVER. As the voice tells you that have failed with it's simple GAME OVER, you look back and ponder on life. How did I get here? Why am I playing this game? What does this game want from me? It has my life, and now it wants my soul. Then you press space and try again. Such a good game. 10/10

Finally, after 7 patches, and the release of all 4 episodes (and the 2 bonus episodes), I am ready to change my original negative review and recommend it. That said, I still have complaints, most notably the microtransactions present for Raid Mode, but that aside, the game is quite good. I am also still unsatisfied with how long it took before multiplayer was implemented (still waiting on multiplayer for the campaign), and the fact that the game was released episodically. That said, at least we now have everything here, which is great. Capcom has also fixed a lot of the FPS, stuttering, and crashes which plagued me on release, so bonus points there too.
A pretty big fan of Resident Evil, if not all Horror games, I greatly enjoyed the gameplay and setting of Resident Evil Revelations. It was good to see the return of Barry and Claire, though I wouldn't have minded seeing more Jill and Ada. Staying true to its history of strong co-op elements, Revelations 2 builds upon this extensively. Whereas in previous Resident Evil games, including the first Revelations, you merely fought with 2 characters, in this one, co-operation between your two characters (Claire and Moira, and Barry and Natalia) is paramount, and the different mechanics of the two characters and how they interact is the standout feature of this game. Forcing you to switch between the two to progress, and with a slew of now customary puzzles, the campaign is solid. But it is in Raid Mode that Revelations 2 truly shines. Having greatly enjoyed the freedom provided by Raid Mode in the first Revelations, I eagerly anticipated the second iteration, and once I could finally play it, I was not disappointed (except for the microtransactions). Great fun, and with multiple characters, weapons, and skills, Raid Mode offers virtually endless replayability. The genuine atmospheric survival horror, and the soundtrack complement the gameplay to produce a worthy addition to the Resident Evil franchise.
In contrast though, the graphics, particularly of the enemies, looks a bit sub-par. The environments and locations look great... but the enemies... slightly less so. While Raid Mode is the best part of the game, microtransactions included, it is seriously grindy, especially if you want to unlock everything. Each character needs to be leveled up separately, and you, as the player, also have a separate EXP system as well. Then there are the skills and in-game cash you need to acquire too. That said, the game is still great fun.

If you like LEGO games in general, you'll like this game (in general).
I got it off the summer sale and have happily played it all through storymode and most of the city missions/bricks.  The game has the same sense of humor and fun as other LEGO games I've tried, pretty much all of them for Xbox 360.  This is the first PC version I've tried out.
I do caution those with lower end PCs (like mine ~7yrs old) you will have to play in the 800 wide mode or you will get every glitch you can google.  Lots of graphics/character glitchings that end level play.  Also fiddle with the video settings and limit useage of the stud multiplier extras as those lag to freeze the screen on occasion.  For the swinging on poles, I have to pause/resume the game for the characters to move on.  Higher-end computers should be fine.
The controls are insane, I'm not sure who designed it but it wasn't with human fingers in mind.  You will have to rebind them before playing.  Or use a controller for simple fix, I unfortunantely don't have one to use.  I'm not really able to complete the game 100% as some of the races I just can't seem to manage with the keyboard - or it's the lag of graphics showing where the next step of the race is supposed to be.  More issue with my lack of tools, but still, slightly annoying.
So yeah... in general I do recommend this game for those who like the brand series and Marvel.  You get to play with the whole of the Marvel universe with a unique storyline.  Some of the missions do get repetitive but I had fun just playing the various characters.

Video games, comic books and LEGO bricks. LEGO Marvel Super Heroes is an incredible game for both LEGO- and comicfans.
The Good:
· A fun story that stays true to the Marvel universe.
· Countless characters like Spider-Man, the Hulk, Thor, Captain America... Basically any Marvel character you can or can't think of. (Even Stan Lee. Hell yes.)
· An open world with tons of side activities, collectable Bricks and breakable LEGO constructions.
· A wide variety of character types that offer for great replayability. Sometimes you will need to replay a level with heroes you have unlocked later on to reach secret areas and so on. For example: Captain America's shield to walk over flames, the Hulk's force to break weak walls, moving metal object with Magneto, and so on.
· Plenty of fun references to the Marvel movies.
The Bad:
· No online co-op, only a local split screen option (that doesn't always respond all to well, unfortunately).
· The game basically requires a controller to play. You can play with the keyboard just fine but there are no mouse controls, which takes away some of the experience. It's not especially a downside, but I thought I'd list it so you know what you're up against if you don't have a controller.
The Ugly:
· For a LEGO game it's absolutely stunning. Gorgeous lighting effects, fun animations, amazing voice-actors... It's a LEGO game to be proud of.
Final Verdict:
An amazing game for both casual gamers, LEGO-lovers and comicbook fanatics like myself. A game every Marvel fan has to own. 9/10

A fun little game if you've got time to kill.
The objective is to outrun a fleet; jumping system to system while facing random enounters, upgrading your ship, and resupplying.
Combat is a side-by-side-view "my ship vs your ship" layout, with weapons, crew members, and ship systems under your control. There is a decent amount of strategy involved in the battles (well, if you plan on not dying then there is).
Upgrade your ship with crew, weapons, drone addons, and so on. Unlock new ships by completing challenges. Each ship generally results in a different battle strategy, depending on the layout and characteristics of the ship (and the loadout).
Overall, it's a fun little game that you can use to kill time on the order of fractions of hours to complete evenings; and all with no lingering commitment and no regrets.

Occasionally I did find the battles a bit too overwhelming, I struggle to see how a casual gamer might cope with the challenges, unless they chose an easier setting of course, sometimes I'd struggle to break through an enemy's armour dealing minimal damage and having to rely on elemental attacks. And this might just be a personal gripe, but in order to unlock all the of achievements, you would have to play the game through multiple times.
Overall, I found the game to be a pleasant and fun experience and would recommend it to anyone who is a fan of RPGs!

Civilization 5 continues the legacy of the Civilization series by completely overhauling the gameplay. While the combat changes need some getting used to, especially if you're coming from older Civilization games, the changes made in 5 can still be seen in the later additions to the franchise, like hexagonical tiles and one unit per tile, etc. Everything has been dumbed down from the previous games for a grater appeal, which works in its own favor.
However, I will give one bit of advice when buying this game; if you didn't like 4X games beforehand, this game could change your mind. It's easy to understand how the game works, especially after a few hours of playing it. The last bit of advice is that I would recommend buying the complete edition. Don't make my mistake and buy the DLC individually. Save yourself a lot of money and buy the complete version.

Risk of Rain is a fantastic game.
That could be my review right there, but I should probably elaborate. This game is fantastic for many reasons, chief among them is the gameplay and music. The gameplay is fun and replayable, with 12 characters (all but one need to be unlocked) all offering thier own playstyles and tactics, ranging from charging at the enemies head-on, to kiting a large group around steadily draining its health. And as the game is roguelike it naturally has unlocks and random-generation, providing many hours of replayability. The music is another selling point (although, while the music is generally well regarded by players and reviewers, it is music, and entirely subjective) as it always seems to fit what is going on on the screen.
I only have one minor gripe with the game, in that there is no tutorial or any form of explanation about how to play, and as a result I recommend watching a video review or a quick explanation. Don't worry about that spoiling anything as the games story is told almost entirely through a short cutscene when you launch the game and through unlockable items called monster logs.
In conclusion Risk of Rain is a fantastic game with great music and gameplay. But little story or explanation.

Shadowrun Returns is a tactical role-playing adventure based off the popular Shadowrun board game. Funded through Kickstarter, this noire detective story is lovingly crafted, boasting beautiful artwork and an interesting text-based narrative. Most characters are forgettable stereotypes - heck, the concept of Shadowrun itself is just a mish-mash of science fiction, fantasy and cyberpunk - but after the initial eye-rolling, the game draws you in.
Even on the highest difficulty setting, the game isn't that challenging until its latter third - but you wouldn't want it to be. Up until that point, you're still figuring out how to best mix and match different upgrades and characters, so it does a good job of building the difficulty. Movement within the combat system can be monotonous, as you have to move each character through halls one slow step at a time, but in its best moments, the combat feels incredibly rewarding, as you task each of your characters with a series of complimentary attacks.
The game is surprisingly long too, lasting roughly fifteen hours. Definitely worth the $3.75 I spent on the sale, though I'm not sure I would have purchased it for anything over $10.
This game isn't breaking any new ground, but it's fun while it lasts.
