Please note that the time played (as of writing, 2.7 hours) is not indicative of how much time I've actually spent on this game -- I played on mobile for a few weeks before this launched on Steam.
Shadowverse is a slick and creative card game unhindered by what other games have done. It uses some classic rules, but breaks others to suit its needs. That is to say, instead of being derivative, Shadowverse uses the genre as a foundation to create its own complex and cohesive game.
I started playing with a bit of trepidation, as I'm not a huge fan of the boobs everywhere art style. However, it turns out that there are also a lot of hot guys, so that's swell. The voices are cheesy at times, but in an enjoyable way. Overall, the game is aesthetically and aurally pleasing. The music's okay, but I admit I typically listen to podcasts while playing.
The port is pretty good. It could use some more hotkeys, but it definitely functions well. I greately appreciate being able to play in 60 FPS on my PC instead of my small phone screen. In terms of running on my computer and the ease of linking my account, it's flawless.
I heartily recommend this game to anybody who enjoys the genre, and would lightly recommend this to players new to the genre. Something like Hearthstone or a MtG Duel Deck might be easier to ease your way in, as the generosity of Shadowverse interestingly makes early ranked matches challenging -- everybody has some half-decent decks to make early, and you need to know how to use them. The game does have a story mode to practice in, but the AI is so dull compared to real people that I stand by my stance of "maybe not your first game, but definitely the one you should stick to later."

Risk Of Rain is a platforming rouglike with it's own interesting universe, easy to understand controls, and crazy gameplay.
This is one of the few games that will help you feel like a
The amount of power you can gain, from being a lowly survivor of the UES Contact Light that dies from a single bite to
Every character that you play stands out from each other, having their own attacks, look, and feel. Not ONE character feels underpowered or overpowered compared to the rest.
Although this game doesn't have the absurd number of items like Binding Of Isaac has...what it DOES have is how every item is viable and doesn't completely topple your playstyle over if you get it. While this does mean there aren't many "weapon changing items", I find so much joy in even finding a common item, as it brings me one step closer to absolute destruction.
That's the joy I find in this game, it's to get as powerful as possible and go as long as possible. There's a nice story under it all (and good reason as to why the items in the game are even there) and if you really think about what you're doing...
You're the villain of this story, whenever you like it or not. The only way you could be somewhat good is if you blaze through the game as quickly as possible and killing as few as you can. The story's optional, though, and you can read about it when you kill foes in Rainstorm or Monsoon difficulties, since they drop logs at a slightly rare chance.
Almost every level has a artifact hidden in it, but you have to be lucky to roll the version of the level that has it. Every Artifact changes up the rules of the game, and gives interesting changes to it. Like, the lower the health something has (including you) the faster you will run, everything exploding with a shower of Creamator explosions when they die, a random skill of yours locking every minute..there's even one called Command that tosses out most of the RNG of the game and gives you chest drops when you get an item. The chest color is the rarity of the items you recieved, and you can pick whatever item from the item table you please. It's balanced, though, that the window you select items is real time, and you cannot move until you pick an item.
When I mentioned "easy controls", this game really does have simple controls. four buttons mapped for your movement, and four buttons mapped for your skills. You can even use a controller.
This game gets interesting when you bring in your pals for co-op, while making it even more chaotic. The game's completely viable solo, but the difficulty becomes interesting in co-op. Do you let your friend take the item drop, or do you snag it for yourself?
There's also a forced item sharing button, which balances out the items for players. Though, me and my friends agree this system is incredibly annoying, so take that with a grain of salt.
The music of the game is an interesting contrast from the chaotic blitzplay of  the game. Even the most intense of the soundtrack is actually quite nice music to sleep too.
If you want my personal favorite piece from the game, it has to be Surface Tension. It's also a boss track, usually used for the Wandering Vagrant boss.
The bosses in this game will be intimidating and will pose a threat, like any boss will, but as you become stronger, you may be able to start one shotting them..and..as you progress even further, normal foes will be replaced by bosses. Ever faced twelve giant magma worms, three overloading ones, six vagrants, and ten colossi at once?
Despite all my praise for the game, though, I do have a gripe about the game. Though, it doesn't bother me too much.
The levels and item count.
The levels will soon feel repetitive, since you will learn their layouts pretty quickly...but at least the levels themselves have different setups. Though it doesn't help that the setups only change the minor places.
The items aren't in a vast quanity, where you will always find new ones...but, hey. Every item is viable to helping you become stronger. I'd rather have this than several items that are "considered" low tier and useless.
Overall, this game, albeit not a masterpiece or a gamechanger for everything that comes after it, it's a really fun game that's even one hell of a ride with friends.
And you know what? That's all I want to ask every once in a while. For the fun alone, I'd highly reccomend the game. The characters are colorful and vastly different from each other (along with having a lot of them) the items you can pick up are ALL great, none are trick items or downgrades, the game chugs on to become blitzplay after you start slaying... It's worth the price.
One more thing to mention. Every item in the game itself has a bit of story on it. Some of the Item logs are even begging for their own stories.
I'd play this over Binding Of Isaac anyday.

Dive into the sprawl and run in the shadows out of the eyes of the Corperations. You are SINless and you are a no one. You're a Shadowrunner. You get by with your skills of hacking/fighting/support/magic/badassery. One day you find yourself in a monetary drought though. Your bank is empty and your bills are piling up. All of a sudden you receive a call on your phone. It's someone you knew from a few years back. He says he's dead. He says he has a million dollars waiting for you. He says you need to find his killer. You grab what little posessions you own and head out on your journey to discover who triggered this dead man's switch. The world of Shadowrun is one of the most engrossing I've played. You'll fall in love with the universe. Yes you, literate person with the eyes.
Gameplay:
The game is an RPG. It feels like it is designed to be an open world RPG at times but it is VERY linear. Throughout the camepaign there was maybe one or two times you had 2 quests you could do. There are branching dialogue trees with options you get to choose yourself for the "role-play" part of RPG. The way you choose your skills is very well done as well, but the menu for the skill selection is a little daunting at first. (It was designed to also work on iOS) At the verry start you get to choose a class. This class selection is merely what preset at the start you want to work with and will not limit you from any other items in the game. If you see mages are cool or you want to be that cyberpunk-samurai you can switch any time! Just know that once you're heavily invested into one tree those points may become rather worthless and you lose them for good. On anything below Hard that won't matter though so experiment away! The pacing is really well done with good amounts of battle and exploration sprinkled everywhere. It never felt like one part was dragging on. The battles themselves are very similar to the new XCOM. There's a cover system with 3 levels of cover, miss chances, action points, and a couple of items you can use. The abilities, weapons, and magic spells all are balanced well with never feeling OP or under powered.
Story:
The universe may be grand but the story is fairly average. It does what you expect and doesn't go anywhere too incredible. It's enjoyable for what it is and a wonderful bite sized RPG. Overall no complaints but no real pros for it either.
Music:
The music is good but rather repetative. And you'll hear the music a lot. The fact I never found it bothersome is a good sign I would assume.
Overall:
If you enjoy isometric RPG's or pine for the CRPG's of old then this may be the game for you.

This game will mess with your head and you will love it.
Antichamber takes place in a series of non-euclidean space (That means you can walk down a flight of stairs into the same room) where you solve puzzles. Puzzles can range from your portal-esc "jump to here" puzzles to staring at an eye until it blinks. Impossible seeming puzzles can sometimes be solved as easily as walking out of a room and easy looking puzzles will have you stumped. The game is completely original in an era of repetition. Even though the game feels inspired by portal I never once felt that this game was a rip-off. Antichamer is never unfair. I never got angry as a challenge because it required you to stand on a certain square or time a jump to the millasecond.
Antichamber is most certainly a Labor of Love. The creators spent years making a wonderful and creative game and I feel like they would have done it for free if they could afford it. The creators do like to throw it in your face from time to time. There are at least two easter-egg rooms that exist just to show off old screen shots or concept art. While this never annoyed me I did roll my eyes once or twice.
The only real issue I have is the story, or lack there of. The story can be summed up as "There is a thing. You catch the thing and then you go into a big place and release the thing. Then the logo." There isn't any real depth or philosphy.
Over all, play it. It's a great game and the world needs more of these.

I don’t have much to say on it, except that the whole game feels like what Fallout 1 and 2 should have been. With Fallout, I remember trying to kill a rat and nothing happened. I’m not sure I even died, I was just locked on the screen pushing every goddamn button I could see but nothing was happening. I felt like an wannabe airline pilot pushing every button in a cockpit with some “off” button that someone else is controlling, and laughing their♥♥♥♥♥off.
But this one is a more clear-cut, FFTactics feel to it. (Which I also sucked at). The mechanics are fairly simple. “Find cover, shoot♥♥♥♥♥♥ reload gun from time to time”. Maybe there’s some complexity down the line but I haven’t noticed it so far.
There’s some RPG to it, naturally. I’m leveling up a few select things that keeps my SMG-wielding girl into a dodging machine. I read somewhere that the “Karma” (Talent points, basically) is a finite resource and I should not be tempted to go “all out”. Therefore, I’m mostly focusing on a couple of main stats, my weapon, with a side gig in Charisma because it usually helps streamline encounters.
But like any RPG with a persuasion mechanic, it adds a fair bit of replayability when you see dialog options you cannot choose. I see “Security” pop up with Police twice now and I’m unable to utilize it, so I may do an extra character or two. And maybe hunt for a profile picture resource some day.
I think I can handle a couple more enemies during some fights. So far the hardest fights were in the prologue, and some fight when rescuing a woman named Coyote where the boss gave himself a heal. He was hard to kill but didn’t hit very hard himself, like most enemies.
If the game maintains its present course, I think I’ll enjoy it for a while yet. It could stand to be a little more challenging (but only a little, I play for fun, not to watch “you died” screens and starting entire levels over).
So far I’m treating it as a sort of “filler” game.
When I figure I can’t get much done in an hour or two on any other videogame, Shadowrun Returns is there to help pick up the slack. Within 30-45 minutes I can usually progress the story one step and get into one fight, which is satisfying for the time.

When I originally played RE:Rev2's first episode on PC< it was a buggy mess. Frame drops, crashes, there were problems. Now that the whole game is released in it's entirety I'm glad to see Capcom have fixed many of the problems that plagued the game at the start.
Resident Evil Revelations 2 put you in the shoes of Claire and Berry, fan favorites from the classic era of Resident Evil. You're joined by Moira,  and Natalia as secondary characters, who help you find hidden objects and to solve puzzles. The buddy system is something I'm not a huge fan of. The AI isn't great, and often stand around and take damage. From a mechanics perspective I wasn't a fan of having an AI partner the whole game.
Luckily for us, the poor AI partner doesn't do much to sully the overall experience. The game is well paced, and throws you into scenarios and presents elements that might be reminiscent to older Resident Evils, something that I really enjoyed. The story is also something I really liked about Revelations 2. Though I feel Moira and Natalia to be something of a chore to play with, they are welcomed additions in terms of narrative. These characters are less like super agents that are so prevalent in the RE series, and more human. You learn more about these 2 and how they're involved in the situation. They're also not shoe horned in, the story's main motivation is from these 2 new chanters. The Story of Rev2 also explores a bit of the series origins which was something else I appreciated.
The game also offers a lot of value as well. For $25 you can expect around 12 or so hours in the main campaign, then an additional 2-3 hours in the bonus campaign. Then there's also raid mode and unlockables which has potentially unlimited play. This is not a bad deal purely from a value proposition.
I feel like the game being released episodically overall hurt REV2 in the end. The first episode was by far the most uneventful and it was pleagued with technical issues. If Capcom released the game in full, and in an optimized state that it is today, I feel like there would of been much more excitement for Rev2, and more positive reviews. Capcom literally put their worst foot forward on this one. It's a shame because the game as a whole is actually quite enjoyable.
Pros:
- Well paced campaign
- Great story (for RE standards)
- Great bang for your buck (good value)
Cons:
- Poor AI
- Releasing this game in chunks (IMO) hurt it in the end.

TL;DR: ...why don't you have this in your Steam liabry if you're a Steam user?
Half-Life 2 is the sequel to the smash-hit debut title for Valve. Half-Life had revolutionary graphics engine, amazing A.I, logical puzzles and an engaging story- nothing like other FPS games that came out before Half-Life. Half-Life won over 50 awards, and is to this date announced as the 'best FPS game ever made'. And Half-Life 2 is the direct sequel to this masterpiece, so it has to live up to its expectations, though cliches with sequels are that they are only made to milk money. THAT is not true with Half-LIfe 2.
Not only Half-Life 2 also had a ground-breaking physics engine called Source, it leaved the 'closed enviorment' atmosphere behind, but used it to make a even better written storyline.
Now, keep in mind that Half-Life 2 was made in 2004. I will be reviewing this game like it came out in 2004, but also as if it came out in modern times.
The Source engine is still a pretty good engine now, but back then, it was amazing. The signature weapon of the game, the Gravity Gun, was made specifically to show out this new physics. You can't play the original Source engine from 2004 because they updated all games that used the engine to have the updated version from Half-Life 2: Episode 2, so you mostly won't suffer from the engines cons, but back then, the sound engine was terrible for the Source.
The story continues right where you left off. You were hired by the 'G-Man' because he was impressed at your skills, and put you into stasis untill the time came. Now, it's time to smell the ashes, and Gordon Freeman, the physicist you're contolling, has to join up with the Rebels to fight off the alien 'Combine' forces. The Combine are this galactic federation that enslaves every alien species come by, and puts them as the member of their 'union'. The humans had a 7-hour long war with them, until the UN HQ burnt down and Earth surrendered.
In Half-Life, the first bit of the game was you trying to get the ♥♥♥♥ out of Black Mesa, the research facility you were working. Then your mission was to save the world from suffering the same misery Black Mesa suffered by killing the invaders' master and ending the invasion. But Gordon was a bit too late, and the invaders found a way out of Black Mesa(which was just teleporting there) before Gordon did. But since Gordon did kill their master, they stopped fighting the humans(except for the non-inteligent ones). Then the Combine came, and this is where you start.
As the story goes along, the level change drastically. You start at a big city, goes to a canal, a dead town, a coast, a desert, a prison, then back to the city to finally blow up the Citadel, the Combine's base of operations for Earth. While the gameplay doesn't change a lot thoughout the game, the atmosphere do.
Now, the gameplay is nothing special in my book- it's pretty good(or above average depending on your look). You shoot guns to kill people. Though you can use physics against your enemies with your special 'Gravity Gun'. The Gravity Gun allows you to pick up heavy objects and just throw them wherever you wish it to. This can definetely result in some funny moments, and can vary up the gameplay.
The playtime for Half-Life is much longer then any other FPS games that came out around 2004(Halo 3, Doom 3, Modern Warfare, etc). The average playtime for those games were about 6~8 hours, while Half-Life's playtime is around 8~10 hours. Nothing special compared to modern games(well, actually maybe it is), but still pretty good for a 2004 game.
The puzzles are back from Half-Life, though this time, a lot of the puzzles are about physics(not because the protagonist is a physicist, but to show off the engine). It involves simple tasks such as moving things to point A to point B, to puzzles like throwing barrels so it makes a bridge(a bit similiar puzzle is from Half-Life: Blue Shift).
Let's talk about some miscellaneous stuff. The graphics were good at the time, but by today standards, it's average(even below avarage). The soundtrack is more of the same with Half-Life 1 actually, with some remixes and a few new tracks. It still takes advantage of the ambient themes.
I probably don't even need to make this review any longer- as you may already have noticed, Half-Life 2 is an amazing game. But many people don't go over the cons for the game, and some of them are blantly obvious.
The A.I. Jesus Christ, the A.I. It's not terrible, but considering Half-Life 1 was revolutionary in its A.I. programming, it was very dissapointing. A good game to compare this is Halo: Combat Evolved. In that game, the enemies flanked you, took defensive positions, etc. While Half-Life 1's A.I. was fantastic at the time, if you compare 1998 with 2004, it's not very different. And Half-Life 2 didn't have much better A.I. then its prequel.(the companions A.I. is a bit improved though)
The game is really really easy. Really really really. I mean, Half-Life 1 was easy, but this game is just out there. I highly suggest not even touching the 'easy difficulty', A.K.A 'you can't ♥♥♥♥ing die difficulty'. There are also vehicles in the game, and while it's pretty fun, some parts are just fillers. Oh, and the ending is not that good. I also suggest buying the 'Orange Box', which includes Half-Life 2, its episodic sequels(that fills up the dissapointing ending), and a few other really great games.
So we come down to the verdict. I give Half-Life 2 a solid(not really) 7.7/10. It's a great game, for reals. If Half-Life 1 was what every FPS should aim to be, Half-Life 2 is a bit more meh. While the Source engine is an amazing engine, Half-Life 2 doesn't do enough to really stand out on its own currently in 2015. But eleven years earlier, it was amazing.
Once again, I highly suggest you to buy the Orange Box, and perhaps Half-Life 1 as well(it's a better game overall except for the story and the graphics). Them, Counter-Strike: Source, and Garry's Mod are a must buy if you're a Steam user.

Risk of Rain is a fantastic game.
That could be my review right there, but I should probably elaborate. This game is fantastic for many reasons, chief among them is the gameplay and music. The gameplay is fun and replayable, with 12 characters (all but one need to be unlocked) all offering thier own playstyles and tactics, ranging from charging at the enemies head-on, to kiting a large group around steadily draining its health. And as the game is roguelike it naturally has unlocks and random-generation, providing many hours of replayability. The music is another selling point (although, while the music is generally well regarded by players and reviewers, it is music, and entirely subjective) as it always seems to fit what is going on on the screen.
I only have one minor gripe with the game, in that there is no tutorial or any form of explanation about how to play, and as a result I recommend watching a video review or a quick explanation. Don't worry about that spoiling anything as the games story is told almost entirely through a short cutscene when you launch the game and through unlockable items called monster logs.
In conclusion Risk of Rain is a fantastic game with great music and gameplay. But little story or explanation.

Risk Of Rain is a platforming rouglike with it's own interesting universe, easy to understand controls, and crazy gameplay.
This is one of the few games that will help you feel like a
The amount of power you can gain, from being a lowly survivor of the UES Contact Light that dies from a single bite to
Every character that you play stands out from each other, having their own attacks, look, and feel. Not ONE character feels underpowered or overpowered compared to the rest.
Although this game doesn't have the absurd number of items like Binding Of Isaac has...what it DOES have is how every item is viable and doesn't completely topple your playstyle over if you get it. While this does mean there aren't many "weapon changing items", I find so much joy in even finding a common item, as it brings me one step closer to absolute destruction.
That's the joy I find in this game, it's to get as powerful as possible and go as long as possible. There's a nice story under it all (and good reason as to why the items in the game are even there) and if you really think about what you're doing...
You're the villain of this story, whenever you like it or not. The only way you could be somewhat good is if you blaze through the game as quickly as possible and killing as few as you can. The story's optional, though, and you can read about it when you kill foes in Rainstorm or Monsoon difficulties, since they drop logs at a slightly rare chance.
Almost every level has a artifact hidden in it, but you have to be lucky to roll the version of the level that has it. Every Artifact changes up the rules of the game, and gives interesting changes to it. Like, the lower the health something has (including you) the faster you will run, everything exploding with a shower of Creamator explosions when they die, a random skill of yours locking every minute..there's even one called Command that tosses out most of the RNG of the game and gives you chest drops when you get an item. The chest color is the rarity of the items you recieved, and you can pick whatever item from the item table you please. It's balanced, though, that the window you select items is real time, and you cannot move until you pick an item.
When I mentioned "easy controls", this game really does have simple controls. four buttons mapped for your movement, and four buttons mapped for your skills. You can even use a controller.
This game gets interesting when you bring in your pals for co-op, while making it even more chaotic. The game's completely viable solo, but the difficulty becomes interesting in co-op. Do you let your friend take the item drop, or do you snag it for yourself?
There's also a forced item sharing button, which balances out the items for players. Though, me and my friends agree this system is incredibly annoying, so take that with a grain of salt.
The music of the game is an interesting contrast from the chaotic blitzplay of  the game. Even the most intense of the soundtrack is actually quite nice music to sleep too.
If you want my personal favorite piece from the game, it has to be Surface Tension. It's also a boss track, usually used for the Wandering Vagrant boss.
The bosses in this game will be intimidating and will pose a threat, like any boss will, but as you become stronger, you may be able to start one shotting them..and..as you progress even further, normal foes will be replaced by bosses. Ever faced twelve giant magma worms, three overloading ones, six vagrants, and ten colossi at once?
Despite all my praise for the game, though, I do have a gripe about the game. Though, it doesn't bother me too much.
The levels and item count.
The levels will soon feel repetitive, since you will learn their layouts pretty quickly...but at least the levels themselves have different setups. Though it doesn't help that the setups only change the minor places.
The items aren't in a vast quanity, where you will always find new ones...but, hey. Every item is viable to helping you become stronger. I'd rather have this than several items that are "considered" low tier and useless.
Overall, this game, albeit not a masterpiece or a gamechanger for everything that comes after it, it's a really fun game that's even one hell of a ride with friends.
And you know what? That's all I want to ask every once in a while. For the fun alone, I'd highly reccomend the game. The characters are colorful and vastly different from each other (along with having a lot of them) the items you can pick up are ALL great, none are trick items or downgrades, the game chugs on to become blitzplay after you start slaying... It's worth the price.
One more thing to mention. Every item in the game itself has a bit of story on it. Some of the Item logs are even begging for their own stories.

This review is coming from a loooooong time Resident Evil fan so I'm probably (read definitely) biased but this is a really really fun game. It lets you play the campaign in two seperate parts allowing you to play as Claire from RE2 and CV in one and Barry from RE1 in the other. The campaign is ok, it's around 4-7 hours depending on how thorough you want to be and has all the classic RE cheese that you'd expect. Don't go into this game expecting a mind blowing adventure though. It falls short of 4, 5 and even 6 in my honest opinion. But still good nonetheless. The RAID MODE however is where this game truly shines. This will most likely be the most polarizing aspect of the game for most people. It consists of really basic/short missions mostly comprised of getting from point A to B while killing everything along the way. You will be earning levels, weapons and parts to customize your weapons with while you complete missions. There are 48 different missions and 13 characters excluding DLC (52 missions and 15 characters with DLC) to play with. The missions have multiple difficulties as well allowing you to redo them with a greater challenge to continue leveling. The reason I say this mode is polarizing however is because it will get very repetitive as you redo missions on newer difficulties and with new characters. This mode is very fun for a little while but it will be best enjoyed by the people who enjoy grinding in videogames because that is what it becomes. I personally love it and expect to play it for a long time but be warned if you're the type to get tired of grinding quickly.
TL;DR
The game is good, the campaign will most likely net you around 6 hours and the raid mode is good for another 6 at least unless you enjoy grinding out levels and abilities on all the different characters in which case you can easily get 100 plus hours of fun out of it.

[Note: The hours shown does not reflect my time with the game as I’ve played the game hundreds of times on the 360 and X1.]
Although 2017 is looking to be a great year for games mired by business practices overshadowing their quality, this year is also the official closures of two great names, Half Life and Dead Space. With the dissolution of Visceral Studios, the DS series has met its untimely end as is protocol for EA to abandon development teams after a massive flop they helped to create. At best, the series will be a prime example of Visceral struggling with the demands of EA to create their own survival horror game; at worst, EA will rework the license to focus it around multiplayer and/or microtransactions after the mess of Dead Space 3.
However, let’s not reminisce in sorrow but in fondness for the original, a game that could have led to EA’s equivalent to Capcom’s Resident Evil for survival horror had they simply let Visceral do what they wanted. While future installments are not bad, the real difference is how pure of an experience the original is because Visceral could create the game they wanted to make without demands of a shoed-in multiplayer or forcing a cooperative mode. Each game has their own moments of brilliance and attempts at innovation for storytelling, showcasing amidst the silent, calm depths of space the foreboding deadness of one’s thoughts could lead to horrors best not pondered by man.
If Resident Evil is defined by the Spencer Mansion as an interconnected environment learned through exploration and working against familiarity with the zombies, then Dead Space is defined by the USG Ishimura, an environment defined by its realism as set-pieces meant to ambush the player at every corner.
The main differences of these series are that their puzzles and enemy placements are grounded more than the absurd, campy puzzles of RE as well as the fact that players move through environments to establish direction. Exploration itself isn’t a priority as players are directed, literally, to set objectives; however, choosing to explore elsewhere will lead to rewards as well as extra risks. Although certain areas of the Ishimura are revisited, their purpose is mainly to establish a sense of realism of the vessel similar to the Nostrumo in the original Alien film. This is accomplished by realistic goals for an engineer throughout all layers of the ship as well as careful usage of Zero G environment to see both the inner and outer layers of the fiction.
Realism, however, leads to events being predictable, which is one aspect that gets a lot of criticism. Objectives remain simple “Go here; flip that” with interesting obstacles or new enemies thrown in to make up for the game’s repetitiveness. Even in its exploration, there are moments that become too obvious they are going to spawn more enemies. However, it’s this dedication to immersion that draws in the player for the horror as well as preventing the player from becoming bored. As many reviewers point out, the UI and HUD, while sometimes finnicky due to camera perspectives, is very intuitive and adds a greater sense of the player occupying Issac Clarke as an avatar even though the silent protagonist adds nothing to the immersion. It’s the gameplay itself from Zero G sound effects inside the pressurized suit to the creaking of the Ishimura and the rustling of a Necromorph clawing its way to you that draws the player into its universe. (Although the massive volume spike of enemies somewhat ruins the moment.)
To describe the gameplay itself is a more refined Resident Evil 4 but with real movement controls and more creativity behind its weaponry that encourages more replayability. As DS is centered around removing limbs, weapons can largely be specialized methods with different enemies in mind. This leads into unique weapons like the ripper, essentially the Gravity Gun from Ravenholm, a hydrogen torch (flamethrower) and the Contact Beam used by miners on dense rock. While there are staples like the assault rifle, the shotgun and a pistol equivalent these weapons have unique changes like the rotation for the Cutter, mines and projectile arc for the Line Gun, and the 360 degree mode for the Pulse Rifle. Like the environment and objectives themselves, most of these weapons are repurposed tools used in everyday life, not weapons on their own, which lends to a greater sense of disbelief to the whole experience by using any tools you can find to make do with what you have.

As one might expect from a loosely Lovecraftian inspired adaptation, Dead Space involves itself in the cosmic horror genre with the slow degradation of madness that manages to be convincing within the storyline present. The lore heavily delves into the daily life, beliefs, economic and government issues of this universe that explains both the larger mythos of DS as well as the slow unraveling of the mystery behind the Ishimura’s radio silence. This universe is one that shows no interest nor remorse for humanity’s concerns, and the hostile threats from beyond the stars is simply another cruel reality of the situation.
In between the maintenance objectives, players are drawn into with Issac’s love-interest to occupy his personal attachment for the mission. Although the outcome of this story-arc is predictable and the overall story is tangently related to the real story of the game, the slow descent into madness with Isaac Clarke comes off surprisingly well after all these years into the sequel that delves even further into his mind. Unlike Lovecraft himself who gave no purpose (or character) to his characters, this simple romantic pursuit is a human, comforting goal that is handled like a dark comedy amidst the larger threat of the Necromorphs, a polymorphic alien species that encounters the Ishimura through what is referred to as the Markers.
As a whole, it’s the immersive qualities and the commitment to drench the player into the story that makes the descent into madness as well as the mystery of the Ishimura work together. Aside from loading screens while riding the tram, no aspect of the combat, the diary entries nor the environments you explore take you out of the experience. (The one exception is the amount of times the game TELLS you to cut off Necromorph limbs instead of letting you discover it on your own.) It’s this approach to crafting a survival horror experience that is derivative but masterfully handled that shows Volition can make a believable place you dread to explore in disguise of a space rollercoaster.
Even nine years later, Dead Space remains an iconic, survival horror experience with superb quality. It is perhaps not the greatest modern title in its genre yet remains an effective experience to this date. Other than mechanics like the Stasis system and its unique weaponry, the gameplay itself is largely derivative by the fact that it’s a more polished game than many other horror titles. (Also, no other game has as much satisfying stomping than Dead Space.) It’s mainly its storytelling and its environments that truly work with the horror elements best, and future titles would further add to the immersion by incorporating more of the Zero-G environments as the third game truly does make effective usage out of them with alternative routes for exploration.
In an ironic case Dead Space has been a two-sided story between the developer’s visions as well as the fans’ commitment to see Isaac at the end of his journey. Perhaps it’s a cruel fate of irony that the series’ devotion would fade away without one more attempt into a disinterested universe that saps away all the ignition left. However, reigniting these games is one more reason to return if simply not to kindle fond memories before saying goodbye.

Is Rev2 perfect and everything we want from an RE game? No, but it's still pretty damn good for what it is. It's certainly a good foundation for this series to turn around on. If they can leep things rolling in this direction going forward, RE may yet return to the top of the horror genre.
Dark, creepy enviroments. Actual zombies that don't wield guns and ride motorcylces. No obligtatory daylight mow-everything-down action sequence.  Pacing that is fast enough that you don't get bored, but deliberate enough that it is unnerving. A story where there was clearly some passion for trying to create interesting and unique plot. Enemies that actually look scary and can be scary to deal with. And arguably the creepiest final boss RE has ever seen. Silent Hill level unnerving if you ask me.
Then there's Raid mode. Which is a million times larger and better than Rev1's. Everything you loved from Rev1 but more more more. More levels, more weapons, more parts, more chars, and now skills added the system. (lots of active and passive skills to choose from, which can dramatically change how you play depending on your combination)
Yes, the performance issues and lack of offline co-op was incredibly stupid. But that has since been patched. Though I still urge Capcom to give PC players an exclusive gift to properly make up for those mistakes. Doing what you were supposed to do in the first place doesn't count as an apology. But giving us something exclsuive like No Mercy modes for Campaign and Raid... that would make up for how you initially gave us the shaft.
I really want some kind of No Mercy mode anyway because if there's any gripe I have, it's that I wish the game would throw more enemies at me some times. This game has the best gameplay engine RE has ever had, but it's kind of wasted on the fact that the game usually throws only 5 or 6 enemies at you at one time. I want those intense moments where there are like over a dozen zombies running at me, and more just keep coming as you kill them. (let me experience craziness like the opening for RE3) So c'mon, add some kind of No Mercy difficult for Raid or something. You owe us something exclusive for botching the PC release. Going back and doing what you should've done in the first place doesn't count.

When I would recruit friends to play the original Killing Floor with me, I would describe it as "Left for Dead, but better." It had the same engaging action, hilarious gore, and rewarding weapon mechanics, while adding a progression system and perks that allowed teammates to cater their play to their own style.
Killing Floor 2 ups the ante on all the features that made its predecessor great. There are more perks, a revamped XP system, and thanks to the new unlockable perk skills, there are more ways than ever to play KF. It's a beautiful experience all the way through, with visually stunning and meticulously detailed new maps, redesigned weapon animations, and a cutting-edge gibbing system. Each kill is more rewarding, but more difficult too: the zeds now have the ability to protect themselves and respond to your attacks.
By far the biggest con is that Killing Floor could run on a toaster plugged into a CRT television, but KF2 is much more demanding on your hardware, especially with all of Nvidia's built-in new high-end antialiasing and physics options turned on. Don't expect to be able to play this game on the computer your grandfather uses to look at pictures of warships.
Killing Floor 2 has become the new perfect game to play when you want to kill time with your friends, but don't have the energy to focus on a competitive shooter, like Counter Strike, and don't want to get bored to death playing Civ for seven straight hours. All you need is a system with some brawn and an insatiable desire to emancipate Zed organs from Zed bodies.

Half-Life 2 is the sequel to the smash-hit debut title for Valve. Half-Life had revolutionary graphics engine, amazing A.I, logical puzzles and an engaging story- nothing like other FPS games that came out before Half-Life. Half-Life won over 50 awards, and is to this date announced as the 'best FPS game ever made'. And Half-Life 2 is the direct sequel to this masterpiece, so it has to live up to its expectations, though cliches with sequels are that they are only made to milk money. THAT is not true with Half-LIfe 2.
Not only Half-Life 2 also had a ground-breaking physics engine called Source, it leaved the 'closed enviorment' atmosphere behind, but used it to make a even better written storyline.
Now, keep in mind that Half-Life 2 was made in 2004. I will be reviewing this game like it came out in 2004, but also as if it came out in modern times.
The Source engine is still a pretty good engine now, but back then, it was amazing. The signature weapon of the game, the Gravity Gun, was made specifically to show out this new physics. You can't play the original Source engine from 2004 because they updated all games that used the engine to have the updated version from Half-Life 2: Episode 2, so you mostly won't suffer from the engines cons, but back then, the sound engine was terrible for the Source.
The story continues right where you left off. You were hired by the 'G-Man' because he was impressed at your skills, and put you into stasis untill the time came. Now, it's time to smell the ashes, and Gordon Freeman, the physicist you're contolling, has to join up with the Rebels to fight off the alien 'Combine' forces. The Combine are this galactic federation that enslaves every alien species come by, and puts them as the member of their 'union'. The humans had a 7-hour long war with them, until the UN HQ burnt down and Earth surrendered.
In Half-Life, the first bit of the game was you trying to get the ♥♥♥♥ out of Black Mesa, the research facility you were working. Then your mission was to save the world from suffering the same misery Black Mesa suffered by killing the invaders' master and ending the invasion. But Gordon was a bit too late, and the invaders found a way out of Black Mesa(which was just teleporting there) before Gordon did. But since Gordon did kill their master, they stopped fighting the humans(except for the non-inteligent ones). Then the Combine came, and this is where you start.
As the story goes along, the level change drastically. You start at a big city, goes to a canal, a dead town, a coast, a desert, a prison, then back to the city to finally blow up the Citadel, the Combine's base of operations for Earth. While the gameplay doesn't change a lot thoughout the game, the atmosphere do.
Now, the gameplay is nothing special in my book- it's pretty good(or above average depending on your look). You shoot guns to kill people. Though you can use physics against your enemies with your special 'Gravity Gun'. The Gravity Gun allows you to pick up heavy objects and just throw them wherever you wish it to. This can definetely result in some funny moments, and can vary up the gameplay.
The playtime for Half-Life is much longer then any other FPS games that came out around 2004(Halo 3, Doom 3, Modern Warfare, etc). The average playtime for those games were about 6~8 hours, while Half-Life's playtime is around 8~10 hours. Nothing special compared to modern games(well, actually maybe it is), but still pretty good for a 2004 game.
The puzzles are back from Half-Life, though this time, a lot of the puzzles are about physics(not because the protagonist is a physicist, but to show off the engine). It involves simple tasks such as moving things to point A to point B, to puzzles like throwing barrels so it makes a bridge(a bit similiar puzzle is from Half-Life: Blue Shift).
Let's talk about some miscellaneous stuff. The graphics were good at the time, but by today standards, it's average(even below avarage). The soundtrack is more of the same with Half-Life 1 actually, with some remixes and a few new tracks. It still takes advantage of the ambient themes.
I probably don't even need to make this review any longer- as you may already have noticed, Half-Life 2 is an amazing game. But many people don't go over the cons for the game, and some of them are blantly obvious.
The A.I. Jesus Christ, the A.I. It's not terrible, but considering Half-Life 1 was revolutionary in its A.I. programming, it was very dissapointing. A good game to compare this is Halo: Combat Evolved. In that game, the enemies flanked you, took defensive positions, etc. While Half-Life 1's A.I. was fantastic at the time, if you compare 1998 with 2004, it's not very different. And Half-Life 2 didn't have much better A.I. then its prequel.(the companions A.I. is a bit improved though)
The game is really really easy. Really really really. I mean, Half-Life 1 was easy, but this game is just out there. I highly suggest not even touching the 'easy difficulty', A.K.A 'you can't ♥♥♥♥ing die difficulty'. There are also vehicles in the game, and while it's pretty fun, some parts are just fillers. Oh, and the ending is not that good. I also suggest buying the 'Orange Box', which includes Half-Life 2, its episodic sequels(that fills up the dissapointing ending), and a few other really great games.
So we come down to the verdict. I give Half-Life 2 a solid(not really) 7.7/10. It's a great game, for reals. If Half-Life 1 was what every FPS should aim to be, Half-Life 2 is a bit more meh. While the Source engine is an amazing engine, Half-Life 2 doesn't do enough to really stand out on its own currently in 2015. But eleven years earlier, it was amazing.
Once again, I highly suggest you to buy the Orange Box, and perhaps Half-Life 1 as well(it's a better game overall except for the story and the graphics). Them, Counter-Strike: Source, and Garry's Mod are a must buy if you're a Steam user.

Well having completed the game I can now write a thorough review.
Gameplay: It’s actually a very fun game. Although it’s made by the same people who created dead island, and has quite a few similarities, it feels more fleshed out and responsive. The main character starts out pretty weak and with a horrible selection of weapons, but that just makes you feel a sense of danger going out into the world. Once you level up a bit, hordes become easier to navigate/destroy.
The special infected are completely ripped off from dead island save for the screamer. Also the “boomer” blends in with crowds pretty well. This along with some special placement can make the game feel cheap sometimes. There are several other instant death situations that feel really cheap and unavoidable, especially when you manage to survive several days/nights. The Volatiles are actually pretty unique though. They only come out at night, mostly...and are pretty difficult to kill even when you level up.
Story: Honestly I hate the story. It feels so cliché and boring. I hated every single character, friend or foe. They tried hard to manipulate emotions and make you feel sad/angry/remorse and such, but I could not feel anything for these characters. There really weren't any memorable missions for me either.
The main character is also ridiculous. He is supposed to be some kind of spec ops infiltration unit, but you can see from the very beginning how pathetic and scared he is. He doesn’t bother in making choices for himself, and allows everyone to look down on him. He just doesn’t come off anywhere near the kind of badass he needs to be, even afraid to curse someone to their face. There are even moments where you can hear in his voice that he expects a betrayal, yet he just continues doing whatever they tell him. Go here, fetch this, find that, save them...The only character I’ve played that’s worse than this guy is the guy from farcry 3.
If I were to do it again, I would wait till this game is on sale. I will probably do that with dead island 2 now. Expect a fun game experience, but forget the story and “character development.

I’m going to break Dying Light into 3 categories. Story, Gameplay, Technical.
Story
A brief understanding of what is happening:
Players assume the role of Kyle Crane, an undercover operative sent to infiltrate the quarantine zone in the fictional city of Harran, based off ancient Turkey, as his mission is to find Kadir “Rais” Sulaiman, a rogue agent who has a file that could destroy the reputation of the agency. But when he arrives, he must choose between completing his mission or helping the other survivors led by Harris Brecken. Watch as the rules that govern civilization crumble to dust. - Wikipedia
I really felt the storytelling was lacking but tried to keep you entertained enough to keep playing. It did exactly what I liked which was to keep me interested but not so interested that I only wanted to complete it first and not experience the games side quests and adventures. I really enjoyed that Techland didn’t try to make it like a Mass Effect where you can pick different choices and have a different outcome. I think it’s important that a game tells you the story they wanted you to experience. I think the team did that great. While it’s not the most entertaining story it does have some good parts in it and I can see the potential. 7/10
Gameplay
Gameplay is the most important thing in a video game. Techland’s previous 2 zombie games, Dead Island and Dead Island: Riptide had great potential but wasn’t enough to be outstanding. In Dying Light, you can really see where Techland learned from their mistakes and executed on them flawlessly. You can also see where improvement can still be had. The parkour aspect at times make you feel like you’re playing Mirror’s Edge. I wish there would of been something more than just a grappling hook such as a parachute or wing-suit to allow the player to get across the map faster but it was still excellent nonetheless. The melee weapons make you feel like you’re just this machete wielding badass. The day and night cycle I saw was getting some criticism about it being tied to missions which is true at times but not most of the time. You can very much run around doing side quests while the cycle’s change and you are terrified trying to sneak around Violates (zombie’s terrifying brother). The part I really didn’t enjoy so much was how frequent and less rare guns were. My favorite part of the Dead Island series has been the melee focus instead of guns but nonetheless it isn’t a bad thing just a personal preference. Inventory, Skill tree, and Traps in the game needed more work though. The Inventory is very cluttered. Every time I would level something up in my skill tree I forgot that I even had that ability till I accidently did it and said, “Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥I can do that.” The traps are so useless that I just never used them but I will say the spikes are hilarious and make me laugh. The gameplay is where this game truly does shine and show that Techland has learned from many of their mistakes. 9/10
Technical
To preface this category I played Dying Light on PC. I have a GTX 780 and it ran not excellent but around 60 FPS on max graphics. The facial animations were my biggest concern in this category as they didn’t match at all what the voice actors were saying. On top of that the same character model was used more than once. The graphics were beautiful besides peoples hair and the occasional pop in textures and some objects including the background of the city were clearly 2D images and didn’t even try to hide it. But nothing ruined my experience as much as the film grain. After 4 hours of playing with it on I looked for a way to turn it off and managed too. Most games nowadays are getting into the near 60GB range but Techland manages to deliver only on 11 and it shows. 6/10
Conclusion
Dying Light tries to fire on all cylinders but sometimes misses the mark. Techland gave me a game that I wasn’t disappointed in and made me look forward to the next project they produce. If you liked the idea of Dead Island but didn’t think it was well executed then this is the game for you. When I bought the game it was around a 87% on Steam and I think that is a valid score for it. So if you like slow motion head slicing while running off of zombies onto a building and jumping into a pile of trash, this is the game for you. Good Night, Good Luck.
9/10

Instead, he has a clear goal with the need to repair or adjust specific parts of the ship. Often, one enemy is enough to wound Isaac greatly, despite his best efforts. Awesome game.  Plenty of options for different playstyles, multiple solutions to puzzles, and ways to make it worthwhile to explore a variety of character types.  The setting is a classic RPG verse that hasn't been explored all that well in video games (there was a well-loved Shadowrun game in the SNES era, but that leaves a gap of decades).
The Dead Man's Switch campaign is good.  It could have been better, but I found it very enjoyable to play.  It's not every game where you can team up a cyborg waitress with a shotgun and a personal grudge against drug dealers, a Native American shaman with the power to summon real spirits and a murdered brother to avenge, and damn near any character type you want to put together including elven mages or cyborg trolls.  A lot of people found Dead Man's Switch disappointing, but overall I like how it turned out.
The Dragonfall DLC campaign is AMAZING!  An improvement in every way.  A whole new setting with more freedom of movement; a persistent crew with their own personalities and goals; a bigger, farther-reaching storyline with interesting and unique enemies; more side missions; several new items and options (though sadly no major overhaul of the rather limiting cyberware installation system); so much more to see and do.
I am eagerly looking forward to the Dragonfall Director's Cut!

When it comes to the enjoyable Action – Adventure , GTA always become a good example of it . Some of it are the best but a few of them don’t . But what happen when GTA hit the 80s Era , let’s find out in my review about GTA Vice City
Story
It was first focus on Sonny Forelli’s order to get the drug . It was Tommy who was set to be in charge for the job . When the meeting started , and ambush start to mess around , made him lose the drug and the money . Sonny was so angry when he knew Tommy loses both of that stuff , but he promised to bring them back by getting into first big problem and silently become a big player in Vice City . The Story starts to make kinda 80s style right when the game begins , and somehow it sounds like Brian De Palma’s Scarface , it’s good but also memorable , due to the great cast of characters . Very Awesome
Characters
Tommy Vercetti is the main character for the game , he was a bit psychotic , smart , and also rough . He plays well in the role of the game . When you realize Ray Liotta was the guy behind Tommy , it will make you entertained through the rest of the game . Although sometimes there are some idiotic character who instead broke just a bit of the game immersion , but it still good to keep the rest of them live up the hype . Like example Avery Carrington , then Kent Paul , Colonel Juan Garcia Cortez , and also our first friend in Vice City and a lawyer Ken Rosenberg . It is good to have them in here .
Graphics
From this side , there only 1 sentence to explain this : “Simple but Good” . GTA Vice City was made for the 6th Generation Consoles , so it is reasonable why the graphics are so old but good . The 80s era didn’t require too much polygon in order to make it beautiful , so in the end Rockstar North decided to make minimalist but good as possible .
Sounds
The Voice Acting was well – received , but beyond that , there is one that can be so memorable . That is the Music . GTA Vice City had a hundred of licensed soundtrack to hear , like Africa from Toto , Broken Wings by Mr Mister etc . It was well – crafted to make a good 80s vibe .
Gameplay
From all the perspective that I reviewed , this one is the best . The Gameplay was well – designed and absolutely FUN . you can make almost every action you made is fast – paced and totally awesome . The control of the vehicles is definitely outstanding  and the gunplay was so fast – paced and fun . The missions itself is well – designed too and always make you want to play it again and again , but sometimes the it can be too hard and unbalanced between the characters arsenal and AI’s power and also for the design itself , it also require trial and error in order to finish it , but overall it was so fun …. Like DEFINITELY FUN AF =D .
Features
There is a ton of features in GTA Vice City and is surrounded in Vice City all over the place . Like RC side missions , Shooting Range Side Missions etc . You can find it almost in every section of the city . In the end it will rewards you with some powerful stuff when you get 100% of the game’s progression
The Good
+ Outstanding Gameplay
+ Great and Agile Vehicle's Control
+ Memorable and enjoyable cast of Characters
+ Loveable and Good 80s Soundtrack (especially on Emotion 98.3 and Flash FM)
+ Perfect mission Design
+ Intense Action
+ Great use of 80s Vibe , it feels like 80
+ Good Story
+ Tons of features
The Bad
- Some punishing difficulty in some of mission design
- The singleplayer‘s story is too short
Conclusion :
if you still have 10$ in your pocket and also if you need a nostalgia , you better get this one , it is beyond than any 80s Game's theme

score: 6.5/10 - solid
similar games: Resident Evil Franchise, The Evil Within, Dead Space
target audience: fans of survival horror
Many people seem to like Revelations 1. They say even if its not true survival horror, it still goes into the right direction. I dont agree with that. Revelations had its moments, but everything in that game was let down by the fact that its a DS port and you felt it every second. So with Revelations 2 we get a proper Revelations game, developed for the main platforms.
Unfortunately this is not an AAA game, Capcom will probably reserve that for Resident Evil 7. That means that the graphics, animations and sound effects are not great (about the same level as Resident Evil 5). The most dissapointing is the level design. Its not bad, but you can really feel the technical limitations. Actually there are some really cool levels in this game, but Im sure with proper technology they could make much bigger and more complex levels.
The combat is the same as always, but less clonky as in previous games. What I like the most is that they added the dodge move (was already in Rev1) which makes combat much more dynamic and makes you think about evading enemies and maybe trying to use the knife and conserve ammo. And you actually need to conserve ammo in this game unlike many other Resident Evil games (on Survival difficulty at least). I also like the "finishers" which returned from previous games, after you shoot an enemy on weak spots they get stunned and you can do a melee attack which makes them fall and take extra damage. This is another way to conserve ammo, but also puts you in risk because you have to get close to the enemies. This would be even better if the melee attacks werent so op. When you target one enemy with a melee attack you are invulnerable while you are attacking and every enemy close to the target will also fall down which makes these really powerful and there is really no reason not to use them (less decisions to make as the player, less depth).
There arent that many weapons in the game, you basicly get a weapon for every weapon type you can think of and thats it. In previous games you also got better weapons of the same type later in the game (this is also in Rev2, but only for 2 or 3 weapons). To compensate they have weapon customisation parts, upgrades which increase stats of the weapons. These are not a bad idea, and are also something to reward players for exploration, especially people who find secrets where they find very rare parts, but the upgrades are boring most of the time, because its just stuff like +5% dmg, +10% attack speed. There are some more fun stuff like a charge shot you can get, but those make the game a little arcady for my taste but hey its better than nothing. Thinking about which weapon to use in combat and changing mid-fight depending on the situation is really fun and you do not simply change to shotgun when close ranged and to pistol when mid ranged, it also depends on the enemies. Some are fast, some slow but tanky, some fly, some have weak spots and stuff like that. However every enemy in this game will be familiar to you from previous games, but unlike previous games, even Revelations 1 which was a DS game, the enemies in Revelations 2 are designed really boring visually. They look like the enemies from The Evil Within, and those also looked boring. Not only that, but they also have really bad sound design, not that Resident Evil enemies had that memorable sound effects, but in previous games you still could identify every enemy by sound, in Revelations 2 however enemies rarely even make a sound. There are like 1 or 2 good enemies, but thats about it. Especially for Episode 3 or at least Episode 4 I expected that they introduce another enemy type, but no. This made Episode 4 a little bit boring, because there was nothing new, they even reused 1 boss like 3 times. Whats weird about this is how much content there is actually in this game. You have the main campaign, which consists of 4 episodes which take about 2-3 hours = 10 hours total, and on top of that you have 2 extra episodes (which I didnt played yet), and on top of that you have Raid mode.
In my opinion they shouldnt make a Raid mode or extra episodes, but instead spent that time on making the main campaign better, more enemies, more weapons, better level design. I know there are people who like Raid mode, but in my opinion its a complete waste of time. Its nothing else than a grindfest, enemies dont even attack you like in the campaign, its extremely easy, arcady, and you can see that this is a game from japan because Raid mode is in the game. The only reason people are interested in it (imho) is because they can get a little more playtime out of their game, at least you can upgrade your character and level up. The thing is the skills you unlock are totally useless and extremely boring. Also the weapons you unlock are useless, cause later you only need 1 weapon (if you upgrade the weapon type you get tons of ammo for it).
What I was surprised by the most is the story of this game. It has the usual cheesy writing of RE games and over top plot, but it also had some interesting characters and was fun to listen to. I mean the characters are still cliche (Moira), but they were good enough. There were some twists and turns and some of them actually surprising, but most of them I was expecting miles ahead. But again, the story was solid, it was fun.
To conclude I only want to say that I believe that this game would be a MUCH MUCH better game if they had done the following things:
1. only 1 playable character, no coop, no parallel storylines
2. take out Raid mode, use the time spent on that on the main campaign
3. no episodes
4. obviously more budget is better, but I guess its fine cause this costs only 25€
And because this game only costs 25€ I can easily recommend it to any Resident Evil fan, but for everyone else there are enough alternatives. If you really find this game interesting for some reason then you wont regret the purchase either.

TL;DR: ...why don't you have this in your Steam liabry if you're a Steam user?
Half-Life 2 is the sequel to the smash-hit debut title for Valve. Half-Life had revolutionary graphics engine, amazing A.I, logical puzzles and an engaging story- nothing like other FPS games that came out before Half-Life. Half-Life won over 50 awards, and is to this date announced as the 'best FPS game ever made'. And Half-Life 2 is the direct sequel to this masterpiece, so it has to live up to its expectations, though cliches with sequels are that they are only made to milk money. THAT is not true with Half-LIfe 2.
Not only Half-Life 2 also had a ground-breaking physics engine called Source, it leaved the 'closed enviorment' atmosphere behind, but used it to make a even better written storyline.
Now, keep in mind that Half-Life 2 was made in 2004. I will be reviewing this game like it came out in 2004, but also as if it came out in modern times.
The Source engine is still a pretty good engine now, but back then, it was amazing. The signature weapon of the game, the Gravity Gun, was made specifically to show out this new physics. You can't play the original Source engine from 2004 because they updated all games that used the engine to have the updated version from Half-Life 2: Episode 2, so you mostly won't suffer from the engines cons, but back then, the sound engine was terrible for the Source.
The story continues right where you left off. You were hired by the 'G-Man' because he was impressed at your skills, and put you into stasis untill the time came. Now, it's time to smell the ashes, and Gordon Freeman, the physicist you're contolling, has to join up with the Rebels to fight off the alien 'Combine' forces. The Combine are this galactic federation that enslaves every alien species come by, and puts them as the member of their 'union'. The humans had a 7-hour long war with them, until the UN HQ burnt down and Earth surrendered.
In Half-Life, the first bit of the game was you trying to get the ♥♥♥♥ out of Black Mesa, the research facility you were working. Then your mission was to save the world from suffering the same misery Black Mesa suffered by killing the invaders' master and ending the invasion. But Gordon was a bit too late, and the invaders found a way out of Black Mesa(which was just teleporting there) before Gordon did. But since Gordon did kill their master, they stopped fighting the humans(except for the non-inteligent ones). Then the Combine came, and this is where you start.
As the story goes along, the level change drastically. You start at a big city, goes to a canal, a dead town, a coast, a desert, a prison, then back to the city to finally blow up the Citadel, the Combine's base of operations for Earth. While the gameplay doesn't change a lot thoughout the game, the atmosphere do.
Now, the gameplay is nothing special in my book- it's pretty good(or above average depending on your look). You shoot guns to kill people. Though you can use physics against your enemies with your special 'Gravity Gun'. The Gravity Gun allows you to pick up heavy objects and just throw them wherever you wish it to. This can definetely result in some funny moments, and can vary up the gameplay.
The playtime for Half-Life is much longer then any other FPS games that came out around 2004(Halo 3, Doom 3, Modern Warfare, etc). The average playtime for those games were about 6~8 hours, while Half-Life's playtime is around 8~10 hours. Nothing special compared to modern games(well, actually maybe it is), but still pretty good for a 2004 game.
The puzzles are back from Half-Life, though this time, a lot of the puzzles are about physics(not because the protagonist is a physicist, but to show off the engine). It involves simple tasks such as moving things to point A to point B, to puzzles like throwing barrels so it makes a bridge(a bit similiar puzzle is from Half-Life: Blue Shift).
Let's talk about some miscellaneous stuff. The graphics were good at the time, but by today standards, it's average(even below avarage). The soundtrack is more of the same with Half-Life 1 actually, with some remixes and a few new tracks. It still takes advantage of the ambient themes.
I probably don't even need to make this review any longer- as you may already have noticed, Half-Life 2 is an amazing game. But many people don't go over the cons for the game, and some of them are blantly obvious.
The A.I. Jesus Christ, the A.I. It's not terrible, but considering Half-Life 1 was revolutionary in its A.I. programming, it was very dissapointing. A good game to compare this is Halo: Combat Evolved. In that game, the enemies flanked you, took defensive positions, etc. While Half-Life 1's A.I. was fantastic at the time, if you compare 1998 with 2004, it's not very different. And Half-Life 2 didn't have much better A.I. then its prequel.(the companions A.I. is a bit improved though)
The game is really really easy. Really really really. I mean, Half-Life 1 was easy, but this game is just out there. I highly suggest not even touching the 'easy difficulty', A.K.A 'you can't ♥♥♥♥ing die difficulty'. There are also vehicles in the game, and while it's pretty fun, some parts are just fillers. Oh, and the ending is not that good. I also suggest buying the 'Orange Box', which includes Half-Life 2, its episodic sequels(that fills up the dissapointing ending), and a few other really great games.
So we come down to the verdict. I give Half-Life 2 a solid(not really) 7.7/10. It's a great game, for reals. If Half-Life 1 was what every FPS should aim to be, Half-Life 2 is a bit more meh. While the Source engine is an amazing engine, Half-Life 2 doesn't do enough to really stand out on its own currently in 2015. But eleven years earlier, it was amazing.
Once again, I highly suggest you to buy the Orange Box, and perhaps Half-Life 1 as well(it's a better game overall except for the story and the graphics). Them, Counter-Strike: Source, and Garry's Mod are a must buy if you're a Steam user.

Killing Floor 2 is a great successor to the original retail release. This came from just a simple but very addictive mod for Unreal Tournament 2004, and today is one of the most addicting shooters to play with any of your friends. The amount of details put into this game are untouchable, to the textures, animations, lighting and just amazing map designs. The gore level in this game is taken to the next level, not with just the blood level and how it stays on the map till the end of the game, but the many ways you can kill ZED's and shred layers of their skin off and shoot off limbs. Tripwire has also one of the best sound design in a game, pushing companies like DICE to bring a better audio and sound design to their Battlefield games.
Tripwire is also very community friendly, they take feedback left about every inch of their game, whether it’s an issue with how the game runs, how weapons work to even just small details missed in textures, they listen and bring another level of community support, that most companies refuse to do now a day. They’ve implemented community weapons and popular maps into the games and it’s awesome to see they respect other people’s work, going back to their roots.
If you loved the first game, you’re going to love this one. If you’re a fps player or enjoy playing the Call of Duty Zombie game modes, you’ll really enjoy this.
PRO
-	Amazing sound design
-	Great lighting effects
-	Great texture details on everything
-	Great map designs
-	Many different classes to play from
-	Lots of different weapons to use
-	Great game support (For updates and content)
CONS
-	Might need a higher end PC to get good performance for the high-end details
-	Can be hard for newcomers
-	Not very many maps (use the Steam Workshop for more)
-	Can get repetitive
-	Very addicting if you like this kind of gameplay
So, what are you waiting for? Grab this game and jump in with some friends!

You! Yes, you.  You like fantasy RPGs? You like strategy games? You like Sci-Fi? Ever wanted to mash 'em together into a delicous nerd smoothie?  Then do we have a product for you.
If you're an XCOM fan, the mechanics are pretty straightforward to you.  Honestly, Shadowrun Returns as simply a game is good, but not great.  The Karma system for leveling allows you to customize your character however you like with no limitations on class, though you'll want to specialize as you approach endgame.
However, Shadowrun Returns -- Shadowrun as a whole -- is so much more than a game.  It's a living, breathing world; a technologically heightened and magic-infused setting for stories of any kind.  Plots might hinge on the epic and esoteric (dangerous research into blood magic by a ruthless, profit-hungry megacorp) or the throwback noir with a twist (being hired by a dead man to find his murderer).  Sure, most of the RP of this RPG happens via old-school plain text, but you know what they call plain text in most places? Books. It ain't broke, so don't fix it!
Character creation remains fun to me, even after a few playthroughs.  It's pretty neat to tell your friends about your human shaman/street samurai who packs enough heat to take on a militia even before summoning his elemental spirits.  Or about your pink-haired elvish techno-wiz equally at home jacking into corporate Matrix blocks or rigging into her homemade combat drones with her very mind.  Moreover, the skills your character chooses will assist them outside of combat, unlocking alternate routes, hidden passages with loot, chances to solve a problem diplomatically (with added EXP!), and more.
The campaign that ships with the game, Dead Man's Switch, is a bit short but satisfying nonetheless.  It's an excellent introduction to the Shadowrun world, and veterans of the series will even see a few familiar faces. Depending on your system, you may encounter a frame rate related bug that can 1) not allow you past a particular door in the beginning, 2) not start a specific mid-game boss fight, and/or 3), cause Isaac to glitch and die on some zero gravity landings.  The game must be running at 60 or less frames per second in order for those scripts to work in the game.  Try either forcing V-sync in the video card control panel, or running a framehog program like FRAPS video recording to bring your frames down on a newer system.  Last alternative is to temporarily enable the in-game V-sync (it's REALLY bad) and lowering the mouse movement to accomodate for the stiffer controls.  Then, just turn it off when done.

The game consists of story segments followed by a dash from one place to the next, usually chased by the police.  I love the clean bright look of the game. It really enhances the feeling of space and freedom as you are leaping about. The main challenge is to discover  where you have to go, while being chased, which leads to repeated "death by bullets",  and you just having to replay the section again and again until you discover the exit. But the constant race to avoid death leads to the game being very rushed, which somewhat undermines it because you can't take in all that  freedom and space.  Personally, I think they would have done better not having the police chasing you everywhere. It really wasn't necessary. Having said that, it's still an enjoyable game and one I have no reservation in recommending.

1. Optimization has definately improved from launch, this can be seen especially in two raid mode levels stage 3-3 (and 5-2 to a lesser extent) was basically unplayable with massive frame rate drops and now runs smoothly. (yes even after they screwed it up and fixed it again, sniper scoping still seems to be unattended to.)
2. The game feels just like resident evil 4 which some people will complain about and some will absolutely love, this one is up to personal preference.
3. Offline co-op is fully instated into the game for story, however two controllers are needed for this, online co-op is instated for raid mode only, capcom has said time and time again that there will not be any online co-op for the campaign, which is sad considering my next point.
4. The one and only major flaw with the campaign that I experienced is that the AI is abhorrently stupidly inept that they have trouble climing stairs, FREAKING STAIRS, to mention nothing of ladders, if you're being claire the AI will stare at you looking dumbfounded as they are repeatedly attacked by whatever is next to them, at least they have regenerating health, that's the only thing that makes them even partially tolerable since they can tank hits and be a nice little target while you pick off the enemy, simply make sure that if you need to switch to moira or natalia that barry/claire are in a completely safe area where they have no chance of being attacked, and forget about taking the AI gun usage skill as its just laughable.
5. The game difficulty is actually very per player basis, if you want a full survival horror game where ammo is extremely limited go for survival mode right off the bat, if you simply want the story but also want survival for the reward, go for casual or normal and gather weapons and ammo to carry over into survival, which I think is pretty nice although a full inventory reset function might be nice for some people to simply have the option.
6. Some say the story is cliche, lackluster, bad, etc. some say it's interesting, again this is personal preferance, although as a heads up there are two endings, (extremely minor spoiler) at the end of claire's episode 3 bossfight there's a small button mashing moment, however if you don't mash the button you can instead switch character to moira and then go, this moment decides the ending of the game (extremely minor spoiler over).
7. Qtes are thankfully mostly gone, there is of course the one here and there when an enemy grabs you and when there's a melee prompt, but you won't have cutscenes full of them like RE6, in fact aside from the one aforementioned (in the spoiler above) moment there aren't any qtes at all.
that's about all I have to say, overall I like the game. (if my hours played aren't already an indication)

An impressive sequel to the original, Killing Floor 2 retains the tight gameplay of the original while adding plenty more to play with.  This game shows that art direction, attention to animation, and proper usage of colors are are much more appealing visually than running a game on the newest cutting edge engine.  Runs great at 144 FPS and has enough graphical options to run smoothly for just about anyone.  If it gets the long term support that the original game had, this will easily be one of the must have games for at least the next few years.  Only real complaint is my own grievance with randomized/slot machine style cosmetics.  While they do not affect the gameplay, I would much rather they just offer all of the skins and other cosmetic items as DLC instead of keeping some items locked behind roll of the dice loot boxes that require money to unlock.  If these cosmetics ever start to influence the gameplay this review could easily change but at the moment the game is almost flawless in executing what it set out to do.
