Risk of Rain is a sci-fi side-scrolling rogue-like game in which your task is to progress through five levels on an alien world and reach your ship where you fight the final boss.
I originally bought this game because I fell in love with the soundtrack, but I put off playing it because I thought it would be too difficult for me. The way difficulty works is that the game gets progressively harder the longer you play it: you start at the "very easy" difficulty, which is raised to "easy" after five minutes, then to "medium," "hard," etc. -- about 20 minutes in you're already at "very hard" and you're only half-way to the max difficulty! Luckily, there is an option to make the game easier -- if you play on "Drizzle" mode it takes twice as long for the difficulty to increase from one stage to the next, so you have more time to deal with enemies and pick up items before the game gets properly challenging.
Items are what can make or break a run. There are various offensive, defensive and support items, and it is possible to have multiple stacks of each, making their effects more powerful. However, you are rarely able to choose which items you pick up -- most of the time they are locked in chests and only rarely do you come across a shop where you can choose between three items on display. The items that you pick up will likely determine the longevity of the run: if you get good items (and plenty of them) at the start, you'll survive longer to pick up more items which will help you fight the increasingly tougher enemies.
There are also artifacts hidden in levels which can make the game more challenging or more random. After you find them, they can be activated before starting each new run. As you progress through the game you also unlock different classes, each of which has different abilities. Although each individual run may last up to an hour, this range of available classes, the randomness of item drops and the addition of artifacts make the game virtually endlessly replayable.
All in all, it's a fun and challenging game with (thankfully) an "easy" mode which makes it more accessible to less skilled players. Also, the music is AMAZING.

The game had a very bumpy start.  For the first month there were a lot of issues with performance and other bugs.  Since then the game was patched and works great now.  So that is why the game has low-ish recomendations.
It's a Resident Evil game, so the story is B-movie material but still enjoyable.  The campaign is fun once you get the hang of switching constantly between your characters, and picks up after the first episode which is really short compared to the others.  There are a lot of unlockables hidden behind high-rank playthroughs as always.
Raid mode does some things amazingly well, but in other areas is a step back from Revelations 1.  The parts and guns system is amazingly additctive and more deep than it was in Rev 1.  There are a ton of characters, and the skill system allows you to play whoever you want and still have the bonuses you want.  The bad news is it lacks much of the fun levels and character that Raid mode had in Rev 1.  Most of the time it is just a small arena.  Also most of the maps are from RE6.  There are no hidden enemies, no hidden BP medals, no voice clips.  But there are emotes, lots of emotes.  And if you really get into it, I suggest picking up the extra storage DLC for parts and weapons.  It's $2 for each so it isn't that bad.  It's still additctive, but it is different from Rev 1 Raid.  There are enough unique skills for the characters to keep things somewhat fresh.  Some get pretty silly.
I'd buy it if you like Resident Evil games for sure.  It plays more like RE4/5 and Revelations 1 than RE6.

I was rather torn when deciding how judge this. It has what I like to call Neverwinter Nights syndrome: It's a construction set that comes with a mediocre campaign to show off what you can do with the game tools. The campaign itself is playable, up until the final mission when it becomes completely awful.
The Dragonfall expansion however, is amazing. The story is good, giving you tough choices on how to complete each run; but the character development is where it really shines. The level design is much better than the vanilla campaign, and many of the runs give you new toys to play around with. Before they announced the stand-alone Director's Cut, I would have recommended this game for Dragonfall alone. Now that you can get Dragonfall by itself though, with all of the modding tools that came with this version of the game, there is no reason to get the vanilla game.
TL;DR version: Skip this, buy the Dragonfall Director's Cut.

50 hours.
That is how long this game takes to complete for an experienced LEGO Star Wars: The Complete Saga player, like myself.  This means that the WHOLE 50 hours consists of me finding/doing something new, and generally having fun.
Okay, so 4 out of 50 hours consisted of me and a few friends screwing around and causing chaos, but that's STILL more fun than going through the same Star Wars level 2 more times in repetitive "Challenge" and "Super Story" time trials, wherein you encounter nothing new. Fortunately, this game does NOT have these modes.
Onto the game itself, it's standard LEGO platforming goodness. If you came here expecting something new and wildly different, you're out of luck.
However, if you're a fan of adventurous, exploration-heavy platformers like Spyro the Dragon and Ratchet and Clank, you can't go wrong with this. The story's quite entertaining, and the characters are likeable. It's really on the easy side, but that just means you won't tear your hair out in frustration most of the time.
Just watch out for the bugs, though. It's not as stable as LEGO Star Wars, and you might get stuck in due to an elevator door closing in on one of your characters, or just being unable to tag/switch to the other active character until heading to a new area.
Also, turn off Vsync when using an LED monitor, or else you'll crash at scene changes.

Dead Space is pretty much like outer space – huge, mostly empty and has no atmosphere.
Usually I feel obliged to complete the game I started – after all, I have already invested my time and money into it. But I had to make an exception for Dead Space, for it is about as exciting as unloading a truckload of bricks, without the benefit of physical exercise. As I trudged through its endless repetitive corridors I was literally falling asleep every ten minutes – not a kind of reaction I expect from a survival horror.
…You walk around a spaceship, slowly and tediously, enter a room and scary music starts playing as a monster jumps out of an air vent. Yawning, you shoot its legs off, you shoot its arms off, it stops moving, some generic guy over the radio says that he urgently needs you to perform yet another mundane task half a ship away, you go over there, slowly and tediously, shooting limbs off monsters, receive new mundane tasks and it never, ever ends…
Sounds like work to me, of a repetitive, mind-bogglingly boring variety. Perhaps the main character, Isaac Clarke, has gone mad due to the sheer tedium of his space engineering job and imagined face-chewing monsters to cheer things up a bit? If so, he failed miserably – Dead Space doesn’t offer anything in a way of excitement, preferring to rip off The Alien, Event Horizon and Halo and wrap its generic plot in some atrociously poorly written dialogue.
Maybe I exaggerate, with Dead Space having received high ratings and suchlike? Not a bit.
A survival horror game, in my opinion, should excel in three respects: plot, atmosphere and gameplay. So let’s see…
For all practical purposes there isn’t any. Isaac Clarke just walks around a spaceship, shoots monsters and repairs stuff. Every plot twist boils down to the following: air conditioning (engines, lifts, Christmas lights, plumbing) breaks down, and you have to fix it. After going through the entire ship, because the trouble always seem to happen as far away from you as possible. Yes, there are alien artifacts and evil cults, but all this stuff is so generic and forgettable that it could have been replaced by pretty much anything without anyone noticing.
And it keeps dragging itself on and on. When Clarke fixes one thing, something else immediately breaks down and he has to go and fix it too. And again. And again. The plot doesn’t so much progress as it meanders about, adding more and more padding to the playtime. I can almost see EA executives saying: “What do you mean the plot fits in two hours of gameplay? Hell no, you have to add at least ten times as much. Make Clarke flush every toilet on the ship manually or something, you are the script writer, do your job”.
Curiously, Dead Space is often described as a true representative of survival horror, a rare gem, a resurrection of all that was good in the genre released at the time most familiar franchises in it have turned into action-y nonsense. I can’t say I am such a huge fan, but I like me a little survival horror now and then.
And frankly, I have no idea what business Dead Space has in this category at all. It feels like people who made it knew that there is a kind of games that are supposed to scare you, but had no idea how it is done.
As a result, when it comes to frightening you, Dead Space depends solely on jump scares. A monster is lying on the floor, seemingly dead? You can bet it will jump at you when you get closer, so after a while you either start shooting corpses from a distance or stop being scared when they, invariably, jump up. A monster leaps out of a vent? Scary the first time it happens, but not when they jump out of every other bloody vent you pass. After the thirtieth time it stops being frightening and start being annoying.
Some say they are terrified by the atmosphere of claustrophobia, horror and hopelessness… Seriously? I remember quitting Silent Hill 2 after a couple of hours because it was creeping me out too much. Dead Space doesn’t induce fear. It induces yawning.
With all this, you probably think that Dead Space at least can be fun as an action. Not so. Controls are clunky, combat is repetitive, and there are some astonishingly bad design decisions. For example – everything in game costs money, including weapons and upgrades for them, and the money you find is probably enough to fully upgrade 2-3 weapons, which effectively discourages you from experimenting and trying out new guns. I don’t know about others, but I have been using and upgrading nothing but the starter Plasma Cutter until the very moment I got too bored to go on. I never felt need in any other weapon.
An excellent illustration of the fact that huge budget, an experienced dev team and a rich publisher do not necessarily make for a good game. Especially if the publisher is EA.

GTA: Vice City is set in the most magical time period of the whole Grand Theft Auto series. It has a certain charm that the other games certainly haven't accomplished to the same degree. The soundtrack is one of the most beautiful, and breathtaking soundtracks in all of gaming. The radio commentators are hilarious and witty, and they accompany the music wonderfully. Fernando Martinez from Emotion 98.3 is a prime example of this, constantly commenting about the way he flirts with women, and other things. The gameplay of this game has always been incredibly fun, but to today's standards, it is pretty barren and empty mechanically. There is no cover system, but you can crouch behind things. Weapons shoot in a very curved way if you leave Widescreen turned on. It looks pretty bad on a 16:9 monitor when using widescreen off. The driving is very arcade-y and turning is very rapid and overall works nicely. The city of Miami (Vice City), however, is the main highlight. This is not only one of the most memorable video game maps of all time, it is also... a beautifully remarkable city of pure nostalgia. While it is minuscule in size by comparison to other GTA maps, it sticks with you forever, especially if you played this game for hundreds of hours as a kid. The game makes me feel like I am back at home, which is an extraordinary feeling. While it certainly is a bit short, (took me 10 hours to beat - a bit of a rushed playstyle, and used weapon cheats only). Storywise, it will remind you of classics such as Scarface.
This is definitely a recommendation, but I also recommend modding it to bring it a bit more to today's standards.

You see yourself roll with every fall, feel every clamber, hear every breath and footfall, and at the same time you have a sense of how quiet and small it all is. Dead Space was released in October of 2008 by publisher/developer Electronic Arts. For its time, the game was an absolute revolutionary masterpiece that helped to bring back the horror genre of video games to the limelight. It's undoubtedly one of the best horror games of the last decade, but time does have a way of ravaging our favorite games and movies. Nearly 10 years later, does Dead Space still hold up to its original praise, and is it worth playing for newcomers to the franchise?
Set in the year 2508, players take on the role of ship system engineer Isaac Clarke. At the beginning, Isaac and his small crew, made up of commander Zach Hammond and computer specialist Kendra Daniels, come across a distress signal that's being emitted from a large mining vessel known as the USG Ishimura. As luck would have it, Isaac's own ship, the USG Kellion, has a guidance system malfunction that causes it to crash right into the USG Ishimura. While Isaac and his crew explore the abandoned mining starship in search of a way to repair either ship, or escape, they come to find that hostile alien life has taken up residence on Ishimura. Needless to say, it doesn't take long to determine what wiped out the crew and prompted the distress signal. However, the plot becomes a lot more convoluted, and in time Isaac discovers everything from a cult, to a mysterious stone marker.
Even though protagonist Isaac Clarke remains silent throughout the game, his character is decently fleshed out through a series of video logs between him and his girlfriend, Nicole. The remaining characters, though not much is provided in the way of their backstories, are generally well rounded. To add to the depth of the overall plot, text and audio logs can be found scattered through the levels, and upon beating the game once, backstory logs are unlocked.
For a 2008 title, Dead Space has held up surprisingly well. Though a modern playthrough is nowhere near as impressive as seeing the game in its original glory a decade ago, the dynamic lighting, environmental effects, and cold, lonely atmosphere are as captivating as ever. The textures and character models still hold up their end of the bargain as well, although there is expected, yet subtle, aging of both entities. The enemies, known as Necromorphs, have a decent variety to their species; from weird baby-like things with tentacles, to fast multi-limbed monstrocities, fat guys that explode, wall-mounted fat guys that launch tentacle pods, creepy ground-slithering aliens with two arms, and the list goes on. Needless to say, the Necromorphs themselves are unlike anything ever seen in a video game, and even though there are only a couple of real "bosses", the amount of foes that one will encounter more than makes up for that neglected factor.
The most chilling factor of the game is just how alone Isaac is. Even though he has communication with the other two members of his crew, it's limited, and his physical interaction with them is very minimal. This means that he's left alone to do nearly every task to help get him and his crew out of the alien-infested ship alive, and at every twist and turn he's coming up on blood-soaked corridors, organic-matter laden rooms, and eerily-lit chambers. With that being said, a good chunk of the way through the 12 chapters, which amount to a 9 hour campaign, it becomes easy to tell when the game is going to throw in a jumpscare, leading to easy predictability. This somewhat reduces the horror aspect of Dead Space, but the surrounding cold, lonely, yet tense atmosphere makes up for the loss.
Not to be confused with your run of the mill, run-and-gun third-person horror shooter, Dead Space does have some survival horror elements; a limited inventory, the need for tons of ammo, health kits, stasis recharges, cans of oxygen, and store credits are just some of the included factors. Upon finding schematics, Isaac can level up his suit, as well as craft new weapons and their ammo. There are also power nodes that can be used to further upgrade Isaac's weapons and suit by increasing their damage, capacity, reload time, air supply, health bar, oxygen amount, and stasis limit. Some of the awesome weapons that players can expect to enjoy are the series-staple plasma cutter, pulse rifle, flamethrower, line-gun, and a ripper that shoots razor sharp blades. Each gun has both standard and alternate firing modes, each which come in handy at least once throughout the game.
Additionally, the gameplay has innovative zero gravity and limited air mechanics. In many places of the campaign, Isaac will be tasked with venturuing outside of the spaceship, or even encountering areas of the ship, where no gravity or oxygen are present. This leaves players racing against the clock to solve the small puzzles of the area before they die of oxygen deprivation. Also not to be forgotten are the kinesis and stasis abilities, which allow heavy objects to be lifted and moved, or fast objects to be slowed down, respectively. Another noteworthy unique feature of Dead Space is the HUD that's displayed on the back of Isaac's armor, and the on-screen inventory and map system, rather than having the gameplay pause or change to another screen entirely.
It should also be noted that the PC version of this game does not suffer from any malfunctions on Windows 10, and runs fine at 144Hz; it even supports Xbox 360/Xbox One controllers for those who aren't so keen on keyboard and mouse controls. Speaking of the latter, the mouse movements are very stiff, even after adjusting the sensitivity level, and as such one may need a larger mousepad area than normal.
Akin to the nostalgia factor brought along by ones first romp through a Silent Hill or Resident Evil game, everyone remembers their first time with Dead Space. For me personally? Well, I was working at Best Buy at the time and bought the game on All Hallow's Eve, then I played through the entire campaign on Halloween night. I nearly wet my pants dozens of times over, and I guess my Xbox 360 got pretty scared too because at the end of my playthrough it displayed the infamous Red Ring of Death; yes, Dead Space effectively killed my console. The game is an absolutely unforgettable experience, and upon beating it there are some hefty unlocks that bring a decent amount of replayability with them. Despite its age, Dead Space still holds up remarkably well, which will invite old players to revisit its horrors, while allowing new players to still enjoy the experience.

Oh, where do I start?
This game is an absolute masterpiece. I've completed it once already, and have decided to run through it again just for kicks.
The art style is minimalistic, and voxel based for the most part.
It's a cleverly styled non-euclidian puzzle game that forces you to think outside the box.
I found myself to be very connected to the overall gameplay, I'm not sure why... But I loved every minute of my experience with it.
Later in the game, once the higher level gun abilities have been acquired, some say that it loses its challenge, and it becomes easy to "rush through" the rest of the game. Not necessarily so. Indeed the gameplay becomes simpler because of your progress in the game, and the acquisition of improved, and more advanced gun abilities.
There is a downside, the game is quite short... It's said that it can be beaten by normal progression in about four hours.
I do wish that the developer would create an addon pack for it as well.
There IS one room though, that seems to be unfinished. I'm assuming that the developer has plans for it in some unknown way, but... It could be there just for the sake of having an obvious dead end.
Unfortunately, the only way to truly experience this game is by playing it. Immersing yourself in the experience, and letting it take hold of you. Become the antichamber. It really is worth it.

GTA 3 is great, but GTA Vice City is greater. Vice City takes what GTA 3 established, preserved it, improved it and added to it. Taking place in 1986 Vice City, you play as Italian American mobster Tommy Vercetti. Immediately upon arriving in Vice City, a deal that was supposed to establish him in the city is attacked, forcing him to leave the goods at the site. The rest of the game involves rising up, killing the man responsible for the attack, obtaining a mansion, killing your former boss and ally, and ruling Vice City. Perhaps the best part of Vice City for me is the soundtrack. Containing many songs from artists like Toto, Hall and Oates, Michael Jackson, Laura Branigan and Foreigner, along with two complete talk show stations, Vice City will keep you busy in the audio department. Unlike the soundtrack of GTA 3 which mostly consisted of stereotypical late 90s pop music and typically left me only tuning to Flashback FM with its Scarface soundtrack, Vice City sometimes left me driving around just to listen to the great music or VCPR, its guests and its bitter Hispanic host, Maurice Chavez. If none of that fascinates you, the PC version supports a custom radio station. Just drag your .mp3 files into its folder, and you can drive to your own music. Sadly, due to the vast amount of copyrighted music, rights expire, and songs are lost. This song being Lionel Richie's "Running With the Night", which was present on the PS2 version but absent from the PC version. Compared to GTA 3, there is alot more things to have and to do. Motorcycles, helicopters and alot more boats are the firsts in the vehicle department. Many more weapons, like revolvers, chainsaws, hammers, combat shotguns, submachine guns, assault rifles, sniper rifles and even screwdrivers are some of the new additions. A lot more is also added mechanic wise, like the ability to dive out of cars, crouch and aim properly are some new additions. Vice City itself is quite beautiful, with many neon, art deco buildings and skyscrapers can be found in the city. Most buildings in the game are just low res textures, but the interiors you could enter are beautiful, like the mansion, the hotel room, the dance club and the strip club. Perhaps the biggest change between GTA 3 and Vice City is the addition of a speaking protagonist. Not only does Tommy Vercetti have a lot more personality and charm, he is more likeable. Another addition is the ability to buy safehouses and businesses. In GTA 3, you are given a safehouse on each island but that is about it. In addition to being more convenient, the latter is also fun and necessary. After killing the man who set you up, you can buy up various businesses around Vice City, like a Car Dealership, a Boatyard, a Strip Club, a Pornography movie studio and a dance club. All of these businesses set up fun missions with them. For example, the dance club opens up a series of bank heist missions, the boatyard opens up a long stunt course, and the car dealership opens up a mission to retrieve certain cars on a list, which will get you both a monetary reward and a bunch of fast cars, like a DeLorean or a race car. There is alot more in Vice City that just have to be seen to be believed. Some features of the PC version include the ability to aim with any weapon, the ability to change the player's skin and, as I mentioned, the ability to make a custom radio station. For the money, Vice City is definitely worth it. Buy it.

"And I ran, I ran so far away. I just ran, I ran all night and day. I couldn't get away." Vice City has it's charm in being set in the 80's. Everything you would expect from that timeline has managed to find it's way here: neon lights, hawaiian shirts, synthwave, everyone being doped up, etc. It looks great aesthetically. Riding a motorcycle and listening to 80's tunes with palm trees in the background is always enjoyable, including the 80's filter that was originally on the ps2 that helps give it a more authentic experience (it can be downloaded on pc with mods). However, after playing this for so long this title feels lacking especially when compared to the other entries. The map is very small and you can drive around Malibu in around 2 minutes. There aren't much attractions other than a dance club and the beach. The characters aren't that interesting and more-so try to fit the 80's stereotypes. Most missions are dull, they include tasks like checkpoints, driving around an 80's rock & roll band or killing someone at a golf course. It makes the character feel like a chauffeur, and the missions tend to have more style than substance. Also, the plot takes the character from faction to faction without trying to bring together a world with interrelated characters and stories, concluding to a rushed ending that comes together sloppily. It's still fun due to nostalgia and if the neon lights aren't a deterrence than Vice City should be enjoyable.

This game was a massive amount of fun especially in Coop. I played through this game entirely in Coop with usually one other person. I describe it as zombie horror survivial without the PvP element. The parkour system was sometimes buggy while zip-lining to building to building and there's usually a specific path you're supposed to take if you don't have the zip-line, but with it you can basically go anywhere. It was a nice addition to the zombie survival to be able to jump across buildings and run across the entire map without having to deal with zombies.
Night-time definitely felt like it was a challenge even with a partner. You had the choice to stay out and gain extra experience or wussy out and sleep in a bed until daytime. The volatiles gave you a sense of fear when night came and half the time we started sprinting to the nearest safe house when we heard the night-time warning over the radio.
The game being in first-person added even more immersion instead of the thrid-person camera you usually have in an open-world survival game.
If you get this game I suggest finding a partner to play it with. It is a lot more fun with a partner or two. And remember to drop kick everything and make sure not to kill yourself with your own elemental weapon.

Doom & Destiny is an RPGmaker game that makes fun of the tropes of its genre while adding tons of references to other games, movies, comics and animes into the mix: it sports some standard JRPG gameplay and story but its self-conscious sense of humour truly makes it an original and enjoyable experience.
-the standard plot is made very interesting by the humour that permeates it, the characters themselves know they're being used for stupid fetch quests but they play along nonetheless -often breaking the fourth wall- with hilarious results
-the whole parody of the rpg genre is very well done and makes fun of things such as same looking npcs, boring quests, being able to steal freely from npcs houses etc
-four party members with tons of loot and powers to choose from
-while the graphics are from RPGmaker they're very colourful and the devs really made sure all locations are filled with little details to make them appear more lively
-wide world map with many locations to find and explore
-good enemy variety
-tons of references from other games, movies, animes, books and more
-good length at least 10/12 hours for the main story+leveling for it plus more hidden bosses and areas available after clearing the last boss for those who wish to grind to be strong enough to tackle them
-there's no transition to the actual battle screen during random encounters, so they might feel thrown in your face until you get used to it
-a few grammatical errors or weird phrasings
-the gold level for side quests can get very grindy
I really enjoyed how self-conscious Doom & Destiny is in its humour, the game doesn't expect you to take it seriously and takes you for a fun ride on the various quirks one usually meets in rpgs. You're free to steal from homes because the king said so in an edict, npcs take their job of walking around aimlessly seriously, characters and npcs quote songs when using certain spells and, when questioned about it, some bosses might realize their plan of kidnapping the princess isn't as smart as it sounds: it's truly a ton of fun and I found myself chuclking at it quite often.
But make no mistake, behind its jokes and references the game is a solid rpg in itself with a good story, a nice power system that lets you tailor the four protagonists to your liking and a big world with lots of stuff to do. Doom & Destiny is absolutely recommended to fans of the genre.

It requires some tweaking via third-party applications to get the frame rate and mouse sensivity working optimally, but once you do, there's a great game that despite those issues, has aged pretty well.
The atmosphere is what really shines here, and it establishes the kind of game it is early on. It isn't just jump scares you'll find here either, some parts of the game you'll hear whispers of dead crew members as you see the grotesque horrors, of which the game has plenty to offer. Lighting is also utilized as they flicker in empty bathroom stalls and as you go down some hallways, there are sudden black-outs leaving you to go forward with only the flashlight from your weapons.
The movement can feel a little clunky, but I suppose that is the devs way of saying "keep your distance". The aiming is one of the few things that does show its age. It's just really unrefined even with the sensitivity fixed for the mouse or if you're using a controller. Apart from that aspect, the gun-play and the weapon variety is very good, with the Plasma Cutter standing out. Each weapon can be used effectively against specific enemies and the additional firing modes can come in handy during zero-g portions of the game.
As for the story, it's pretty good, though it isn't the best aspect of this game. There is a twist that is subtetly planted throughout the game that ties to the first thing you see at the start of the game, so it works well and you become invested in some of the characters. I found the audio logs of deceased crew members to be pretty interesting, and made exploration worth while as they tended to be put with ammo and other supplies.
Overall, I think Dead Space is a solid game that's worth experiencing if you're a fan of horror and/or Sci-Fi. It does invite replaying, with items that unlock after you complete the game for the first time, so perhaps that's something I'll do in the future, but even just for playing through it once the price is definitely fair.

Alright, maybe that wasn't as well of a explanation that I thought, but FTL is hard as♥♥♥♥♥♥ You'll be multi tasking and focusing on so many things, it's insane. The game is a pixelated rouge like, being when you die, you die. But not your character, your ship. There's two ways for you to lose in FTL: Your ships hull breaking, causing a massive atomic bomb going inside the ship, being able to compete against the explosion of the Deathstar from A New Hope.
Alright, that too seemed exagerrated. The games premise is that your part of the Federation, you just found some secret blue prints on destroying the Rebel Flagship:   the big momma of the Rebel ships. I'll get to that thing later. But, you'll be travelling beacon to beacon, fighting ships, and going through choices. Now, each choice will depend on your ship, your arsenal, and your crews life. There'll be a dice roll going on behind the scenes choosing your every fate. I know I may be rushing through this, I'll probably revise it later, but let me talk about the final boss: The Rebel Flagship.
Good God is this thing impossible to kill. It's not only hard to reach the final sector, but you have to fight through a 3 part boss with this thing, while it's trying to reach your central base. The thing is absolutely insane, having such a dense shield, a large amount of crew members, drones, and arsenal.
Let me just leave it here, this game has good music, gameplay is satisfying, it's good overall. Just don't get your hopes too high on defeating the final boss.

I got a bit worried at first, but put my faith in, and preordered the game + season pass. So far, I am NOT disappointed!
Pros
+Its zombies! all types! Fast, Slow, Scary, Wimpy, Ranged, Melee, Big, Small, etc, etc!
+Fun crafting like Dead Island, but with more purpose and apparent effect!
+A great parkour system that lets you realy enjoy the well built maps, and take on any challenge multiple ways!
+Night time is genuinely terrifying! When you cant rush, and are reduced to a sneak for fear of being shreded by monsters that are faster than you, and have ony the advantage of UV light and Climbing speed to get away, you know night has been done justice!
+Night Hunter invasions are fun once you get experienced on both sides!
+Graphics are AMAZING. Holy cow, I got in and had to stop and just walk for a bit to really appreciate how great it all looks!
+You get better at skills by USING THEM! Want to be faster? Run, climb, and vault, and youll get there! Want to smash heads quicker? Swing, crush, stab, and slice, and you will be fighting better in no time!
Negatives
-Night Hunter invasions come so fast that you get no down time once you get caught in them. (they are fun though, and if you get to a safe zone in time, they can be avoided)
-Optimization. I have a great laptop, but the default settings will be too much right now for almost anyone on PC. Its just not optimized enough as it is. I have to run it on "low" settings to avoid crashes and hitching, but it still looks amazing.
I gotta say, I recommend this game, and lets hope it continues to wow me, and all the others who play. See you at the Tower, and make sure your there before dark! :D

So, for the immature people that are going to scream "fanboy" or "dumbass" or the like, I can care less about what you say. For the people that actually have honest opinions and valid points, heres my overall summary of the game.
Pros:
* The parkour system, is not awful, infact its extremely well made. The animations are very nicely done, with only a few clipping issues and entertaining bugs. Which, depending on the person, may cause a negative or postive reaction.
* The combat feels much more interactive then dead island, and there is more control over it. Even with a one shot weapon, your stamina with every skill other then infinite, still prevents you from killing an entire crowd, and the repair system balances it nicely.
*The night system was decently well implemented, albeit with some balance issues in the late game it still feels rather well done.
Mixed Judgements:
The repair system is a great idea in theory, and later in the game it doesnt matter. I easily find better weapons then what Im using, they are terrifyingly common. Early on, weapons become pointless and fighting is less relevant, which is what the devs were going for. They give you high speed and parkour abilities, they want you to use them not walk down the road and beat every zombie you see to death like in Dead Island. This game is NOT dead island, its Dying Light. Judging it based upon its afiliation with techland and dead island is nine times out of ten, biased. The character system, which compared to its "Spiritual Predecessor" (I use the term very lightly) Dead island, is insanely improved. The ability to change what you look like, is great. However.. Peoples arguments about the clones and such are completely justified in the sense that there arent many clothing options and no actual -character- customization options.
Cons:
*Weapon balancing is a definate problem in this game, you can see it once you hit sector 0. You go from hitting the same zombie 3-4 times to one shotting 1-3 in one swing to the head. As I stated earlier, the combat is more interactive as a whole, but late-game it can still become pretty bull.
*Difficulty curve is way, and I mean wayyyyyy to easy to see. This is mainly because of weapons being unbalanced, but the zombies dont ever get stronger like they do in dead island. They simply... are there.. They dont get more numerous, or get more health. A difficulty setting is definetly needed using damage and health multipliers being preferred.
* The mod support. Or rather the lack thereof. A mod developer should be thanked and appreciated, mabye even learned from. Mods, in this day of pc gaming, are what make a game grow and develop even after the devs move onto other games. This is what keeps most games alive years after they have been forgotten. Preventing mods on your game is like telling your support team to ignore customer requests, its downright rediculous.
*The Optimization, nuff said.
With 30-60 or more FPS, easily a 7/10, mabye a 6/10 with lack of mod support.
With less then 30 FPS, and low frame tolerance, 3, mabye 4 if your generous out of 10.
One of the best games of the year, completely ruined by bad optimization.

She can point out hidden items and she's got a flash light that can stun enemies and AI Claire would round house kick them to the floor where I could run in and perform a killing move. It worked really well to attack with Moira's melee weapon because if I started getting into trouble, usually Claire would shoot them up a bunch and stop their attack and I could keep whaling away on enemies with Moira's crow bar. Barry is partnered up with a little girl who can see enemies through walls (and also spot hidden items like Moira)  and some enemies only she can see at all. Some of my favorite moments were when she'd point her finger out at these invisible enemies and I'd get behind her to try to line up my shot to where she's pointing. There's also this strange disorienting effect that takes over when those invisible enemies get too close. It was a nice touch.  Unfortunately, there isn't a huge variety of enemies and most enemies are not visually interesting at all. Overall they seem very generic. The combat was fun, though. Classic clunky resident evil controls are still here. Along with the campaign and Raidmode, theres a couple of short stand alone chapters to play. One that's essentially a horde mode where Moira and her new friend go hunting for food and monsters. The second one is all stealth where the little girl, Natalia, sneaks by monsters through a series of locations from the campaign. They're both short and are ok. It's always nice to have a little bonus something to play when the main game is over. I've only played a little bit of Raid mode, but its really just Merceneries, which is not a bad thing. The graphics are functional. They look about as good as RE5 did. The voice acting is competent. Revelations 2 is not as good as the recently released RE1 Remaster (99% of games aren't), but it was still a lot of fun. It's an EASY recommendation, especially to RE fans.

A highly-entertaining satirical game that pokes fun at the RPG genre while being a solid addition to it. It's a throwback to old-school pixelated RPGs like Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest, with an entertaining twist and ongoing meta-commentary about the tropes that made so many of those games fun. The battle system is turn-based and the class system uses points to equip abilities that unlock through leveling up your stats, so you have an impetus to keep your characters at least somewhat balanced in order to maximize your point spreads.
My favorite part is one of the characters calling upon the Flying Spaghetti Monster to cast healing spells. 10/10 would heal again.

Moira's inability to use firearm is not as frustrated as I first thought, and though Natalia can't use weapons at all her ability to sense enemies from afar is useful. There aren't many puzzles in this game, but some does require the corporation of two characters, or the unique ability of a character in some way. However, this create a problem in single player campaign on PC as there's no co-op, and continuously switching between characters does lengthen the finishing time. I don't have any issue with the graphics, I think it looks fine and I don't complain as long as the gameplay is fun.

Shadowrun Returns is a beautifully crafted game, with an amazing job with the story and setting. Based off of the roleplaying game, Shadowrun; You the player create your own Runner. A freelancer. A Merc. A person who's whole purpose is to make money doing the seedier things that society dust under the carpet.
With this game, it provides an interesting media to portray your antics. Allowing for most situations to be handled however you want to. Want to hack a turret to fight for you? You can. Want to mow down enemies with a machine gun? Have fun trying. Want to charm enemies into allies, or summon elementals to fight for you? Get started sparky. This game does a great job bringing in just about every aspect of the roleplaying game. Mind you, it does have some constraints.
You are following a premade story, so there are limits on what you can and can't do. But with the addition of Daggerfall, you get a little bit more freedom with how you do the story.
In the end, the graphics are nice. Music is very fitting for the setting, and the story is wonderful. The fact that it has a user workshop and the tools to make your own story is also greatly appreciated. There are many nicely made user stories out there, and most allow you to bring in your Runner from the main campaigns. Which really does fit well with the idea of the original game. So overall, I give it a 8.5/10. And remember kids, don't trust anybody. Not even your closest friends.

I've had an amazing experience in this game. Most horror games I've played previously tended to have a faster pace in comparison to Dead Space but this slow pace was a pleasant surprise. The graphics are mediocre in this day and age but accomplishes amply in setting the ambience. This in combination with the baffling intensity of detail with the atmospheric sounds makes this a marvelous masterpiece of suspense. The sound in Dead Space is something that evokes dread while playing. I've always preferred to progress in a sensible manner and I never felt that I was rushing through the game or that the pace was too slow. I explored most areas and it took me approximately 12 hours to complete the game story wise. However, there are a lot more to explore and many more experiences to be had in this game. Not to mention various play styles. It became clear that on higher difficulties you need some hasty reflexes in order to survive and it took me a while to get used to the 3rd person mouse controls. I were initially slightly deterred by it but you get used to it rather quickly. However, there are some unfortunate minor hurdles you need to get past before you can play the game pleasantly on a modern PC.
I personally followed a
made by Bropalm on Dead Space's community guides. I chose to download the DLL fix and changed the Vsync for Dead Space in NVIDIA Control Panel to [ON] which sets the game FPS to your monitors refresh rate. The default Vsync within the game is set to 30FPS and with it set to [OFF] the game will run at several thousand and overwork your GPU and CPU while also causing screen tearing. The game ran and runs fine for me after I applied the changes.
I definitively recommend this game to anyone that remotelly enjoys ambient settings and horror. I'll surely play the sequels.
Posting your own experiences with Dead Space whether good or bad assists potential newcomers in making their decision in whether to purchase the game or not.

Quick Summary: Dead Space is an action/horror/shooter game similar in gameplay to Resident Evil 4, but with more emphasis on gunplay and less on puzzle solving. If you’re a fan of inventory/ammo management, careful aiming, creepy dark rooms, and jump scares in a sci-fi environment you will love this game.
You play Isaac, an engineer who is part of a small crew tasked with reestablishing contact with the mining ship Ishimura somewhere in deep space. Your mission goes awry due to circumstances beyond your control + nasty creatures. As one of the few surviving members of your crew, your job is to run around the Ishimura fixing what needs to be fixed in order to get the hell out of this hellhole. It turns out that an “alien” artifact has been discovered that causes not only widespread insanity, but grotesque mutations, transforming the ship’s former crew (both alive and dead) into vicious bloodthirsty monsters called necromorphs.
The game is played in third person over-the-shoulder perspective, similar to Resident Evil 4, 5, and 6 though you can still move at a reasonable speed with your gun drawn and aiming. One of the unusual elements to Dead Space is that unlike other shooters, you should not be aiming for head shots. The necromorphs are far more vulnerable to dismemberment, meaning that if you shoot off their arms and legs you’re doing a lot more damage to them (also slowing them down more since they’ll probably keep crawling after you). There are also a few gameplay variations to spice things up (asteroid shooting, zero gravity sections, etc.).
You should play Dead Space if:
+You’re a fan of horror games with jump scares, dark spooky environments, and really nasty tumorous looking aliens.
+You liked the Resident Evil 4, 5, and 6 type of action shooter gameplay but wished it was faster and more “fluid” (run & gun).
+You like scavenging dark corridors for loot such as money and ammunition, and managing your small inventory to only keep the stuff that you’ll need to get through the next section of the game. There are a variety of different weapons in Dead Space and they all use different ammunition that takes up one of your precious inventory slots. If you fill your limited inventory with the ammunition types for your guns, you won’t have any space for other loot that you come across.
You should NOT play Dead Space if:
-You dislike jump scares, grisly death animations, or dark squishy environments. Dead Space 2 is even darker, but you get a flashlight in that game.
-You’re a Scientologist. You’ll understand what I mean if you play the game and read the logs scattered around the Ishimura.
-You’re a more casual player and dislike messing around with small inventory space or limited ammunition.  Upgrades for your guns are purchased using semi-rare “power nodes” that cost a small fortune so if you’re not playing on easy mode you’re not going be able to fully upgrade all your guns. Pick one or two that you want right from the start, and only upgrade those.
-Annoying mouse control (stuttering) when aiming your gun. This is a well-known bug for the PC version of the game but there are workarounds.
Overall Dead Space is an awesome game experience (about 12 hours to beat) and well worth playing. Be aware that you might get a mild headache playing the game until you get used to the movement and perspective.

Holy tap-dancing Christ, what is this? This is FTL, also known as "one of the two good things that ever came out out of a Kickstarter project", and that says a lot. You know what else says a lot? The ♥♥♥♥ing difficulty.
FTL is a little roguelike space combat / spaceship management game where you get to pick a vessel of choice and manage its weapons, systems and crew as you travel across sectors of the Galaxy during an all-out civil war to deliver a message to Federation command while at the same time making mincemeat of any scum that dare stand in your way including rebels, pirates, slavers, brainwashed aliens, and just generally douchenozzles. What does make Mirror's Edge a good game?
First, Mirror's Edge is probably a unique game. Unlike many games that used acrobatic with a third-person view as a game mechanic, this one uses a first person view. Believe me: the system is really well done. However, it might be tricky to play this game with a keyboard. Using a controller is a great solution if you have difficulties to play it with a keyboard + mouse.
Second, the environment is really well done. It always stay consistent, which is nice because it helps you to stay focused on the game. The colors help you to react when you must face a situation. The cinematics and the story are well adapted to the world in which they're set.
Third, the game is well optimized for PC. If your computer is not too old, it should run just fine.
My only complain is that Mirror's Edge is rather short and linear. I'm pretty sure you won't play it 10 times. However, if you can have it at a low price you won't regret it.

Half-Life 2 is, to put it simply, one of the most masterful games ever created.
Now, if the New Tens (or later) is the first time you're playing, you'll probably think that it's a cliche storm.
However, quick history lesson for aspiring geeks: This game came out in 2004. A lot of first-person-shooters that share many tropes with HL2 came out after 2004.
Not to say those aren't good, too. I mean, I play CoD on occasion, but HL2 is the best FPS I've played yet.
If you want to play this first without the original, here's a quick backstory (spoilers ahoy!):
The player character, Gordon Freeman, was performing an experiment in the Black Mesa Research Facility that caused a "resonance cascade," causing aliens to start teleporting in from an alternate dimension. The only reason he didn't die is because he was wearing an "HEV" Suit. He hacks his way through the facility, aliens, and the military to get to the Lambda Complex, where he teleports to the alien homeworld Xen, where he kills the alien's leader: the Nihilanth. Then,  a mysterious figure known as the G-Man offers him a new job. Freeman accepts, and he is put in stastis.
He wakes up on a train, arriving in one "City 17". This is where Half-Life 2 begins.
Now, why don't you put down $10 (or less, if you get it on sale) for this slice of gaming history?
P.S. Also download the Half-Life 2: Update mod, which pretties up the game extensively.

Now, while I may have only played about 2 hours of the game as of writing this review, I can honestly say I would adore this game if it functioned properly.
When I can combat roll on the spot, and activate my abilities (and basic attack) it has a tight, amazing feel to it, and I know that every mistake is my own.
When the game decides to lock up and continue to use an ability every time it cools down, or spam the basic attack non-stop, it is utterly infuriating. It is so annoying when I'm doing well, dodging a boss, and my character decides to start spamming Machine Gun which considerably slows him down and or locks him in place, and the only way to move is awkwardly jump to and frow, smashing the various abilities in hopes that it stops.
I really like this game when it works, but when it refuses to, I could lose it. I've tried various fixes, including resetting my computer, the game, steam, and checking the buttons themselves, but they all seem to be functioning normally. Risk of Rain is great otherwise, but with this glitch, it's next to unplayable.

A rather simple card game to pass the time, Faerie Solitaire is literally as the name implies--a slightly glittered-up version of solitaire. It is something to play should you want to just aimlessly pass the time away. If you have any other games on your list to play, then I suggest playing them first. Don't get me wrong, the game is decent in its own right, but mainly for younger ages, casual gamers, grandparents, or those odd people who actually classify themselves as "gamers" because they play facebook games. It has a few unique factors to it such as pets, achievements, and objectives, which utterly make it seem more and more like it truly does belong on facebook.
Objectives start out easy and gradually increase with difficulty as you progress through the short and thin plot of the game. If you do not complete an objective on that level then you must start it over completely. This is something that will utterly allow you to waste more time should you so wish. Achievements vary but are relatively simple to grasp and accomplish by just playing the game. Lastly, you can find eggs and other "mystical" items as you progress, and they allow you to hatch them and raise your own pets/creatures over time. There are baby and adult versions of each creature--it evolves when you acquire the appropriate materials and earn enough exp (which you attain by simply putting time into the game I believe). The point of the game is to fill "Faerie Land" with creatures and release trapped Faeries by playing the card games somehow... Overall, I recommend Faerie Solitaire only if you are truly bored or have a younger sibling/child you wish to entertain while babysitting them.

Hey. Do you like games that don't shove micro transactions down your throat? Do you like paying one price for about 50 or so hours of content? This is the game for you. The combat is great and you never feel overpowered (at least where I am) the zombies can mess you up if you dodge at the wrong time or mess up a grapple. It's the little things that can ruin you, you can only upgrade your health in 25 hp increments maxing out at 175 meaning you can take some punishment but you will never have 600000 Health. You can become an athlete at both running and fighting but you never can just chop through a hoard without expecting to get hit at least a little.
Things I liked:
-The climbing and fighting feel great.
-You upgrade each of the three skill trees by actually doing things that are involved doing them. (Agility is from climbing and falling safely, Fighting is from killing and hitting enemies, and Survival is from collecting air drops and helping out random survivors.)
-The costumes for the most part look fine.
-The side missions are oddly satisfying for me to do, like more than most RPGs. (I can't figure out why.)
-The main story moves rather fast and didn't leave me feeling like what I was doing didn't matter. Just don't expect a really good story this is a GO BANANAS GAME.
-Crafting and modifying weapons are effecting and easy to get the hang off.
-This game is FUN AS HELL. (DROPKICKS)
-The human enemies sometimes actually RUN from you after you kill their friends and you get to either let them get away or chase them down.(Best AI 2015 so far.)
-Co-op seems like it'd be a blast with a couple of friends.
-The Volatiles that only come out at night are scary and you don't want to take on too many too early.
-You can play as a zombie and be a kind of predator to kill other players.
Things that I didn't really like:
-You can't customize your Crane other than the set outfits.
-Sometimes deaths can be a bit cheap but this can be easily taken off if you listen well.
-Some animations look awkward in first person if you aren't looking at a place causing you to jump at places that may get you killed.
-Weapons are rather boring early on, guns are sometimes useless due to noise but it's cool that they are in the game.
-Bombers are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
-That Rais' men sometimes arrive at airdrops RIGHT IN FRONT of you.
Seriously though. This is a great game. It's really a no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t fun game if you like melee combat that feels good, running errands, and climbing high stuff. Dropkicks are the best thing.

What could I possibly say that hasn't already been said already.
Well... let's tell my story.
When I was a kid, I fell in love with a game called 'Shining Force,' which some may have heard of, and others not so much. Anyway, it was a top down "tactics" game: you controlled a rag-tag bunch of Medieval fantasy-style characters on a quest to purge the darkness that had been unsealed. One of the main draws of this game (and one of the main reasons I'd still return to it in the present day) was its simplicity; you had options, but you mostly had to rely on formation and non-fog-of-war tactics to really succeed.
While I did, as I aged, fall in love with other (console) tactics games for various reasons - Final Fantasy Tactics, Disgaea, Front Mission, Advance Wars - none of them retained the complexity of those of the earlier games in the Shining Force series (especially Shining Force II) by way of simplicity, but rather by way of introducing complex or quirky mechanics that, while amusing for the first few implementations, grew steadily into automotonic repetition... or by quasi-forcing you to grind your way to the top (You technically could grind in Shining Force, but you didn't often NEED to as much as you might in, say, Disgaea).
Which brings me to XCOM. I'd been introduced to it indirectly by a number of YouTube LPers, and fell in love with the crazy antics and frustrations they experienced... especially the ones they inflicted on themselves by hacking into the game and ramping up the difficulty beyond even that of present-day Impossible mode, just for the challenge of it. When I later saw that there was to be a new edition (and even later, saw the amazing graphics of said edition), I jumped on the bandwagon as soon as I had the time and money to do so, and I have not been disappointed.
XCOM will always keep you on your toes; unless you're a master at the game playing on Easy or Normal perhaps. I myself have not yet mastered this system (years of fuddled implementations of "flanking" rules are still wreaking havoc in my brain), but success in the game relies more on simple squad tactics than it does on any sort of weird crafting, class, or combat, or other system. You need to think ahead practically all the time on the field (and off), carefully cross terrain and explore the map, and hopefully only ever uncover a group of aliens when you can actually handle them in one or two turns. Every battle challenges you to choose the right strategies every turn, whether the best option is to play more defensive or more offensive, play economically or in more of a rushdown style (either of which can backfire horribly). And because dead characters are dead... not resurrectable as they might be in the more lightweight tactics games of modern day (save Fire Emblem), I actually tend to really "care" about them. Any alien that blows up my main avatar is going to die in the most gruesome way I can manage.
Coupled with an amazing combat engine, XCOM also challenges you with managing the actual base of your operation (in a much simpler and streamlined fashion than in the original), which again challenges you to think about how you ultimately want to build your base, and when to build which structure, and when to do which research, and which items or weaponry or armor or accessories to purchase or upgrade... all on a budgeted income. Perhaps it's an odd thing to say, but the limitations imposed upon you actually help to drive the game, and help to make the game an enjoyable one. While I did enjoy the slight period in time that I could relatively ROFLstomp the enemy due to overpowered weaponry, I find I still have the ability to so long as I size up the enemy first and plan intelligently my assault... it just takes a bit longer to do so.
I have not played Enemy Within... but I look forward to a purchase in the near future. Still, even without the expansion, XCOM: Enemy Unknown delivers... alien heads on a platter.

Very fun survival horror action. I love how it gives you "safe" places, like save stations and stores, but occasionally invades them to keep you thinking. The game's length is very appropriate: after you become accustomed to design patterns and enemy tactics, it's halfway through the game and you're becoming a force to be reckoned with. The endgame has a few easy fights that just made me feel strong before the final few challenges.
Hard to believe it was a 2008 release. Environments are cramped but filled with detail. Sound design is incredible, the main reason I was on edge for most of the game.
Deep and interesting world lore, though the immediate narrative is often dull. "Go fix this", "Good, now go fix that", repeat each chapter. The general repetition throughout the game can be boring, even though encounters stayed fun for me. I feel a lot went into minimising repetition through frequently mixing up gameplay with zero-G and vacuum areas, and various different enemies you need to learn how to deal with.
Highly recommended, especially due to the low pricetag (for some reason, only £10 UK = <$15, while it's $20 on the US store). If you're patient and want a longer experience (one run took me 12hrs), play Hard!

First, I recommend this game more on a scale of Shadowrun games to date. It's not the best, but compared to all of the games to date, it's my second favorite Shadowrun video game.
This game is hard for me to rate one way or another. I love the Shadowrun setting. I have played the tabletop RPG, and most, if not all, of the video games it has spawned. The best game, and the one this most closely resembles, the 1993 SNES Shadowrun, is still my favorite game. It even contains a few cameos by that games player character. If you are drawn to this one because of that similarity, let me explain where it differs. This game is extremely linear. There is no going back to areas to explore, the only place you can exit to is the place they want you to go next. You quickly realize that you aren't in charge of anything, you can't leave without doing what needs to be done, and you don't need to worry about where you're going next, it will make you go there. Searching and examining things will yield very little of use in the long run. The few times that you have to work things out through clues and context are so rare that they seemed out of place. I would have enjoyed more of that, but if you're only going to do it two or three times in the story, it feels forced when it happens. The last issue I have with the game is that if you want to play the same character in both of the currently available storylines, you have to use a user generated patch to load a previous character. I imagine that this had to do with balance, but I expected to be able to take my character right into the second story after finishing the first. My large reward at the end of it was useless as it didn't even transfer with my character, it may as well have said "you get all the money in the world" since I didn't get anything I could actually spend before the game began rolling credits. If you understand all of that going in, and you want to play it knowing that, you will be happier with it than if you'd gone in hoping for the experience of playing the game this one attempts to recapture.

Resident Evil Revelations 2 Is a huge step up than the first one in my opinion. I first played RE Revelations on my 3DS and I had expected a lot from it given the whole point behind it was what this game had finally done. I wouldn't say it exactly put you into the series' roots but it has some of the older ones feel (RE4/RE5). Everything here is considered an improvement including the story. I was satisfied by this game and I easily would support the developers doing more of this gameplay style. However, not every game is without its drawbacks. There are 2 characters in each campaign and I suppose I was bothered by the fact that there is one character in both Claire and Barry's campaign that is able to find hidden items across the map. Of course, the player would not ignore to look for these items and the AI doesn't help you finding these items if you are playing single player. So, this resulted in me sticking with playing as Moira/Natalia throughout the whole campaign which really annoyed me since I wanted to have my leisure time to switch between characters. Nevertheless, it was an entertaining game and I would forget about the blunder the developers made in RE revelations 1 now that this game has at least some redeeming qualities. The extra episodes weren't worth it, they didn't reveal anything about the story so I would only recommend the main campaign. Raid mode was alright to wait between episodes but it didn't exactly draw me for more than a few hours. Good game. I'd also recommend getting it on a sale, it isn't exactly all the rage to buy on full price.

Resident Evil Revelations 2 offers some new likable mechanics into the age old formula but still rests on the side of action rather than pure survival horror. There's a fine mixture of puzzles versus exploration and some clever moments fused with equal amounts of frustration that create much satisfaction once bested. Some elements are a bit wonky and could be better polished in terms of control, but in general the game serves its purpose and is easy to pick up and play for newcomers and vets alike.  There's ample variation when taking into consideration the two extra episodes which focus on stealth and team based combat making a well rounded package that's cheap and reasonably polished. Whilst there are some moments where nothing seemingly happens and enemies appear sparse, when they do jump out there's some neat gameplay mechanics (more-so in  Claire's campaign) to give the game is own identity within the long running series. Whilst it doesn't re-invent the wheel, it's a pleasing and gratifying game offering some interesting concepts, an engaging story with some familiar faces. If you're a fan of the series then this is a no-brainer and well worth checking out. Action fans will also find some entertainment here although might find some of the puzzles interrupting the flow a little. If you can ignore the abundance of cheese in the last moments of the story and bask in the game's extra content you'll find a worthy game to add to your collection.

Instead of a quote, i will start this review by telling you this: "This game is a love letter to Resident Evil fans". The return of Barry Burton and Claire Redfield deserves a big thumbs up to Capcom. The old B-movie like story is back with an interesting antagonist, which some fans have been waiting for. The game has a lot of self-awareness, making quotes now and then that fans will remember, like: "I was almost a Claire sandwich" or "Who's the master of unlocking now?".
Claire Redfield works at an anti-terrorist organization called Terrasave. Barry Burton's daughter Moira recently joined Terrasave. Terrasave is hosting a party, which gets crashed by mysterious mercenaries, and injects everyone with something. Claire wakes up in a cell in an unknown location. Shortly after she finds Moira also locked in a cell. Both are wearing strange bracelets through where a mysterious woman is speaking, quoting poetry and giving instructions. Claire and Moira must find out where they are, who this woman is that is speaking to them, and how to get away from this place.
The gameplay is very similar to Revelations, over the shoulder third person action, with a little bit of survival horror here and there. scarce ammunition and though enemies make for some tense moments. Next to Claire Redfield and Moira Burton, you will also be able to play as Barry Burton accompanied by a girl named Natalia. The game uses an episodic structure in which you play a part of Claire's story and a part of Barry's story. Side characters like Moira and Natalia won't use guns, but have another special ability. Moira has a flashlight, which she can use to slow enemies down and stun them. Natalia in Barry's campaign has the ability to spot enemies from a distance and through walls. This is useful for Barry to easily sneak kill the enemies. The main campaign has a big focus on story, and a fine mystery to solve, but the gameplay is much like every recent Resident Evil game. The place where the gameplay really shines though is at..
The raid mode is back from Revelations, and better than ever. More characters and more stages to play makes for a very fun experience.  Many unlockables and special weapons to achieve makes the new raid mode very, very addictive. Many critics have praised the raid mode in Revelations 2, it's like a little RPG hidden in the game. for those of you who are not familiar with the raid mode. Raid mode has you run through an area, killing enemies with your selected character and loadout. You can achieve medals in each of the stages to get a higher score. At the end of the stages you'll be rewarded XP to level your character and improve in your skills. The raid mode in Revelations 2 is very addictive and fun, and might even be worth the price alone.
After all the praise I gave the game, I can't help but say that the pc launch of this game was horrible. A very bad port from the start with huge performance issues, which has been fixed a few days ago. My pc can run almost every new game on ultra, and I couldn't play this game on low without huge fps drops. Luckily this has all been fixed now, making it possible to play this game on ultra fluidly. I can barely forgive Capcom for this horrible launch, but after all the fixes, i can't help but say that this game is actually very, very good.
With a horrible launch, Resident Evil Revelations 2 got a lot of dislike thrown towards it. Now that all the episodes are released and most of the bugs fixed, this game became a solid entry in the Resident Evil series. The return of Claire and Barry is a true love letter to fans, and the cheasy B-movie style story like we all love from Resident Evil is back big time. The addictive Raid mode would be worth the game alone, but the main campaign is a lot of fun, and might be one of the best Resident Evil games since a long time.

If you liked Portal and wanted to play something else like that you're in tough position. There's simply not many things like that. Then there's Antichamber. It can't really be compared to Portal as it's a completely different kind of game apart from being a first-person puzzle game, but if you enjoyed "thinking with portals" you should check it out.
First thing you see on the promotional materials and after starting the game is the incredibly simplistic and sterile art direction. Accompanied by subtle and fitting soundtrack, it sets the tone for the whole game and dramatically helps it being what it is. Antichamber simply wouldn't work with more realistic approach to graphics.
As for the game's mind-bending properties - they're there, but mostly in the first part of the game. New game mechanics introduced to the player along the way are not particularly special or interesting although not bad either - what's bad is their use. It comes down mostly to solving yet another puzzle embodied in the wall in order to open yet another door. It's rather disappointing and makes the game not use most of its potential.
Story-wise, there's literally nothing to guide you. Not a single word of explanation who you are, where are you, what are you trying to do etc. You have to think for yourself. And it works. I really liked how it's all very ambiguous yet not pretentious, and this approach fits the game perfectly. Plus the ending is very cool. It kind of saved the overall experience for me as I was getting more and more tired and disappointed in the middle section of the game.
In overall I really think this is a game worth playing. It has its flaws - mostly poor use of mechanics and repetitiveness at some points, which is a pretty major thing - but makes up for it in other aspects. There's not enough of games of this kind to miss this one.

One of the bigger surprises of 2012 is FTL.  Considering the price this is one of my top games of 2012.  Like almost all great games, it is simple in it's concept but has layer upon layer of depth the more you dig into it.  Getting your small ship with a skeleton crew across 8 sectors of mostly hostile space with an overwhelming rebel fleet at your back is at times thrilling and other times soul crushingly brutal.  Expect to use your entire arsenal of curse words as you and your crew will die in dozens of brutal ways.  Having your ship blown apart is only the begining.  Death by fire, lack of oxygen, being sucked out into space, being evisacerated by space farring Manti, being mind controlled by space slugs and having robotic drones teleport aboard your ship and tear it apart from the inside are all par for the course.
This game is tough as nails.  But with each death comes a painful lesson.  Running your crew around to repair systems, fight fires and transfer powerr between systems becomes second nature.  Also as you play and stumble across new ships and weapons, these are unlocked and you can use them at the begining of subsequent ventures out into space.  Along with your increasing skill at the game, these unlocks make future voyages slightly easier.  But still expect to die the majority of the time.  Very few games can remain fun when you suceed less than 1% of the time.  FTL is one of those games.

Okay, to start I NEVER write reviews so please read with that in mind... I found this game so enjoyable to the extent that i decided to finally write one in hopes of supporting what is now one of my favorite games. This review is completely opinionated (OBVIOUSLY) so take it as such. At this point i have not finished the game but believe to be on the last mission. I will not talk about story whatsoever because of my terrible hate of spoilers (sorry!)
Gameplay:
The gameplay in Dying Light mixes first person melee combat/some FPS and parkour. As a gamer before this game I would actually avoid a RPG if it was first person melee. I just never found it too enjoyable and always felt it was clunky, no matter the game. I never finished Skyrim or Dishonored because of how much i disliked melee combat, absolutely nothing negative to say about those games, just first person melee was never my thing. That being said, the combat in Dying Light is the best that I have seen first person melee done. Think almost Skyrim and Darksouls mixed. You have a stamina bar so you cannot just sit there hacking away at a pack of twenty zombies until you have leveled up a bit. Each swing feels like it has weight to it when using a blunt weapon, and yet take a sword out and the combat seems much more fluid as you slice limbs off whatever you're fighting. Melee weapons can break and have a limit to how many times they can be repaired before becoming ultimately useless. This can be somewhat aleviated in the skill trees to an extent. For example having the chance to not consume a repair charge when repairing a weapon, which is extremely useful.
Progression:
Leveling in Dying Light is pretty straight forward once you are in game and can look at the three talent "trees". The trees are: Survivor, Agility, Power (names might not be exact but you get the point). Survivor includes talents like decreased shop prices, better crafting, etc. Agility is all parkour, and Power is... well... COMBAT :D. The three trees level independently from eachother, meaning in order to level survivor you need to do missions (dying causes you to lose survivor xp, to my knowledge you will not de-level if at 0xp in the level at death), agility is leveled just by parkouring around the city, and power is earned fighting, killing. I would highly recommend taking the game slowly, leveling up as much as possible before believing you are all powerful and any zombie you see should die.
Day/Night:
One of my favorite things in the game. During the day you honestly wont fear much once you are established in the game. Not even the bigger zombies will be able to stand much of a chance... But at night... The entire game's atmosphere changes into that of a survival feeling (which i didnt really feel during the day) zombies become more aggressive and the hunter zombies come out which will chase you down in a heartbeat early on.
Fun things to do:
I wanted to add this section because there are so many fun things to do in the game.
1st. Find a huge horde of zombies. get on the roof above them. drop a firecracker. wait till they all group up on it. MOLOTOV!!!!!!!!! sit back, laugh, watch the xp roll in.
2nd. As soon as possible make an electric weapon. Its not really over powerered or anything. Just suuuuuper funny to watch the zombie you hit have a seizure from the jolt.
3rd. Honestly just parkour around. I found myself spending hours just running through the city, not even killing anything. Just having fun with an unbelievably well done implementation.
Sorry i jumped around and if you stuck around I really appreciate your time and hope this helped! And remember this was my first one so it probably wasn't too well structured (sorry!)

Do you like rougelikes? Do you like getting an assortment of items that do different things to help you survive longer and not die? Do you like the
trope?
If you answered yes to any of those questions, drop what you're doing and get this game right now...unless you wanna wait for it to go on sale, then get it once it's on sale.
Risk of Rain is, at its core, a rougelike but also a game about survival on a planet of creatures that weren't hostile until your character crashlands on the planet and then everything wants to kill you for some reason (maybe they can sense your hidden murderous intent).
At first you only have one character you can play as, with a total of 12 after you unlock everyone. The more you play, the more stuff you unlock with which you can do even more stuff to unlock even more things and so on.
You can also unlock up to 110 different items to help you outlast your enemies longer. Thirdly, there's artifacts you can acquire/unlock that change how the game plays should you switch any on.
You can use either keyboard controls or gamepad controls so there's something here for both parties.
For each run, you start off at level 1. You gain experience and money from killing enemies and after getting enough experience you level up, increasing your health and how much damage you output from attacks. The money you get goes towards buying chest (opening them) and activating stuff that can give you items.
The main goal is to find a teleporter to advance to the next level. When you activate it, a boss enemy shows up. Depending on what difficulty you play on, the timer for the teleporter to activate differs, being 90 seconds on Drizzle(easy) and Rainstorm(medium), and 120 seconds on Monsoon(hard). The longer you play, the stronger enemies become so don't stick around levels too long.
When you do die, anything you unlocked remains unlocked for later runs. Enemies sometimes drop enemy logs that have information on them you can view at the main menu and every item you unlock has some flavor text giving you more background info on different items.
In total, there's 5 stages you can play in, with a 6th stage housing the final boss. By 5 stages, I mean you only go through 5 stages and of the 5, there's 2 possibilites per level. In one run you could get one starting level but in another you could get the other possible level. The level rotation is randomized so you don't always get the same set of levels every run, but the final level is always the same.
My only gripes are the multiplayer and framerate dropping if you have too much happening on screen at once.
Risk of Rain is not for everyone but for you rougelike fans, give this one a gander. It has nice music too :^)
