Heads up, game fans! It's time to review the new zombie apocalypse game that so many people are playing and talking about: Dying Light. I've had a taste, and I want more, but will you? Read along and hopefully find out. I'm not going to tell you everything, and I'm trying to avoid any serious spoilers, but I will give you just a taste so that you can judge for yourself. Please keep in mind that this review is current as of the date of publication, but I have no idea what features may change, improve or get nerfed after this point. I am not including in this review aspects of the DLC, but I may review that later. Or not.
If I had to give just a brief idea of what this game is like, take a little bit of Fallout 3, just the tiniest taste of Crysis, a dash of Skyrim, a sprinkling of Far Cry 2, a little more FC2, toss in some inspiration from L4D2, and then top it all off with some Mirror's Edge, and you might get an idea of what this game is like. Maybe. Also throw in some optional asymmetrical fps with some rather unfortunate choices on the part of the developer to get even closer to the full experience.
You start off parachuting into a situation in a quarantined city somewhere seemingly in the Middle East. You have to find that one guy that your organization needs you to find; you know the one. You get infected, and you need medicine. That's how you're compromised, and that's how you begin working your way into the local sitch. You make yourself at home and begin doing odd jobs to improve your standing, gather intel, and make reports back to the peeps in charge in the rear. You can probably guess where this is going, so that's all I'm going to say about the back story. If you don't get medicine regularly, you get sicker and could possibly turn. So far it hasn't affected my gameplay as much as the same mechanic that was used in Far Cry 2, but I haven't gone very far in the main story line either. In the relatively brief time I've played this game, I've only had convulsions the one time.
You spend all your time climbing, running, jumping, ducking, dodging, and generally trying to outmaneuver, overpower, or out-think your opponents. You constantly have to think about where you're going next and how. The game has freedom, but with it also comes a terrible price. Sometimes you choose wrong, and it hurts so bad when you do. Conversely, when you choose well, and it works, it feels really good, too.
You get three skill trees, each with a different focus--one for gear, one for agility, and one for power. The things you do build your skills in the respective area, and if you want to get better at something, try doing it repeatedly or things closely related to it. Craft items and you'll be able to craft more items. Take on zombies one on one in melee, and you'll get better at it. Try extreme stunts, and you'll become a world-class parkour... -er (actually, the proper term is "traceur" if you didn't know... I didn't).
Your opponents are a blend of frightening zeds with some specials mixed in who will not always stand out at a distance the way they will in L4D2. Once you know what you're looking for they will be all too apparent in most cases, but there is a slight learning curve involved. Yes, the big guy with the insane hammer is easily spotted in any crowd, but the little screechy ones not so much. There is a level of unpredictability to every encounter. One guy goes down with a single blow, another saps your weapon of its remaining strength. Be wary of that. Weapons can only be repaired a few times. Also, if you upgrade a basic weapon, apparently you cannot then use it as part of crafting an advanced weapon. And when you can no longer repair a weapon, don't forget to dismantle it for the spare bits.
You can find a lot of loot everywhere you turn, but most of it (especially the better stuff) is behind locks that you can pick. If you've played Skyrim, you shouldn't have any issues doing this. I've heard Thief players should also know what's what. If you've played neither of those, watch a video before playing your first time to get a sense of how it's done. If somebody says you need tons of picks everytime you go looting, don't listen to them. You only need tons of picks to practice with until you're good. Skyrim players who've already cut their teeth on these locks should have no issue even with the toughest locks in this game.
During the day it's a parkour rpg with FPS elements, but at night, if you're out, it's totally stealth. At least until you know what you're doing. Bold precision pays off in this game. The developers have relied on player fear to a good extent, but how can you know the limits until you have tested them. Climb to the top of that communications tower. You never know what you might find. Plan your exit strategy and then hit that guy with the tank on his back. After he explodes, if you survive the swarm that will descend upon you, you will come out the other side stronger for it. Stronger or more agile, or both. Make your painful mistakes early on, because if you wait until later, you will feel the pain as you lose tons more points as a higher level character dies for the mistake of not being bold early on. Clear all your safe zones straight out from the prologue before you complete any quests. I did it my first day after the prologue, with the exception of the last one which was too well defended.  I think the daylight cycle might be tied to story progression and perhaps even side quests. Also, another pro-tip, if you're stuck, consider leaving the game and coming back because there are still glitches and bugs to be worked out. Can't reach a certain post from the roof of that one building? Maybe you're not supposed to. Trust me and see.
If you want to know what awaits you in the dark, play the Be a Zombie mode. You get to play as the Hunter, which feels like a cross between a vampire or werewolf and Venom. You get to play as one, that is, if you can find a match where people don't automatically leave as soon as you join. In my experience almost every one of the matches where I was actually able to stay and play, the human players knew what to do. If you decide to play this mode, expect some frustrations as a result, from the learning curve or from the game mechanics or from the matchmaking system. Being the Hunter is fun, but frustrating--until you get better at it. And you will get better if you stick with it. I feel the system is kind of limiting and almost misleading, because you aren't playing as any of the other zombies, only the Hunter.
One of the poor choices I feel the developer has made is seen in the multiplayer part of the game. You have extremely limited options in controlling online game play, and the game doesn't distinguish between sides. Say you go into Be a Zombie mode and open your game to public games online, when you go back into your solo campaign, it's not solo anymore. You have to go back into online settings and set it to solo once more. I wonder if this isn't part of the reason behind the large number of players who quit when a Hunter joins their game. Also, apparently, though I have yet to play with friends on co-op, I can tell you the voice communications in multiplayer are set to be strictly always on or always off. No push-to-talk. Perhaps they will fix this in the next patch. We can hope. Until then, better consider your third party options for game chat. Headphones, people. Wear. Your. Headphones. And play in a quiet area or turn off your mic please, for the love of all that is good and true.

What could I possibly say that hasn't already been said already.
Well... let's tell my story.
When I was a kid, I fell in love with a game called 'Shining Force,' which some may have heard of, and others not so much. Anyway, it was a top down "tactics" game: you controlled a rag-tag bunch of Medieval fantasy-style characters on a quest to purge the darkness that had been unsealed. One of the main draws of this game (and one of the main reasons I'd still return to it in the present day) was its simplicity; you had options, but you mostly had to rely on formation and non-fog-of-war tactics to really succeed.
While I did, as I aged, fall in love with other (console) tactics games for various reasons - Final Fantasy Tactics, Disgaea, Front Mission, Advance Wars - none of them retained the complexity of those of the earlier games in the Shining Force series (especially Shining Force II) by way of simplicity, but rather by way of introducing complex or quirky mechanics that, while amusing for the first few implementations, grew steadily into automotonic repetition... or by quasi-forcing you to grind your way to the top (You technically could grind in Shining Force, but you didn't often NEED to as much as you might in, say, Disgaea).
Which brings me to XCOM. I'd been introduced to it indirectly by a number of YouTube LPers, and fell in love with the crazy antics and frustrations they experienced... especially the ones they inflicted on themselves by hacking into the game and ramping up the difficulty beyond even that of present-day Impossible mode, just for the challenge of it. When I later saw that there was to be a new edition (and even later, saw the amazing graphics of said edition), I jumped on the bandwagon as soon as I had the time and money to do so, and I have not been disappointed.
XCOM will always keep you on your toes; unless you're a master at the game playing on Easy or Normal perhaps. I myself have not yet mastered this system (years of fuddled implementations of "flanking" rules are still wreaking havoc in my brain), but success in the game relies more on simple squad tactics than it does on any sort of weird crafting, class, or combat, or other system. You need to think ahead practically all the time on the field (and off), carefully cross terrain and explore the map, and hopefully only ever uncover a group of aliens when you can actually handle them in one or two turns. Every battle challenges you to choose the right strategies every turn, whether the best option is to play more defensive or more offensive, play economically or in more of a rushdown style (either of which can backfire horribly). And because dead characters are dead... not resurrectable as they might be in the more lightweight tactics games of modern day (save Fire Emblem), I actually tend to really "care" about them. Any alien that blows up my main avatar is going to die in the most gruesome way I can manage.
Coupled with an amazing combat engine, XCOM also challenges you with managing the actual base of your operation (in a much simpler and streamlined fashion than in the original), which again challenges you to think about how you ultimately want to build your base, and when to build which structure, and when to do which research, and which items or weaponry or armor or accessories to purchase or upgrade... all on a budgeted income. Perhaps it's an odd thing to say, but the limitations imposed upon you actually help to drive the game, and help to make the game an enjoyable one. While I did enjoy the slight period in time that I could relatively ROFLstomp the enemy due to overpowered weaponry, I find I still have the ability to so long as I size up the enemy first and plan intelligently my assault... it just takes a bit longer to do so.
I have not played Enemy Within... but I look forward to a purchase in the near future. Still, even without the expansion, XCOM: Enemy Unknown delivers... alien heads on a platter.

Shadowrun Returns was one of my most anticipated games for 2013. It didn't disappoint, despite the endgame mission being a bit... disappointing. I won't spoil it, but put some points into shotguns. It plays much like XCOM using half and full cover, you can build your main character any way you see fit in classic Shadowrun style. The storyline is deeper than most games you'd find today and without a voice cast, you are almost forced to read it, kind of like a story!
The community support is probably not as big as Harebrained thought it would be, being that the content editor is admittedly difficult to use and most people have lives and jobs. However, some of the player generated material is actually better than anticipated, some of it doing things no one expected could be done: Random generated missions, personnel escorts, etc.
All in all, it's a good game and if you're unsure about it, the game goes on sale pretty frequently and it's good for about 20 hours of gameplay. Dragonfall (the DLC) is even better than the original game and although I've yet to finish it, the story and the characters are diverse and it makes you want to press on by adding additional information about your crew as time goes on and they warm up to you.
I know that I've mentioned the story in this review a few times and I think that's what I'm trying to get at: So many of today's games focus so much on graphics, combat systems, crafting systems, skill trees, and so many other things that they mostly forget that there's got to be something beyond that to make it interesting.
This game is therefore a breath of fresh air. It doesn't have the best graphics, it doesn't have a voice cast, the combat system is mediocre and even troublesome at times. It doesn't have a lot of the features you'd typically have in a game today, but it does have something most games don't: a personality.

Man, I really don't know where to begin with this review... But here we go.
Doom & Destiny is a turn based RPG that basically jokes about/steriotypes Tabletop RPGs as well as the "nerdy/geeky" lifestyle in a sense. It is very humorous, almost everything about this game will make you laugh if you understand it.
So here is a short list of pros and cons to this game.
Pros-
Graphics, this is a "if you like these kind of graphics" thing. Personally, the graphics are nice, bringing back memories of some of the classic pixelly RPGs of old.
Audio/Music, the music and audio are nice. Not really sure how else I should explain this... So there you go :-)
Combat, the combat is turn based, which I definitely like. Skills/Powers and there uses actually matter, the proper timing of a skill could really determine whether you end the battle in victory or in defeat. Strategy actually matters!
Skills/Powers, there are a lot of them! Plus, you get to choose basically any of them you want! In the game, you basically purchase your skills and give them to the characters, each character being able to equip a certain number of skills.
Character Development, you are basically able to shape the characters however you want. Although the characters have a class that they are given initially, the terms of what these will become is vary vague, and up to your personal interpretation. Want a Ranger? Make one. Want a Paladin? Make one. Want Kirito from SAO? Make him!
Alright, that is enough pros I think except from some more minor things, so lets continue with the cons.
Cons-
If you don't like "RPG Maker Games" or their like, then you probably won't like this one either. But let me just say, this is not your "cheap made RPG maker game", this is a milestone for games like this and it should not even be remotely compared to some of the other RPG maker titles currently on Steam.
Combat, but didn't I have combat in pros? Well, I like the combat, but it seems like others do not like it so much. Like some turn based games, the combat may feel slow at points or feel repetative. This leads to the next point...
Grinding, expect to grind some if you want to level your characters. Although for the most part you can just do quests and keep the action moving, you will need to do some actual leveling in order to proceed. Personally I have nothing wrong with experience hunting, but I understand that others do not like this so much usually, so I thought I would point this out.
Conclusion-
Doom & Destiny is definitely a game that is worth the money, if not for the gameplay (which itself is amazing), then for the comical aspect of it. It is definitely a unique game like nothing else I have seen previous. You should definitely get this if you want to play a fun, casual game with lots of humor.
May your adventures be many and always end in reward!
-Donoknight, Founder of the Tabletop RPG Gamers League

This review is based on the original campaign Dead Man's Switch, I haven't played Dragonfall.
Pros: The setting is one of the coolest and most original ever - Tolkien-style elves, trolls, mages and such in a William Gibson-esque cyberpunk world. I love the art and music, it's very cool and atmospheric. I dig the turn-based battle system so it's possible to take your time and plan your moves. As a Kickstarter supporter, I wasn't let down...
Cons: ...except for one thing: if you don't have the right character build, you probably won't win the final boss fight. Even worse, there aren't enough side-quests available to grind to build your character before heading to the final confrontation. I wouldn't go so far to say the original campaign sucks but it's way too linear and lacks flexibility for alternate character play styles, especially the final fight. The boss battle is pure brute force with very little strategy involved. If you have a character that requires finesse, you will lose.
UPDATE: I finally went back and tried the boss fight again and won, after reading a few different strategies. I still stand by my initial critique; if you don't have just the right team, it's a slog.
The cool thing is, there are player-created campaigns and DLC, which is where a highly moddable game like this really shines. If you like RPGs and turned-based strategy, there's no reason not to get Shadowrun Returns.

I was a little disappointed with the overall game. One thing everybody seems to complain about is the physics and the overall demand to constantly move to build momentum in this game. I personally thought the physics were fun and easy to work with, and even if I lost all my momentum, I felt like I could still accomplish what I wanted to accomplish. This game had about as much replay value as the first two Max Payne games in the sense that once you get through the initial story mode, everything else is difficulty settings and time trials. What I didn't like was the story of the game. The setting was a PG-rated combination of Aeon Flux and those E*surance commercials with the pink haired spy chick (the cutscenes even had the same animation). It's every "parkour chick vs. the evil government faction" trope you've ever heard of, but with a safety net, almost to shelter the player too much. Aside from that, amazing graphics and pretty fun levels of jumping, running and disarming SWAT teams.

Shadowrun Returns: Dragonfall
The DLC of the original SR is a full campaign in the Anarchist state of Berlin. When a milk-run goes bad it's up to you to fill in the shows of your now dead partner as leader of a band of runners and by extension your district. With shadowy organisations, rogue AIs and even dragons veing for power, can you investigate your partners death and how it ties into events now lost in the past?
A more worthy sequel that definitely has a better feel than the original campaign, with a consistent crew of runners and some well expanded backstories to explore this feels more cohesive than "Deadmans Switch". My minor gripes is that it feels a little long in the tooth in places as opposed to DS witch felt rushed. My other gripe is that when the central dilema revolves around "I'm going to do something ghastly but short term to solve something long term" then at least having the option to agree should be given. Even if you get a "bad end" it should be an option.

I know that this game is some kind of a holy grail to some people. And yeah, sure, it's got a story. But that doesn't save it. It doesn't look bad, sure. But that doesn't help it that it just didn't age well...
This game is from a period where PC games where generally quite bad, and pretty much all AAA-titles were bad ports from consoles. And that's just really sad, cause this game does have some potential to become a classic. But it didn't use it, at least not on PC. It's got pretty much the clunkiest gameplay I've experienced in a long while. It tries to scare you, but it doesn't go anywhere with it, it just stays at boring attempts with no real consequence. It artificially bloats up playtime with tons of unskippable animations. Melee-fighting isn't great either, it's pretty much random whether or not you hit an enemy that's right up in your face. And then there's those stupid enemies, crawling up a wall being just invincible until they jump down.
No, this isn't a classic. This wasn't that great to begin with when I played it on Xbox, and it's just worse now on PC. Sadly.
You should definitely not spend 10 bucks on this, and you should really think about whether you can bear clunky, repetitive gameplay for a somewhat good story. I have a hard time doing just that.

"The canon ending to this game is the best ending in the Resident Evil series EVER."
This game exceeded my expectations. I didn't have much faith in the story mode and only bought the game for Raid mode. I can say in all honesty, this is arguably the best story since RE 4. Characters are interesting and Moira is a blast. And don't worry, these developer seem to be in touch and know what made Barry so great 20 years ago. He hasn't changed a bit and it's great. The episodes are paced fairly well, and if you're a fan of the RE series since the original then you will appreciate every reference that is made until the end. My goodness, the canon ending to this game is fantastic by the way. I won't spoil anything but I was left with a smile the whole day after I completed the story. The canon ending to this game is the best ending in the Resdient Evil series EVER.
Gameplay has imporved since the first Revelations which played alot like RE 4. Revelations 2 plays more towards RE 6, but with smoother controls and animations and the FOV is much better. The game is both playable on mouse and keyboard as well as a Pad. I personally use a pad for these types of games, but that is just preference. During the story mode, you're able to swtich between two characters at a time (Claire and Moira/Barry and Natalia) and this is a much welcome feature. No longer do you have to deal with the A.I. being dumb as you can quickly switch to them and help their situation if need be. The character swapping is a lot like Zero and it adds a dynamic to the gameplay other titles have been lacking since Zero. Gunplay is nice and responsive as you are able to crouch and shoot and we fianlly have a dodge feature that is easy to use to avoid enemies and attack with skill. All in all, gameplay is great.
In Raid mode, you'll be running around shooting enemies till they drop or defending your base crystals from on coming hordes. In many respects, Raid 2 is different from the original Raid. You still get random weapons, but you have to open chests to find them. You still level up, but each character has their own level. Raid mode is a ton of fun, just like the original and you could find yourself spending hours just playing Raid 2. My only complaints for Raid 2 is the unnecessary insertion of microtransactions and it's DLC model. DO NOT support the MC and DLC aspects of Raid 2. You will never need life crystals, just restart the mission and take the exp you earned before you dropped dead. You don't need to buy guns as you can earn them in game. The other thing to note is that Raid 2 uses a lot of RE 6 stages. I mean A LOT. You hardly see the game's title content in Raid 2 and thats a shame as the levels here are more interesting than RE 6 was. Besides those gripes, Raid is a blast.
Since RE 4, the music of past RE titles have been forgettable in my honest opinion. The music in 5 sounded very generic and 6 I can't even remember apart from the tracks they use in this game. That's not the case in the Revelations series. The first game had a great soundtrack and the second is no expection. In fact, I feel Revelations 2 exceeds the first. From Theme of Barry to Lost (Enhanced Ver) the music is beautiful and a lot of the score reminds me of Code Veronica which is great. My only gripe is Raid mode's selection which is very short on tracks and you will often here the same music over and over through out the missions including selections from RE 6. The sound effects of the game are improved from the first Revelations as well. Guns sound as they should with powerful pops and blasts. The voice acting is top notch and the new voice actress for Claire has won me over (I still miss you Alyson Court). Overall, Music and sound is great.
At launch and it's first month you could say this game was in beta. In fact, I'm convinced early adopters who purhcased the game as the episodes were coming out were beta testing the game. Performance was awful with framrate drops in both story mode and Raid. Characters would stutter like they just drank a mountain of 5 hour energy and slow downs would throw off your aim in crucial moments. Thankfully on it's retial launch week, March 18th, we got a performance patch shortly after and it fixed almost all the issues allowing me to write this review. Framrates have gone to awful to good with steady 60fps on all high and the stutter is all but gone. It was a night and day difference as I was an early adopter and it's a relief and a joy to play the game as it should be played. Performance was saved and it's good.
For being a budget title, Revelations 2 has far exceeded my expectations. The story mode is just fantastic and any RE fan will adore the many references through out. Barry is just as amazing as he was 20 years ago, and it's nice to see Capcom as well as the developers acknowledge what made him so great to begin with. Gameplay is nice, responsive and smooth and Raid 2 is overall a blast to explore. Music is fantastic with memorable tracks and performance has thankfully been fixed. If you enjoyed the first Revelations, you will more than enjoy Revelations 2. If you haven't played a RE title then this is a good game to get into. If you rage quit the series after 6 then I say welcome back as this is the game you're looking for. Overall, Revelations 2 and the Revelations series proves it's ground in the RE universe and I would dare to say it surpasses the main line from 5 and 6. For $24.99 (Complete Season) or $39.99 (Complete w/Extras) you can't go wrong and I highly recommend this title to fans and new commers alike. Hopefully after it's shaky launch, this game succeeds and we get a third entry. Here's hoping for Rebecca and Billy!

If you liked Portal and wanted to play something else like that you're in tough position. There's simply not many things like that. Then there's Antichamber. It can't really be compared to Portal as it's a completely different kind of game apart from being a first-person puzzle game, but if you enjoyed "thinking with portals" you should check it out.
First thing you see on the promotional materials and after starting the game is the incredibly simplistic and sterile art direction. Accompanied by subtle and fitting soundtrack, it sets the tone for the whole game and dramatically helps it being what it is. Antichamber simply wouldn't work with more realistic approach to graphics.
As for the game's mind-bending properties - they're there, but mostly in the first part of the game. New game mechanics introduced to the player along the way are not particularly special or interesting although not bad either - what's bad is their use. It comes down mostly to solving yet another puzzle embodied in the wall in order to open yet another door. It's rather disappointing and makes the game not use most of its potential.
Story-wise, there's literally nothing to guide you. Not a single word of explanation who you are, where are you, what are you trying to do etc. You have to think for yourself. And it works. I really liked how it's all very ambiguous yet not pretentious, and this approach fits the game perfectly. Plus the ending is very cool. It kind of saved the overall experience for me as I was getting more and more tired and disappointed in the middle section of the game.
In overall I really think this is a game worth playing. It has its flaws - mostly poor use of mechanics and repetitiveness at some points, which is a pretty major thing - but makes up for it in other aspects. There's not enough of games of this kind to miss this one.

A prime example of excellent atmosphere-making. The slow, heavy breathing, the variable heart rate, the occasional whispers, the voice of the ship's announcement system ("Entering zero gravity." "Entering vacuum."), the hum and beeps of holographic displays and HUD, the slow onset of suffocation in vacuum and the omnipresent ominous music and ambient sounds. All of those things and more (like the design of your enemies, the Necromorphs) are the engines of horror running this amazing sci-fi shooter. The game will put you to a test of your survival instincts, quick trigger finger, strong stomach and orientation in space by putting you in areas with zero gravity, where you can jump from wall to wall to reach your objective. The objectives are very variable and original as the story will walk you through all of Ishimura's decks, mainly in order to fix something (your vocation is ship systems engineering). Isaac, go there and fix that. Oh no. Something is blocking the path. You have to first clear that mass of undead crap in order to get there. You and your colleagues are communicating by holographic video transmissions and you are constantly being given directives while they sit tight in safety. It's better though, for the atmosphere, that you are alone all the time. The gameplay offers a nice variety of enemies and weapons for you to enjoy, but I found many weapons to be too weak without upgrading them and power nodes used for upgrading are few and far between. Graphically the game is very well-done standing the test of time. I recommend turning off the blurry in-game AA. In-game vsync caps the game at 30 FPS. Download a fix for the game's terrible mouse support. Play on Hard. While maintaining a nice difficulty level, the game showers you with resources and you can buy what you need in the Store. Pressing Continue game in Main Menu causes the game to set the difficulty to Normal.

Killing Floor 2 is both the same and different to Killing Floor. It shares most of the same enemies, it has an unusual array of characteres to choose from and the whole package is wrapped up nicely in a way that will help alot of players feel at home. Not too much has changed in that if you played the first game, you know what to do here.
The addition of sprinting and customization brings the game in line with most other shooters these days and the monetisation isn't handled too badly although it gets a little pricey if want more than a woodland camo or a beanie. At least this is potentially offset by an item drop system that gives you 1 item per day every day. This is all well and good unless you are unlucky enough to get repeated "crate" drops that require keys bought with real money to open. You CAN get some great drops, but WILL you? That is up to a bunch of random numbers and luck is not on everybodoies side.
But let's be honest, Killing Floor is about 2 things, killing and... er floors.  The killing is fantastic, the shooting is tight and fun with body parts and blood spraying everywhere. You will need decent aim though or you will be overrun. The floors are ok, but you won't be able to see them through the blood after a few rounds so not to worry.
All in all, it's a fun game and should be in every shooter fans library. Even better if you have a few friends to play with but online games with randoms aren't always bad, just choose a difficulty that suits your skill level or you will find yourself getting kicked, maybe before you even start to play

So, for the immature people that are going to scream "fanboy" or "dumbass" or the like, I can care less about what you say. For the people that actually have honest opinions and valid points, heres my overall summary of the game.
Pros:
* The parkour system, is not awful, infact its extremely well made. The animations are very nicely done, with only a few clipping issues and entertaining bugs. Which, depending on the person, may cause a negative or postive reaction.
* The combat feels much more interactive then dead island, and there is more control over it. Even with a one shot weapon, your stamina with every skill other then infinite, still prevents you from killing an entire crowd, and the repair system balances it nicely.
*The night system was decently well implemented, albeit with some balance issues in the late game it still feels rather well done.
Mixed Judgements:
The repair system is a great idea in theory, and later in the game it doesnt matter. I easily find better weapons then what Im using, they are terrifyingly common. Early on, weapons become pointless and fighting is less relevant, which is what the devs were going for. They give you high speed and parkour abilities, they want you to use them not walk down the road and beat every zombie you see to death like in Dead Island. This game is NOT dead island, its Dying Light. Judging it based upon its afiliation with techland and dead island is nine times out of ten, biased. The character system, which compared to its "Spiritual Predecessor" (I use the term very lightly) Dead island, is insanely improved. The ability to change what you look like, is great. However.. Peoples arguments about the clones and such are completely justified in the sense that there arent many clothing options and no actual -character- customization options.
Cons:
*Weapon balancing is a definate problem in this game, you can see it once you hit sector 0. You go from hitting the same zombie 3-4 times to one shotting 1-3 in one swing to the head. As I stated earlier, the combat is more interactive as a whole, but late-game it can still become pretty bull.
*Difficulty curve is way, and I mean wayyyyyy to easy to see. This is mainly because of weapons being unbalanced, but the zombies dont ever get stronger like they do in dead island. They simply... are there.. They dont get more numerous, or get more health. A difficulty setting is definetly needed using damage and health multipliers being preferred.
* The mod support. Or rather the lack thereof. A mod developer should be thanked and appreciated, mabye even learned from. Mods, in this day of pc gaming, are what make a game grow and develop even after the devs move onto other games. This is what keeps most games alive years after they have been forgotten. Preventing mods on your game is like telling your support team to ignore customer requests, its downright rediculous.
*The Optimization, nuff said.
With 30-60 or more FPS, easily a 7/10, mabye a 6/10 with lack of mod support.
With less then 30 FPS, and low frame tolerance, 3, mabye 4 if your generous out of 10.

Faerie Solitaire is an attempt to wrap a story around a game of solitaire where you attempt to "clear" the play field of all the cards. There are additional aspects like win money to buy upgrades, and collect creature eggs and ingredients to evolve them. However, the difficulty curve is uneven, and the various aspects never integrated into a cohesive experience.
Basic gameplay is solitaire, the kidn where you have a bunch of cards, only some were open (but the unopen ones may be face up so you can plan better). You have the remainder of the deck, and you have ONE open card. The objective to to match your open card with the open card on the deck that's one higher or one lower (color/suit is irrelevant) and attempt the clear the entire board before your deck runs out. You can achieve partial success by removing most of the cards (which fills up the purple power meter), and if you managed to clear the board you get "perfect" hand (and bonus reward)
You will also need achieve up to 3 objectives by end of 9 hands, which consists of a level. Each "stage" is composed of multiple hands, and there are 8 stages overall, resulting in a lot of solitaire play. Some additional complications, such as "frozen" or "thorn-locked" sections and timed goals makes things interesting, but this game is really for people who can play LOT of solitaire... of one kind only.
The story line and combat is not really integrated into the game itself, much like Puzzle Kingdom or Puzzle Quest. After all, this is solitaire, with no competition except against oneself. So somehow, while the story is fairly compelling, with a twist mid-game, the game doesn't quite "feel" much like going on a quest, but more like uncovering sections of a story book, doing some unrelated stuff to unlock the next chapter. And that really distracts from the game.
Furthermore, the game's difficulty curve is not even. The powerups that you can buy can affect the game greatly. There are a stage or two where you need to get THREE perfect hands out of nine hands total. That turned out to be VERY very hard without a certain powerup.
To add some "value" to the game the developers added "pet collecting", as you can find magical ingredients and occasional some magic creature eggs when you clear the board (i.e. get "perfect" hand) and if play with the baby creature enough hands, and have the right ingredients, you can "evolve" the creatures into "adult form". However, there seem to be no relation of the creatures to the story OR the game, so it felt as if it's tacked on to FORCE some completionists to replay the game to get all creatures and/or their adult forms.
There are some challenge levels not related to the adventure mode, but that's not much fun there.
As you win each hand you accumulate some monetary winnings that can be used to buy certain powerups, which gives you extra UNDO, peek at the next card in your deck, and so on. Those can be quite expensive but can make your late games easier, esp. the power to "zap" a card off the board. But again, the monetary value isn't integrated into the story much.
One very annoying aspect is sometimes there are timers, like "fill the purple power bar in 2 minutes", but there is no timer on screen that tells me when my 2 minutes is up!  (And there's an impossible achievement: get a perfect hand in under 1 minute)
All in all, Faerie Solitaire is an indie game that tried to marry a story to soltaire play, but didn't quite succeed, as the various elements sucha s pet, money, and story don't mesh.
The game ended on a cliffhanger, leaving it to the sequel. Let's hope the sequel is more... integrated than this first attempt. But NOT recommended, unless you REALLY love playing soltaire.

At face value this game seems like a clone of Hearthstone. If you tried Hearthstone you'll feel right at home with how the game works at it's core but with some distinct differences for the better.
- RNG element in cards is much more limited. In the cards i got from the starter packs i encountered maybe a single card that pulls something random from the deck.  Not a madhouse of RNG like Hearthstone is.
- It's systems although not overly complex, Hearthstone isn't complex either though. The evolve mechanic is really unique and feels quite "anime-like" in my opinion. You can choose to get a more powerful version of any card 2 or 3 times on each match.
Also when cards evolve have another VO and a new art. Which is very nice indeed.
- It is more "pretty" than Hearthstone. Artwork is top-notch for what it is, anime-styled artwork. There are more emotes to choose from to communicate through your hero, the cards are just so nice to look at.
- Foil cards are just very, very nice looking. I sincerely never bothered with foil cards. In HS i just converted them to spirit. In Shadowverse they just look, very nice.
- The game is very generous with it's rewards and the starter cards it gives you. I think it's like 40 packs plus boosters cost like 1 dollar each, getting Rupies doesn't seemed too hard either. I would say it's even more generous than Duelyst. And i believe Duelyst is quite generous.
And now some bad things:
-----------------------------------
From what i read, this is a port from an android app. It feels and looks like it quite a few times sadly and the interface is generally clunky and unusual compared to your standard PC game. Also there's game menus that prompt you to "Tap" here and there. Hopefully the UI will get ironed out if there's success for the PC platform.
You can't mix and max faction cards together. That's a pet peeve of mine, because i believe it really limits you to just try and create with a much more limited card number and strategy available.
As a sidenote if you enjoy japanese VOs more you can do it, there's a post in the Steam forum explaining how.
All in all it's a pretty, enjoyable game with simpler yet enjoyable mechanics, affordable for the free to play player and easy to learn, especially if you tried Hearthstone before.

Super Hexagon is a great idea for a game. Simple but challenging gameplay, fast-paced, and frustrating but fun. It does all of these things very well! There are a couple things that I did not like about the game though, which the majority of people will not find as bad as I do. They are as follows:
Upon a game over, a flash occurs. You WILL game over very frequently, and if you have blinking tics- like I do- these flashes will not be your friend. It is inconvenient enough to have to close your eyes while playing a video game, but with Super Hexagon, more than an eighth of a second can spell your doom. The flashing really sets off my eyes and adds a new level of personal frustration, but I know that is not the case for probably 98% of people, who don't have these tics. Secondly, I own a mac computer (yes I know, I catch a lot of heat for it, don't worry your job of shaming me has been done for you), and while I have a compatible Xbox 360 controller, the mac version of this game does not support the Xbox 360 controller. Contrary to what the product description may advertise, there is absolutley no controller compatibility for the mac. Those are my only two issues.
It is not the most enjoyable game on Steam for me to play, but I am recommending it anyway! Becuase what the game does, it does extremely well. It is fun, trippy, challenging, and it has great music. Just do not play it if you have anger issues or a fear of failure. If you can check those two of your list, make sure you can also check off blinking tics and a mac computer with Xbox 360 controller. Then you will have many fun hours of staring at moving colors, listening to EDM, and cursing loudly at your computer.

Resident Evil is back! There is plenty here to keep oldschool and newschool fans of the series entertained.
Campaign Mode has a traditional mix of story, puzzle, action and suspense.
Actions alter the way it plays out as you progress adding replay value without the chasing after Emblems and extras. SP are awarded for gathering gems and completing various tasks and performing well. Enabling you to power up on future playthroughs.
Raid Mode turns up the pace for the run and gun addicts. Progression awards unlocks and skills to power up characters as you level them up. Daily missions are available while connected to steam online. Online co op when added should be interesting but split screen is more than acceptable for the time being.
The control system works well and feels smoother than Revelations 1. New mechanics for campaign partner add strategy to the mix. Offline co op works especially well here.
The negatives are that rushing through raid mode before completing the campaign could potentially spoil later chapters. Also Capcom having difficulty with optimization on initial release has soured the experience. Thankfully patches have been implemented and they seem intent on keeping this up until everything is fixed.
The things that are  missing:
An online co op for campaign mode (Online co op for Raid due 31st March) I can understand the reluctance to supply a LAN option.
More customisable graphics and controls settings. If users could reduce particle count on effects themselves, and turn off filter options for things like film grain as a preference. Capcom wouldn't have to worry as much about fps drops on older PC systems.
Dual monitor support for PC! (If Capcom can supply this feature in future it will be amazing) the skewed black borders need to become an optional thing. Forcing local co op is fine as long as the option for separate screens becomes available.
8/10 (somewhere between 5-7/10 whilst suffering the fps drops, depending on severity)

Half-Life 2 is, to put it simply, one of the most masterful games ever created.
Now, if the New Tens (or later) is the first time you're playing, you'll probably think that it's a cliche storm.
However, quick history lesson for aspiring geeks: This game came out in 2004. A lot of first-person-shooters that share many tropes with HL2 came out after 2004.
Not to say those aren't good, too. I mean, I play CoD on occasion, but HL2 is the best FPS I've played yet.
If you want to play this first without the original, here's a quick backstory (spoilers ahoy!):
The player character, Gordon Freeman, was performing an experiment in the Black Mesa Research Facility that caused a "resonance cascade," causing aliens to start teleporting in from an alternate dimension. The only reason he didn't die is because he was wearing an "HEV" Suit. He hacks his way through the facility, aliens, and the military to get to the Lambda Complex, where he teleports to the alien homeworld Xen, where he kills the alien's leader: the Nihilanth. Then,  a mysterious figure known as the G-Man offers him a new job. Freeman accepts, and he is put in stastis.
He wakes up on a train, arriving in one "City 17". This is where Half-Life 2 begins.
Now, why don't you put down $10 (or less, if you get it on sale) for this slice of gaming history?
P.S. Also download the Half-Life 2: Update mod, which pretties up the game extensively.

Killing Floor 2 is an action-filled, blood and gore-fest co-op zombie shooter just like the original, Killing Floor. If you are a fan of the original, you will definitely love the sequel. The strategy and gameplay hasn't changed much but the sounds, animations and graphics to name a few have improved.
For those who aren't familar with Killing Floor and its style, the game is wave based surivial with 1-6 players (Upto 20+ players on modded servers/lobbies) fighting hordes of enemies made up of mutated humans and rampant experiments known as "Zeds" that are out to wipe you and your squad of players out, as you defeat more waves, the stronger the "Zeds" become, to counter this you MUST buy armour and better weapons, after a certain amount of waves based on game length chosen a boss "Zed" will spawn that you MUST defeat, the game ends in either a Victory with you defeating the boss or a Defeat with your entire squad getting killed at any point during a match.
Some Pros and Cons to this game are...
+Pros
+More perks as well as unique skills to them that you can choose (10 as of this review) compared to KF1 which had 7
+Improved graphics and animations
+Improved sounds and soundtrack
+BLOOD, GUTS AND GORE
+New and old characters
+Steam workshop
+New VS mode (PvP where players can be the "Zeds")
+Friendly community (unless you join a Hell on Earth server as a level 0 player or get salty over dying from teammates being unable to help because you ran away from them)
-Cons
-Still a bit of a grindfest with perks (roughly the same time to reach max level perk as KF1)
-Low level players joining higher difficulty servers (not a game problem, just a community/player problem)
-Major updates CAN be few and far
-ZEDconomy aka Micro Transactions (Personally I don't mind this since it doesn't affect gameplay as it's only cosmetics in the ZEDconomy, plus you can get the cosmetics randomly from finishing a match)
Overall Killing Floor 2 is a great game for a co-op shooter full of gore whether you play solo or with friends online, 8/10 would recommend!

I've been playing this game for some time on my mobile phone (not as much as Duelyst though), so don't mind the Steam hours.
This game plays like a HearthStone clone, but in Anime style and with a big gameplay twist. You can "evolve" cards mid battle to give that card a small stat boost and allow them to attack an enemy minion in the same turn you've summoned them. Some cards have an effect that gets activated when you evolve said card, adding a few more strategies which are not present in HearthStone.
The grind for cards is not much, generous even. When you start out, you gets tons of boosters to open. You get enough gold from daily challenges and the daily log-in bonusses to buy 1 pack each day, often you even get a daily challenges that rewards a card pack. You also get gold by playing the story missions of the various heroes, but also from achievements (some reward card packs too) and getting a higher rank in ranked MP.
There is also a gauntlet/arena mode which yields rewards, but you only play 5 matches each run. No matter how often you won or lose, but the rewards are getting higher the more you win in a run. There is also 1 major difference between Duelyst's Gauntlet/HearthStone's Arena and Shadowverse's Arena, in the former 2 you pick 1 card out of 3 shown cards before another 3 cards get drawn to choose from. In Shadowverse you're shown 2 pairs of cards to pick, you have to pick a pair. But sometimes it can happen that a good card is paired with a bad card. Which a pretty unique twist.
There are some things that could be improved on. For starters you can clearly see it's a mobile game. The textures of everything except the cards are ehhhh, and there is a big lack of Anti-Aliasing imo. There is a huge hero potrait on yourside of the field which could've been smaller.
Another thing I'm not too fond of is how the handle the balance between which player goes first and which goes second. Player2 may draw 2 cards from his deck in the first turn, has 1 evolve point more then player1 and also player2 may evolve a turn earlier then player1. So I'm kinda schratching the back of my head right now wether it's unfair or not, because it sometimes feels unfair.
Also there is this: I'm not sure wether it's because of the mobile screensize limitations or just a design choice for gameplay, but you can only have 5 cards on the field on the same time. Which can be annoying if you have 1 or more non-countdown amulets on the field.
I do recommend anyone who isn't bothered by the Anime style and in search of a good HearthStone like game, with a generous grind, to give this game a try.

Shadowrun Returns is a decent game.  Even though there's a graphical interface and pretty pictures, it's an old-school, turn-based, text driven game.  There's a lot of reading to do, but that's not a negative.  Instead, the writing is very nicely done and your brain fills in the details we normally get with fancier graphics and super-duper cutscenes and voice acting.  It's really nice.
There are several areas where the game falls down a bit:
- Pacing:  about halfway through the story you start wondering if this is the last scene or not.  The story implies an ending, but doesn't get to it for a while.
- Dialog choices:  adding more Charisma is supposed to open more dialog choices.  But, as far as I can see, there were only four or five places where those additional dialog choices existed.  Plus, I believe that there was only one type of extra dialog choice that was used more than once in the game.
- Inability to progress:  because the story goes from one area to the next with no ability to go back or do other things, you can get to a point where you're stuck.  Maybe you need more money to hire a team or buy stuff.  If you don't have it, you're SOL -- there's no way to go off to earn it and come back.
- Mission ambiguity:  when you're given a mission, you're told to buy a team to help you.  Yet, you don't know enough about the mission to know if it's purley physical or will involve decking.  So, you really don't know who to put on the team.  This is made a bit worse by the design choice of not assembling a permanent team that you develop and train.  With a permanant team, you could produce multi-talented people to cover all the gaps.
- No sharing:  you can't move items from one character to another.  This is especially troublesome with things like med kits and resuscitation kits.  I ran into many cases where the character carrying those resuscitation  kits died and I could neither transfer one out to another character before-hand or walk over to the corpse and take one out of his pack afterwards.
- Development tree:  some of the character developement tree doesn't seem to be of much use.  For instance, I played a Decker.  Theoretically, I should have focused on the Intelligence/Decking aspects of the tree.  Yet, Decking only happens in a few spots in the game.  Since the character you're playing is the single point of failure for the whole game (i.e., if he dies, the game is over -- whereas if a team mate dies, you can resuscitate him or carry on without), you're better off focusing on pure physicality and survivability and hiring the specialists as needed  (assuming you knew when they'd be needed).
Of course, I've got to temper that by saying that all of that stuff is based on the sole developer-provided scenario.  There's another one in the Dragonfall DLC available here and there are oodles available for free in the Workshop.  So, with the proper writing, those issues could go away.  So, the game, especially considering it's a framework for other stories, is decent.

There are very few games I can define my experience with as being my discrepancy of "fun", but the LEGO Video game franchise has never failed to deliver that to me. Meaning this game is no exception, it has met and well exceeded my expectations from a LEGO game and from a superhero game. It is well balanced but at the same time the characters feel very unique and powerful in their own respect. The game runs great on my PC, I havent had a single texture or hitbox error of the sort you would expect from a low budget PC port, if that is indeed what this is. The physics feel very solid if it were not for the controls being almost frantic, adding super power combo controls to the 4 buttons used in a normal LEGO Video game configuration. The LEGO pieces feel very realistic and have a very plastic weight to them as they would in their actual form, thats not to say that the models that are sold dont feel sold. As for the storyline and the length of the main missions, I believe they are ideal, 15 missions (If im not mistaken) each running about an hour if you really get into exploring the whole level. The story is as good as you would expect from a LEGO game if not a bit better, given that it has character voice actors (Who do lego models a lot of justice for having a voice). All plot lines are well paced and have more than a few catch yet subtle jokes and references, making it a more than enjoyable experience even with the narratives lighthearted tone.
In closing, The only thing to say more would be that this is the only review I have every felt necessary enough to post on steam, being a fan of the LEGO Video games and naturally scrutinous of squals, this is easly a 10/10 for the LEGO franchise.
Recommend to fans of LEGO, Superheros, and Video games in general.

A largely luck-based game, solitaire is an unusual game to think of for a game where they rate you on how many "perfect" games you can get, but that's exactly what they're doing.  They make it easier, at least in the early levels, but it's still by and large luck, and you'll occasionally get a board start with all the 4s in a row on the bottom, and all the 3s and 5s behind them so that it's flat impossible to play that hand.  Want to reset so you get a hand you can play? Too bad, you have to do a set of 9 hands in a levle, and resetting means losing all your cash and items and starting back from the beginning of the hand, meaning you wasted the last 8 minutes you were playing.  Like real solitaire, it's luck-based, but real solitaire just shrugs and lets you play again.  In Fairie Solitaire, it lets you know you're a failure for something beyond your control... other than just not playing the game.
Of course, even if you are a perfectionist, there's very little reason to want to go back.  There's an award for beating a hand in less than a minute, but a more reasonable pace is about 2 minutes a hand, and there are 9 hands a level, 5 levels a stage, and 8 stages... That is, 6 hours if you never have to repeat things... and you WILL have to repeat things.
Hands and levels are little different from one another.  They do have things like a "thorn patch", which is a line of cards that only opens up when you clear some other line of cards, or an "ice wall", which is a line of cards that only opens up... when you clear some other line of cards.  Basically, it's the same tricks over and over, but with a different icon for it. Get ready to grind, because they couldn't think of anything more to add to solitaire.  (Note that even the positive reviews here say that this game is EXTREMELY repetitive.)  Note that levels basically repeat the same placement patterns and hoops to jump through, just the exact order of cards is different, so expect repeating levels to get VERY old VERY fast.  In a supposedly 6 hour game, some of these people have 20 hours or more...
There's voice acting, but it's tied to the music volume for reasons I can't comprehend, and the music is far, FAR louder than the voice, so you have to crank it down to a whisper so the music doesn't deafen you.
There's a "pet system" but it's really just randomly getting things about 0.01% of the time when you clear a line, and then getting told you are "leveling up" this thing by just doing what you were doing, anyway.  Pets do nothing.  At all.  You can't even see them in the corner of the screen as you play.  They just require you select them to have them invisibly gain XP to invisibly grow up (after you give them resources that are also random drops) so that you check another box off on the way to completion.  Plus, there's a ton of them there, since, of course, if you're going to tack these things on just to extend gameplay, you might as well make them drop rarely, have a ton of them, no player control over what you get, and put out an achievement for it if you Gotta Catch 'Em All.
It's also bizzarely unoptimized, lagging on my computer and using up all the CPU it can get in spite of it being a rock-simple sprite-based game.
Also, if you look at the art and think you might want to play it just because you like fairies or something, keep in mind that they basically don't appear much.  Even the pets are things like robots instead of fairies, at least the ones I got, and most of the time, the fairies are just yellow glowy bits in a jar you get to release for nothing more than a "Thank you :D" at the end of a level.  99% of the game has no fairy onscreen, just cards.  They only appear in a few still images, all of which appear in the screenshot gallery, or between stages.
All told, it looks feels, and plays like the sort of game marketed to older women who don't play anything but casual games, and the amount of quality and effort that went into the game reflects the sort of mentality of someone with only enough skill or dedication to pull off something just barely excusible to ship to a less discriminating customer base if you just have a fairy theme in it.
I got it for $0.50 on a 95% off sale, which says a lot about the game, and I sold the cards for nearly enough to pay for itself, but it still wasn't all that great an experience...  Definitely only buy on sale when you have enough in your Steam Wallet to not even notice the money spent, if at all...

Antichamber is a minimalist 3D FPS puzzle platformer where you solve non-euclidean spatial puzzles using an evolving block gun which can place and remove blocks. Many of the puzzles are obscure, requiring a fair bit of thought to figure out what was going through the developer's mind, and some will present a challenge. There are also some collectible doodles that you can find by exploring everywhere. From the menu to the puzzles themselves, it's all done very simply and elegantly and it's very easy to pick-up and play. It's fun and gets moreso as you get more abilities, but it is best taken in chunks rather than all at once because of the nature of the game. There are a good number of puzzles and it will probably take at least a few hours on a first play.
The abnormal spatial organization of the game's world will lead to some surprises, but also a fair bit of getting lost and retracing your steps. The soundtrack is subdued and if there's a story, it wasn't apparent in my playthrough - It would have been nice to have a reason for the puzzles rather than just for the sake of puzzles.

Grand Theft Auto: Vice City remains, and most probably always will, the best game of the series (in my view). There's a remote controlled helicopter mission in particular that is possibly even as famous as the game itself, and will have even the most level headed gamer contemplate homicide.
The soundtrack is a major draw card if you are of an age (that means older than 20) and plays a integral role in creating the feel of the era in which the game is set, Tommy Vercetti is an enjoyable role to take on and is easy to identify with, and the missions range from simple to only moderately difficult.
It has more similarity with Grand Theft Auto 3 than it does Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas (the two games in the series released directly before and after); with a more detailed protagonist it feels more like an RPG than did GTA3 but while it lacks the extensive customisation that San Andreas offered, because it doesn't have this, you don't feel that the story and the missions are being pushed aside so you can spend a few in-game days strengthening your biceps.
I'd easily give this 8/10 and absolutely recommend it to any Grand Theft Auto fan that hasn't experienced it yet.

Dying Light is the best new zombie game I have played to date. If you love Dead Island (and Riptide) you will love this latest iteration.
Some key points which make this a strong recommendation to buy this game after 30+ hours of play:
1. The open world design of the city. As you progress and gain abilities you have new ways of traversing the city. The logical way this is unlocked is very well designed.
2. You are not forced to follow the main storyline all the time. There are plenty of random events that pop up that lead to new objectives. Missions hubs open up as you help survivors in the city.
3. An excellent variety of weapons and skills to play with that leads to creative and fun ways to kill the infected (and enemy humans). As you level new weapon drops are revealed with high levels. Completing events also unlock new purchasable weapons from quartermasters.
4. The crafting system is easy to understand while still offering some variety of weapon effect choices. Unlike other games I do not find crafting annoying and the plentiful loot drops make it easy to constantly craft new weapons and upgrades.
5. Yes many (if not all) of the game mechanics in Dying Light have been copied from other games but the way they work so well together in Dying Light makes the game pure fun to play.
6. The performance of this game on my system has been better than I expected. The graphics are very detailed yet run smoothly on my GTX780 and 4770K. Framerate averages between 40 to 80 fps at 1920x1080 resolution depending on the action. At no stage was it unplayable for me.
7. The co-op mode is great fun and works seemlessly within the campaign. There is a teleport function to immediately travel to your friends location. The co-op mode not only features objective sharing but you can also compete in optional challenge modes for extra rewards.
8. I have no negatives for this game. If I was nitpicking all I would ask for is more detailed graphics options to fine tune the framerate. The game has never crashed once on my system after 30 hours of play.

You'll find that being the hunter, especially at early levels, is excruciating. There is a leveling system, and it's nearly impossible to win until you've at least unlocked a few of your skills. Otherwise,
will be hunted down and killed by survivors that know what they're doing. It won't feel balanced.
Joining a game on its own is frustrating as you'll constantly find yourself unable to connect or dropped before the round starts. And this because hunters are frequently attempting to invade the same instance. Most of the time you'll be overrided by another hunter joining the same game. Other times, the player will simply drop out because they don't want to play that mode. And as a survivor, leaving the option for invasions on is a disaster. I wasn't expecting all that much from this game, but in the end i was pleasantly surprised by it.
The base game provides you with the story 'Dead Man's Switch' to play through and it exists as a piece of content, inviting modders to create their own stories in a similar manner.
Given the way the game has been constructed and given the game's origin through kickstarter to create something specfic for its fans, its worth approaching this game for what it is, accepting its rough edges and lack of development of many aspects and focusing on what the developers put their time and obvious enthusiasm into.
So for instance.  If you skip through the dialogue, you're doing it wrong...  Its generally well written, there's great characterisation and although often all paths often lead to the same place, there are options to pick from and ways to roleplay your character.
If you're expecting the turn based combat to be on par with say, Baldurs Gate, Xcom EU etc...then don't.  Its not.  Its basic at best.  Guns are just superior to magic, cyber mods didn't seem necessary and the combat was often just a game of rng for whether you miss or not.   Fortunately it isn't too difficult either so for me i was just playing through it to get to the next plot point, rather than playing it as the focus of the game.
Cyberpunk.  Yes... this game scratches all those itches if you love the genre.  Running the shadows...bad deals going down.... brilliantly gauche 'slang'  (thats so drek, chummer), physically going into the interwebs like we all throught was the future way back when... And the music... The music may actually be the best thing about this game.   The music provides all of the atmosphere, all the cyberpunk feels, the heightened excitement in combat... Its memorable, its what you'd expect for the genre and it almost single handedly makes the game.
The main campaign takes about 10-12 hours.  Its not the most original story but it is written by people who obviously love the genre.
There's lots of easy targets to nitpick about the game, the animations are terrible, the pre-fabbed backgrounds actually seem to make the limited points of interactability that much more obvious.  The bad UI... (looks like this has been fixed in the new standalone Dragonfall).
But if you can get past that, and you love the cyberpunk setting, a good pulpy story and turn based combat (i.e thinking combat rather than twitchy combat)  Then you'll get a good amount of enjoyment from Shadowrun Returns, especially now it you'll likely be able to pick it up pretty cheap on a sale somewhere.

This review is changed from NOT RECOMMENDED to RECOMMENDED as of March 19!
Thanks to the performance patch, the game now finally functions as intended.
Excellent story with interesting character cast with plenty of familiar faces and some newcomers.
Revelations 2 deliver a solid gameplay by focusing on the survival aspect of the series while putting a heavy emphasis on utilizing every character's ability in order to survive. The controls are fluid, the asymetric team gameplay is enjoyable, while the dodging mechanics from the previous Revelations is vastly improved!
If you are fan of the older Resident Evil games and disillusioned by the recent entries in the series, Revelations 2 might just change your opinion and give you some hope for the future of the Resident Evil franchise!
The story is pretty good, and unlike Revelations 1 it actually leads somewhere. With a terrible pun, you could say there's a revelation actually. The events of Revelations 2 take place on an unnamed island where Claire and Moira are kidnapped and exposed to horrific experiments by an unknown antagonist, while months later Barry finally locates the island and begins his search for his missing duo, accompanied by a mysterious girl named Natalia.  The idea of retracing the events of the past is kind of unique, and the plot twists at the end of each episode manage to keep up interest to the very end. The new character cast is interesting and enjoyable, especially Natalia. Even Moira is likeable despite her terribly written lines. However the highlight of the story for me was the interaction between Barry and Natalia.

Since we are talking about a survival horror game the first thing I should start with is the atmosphere. The game isn't scary at all and there aren't many jump scares either. But is that a bad thing? Well if you want a game that scares the living hell out of you then probably this isn’t the one you should get, however despite that, it's a very atmospheric game, with plenty of details. Each chapter during Claire's segment of the episode you walk through a set location, while playing Barry’s portion of the episode you revisit them. It might sounds kind of lame, that Capcom just recycle the same locations, but it actually works pretty well. All locations go through major changes due to the 6 months difference between the story of Claire and Barry: some routes are blocked away, some paths are opened up. They are the same locations yet they feel and play quite different. The enemy line-up is also different, however there's one small detail I really liked: in Claire's campaign the enemies are lively, mutated humans but in Barry's campaign those same enemies are rotting corpses since several months have passed. It is indeed a small detail but it was a nice addition for the atmosphere.
The research notes and survivor letters scattered throughout the game also shed some light on the events of the story.
The focus of the game is survival (unlike recent RE entries) as the supplies are limited and your characters are quite vulnerable. The game doesn’t have many enemies, however they are very well placed, and hit pretty hard. There’s a heavy emphasis on utilizing every character’s abilities in order to progress: Claire and Barry are the weapons experts, while Moira and Natalia play as support, helping you open up otherwise unreachable paths, locating hidden items and stun enemies. It is basicly asymmetric team gameplay done right. The AI is certainly not the best, however the support characters have regenerating health, so you don’t really need to worry about them. They can mess up terribly sometimes, by not following orders, but it doesn’t happen often!
Puzzle elements return, but they are mostly rather simple ones and there’s plenty of fetch-styled puzzles as well. They are not too bad, but some of them were just awkward and out of place.
Overall the gameplay offers solid gunplay and smart team management mechanics allowing you to switch between characters. The controls from the previous Revelations are improved and the revamped evade mechanics works perfect!

Despite he game is supposedly a budget release, I would say it is quite decent. The graphics are certainly not the best, but the game looks nice enough (minus the film grain effect, which can be rather annoying in dark indoor areas) and the lighting effects are particularly well done.
Where the smaller budget shows however is how the animations were done, there are plenty of clipping, and some of the animations look sloppily executed. (Enemies spawning in front of you and the hitboxes are pretty inaccurate: you get grabbed even though the enemy attack animation isn't finished just to name a few of the problems)
Music was enjoyable, though aside from two tracks (escape theme and EP3 boss fight), I wouldn't say the soundtrack was memorable.
As for the voice acting, it was good. Many expressed their disappointment that Alyson Court didn’t return as Claire, but I must say the new actress was doing well, aside some oddly delivered lines. Barry’s and Natalia’s voice actors were great and the interaction between them felt natural. The weakest voice was probably Moira’s but I blame it on her horribly written lines. Every time she spoke it just felt….wrong.
The length of the game is fairly short, so with an average pace you can finish the story on your first playthrough in about 8 hours. Despite the main campaign being short there's plenty of replay value thanks to Countdown and Invisible modes. Both are challenging in their own way. There are plenty of unlockables ranging from Secret files which add more depth to story, secret weapons (such as the Chicago Typewritter, a katana and even silly ones like the Bubble gun, just to name a few) and the usual figurines and concept art. Also good news for those who were missing Claire's biker suit and Barry's STARS outfit that they can be unlocked as well for finishing the story under certain conditions!
The initial release was a horrible mess, but as of March 19. Capcom adressed most of the performance issues, such as framerate drops, stutterings and crashes for both story and raid mode.
- Interesting story
- Excellent atmosphere focusing on building tension rather than mindless action
- Gameplay finally resembles old school Survival horror
- Solid team-management mechanics, which also add a new layer to environment puzzles

- High replay value thanks to several extra modes for the main campaign and Raid mode.
- Cheesy one-liners and references to Resident Evil 1's Barry moments
- Animations could have used more polishing.
- Lots of pixel clipping.
- The annoying mouse shaking QTE is back!
- Short campaign

+More perks as well as unique skills to them that you can choose (10 as of this review) compared to KF1 which had 7
+Improved graphics and animations
+Improved sounds and soundtrack
+BLOOD, GUTS AND GORE
+New and old characters
+Steam workshop
+New VS mode (PvP where players can be the "Zeds")
+Friendly community (unless you join a Hell on Earth server as a level 0 player or get salty over dying from teammates being unable to help because you ran away from them)
-Cons
-Still a bit of a grindfest with perks (roughly the same time to reach max level perk as KF1)
-Low level players joining higher difficulty servers (not a game problem, just a community/player problem)
-Major updates CAN be few and far
-ZEDconomy aka Micro Transactions (Personally I don't mind this since it doesn't affect gameplay as it's only cosmetics in the ZEDconomy, plus you can get the cosmetics randomly from finishing a match)
Overall Killing Floor 2 is a great game for a co-op shooter full of gore whether you play solo or with friends online, 8/10 would recommend!

Antichamber is one of those games where you can sit down, aiming to complete it within the set 01:30:00, and get up after that time having only run around aimlessly with no knowledge of where to go or what to do next. You will leave the game dazed and confused. It's brutal; it plays with your head, and it does things no puzzle game ought to do.
I can't recommend it on the basis of consistent playability; I've played a mere three hours, and they're on-and-off as I occasionally fire up the game in order to lose myself a bit more. I've also never completed the game, or felt I've ever been close to doing so. What I can recommed it for, is the way it makes you rethink the situation at hand; the way it forces you to think outside the box; the way it pushes you into the unknown and is then quite happy to string you up like a puppet and watch you repeat the same futile exercises over and over, hoping something will change, hoping that you will find another room in which it can mess with your head a little more.

Dying Light is the best new zombie game I have played to date. If you love Dead Island (and Riptide) you will love this latest iteration.
Some key points which make this a strong recommendation to buy this game after 30+ hours of play:
1. The open world design of the city. As you progress and gain abilities you have new ways of traversing the city. The logical way this is unlocked is very well designed.
2. You are not forced to follow the main storyline all the time. There are plenty of random events that pop up that lead to new objectives. Missions hubs open up as you help survivors in the city.
3. An excellent variety of weapons and skills to play with that leads to creative and fun ways to kill the infected (and enemy humans). As you level new weapon drops are revealed with high levels. Completing events also unlock new purchasable weapons from quartermasters.
4. The crafting system is easy to understand while still offering some variety of weapon effect choices. Unlike other games I do not find crafting annoying and the plentiful loot drops make it easy to constantly craft new weapons and upgrades.
5. Yes many (if not all) of the game mechanics in Dying Light have been copied from other games but the way they work so well together in Dying Light makes the game pure fun to play.
6. The performance of this game on my system has been better than I expected. The graphics are very detailed yet run smoothly on my GTX780 and 4770K. Framerate averages between 40 to 80 fps at 1920x1080 resolution depending on the action. At no stage was it unplayable for me.
7. The co-op mode is great fun and works seemlessly within the campaign. There is a teleport function to immediately travel to your friends location. The co-op mode not only features objective sharing but you can also compete in optional challenge modes for extra rewards.
8. I have no negatives for this game. If I was nitpicking all I would ask for is more detailed graphics options to fine tune the framerate. The game has never crashed once on my system after 30 hours of play.
