Since everyone is comparing it to Hearthstone anyway, lets run the list:
PROS
+ Toned-down RNG. Most RNG cards can be manipulated, which is the right way to do RNG (for instance: if a card deals 1 damage to a random enemy follower, you can manipulate the board to get the hit you want, unlike Hearthstone, where you can always hit face and lose the game).
+ Evolve system is this game's Coin, but unlike Coin it's a full mechanic with depth, strategy and it will happen at least five times a game.
+ Somehow the cards feel more balanced than Hearthstone - a couple of Japanese guys beat a multi-million company in design? (for instance: most early-game cards are weaker because of how much tempo they can generate)
+ The monetization. I'm playing this game for two days and I think I already have most of the cards I need for my two decks. You get Gold and Pack Tickets for almost everything. You have challenges that give you Gold.
+ Animated (Golden) cards cannot be crafted, so it still makes sense to buy packs.
+ Anime boobs everywhere.
CONS
- The UI could use a bit of work, it's not as responsive as Hearthstone.
- The PC UI is a straight-up lift from the phone version. It's not terrible, but sometimes it shows.
- Take-Two, this game's version of limited/Arena isn't that great, it my opinion. But it's price structure is a lot better than Hearthstone. There's also space on the UI for other versions of Arena.
In short - RIP Hearthstone, unless they manage to screw this one up, somehow. DON'T SCREW THIS ONE UP

Techland really improved on all the elements from Dead Island from crafting to combat. The parkour is smooth and satisfying. Yes, it did remind me of Mirror's Edge. It's a nice experience running past crowds of zombies and jumping across rooftops especially at night. Playing through the campaign either solo or cooperatively just works. The added coop challenges were a good idea. You should get it once you and perhaps a friend find a price that's within your budget. Sitting at 24 hours, and I still haven't finished the main campaign. I am personally hoping they add more content in the near future.
You'll find that being the hunter, especially at early levels, is excruciating. There is a leveling system, and it's nearly impossible to win until you've at least unlocked a few of your skills. Otherwise,
will be hunted down and killed by survivors that know what they're doing. It won't feel balanced.
Joining a game on its own is frustrating as you'll constantly find yourself unable to connect or dropped before the round starts. And this because hunters are frequently attempting to invade the same instance. Most of the time you'll be overrided by another hunter joining the same game. Other times, the player will simply drop out because they don't want to play that mode. And as a survivor, leaving the option for invasions on is a disaster. As soon as there's a chance, you will get invaded. And it'll happen over and over until you turn it off. I imagine that's not what the developers had in mind, but at the moment the zombie mode is oversaturated while most players are content to play the game sans invasions.
Despite these issues with Be The Zombie, once you find a game after gaining some experience, it's pretty challenging for either side, and it's quite fun if you're looking to play it.

First off I'm not a fan of turn-based games but XCOM really blew my mind.
The gameplay is just so well made with it's cover system, the weapons and what damage they do to the environment and how you feel connected to your soldiers.
As each soldier has their own nationality, facial features and names (facial features and names can be changed) it makes every single one stand out and sometimes you'll do anything to keep them alive. There's also an option that prevents you to save during missions which will make you think twice about what move you're going to make as every single mistake can change everything during a mission.
There's 5 classes (6 in enemy within) all with their own very important roles. Each time they level you get to choose a perk in their skill tree, normally each class has their set perks to choose from but there's an option that makes the perks random so you could end up with a soldier that has a perfect set of perks from different classes.
XCOM also offers the ability to build up your own base, do research and create items and weapons and it's more or less up to you in what order you want to do things.
The Enemy Within expansion gives you a new class, a heavy cyborg/mech kind of class aswell as implants for regular soldiers that will boost them quite alot.
The missions in The Enemy Within are the same as in Enemy Unknown so if you think you'll only be playing the game once I would really recommend getting the expansion right away as it offers alot more options to your playthrough.
Even if you're normally not a turn-based gamer I would recommend trying this game, you won't be disappointed.

Shadowrun Returns (Dead Man's Switch) has some of the best writing of any game I've played this year, but the early going can be somewhat frustrating as SR unfortunately plays its cards close to its chest before opening up the world. After an extended prologue, though, the game blossoms into a story that pulls from classic noir fiction like Raymond Chandler's Marlowe stories and Polanski's Chinatown coupled with the richly detailed background fiction of the Shadowrun universe. "Cyberpunk and magic" is a concept that should, by all accounts, collapse into utter silliness, but somehow SR manages to keep finding interesting (and sometimes amusing) twists on both of these themes.
While the art style is clean and the interface generally functional (inventory management is a sore spot), be aware that this is a game that really only gives as much as you're willing to bring to it -- there are no 3D environments, voiced dialog, or cut scenes, but the game manages to be immersive in the same way that dreamily browsing through a gamebook and conjuring adventures can be. Some reviews have faulted the plot for being overly linear, and while I always appreciate more player agency, it really wasn't an issue for me here.
My main complaint is the way the game paces itself in doling out the fun skills and cool toys. Early on it's hard to understand why I'd want to invest in particular skill sets when there's little explanation of how they function or game scenarios that take advantage of them. It's not until the midpoint of the game that distinctive SR features like rigs, decks, and chroming really even come into play which makes it frustrating to define your character without knowing what kind of build you're even shooting for. While I have no problem holding back some surprises, I would have rather seen the advanced stuff up on the shelf early on so I had a better idea of what I could aspire to be. In the worst case, you can never go wrong with shooting something with a gun or throwing a fireball at it, though a lot of the fun in SR comes from mixing and matching all the different combinations available.
But the story and characters are well drawn, the dialog full of personality, and once events pick up steam I felt compelled to chase down the conclusion. By the end I'd developed a lot of affection for both my character and the friends she'd made along the way; I was sorry to see them go (and that there are currently no plans to continue their story) but based on the strength of this initial foray I'll definitely be checking out the sequel, Dragonfall. Definitely recommended.

A respectable update to Civ IV.
$8.24 (Steam Sale)
I was quite late to the scene with this game. Civ V had already been out for a while, yet I was looking for a modernized experience to that I had in Civ IV. Both are great games, but certainly Civ V does have its shortcomings.
Right off the bat it’s easy to tell the graphics have been updated. While you won’t need some crazy system like mine to play with detail, the upgrades in textures and fidelity is appreciated.
Beyond the graphics department, we can see it has native touch support in Windows 8 and above. I don’t have Win 8, but I did have a chance to play with Nvidia’s 3D Vision. The game looks great in Stereoscopic 3D, but it’s not must see experience (Unlike Mass Effect 2/3 with Helix Mod).
Gameplay has been tuned towards the more serious Civ fans. Hexagon tiles are now used, which prevents "cheating" by gaining additional distance by moving units diagonally in Civ IV. With certain elements however, I find myself turning them off each new gameplay, such as minor factions. While certain “civ buffs” like them, I know I can’t overly criticize them without receiving major downvotes.
Overall, if you have a good few solid hours (5+) you will find yourself enjoying this title, and the workshop support it brings to the table. This would be one of the few games I’d play in a LAN party, as taking turns in multiplayer games has always had issues (especially against Civ fanatics).

EDIT: I have played this game on PS4 for 20+ hours prior to this review.
Dying Light is a breath of fresh air, in this landfill of games that copy one another. If you enjoyed the likes of Dead Island, or similar games, you will be right at home with this game, but be wary, there are major differences between the two. The parkour mechanics are very reminiscent of EA's 2008 cult classic, Mirror's Edge.
The combat system can be clunky at times, and it is easy to get flustered especially in the early hours of the game; Upgrading weapons is highly recomended if you plan to survive in the late game.
Now to talk about what makes this game special. The day and night cycle.
During the day, the zombies are your adverage infected that you have seen before, plus a few special infected types.
Night time is when things get interesting. A new, fast, and very powerful infected type come out during the dark. Best bet is to always have flares and firecrackers.
In conclusion, this game does have a few bugs, but they aren't substantial enough to cause a drop in score.
Final verdict: 9/10.

First off I'm not a fan of turn-based games but XCOM really blew my mind.
The gameplay is just so well made with it's cover system, the weapons and what damage they do to the environment and how you feel connected to your soldiers.
As each soldier has their own nationality, facial features and names (facial features and names can be changed) it makes every single one stand out and sometimes you'll do anything to keep them alive. There's also an option that prevents you to save during missions which will make you think twice about what move you're going to make as every single mistake can change everything during a mission.
There's 5 classes (6 in enemy within) all with their own very important roles. Each time they level you get to choose a perk in their skill tree, normally each class has their set perks to choose from but there's an option that makes the perks random so you could end up with a soldier that has a perfect set of perks from different classes.
XCOM also offers the ability to build up your own base, do research and create items and weapons and it's more or less up to you in what order you want to do things.
The Enemy Within expansion gives you a new class, a heavy cyborg/mech kind of class aswell as implants for regular soldiers that will boost them quite alot.
The missions in The Enemy Within are the same as in Enemy Unknown so if you think you'll only be playing the game once I would really recommend getting the expansion right away as it offers alot more options to your playthrough.
Even if you're normally not a turn-based gamer I would recommend trying this game, you won't be disappointed.

I've been a big fan of south park my whole life. When i first learned that this game was coming out i was estatic. I even preordered it - something I never do.  However when I was done with the game (14.4 hours later) I felt let down. I'll lay it out in positives and negatives:
Positives:
-Looks incredible - just like the show. Visual experience is amazing
-Pretty much every south park character you could ever want makes an appearance.
-Embodies the spirit of the show very well.
Negatives:
-This is my main gripe - very little fresh content. By this I mean most of the jokes and characters are just a simple rehash of certain episodes. If you've watched a lot of south park over the years then you've already heard 90% of the jokes. Many of the scenes in the game are borrowed from episodes. I was expecting a lot more new content. If i want to watch an old episode of south park then I'll go watch an old episode of south park.
-This game is easy. So ♥♥♥♥ing easy. Jesus Christ. I rarely felt challenged throughout the entire game. The 2nd half of the game was a joke.
-This game is short. 14.4 hours was more than enough to beat the game. I also did every side quest I could and found most of the items. This brings me to my next point.
-Zero replay value. I mean i didn't expect much but damn all the side quests are pretty short and there is very little incentive to collect everything. The last boss is so easy already it's not worth getting the top tier gear (not like it's very hard anyways)

A Return, indeed.
Shadowrun, for those not in the know, was an 80s/90s tabletop RPG that functioned similarly to Dungeons and Dragons. Except, your setting was a dystopian, cyberpunk and futuristic atmosphere. Always set sometime in the 2050s and much later.
The series would see some video game releases during the 90s, finding titles on the SNES, Genesis and Mega CD. Players back then were torn between the SNES/Genesis versions as they both had strong representations but also a few things lacking. However, it was the SNES version that seemed to have been favored out of them all. It wouldn't be until the mid 2000s that we got another Shadowrun release, on the X-Box 360 console. Gone were the RPG aspect of what makes Shadowrun and in came this FPS hybrid that didn't really catch on to those familiar with the lore. Thanks to that release, it kinda gave the series a bit of a genre identity crisis and an uncertain future that might've been doomed of seeing anymore entries.
Until this game came.
2013 saw this game developed by Harebrained Schemes and come to Steam. This is what you would call a proper return to form.
Shadowrun Returns highlights and shows what it's all about and what it's supposed to be:
- A rich story. You have to start somewhere and Shadowrun has a lore in which there can be a story for anyone and it can go for as long as the imagination and writing allows.
- Turn Based RPG. The core of Shadowrun is intact here in this game. Sadly though, you are subjected to the RNG gods who may favor or work against you on all odds in your journey.
- Style. Everything about Shadowrun is captured here and it's wonderfully projected thanks to the isometric view the game has. While isometric doesn't give you a good picture of everything, it's good enough to give you an idea. It does a fair job of showing you the cyberpunk future that surrounds you.
- Music. That lovely techno bumping music and electronic ambience that can be heard in this game. It helps move along the mood nicely when you're knee deep into the story or the combat of the game.
All of these perks alone help bring Shadowrun back to it's elements that seemed to have long been forgotten.
I will say that the campaign this game comes with could've been more explored, but for what it has going for it, it'll keep you busy for a few hours. It's nice to have that Workshop support since it'll encourage people to make more campaigns and add things to this game to help spice it up a little.
I do love some of the nods this game also provides. The more bigger nod to me is having Jake Armitage in the game as a cameo. If you didn't know, he's the protaganist in the SNES Shadowrun game many, many years ago.
I don't have a lot gripes against this game because it can be shrugged off with the sheer appreciation I have towards this title. For finally having brought a seemingly dead series back to life in the modern times and continue that momentum with a couple more releases along the way with Dragonfall and Hong Kong.
Recommended. Now go run in the shadows, chummer.

Shadowrun returns, isn't a bad game, but it isn't very good either.  Based off an earlier edition of the rules so you still have good ol cyberdecks and physical connections, you build your own runner and go through an extremely linear campaign.  The dialogue isn't bad, and it's nice not being tied down to player alighnments or some sort of morality system which makes it refershing when it comes to most wrpgs these days.
Building characters, either due to the lack of depth in character abilites and equipment in the game or because of the system, tends to be very straightfoward, there are good spells, and then there are useless spells, (slow, silence), class balance seems to be all over the place, Riggers have been near garbage from what I've seen, since part of why they were important in the tabletop (being able to drive and fly everything) is gone.  Deckers rely entirely on if there's anything to even hack, and about 70% of the time there isn't. Adepts seem to be garbage, since they'll have worse hitrates in melee compared to a samurai shooting across the stage.
The game offers 'Etiquettes' or different kind of social groups your shadowrunner can be familiar with, and honestly I'm pretty sure some of them only showed up once or twice in the entire game. Dialogue, while there's a decent amount and each choice tends to give you a different blurb, doesn't really effect much. There's only one area in the entire game that allowes multiple approaches. You can't plan out your own runs, the stages are linear as ever, and you have no set team,  which I'm told is fixed in the expansion.
Another gripe with the game is that once you're in a combat area you can never leave combat mode until all the enemies are defeated, reguardless if none are visible or attacking your characters, this makes it extremely tiresome if you're moving your group just trying to explore the area, or even prepare people for the next encounter.
The final stage of the campaign isn't exiciting or thrilling, it's a slow, boring trek through tunnels.
The campaign isn't BAD, but it's so uninspiring, and overall the game feels more like a construction set than an actual game.
The music is okay, it's no Deus Ex or ghost in the shell.
At least people can finally forget the awful shadowrun console shooter now.

A horror game in all its glory. From the tight claustrophobic elevators, to the gargantuan rooms filled with corpses, the game manages to impress through sheer fear. The weapons give out a sense of relief, every time you see the full clip, making you think "I`ll make it...I`ll survive through this level" Although managing their upgrades is a top priority because the bigger and meaner monsters throughout the game.
The enemies are quite repetitive at some point and at one point the sheer amount of them makes you pull your hair out, especially with the indestructible one that keeps regenerating.
The story lacks perspective and it could be a bit better if the game wouldn`t focus so much on you doing your allie`s chores. "Go do this", "Repair that", "Kill that giant space thing". It easily gets frustrating at times seeing your comrades just sitting there, waiting for you to finish a task just to send you on another one. I often find myself questioning why i was in a specific location and why the main protagonist was even on the ship. There should have been a bigger emphasis on his love interest (that being the reason why he`s even doing this).
Through the game`s ending I would rapidly go from room to room, killing enemies and doing the puzzles just to be expected to do it all over again after i switch stations and chapters.
The game`s main focus "fear" is it`s best asset. tight rooms, scary sounds, corpses lying arround, they all make for an excelent horror game. The blood on the walls amongst the weird messages and alien writing offer a unique atmosphere to the game. Not only does it make you question what happened in that room before you came, but it gives a sense of history to the place.
The mechanics of the game show it`s true age. Slow movement, hard to control, weapons function very slow as well. Although a decent, fun and playable game, I found myself many times getting annoyed by how close up the camera was to the main protagonist`s back, making me miss my target. Speaking of target, the aim seemed to be a bit clunky. I do recommend that the game be played with a controller as it gives immersion and also offers better aiming compared to a mouse.
All in all, taking for account the game`s age and how well it passed the test of time, I strongly recommend it. A fun and at the same time scary third person shooter that manages to hold your attention, althought it can be rough at times.

3rd person, action, shooter, bio weapon post-apocalypse, inventory management, survival game. It's little bit of those things. Basically it's a story driven game focused on single player, similar to Resident Evil: Revelations, though this time around you're on an island instead of a ship.
It's episodic rather than full day one release (at least if you bought it at launch, you was only able to play one episode, and wait week between the next episodes). I found that frustrating, because I like to play games in couple days, and not sit idle for month to actually be done with it. But that aside, if you get it now, when everything is released it's all good right, well not really. Game still suffer from bad optimization, no multiplayer Raid co-op, even though Capcom confirmed they screwed up with store page information and misled a lot of people.
Gameplay wise game is similar to it's predecessor, yet lacks same kind of polish. You go through fenced levels, complete puzzles by finding right set of levers and doors, pick up ammo, weapons, upgrade parts on the way, visit occasional bench for modification, basically same. Yet this time around, you have ability to switch between characters, as you tend to run in constant duo team. Need to open specific door? = switch to other character; need to find hidden loot? = switch to character with flashlight (their new finding secret loot mechanic), etc. We all know that Revelations was kind of intended to be the single player series, "in between" main Resident Evil games, but this clearly looks like a co-op feature, yet is only available for local split screen co-op, go figure, why even bother adding that complication. Could have spent all that time on optimization.
Enemies are somewhat smart, they will dodge if you aim at them, usually charge you, some stay at range and lob nasty stuff your way, others are invisible or have special weakspots you have to destroy to kill them, etc.
Game environments look boring, with plenty of horrible texture work and effects yet with increased system requirements for no reason. Character models look mediocre, with good textures yet ugly face features on female part, especially on Claire, Gina (I don't know how hard it is to hire some competent 3D modeler to make decent face).
Story wise it's weaker than 1st game, by A LOT. Character interactions feel emotionless most of the time, there are crazy cut-scenes once in a while that show full potential of how game should have looked, because they are clearly made using same engine, yet looks nothing like real game. Story was not interesting for me at all, when I saw main villain I was like: Are they serious, how lazy was that? They couldn't find any other suitable character? Next time they will just add cousins that suffer from "World Dominance Syndrome", seriously. The most I enjoyed out of the whole story, were part you play as Moira and Grandpa as the bonus episode. That's how enjoyable story was for me, basically that episode is more like a extended Raid mission, rather than story.
Thus we get to the best part of the game, the mode where you kill infected, get medals, unlock new weapons, level up, get new skills, play with different characters on different levels - aka RAID. That is the most fun I got out of this mess, I know that at least 50% of the campaign used similar level assets from 1st game, and Raid mode had A LOT of levels from previous Resident Evil titles, but it's fine. Gina was by far the most fun character to play as, mostly because of her looks (at least from behind, face was fugly as hell though). Compared to Raid mode in 1st game, this was well made, with better difficulty choices. Not much in terms of costumes, nothing for Gina just your default secretary outfit, but who cares.
ANYWAYS, this has been mostly "how I feel about the game", so it's my opinion, I'll stick to mine, you stick to yours, think of it what you may. Maybe some of the info will provide an insight. Verdict is simple, if you're true Resident Evil fan, you don't need reviews, you already bought the game, if you're skeptical, get 1st episode, see how it goes, how it runs on your PC, if you like, get next, etc. Good luck.

Dying Light is the best new zombie game I have played to date. If you love Dead Island (and Riptide) you will love this latest iteration.
Some key points which make this a strong recommendation to buy this game after 30+ hours of play:
1. The open world design of the city. As you progress and gain abilities you have new ways of traversing the city. The logical way this is unlocked is very well designed.
2. You are not forced to follow the main storyline all the time. There are plenty of random events that pop up that lead to new objectives. Missions hubs open up as you help survivors in the city.
3. An excellent variety of weapons and skills to play with that leads to creative and fun ways to kill the infected (and enemy humans). As you level new weapon drops are revealed with high levels. Completing events also unlock new purchasable weapons from quartermasters.
4. The crafting system is easy to understand while still offering some variety of weapon effect choices. Unlike other games I do not find crafting annoying and the plentiful loot drops make it easy to constantly craft new weapons and upgrades.
5. Yes many (if not all) of the game mechanics in Dying Light have been copied from other games but the way they work so well together in Dying Light makes the game pure fun to play.
6. The performance of this game on my system has been better than I expected. The graphics are very detailed yet run smoothly on my GTX780 and 4770K. Framerate averages between 40 to 80 fps at 1920x1080 resolution depending on the action. At no stage was it unplayable for me.
7. The co-op mode is great fun and works seemlessly within the campaign. There is a teleport function to immediately travel to your friends location. The co-op mode not only features objective sharing but you can also compete in optional challenge modes for extra rewards.
8. I have no negatives for this game. If I was nitpicking all I would ask for is more detailed graphics options to fine tune the framerate. The game has never crashed once on my system after 30 hours of play.

Techland really improved on all the elements from Dead Island from crafting to combat. The parkour is smooth and satisfying. Yes, it did remind me of Mirror's Edge. It's a nice experience running past crowds of zombies and jumping across rooftops especially at night. Playing through the campaign either solo or cooperatively just works. You'll find that being the hunter, especially at early levels, is excruciating. There is a leveling system, and it's nearly impossible to win until you've at least unlocked a few of your skills. Otherwise,
will be hunted down and killed by survivors that know what they're doing. It won't feel balanced.
Joining a game on its own is frustrating as you'll constantly find yourself unable to connect or dropped before the round starts. And this because hunters are frequently attempting to invade the same instance. Most of the time you'll be overrided by another hunter joining the same game. Other times, the player will simply drop out because they don't want to play that mode. And as a survivor, leaving the option for invasions on is a disaster. As soon as there's a chance, you will get invaded. And it'll happen over and over until you turn it off. I imagine that's not what the developers had in mind, but at the moment the zombie mode is oversaturated while most players are content to play the game sans invasions.
Despite these issues with Be The Zombie, once you find a game after gaining some experience, it's pretty challenging for either side, and it's quite fun if you're looking to play it.

Dead Space is like Resident Evil 4 in space, but without the charming B movie dialog, and with a few more deliberate scares instead of a creepy mood pervading everything like in RE4. I vastly prefer Resident Evil 4, but both exist, and given how cheap you can buy them both, chances are you get can both if you'd like when they're on sale.
In Dead Space, you go to investigate a ship your girlfriend was on, and a bunch of mutant zombie critters attack you. The gameplay loop is a third person shooter where you go where characters boss you around to go to, and along the way, mutant zombie critters attack. The game's big gimmick, which is admittedly pretty darn entertaining, is shooting off the limbs of enemies. There's pretty fast and dangerous, so you can blow a leg off to take them to the ground, blow an arm off to reduce the chances of getting swung at, etc. It's actually pretty darn fun.
I feel like the game stretches out a little bit too long, and could have cut a few levels and been a product that was as good if not better. I'd certainly feel more inclined to play through it more frequently if it didn't feel like it dragged on so much at parts. But I digress. There are upgrades for your various weapons throughout the game, as well as your health and stasis (slowing enemies to nearly frozen in time). I definitely recommend it and other than being a bit too long in my opinion, it's a very good game.
UPDATE: Having just finished replaying the game, I think I would add that the game isn't necessarily too long based on the story it has and the things they have you do in the game. What drags on, in my opinion, is the game's environment. This game has a lot in common with Resident Evil 4, from the death animations, to the third person horror with limited inventory space, safe rooms with shops and save points, etc.
However, if you've played RE4, think about the environments. You get a village, a castle, and an island with military/industrial architecture. In Dead Space, almost the entire game looks much the same (brown metal floors/walls, tram stations, etc.). I believe that if Dead Space had more variety in its locations other than stand-out memorable rooms amidst a samey 'tileset," it would have been more enjoyable for me...not that I didn't like it. This is my third time to complete the game (second time on Steam).
I played Dead Space 2 on PS3 when it first came out, but I barely remember it. I'll grabbing it the next time I see it on sale for ~$5, and will be curious to see if they rectified this issue there or not.

The nail-biting, everything-to-lose, life-or-death battles are what really make this game something special. Death is waiting around every corner, and as with any roguelike, death is permanent. If that's something you'd be into, and I certainly don't want to know you if it isn't, then do yourself a favor and grab FTL.

Dead Space is a good Horror-Action game, with an interesting tactical mechanic of dismembering aliens. You play as a normal mechanic on a simple mission to repair a spaceship. And you can shoot horizontally with your starting weapon if you aim down sights and press middle mouse button. I give this game a thumbs up :).

An engaging story, well-scultped background art, and dynamic soundtrack make for an excellent comeback game. Fans of the tabletop RPG, SNES, or Sega Genesis games will be pleased, as will fans of games like the X-Com and Fallout series.
The game and the storyline are both very linear, but as long as you are okay with that, you will really enjoy it. The way I see it, this release is more or less the Shadowrun adventure engine, and Dead Man's Switch is a good starter adventure. From what I've heard, Dragonfall takes more liberty with branching and plot twists and the like, and gives you more freedom to explore.

This game exceeded any expectations I might've had for it, based either on Resident Evil: Revelations 1, or the entire Resident Evil franchise. I didn't have the highest hopes, but I was also really looking forward to playing it. The episodic release provided a nice structure to give me a chance to come up with my own theories about what was going on, while remaining spoiler-free. It was fantastic to experience the story as it unfolded. If you're a big fan of past Resident Evil games, you'll recognize a ton of references scattered throughout the game, paying a nice homage to the game's predecessors and making some ties to previous games in the series that you might not have expected. The game does a great job at connecting other games in the franchise with in-game dialogue, text files, and secret unlockable files - and I've still just scratched the surface on those.
If you do compare it to Revelations 1, or if you have played that game and are on the fence about this one: the only thing I really can say is that Revelations 2 achieves everything that Revelations 1 did not. The story presentation, dialogue, and writing were all phenomenal. The voice direction worked beautifully. It really feels like with this game, the spinoff series could very well be a successful standalone experience.
For extra content - there are two bonus episodes (campaign), as well as three difficulties for the normal campaign, and two separate bonus campaign modes: Countdown, where you race against the clock, earning bonus time as you progress through the episode; and Invisible Enemy, a throwback to REmake where the enemies you face are all invisible, until revealed by Natalia or Moira's support abilities, or when you successfully attack them. On top of that, Raid Mode makes a very big return with a vastly improved structure, the introduction of Skills, and over 140 stages, featuring familiar enemies from other recent Resident Evil titles. There's also a nice cast of playable characters, all with their own unique skill-sets, and they each add their own kind of variation to the way you can play the game to keep things interesting in the long haul.

I call this my “Old Games Series” and Dead Space was the first game I played on it. The main reason for reviewing it was to see if it was still as good as the games coming out now when it comes to story and game play.
One of the things I was expecting when I went into the game was for it not to be as good looking as current gen games and obviously, this was the case since technology now can produce some of the most amazing graphics. As well as computers being able to handle more polys on the screen than a game could when Dead Space came out. That being said Dead Space looks really good, occasionally there was the stretching of textures when it came to animations and certain poses, this also happened regularly when a person died and their body rag dolled. This happened a lot with the necro-morph, when they died in awkward places, mostly near a wall, they would get caught in an unseen seam and jitter about causing a very strange and awful slapping noise.
When it came to the game play, this is probably the area I find has the most problems, the main issue was the sensitivity of the game. The movement in the menu was fast, making it very difficult to move the mouse about and change the settings, I know that you can use the arrow keys to navigate the menu, but it is much easier to use one device for everything instead of having to change between mouse and keyboard for navigation. Other than this the sensitivity for aiming in game was extremely slow, it made changing targets very difficult, it also made the fast action points very frustrating to complete. I ended up spending a lot of time in the menus constantly tweaking the sensitivity trying to get it to the sweet spot between menu navigation and aiming controls, but unfortunately, I never found it.

FTL is one of my favourite games and I feel that it gets so much right. The balance of the game is excellent, the mechanics are almost perfect, it's never a chore to start up a new game and every time you play you have the chance to experience an amazing adventure with lots of ups and downs.
The game creates amazing narratives as you play. You can experience that wonderful feeling of having turned around a tight fight by redistributing power to a different system and pulling off some awesome tactical move. Or you can go through the nightmare of wondering what could have been if you'd just invested a little more into your engines as a missile collides with your hull and destroys your ship and with it your chances of saving the federation!
If you manage to survive until the final sector, the final boss fight is an adrenaline fuelled, heart-pumping, chaotic and totally crazy climax to the game. It will have you shouting instructions out loud and fist-pumping as you desperately try to lead your ship, and your crew, to victory. If you are victorious, it's a great feeling every time, and if you lose, well then it's clearly time for another run!
The focus of FTL is very much on the gameplay although there is somewhat of a story and there are little snippets of lore about all of the races in the game which come up as you play. The style and music are a big plus for FTL too as I think both are of an extremely high quality. I cannot emphasise just how amazing the soundtrack is because it really adds to the experience and makes the game even better. The artistic style of the game in general is just really awesome.
FTL has three different difficulties (as of Advanced Edition) so you can set the level of challenge that suits you although it is worth noting that the game is quite difficult in general. There is a hell of a lot of content and fun to be had with FTL with new ships to unlock, different difficulties to try out and various achievements to try for as you play.
FTL is such a fantastic and addictive game!  Fairly easy to pick up and play but, at the same time, has layers of complexity beneath the simplicity. It's great fun to play and really well done. A game that I can tell I will be coming back to again and again. I mean, what's not to like? Sci-fi setting, running your own space ship, roguelike elements, randomisation (different every play through), easy to pick up and play but tough to master, super fun and super addictive. Even the soundtrack is totally awesome! It's a very cool game indeed, and I couldn't recommend it more.

Despite its age, Grand Theft Auto: Vice City is still an extremely fun game. I have played every GTA game to date and despite my love for Grand Theft Auto 5, I still prefer Vice City and in the paragraphs below I will attempt to explain why.
I love GTA 3. The game has quite a lot of enjoyable gameplay and during my most recent playthrough, I didn't have too many issues (besides the races), which was fairly impressive for a game of its age. This certainly does nor mean the game is amazing. In 2016 the game is both a bit clunky and also lacking aesthetic wise. The game was a good starting point and a great transition from the 2D gameplay of old into the 3D realm we know today. I understand how revolutionary GTA 3 was, however looking back in 2016 with the incredible GTA 5 out as well as some decent competitors such as Watch Dogs 2 and Mafia 3, GTA 3 doesn't stand up as well as it used to. Vice City (in my opion) does.
Open worlds are getting bigger and bigger as both time and hardware move forward. In an era full of games with huge landscapes that take hours to explore, revisiting Vice City was very refreshing. It takes about 10 minutes maximum to traverse the map and that is without counting for the race cars which can be found around every corner. I feel I have to truly get into a game in order to play it nowadays. You can't just sit down, do a quick mission and then leave again. This is mostly personal but a lot of Vice City's charm comes with its simplicity, in my eyes at least. Of course, the game isn't "simple" as I put it but compared to modern open world games it's far from complex; thats why I love the game. It's so easy just to do a few missions, save and quit. I think if the game tried to be complex it would've been left in the dust as time went by, but the games simplistic charm is what truly makes it timeless.
My main quarrel with this game is it's aiming mechanics and this is stemmed from the lack of over the shoulder aiming. Shooting accurately in third person is a pain. Let's say you have someone directly in front of you that you need to shoot. You aim your crosshair at them, but due to the camera angle, this makes you look at the ground missing your target. Instead, you aim above the target so you shoot straight in front of you (in theory). You shoot into the sky. This is quite easily fixed by scoping with the Assult Rifles however that makes 2/3s of weapons redundant. This is mainly a sign of age, however, the Assult Rifles spoke of earlier are not hard to find.
Driving is very smooth for keyboard and mouse and is both playable and enjoyable. The flying is rather hard to get used to. In the modern day, it is rather rare to use the num pad to control anything let alone something as complex as a helicopter. It is very hard to control at first, however, upon getting used to can be fun to use. Boats are ok but a bit odd due to the physics engine.
The physics engine for this game is both a bit clunky and also glitchy due to its age, however it is rare to have an issue with it in normal gameplay. Cars occasionally slide upon collision and some bigger vehicles can seem weightless and tip over but these issues are rare.
The story follows Tommy Vercetti as he is forced into the crime underworld of Vice City, a Miami-inspired metropolis filled to the brim with gangs, drugs and greed. You, through the eyes of Tommy, rise up through the criminal world and slowly build your empire gradually making more and more money. Admittedly the story can be a bit cheesy and predictable but this fits the pumped up 80s action film tropes that this game likes to both mock and mimic. Most missions are fun and interesting. You can go from stealing a phone from a gang of chefs to blowing up part of a mall and attempting to escape with a 5-star wanted level. Of course, a few missions are difficult and require multiple runs, but that just adds playtime.

I played Vice City for the first time when I was 7 years old on my older brother's PS2. All I did was drive around and shoot at people with no real objective. I would watch my brother play through the story even though I didn't really understand any of it. I remember playing a small bit of it again when I was a bit older and I got into it and decided to buy it on steam. Boy am I glad I did.
We got a dude named Tommy Vercetti who moves to Liberty City after his Mafia boss buttboy, Sonny tells him too. A coke deal goes bust. His boss calls, and Tommy don't got the money, Sonny. So Tommy works for a lot of dudes and turns into scarface in 2 weeks.
The Story is really good. A really big improvment from GTA 3's barebones story. This time, the main character actually talks. Tommy has some character too him, and he might not be mighty complex, he's atleast interesting.
Although the gameplay doesn't have a huge improvment from GTA 3, it feels a lot more polished. One of my major critisims of GTA 3 was it's insane difficulty towards the end. Vice City does have a few frustating missions, but still feels easier to play and complete than GTA 3. The shooting was made easier and the driving was made smoother.
The graphics are still 2002 PS2 graphics and aren't that impressive by today's standards, but the atmosphere of bright neon pink and yellow, makes the game a nice sight. Cinematics are actually intreging and interesting this time around and don't feel like a necessity to understand what's going on. The dialouge between the characters is very well written, which makes a lot of cutscenes memorable.
Of course a game set in the 80's is gonna have a lot of 80's music! The soundtrack in this game is the best in the series. Even if you think you don't like 80's rock, give the stations a listen, most will still jam.
I really like this game. I didn't feel like I was trudging through it like I was with GTA 3. I got all of the hidden packages, and I got to about 80-90% completion before deciding to play San Andreas next. This game was a blast from beggining to end! I strongly suggest that anyone that hasn't tried this game out, to do so.

Have you ever spent hours on a Windows PC playing Hearts, Solitaire, Spider Solitaire, Freecell, or any of those other card games?  Expect to spend a lot of time with this title!  Unlike the other standard Windows offerings, this game includes rpg elements such as a type of in-game currency (no microtransactions here though!) where you can purchase various upgrades, and a "pet" system that lets you change the background of the cards in your deck.
Now there's an alleged story element as well, demonstrating itself as nothing more than powerpoint slides with some voiceover narration.  It would work well on its own as a children's fable, but as it stands it is simply jarring and distracts one from the experience, and gets in the way of the card game.  The story element might count as a visual novel, if one was willing to disrespect the vast genre of visual novels by including this game's "story" in its ranks.
The game itself is great, and that aspect alone is worth several bucks.  Be warned that the cutscenes are far less engaging than usual, though!

True to it's origins, it gets some of the best features that made the first KF a great game. With guns ranging from a 9mm pistol to a big futuristic Microwave emitter, there is a choice for all tastes. Just log in, get a weapon and smash them to pieces!
Pros:
- Possibility of SP, Coop up to 5 players and PvP (yes you read it right, you can be any Zed even a Zed-Boss in this game)
- Complete and balanced perk system with a lot of perks to choose from.
- Very detailed graphics with a special option for Gore lovers
- Very detailed weapon design (Tripwire have been the best gun-designers in the gaming industry for a while having inspired f/example games like battlefield to step up their gun/gun sound design)
- Daily drop system with possibility to sell content in steam marketplace
- Great dev team that listen to community feedback.
- Regular free content
Cons:
- Lack of a campaign/Story mode (They have enough material to do something about this topic, let's hope for it in KF3)
- Might get a little repetitive if not played with friends. (The development of new maps and weapons might mitigate this a little bit)

I think it is a solid card game.  A bit of a clone of hearthstone but it does have several unique mechanics or adapted ideas from MTG + hearthstone style games.  Each class is very unique from each other, although they are very much analogs from Hearthstone with a twist.
They love to throw packs at you, and opening packs is fun...
Their draft mode (take two) is very good.  You are shown two pairs for cards and you pick one of the pairs to add to your deck.  You do this 15 times to create a 30 card deck.  You then play 5 matches and are awarded based on how many you win.  This is a bit of a departure from hearthstone, which is great.  Although I like that there are less games per a run, I wouldn't mind getting a second shot at 5 win reward (cause it's like double the 4 win reward) even if you lose once.  At the same time, the format makes it feel a bit more rewarding as it mimics ladder a bit better.  Less games per run means you can draft more decks in the same amount of time.  And drafting can be quite fun in the game.  You can easily farm this mode I think.

However, I am not jesting about the 10/10. Or being restrained.
Super Hexagon is a simple game about a small triangle revolving around a center hexagon, dodging shards seemingly made of other hexagons. You are the triangle. You cannot touch the shards.
As opposed to the original Flash version (which had one level and two colors), Super Hexagon contains six levels, each requiring you to stay alive for one eternity-- er, minute. Oh, and there's more colors.
The game is unrelentingly difficult, but oh-so-addicting. The game plays with only two buttons during gameplay, and has several ways of doing so (arrow keys, mouse buttons, gamepad triggers). The game's visuals are psychedelic, color changing and, in the first two levels, seemingly on an axis. You better be darn sure that you're not epileptic or have motion sickness. However, for a person with neither (yours truly), the effect was mesmerizing.
The six levels consist of three different levels (Hexagon, Hexagoner, Hexagonest), and then three "Hyper Mode" versions, which are faster and with different patterns. Trust me, you WILL work to complete every world.
Despite the theoretical six minutes of gameplay that this game would (theoretically) provide, hours will be poured into trying to complete every level... and then some to break your own (or someone else's) high score. Heck, it took me 17 hours to beat a $4 game, and, I tell you, I feel like I need to be locked up on robbery charges at that price.
6 levels, 6 sides, 60 seconds. Yep.
Also, I legitimately cried at the end. That's actually true.
I have never said that a game is perfect before. Even my favorite games that I hold in such high respect still have several flaws which I acknowledge. However, due to the concentrated nature of Super Hexagon's gameplay, it is impossible to find any faults within it. Really.
At this point, it sounds like I'm simply ecstatic about the game, and will shout praises and begin handing out brochures about the dangers of other games. The truth it, I feel that everything I wrote here is true. Every last word.
Except the beginning joke.
Seriously, 10/10 "would buy again"
And yes.  I actually would.

This is a cool game in that the genre of cyberpunk is well communicated.  It is like experiencing an interactive Shadowrun novel.  Shadowrun, for those that don’t know, is a future time when the major business corporations pretty much rule the planet.  Money (nuyen) is definitely king, and it can be a very bleak place to live for the have-nots.  There are great technological innovations, which basically allows cyborgs.  There is also magic and spirits.
The game is turn-based combat and moves much more swiftly than the pen-and-paper RPG game, of course.  The power level of the game is lower than the pen-and-paper game, with less cool cyberware and adept powers for instance.  It does not follow the Shadowrun rules, and the rules aren’t detailed for the min-maxers.  Still, I thought the overall game play worked well.  All the Shadowrun elements are there.  You can be a decker, rigger (of drones), mage, shaman, physical adept, samurai, or any combination thereof.  There is plenty of karma during the game to develop your character.  The games centers more on combat than sneakiness or creative shortcuts.  You have several difficulty levels.  You can further adjust the difficulty by choosing which and how many fellow (NPC) runners you bring along (up to 3).  You can also of course, not choose to over-optimize your character or carry illegal weapons and armor (which the game allows you to do without penalty).
I liked the original story, The Dead Man’s Switch.  It reminded me so much of classic Shadowrun stories.  The next episode, Dragonfall, probably was even bigger than the first story - there is plenty to do and more cool gear and cyberwear to do it with.
Possibly, the coolest thing about this game is its Editor.  There is already a great deal of fan-made content, including new campaigns, new equipment, and changes to the rule set.  You are free to choose any of the stuff you like that other people have made or make your own.  There is also a wiki and forum up for the game.
This game was built on a low budget and that shows in some areas.  Areas for improvement include the graphics, which are hardly better than Balder’s Gate (1998), and the soundtrack.  I don’t even listen to the game’s sound at all.  There should be voice acting, good city ambience sounds, and more meaningful combat audio clues, as well as more varied background music.  A great manual with links to the forum should be presented.  We don’t need to discover how to use controls or what the hard coded rules of combat are – we should be told.  Even with these minor drawbacks, I am very impressed with this game’s value.  I think it gives a lot for its rather minimal cost.  I suggest you give it a try if this sort of thing interests you.

So, I never played the paper based version of this game although it was something I was aware of in my teens,  I picked this up in the Steam Summer Sale as something of an impulse purchase and, idly lookng for something to play fired it a week or too back and I've been playing it ever since.
It's set in a sort of post-apocalyptic future world where after magic reawakens and the world is suddenly awash with Magic, Elves, Dwarves, Trolls and all the trappings of standard fantasy tropes, but retains guns, computers and technology. If you have ever read William Gibson's Neuromancer (and if not, why not?) then it's that world. But with magic. Governments have seemingly collpased, Dragons run rampant and Mega-Corporations now run the world. Into this your little band of mercenaries - shadowrunners - instigate heists, perform assassinations and generally do whatever they can to survive.
Gameplay wise it's basically the Fallout & Fallout 2 model - you explore your environment and find stuff to do and, more often than not, end up in a turn based combat system. There are plenty of different character classes to choose from, ranging from street samuri (your tanks) to battle mages, shamen, Deckers (these guys are your computer experts and hack into "the matrix" (which is exacly what it sounds like)) and RIggers - guys who control robots to do their fighting. There are others too, and you can specialise how you like even mixing classes if you want to - although the jack of all trades is master of none, especially in this world. As you progress you earn Karma to spend on skills that your character class uses to improve and become much more effective in-game.
The game is very solid - graphics are solid  for a kickstarted game, there are few minor bugs but nothing major - and the game stands very much on the quality of it's writing, which is very good indeed. The first campaign from the kickstarter (Dead Man's Switch) is very involving, and although I thought it lost its way towards the end at least gets you there - you'll want to know how it's all going to end. The combat system works as well - you'll be using cover, buffing your team mates and working out how to get the drop on your opponents. However it lacks some character development (for example you can only hire other shadowrunners, so you don't develop a team you get to know) and outside of the main quest there isn't much else to do. You can explore a bit, maybe find a few fetch quests but that's it.
The expansion DLC Dragonfall is where this game is at though. It maintains the quality of the writing, it's got proper character development and you get a team of shadowrunners to get to develop and know as the game progresses. There are plenty of missions outside the main mission, with some real decisions (and consequences) to work through as you take them on. The main hub you retreat too a large area with plenty of other NPCs to chat to, some of who will give you some side missions, others of whom need you help.  It is a great little RPG and really deserves a lot of praise.
Where game falls down is in two areas - there are too many character classes to choose from and to be honest many of them are essentially identical - only one set of classes use technology and other use magic. The only distinct class are the Deckers, but unfortunately the Matrix sections of the game are distinctly underwhelming - you basically run around a white wireframe world while red blobs shoot at you - and it doesn't really work. I have a lot of sympathy for the developers there - short of developing an entire differnt game for the Matrix bits I'm not sure what else they could have done - but it does sell the game very short.
However don't let that put you off - there aren't many of them and the Dragonfall campaign leaves them entirely optional.
Finally th developer has released a full editor suite of tools for you to make your own campaigns and release for public consumption. As good as they are, the developer campaigns aren't that long (Maybe 12 hours or so to complete) and so having fans with the ability to make their own efforts gives this game a lot more replayability. Some of the ones released so far are pretty damn good - Ashron's 'From the Shadows, Run' being a particular stand out.
So yes, this is a good game with a lot of longevity. If you liked the original fallouts, Jagged Alliance, XCOM etc then you'll love this. It's got a few rough edges to be sure but they don't detract from the main game and it is more than worth a purchase.

FTL reminds of a board game I played called Battlestations.  An overly complicated, geeky spaceship resource management that you really wanted to love but no matter how hard you tried you just couldn't due to all the pieces and crap you had to keep track of.  The whole time I was playing it I was thinking this would make a great video game and what do you know, it does!
Everyone here should know by now that I love Dark Souls and with that stems a love for Roguelike games.  FTL follows a truer roguelike formula than Dark Souls where when you die, it is game over.  You lose everything, which can be infuriating at times but also adds a feeling of urgency and threat that you just can't get from save/restart games.  To add to that the entire game is random, which can put you in some rough situations if you’re not prepared.  In one play through you could come across a stranded ship and where you get an extra crew member, the next stranded ship however could blow up and take half your hall with it.  I swear, every time I think I’m doing awesome something goes very wrong to show me that I really have no clue what I am doing.
Maybe it’s Battered Persons Syndrome or maybe I’m just sick of games hand holding players but there are two things I want when I buy a new game.  Challenging game play and replay value.  FTL is no exception but what  I think will put this over the top for you as an awesomesauce game is whether or not you loved FireFly/Star Trek/BSG and ever day dreamed of being a captain.
Finally, don’t let the graphics put you off, what the game lacks in visual appeal it makes up with gameplay and the soundtrack/effects are really well done.  The sound of rocket fire and lasers just helps enhance the music playing the back ground.  It’s hard to explain, let me just say that this is a game you want to play with the sound on.

I'm a big fan of Resident Evil, and the original Revelations on 3DS was one of the better entries in recent memory. RE2 has always been my fave, so when I heard this game would star Claire Redfield, one of my favorite video game characters, and it would be a sucessor to the fantastic 3DS game, I was all in. Unfortunately, the game is a huge letdown.
Local co-op controversy aside, the game is a shoddy port. The game stutters and freezes horribly, and a game this ugly has no business doing that on my PC. It's especially bad if you die and have to reload a checkpoint. As the level loads again the game completely freezes, though enemies will still attack and kill you again while you're unable to play.
Besides technical issues, the game is horribly unbalanced. There's two co-op partners who serve no purpose in this singleplayer only game, and since they can't effectively fight back they're a walking liability. You have to juggle between characters in the middle of combat to try and perform co-op actions and defend yourself at the same time. This becomes increasingly difficult, as the game throws you tons of enemies to fight and practically no ammo. It's like they tried to recapture what was fun in Revelations and RE4, but with the limited supplies of the classic games, and it does not mix. It's unbalanced and just plain unfun.
I love Resident Evil, and the Raid mode is actually still okay(albiet made up of reused geometry from other RE games), but I cannot at all recommend this game. It's an unfinished, badly ported mess. Almost any other game in the franchise is a better buy than this.

This is the ZOMBIE GAME that delivers. Incredible graphics throbbing with excellent optimization. I had my LOD set to 0 yet i was still getting mind blowing far off views. I can only imagine what its like set to full. Npcs are lifelike in appearance and the world is so fully realised in its detailed environments i feel like am actually there. The only way it could get any more real is with one of those up and coming virtual reality headsets.
Audio and music brings home the classic eerie nightmare feel of a George Romero, Lucio Fulci, Ford Brothers zombie movie with just the right balance of real life ambience and theatrical stimuli. Voice acting is marvelous giving life to npcs and your character while enhancing further the believabilty of the amazing highly fleshed out world.
As you play through the game your character will level up getting skill points depending on what he does most in the game. If they are a runner type their agility tree will get skill points to use on different strengths. If they are a smash and kill every undead in sight type they will get skill points in their power tree etc.
The environment is very tactile with tons of things you can interact with. From turning on radios to collecting common day items you can then use to craft new things with like weapons and home made health kits. You can pick locks of different levels of difficulty but be weary time will not stop and a zombie may chomp into your skull because you didnt pay mind to its shuffling feet as you greedily picked a locked chest. You can rummage through buildings for food and money while coming across people in need of help. If you decide to help them it will effect how they view you. If not oh well you scoundrel you! Movement is also another spectacular very natural feeling action executed in spectaculer fashion by DYING LIGHT finding myself climbing and jumping onto and off buildings, diving under things etc etc. Usually i suck at games that have acrobatics but in DYING LIGHT it all felt so right with the parkour system.
You will see npcs going about their daily lives while having to deal with the horrors of the zombie plague. One time i came across a bunch of children in a day care school setting in a apartment building as a female teacher read them children stories. Another time i listened to one of the many varied accounts of those fighting zombies as i explored a building.
Combat is alot of fun as well as quite scary. While you engage zombies your stamina will go down making your attacks less effective and you more vulnerable to a zombie(s) assault.  Zombies may be slow moving but they will tear you apart as you scream in horror when you suddenly find yourself surrounded by a slow moving horde of rotting corpses.
Your weapons have wear and tear which means that metal pipe will be useless after one too many door smashed open by it or zombie skull caved in. Fear not though for you can repair your items back to working shape with items you salvage in the world.
DYING LIGHT its the ELDER SCROLLS and METRO 2033/METRO LAST LIGHT of zombie games. Truly a mind blowing masterpiece that will give you hours upon hours of endless gameplay with a awesome campaign and plenty of side quests.
To have this much enjoyment from my i5-3570k 3.40ghz with 8.0gb ram, Radeon HD 7770 card at a resolution of 1366x768 is miraculous. All i can say is thanks and DYING LIGHT is definitely a title worth playing and paying full price for.
DYING LIGHT a magnificent and rare treasure of a game.

There are still some issues with infinite uploading & casual Raid-Mode crashes for some people. If you waited for the performance to be fixed before buying the game, then now is the time to buy it without regret!
You play Claire Redfield & Barry Burton’s Daughter Moira. You get kidnaped and wake up in a prison cell with a bracelet around your arms that change colour in response to fear. Now it’s on you to escape the place and to find out who did this to you. The all so ever faithful co-op partner system of modern Resident Evil games is in play here.
You can switch characters on the fly to solve puzzles, organize your inventory and defeat monsters. Unlike previous games only one of the two characters (Claire) will use weapons, the other one (Moira) uses a flashlight to blind enemies to beat them up with her crowbar or to have Claire take them out with brute firepower. Moira’s flashlight can also detect hidden items in the vicinity by shining the light on it. In between episodes, you can unlock special abilities for use in the campaign with Bonus Points (collected as gemstones ingame) to make it easier for you to survive the horror.
In the second half of each of the four story-campaigns you play as the man Barry Burton himself that came to the place to rescue his daughter Moira. He soon meets a small girl (Natalia) that can sense enemies in the environment for Barry to plan his next move. You might think Barry’s part is a pure shooting gallery, but it’s not. Preparation and planning is as important to survive in the Barry/Natalia part of the story as it is for Claire & Moira.
Additional Modes can be unlocked after finishing the episodes. Including a Countdown (Speedrun) & Invisible Enemy Mode in which partner swapping is a must to survive. There is actuall a ton of unlockables & achievments besides the usual Secret Documents, Figures, Artworks to unlock.
But don’t expect any unique gameplay elements here. Revelations 2 recycles & uses many elements you already found in countless other games of the last 2 years. If you take a closer look you will realize (mostly series veterans) that Capcom seemed to have put together all the good and sometimes bad things from previous games in the series. But you will be glad to find out that the good things overweight. Revelations 2 is a high quality entry of the franchise. Capcom abandoned the action firework style of Resident Evil 6 and created a very atmospheric, sometimes creepy game. Will it scare you? Maybe. But don’t count on that. It’s far from being Resident Evil Remake.
There might be lots to unlock in the story campaign that can bind players for countless hours & gives completionists a reason to continue playing. But it’s nothing compared to the second incarnation of Revelation 1’s Raid-Mode.
You pick from a decent amount of characters that all start from level 1. You then enter the first of up to 200 stages. You will shoot monsters, gather experience & gold. You will loot weapons & weapon modifications. You will finish the stage with up to 5 medals rewarded for sticking to certain requirements and level up the character you used.
Weapons & modifications can then be kept or sold for gold which you then use to buy new equipment in a store. Experience points can be spend on various active & passive skills to strengthen the character. But you want more loot, more gold & more experience: So you start the second stage and keep on going until your character is level 100.
Level 100 is only the beginning. You keep on playing for more weapons, more skillpoints, gold & modifications. You might even try to use other characters to find out what their special abilities, advantages & disadvantages are. Skills of characters can be unlocked for other characters to use. Sooner or later you will realize that you are addicted! That’s Raid Mode in a nutshell.
Why do I recommend the game? Well, mostly for Raid-Mode. Raid-Mode alone is worth the $6 for Episode 1, even though you don’t get all characters, weapons & stages. But you will always have the ability to upgrade to the entire set for $25 for more of it or $40 for everything (including DLC you would need to buy if you get the package for $25).
Revelations 2 features an interesting & compelling Story-Mode with well written storyline & cliffhangers that keep you guessing.

A limited but fun little tactical turn based RPG set in the unique cyberpunk/magical Shadowrun universe, where the future is dominated by corporations and the rich, the poor are often little more than slaves and everyone seems to be simply struggling to get by. If you can't tell, it's not a nice place.
But then you're not exactly a nice person either. You can choose from up to 6 classes, from fairly standard mage or warrior (shadow samurai) to the more unique like Deckers (hackers, more useful than you'd think) or Adepts (magical close combat specialists). As you "level up" you gain karma points that you can spend in any of the different attribute areas, allowing you to customise your character however you see fit. Don't like the damage your decker is doing? Throw some points into a ranged weapon and watch them be (not as) useless in a firefight. Want your heavy gunner to get a healing spell? By all means. Ultimately the campaigns are too small for expansive customisation so it is best to specialise, but you can easily put points into a few different areas without handicapping yourself.
The stories are generally well written, with Dragonfall (the DLC) being better than the one that comes packaged with the game (Dead Man's Switch). The characters are also well written though, again, I found the ones in Dragonfall to be a higher quality.
Combat is turn based and works similar to the recent X-Com title, where angles and cover play a large role in damage mitigation. It's generally fast, coming in short bursts which keep it from getting stale. In between you're able to talk, sometimes avoiding combat altogether, while you piece together just what in the hell is going on.
Graphically it's not card breaker, so lower end computers shouldn't have a problem running it. It's stylised, with vibrant, neon colours clashing with the darker, grimier parts of a bad world. Honestly though, just look above and see if you like it or not.
There's also a full game editor and a decent amount of user created content. Obviously the quality varies but it's a decent way to prolong the game beyond its pair of campaigns. The problem I have here is it feels like this feature was/is relied on for content in general. The default campaign isn't amazingly long, though Dragonfall is longer. Still, they're two seperate campaigns and could be looked at as 2 seperate games and neither, I feel, are long enough for this kind of RPG. But I can't fault them for having this.
So ultimately, if you're a RPG fan I'd recommend this. If you're not I'd probably leave it, unless you decide to give it a chance during a sale.

FTL reminds of a board game I played called Battlestations.  An overly complicated, geeky spaceship resource management that you really wanted to love but no matter how hard you tried you just couldn't due to all the pieces and crap you had to keep track of.  The whole time I was playing it I was thinking this would make a great video game and what do you know, it does!
Everyone here should know by now that I love Dark Souls and with that stems a love for Roguelike games.  FTL follows a truer roguelike formula than Dark Souls where when you die, it is game over.  You lose everything, which can be infuriating at times but also adds a feeling of urgency and threat that you just can't get from save/restart games.  To add to that the entire game is random, which can put you in some rough situations if you’re not prepared.  In one play through you could come across a stranded ship and where you get an extra crew member, the next stranded ship however could blow up and take half your hall with it.  I swear, every time I think I’m doing awesome something goes very wrong to show me that I really have no clue what I am doing.
Maybe it’s Battered Persons Syndrome or maybe I’m just sick of games hand holding players but there are two things I want when I buy a new game.  Challenging game play and replay value.  FTL is no exception but what  I think will put this over the top for you as an awesomesauce game is whether or not you loved FireFly/Star Trek/BSG and ever day dreamed of being a captain.
Finally, don’t let the graphics put you off, what the game lacks in visual appeal it makes up with gameplay and the soundtrack/effects are really well done.  The sound of rocket fire and lasers just helps enhance the music playing the back ground.  It’s hard to explain, let me just say that this is a game you want to play with the sound on.

However, the steam version is a headache and then some. Here’s some of the several troubleshooting issues you’ll have to go through.
DirectPlay. Firstly, you’ll have to enable this, the path is Control Panel > Programs and Feature > Turn Windows features on or off > Legacy Components > Direct Play.
Next, it’s not compatible with your OS unless your running 98 or XP, if so, you have more issues to worry about. Go to compatibility, select Windows 98, also, reduce the colour mode, along with the bits, alongside applying it to run in 640 x 480 resolution.
Think you’re done? Nope. You just applied for a part time job as a computer technician.
Next issue, it will ask you to insert the CD. That’s right, the digital copy you purchased, most likely for the main reason of having easy access to a childhood game, will ask you for a CD.
So, the main way you’ll be able to resolve this is if you delete the audio folder in your steam apps, and replacing it with the CD versions audio folder, thankfully, I kept my CD for this part, if not, you have to illegally torrent the game, but if you do so, you won’t have the fun of troubleshooting.
Don’t worry, it gets better, the game can now load and you can play it, however, the audio will not be compatible with the game itself, so you won’t hear anything. No awesome 80s music or Haitians dying in the streets.
The final step, refund this mess that steam provided to you, with no warnings or disclaimers and throw that CD that you kept in perfect condition for the last 14 years at the wall.

All right, first of all, I, like so many other, am an RE-Veteran. I started this series with the first part back in 1998 on the original Playstation. Played the grande part 2, the mediocre part 3 and then lost track. Some time later I played RE 4, which is the second best one (after RE 2) and then 5 which I enjoyed a lot in Coop-Mode with my gf.
Then something ugly happened and voila: RE 6 and Operation Racoon City.
After the Quick-Time-F*ckfest named RE 6 (god I hate this game, everything related to it feels so wrong) I was not sure if I ever play a RE-Game again.
But hooray Steam-Sales, I bought Revelations and now Revelations 2. Let's forget about Revelations, its mediocre at best, and dive right into a surprisingly entertaining R2.
It is the first RE-Game since 4 that has a somewhat slower pace. There are absolutely no QTE's which is splendid and the overall atmosphere is great. It is more of a horror game, just like the early parts and less of a Micheal-Bay-meets-some-fancy-japanese-tentacle-fetish-thing.
The story (I played halfway through episode 2) is ok. The setting is nice, even though the graphics are an insult for any gaming pc. Still, overall it's a good game.
If you like the pace and the feeling of the older Resident Evil-Games and are older than 12 (and therefore hate RE 6), this is a great game for you. Absolutely recommended. Especially as it is sold in parts. Buy part one, see if you like it, then buy (or not buy) the rest. Awesome.

FTL reminds of a board game I played called Battlestations.  An overly complicated, geeky spaceship resource management that you really wanted to love but no matter how hard you tried you just couldn't due to all the pieces and crap you had to keep track of.  The whole time I was playing it I was thinking this would make a great video game and what do you know, it does!
Everyone here should know by now that I love Dark Souls and with that stems a love for Roguelike games.  FTL follows a truer roguelike formula than Dark Souls where when you die, it is game over.  You lose everything, which can be infuriating at times but also adds a feeling of urgency and threat that you just can't get from save/restart games.  To add to that the entire game is random, which can put you in some rough situations if you’re not prepared.  In one play through you could come across a stranded ship and where you get an extra crew member, the next stranded ship however could blow up and take half your hall with it.  I swear, every time I think I’m doing awesome something goes very wrong to show me that I really have no clue what I am doing.
Maybe it’s Battered Persons Syndrome or maybe I’m just sick of games hand holding players but there are two things I want when I buy a new game.  Challenging game play and replay value.  FTL is no exception but what  I think will put this over the top for you as an awesomesauce game is whether or not you loved FireFly/Star Trek/BSG and ever day dreamed of being a captain.
Finally, don’t let the graphics put you off, what the game lacks in visual appeal it makes up with gameplay and the soundtrack/effects are really well done.  The sound of rocket fire and lasers just helps enhance the music playing the back ground.  It’s hard to explain, let me just say that this is a game you want to play with the sound on.
