Unfortunately I cannot recommend this game. The game is not bad, but it most certainly is not very good either. I did enjoy the art style and just playing through the story to find out what was going to happen next. If it weren't for the 'crashes' that forced me to start from the last save again, or the bugs that forced me to restart an entire level, I may have recommended Shadowrun Returns to people that enjoy a 'casual playthrough'. However, these game breaking bugs weren't the only problems I had with the game:
- It lacks the depth I was hoping for. Of course it was partially my fault, expecting a lot of depth in a game with this price usually does not turn out well. Still, when starting the game the player can choose from 5 different races and a whole lot of classes. These races and classes did not appear to have much of an impact though. It would not surprise me if it is possible to finish the game without ever spending 'karma' (equivalent of skill points) except for a few points in the ranged weapons skill in order to be able to use better weapons. There are no actual alternative options available in the game whatsoever, regardless of the class and skill level of the player.
- On 'hard' difficulty I did not encounter an actually difficult part. I could still get through every combat sequence with incredible ease. The only times I had to load a previously saved game was when another game breaking bug occurred, never because I died due to difficulty.
- The game is extremely linear. Sometimes the player has a choice between a few different dialogue options, but they don't seem to have an impact at all: it makes no difference if you are acting like a professional or like a streetganger. There is also only one path through each level, with perhaps one of the last levels being an exception with two or three vents your drones can move through if you happen to have those with you. This alternate route did not really seem to have any advantages over the main route though.
This lack of alternative routes and options also makes the whole class system a bit useless. I chose to be a 'decker', which is basically a hacker that moves around in cyberspace to retrieve data and/or take control of systems. There is only a single level in which the player actually gets the OPTION to hack into a system to gain an advantage. In all the other levels where a 'decker' is required, one will be provided by the game because you are forced to hack into computers to progress. The best party-member composition probably is a party with only large, powerful guns and no support characters. More situations with optional hacking to, for example, disable security would have been very nice.
- The levels feel very empty, both indoor and outdoor levels. Even when there are quite a few people displayed on the streets it feels as if there is no-one else but the player and its party, because the NPCs are simply static scenery and don't move at all. Something that adds to the emptiness is the complete absence of ambient sounds. This game made me realize how important ambient sound is in a game, because without them a level feels very lifeless.
- The story is not all that original and somewhat anticlimactic. It does not make too much sense in my opinion. At least it was enjoyable enough for me to keep playing, despite the annoying game breaking bugs.
I have not played any user created content for this game, so I have no idea if there are great workshop entries out there that fix some of these problems. I sure hope so, because I was kind of expecting a modern, although shorter, Arcanum: Of Steamworks and Magick Obscura in a cyberpunk setting, which this game just is not.

I can't say I "highly" recommend the game, but it is quite enjoyable for what it's worth and the humor and various cameos help move along a very unpolished product.
And I do mean unpolished: the controlls are a mess, one button has up to three functions simultaneously, the driving and flying control like bricks (heh), the physics are wonky as hell, and there's some very questionable design and balancing choices. Furthermore, the game is padded out like hell: New York city is a sizable sandbox with tons of things to do, but sadly a lot of the quests end up being basic point-A-to-Point-B-and-back fetch quests, the worst of all include you escorting people (has anyone ever said "What this game needs is escort missions"? Anyone?) who are slower than you, can't get into vehicles, and routinely get stuck behind ankle-high pavement. The ♥♥♥♥♥♥ voice acting and excessive use of puns is also very noticable.
Still with me? Good, now here's why I actually do enjoy the game a lot. If you've ever played any of the previous LEGO titles, you'll know the basic outline of the game: Every mission has to be beaten once using a select group of characters, all of which have their own special abilities, and once you've beaten them you re-thread the stage with the ability to select any character you've unlocked and then search for hidden items and such. The game's abilities and heroes are varied and fun; there's amazing detail shown to every single cast member, most of whom have their own special animations for attacking and their own crosshair icon. Statistically speaking, your favorite Marvel character is somewhere in this game playable, and unlocking people is very fun. The level design is top notch, with every one forcing you to keep a keen eye out for hidden goodies and I never once found any particular puzzle to be annoying or obtuse. Finally, the music in the game is quite good, which took me for surprice. I'm particularly fond of the racing theme.
Overall, it IS a good game, only that the seams are more visible than Hulk rampaging through a kindergarden. If you can forgive its many, many technicall fault you're bound to fall in love with a game that was clearly put together with lots of care.

Imagine a world filled with your wildest imaginations. A futuristic world where humans, trolls, dwarves, elves, and orks exist and live together. Imagine the presence of mages, cybernetic freaks, skilled hackers, deadly swordsmen, chi-casting masters, wicked shamans, and one-shot marksmen. No, let's not stop there! Imagine an organized group of people called Shadowrunners, who take missions from clients, avoid the influences of corrupt businesses, and lurk in the shadows. All of these ideas I mentioned are the world of Shadowrun Returns.
Shadowrun Returns is an immersive, intelligent, and fun game that is influenced by many references. It's a strategy cyberpunk RPG game that gives you freedom. In order to keep this review short and sweet, I'll make a Positives vs. Negatives list of Shadowrun Returns.
POSITIVES:
-Main campaign has an engaging story that dives you into the mystery of your friend's murder. DLC campaign also has an engaging story that makes you uncover the secrets about an infamous dragon and the chosen one who defeated it.
-Twists and turns occur just when you think the story is over
- Lots of Races to choose from right from the get-go (Human, Elf, Troll, Ork, Dwarf). Each have special qualities and set-ups.
- Lots of Classes to choose from right from the get-go (Street Samuari, Decker, Shaman, Mage, Physical Adept, Rigger). Each have special qualities and differ in gameplay.
-A wide cast of characters who are surprisingly relatable and interesting
-A DLC campaign (Purchased Separately) that explains an aspect of the story more and provides a different experience from the main campaign. The DLC campaign is about as long as the main campaign. The DLC can be longer if you do all the side content there.
- Complex world with interesting atmopsheres. Game created its own terms (ex; chummer, nuyen) and has its own glossary in-game. Shadowrun is a combination of A LOT of influences. The decker class is heavily based on a book.
- Karma system (Skill tree) that enhances gameplay and abilities
- Game allows you to choose multiple conversation paths, making the plot more immersive.
- Depending on what class, race, and ability you pick, you will have more options to choose from when you converse with NPCs
- Some side content is avaiable in both campaigns
- Has a User-Generated Content system, which adds replayability value and allows the players to create their own stories and levels (just like the developers!)
- You can save ALMOST anytime (Can't save between conversations). There are also autosaves.
- You can hire other Shadowrunners to experience other classes and accomplish missions.
- Solid and unique RPG gameplay that is easy to learn
- Difficulty is scaled well, especially at the end of the game
- About 20 hours of content in main campaign. About 30 hours of content in DLC campaign. More hours of content when playing/making user-generated content.
- Solid music
NEGATIVES:
-Game doesn't have a lot of side content, making it seem linear at times.
-Sometimes, the game can get too complex in background story. (Might be just me)
-Occasional glitches and bugs, especially with the user-generated content.
Of course the game has negatives, but look at how the positives outweigh them! Without a doubt my favorite Lego game. Might even be one of my favorite games of all time.
Lego Marvel features an impressive roster of characters, with over 150 characters (excluding DLC) to choose from. The impressive part is that each character has a unique moveset (some character even have a completely unique move) that helps keep them as individual characters and not copies of each other. Venom and Spider-Man or Wolverine, Beast and Sabretooth or even Hulk, Abomination and Blob might play the same but they don't really feel like a lazy palette swap of each other.
The story features 15 levels and has been crafted specifically for the game. Like its predecessors, Lego Marvel doesn't lack the usual Lego humor, as the game is full of the same light-hearted humor that has been precent since Lego Star Wars. The story itself is somewhat decent and characters that make an appearance have the same-ish personality as they do in other forms of media they have appeared in.
The voice cast features familiar voices of Nolan North (Cyclops, Deadpool, Magneto...), Troy Baker (Hawkeye, Loki...), Tara Strong (Mary Jane Watson...) amongst a dozen others that help give each character a personality. Adrian Pasdar, Fred Tatasciore reprise their roles as Iron Man and Hulk respectively and even Clark Gregg is present as Agent Coulson, not to mention Stan Lee as himself.
Speaking of the audial, both the soundtrack and audio itself are really well-done. Skydiving from the helicarrier high above or racing is accompanied by an intense, gripping piece of music whilst running around the city feature a slower, more mellow melody. That's the best way I can describe the music of the game, it's fitting in the pretty much any context.
The visuals of the Lego games have always been impressive for their time and Lego Marvel follows that tradition with bright, inviting, colorful visuals, a stark difference from the dark and gritty atmosphere of Lego Batman 2.
Gameplay wise, there is little Lego Marvel adds that hasn't already been present since day 1. You go from level to level, collecting studs and minikits, using aforementioned studs to buy new characters, vehicles and Red Brick extras, then go back with the ability to play as anyone to fully complete the level. It becomes tedious at times as many of the levels have you constantly switching out characters because only Magneto can move magnetic objects or because only Sandman can traverse sand tunnels.
In free roam you wander about, finding lose Gold Bricks, tokens and even helping Stan Lee who has somehow found himself in various predicaments around Manhattan, take part in racing challenges or fetch quest a lá Lord of the Rings. At first it seems like the map is littered with endless challenges and for most of my time playing I felt exhausted just looking at all the things scattered about on the map.
The challenges also sometimes suffer from feeling uninspired. Most of them are just beating up bad guys, fetching something from the other side of town or escorting a lost cat to its owner. Thankfully each challenge has unique voice acting, so you're not hearing the same thing over and over again.
I musn't forget about Manhattan, the open-world map you're given to explore. Swinging around from building to building as Spider-Man, rampaging through traffic as Hulk or rocketing across the sky as Iron Man is really fun and never really ends up feeling dull, given that so many characters have different ways of moving about. Even driving feels responsive and stranely enough handles better than many racing games where driving is the main focus.
Though not big (certainly a bit smaller than Algonquin of Liberty City), Manhattan has been faithfully recreated. You can visit areas like Chinatown, Times Square, Harlem and the Financial District, each are designed in a way that makes them stand out from one another. You'll come across famous landmarks such as the Empire State Building, Grand Central Station, Central Park and Columbus Circle, though the strange lack of Chrysler Building and United Nations Headquarters doesn't really detract from the island as a whole (perhaps there wasn't enough room, I don't know).
Free roam also introduces some much needed changes with the most relieving of them being the inclusion of a mini-map, something Lego Batman 2 and Lord of the Rings sorely lacked. The ingame map itself is even an improvement, you can now tell which direction your character faces and whether a collectible or objective is below or above you. The best of all is that the map is actually readable and less cryptic in all regards. Fast Travel is present, making short of having to cross the entire city for an objective (not that it takes a long time anyway).
Gone is the inventory system of Lego Lord of the Rings which means that you have to switch characters more often, leading to situations described above. I think the reason being is that it really wouldn't fit in the game all too well.
Flying controls (in my opinion) has also been changed for the good as they are way more precise. Now It's easier to fly up onto a building and you won't overshoot it half the time. Still, the button for descending and turning off flight is the same, making some of the flying racing challenges unintentionally annoying. A step in the right direction anyhow.

After split-screen was added to the PC version, I have almost nothing but praise for this iteration of Resident Evil. It's the best new entry in the series in nearly six years and is packed with plenty of content for its very reasonable price tag. The gameplay dials back the ridiculous action focus from RE6 and delivers a few clever puzzles and some genuine tension at times. Progression is still linear and chapter based but the campaign offers a good deal of exploration. Combat (on Survival difficulty) is satisfying and risky, and even the forced co-op is actually designed with single player in mind since it's now more reminiscent of the partner system from RE Zero than RE5 or 6. Hell, the writing and voice acting are unexpectedly great with some truly chuckle-worthy banter and just the right amount of cheese peppered through a fun-and-silly story. There's lots of fan service and even some successful tugs at the heart strings which makes it easier to forgive some of the sloppier characterization on Claire's end (and the very depressing replacement of her voice actress).
That's not even to mention all of the content and longevity supplied by Raid Mode. It's a clearly budget-made RE and has some roughness on its edges, but Revelations 2 puts its heart in all the right places. The series hasn't yet achieved the mythical "blend of classic and new" Resident Evil yet, but this is the most potent example of it so far.
EDIT: All episodes are now out and with everything on the table, I have to say I like the game even more than when this review was published. A nice optimization patch has helped performance (though it wasn't much of an issue for me beforehand) and the game offers a ton of unlockables and replay value, including multiple endings! Sadly, the less satisfying of these two endings is triggered far too easily and obscurely, but for folks who managed to finish Episode 4 with the good ending will really be in for a memorable treat.
The bonus episodes aren't crucial selling points, but they are fun hour-ish long diversions that mix up the gameplay mechanics and flesh out some bits of the narrative.
Ultimately, even if you just snag the $25 season pass without any additional content you'll more than get your money's worth.

Half Life 2...well, my original review was less than positive, as I gave it a punishing 4/10. After replaying Half Life 2, I've appreciated it more, but it still has some really glaring issues.
Now, Half Life 2 is pretty much a must-own for any Steam gamer, as it offers a view of a truly revolutionary game. However, its main issues lie mostly in the overall length and story. So a large portion of the game (specifically the Highway, Sandtraps, and Nova Prospekt levels) feel like filler and drag on for far too long, and end up getting really tedious. You're also stripped of story for almost the entire middle section.
Half Life 2 really shines in the beginning and end levels. The first level in the game is perhaps the best introduction of any game I've ever played, and the following levels are strong as well. The ending levels are also excellent.
Overall, Half Life 2 is really a game anyone should buy, just don't expect it to outshine every other FPS.

Having been a roleplayer a large portion of my life. I always wondered what it would be like to actually live out one of the many adventures I had played late night with my friends. Doom & Destiny approaches this in true form. Bad jokes, immaturity and plenty of junk food. Except instead of high amounts of calories, you get HP and MP. From the moment the game starts it delves into the meta and lampooning everything you loved about RPGs. Now you can expect the standard helping of RPGMaker Pixel graphics, turn based combat, hundreds of items/spells and huge overworld to explore. What makes Doom & Destiny rise above the rest, is its dialogue and characters. Why are they on this crazy adventure? Who cares. Just have fun is the mentality, and It shows. With 20 hours of core story and plenty of side quests. Doom & Destiny is wonderful homage to late night roleplaying sessions with friends, having an adventure of a lifetime!

Based on the first 3 episodes and over 28h spent on the game so far, I must say that Resident Evil Revelations 2 is a surprisingly good title.
I say that, because it was kind of obvious to me, that this title is only for the hardcore RE fans out there, but after playing both the campaign and the bonus Raid Mode, I see that it is way more than the Revelations 1 ever was.
Instead of a cheap port, we got something between that spin-off and an AAA title like Resident Evil 6.
In places it feels like it had a smaller budget, but quite often I find myself to like it more than RE6. It is much less chaotic, the story makes sense, and makes you more invested in it.
Gameplay is still action based (despite people claiming otherwise), but the different playable characters do give a change of pace and style of gameplay. In both cases though, it is darker and a little bit more scarrier than the latest RE titles that we were given. And that is a step in right direction!
Episodic content is a weird marketing choice for me - a RE fan - but perhaps it is a smart move if they want to bring in some new blood. You don't risk much if you buy the first episode, and it's quality may positively surprise you.
I'd give the game 8/10 + I see a lot of potention for Revelations 3 or more episodes. If they were to give us the same quality, I wouldn't hesitate for a second.
Game is based on RE6 engine, so maybe it has an easier start, because I actually like it more than the RE6.
I can imagine better graphics, especially some models (the cars...) but most of the stuff looks good enough (especially character models), which you can't say about the old REV1. Bland rooms and corridors are no more, but I wish that I will live long enough to see RE game on Unreal Engine...
Also keep in mind, that many things have been patched already, with future patches planned, so I hope that the mixed reviews will soon change into positive ones. :)

The world is familiar yet so different. Bright lights of an urban metropolis help make the shadows even darker. These dark areas are occupied by all sorts of seedy people. None more elusive than shadowrunners, operatives offering their services to the highest bidders. Mostly it’s just multinational corporations trying to steal valuable technology or information from each other. But there are also those who have more personal agendas. Whoever they are and whatever they set out to do, they get the job done. And that’s the role you’re able to play in Shadowrun Returns. In the process you’ll get to experience a unique cyberpunk setting where technology meets magic. It really feels interesting from the outset and makes you wonder why there aren’t more cyberpunk games around.
When you create your own custom character, you’ll be able to choose standard things such as gender, class and race. Apart from humans, Seattle in 2054 is also home to elves, dwarves and orcs. This makes for some interesting class options such as the Street Samurai elf who wields a katana and a sub-machine gun or an orc Mage that casts a variety of spells but is also knowledgeable in hacking. The player is tasked to uncover the shady circumstances surrounding the death of a fellow shadowrunner and is hired by the deceased himself through a gadget called the dead man’s switch. You can do it out of loyalty or for the money or both. But you will get it done because you’re a shadowrunner, it’s what you do. From there you’ll stumble upon a gruesome serial killer, you’ll investigate a religious cult and break into a megacorp.
The storytelling is delivered through text-only, mostly through dialogue with various interesting characters. The writing is strong and the story is genuinely interesting. Unfortunately, it does wander off into a pretty silly direction towards the end, but it’s not a deal-breaker. The graphics are simple but pleasing with a mix of 2D environments and 3D characters while the audio is solid if a bit repetitive. All of these elements create an interesting game world with a strong atmosphere. The gameplay consists of a lot of multiple choice dialogue, some very light puzzle solving, a bit of exploration and a turn-based combat system. It’s very well put together, the pacing is solid and continually mixes up the combat and the downtime moments. The combat plays out like a rather simplified version of XCOM. You control a party of up to four different characters and you’ll use their unique abilities and the environment against your enemies.
You can also level up your character in well familiar traits such as strength, willpower, charisma and so on. Shadowrun prefers specializations as opposed to dabbling in too many abilities, the game itself warns you that a jack of all trades is a master of none. So if you’re a Mage, you better commit to it as you won’t be getting that many karma points for upgrading. However, you cannot upgrade your party members. Even though most of them are directly woven into the story, they tend to pop in and out depending on what’s going on and most of the time you’ll have to fill out empty spaces in your party with hired goons.
There really isn’t a whole lot of depth or breadth in here, Shadowrun Returns is a compact, bite-sized RPG. It’s entirely linear and relatively short which is fine because it is reflected in its price. However, it lays a very solid foundation for grander things to come hopefully and it’s simply an enjoyable game on its own terms. I love that Shadowrun is back and I already want more of it.

Then I came back after a couple months and my save game is deleted.  I looked online and this is a common issue, and the game does not and according to the devs will not support Steam's cloud sync.  Better find and back up your save game regularly.  Maybe even before finishing each level, because some of the tasks get really annoying when you play ten rounds to find that you didn't win enough of them, so start over.
So bottom line, it's cheap, tho not as cheap as that Klondike or Spider solitaire built into your Windows install.  You might see where the story is going long before they reveal it.  You may rage quit when you play fifty games in a row without an egg drop.  Your save game may just magically cease to exist. I dont know how to do reviews so here a good recipe for banana bread
2-3 very ripe bananas, peeled
1/3 cup melted butter
1 cup of sugar (can easily use 3/4 cup, or drop it down to 1/2 cup if you want it less sweet)
1 egg, beaten
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
1 teaspoon baking soda
Pinch of salt
1 1/2 cups of all-purpose flour
METHOD
Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C), and butter a 4x8-inch loaf pan.
In a mixing bowl, mash the ripe bananas with a fork until smooth. Stir the melted butter into the mashed bananas.
Mix in the baking soda and salt. Stir in the sugar, beaten egg, and vanilla extract. Mix in the flour.
Pour the batter into your prepared loaf pan. Bake for 1 hour to 1 hour 10 minutes (check at 50 minutes) at 350°F (175°C), or until a tester inserted into the center comes out clean.
Remove from oven and cool completely on a rack. Remove the banana bread from the pan. Slice and serve. (A bread knife helps to make slices that aren't crumbly.)

I've been looking for an old-fashioned RPG ever since playing some old favorites from the Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest series recently. I tried a few JRPG's on Steam that just weren't doing it for me and came across Doom & Destiny while browsing the RPG section and decided to buy it on a whim. It was one of my best impulse buys in a while.
D&D was exactly what I was looking for in an old-school exploration/grinding RPG and on top of giving me the experience I wanted, it also made me laugh along the way. Now, the humor relies heavily on the assumption that the player has a lot of experience with the RPG genre, but I assume if you're interested in this type of game, then chances are you are quite familiar with the games that it lampoons.
Aside from being funny, the gameplay is pretty solid. There's a certain amount of customization that goes into leveling your characters and deciding which powers you want them to equip. The combat can seem a little repetitive, but if you're not a fan of grinding, then you probably shouldn't be playing this type of RPG to begin with. Add in the fact that there's literally hundreds of weapons and items to use, and you have quite a lot of game packed into this little indie. I just finished the main quest which took about 20 hours, but for the hardcore players out there, there's at least 20 more hours of gameplay that you can do after the main story line.
I can't wait to see what these guys develop next and hope that a D&D sequel will arrive someday.

If you were to cross Bladerunner with The Dresden Files into a quality tactical strategy RPG hybrid, the result would no doubt be something very akin to Shadowrun Returns. Shadowrun Returns excels at story telling, the game is rich with lore, well written dialogues that feel more conversational than what most games accomplish, and a structured story full of plot twists and interesting characters. Perhaps my favorite point about the story is that it starts out small-scale, you are on a simple mission to look into the death of a friend, but it slowly ramps up into something larger as the story progresses. To top it off the game is set in a beautiful futuristic game world and has solid tactical gameplay to boot.
More than anything this game to me was about an awesome sci-fi detective story. The mystery and intrigue suck you in, the stellar writing especially in regards to dialogue keeps you hooked. I'm not saying the game mimics what street talk may actually be like in the future, but it was great enough to get me immersed in the street life of futuristic Seattle. The characters within the game range from annoying (intentionally so), charming, grumpy, and likeable; chatting with the regulars throughout the story and going through the different chat options was something I enjoyed doing (shout out to Mr. Kluwe, you're the man, man!). The game's audio and visuals do justice to this story, bringing it to life with stunning hand drawn environments and appropriately mood setting music.
The game's combat also leaves little to be desired. Although I felt the large scale management of the game to be a little inconsistent...for example the money you earn throughout the story can go into temporary lulls, and if you need to do a mission when you aren't expecting it you may find you don't have enough money to buy a full team of mercs. The game runs similar to most other tactical RPG games, especially similar to the XCOM series. You use the terrain to your advantage and in a turn based fashion you move your team about and order them to attack or use utility items/spells. On hard the game isn't terribly difficult and you shouldn't have to think deeply each turn on how to best arrange your team and how to best utilize there action points (how many actions they can take per turn). The combat is a bit sparse at the beginning of the game but as you progress further you start to battle the baddies more often and that's when the fun starts.
Shadowrun Returns is a solid tactical RPG game, and with the addition of the Steam workshop can keep you playing well beyond the twelve hour campaign. The game's story is strong and the characters within are fun ones. It's nice to play a detective style game that isn't a point and click for a change. The game is quite gripping and just like any good detective novel it kept me at the edge of my seat until I got through to the end.

This incredibly atmospheric and scary survival horror science-fiction game, released back in 2008, has recently received a sequel, so why not go back where it all started, to the beginning of the nightmare?
On the colony planet Aegis VII, in the year 2508, a large stalagmite-like structure covered in strange runes is discovered. This ancient artifact, known as a Marker, soon becomes quite dangerous, driving colonists to mass murder-suicide. Soon after their deaths, a mysterious virus entered their bodies, re-animating them in grotesque ways. The resultant beings, known as Necromorphs, seek only to kill others and make more of their kind, with their sharp appendages, tentacles and infected projectiles.
When it was removed to the mining ship USG Ishimura, the Marker began affecting the crewmembers similarly to those on the planet, driving them mad and eventually to killing themselves. Then the Necromorph-creating virus was then somehow brought on-board. It is up to Isaac Clarke, a lowly engineer protected by a hard mining suit designed to protect in cases of zero-g and vacuum incursions, to discover the source of the Necromorphs and destroy the Marker.
Gameplay adheres to the survival-horror staples introduced as early as Resident Evil, though Electronic Arts changed things up a bit; you could strafe (move side-to-side) while aiming, the aforementioned zero-gravity and vacuum areas (in which you had to keep topping up your oxygen with found canisters) were added, and the biggest change in games of this type: headshots do not necessarily kill instantly, bringing into gameplay a tactic known as strategic dismemberment.
The Necromorphs’ life force does not seem to be concentrated in their heads like most video game enemies, but through their whole bodies. Cut off a limb with the decidedly mining-inspired weaponry, and they’re slowed down; cut off two or more, and they’re down for good.
Isaac’s heavy mining suit makes him very slow (there’s no full-on sprinting in this game) but aside from being upgradeable at special workbenches (along with his weapons), is equipped with heavy gauntlets and boots that allow him to finish the job on recalcitrant Necros. It’s also a good idea to stomp any bodies you come across as well, so they cannot rise to harass you later.
This is a very good-looking game, for what it is: extremely gory. You will see bodies of Necromorph victims splattered throughout the Ishimura, and the Necros themselves are, on the whole, totally disgusting; for better or worse, you won’t have any misgivings about putting them down. Actually doing the deed, however, is a different story; as with all survival horror, the main objective is to survive near-insurmountable odds, which sometimes entails watching poor Isaac die multiple times until you get the path of destruction just right. Fortunately, the story is strong, the gameplay solid and the presentation compelling. Five stars out of five for this first game!

My review/appreciation for this game might be considered to be both too little and too late, but 'Mirror's Edge,' despite a few critical missteps, still deserves a heap of praise. Not since 'Chronicles of Riddick' has the first person perspective and moreover, the depth of immersion, been achieved in a first person game. It's believed to that in most encountered situations of adversity, the human instinct is fight or flight. And while 99% of the shooters we see on the market wholeheartedly encourage the player to fight, 'Mirror's Edge' not only allows, but encourages the latter: FLIGHT!!! And that's where the game succeeds. The protagonist in Mirror's Edge is part Mary Lou Retton, part Flo Jo, part Trinity, nicely wrapped into a package of cyberpunk. And you get to enjoy all of her gifts from the always reliable first person perspective. You'll from running to sliding, to flipping to disarming to hanging (and falling if you don't master the jumps) all from a first person perspective.

The setting is new to me, so I can't comment on it, other than, you know, it's got sodding orks and elves in it, like every other vaguely fantasy setting, even if this one is cyberpunk. The combat is very new x-com-esque, and will probably scratch that itch if you're needing a tactical fix. I rather enjoyed it.
Pros:
- Functional story with a few twists and good writing (we're not talking Torment good, but there's nothing to cringe at)
- Good range of character options with no single thing being mega OP
- Deep without being overwhelming turn-based combat system which offers plenty of options
- Lets you choose your team of level-appropriate mercs, freeing you from managing loads of characters skillsheets
Cons:
- Leaves you to read the tutorials tucked away in the menu rather than explaining the systems (possibly a plus if you're old school and find modern tutorials slow)
- Decker classes are probably awesome the 2 or 3 times you need them to do their matrix thing, but have limited options in the real world, largely due to the lack of computers in most environments and effectiveness of shooting things instead
- Arguably too easy if you use the options available to you: none of my characters ever came close to dying in the campaign, but this was normal mode and it's possible I'm a tactical genius and didn't notice.
- A special weapon required for the final mission is intentionally short ranged and small-magazined. This is slightly annoying.
- (Possibly a tiny bit on the short side for those used to epic RPGs, but there's no filler here, so I'll take no issues with it)
I'm told the new campaign is even better, which sounds pretty good to me: wishlisted, as the cool kids probably don't say.

Very good third person action/thriller/splatter game. Great gunplay, shooting the limbs off of your enemies is incredibly satisfying especially since they will change tactics depending on which limbs you shoot off. Shoot off a necromorphs leg, he begins to crawl toward you with alarming speed using his arms. This is NOT a horror game. If you play this game to be scared, you will be very disappointed. In short, buy this game, or be haunted by a vengeful ghost waifu forever.

WARNING: MIGHT CONTAIN SPOILERS!!
My PC specs:
i7 4790
AMD R9 290 4GB
8 GB RAM
Win 10
First off let me start by saying that I haven't purchased the game at launch, I only got it after the supposed PC "fix" came in November.
Now, given my PC specs, I can say that, personally, I had absolutely no performance issues with the game, I was just lucky enough to be part of the group of people who could ran it fine. The only issues I had were stability issues. The game crashed quite a lot for me.
Now I am very aware a lot of people did have performance issues even with better configurations than mine, so on this note I do not recommend this game.
It is simply inexcusable to release such a bad PC port.
With the performance part out of the way lets get to the game itself.
If you are a Batman fan and have some knowledge of the character, the universe and the villains, the identity of the Arkham Knight (which Rocksteady claimed to be an original character) will become very obvious from a mile away. This will eventually make the reveal at the end very unimpressive.
However, the plot of the game is quite good with a few twists and turns (which again can be very predictable). I'm not going to go into further details so as not to spoil too much of it.
Gameplay wise the game is just as good as Arkham Asylum or Arkham City with the exception of: the Batmobile. This new addition to the series, which a lot of people asked for, seemed to be very out of place. It tends to break immersion when you start rolling through the streets in your highly advanced battank, blowing things up left and right, and ultimately causing more damage to the city than the villains. It can be impressive, visually speaking, but thats about it. This is only made worse by the racing challenges set up by the Riddler which can get quite frustrating if you decide to do them all.
The combat in the game is pretty good with some new gadgets and a few new moves added to Batman's arsenal. The counter-based combat mechanic remains just as easy to pull off and as fullfilling as in the previous titles, especially when you manage to chain up your attacks to take out an entire room full of goons by punching their faces in.
A new addition that could've been used more often is the character switching during combat. There are several points during the sidemission where you are joined by one of Batman's allies in combat and you can switch between characters while performing combo takedowns. It is just too bad that there was less of an emphasys placed on this than on the Batmobile sections.
As a conclusion, I want to mention that, even though I have set this as recommended, there are 2 sides of the coin here.
From a gameplay and storyline point of view I recommend this game BUT from a performance point of view I cannot. If you cannot run it comfortably on your machine simply refund it.
It is quite sad that Rocksteady managed to botch this in such a manner. Being the final chapter in their Arkham games series it boggles the mind how they did not strive to put out the highest amount of effort to go out with a bang.
These being said the game offers a very satisfying conclusion to the Arkham series.
TIP: In order to get the "real" ending of the game, you will have to collect and complete all the Riddler challenges scatterd around the map.

Warning for potential buyers: This game requires a controller or gamepad. The keyboard controls are absolutely unacceptably atrocious. They want your right hand to be on HJKL and also hit the arrow keys. That will never happen. Luckily, I had a 360 PC controller, plugged it in, the game automatically recognized it and switched to controller mode, and the controls work beautifully. Play it with a controller!
Aside from the initial shock at how immensely bad the keyboard controls were, this game is really fun. If you like LEGO anything, you'll probably like LEGO Marvel. You can play as a vast array of different heroes and even villains, and beat up bad guys. The game really opens up as you progress, allowing free-roam of New York City after a certain point. It plays a lot like other free-roam games, you have a map with objectives and you can do side-stuff along the way, collecting and unlocking as you go.
The main plot is the only true drawback for me. It's definitely there, but each mission feels disjointed. There's so much that you have to skip because you haven't unlocked a character yet. I spend more time trying to figure out if a shiny unbreakable object is something I can activate than progressing. Fortunately there are a lot of details from Marvel canon and beyond that the development team added to make even the dull parts amusing.
And as always, the gameplay is top notch. LEGO games all feel the same and I like that about them, but they went above and beyond in LEGO Marvel Super Heroes to make each hero play differently. I'm not halfway through the game yet and I've already played as probably 15 different heroes, each with a unique style and skillset. It's just downright fun.

You have four base classes to choose from.  Your sniper deals deadly damage from afar, and unlockable skills come from promotions that make the sniper even more deadly, such as the squadsight, which allows your sniper to shoot at an enemy that any of your team sees, so long as he has a clear line of sight.  Give the sniper armor with the jetpack, or grappling hook, and put her up on high ground and watch alien heads explode.  Fun, fun!
The heavy is for blowing the bejeezis out of stuff.  The heavy can also unlock the suppression ability to pin down an enemy, while another player flanks for the kill.
Your support class is most often equipped as the medic of the squad, but can also learn the suppression skill to help trapped soldiers get out of a tight spot, and can also deploy the smoke grenade to make your people harder to hit.
The assault class specializes in getting in and out of a fight quickly, and with special training, can dodge incoming enemy fire, run and gun, or blast any enemy foolish enough to get too close.
It's more than a shoot-em-up game.  You have to manage your team's finances and research as well, including making decisions involving diplomacy.  Keeping all of the member nations of the XCOM council is a difficult balancing act, and you should build up your satellite and ground station tracking resources quickly, saving those resources where possible in case you have an alien panic that threatens to cause council members to leave.
Researching alien artifacts gives your squad valuable upgrades that will help with the battle, when the alien enemy rolls out the more challenging enemy soldiers.
Overall, I think the game stays true to the original game, but adds plenty of twists and really good game play to update the old classic.

The first Resident Evil Revelations managed to be a great game in it's own right, both on the 3DS and other platforms, unfortunately, there is no doubt that Revelations 2 is nothing more than a poor cash-grab, with next to no effort put into it, at least not on the PC.
The stiff and clunky control is not the typical Resident Evil control from more modern titles, those usually work out well, they feel responsive, and I have never had an issue with them, but in Revelations 2, both aiming- and movement wise, it feels like it was put together in a matter of seconds, without testing the feel of the movement further.
With terrible feedback from using your weapons, the return of the worst element of Revelations 1 (the scanning) but this time with flashlight and pointing fingers (even if you spot a shiny hidden object, you still have to "aim" as if it was an enemy, before you can pick the item up, terrible AI that can easily result in a cheap deaths, episodic segmentation, day-1 DLC practises and originally no co-op implemented for this port, makes it more than clear, that Revelations 2 is not worth your hard-earned money, until Capcom puts some actual effort into fixing the problems with this title.
To make matters worse, the character models have a strange animation skip from time to time, which can result in awkward-feeling movement when controlling your respective character.
Minor fade-outs when opening doors are also present in this title, and we are not talking about the classical "only the door opening"-animation, just a simple opening of the door, just like in Revelations 1, but with an added fade-out to a black screen for 1 second, a flow breaker, and a unnessesary element, which serves no purpose, in an already off-track trainwreck of a title.
The return of beloved characters such as Barry Burton and Claire Redfield are simply not enough to justify the abysmal "production value" of this PC port.
I recommend getting any Resident Evil title, available on Steam, but this one.
Even Resident Evil 6 plays fantastic on the PC in comparison to the 360 counter-part.

Dead Space is one of the most memorable survival horror experiences of the past generation and for good reason. It has a horrifying and bleak atmosphere coupled with the most disgusting and disturbing cast of enemies in addition to a unique combat system and puzzle solving mechanics.
Story: Its the 26th century and humanity has cast out to the stars in order to acquire enough resources to survive, Earth's being exhausted. To do this, special ships called Planet Crackers were built, The USG Ishimura was the first and most famous. One an expedition to Aegis VII, the Ishimura has lost communications with the Concordance Extraction Corporation which is responsible for building the Planet Crackers and saving mankind. The CEC has dispatched a small repair team which includes Security Chief Zack Hammond, Computer Specialist Kendra Daniels, and Systems Engineer Isaac Clarke. Isaac had volunteered for the repair mission so that he could meet up with his girlfriend, Nicole Brennan. They arrive on the Ishimura to find it absent of any people. Soon there after, the Necromorphs attack killing two of the crew members and separating Isaac from Hammond and Kendra. Now Isaac must work to meet up with his crew, rescue Nicole, and escape the Ishimura, little does he know of the true evil behind the outbreak.
Overall Score for Story: 10/10
Gameplay: The gunplay in this game is extremely unique and makes for a memorable experience. To kill the Necromorphs you must sever their appendages which differ from each type of enemy.  The weapons emit a laser sight that lets you know what kind of area they affect and what kinds of enemies they are effective against. In addition to that they all have a secondary fire mode which makes them all the more deadly. You'll be able to upgrade them and your suit via power nodes that are scattered across the ship which will make you able to deal more damage, withstand more hits, and carry more oxygen with you. At first the game is very difficult due to your weak and limited equipment combined with the difficult combat. You will however get better as you purchase new weapons, upgrade your equipment, and learn to kill enemies faster. The puzzles in this game are also pretty fun though they aren't exactly brain busters. You'll have a Stasis ability which slows down enemies and physics objects allowing for you to line up shots or pass through dangerous areas. You'll also have a Kinesis Module that allows you to pick up physics objects and throw them at enemies or fix equipment. Despite the intense combat and puzzles however, this is still a horror game at its core. Enemies will jump out at you, you'll hear strange noises, witness strange events, and be under a constant feeling of dread. The scares are thankfully not recycled over and over and the few that are are easy to counter by attacking first. What makes the game so scary is the developer's ruthless enemy design (you'll have to play it to see it) which instills a sense of shock at first, and the tight, close quarters environment which puts you on a constant state of alert and paranoia. All in all this game plays very well and holds up to most of today's AAA horror titles.
Overall Score for Gameplay: 10/10
Characters: The characters in this game give it much further depth and discomfort. Isaac is a silent protagonist, yet his body language, hallucinations, and few but impacting facial expressions tell you exactly how he feels about the situation he's been forced into. The rest of the cast begins as very typical characters but develop heavily by the game's end. The conflict and mistrust between them turns reunions aboard the ship from what should be something comforting and safe to a tense and paranoid encounter. They are all voiced exceptionally well and are all very intriguing.
Overall Score for Characters: 10/10
Graphics: For 2008, these graphics looked amazing and they hold up very well today. The textures look very good and are convincing. The game is easy to run at 60FPS and can be played at 1080p. There are some nice mods out there but they aren't necessary as the game looks fine in its vanilla state.
Overall Score for Graphics: 9/10
Soundtrack: The soundtrack in this game is also very nice though it is not pleasing in any way. It is mostly meant to add to the frantic and terror inducing feeling of the Necromorphs and it does its job very well. There are a few emotional moments as well and the soundtrack does them justice but due to the pacing of the game itself most of the music is either scary or a slow buildup that's meant to create dread within the player.
Overall Score for Soundtrack: 9/10
Sound: The sound design in this game is very good. The weapons sound powerful and impacting, the footsteps are heavy, the breathing and interaction noises are good. In addition to that the Necromorphs sound frightening and monstrous while emitting the most disgusting sounds as they walk and move. The ambient noises are also very convincing and they make the experience all the more scary.
Overall Score for Sound: 9/10
Dead Space is an amazing horror title. Although dated it still looks and plays great. I'd recommend this game to anyone who enjoys horror games and a challenging shooter. I do however recommend a controller as the controls for this port aren't good at all (personally I prefer the Xbox One controller but a 360, PS3, PS4 or any other controller besides the steam controller would do well). Also, for many modern rigs the Vsync should be disabled as it causes the game to lag a ton. Both these things are easy to fix however and won't make you enjoy the game any less unless you hate controllers.
Overall Score for Game: 9.6/10

I dont know how to do reviews so here a good recipe for banana bread
2-3 very ripe bananas, peeled
1/3 cup melted butter
1 cup of sugar (can easily use 3/4 cup, or drop it down to 1/2 cup if you want it less sweet)
1 egg, beaten
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
1 teaspoon baking soda
Pinch of salt
1 1/2 cups of all-purpose flour
METHOD
Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C), and butter a 4x8-inch loaf pan.
In a mixing bowl, mash the ripe bananas with a fork until smooth. Stir the melted butter into the mashed bananas.
Mix in the baking soda and salt. Stir in the sugar, beaten egg, and vanilla extract. Mix in the flour.
Pour the batter into your prepared loaf pan. Bake for 1 hour to 1 hour 10 minutes (check at 50 minutes) at 350°F (175°C), or until a tester inserted into the center comes out clean.
Remove from oven and cool completely on a rack. Remove the banana bread from the pan. Slice and serve. (A bread knife helps to make slices that aren't crumbly.)

I got this game for 95% off, expecting a crappy game but cards to turn a profit. I was surprisingly impressed.
Faerie Solitaire is surprisingly solid and engaging, easy to play and still satisfying with crisp sounds and a nice style. Gameplay is random but still functional at the start, with new mechanics added gradually to alleviate the problems of random card draws. In a few hours, you can 100% any level by pure skill and planning. The progression system is solid, although collecting all the eggs is too random. The only bug that stands out is the first card not counting for Aura Ring if unused. It can be worked around by drawing the next card and using Undo, but it's something that should've been noted and fixed.
It is basically a free game that would be played online or on mobile, but it is polished and engaging enough to be worthwhile. I probably have 30 hours that haven't shown up due to playing offline. Offline play is one strength I would also consider; achievements unlocked offline will pop on Steam when you check the in-game achievements while online. Keeping this in mind, you can save the last Faerie Land purchase or Challenge stage to complete online, hitting all the offline achievements without backtracking.
There is a fair amount to enjoy in this game, but it will get old after some time. But 40 hours of enjoyable gameplay is worth a purchase for those interested. I'd recommend the game at 75% off or better for most players.

Civilization IV is my favorite game, period. When Civilization V was announced, I was ecstatic as you could imagine. However this game is a let down, even with the DLC's.
The interface is vastly improved, and the game is simpler to play, which is a good thing. Civ IV could be confusing in several aspects, and CIV V is less confusing and more inviting to new players.
However, the big issue I have with this game is warfare. I am very militaristic when it comes to these games, however this game punishes you for it. The One-unit-per-tile rule makes managing a large army a pain in the butt. You have to move each unit one-by-one, every turn. If you move them several tiles away, they will run into each other and cancel out the orders.
If it wasn't for this one flaw, I would love this game. It is honestly a good game besides the military aspect. Unfortunately, this is a Civ game and military is one of the most important aspects, and this game is crippled as a result.
It's still worth getting on sale, especially if you are a peaceful player.

This game will eat up a great deal of your available free time, but it's well woth the money.  Those of us who remember the original XCom will see many of the same features, with some new ones.  The only thing missing from this version is the base defense, but that makes an appearance in the add-on pack, Enemy Within.
You have four base classes to choose from.  Your sniper deals deadly damage from afar, and unlockable skills come from promotions that make the sniper even more deadly, such as the squadsight, which allows your sniper to shoot at an enemy that any of your team sees, so long as he has a clear line of sight.  Give the sniper armor with the jetpack, or grappling hook, and put her up on high ground and watch alien heads explode.  Fun, fun!
The heavy is for blowing the bejeezis out of stuff.  The heavy can also unlock the suppression ability to pin down an enemy, while another player flanks for the kill.
Your support class is most often equipped as the medic of the squad, but can also learn the suppression skill to help trapped soldiers get out of a tight spot, and can also deploy the smoke grenade to make your people harder to hit.
The assault class specializes in getting in and out of a fight quickly, and with special training, can dodge incoming enemy fire, run and gun, or blast any enemy foolish enough to get too close.
It's more than a shoot-em-up game.  You have to manage your team's finances and research as well, including making decisions involving diplomacy.  Keeping all of the member nations of the XCOM council is a difficult balancing act, and you should build up your satellite and ground station tracking resources quickly, saving those resources where possible in case you have an alien panic that threatens to cause council members to leave.
Researching alien artifacts gives your squad valuable upgrades that will help with the battle, when the alien enemy rolls out the more challenging enemy soldiers.
Overall, I think the game stays true to the original game, but adds plenty of twists and really good game play to update the old classic.

Dead Space was a game I originally played on the Xbox 360 when it first came out. So when I transitioned into PC gaming and saw that this game was on steam, I had to have it. Unfortunately, this was not the game that I once knew and loved, it was plagued by a poorly optimized pc port. V-sync would cause a weird kind of delay on the aiming making it especially difficult to target enemy weak spots. Pro Tip for Nvidia card users: Force V-sync through the nvidia control panel and then turn it off in game and most of those issues should be fixed.
In this game you play Engineer Issac Clarke sent to the USG Ishimura on a repair mission as well as a romantic rendevouz with your girlfriend Nicole. Once you arrive you are greated by bloodthirsty monsters that want nothing more than to kill you. Using your engineering skills, it is up to you to save Nicole and escape the nightmare aboard the Ishimura.
This game is great fun (once you fix the v-sync), while most of the missions are basic go there or grab this; this game really shines with its atmosphere and sound design. If you listen closely you can always hear something scurrying around in the vents or off in the distance. Decently long game will take approximately 6-8 hours for new players on the medium difficulty setting,
I would recommend this game to any person that is craving a horror game where you can actually defend yourself from the monster instead of having to play peak-a-boo in the closet until it loses interest and leaves. As well as players who like to try and stay calm under pressure while trying to strategically remove monster limbs while they attack from all sides.

Seriously for £3.50 in the steam sale I cannot recommend this enough, that's about what a pint costs these days, I've played this for hours on end before it was steam cloud synced. It's worth every penny.

This review is for Shadowrun Unlimited....a dlc created by Southwind. Basically, this add on takes Shadowrun Returns & makes it the game it should have been. Don't get me wrong, SR is a very good game in itself but it tells a very linear story that takes around 12 hrs to complete. What Southwind did was take the basic gameplay & created a sandbox like game that a lot of fans of the table top version were hoping for. In Unlimited you have a back story of avenging your brother but while trying to accomplish this you have to become an experienced runner first. To accomplish this you start gaining contacts for different job types you can choose from such as being a bodyguard, cleaning up problems, asassination & delivery jobs. You also meet other runners which you can contact to help you on the different jobs you take on. You have  a lot more different areas you can travel to & different options to complete your missions. I've played about 4 hrs at the time of this review & I am still working on just building my character up for better jobs. That is what makes Unlimited so much better than SR....it gives you a feeling of being in the Shadowrun world rather then just getting to the end of a story.
Unlimited introduces some very cool game elements that expands on the game & helps make you feel even more in this world. You can rent different safehouses to heal between missions & store your gear. You also have 3 new "stats" to check on. Street cred, which affects the quality of missions you can get. There is noteriety, which can cause you problems with the different gangs & corps. Lastly, there is heat. This one is for how the Lone Stars (cops) treat you.
My understanding (this is the best part) is that there is no "end game" for this. Southwind & others are working to continually expand on what is already in play by adding more missions, maps & characters. My only hope is that once the backstory is finished a new one will take it's place. The only downside to this game is I don't think you can import an already created character but it is definately worth starting a new one for this.
In closing I feel that Unlimited took what the dev's put together & made it so much better. If you already have SR than this is a must have. If not but were thinking about it Unlimited should give you that little push to get the original just so you can jump into this excellently done add on. Oh, by the way, Unlimited (not Shadowrun Returns) is free.

I got a 90% off coupon to get this game when I completed a badge, and I thought “What the heck, solitaire is fun sometimes.” Now, I have almost twenty hours on record, and I don’t plan on stopping any time soon. If you see this game on sale and you like card style games even a little bit, it’s worth it to pick it up.
The gameplay is simple enough. You are dealt a board and you have to make chains from your foundation card. In order words, say your card is an eight. You can place a nine or seven from the board onto your foundation, and you can go up or down. As you remove cards from the board, other cards get revealed. It’s simple enough until they start throwing ice cards at you that have to be “unfrozen” with a fire card, or thorns that you have to untangle by uncovering all the cards on a rose. Then, as you remove cards from the board you might suddenly come across an egg. You can hatch your eggs for little pets. Do these pets do anything? Nope! But I have a baby unicorn!
So yeah, this game is highly addictive. Find the game too easy? Try the challenge mode and bang your head against the keyboard. Find the game too tough? Try quickplay or adventure mode. You can also spend in-game currency to unlock “talents” that help make the game easier like the ability to preview the next card in your deck, or the ability to know how many cards are remaining in your deck.
So, to wrap it up, I understand that ten dollars is a lot to spend on a solitaire game, but honestly It’s a great game and definitely worth it to pick it up on sale. The only thing that might turn people off is the “fairy” package the surrounds the play style. Yes, it’s a bit feminine but honestly it’s not going to stop your enjoyment in any way. (Baby unicorn!)

After reading some of the reviews of this game, I started to wonder if we were playing the same game.
First off, there is as far as I know still no CO-OP (Today the 3rd Episode was released) and the framerate is still bad at times.
I first want to comment on the gameplay.
While the controls are OK (basically the same as Revelations 1 without the stupid scanning gimmick, weight off my shoulder). But then they go and "fix their oversight" by giving you this useless sidekick. The second charater is basically pointless and I can not for the life of me think of a possible scenario, why someone, when playing CO-OP, would want to play as the second player. It's a tag along, the character for players, who don't like to play games or don't like horror, just a complicatd USE KEY, nothing more. When they were attacked, I never saw them defend themselves or help out in a fight (Compare this to RE 5 & 6, in 6 in particular the Partner AI was great).
Moira blinded an enemy maybe once of her own volition. You just need those characters to get items, which you basically already see shining but can't pick them up because apparently they weren't shiny enough. You have to use their flashlight/ ability. When you play as Moira you at least have the crowbar to melee through, but since many enemies are walking puss bombs, why would you want to come close to them when they smear your screen with green goop and take a big chunk of health when you're close while they explode. It doesn't stop there. This game is full of those unexplicable design decisions. Like for example the fact, that the custimization parts take a place in your inventory. Not so bad you might think. But here is the kicker. In order to accomodate this change, there are fewer upgrade parts compared to Revelation 1 and you have to get those parts to a workbench to use them and get them out of your inventory. If the ammount of part would have stayed approximatly the same, it would have screwed up their limited inventory system. The skill tree is also a new introduction, that adds little and erodes immersion. You have to BUY the ability for AI controlled partners to protect themselves and fight back!
Another thing that I noticed is the games "funny" notion to trigger spawn enemies out of thin air. RE5, 6 and Revelations did this to a lesser extent. The new enemies would come out of ducts, windows etc. On several occations I got attacked during an encounter and was running between the start and midpoint of the map. I just passed the whole beginning of the map and cleared the whole area. There was no chance some walking puss would have gone undetected and still, somehow one found it's way up even though I just cleared it and there was no way one of those slow asses could have reached me. This happend a lot, especially in episode 3, where they either pull this crap or place the monster in a way that you just couldn't predict. When I say predict, I don't mean the actual "scare" but predict in a sense, that the game wants you to run away, you turn a corner and run into a proximity mine in form of a monster. This isn't there to scare the player or build tension but to annoy. I've gone on about gameplay and I still could go on about the hacking mini game that just had to be there. Hey Capcom, as with your cover system in 6 you apparently heard, that lockpicking exists in other games but never bothered to pick up a good one and copy that. Enough said about that. 1.Stating the obvious
2.Reaction to events don't fit the actual events
3.Reaction to what the other person is saying in conversation doesn't match.
In the 3rd case it's like watching two people have two different conversations. In RE 6 for example, which had also aweful dialogue, the awefulnes comes from the fact that the developer didn't know which campaign the player would play first. So in order not spoil the other two campaigns, the dialogue for the most part was inconsequential and vague. Especially the Leon campaign had this problem. It got annoying very fast. It just makes her look like a spoiled brat. I swear, everytime she opens her mouth, I want to slap her. " Go jump on a Di*do" - This is a sentence, that actually happend. Someone was paid to write this drivell. I had to double check I read it correctly, because I couldn't believe my ears how stupid, out of the blue and non sensical that sentence has been.

I remember starting Hearthstone and quitting within a week a couple years back. Picked up this game a month ago, and still play it now.
TL;DR
With an easy learning curve and rewards being thrown at your face right at the start, it's difficult to not recommend. Matches are decided in the middle of the game, rather than at the starting hand, so it feels a lot more enjoyable. Characters feel both unique and special, and are fun to switch between. Grinding for cards and decks are also made accessible so that paying for cards doesn't feel like requirement to start the game.
-----------
If you want to jump right in, you're given a total of 16 packs (10 from tutorial, 6 from linking to steam), and can build a half decent deck right from the start.
As for the grind, there's all sorts of ways to get packs, coins, and materials. This makes it feel a lot more like playing the game, rather than having to grind for X amount of hours to be "good."
-Achievements
-Monthly competitve score rewards
-Daily log-ins rewards
-Daily missions
-Arena mode (guaranteed 1 card pack)
-Story mode
For measure, packs are 100 coins, and the common coin rewards are 20~40 each.
If you're into that pay-to-win stuff, be ready to spend a lot. The one-time deal is 600 crystals for 6 dollars, and the packs are priced at 100 each, with the daily offer of 50. There's no premium card pack to buy, so you're spending money to buy the same packs that others will get for free, while at the same draw rates for higher tier cards.
For deck variation, there are a set of neutral cards, and a set of cards specific to each character. Building a specific deck might take a while, but I was able to build a strong deck with playing on-and-off in a month's worth of time. That being said, you can probably get a strong deck in a week or two if you play the game consistently. Just be sure to commit to a certain character before making a deck, as each character will work drastically different than the next. Also a character has at least two different play styles, so be sure to pay attention to which ones you're aiming for.
The basics are exactly like hearthstone. Summon creatures to fight, cast spells to control the battlefield, and bring your opponent down to zero to win. During actual gameplay, RNG feels a lot less apparent than in other card games. At the start of each game, you draw three cards, which you can then recycle back into your deck if you choose. Even if you get high cost cards afterwards, the Evolve mechanic of the game lets you stall or turn the game around in your favor to give you a fighting chance.
For Ladder mode, your rank is an EXP bar that will fill as you win, and deplete as you lose. When starting out, you're guaranteed to play with other new players, because after reaching a certain rank, you can't revert to the prior tier. This keeps players who have played longer potentially better decks within their same area, while letting newer players learn and enjoy the game.
In Arena mode, you select one of three random characters, and create a deck to fight others with random decks. Creating a deck is done in pairs, so you're choosing between 2 pairs 15 times to make a deck of 30 cards. After five rounds, you're given a reward based on how well you've done. Regardless, you're guaranteed one card pack per entry into the arena, making you feel a lot better after losing five rounds in a row. Just make sure you're using the tickets, since the normal price is either 150 coins, or a 150 crystals.
Private matches also allow you to play against someone in either standard mode, or in the arena's Take Two mode.
With an easy learning curve and rewards being thrown at your face right at the start, it's difficult to not recommend. Matches are decided in the middle of the game, rather than at the starting hand, so it feels a lot more enjoyable. Characters feel both unique and special, and are fun to switch between. Grinding for cards and decks are also made accessible so that paying for cards doesn't feel like requirement to start the game.

It may have performance issues (depends on your rig). It may disappoint you in terms of the gameplay (there's an unnecessary amount of Batmobile focus).
But even still, I keep coming back to Arkham Knight. The environment of Gotham is great, the visuals are the best they've been, and the quality of life upgrades are just too good to overlook.
Plus Red Hood. I'm a sucker for Red Hood.

It is very hard to write a review about this game without making comparisons to Hearthstone, so I will just compare it to Hearthstone to make it easier, and I will use terms that experienced Hearthstone (or other CCG) players should be familiar with, so if some of the terminology goes over your head, just trust me, the game is good, it costs nothing, so give it a try.
This is the game that Hearthstone could have been.
Shadowverse was designed by a development team led by Jun'ya Iyanaga, who is a Magic: the Gathering world champion and has five MTG Grand Prix top 8 finishes. Even if you have no idea what that means, point is, he is pretty good at card games, and also pretty good at understanding what makes for a good card game.
The dev team at Cygames has learned a lot from Blizzard's mistakes. As of the steam release, they have increased the number of deckslots, added a free arena mode in friendly matches, and released an intelligently designed new expansion that brought the priest-class equivalent to the forefront of competitive play while retaining a fairly balanced class representation on the ranked ladder. Balance isn't perfect, but their balance philosophy is to change cards through relatively frequent, small nerfs, rather than to kill an entire archetype in one go, once a year, as per the Blizzard standard.
The other elephant in the room is the matter of art design and general visual aesthetic. I personally like most of the art, but this is something that is subjective and not really up to me to tell you if it's good or not. But one thing I can say is that if artstyle is the dealbreaker for you on a game that is actually pretty damn good, you ought to rethink why it is you even play games in the first place.
You'll notice that I've now spent several paragraphs talking about this game without actually talking about the gameplay. This is because for those of you who are Hearthstone players (and who this review is intended for), this game is going to feel very familiar. Each turn you gain one mana, and you can play cards from your hand by using that mana as a resource. The differences are in the lack of hero powers, the limited amount of RNG effects, and the presence of the Evolve mechanic.
Evolve is an ability that is given to the first player starting on turn 5 and the second player on turn 4. The first player can evolve 2 times per game, and the second player can evolve 3 times. What evolution does is make your minions stronger, as well as give them the ability to attack enemy minions on the turn that they are played. Ordinarily you need to wait a turn before a minion can attack, but evolve somewhat bypasses that limitation. Certain cards also have additional effects when they evolve, such as dealing 3 targeted damage, or making some smaller minions.
Evolve therefore acts as a safety valve and comeback mechanism. The ability to turn any cheap minion into a removal spell attached to a body is incredible tempo and is much more powerful when you are behind than when you're winning. In this way, there is an inherent safeguard against face only aggro decks because it is possible for all decks punish overaggression extremely hard. On the flip side, since evolution is such an insanely powerful comeback tool, it is sometimes correct to evolve an minion thats been around for a turn purely for face damage, and to expose yourself to an incredible blowout and waste of an evolution point. The dynamic where evolves are a precious resource, but at the same time a necessity to use so as to not fall behind creates a very engaging midgame and lots of back-and-forth tempo swings.
The other thing I'd like to talk about is the lack of hero powers and general card design in Shadowverse. The lack of hero powers means that for classes to feel diverse, their cards need to feel diverse. This was achieved by limiting the neutral card pool, and by expanding the class specific card pools. Each class also has several different mechanics and synergies to explore, which means that just because you're queueing up against a Runecraft deck, it doesn't necessarily mean you'll be dying to Dimension Shift OTK.
This leads to my penultimate point. The existence of OTK and extreme burst decks in this game. This is the thing that can be a dealbreaker to some, and I openly acknowledge that about this game. As of now, there are many top tier decks that either kill you in one turn or burst you for such immense amounts of damage that it is an OTK almost every time anyway. I would argue that this is a design choice that they made on purpose. The very existence of these kinds of decks, as well as the inability to overheal past starting life, means that control decks can never be too greedy. There will never be a control warrior equivalent in this game because of the existence of Dimension Shift OTK. The presence of these kinds of decks puts a soft limit on the number of turns that a game can go to, and therefore a limit on how much time it takes to play a game. While this sounds like a polarizing design choice, and it is, the end result is actually pretty good. Barring some times when those decks were too good (and were subsequently nerfed), the meta usually ends up stabilizing somewhere between a 1/3 aggro, 1/3 midrange, 1/3 combo/control split, which I think is pretty ideal.
I get it, dying to an OTK is not really that fun, but they're a necessary evil, and really, they're basically the same as losing to control warrior anyway. When you lose to CW in Hearthstone, you're frequently just dead long before they actually have lethal. Sometimes the control warrior just draws all their removal and you just run out of gas. You're not dead, technically, but you basically lost already. Dying to DShift OTK in Shadowverse at least cuts out all the waiting because when you're dead against that deck, you have 20 something points of damage headed your way.
Again, balance is not perfect, but I have faith in Jun'ya Iyanaga. Faith that I no longer have in Blizzard's design team. And even though the game is not perfectly balanced, it is pretty damn close. Ladder representation of each class is somewhere in the 10-18% range, which is exactly where it should be for a game with 7 classes (perfect distribution would be around 14% for each class).
Lastly, I want to briefly touch on the topic of game progression for F2P players. I've been playing the mobile version since early August, and I have almost every legendary in the game and own nearly all the top tier meta decks. It is incredibly easy to earn currency, and there is a ton of free stuff given out on fairly regular basis. Just a little while ago they did a promotion that gave out a copy of every neutral legendary for free. With the steam release, they gave 11 free packs. At the time of this writing, there is a twitter campaign for even more free packs.
For those of you who stuck through this long wall of text, thank you for reading. Shadowverse is a game that I am very passionate about because it really just does a lot of things right that no other CCG on the market does. For those of you who are like me, in that your patience with Blizzard has long since run dry and you're looking for somewhere else to spend your time, look no further. Shadowverse is an elegantly designed game that takes all of the good that Hearthstone had, and polishes it to a mirror sheen.
