Zombie games have really come into their own during the last decade; I for one enjoy picking up a zombie survival game now and then just to cause havoc throughout the world. The idea of an open world survival zombie game isn't new and to be honest the last few games such as H1Z1 and Day Z have been somewhat of a letdown due to unfinished content or their empty promises. Dying Light feels like a push in the right direction for all those who try to master the survival zombie genre.
Now I can honestly say this game plays more like a Far Cry or a Dead Island game more so than a true survival game we've been forced fed over the past few years, but I am really quite happy about that. When an open world survival game such as H1Z1 is released I feel discouraged when playing for a few hours only to realize that I am playing a very unfinished game with little to no polish what so ever. Opening up an AAA title such as Dying Light makes the experience so much more enjoyable when things just work.
The campaign showcases the game which is great to see. Instead of hand holding quests and boring gathering missions the game tries to introduce different elements to the user with every quest. The player can experience most of the game’s content without having to do the campaign, but if the player wants an explanation or reasoning behind elements of the game they can find out through side quests and story missions. For example, experiencing night for the first time was a daunting experience due to not knowing what the hell going on, but completing some story missions I find out that “volatiles” appear during the night and are pretty much zombies on steroids and 52 red bulls.
The story plays out well, set in the fictional city Harran. You come across survivors that feel like survivors not just random people who found a gun on the side of the road. The story throws you in the midst of a war between a rebel-ish faction and a pure survivalist clan. I was surprised to see the scare factor really got to me during some story missions. One mission when exploring an abandoned school had me expecting jump scares around every corner. Weaving and ducking around corners only to die from a rebel wielding an axe.
Character development and interaction is another highlight, I usually find myself disagreeing with the protagonist in these types of games, but the background of the main character is pretty strong even in the diplomatic situation he finds himself in. The typical character types are throughout the game as well, the boss man with the ridiculously big chest tattoo, the kid who needs to prove himself, tough female combat commando and the old man who just wants everyone to be friends.
The free running aspect of the game is pretty enjoyable, if mirrors edge was your thing, but you found it a little too easy, Dying Light would be right up your ally. Not knowing if that jump is a little too far or if the roof was going to collapse is a fun experience when throwing hordes of zombies into the mix. There really is no limitation on what can be scaled or leaped from, which is what I really do enjoy about open world titles such as Dying Light.
The night and day cycle is pretty great. The game gives you an opportunity to sleep through the night at a safe house or roam the streets at night, risking those pesky volatiles and hordes of stealthy zombies. Planting a flashlight in your hand, the game wants you to venture out during the night, I am still unsure if free running on the tops of buildings or sneaking through the cover of darkness is the way to go when dealing with night time. It is a dynamic change up in the way the game plays and functions from day to night and would most definitely recommend going out at night and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ your pants when a volatile gets a hold of you.
I usually have an issue with AI in games like this, but Dying Light really showed me how smart zombies can actually be. The way that the zombies move can range in speed, but they always seem to flank me when I least expected it. Different zombies have the ability to climb up walls to meet you for some fisty cuffs on rooftops and other can spit vile fluids at you from below.
Like Totalbiscuit, I too can be prone to sickness from staring at a game with a smaller field of vision. It is true that Dying Light has a FOV slider which can dramatically help with headaches and eye strain, but unfortunately in this case it also came with some bugs when doing so. Changing the FOV to full caused NPCs to oddly pause as they go off-screen in cinematic and perform weird combat animations that interrupted combos. These bugs aren’t game breaking, but it took me out of this amazing world of zombies and made me think about climbing an invisible pole due to the FOV slider.
Three talent trees add some unique gameplay, which felt like it would be needed if the game became stale after 60 hours or so. Splitting the trees up into survivor, agility and combat was a smart idea to allow the player to focus on one aspect if it seems to be lacking. Skill points are generated by experience which can be farmed if need be.
Now the combat is where the game in my opinion becomes difficult. As an experiment, I tried to lure as many zombies as I could see if we had another Batman: Arkham style combat system, whereby only one enemy could attack at once and if it could be possible to defeat whole armies. Nope, I got squashed. Combat is hard and I haven’t seen anything quite like it in a while. I was lucky enough to find a gun in the first few hours of gameplay, but with the very (very) limited ammo around I only had about 14 shots. Using melee weapons I found myself running away from most hordes of zombies and that is what I really wanted from this game.
The crafting system is pretty stock standard; you can buy or find different blueprints which permanently allow you to craft a weapon. With the amount of resources around the world, it was quite easy to craft very simple weapons without feeling the need to bash zombies over the head with only fists. An issue I found with the weapon system was how expandable the weapons are. Buying weapons from the vendor seemed quite pointless due to the repairing mechanic whereby once a weapon cannot be repaired anymore it is rendered useless.
Dying Light was pretty much the game I wanted; I got a little too scared at times, but it added to the frustration upon death and the sense of self worth when completing a difficult task. Not being a fan of the under developed zombie games floating around, Dying Light was an extremely fun time and I don’t think I will stop playing anytime soon. If you're into Parkour and zombies I suggest picking up this game and killing some infected with friends or just by yourself.

I'm asounted at the level of whininess and belligerence directed at this game. Performance issues aside, Resident Evil Revelations 2 is quite good. Many of the people attacking it aren't judging it as a game, and half the criticism comes across as petty and irrational. I never would have expected anyone to get so bent out of shape over no local coop. That's LOCAL coop. As in not online coop. I don't even care if it was mistakenly advertized, the backlash came across as more of a childish manufactured mass temper tantrum than a legit complaint.
anyway
tl;dr version: campaign is quite good. raid mode (while it hooked me) is ok but lazy and very simple to break and make TOO easy.
This game is running off the same engine used for RE6. At first I was worried since RE6 was a terrible game with a terrible engine, but its been tweaked. The controls are tight and fluid and have been reconfigured to be more intuitive and arcadey. It works. Graphically, the game looks great but isn't perfect at the moment. There are frame rate issues, some stuttery camera issues, and some animation issues. Mostly because the game is still new and hasn't been optimized yet.
Anyway, Revelations comes in 2 flavors: campaign and raid mode.
Campaign:
This mode has been polished the most performance wise. Revelations 2 has some stuttering, frame drop issues and goofy graphics issues, but once everything is loaded and working proper, it looks and animates really well. I'm making a point of this since its not the same for raid mode.
If you buy the game for the campaign, you're in for a treat. It is quite good. The story thus far is compelling and mysterious. Capcom has made an attempt to get back to the game's roots by making items and ammunition scarce in turn making the enemies more scary and dangerous as a threat.
However, there are permanent character buffs and weapon modding systems in place that do make the game easier potentially turning it into cakewalk like most recent REs allow.
Also, and I don't know why Capcom keeps doing this with RE games, they've designed the game around a partner system again. So you've got a real dumb AI sidekick that tends to help you in battle by starting at you and getting hit by enemies. Thankfully you can switch between the two characters so if you get downed, you can switch and pick your partner up. Very unlike RE5 when your AI controlled partner would stand next to you and watch you die.
Raid Mode:
Just like Revelations 1, this is the arcadey action mode of Revelations 2. Kind of like mercernaries mode in the older RE's, but expanded upon.
performance wise, raid mode is terrible. Certain maps will frame stutter and lag badly. I have an R9 270x video card, and the first 30 seconds map 6 in gauntlet I is like a slide show no matter what the game's settings are.
Raid mode in Revelations 2 is a departure from Revelations 1's. In Revelations 1, each map was a sequence taken from the campaign and modified into a 3rd person shooter stage. It threw in level progression that would unlock various weapons, characters, and power ups. You could also farm stages for better items. Playing the same level on a harder difficulty yielded different enemy spawns and spawn locations, so each difficulty made the same stage completely different.
However, in Revelations 2, each map is tiny and short and is ripped from RE6 and rarely from Revelations 1 (wtf?). Enemy spawns and spawn locations NEVER change between difficulties. Harder difficulties merely speed enemies up and add more obnoxious status/elemental buffs. Oddly, when enemies spawn they stand up at the same sluggish easy to shoot in the head rate regardless of difficulty. Its actually quite boring. I don't know if this will change once all the chapters are released, but this is what raid mode is currently.
In contrast to the boring levels, Revelations 2 fleshed out the character system tremendously. Instead of having a player level shared between all characters like in Revelations 1, each character has their own individual experience and level gains. As characters level, they unlock new slots for skills and weapons. They also come with their own personal skill sets and earn skill points to purchase and upgrade said skills. Its neat, but seems a bit wasted next to how basic the stages are.
The only thing that remains mostly the same in raid mode is the weapon system. Weapons still come with their own level, but the level no longer exists as a restriction (a lvl 1 guy can use a lvl 75 gun which is nerfed to lvl 1 strength). There are also uncommon guns, gun titles, as well as rare named weapon variations same as Revealtions 1. Rev 2 retains the gun parts system where you earn and pick up and attach gun powerups. Power ups seem to be a little more generic this time however. Currently, its very possible to upgrade a weapon that makes raid mode boring and easy. Very unlike Revelations 1 where the hardest difficulties were still hard as f*ck even if you had a fantastic weapon.
my biggest complaint with Resident Evil Revelations 2: I can't play as the guy who looks like Conan O'brien from Resident Evil Revelations 1.
Anyway, if you made it this far, good job. I wasted too much time typing up a review that will likely not be read.

So far pretty good (currently through episode 2)! I came into RE:R2 with pretty low expectations. I've played through most of the RE's and didn't really like the direction the series went with RE4, 5, 6 - being a fan of the slow paced fixed camera/tank control/very limited inventory system. The original Revelations was also just plain weird and over the top and wouldn't even feel like a RE game if it didn't have Jill and Chris in it.
That being said, Revelations 2 exceeded expections. The game has been slowed down dramatically and ammo is more scarce, placing an emphasis on survival and the story has been decent, if not a bit Silent Hill like. What I do know was near the end of Barry's level of part two, I was praying that the episode would end soon as I had exhausted almost all of my ammo and herbs and knew that I would not survive another enemy encounter. I've not had this type of anxiety in a game for a long time and it was REFRESHING.
Claire and Barry make a welcomed showing, and brings back references from prior RE's (Jill sandwich). On the other hand, Moira and Natalia are more forgettable, especially their pointing finger/flashlight play mechanic. Apparently Claire and Barry can't see ammo boxes and herbs on shelves right next to them without the the other two pointed them out. I do have more hope for Moira though, as her lines are fairly entertaining sometimes.
Raid mode is where this game really shines, and works almost like a mini Borderlands-esque instance. There are level ups for characters, skills, and weapons and the monsters scale with whatever level your hero is. There are also dailies that provide an extra boost in Exp and money. There is a cash shop but it seems that everything offered in the store can be earned through gameplay (so far). Online co-op has NOT been added yet and that is my main complaint. My other disappointment was the throwback map pack. I was hoping to see remakes of original RE 1, 2, and 3 levels, but it ended up just being rehashes of RE 6 and Revelations 1 maps.
The way this game is going so far I would definitely recommend it. Capcom has priced this game fairly and this is a strong selling point for it.

Supposedly this game has less RNG than Hearthstone, but obviously you could still get screwed over through card draws while your opponent has perfect curve.
Evolving is the biggest thing seperating this game from Hearthstone, which helps mitigate bad RNG with good play, but despite this there are still unwinnable scenarios and evolving only does so much. Like Hearthstone, going first vs going second has distinct advantages, and players need to keep this in mind when deciding when to evolve.
Class variety is great, as what seperates each class is not a hero power but their abilities (passives) that change how their class cards play. For instance, many of Bloodcraft's cards become stronger when they are at or below 10hp, so it becomes a class with high risk and comeback potential. Runecraft boosts the spells in their hand, becoming a class where most of their advantage is hidden until they play their hand.
There is effectively no notable single player experience. There is technically a story mode, but it's short and the core gameplay is in online matches and arena. Perhaps there might be more story in future patches, but I wouldn't hold my breath.
Overall, a fun children's trading card game. If you've played Hearthstone, most of the fundamentals will carry over to Shadowverse. If not, it's simple enough to pick up and Cygames is generous with card packs when you start out. However, this is a competitive game by nature, so as you improve, games will inevitably get more rage-inducing, so be prepared for that.

The original Civilization V was great, but when you install the two expansions, this game gets really amazing.
The level of details, situations and events amazes me. The technological tree is great, the trade routes make the game really hard, since you need do trade with other civilizations in order to pay for maintenances, trops, etc, and you can't be self-suficient like you could in the past versions of this game (it's part of the Brave New World mechanics).
The combat system is fairly simple, big units kill smallers units, but there are so many types of promotions that each unit feels different in some way. Sometimes a small army can defeat bigger and stronger armies, if you play it strategicaly.
There are few things that could be better, though. The computer doesn't have a good AI, sometimes they send an invasion army against you, but they send few units each time instead sending them all at the same time, but you can play it at unfair levels and give them lots of advantages to compensate their lack of strategy.
Also, with the Brave New World expansion, winning the game by diplomatic victory is kinda easy.. Too easy for my taste, but you can disable this type of victory.
I'd recommend this game (with the two expansions) anytime, anywhere, always. It's one of the best games I've ever played, and after years I still play it A LOT (more than 1.100 hours so far), making it a game with amazing replay value.

This is in my opinion the best game in the Batman Arkham series. The two previous games were excellent in their own right, but they felt somewhat limited in scope to me. I was always slightly bothered by how I felt contained by the enclosed environments. But in Arkham Knight, Gotham City finally feels complete and whole. You literally do have the entire city to explore, and it is as fully realized as the cities in any Grand Theft Auto or Saints Row games.
If you get the Season Pass with the bonus missions pretty much every major villain is represented, most of them having their own side missions. The Batmobile is something a lot of people complained about, and early on in the game it does feel like you are chained to it at times (though I do understand that the developers wanted to showcase the new toy they put into this game). Once you get used to it though it's a fantastic way to get around the city, and for the majority of the game you don't need to use it at all if you don't want to. There are some mandatory racing or chase sequences though that if you struggle with, you will find very frustrating.
Thankfully there are fewer Riddler puzzles in this than in Arkham City, and for the most part they are solvable enough. There are some race against the clock ones that can be quite frustrating though. While the identity of the Arkham Knight will likely surprise no one, he still makes for a compelling and interesting villain throughout the story. And what they did with the Joker in this game...I absolutely LOVE.
There were lots of complaints about the PC version of this game early on, but I've never had any troubles with it myself, aside from very rare random crashes, but when I restart the game I always pick back up without incident. If you have a PC that is capable of running most current games, you should be totally fine here.
This is definitely in my mind the most satisfying game of the series, with it's very rich story incorporating tons of villains and having the entirity of Gotham City to explore. Highly recommended!

In 1994, a stratgey RPG titled: X-COM UFO Defense was released on the PC. It was a hit, and the series continued, it eventiually got very far away from its turn-based RPG roots (See XCOM: The Buereu). Now, Firaxis has brought everything back to the start with a reboot of the series. It is definatley a triumphant return. The game has been very changed, and even those who played X-COM to death will have a new experience in XCOM. Without getting into every detail, the one thing this game does is simplify the experience. Each unit has infinite ammo packs, there is only ever one XCOM base, and so on. This serves not only to say that this is a modernized version of the classic game, but also as a completely new one. Now, the best part of the game is the customization options. If you get both of the DLCs, the game has a number of different voices, races, hair styles (even Guile hair!) to choose from, allowing you to make a team of whoever you want, and not just having generic soldiers. Personally, my team was Hewiki "Stoneshot" Ignika, Raida "Radio" Justice, James T "NotaRedShirt" Kirk, Barry "Magnum" Burton, Jill "Sandwich" Valentine, and Shaquille "Slam-Dunk" O'neil. When you give your soldiers names, themed armor, and everything else, the game manages to make things personal. When a soldier gets critically wounded, the game will make you freak out. Somehow, the game makes you care for these soldiers, and that is the strongest point of the game. However, the game also has some serious problems. It's pretty hard to care for your soldiers when one of them gets hit, and then falls through the floor, you kind of get taken out of the experience. In my experience though, it hasn't ever crashed, just had some problems with registering flanking, aim calculations, and clipping. Major problems with clipping.
All together, with the amazing experience and the replayability the ghame has, with the buggyness in mind,

This is a game where I wish there was a third option between "recommend" and "not recommend". But I guess I am engaged with the game enough to keep playing it, so I am going the "recommend" route.
To begin with, this game is my introduction to the
IP. I never played the tabletop RPG, nor any of the other related video games. And really, this particular blend of genres doesn't really do it for me. If you don't know, in the world of
, magic and fantasy-type races typical in most fantasy (orcs, trolls, elves, dwarves) genres have "re-awakened" in a futuristic, cyberpunk setting. So basically, you've got elves casting spells alongside cyborgs hacking their way through cyberspace. For me, this is just a mashup that I don't find that intriguing, though I can see how some might think it's really cool.
So then, what pulled me in to trying out this RPG with turn-based combat? I guess it was the beautiful visuals of the isometric maps. The game world is very pleasingly portrayed in great detail.
Unfortunately, you can't interact with much in the game world except for certain areas (hotspots denoted by various icons) where you need to search for plot-specific items that you need to advance the story, or when you need to talk to someone, or open a door. And here I'll point out one of the minor technical gripes I have with this game. Sometimes when I try to click on one of these interaction icons (to open a door, for example) the game doesn't respond to the click. It seems like it happens when my character is moving from one point to another. If my character is in motion, then clicking on a "open door icon" isn't going to work most of the time until the character stops moving. Minor nuisance, I guess.
The other thing I don't like about the game is the inventory system, which I find confusing.There is only so much stuff that you can carry and so you have a stash for anything you don't currently have equipped. However, when going on a mission, you usually have one or more other characters going with you and they each have their own inventories. However, sometimes in the game, it seems like these other characters have their own stashes, but it's not clear to me how to access their stashes. Furthermore, when you go to hire these other characters in your party, you have to commit to the team you've just hired and then embark on the mission. You can't hire your team and then go buy equipment for them. You have to by all the weapons, health packs, spells, fetishes, etc. BEFORE you hire your team but then, how are you going to know which gun, for example, will be most effective with which team member when you haven't hired your team yet to look at their stats. Even when I have tried to buy ahead of time for team roles I am going to hire, when I get to the "loadout" screen before embarking on a mission, I try to equip these things on various characters, and then either don't show up (presumably because the character isn't skilled enough to use the item) or they are incompatible with some other item that the character already has. But there is not enough information provided to the player to know what spells, items, etc are or are not compatible with which characters.
Here's an example, I bought some grenades and when I tried to equip them on my shaman, I got this message that said that the item I was trying to quip was not compatible with the level 5 summon elemental spell the shaman already had equipped? Uh, why exactly? I have no idea.
Not to harp on the inventory problem too much, but here is another example. My character is a decker (a hacker class) and I have leveled up to where I can use better decks(like a portable hacking keyboard or laptop) that hold more ESPs (Expert Systems Programs) and other programs to help me hack in cyberspace. But I have never been able to figure out how to get those programs that I buy from my stash INTO my deck. So I usually end up hacking in cyberspace without any of these useful aids.
So other than the beautiful graphics, I have to say that the writing is pretty good in this game. The character dialog makes the characters have their own personalities, and their motivations are usually clear. The load times between "areas" of the game can feel long at times, but there is usually some good flavor text that gives you some setting and atmosphere for the area you are entering. The story is pretty engaging and starts out as a story about bringing your friend's murderer to justice, but through some twists and turns ends up in the familiar, "save-the-world-from-some-evil-from-beyond" territory.
The turn-based combat is also pretty good and implements a cover system. You have plenty of options when it comes to fighting: melee (fists, bats, swords), ranged (pistols, machine guns, grenades), AoE attacks (some spells and grenades), and buffs and debuffs (in the form of spells or various drug-like substances). Shamans can summon elementals to fight for them, but at a risk. These summoned pets might decide to rebel against their masters and then you have one more enemy on the map to fight.
So even though I have some gripes about this game, I guess overall I would recommend it for those who like isometric RPGs with turn-based combat. I am not sure if fans of
will think this game does the IP justice or not, but to me it seems like they would like this game.

Faerie Solitaire shouldn't be engrossing. It shouldn't be addictive. The artwork is beautiful and the sound effects are pretty nice, but the UI is just north of mediocre, in that it's pretty lo-fi (even for 2010) and the number of different fonts used on a single screen is kind of distracting. There are things that are gimmicky and don't really make sense: the hatching and evolution of pets that do nothing, for example. The writing could use an editor and the voice-acting is…meh. The story is repetitive (once again, I again, yet again), to the extent that I eventually just started skipping the narrative (kudos to Subsoap for allowing this).
Sounds pretty bad, right? And yet, I played through to the rolling end credits in a single sitting, then returned to try for some of the more difficult achievements. Faerie Solitaire is much more than the sum of its parts. It's relaxing and entertaining, and it kept me interested with frequent pet discoveries (I like unlocking things). The only gameplay complaint I have is that, in a casual, play-at-your-own-pace game like this, I really don't like the introduction of timers. Some of the objectives require you to finish within a certain amount of time, and I'm just not a fan of time-based challenges.
I really enjoyed this game. I put about 20 hours into it, which works out to 50¢ an hour at its regular price. Mostly because the presentation is outdated, it's a little difficult to recommend Faerie Solitaire at full price when Steam has so many quality titles on offer for a fraction of the price, but I still think it's worth it, and I'm very interested to see what they've learned and improved in FaeVerse Solitaire.

This is an updated review as of the time of Episode 3. This review primarily focuses on comparing RER1 and RER2.
RER2 got off to a somewhat rocky and "meh" start with the first episode but EP2 and EP3 are significantly better.
Pros:
+The game mechanics are improved from RER1 and they've maintained the fun stuff from RER1 while adding cool and interesting new stuff like the skill trees. The partner mechanics are fun and allow for plenty of on-the-fly switching during combat for strategy.
+Claire and Barry are back! This might seem like not a big deal but if you are a longtime RE fan it's nice to see them back, and they are handled perfectly.
+Good soundtrack. Not amazing but it is atmospheric and gets the job done.
+Good replay value for collectibles and medals-- chapters are short, and they're easy to quickly replay to go back and get extras.
+Raid Mode is more fleshed out and is a full-fledged gameplay mode this time, as opposed to it being an afterthought in RER1.
Cons:
-The story has gotten better with EP2-3 but it's really hard to believe they're going to tie all of this up nicely in EP4.
-Difficulty is a bit average. Especially if you run chapters again to get extras, you will end up with massive stocks of ammo and tons of BP to spend on skill trees, which kind of trivializes the need to bother managing ammo. If you're looking for a challenge, I recommend you play the game straight through once, and don't replay episodes until you've finished the game.
-No online campaign co-op. This was "acceptable" in RER1 since it was a port of a 3DS game but it just feels like a silly omission here.
-As of this writing there are still some stuttering/freezing issues. I've only ever had the game totally freeze on me once, but the stuttering issues are frequent and irritating. They seem to be working on this so hopefully it will be fully fixed.

Played since closed beta on mobile:
Shadowverse is a CCG that will be similar to Hearthstone, to those famillar. Minions, in this game, Followers, have attack and hit points, trade against other minions, and die when their HP falls to zero. If your hero's HP falls to zero, you lose. If the enemy hero's HP falls to zero, you win.
However, Shadowverse, for me at least, is a more enjoyable experience. Here's why:
-Consumer Friendly-
More F2P friendy:
-Free Packs are given out on a pretty regular basis. For example. the new expansion gave out 10 free new packs, new accounts get 10 packs, maintenance compensation and social media events also hand out packs.
-Easier gold generation: Arena mode runs last only 5 games, but you play all 5 games regardless. Entry fee of 150g, and if packs are valued at 100g, break even point is ~2 wins and going infinite requires you to win all 5, but generally 4 wins grants you almost an entire next run, usually around 110-130 gold.
-Hearthstone's quest refresh system is that you gain only 1 quest per day with one refresh and you can stock up to three at once. In this game, you get three quests, but they refresh every 24 hours individually. So if you finish all three quests you will gain another 3 in 24 hours. However, Shadowverse does not grant gold per 3 wins or anything of the sort like in Hearthstone. Therefore the gold value generation in Shadowverse is, on average, equal or higher than Hearthstone's but does not require you to grind out 30 wins, only finish 3 quests.
-Story Mode and Elite AI Practice all grant gold, vials, and or Take 2 Tickets on completing stages/battles, again good for beginners getting a kickstart.
Gold Purchasable Aesthetics:
-Exactly as it sounds, Hero/Class skins are purchasable with both gold and crystals.
-Game Design-
Less RNG:
-In Shadowverse, there is, for the most part, lesser RNG involved in the overall card design. Most random damage cards will only target minions, such as Archer (the Knife Juggler equivalent), Archsummoner Erasmus (Ragnaros equivalent, but can attack as well), and Elf Child May (Flame Juggler). All of these cards in this example have random damage effects equal to the stated Hearthstone cards, except they cannot target the face.
No Weapons:
-The lack of weapons in Shadowverse means that your minions are much more impactful and meaningful when played. No specific classes have access to weapons (or their equivalent) that provide card advantage at the cost of HP with little thought involved.
Overdraw = Instant Death:
-This makes sure that decks that do nothing but stall for time have a limit and ensures that games will never drag on past a certain point, as in you will not find any deck that is like Fatigue Warrior that goes past 40+ turns (Decks have 40 cards in this game)
Classes Feel More Unique:
-Compared to Hearthstone, where classes feel rather similar, as most end up simply playing similar archetypes, Aggro, Midrange, Control, and Combo, classes in Shadowverse feel and play much more differently from each other. Every class has mechanics unique to their own class, and will be listed after this part, and thus there are specific archetypes that classes can specialize in:
Forest - Combo Mechanic
Rune - Spellboost and Earth Rite
Dragon - Overflow
Blood - Vengeance
Haven - Amulet Countdown Acceleration
Shadow - Necromancy
Sword - Follower Traits
Better Rank Rewards:
-Every time you promote a rank, you gain a reward of 100g, and every tier you unlock a title instead. Your rank does not reset every season, but this allows for new players to gain an early boost in gold to get started. Instead, every monthly season the amount of Rank Points you gain will stack into your Seasonal Score Rewards, that is the more you play, and win, the more prizes you get. This includes gold, Take Two (Arena) tickets, Card Pack tickets, and Icons/Card Backs. There is actually incentive to play ranked every season even if ranks do not reset, along with the fact that you are rewarded constantly throughout the season rather than given nothing until the end.
Private Take Two Matches:
-This just means you can play Take Two with your friends as there is an interface to draft and battle your friends with Take Two decks for free, but you don't get any rewards.
-Neutrals/Cons-
No Legendary Limit on Decks:
-This allows for more consistent decks but increases the average vial cost of "meta" decks. However do remember that packs in this game contain 8 rather than 5 cards.
Holographic Cards Cannot be Crafted:
-This does not really have an effect on gameplay/balance but to obtain foil cards you have to rely on RNG, but when you do get them they feel more special/exclusive.

Shadowverse is a class-based collectible card game, there are 7 different classes in the game for which you can buy cosmetic costumes to look like a vampire loli, freedom bird, etc.
If you’re looking forward to playing SV, you most likely came from HS or other CCG background so it should be fairly easy to get into the game.
This game rewards you with a lot of freebies, like card packs, take two(arena) tickets, vials (used to create cards) by completing the story mode or by completing several achievements.
It is usually pretty generous as well with the downtimes as they give you some free packs. (I started with like 20 free packs right off the bat)
It should be worth to note that unlike HS you won’t face only the same archetype nor class repeatedly so fear not! All classes are viable in competitive/take two with more than one archetype even though ones are stronger than the others. Also the RNG is this game is practically non-existant apart from the draw.
One unique mechanic (among many) of SV is the evolution, around turn 4-5 you can evolve your creatures for evo. points (Player who goes first gets 2 points, player who goes second gets 3 points) allowing for some insane combos or tempo control plays.

Does it have all your favorite characters? Sure. Does is have all the offensive things you remember? Oh, yeah.  Does it leap gleefully over the line of good taste, and then keep going?  You're damned right it does.  This is a faithful recreation of an authentic South Park experience. If you are a fan of the show, then you should almost certainly consider picking up the game.
Is it a good game? Um, yeah, I think it is.  It pretends to be a great number of games -- a pixel-hunt adventure, a fighting game, a role playing game -- and doesn't really go deeply into any of them. It makes it a relatively casual game, that lets pretty much anyone pick it up and enjoy the ride. There's a battle or two that made me rage-quit a few times, but all in all, it is very casual. The only complaint I can really lodge against it is an infuriatingly inconsistent savegame feature, that only actually triggers when it wants to, regardless of what the menus promise, and will often gleefully throw away your character customizations. That, and be sure you remember to park your mouse down in the lower right before gaming, or that stupid little arrow will sit on the screen the whole time...

Zombie games have really come into their own during the last decade; I for one enjoy picking up a zombie survival game now and then just to cause havoc throughout the world. The idea of an open world survival zombie game isn't new and to be honest the last few games such as H1Z1 and Day Z have been somewhat of a letdown due to unfinished content or their empty promises. Dying Light feels like a push in the right direction for all those who try to master the survival zombie genre.
Now I can honestly say this game plays more like a Far Cry or a Dead Island game more so than a true survival game we've been forced fed over the past few years, but I am really quite happy about that. When an open world survival game such as H1Z1 is released I feel discouraged when playing for a few hours only to realize that I am playing a very unfinished game with little to no polish what so ever. Opening up an AAA title such as Dying Light makes the experience so much more enjoyable when things just work.
The campaign showcases the game which is great to see. Instead of hand holding quests and boring gathering missions the game tries to introduce different elements to the user with every quest. The player can experience most of the game’s content without having to do the campaign, but if the player wants an explanation or reasoning behind elements of the game they can find out through side quests and story missions. For example, experiencing night for the first time was a daunting experience due to not knowing what the hell going on, but completing some story missions I find out that “volatiles” appear during the night and are pretty much zombies on steroids and 52 red bulls.
The story plays out well, set in the fictional city Harran. You come across survivors that feel like survivors not just random people who found a gun on the side of the road. The story throws you in the midst of a war between a rebel-ish faction and a pure survivalist clan. I was surprised to see the scare factor really got to me during some story missions. One mission when exploring an abandoned school had me expecting jump scares around every corner. Weaving and ducking around corners only to die from a rebel wielding an axe.
Character development and interaction is another highlight, I usually find myself disagreeing with the protagonist in these types of games, but the background of the main character is pretty strong even in the diplomatic situation he finds himself in. The typical character types are throughout the game as well, the boss man with the ridiculously big chest tattoo, the kid who needs to prove himself, tough female combat commando and the old man who just wants everyone to be friends.
The free running aspect of the game is pretty enjoyable, if mirrors edge was your thing, but you found it a little too easy, Dying Light would be right up your ally. Not knowing if that jump is a little too far or if the roof was going to collapse is a fun experience when throwing hordes of zombies into the mix. There really is no limitation on what can be scaled or leaped from, which is what I really do enjoy about open world titles such as Dying Light.
The night and day cycle is pretty great. The game gives you an opportunity to sleep through the night at a safe house or roam the streets at night, risking those pesky volatiles and hordes of stealthy zombies. Planting a flashlight in your hand, the game wants you to venture out during the night, I am still unsure if free running on the tops of buildings or sneaking through the cover of darkness is the way to go when dealing with night time. It is a dynamic change up in the way the game plays and functions from day to night and would most definitely recommend going out at night and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ your pants when a volatile gets a hold of you.
I usually have an issue with AI in games like this, but Dying Light really showed me how smart zombies can actually be. The way that the zombies move can range in speed, but they always seem to flank me when I least expected it. Different zombies have the ability to climb up walls to meet you for some fisty cuffs on rooftops and other can spit vile fluids at you from below.
Like Totalbiscuit, I too can be prone to sickness from staring at a game with a smaller field of vision. It is true that Dying Light has a FOV slider which can dramatically help with headaches and eye strain, but unfortunately in this case it also came with some bugs when doing so. Changing the FOV to full caused NPCs to oddly pause as they go off-screen in cinematic and perform weird combat animations that interrupted combos. These bugs aren’t game breaking, but it took me out of this amazing world of zombies and made me think about climbing an invisible pole due to the FOV slider.
Three talent trees add some unique gameplay, which felt like it would be needed if the game became stale after 60 hours or so. Splitting the trees up into survivor, agility and combat was a smart idea to allow the player to focus on one aspect if it seems to be lacking. Skill points are generated by experience which can be farmed if need be.
Now the combat is where the game in my opinion becomes difficult. As an experiment, I tried to lure as many zombies as I could see if we had another Batman: Arkham style combat system, whereby only one enemy could attack at once and if it could be possible to defeat whole armies. Nope, I got squashed. Combat is hard and I haven’t seen anything quite like it in a while. I was lucky enough to find a gun in the first few hours of gameplay, but with the very (very) limited ammo around I only had about 14 shots. Using melee weapons I found myself running away from most hordes of zombies and that is what I really wanted from this game.
The crafting system is pretty stock standard; you can buy or find different blueprints which permanently allow you to craft a weapon. With the amount of resources around the world, it was quite easy to craft very simple weapons without feeling the need to bash zombies over the head with only fists. An issue I found with the weapon system was how expandable the weapons are. Buying weapons from the vendor seemed quite pointless due to the repairing mechanic whereby once a weapon cannot be repaired anymore it is rendered useless.
Dying Light was pretty much the game I wanted; I got a little too scared at times, but it added to the frustration upon death and the sense of self worth when completing a difficult task. Not being a fan of the under developed zombie games floating around, Dying Light was an extremely fun time and I don’t think I will stop playing anytime soon. If you're into Parkour and zombies I suggest picking up this game and killing some infected with friends or just by yourself.

For some, Shadowrun: Returns was a disappointment; a Kickstarter investment that didn't quite live up to their expectations. To others, it was good enough. For some, like me, the game was a very happy surprise that engaged them more than they had ever expected.
Shadowrun: Returns is, as one might gather, a return to the Shadowrun universe, based on the Pen & Paper role-playing game and the previous NES RPG tied in with it. Following its roots, it is of course a role-playing game, played from an isometric perspective not unlike the older Fallout titles. When seeing this perspective, you'll probably note how absolutely striking it is: The first thing that struck me about this game is how absolutely beautiful it is. The artwork is wonderfully designed and it carries a dark, gritty cyberpunk tone that will bring you back to stories such as Neurmancer and Blade Runner.
The centerpiece with many worlds is, of course, the story, and again, this is an area where Shadowrun: Returns truly shines. Although the story itself might not be the strongest out there, the overall writing makes up for it: The character and story are written with a high quality, and this breathes life into the story, making it engaging, making you curious as to what might happen next.  The written dialogues contain plenty of wit and intrigue with interesting conversation options, very much making up for the fact that there is no voice-acting present in the game.
So, if the story is wonderful and the world equally so, you might begin to see where the detracting factors come in that made this game disappointing for some: The gameplay is where Shadowrun: Returns is lacking. Unlike its late 90's - early 2000's peers Fallout and the Infinity Engine games, Shadowrun isn't very open-ended. It's a linear story that you follow. Sure, there are a few optional sidequests, you can talk to people and you have plenty of freedom when it comes to building your character, there isn't too much free-roaming through the game's world. The world is wonderful, yes, but it could have been utilized way better if there was more freedom.
The combat falls a bit short along with it. It's tense enough, and there is a little strategy involved, but very weak animation and sound design deliver a very hard blow to a system that would otherwise be pretty solid; It feels weak and unsatisfying, despite being quite exciting in some of the harder spots of the game.
Finally, the RPG mechanics are lacklustre when compared to other titles. Although the progression tree does its job pretty well, there is no proper way to equip yourself during missions, no true 'inventory' besides utility and weapon slots and generally it feels as if there are just a few features missing in this department that would have truly helped the game become better.
So, what do we end up with? A very story-oriented game with a wonderful world to play in. The gameplay might not deliver all the time, but it's just strong enough to hold together the rest, and if the combat doesn't provide enough motivation to keep playing, the writing most probably will. If a darker, cyberpunk world to play around in for a bit appeals to you, Shadowrun: Returns is most definitely worth playing.
As a final note, it must be said that the game is packed with a reasonably strong modding tool and Steam Workshop compatibility, so when you're done playing you can play user-created content or have a go at making some yourself!

I purchased this game on a whim. When a game is on sale for less than five dollars it is difficult to talk yourself out of purchasing it. This might just seem like every other roguelike pixel art game that crawled forth from the bowels of uncreative game design...but this one is different. This game actually gives you the feeling that you're lost on a distant planet because you don't know what to do.
One of the more attractive parts of the game is how skill based the gameplay can be. Sure, if you're lucky with item drops and can manage to purchase enough to make yourself an aoe wood chipper the game becomes fairly easy. But it takes a lot of time as the amount of enemies spawning increases almost as much as their power. This makes it much more efficient to be better. If you can use the character you are playing efficiently you can beat this game in anywhere from 30 minutes to two hours. This brings about the main reason you play the game, the more times you beat the game, the more enemies you defeat, and the more creatively they are destroyed, the more you are rewarded. The ways you unlock items and characters are almost as satisfying as the unlockables themselves, with requirements ranging from beating the game to aquiring all of the food themed items in one run through.
The characters are shining beacon in this games portfolio of awesome. Each one is completely different in feel from the last. This totally reinvigorates the game with every unlock, as the game feels completely different with some characters requiring twitch reflexes to survive, and others leaning more towards skillful combos to be successful. The bottom line is that each character feels different, has a distinct and colorful personality, and is well balanced with none seemingly overtly overpowered.
If I had one bad thing to say about this game it would come in the form of the multiplayer, although you don't need to port forward to play online it is unnecessarily complicated, making this a better game to be played on LAN or just hot seat. Besides that multiplayer is very satisfying and becomes a grudging competitive co-op experience since the items are not shared. You of course want all the sweet swag to mow through enemies, but you also want your partner to be helpful in the late game, so it becomes an interesting balancing act of greed and charity.
To wrap up this gushing session of my love for this terribly underappreciated game, I just want to say at least put this on your wish list. This is something that I could have completely missed out on and never been the wiser. But after playing this game I can honestly say that I will never stop playing this game. It may not be my most played, I may not ever unlock everything, but I can say that I will always come back to this game when I'm looking for a good time.

SO I have finally got round to playing what people refer to as one of the greatest games in histoy. I was looking forward to seeing what the hype was about, and have come to the conclusion that I really just don't get it. Was it a bad game, definitely not.
People go on about how it was revoluionary in graphics, combat, atmosphere and story. I am not going to compare it to modern games, rather games that came out at the same time or before. Keep in mind that DOom 3 was released 3 months BEFORE Half Life 2, as I will be using this in my discussion.
First off, the combat. This is something that I found to  be a major let down. The guns did not really feel great. The best gun feel as of the time of release (for me) was the single barrel shot gun from Doom. It just had the right kick, and was a pleasure to use. The Sniper rifle from Unreal Tournament, another gun that just felt satisfying, regardless of whether it was a head shot or not.
What the combat did do right was AI. The AI in this game is awesome, and the different enemy types were very varied in how you would deal with them. The use of physics objects to change their pathing was definitely something that kept the game interesting.
Now I will move onto graphics. The graphics for the time were definitely good. No two ways about that, they even hold up ok today. But compare this to Doom 3, where many people for many years after release were not able to run the game on full settings, I find the graphics in Doom 3 to be extremely well done, even by todays standards, you can still happily enter and see reflections, blood splatters that don't look aweful, amazing lighting, etc. Half Life 2 had the advantage of showing off with large spaces, but Doom 3 excelled in regards to the fine detail.
Atmosphere is something Half Life 2 nailed pretty well. Again I compare to Doom 3, where the atmosphere was also exactly how I expect the developers wanted. You felt like you could be jumped at any second, the lighting flickering was great, etc. Half Life 2, again being a more open game, did its job rather well in making the world feel large, and the city feel alive. The numerous NPC's scattered around the place really gave a sense of survival under opression.
Now finally, the story. I can see that this story could have been amazing. But none of it is really explained at any point. And whether that is a quirk of the series, or whatever it is meant to be passed off as, it prevents me from caring about what it is that I am doing. I keep going to places because I am told to. I felt nothing for any of the characters, and this could come down to the silent protagonist. I personally am not a fan of that in story telling as it jsut doesn't give me a sense of what the main character is thinking. And as for the administrator, I have no idea who this guy is and what his role is, or whether or not I should take up some offer that he makes, because there is absolutely nothing to give away what he is offering. A lot fo the dialog just feels like filler to me, without ever really driving the story forward. And then there is G Man... Again, story really looks like it could have been absolutely incredible, but this is only really hinted at,
Two things I found really annoying:
- The vehicles: The implementation of the vehicles was infuriating. I could not believe how poor they were to control. I've used them plenty in Gary's Mod, and hoped that Half Life 2 would have some better control for them, or less "realistic physics". Honestly, going for game play is a much better idea, because that will lead to fun. Going for physics is a gamble, and might be interesting for a short time, but wears down quickly, especailly when there doesn't feel like there is any weight to the thing you are driving. Seriously feels like I was flying around ina  tissue box in the air boat, not a large metal thing.
- Trying to figure out where the hell to go: On numerous occasions, there is someone calling out to you, or someone says "go to X" (seriously,m get to the horse was one of the worst ones). You are then looking around trying to figure out how to get somewhere after you have identified the destination. Now it would be more acceptable if it was some form of physics puzzle, but trying to find a tiny little beam that goes in theopposite direction from the objective, and leads to a little ledge really isn't good enough indication.
Other than some of the destination finding, the map design was really quite good. The environments felt large, and even the vehicle sections that I didn't like had good map design for the purpose they needed to fulfill. Ravenholm was really a brilliant map, and was a pleasure to work my through, both horizontally and vertically. Really, really good job on that one. Not really sure that there was a problem with any of the maps, most of them were of very good quality.
SO, in closing, i finished the game in around 9 hours, and that is about it. I am neutral on the matter. It had some cool features, mainly the AI and some of the physics, and it had some really poor ones, like the vehicle control and the trying to figure out where you are going.
I'd give it a 7/10. Get it, but don't expect one of the greatest games, expect a decent FPS with some neat tricks.
You start the see the cracks and faults very quickly.

Shadowverse is a class-based collectible card game, there are 7 different classes in the game for which you can buy cosmetic costumes to look like a vampire loli, freedom bird, etc.
If you’re looking forward to playing SV, you most likely came from HS or other CCG background so it should be fairly easy to get into the game.
This game rewards you with a lot of freebies, like card packs, take two(arena) tickets, vials (used to create cards) by completing the story mode or by completing several achievements.
It is usually pretty generous as well with the downtimes as they give you some free packs. (I started with like 20 free packs right off the bat)
It should be worth to note that unlike HS you won’t face only the same archetype nor class repeatedly so fear not! All classes are viable in competitive/take two with more than one archetype even though ones are stronger than the others. Also the RNG is this game is practically non-existant apart from the draw.
One unique mechanic (among many) of SV is the evolution, around turn 4-5 you can evolve your creatures for evo. points (Player who goes first gets 2 points, player who goes second gets 3 points) allowing for some insane combos or tempo control plays.

Intriguing, mysterious, and intense; words I’m surprised to find myself using to describe the pixel art styled Risk of Rain.  Mind, I might be over impressed by a bit since my tastes tend to lie in games containing HD explosions, but I’ve got respect for a game with this depth of detail on multiple levels.  Side scrolling roguelike Indies don’t tend to keep my attention for long, let alone so thoroughly and engagingly.  Panic, pace, power, and other words to compliment that alliteration will decide whether you thrive on the bounty of fallen enemies or fall to the overwhelming strength of your opposition.
The gameplay elements held within are a maddeningly delightful conglomeration of luck and skill, with different ways to set up each game uniquely and provide a new experience.  Most of the characters and items you will come to know and love need to be unlocked through various tasks.  In light of its position as one of the hardest games I’ve ever played, Risk of Rain does let you start off slow.  Each game can be set with one of the three base difficulties: drizzle, rainstorm, and monsoon.  After starting any round, the base difficulty will slowly increase every subsequent minute starting from ‘Very Easy’ and escalating to ‘HAHAHAHA’, producing more powerful and numerous enemies.  Playing for the first time on drizzle is akin to riding a bike for the first time; if the bike’s handles were actually arms actively trying to punch you right where the sun don’t shine.  Also, the bike is slowly growing more arms specifically to hold you still.  That is to say, it’ll be even harder than you think at first while still being fun, and by the time you hop on your hell cycle that travels just under the speed of light and is comprised entirely of the pure essence of your own doom,  you’ll be ready from slowly working up to that point.
You aren’t totally on your own on your hypothetical abuse bike, fortunately.  Scattered around the mysterious planet are various chests, shrines, and pods filled with tiny imps to slaughter for items.  With a wide array of functions performing defensively or offensively, passively or actively, you’ll spend most of your initial playthroughs learning what items do what and dying.  With no modifiers unlocked, luck will be a large factor in your survival as you learn maps and their variants, what gives items with varying luck/cost/frequency, and just how fast some enemies can make you weep with frustration.  Better yet, weep with your friends in up to four-player cooperative play!  Also make sure you’re distributing items properly, or doom your allies into utter defenselessness.  Items can range from almost-useless-but-fun to actually-useful-because-LASERSPEWPEW, with things like barbed wire, to damage one close by enemy at a time, or the ceremonial dagger, to cause enemies to fire heat seeking unholy bolts at the opposition.  Conveniently for you (inconveniently for the characters), you’re stranded on a mysterious planet after being shot down in a space train carrying a large amount of special cargo, so there is no shortage in number or variety of relics and munitions to fight with.
What really got me with Risk of Rain was the lore behind everything.  Normally I just hop in and play a game with little concern for why I’m running from point A to point B obliterating everything in between, but the endings each character receive on beating the game caught my attention.  Without spoiling anything, even just the couple lines of text provided to conclude a character’s experience provides a secondary perspective, wrapping everything up in an eerie package.  The enemies in game are fun to fight, appear appropriately otherworldly, and vary from map to map, but the art and descriptions in the item and monster log paint a creepy picture of the twisted nightmare the survivor(s) face.  Wrecked on an unfamiliar planet, alone, with only supplies to scavenge, one can only imagine how disheartening it would be to see these malevolent creatures in endless attack.  A mask constantly erupting in flame, focusing extreme heat over long distances.  Floating, teleporting beings with a single red eye always locked on theirs, slashing with razor sharp talons.  Beings seemingly made out of light towering overhead, materializing to deliver crushing blows that shake the very ground on which you stand.
Even the items you depend on for survival imply long term consequences even if you survive.  Take the jar of souls; upon use, it creates ghosts of all the enemies on screen that fight on your side.  Neat!  What’s the description?  “The recording only contains wailing and screaming.”  Jeez man, that’s freakin’ dark.  The ceremonial dagger I mentioned earlier?  “Finally found the heretic.  Foolish boy, thinking he could save his sister.  With the knife returned, we can continue our rituals.  Ah…  That should please Her.”  Holy crap, what am I even using?  It makes you wonder what it’s like to do what it takes to survive, only to find out that victory only brings living with the results of shooting yourself full of Soldier’s Syringes just so you can attack faster until the drugs likely do you in anyway.  Heck, even considering all of this made me hear the soundtrack itself differently; it sounded more suspenseful, alien, and all around captivating…
Visions of potentially endless horror and scarring aside, everything about Risk of Rain bundles into one amazing struggle.  I didn’t even mention the various artifacts one can find and different map variants to provide new elements such as Glass Cannon, where you do 500% damage, but also have only 10% health.  Different modifications can shift a game more towards skill, luck, or just how dead you wanna be in the fastest possible way.  For the most fun, in my opinion, grab a friend, skip right along into almost certain doom, and make dominate the very concept of death and conquest.

I love the graphics on this game. Very immersive, very dynamic, and truly gorgeous (for being an apocolypse). I tend to play with the graphic settings a LOT in all the games I play to get the best possible graphics while still managing decent framerates. After reading other reviews stating that this game requires some beefy hardware to play maxed out, I was worried that my system may not be able to hang. After spending some time in the video settings, I was pleasantly surprised to find that my machine can play this game very well at high settings (note, no Ultra settings as of yet).
My Specs:
i7 2.8ghz (first gen, not overclocked)
nvidia 760
8gigs of 2000mhz RAM
128gig SSD drive
Video Setting Adjustments:
1920x1080, fullscreen
All settings turned "High" or "On" (unless otherwise noted)
Motion Blur- OFF (this one killed my fps, def need a better graphic card to enjoy this feature)
Vertical Sync- OFF (plays with less screen tears, but max fps is 30. Compelling evidence shows a nice visual @ 60fps)
View distance set a click or two ahead of 50%
I play with these settings and average 43-62fps, with occasional dips. Only the cutscenes seems to drop my fps to 17-28fps. Personally, I don't mind laggier cutscenes as long as the actual game isnt giving me problems.
To squeeze a few extra fps out, turn "nVidia Depth of Field"-OFF.  Its a nice, subtle effect, but it can cause dips for the 760 vid card.

In short, this is a worthy successor to the throne, whilst creating its very own in the process.
Being a veteran of the old X-Com series from Enemy Unknown (1994) to X-Com Apocalypse (1997) with a touch of the spinoffs like Interceptor, it would be humble of me to state that I'm a fan of the game, its universe, and the genre it resides in.
Admittedly, the news of a new X-Com game was a mixed blessing to my eyes. We all wanted the original to be remade in next-gen glory. What we get now is an honest homage of the original, lovingly reimagined for today's audience complete with its focus vs aliens (with a majority returning with a reimagined and even cooler look), turn-based squad tactics with global defense strategy on top, and in my eyes, more than a worthy successor to the throne that X-Com sits on and moreso, becoming its own thing. This is why I refer it to XCOM, instead of X-Com of old.
I would highly recommend this to anyone who loves strategy (SRPG/TRPG-style like FF Tactics would feel at home), loves emergent stories from your experiences (that favorite soldier making a valiant last-stand to save the rest of his squad will stick to you far longer than a ham-fisted voice-acted cutscene that many other AAA titles try to pass off as something important), and loves to play the odds, which are always stacked against you.

Does it have all your favorite characters? Sure. Does is have all the offensive things you remember? Oh, yeah.  Does it leap gleefully over the line of good taste, and then keep going?  You're damned right it does.  This is a faithful recreation of an authentic South Park experience. If you are a fan of the show, then you should almost certainly consider picking up the game.
Is it a good game? Um, yeah, I think it is.  It pretends to be a great number of games -- a pixel-hunt adventure, a fighting game, a role playing game -- and doesn't really go deeply into any of them. It makes it a relatively casual game, that lets pretty much anyone pick it up and enjoy the ride. There's a battle or two that made me rage-quit a few times, but all in all, it is very casual. The only complaint I can really lodge against it is an infuriatingly inconsistent savegame feature, that only actually triggers when it wants to, regardless of what the menus promise, and will often gleefully throw away your character customizations. That, and be sure you remember to park your mouse down in the lower right before gaming, or that stupid little arrow will sit on the screen the whole time...

As someone who is very fond of the likes of Final Fantasy Tactics and Tactics Ogre, I picked this up with little trepidation.In short, this is a turn-based strategy game in which you control a team of up to 6 soldiers in battles against alien invaders. It's quite easy to pick up while the aliens are ruthlessly efficient at murdering your poor soldiers. It's not a resource intense game to run (score if, like myself you rely on a laptop for your PC gaming fix) thankfully. Due to the small amount of soldiers you command compared to previous titles, you really have to think strategically in order to outsmart your extra-terrestrial foes. Using less important members of your squad as bait just isn't an option. I've sank quite a few hours into this as I feared I might. The aliens are nicely varied and require different strategies in order to be vanquished. The level and mission design is less so but this isn't a big problem.
There are issues, however. These range from slightly irritating such as the frame rate dropping to single figures when a beserker moves to aliens spontaneously appearing behind your squad. There's also a high number of bugs, reportedly though I've only had to reload a level once.
Overall, I'd consider this to be one of the best games I own. With the expansion out, there's no reason whatsoever not to pick this up if you enjoyed the older games, or have even a vague interest in using your noggin instead of the usual run-and-gun approach.

I've played turn-based strategy games for over 30 years, and I have to rate this in the top ten.  Excellent Turn-based strategy game.  This is squad-based, with up to six characters that you control in a round-robin.  You can select them out-of-order on your turn if you need to make tactical changes.  The weapons are varied and interesting, and the story line is pretty involved and takes a while to get through.  The replay value is pretty high.  Although there are a finite number of scenarios and maps, where the aliens show up on those maps varies.  For the UFO landing and crash sites, the insertion points are randomly generated.  Well-thought out and pretty polished.  I've yet to run into a game-related bug, and in an era of buggy releases, that alone gets it a high recommendation from me.
Drawbacks:  Flying units are at times difficult to position.  Try changing the camera angle if there is a movement spot that you just can't seem to get to.

Its hard for me to put into words just how great this game is, I honestly can't sing enough of its praises to be truthful. The entire game is rich and full of atmosphere, really setting the mood for the setting it is placed in. The game had me firmly in its grasp the entire time I played it and not once did it let me go, never breaking character or form in a way that jarred me out of the experience.
The game's character creation is really straight forward and easy to understand and especially flexible, so if you find yourself dislikeing the path you set yourself on but happen to like another class as long as you do so early enough you can more or less cross class and still be rather effective!
The game is turn based so if that's your stick hop right on in! It's challenging, but not in the punishing way.  I've never had something in the game bad happen to me that was anything less than poor performance on my part. It's never made me feel like I've been cheated out of a win or into a death. Only that I made a stupid move and ended up dead or lossing the battle becuase I failed a requirement.
Every character I ran into was full of life and unique in their own right, I've never met someone in the game I've even actively disliked! Well, save some of the villians and that was only in the sense of. "Jeez, what a♥♥♥♥♥♥" Rather than the usual, "Ugh what a cliched loser." The only real complaint I have in the area is that you dont really get to associate much with the some of the npcs. By that I mean become real tight friends with them. Ie: Lets say I stroll along and help out vendor A or give him something he wants. While it's acknowledged that I've done right for him verbally, they dont really give you any discounts or anything.
Heck other than really asking them about their past and getting to be chummy with them you don't really get to interact with them much outside of that, save with the exception of like: Coyote. None of the npcs really give you any discounts and the like. Though if your playing the game right you wont really need the money to be honest.
Though I suppose in the end its only really a minor set back if even one at all, considering that they were very three-d and interactive characters. It was a significant step up from all the two-d card board characters that you get for npcs a lot lately. I could actually feel and even would go so far as to say, loved going back to talk to them on a regular basis.
Another thing I loved was the fact that I had all sorts of ways to solve any problem I ran into, each class had its own unique way to solve or deal with things that they ran into. Especially out of combat and I rarely ran into a problem that I couldn't solve in muliple ways myself.
I'm going to stop here because I'm more or less fan girl rambling at this point, but seriously if you've got the spare cash to shell out for this game. Do it, it is well worth the price, I've frankly had significantly less fun on sixty dollar games. For fourteen ninty nine this game is a total steal. I can't believe I how lucky I got on the flash sale back with this, I almost feel half  guilty for getting it as low as I did.
But long story short, the game is great, damn great if you wanna get down to it. I only hope that they pump out more dlc for this. All the content I've played so far is a massive explosion of awesome. Any of you guys still on the edge for trying it just give in. Trust me its worth that price and that much more if you can afford it.

2002.
GTA: VC is coming out.
This was a game way ahead of its time.
If GTA III was, no doubt, a breakthrough, it wasn't that perfect.
Vice City, on the other hand, was.
The main change of time and place was spot on. Miami, 80's, blood, drugs, sex and rock'n'roll.
With combination like that it couldn't go wrong, and it didn't.
Polishing the predecessor's engine and graphics, VC expanded everything: map, weapons, cars, abilities and so much more. But the most important part was that it did it more subtle than San Andreas, for example.
To have this kind of freedom and variety in the open world game was completely mindblowing 14 years ago.
And I still think that this is and probably always will be the best GTA game for me.
The story is a classic from-bottom-to-the-top-Scarface-like journey. And although it's nothing spectacular, all well-written characters, funny lines of dialogue and memorable missions made it special.

This unassuming rogue-like indie which at first appears simplistic in both aesthetics and game design quickly proves to be both a deeply challenging and immensely rewarding experience. Featuring a permanent death game mechanic, you take control of one of several unlockable classes, all with vastly different play styles which dramatically change the way you play the game. As your character moves through the five randomly generated levels you gain XP and unlock passive and active abilities which can have a huge impact on how your character performs in combat. One of the most interesting aspects of the design is the concept that time=difficulty. The game begins at "Very Easy" and simply through the passage of in-game time slowly ticks over to "Easy", "Normal, "Medium", etc., there's an achievement for surviving 40 minutes and trust me when I say you won't get there on your first play-through. Once you die, you start again from the very beginning (hence, 'permadeath'), however this is much less frustrating than it sounds and in fact you never feel cheated by the game, chances are if you died it was probably your own fault. With plenty of different classes, secrets and unlockables, there's always something to strive for even if you've beaten the game. To top it off the game also offers both local and online co-op. Another great example of how indie game developers are creating some of the most unique gaming experiences that are easily on par with AAA titles in terms of both challenge and pure enjoyment.

"Like Hearthstone, but better" is pretty much the simplest way to explain this to most people.
The game takes a lot of the core design elements from HS to make for smooth online play. Each player has their turn, there are no interrupts, etc. Where HS leans heavily on RNG and has questionable balance between classes, though, SV goes very light on the RNG has has multiple viable decks for all classes at all levels of play.
SV also trades in a lot of HS staples like Weapons, Hero Powers and Secrets for new tricks like Countdown Amulets, Necromancy, Spellboost and the biggest mechanic of all: Evolve. Evolve is a game-changing, tempo-gaining mechanic that seems simple at first but has quite a bit of depth. You start the game with a few Evo Points and starting on turn 4 or 5 you can Evolve any follower you control which typically gives it a buff (usually +2/+2) and Rush (like Charge in HS but it can only attack other followers) but special followers will have other effects when evolved. Evo Points are POWERFUL and really set SV apart from HS and it's other clones.
As for the business model, it's F2P and very fair. At least on par with HS, if not better. Newbies get a lot of freebies and there are login rewards, daily missions and monthly score rewards that all feed you a steady stream of cards. There is also a crafting system much like HS's whereby you liquefy cards you don't need and use your vials to create new ones. I'm quick to knock bad F2P practices but I have nothing to complain about here.
Did I mention free friendly Arena matches? There are also free friendly Arena matches.
Verdict: Try It! It's free!
