Shadowrun Returns is a great game.
Think Lord of the Rings meets the Matrix for the setting : orks, elves, trolls, dwarves and regular humans dwell in the shadow of mega-corps, facing the many perils of a cyber-punk low-life. They fight, charm or oustsmart their way around the many dangers of this world with guns, cybertech and magic. The general setting is vibrant and offers a great potential for many stories.
The official first campaign is good, but the excellency comes from the User Generated Contents, some of which are better than the original game. Shadowrun's online community offers a lot of different storylines that make this game virtually immortal : play as an elf shaman, a troll bruiser, a dwarven mage, an ork street samurai or a human cyber pirate (or any combination of them, or a character of your own design), assemble your team of runners and advance through the myriad of high-quality mods. Each character has its advantages and drawbacks, so a balanced team is often the best option, though sometimes brute force, magic or technological capacity can make the difference.
On the gameplay, it is rather intuitive : 50% RPG, 50% turn-by-turn tactical fighting (à la X-Com) with varyinng proportions depending on the mod.
Some "classes" are better suited to some roles than others but the progression system allows you to create your own build : do you want your shaman to have proficiency in firearms ?  Do you prefer him to be a pure spellcaster and go mage/shaman ? Do you want him to be extra-tough ? Do prefer to concentrate on invocations and shamanic support spells ? Do you want to sacrifice some of your spellcasting capabilities in favour of cyberware ? All builds are possible and all of them work, with various advantages and drawbacks !
The different races help for the feel of the game but have ultimately little impact gameplay-wise apart at the very begining or at the very end of a campaign. Choosing to be a tough troll or a gracefull elf will give you some minor changes in starting stats and a different ultimate potential, but for most of the game the different races don't really matter.
Overall, this great game is made awesome thanks to the online community (most of which is here on Steam).

I wish I could recommend this game. I really do. In terms of the positives, the gameplay is fun, although simple. There is a robust cast of characters from the Marvel universe, each with their own unique abilities and many of which that have multiple costumes and so forth. There are some puzzle areas where characters must work together to overcome an obstacle. There are plenty of collectibles to keep you playing and keep you coming back.
Now for the reasons I cannot recommend this game. I cannot tell you the number of times I ran into gamebreaking bugs. There were so so many and all of varying types. In some areas where an event is supposed to trigger, it simply doesn't and you can no longer progress, forcing you to restart from your last save point or the beginning of the mission. Other times, your character can end up in an infinite death loop, again making it impossible to progress. Then there are times when you switch to controlling one of your other characters who the A.I. managed to trap behind a ladder. Try killing him and he respawns in the same place, right behind that ladder, still stuck. Again, this makes it impossible to progress. Add to this the occasional crash and there you have it. The game becomes too damn frustrating to want to play anymore. And this isn't a once-time or occasional thing. These game-breaking bugs occur REGULARLY. When I looked some of these bugs up, I found guides to the game that specifically had to warn you about these bugs and actively show you how to avoid them as part of the game guide. It's like there was absolutely no QA testing on this game. The Lego franchise games are usually terrific, but this one was a terrible misstep in the series, which is unfortunate because it had the potential to be one of my favorites considering the universe in which it is set. Do not play this game unless you have the patience of a saint.

losing xp-

no fast travel or vehicles-
sometimes you die  at night just meters away from a mission objective and it sends you across the map.like...great....thanks....let's try that again in 15 minutes
gameplay in general-
at first i was like wow! this game. but each hour has shown cracks and leaks and fractures. and to be honest the story is tacky. Your character volunteers for everything. the man can't say no! he's lifeless. there's a tower with the last 30 people left alive in it and they didn't notice a guy on the roof was selling drugs!!! the loot is unrewarding and shallow. and the combat just goes AWOL at times. you can't hit a zombie with a baseball bat but it has enough reach to smack you. it's repetitive. very. but worst of all the game just seems to turn on you at times. with everything i listed above all at once. even weirder the game plays fine untill you just hit a 20 minute skid where the game just goes from difficulty and skill to being flat out against you.
final answer:
All in all the art, world, and feel of this game is worth the ticket of admission. I had seen this game get featured in various articles before its release and I'll admit that I kind of let this game slip under my radar until after release. Since this happened, I've been working on ways of preventing this from happening in the future. But I digress. After seeing what the game was about post-launch, I was interested in picking the game up very soon though lack of funds prevented me from getting the game initially. Thankfully, a good friend of mine gifted me the game. FTL: Faster Than Light is a rogue-like, real-time spaceship simulator. In FTL, you must fly your spaceship through hostile space, fight pirates, make diplomatic decisions, and avoid losing your entire crew and/or ship to the cold blackness of space. This game has you flying through various sectors of space collection equipment and scrap (currency) to improve the ship as well as meeting new races and seeing new regions of space. All the while, you must outrun the Rebel fleet that is trying to catch you before you reach the waiting Federation fleet.
You're the captain of a starship for the Federation fleet that is being pursued by the overwhelming Rebel fleet. Why? Because you've learned important tactical information on how to defeat the Rebel fleet. You must deliver this information through a harrowing gauntlet of star systems and planets, avoiding overwhelming danger and surviving the odds. There are eight very dangerous sectors of space before you arrive at the Federation's Last Stand. There are up to four different paths you can take in each sector where a randomly generated situation will either benefit or debilitate your situation. After surviving the eight sectors, you'll join up with the Federation fleet to take on the invading Rebel fleet. At which point you must attack the Flagship of the Rebels directly while the Federation fleet attacks the Rebel fleet itself. Its game over if your ship or crew die at any point. For the most part, your choices have immediate consequences which will build up over time and may lead to success or failure. There are only a couple of choices you can make that will affect anything in the long-term. Generally, there are the prerequisites to acquiring new cruisers.
Each new cruiser you acquire is built and balanced differently from each other to fit a certain play-style. Some are better at stealth, some have better offensive weapons and some are better at taking over the enemy ship or removing all of the crew members. Each cruiser also comes with a B-layout that changes what crew, weapons and modules are included on your ship as well as the color of the ship. There is a great variety of ships for FTL, its just unlocking them can take a long time. When starting the game you get to choose the ship, the layout, the name of the ship and the name of your initial crew, as well as which gender your Human crew are. You can also choose the difficulty setting easy or normal. However, I think they mislabeled these and its more like hard and insane. Not that its a bad thing, but "normal" is not as easy as you would think in most games. Once you've done all this, your ready to start out on your adventure through the stars. You can choose which planet you get to jump to from the galaxy map. Just keep in mind that every jump you make means that the rebels come that much closer to catching up to you. Even if they do, you can fight them off. Its generally not recommended because the only reward you'll get for beating them is one unit of fuel and no scrap. Scrap is the currency you use to repair your ship, buy new weapons and other miscellaneous items.
While the main story may not be that strong, the real story is the journey you take in this harsh universe. Will you lose most of your crew in a freak accident only to survive all the way to the last sector on a wish and a prayer? Or will you escape from a sun's solar flare only to jump into an asteroid field and watch as your ship gets ripped apart by the asteroids and the nearby pirate's lasers? Or do you send your crew down to a randomly planet's distress call only to lose some of them as they are attacked by rebel forces? The story is played out with a lot of different text screens as you jump from one place in the galaxy map to the next. You'll encounter many different races, each with their own set of needs and personalities which you'll then have to decide what's best for your ship's continued survival. That's the fun with games like this is that you get to create the story in your head as you go along. It happened more than once that I would say "ENGAGE" at my monitor as my ship escaped a brutal battle or mourned over the loss of a comrade who bravely defended invading forces from taking over the ship. So, while the base story might not be much, its what you create from the universe that will really engage your interest in the game.
FTL: Advanced Edition fleshes everything about the game out, it's that simple. The new alien race adds a new mechanic where they suck the air out of the room they are in. There's new ships as well. It also comes with more music, weapons, encounters to overcome and UI enhancements to boot. It's a free expansion so no reason not to enjoy it. It can be disabled if you're wanting the vanilla FTL experience.
FTL's settings are a bit lacking. You only have a few options to control the size of the game on your screen. Those included are: windowed mode, full-screen (stretched), full-screen (black borders) and full-screen (FTL's native resolution) which is not your monitor's resolution. You also have no control over key bindings, though the default keys are pretty smartly placed. There are also a bunch of other minor settings you can enable or disable to your liking and you can see in the screenshot above. Overall, my biggest criticism of the settings choices would be the lack of resolution options as I'm not a bit fan of the current ones but they should work well enough for you. The game also features a good tutorial to get you up to speed on how to play. There is also a Stats screen which contains your best performance and achievements for each ship you've flown. The game is well polished as far as being free from any bugs or crashing problems are concerned.
FTL is a fantastic game and I don't think I'm saying anything new there. There's plenty of content and challenge, as I got 30 hours out of it. Though the RNG can easily ruin a run and I'd classify it as overly harsh, but there's something to enjoy every run. It's one of the few games that genuinely gives the feeling of being a starship captain. If your looking for a starship simulator that is an enjoyable, simple, and well crafted experience, then give FTL: Faster Than Light a look. This became my Game of the Year in 2012.

Do not let the horrible RE 1 fans keep you from playing (and most likely really really enjoying) this game. This has quite a bit more action than RE 1 - 3 which will, naturally, leave the earlier fans crying in their diapers. This is, legitimately, my first time writing a review for anything, but after seeing the completely heat-of-the-moment, horribly explained reviews I felt that I had to butt in.
To start off, yes, there are some areas in the game where the FPS will drop and you may need to drop your graphics settings down for those areas or you may not. Regardless of what common, completely uneducated opinion might state, games can not run perfectly on every form of machine in the world, they just can't. So everyone shouting "CRAPCOM" when their toaster or AMD machinery doesn't work the way they want them to, I'm sorry (and I'm certain capcom is too)
So, since this seems to be the way to do these sorts of things, I will list the pros and cons in my opinion
-PROS-
1.) Controls are smooth, this is against what others have thought, but after you play for a while and work with the skill tree (yes there is a skill tree now) you will see that the game is actually very very smooth in terms of combat and 'feel'
2.) The atmosphere is absolutely enticing. You may very well crap your pants at times (be warned)
3.) The boss fight was incredibly fun (there has only been one in all 4 parts to date [no Pedro wasn't a boss people])
4.) The story is actually very thrilling and can drive you in and hook you, leaving you waiting anxiously for next week
5.) I really happen to enjoy the whole episodic function of these games, it ties in with RE development really well (you might feel differently)
6.) The difficulty level of the game (I play on medium difficult) is really enjoyably challenging, I can't wait to do it over on hard mode later on
-CONS-
1.) The stuttering in certain areas should be fixed, it ruins the atmosphere and can be annoying during combat
2.) I've read that a lot of people have their mouse on the screen even when playing on a controller. I also play on a controller, even though its whack for aiming, and do not have this problem. This problem, however, can be quickly (in about 5 to 10 minutes) solved with a little google magic.
3.) Having to listen to all the idiots post about how not having split screen coop is game braking. Since when does being able to play my game on half my 17 inch screen become a requirement? And who the hell would do that to themselves?
4.) On the other hand, having online coop for both story and Raid Mode would be an excellent addition to this game, and like DLC, I really look forward to it in the future.
All-in-all, it is a really great RE games with actually believable story, for the most part. Combat is fun, challenging, and at times left me with a smile on my face (whether I was getting slaughtered or commiting the slaughter)

Shadowrun Returns is not in itself a game. It is a platform that supports the creation and play of Adventures, both developer and community created. "Dead Man's Switch" is the initial campaign that you get at purchase and is a well constructed adventure. It has almost all the things you might expect to see and hear in a shadow run adventure. The combat is a xcom esque entertaining and at times very challenging. The characters are interested and likeable. The leveling system is more or less an intuitive waterfall setup. Attributes unlock skills, and skills unlock specializations i.e. Quickness[1] -> marksmen[1] -> rifles[1]. Though the game could do better on conveyance in general. Most important though is the adventure is fun and the game mechanics are solid.
I do have minor grips with some of the unanswered mechanics issues and other game play short comings. But before that I can safely say that if you are a fan of shadowrun or have ever enjoyed playing the paper and pen or older SENS games you will enjoy this one.
** My final recommendation: If you like Shadowrun you will like Shadowrun Returns - Dead Man's Switch **
Now If you are interested in an runners ranting here are some of my misgivings about the game.
-Characters should be persisten between adventures. Starting a new character every adventure is a little disheartening. (This being between Dead Man's Switch and dragonfall)
-Send to stash: sending things to your stash doesn't seem to send said items to your stash.
-Hit Chance: a legendary marksmen shouldn't consistently miss from half a room away just because the target is behind a half cover desk.
-The lack of stealth is a real bummer, coupled with that is the lack of ability to use your etiquettes to aid in undercover stealth sections.
-The absence of a local net on runs to disarm alarms, disrupt communication, shut off lights, lock doors, est. Mostly the disarming alarms before they go off bit.
-Magic is also very spartan in comparison to the physical combat skills and interactions. You can summon spirits at predetermined locations
-Having to run into an enemy or ambush to trigger combat mode is very disconcerting. The ability to freely toggle combat mode would have been greatly appreciated.
-Riggers: Not being able to pilot drones outside of combat is a bit of a disservice to the rigger characters. As setup is a key part to the rigger play style.

This game is a little bittersweet for me. But it also lends hope for the series.
I should start off by saying I really enjoyed RE:REV1. It had, at least for me, good horror, rewarding gameplay, and replayability. Both of the Revelations games are a stark departure from the usual RE formula, and Revelations 2 departs from its predecessor just as much. Returning themes are the gun customizations and BP. That’s ... about it I think.
I've played through the first two episodes so far and impressions are a little mixed. We'll start with the pros for those without much patience;
- Claire looks like an ACTUAL women. REV1 was mostly you staring at the tight♥♥♥♥♥of Jill from third person. Fan service, really. But Claire is realistic and I like her much more for that.
- You get about 2 hours of gameplay for 6 bucks. I think that's fine for just one play through.
- If you grew up with this series or played and liked the original REs, there are a few references and fan services for you. Including sandwiches.
-Scavenging is key. I thoroughly enjoyed the Metro series for it's rewarding scavenging and REV2 usually delivers on that.
- I like the split story telling between the two groups. And each side has their own sort of style of gameplay. Both are potentially fun for me.
- Aside from the film grain, the game looks really good. It's more of a gritty and realistic take. Through, I have preferred to sort of style that RE4 and 5 had graphics wise.
- I just can't seem to get enough of Barry's voice actor ... or Barry himself for that matter.
-It seems like Revelations is becoming REs proving grounds to experiment. That lends a lot of hope for the atrocity that was RE6. I enjoyed RE6 a lot, actually, but it was a huge let down from RE. If REV2 didn't have the RE name, I would be fooled in to thinking it's an entirely different franchise. It seems to take a lot of inspiration from The Evil Within and even the Metro series. The enemies and settings really remind me of The Evil Within and I'm pretty sure one of the earlier heavy enemies is a subtle reference to Pyramid Head. I hope they go on to maintain a sort of main series and then a sub series in the Revelations' vein. That way if they want to cram as much Quintin Tarentino-y action in to a game as they can like in RE6, the rest of us can still enjoy a sub series.
- Adding on to the previous point, this game is cheap. Despite having the small price tag, this is a full game. Like I said, this is probably their place to experiment and the lower price tag sends me the message that they understand this isn't meant to a super Triple A game. It's a side story to add on to the series. So with that lower expectation I was left marginally surprised, in a good way.
And now for the cons;
- Killing enemies no longer gives you ammo. This is practically a deal breaker for me. One of the things I loved most about RE4,5, and REV1 was that I could wean ammo from enemies. I liked playing through once with difficulty, then playing through a few more times to grind ammo and just enjoy having that surplus to get my revenge on the harder bosses or enemies. You might sort of do this in Raid Mode but it's just not the same for me.
- There is an incredibly annoying film grain overlay. The Evil Within also had this and I hate it here just as much as I did there. I can't seem to find an option to turn it off, unfortunately. I'm sure they thought this would add to the ambiance but it just becomes distracting. Some may like it and many probably won't notice it as much as I do, though.
- This game acts like a very half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥console port. Enemy path-finding AIs get tripped up, a few graphical bugs, desynced audio on some cutscenes. and unresponsive partners (Very reminiscent of Sheva) really break any immersion you manage to achieve.
- This might be because I'm bad shot and play with a gampad (I usually don't use controllers), but the game can sometimes go beyond hectic and just become unfair or annoying. Ammo never seems to last or be enough. In my experience, I seemed to run out of ammo at the worst possible times. But, again, could just be me.
- I'm not too sure I like the episodic format. This is just personal taste. On the bright side, if you are very short on cash you can spread the cost of the game out and it does a good job of bringing you back for the next episode. And, you could just wait until all the episodes are out, buy the bundle, and play it all through.
All in all you can only end up wasting 6 bucks if you give the first episode a try. And despite the quirks it has, I've ended up liking it. It's a pretty innocuous investment and if you like it you can get the other episodes when they come out or just wait until they're all out and buy the bundle.

It’s really quite remarkable how South Park creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone have slowly ramped up the shock value over the past 17 years to keep the show sharp. Whether they and developer Obsidian could pull off the same for a 14-hour game instead of a 22-minute show was never a sure thing. But there I was, shrunk down to Underpants Gnome-size, crawling up Mr. Slave’s orifices to retrieve a WMD, slicing through gobs of bodily fluids in turn-based JRPG combat and climbing up half-digested corn-on-the-cob as I went, laughing hysterically the whole way. I’m floored at how consistently funny it is, and at how well the outrageous comedy melds with the relatively simple gameplay to create not just an amazing South Park game, but an intelligent and witty satire of roleplaying mechanics.
As for the story, it’s a clever premise that allows The Stick of Truth to take place in a recognizable and painstakingly recreated South Park setting, but also brings in all the usual fantasy roleplaying tropes through the power of children’s imagination. It’s a trick used many times in the show, and it works great for the game, too. An epic LARPing session (as casually set up by last year’s “Black Friday” trilogy of episodes) has your custom-created new kid in town joining either Cartman’s Humans or Kyle’s Elves, all dressed in amusingly bad makeshift cosplay outfits. True to the show, things escalate wildly and hilariously, leading to conspiracies involving the government, aliens, and Taco Bell.
Though it manifests itself in typically over-the-top South Park-ian ways, The Stick of Truth is a Paper Mario-esque RPG-lite. You and your single extra party member (you’ll unlock several South Park regulars, though only one can fight with you at a time) take turns battling formations of enemies, be it the Gingers, crazy homeless guys, aliens, and more. Typical buffs and debuffs are ably skinned in screwed-up fourth grader verbiage (throwing feces to add “gross out” effects) mixed with mana-powered spells and timed button-press attacks and blocks to keep you on your toes during combat. It keeps things simple enough while still leaving room for some tactical depth. And Obsidian refreshingly leaves out time-sink annoyances like character encumbrance and random battles you can’t avoid.
I couldn’t resist the curious lure of playing as the Jew class over the archetypal Fighter, Thief, and Mage options, but the differences between them turned out to be

Sure, each has their own special abilities, but there are effectively no class-specific weapons or items, and there’s nothing to stop a Mage from choosing melee-enhancing gear and carving up foes with a blade just as well as a Fighter. All classes eventually learn special farting magic (a crude parody of Skyrim’s Dragon Shouts) though both the thumbstick motions and especially the tutorial sessions for your powers of flatulence tend to be cumbersome. Achievement or Trophy hunting aside, this lack of class differentiation or significant choices in the story are big reasons why I don’t feel much incentive to replay the campaign.
The other unfortunate offense is that some extremely useful things are poorly explained, if they’re even mentioned at all. Tricks like being able to switch your Buddy at any time by pressing down on the D-pad to access the Party menu, or taking the first swing at overworld enemies so that you get the first turn when the battle starts, and what your Buddies can do and are specifically good at are all up to us to discover accidentally. One other puzzling issue is the slipperiness of the action-selection wheel during combat – it’s strangely difficult to get your pointer to stick on the option you want, particularly if it’s in a diagonal slot on the wheel.
But that’s about the extent of the damage. Aesthetically, The Stick of Truth might be the most beautiful crappy-looking-on-purpose game I’ve ever seen. While it may seem trivial to make a role-playing game resemble the crude, construction-paper cutout style of the show, it’s executed so well here that the two mediums are almost indistinguishable. You’ll never see a HUD when walking around town, for instance, unless you tap the Y/Triangle button. Only the very rare stuck animation on an overworld enemy and (on both consoles, but not a capable PC) the occasional frame rate stutter when a new area loaded in for the first time reminded me that this was a game and not the show. And that was the extent of the technical problems I encountered.

I love the graphics on this game. Very immersive, very dynamic, and truly gorgeous (for being an apocolypse). I tend to play with the graphic settings a LOT in all the games I play to get the best possible graphics while still managing decent framerates. After reading other reviews stating that this game requires some beefy hardware to play maxed out, I was worried that my system may not be able to hang. After spending some time in the video settings, I was pleasantly surprised to find that my machine can play this game very well at high settings (note, no Ultra settings as of yet).
My Specs:
i7 2.8ghz (first gen, not overclocked)
nvidia 760
8gigs of 2000mhz RAM
128gig SSD drive
Video Setting Adjustments:
1920x1080, fullscreen
All settings turned "High" or "On" (unless otherwise noted)
Motion Blur- OFF (this one killed my fps, def need a better graphic card to enjoy this feature)
Vertical Sync- OFF (plays with less screen tears, but max fps is 30. Compelling evidence shows a nice visual @ 60fps)
View distance set a click or two ahead of 50%
I play with these settings and average 43-62fps, with occasional dips. Only the cutscenes seems to drop my fps to 17-28fps. Personally, I don't mind laggier cutscenes as long as the actual game isnt giving me problems.
To squeeze a few extra fps out, turn "nVidia Depth of Field"-OFF.  Its a nice, subtle effect, but it can cause dips for the 760 vid card.

Pros:  All in all, I like it. Has a very "FarCry" feel to it. Storyline, layout, map, quests, etc. The story and voice actors are all really good.  Although its kind of clunky, I like the Assassin's Creed style movement (parkour). Makes traversing the city a lot of fun (and gets you out of tight spots frequently).
Cons:  Not as survival-based as I would have liked. I guess I was hoping for more of a "State of Decay" style of survival where scavenging was necessary because you had to eat and drink. Instead, the game presents a "FarCry" style of play where survival is more of a concept strictly for the main story than a necessity. I would have loved if there were some form of stealth or sneaking. Lastly, I find it comical how the zombies turn into wii avatars when they notice you by putting on "pointy teeth" stickers over their mouths.
Even though I'm not blown away by this game, I am enjoying it. So for that, I give it a thumbs up.

This is a neat little game with some very big frustration.
The premise is simple, you command the crew of a small starship who must escape from an ever advancing enemy armada in a desperate attempt to reach safety with your own fleet. Along the way you'll find yourself fighting other ships in individual combat and engaging in random events whose outcomes are decided primarily on random chance, crew selection, and equipment selection.
As you jump into each new sector, the difficulty will ramp up considerably, meaning if you are unlucky or adopt poor tactics, you will quickly die. This can and usually does result in frustration and may put some off from playing the game. Keep in mind there are no retries in this game, so each death means you start over from scratch.
If you like a very challenging strategy game, you might try this, but dont expect any huge fleet type battles. This is strictly a one on one fight kind of game.

It's Dungeons Of Dredmor and The Binding Of Isaac but  in space. Faster Than Light is a roguelike game, meaning that if you die, it's truly game over. There's no reloading savegames, checkpoints, anything. You have to start all over again, except for a few things (like new ships or layouts) that you'll unlock during your games.
The whole game is randomly created so you'll never play the same game twice. There's also a bit of micromanaging. Scrap the 'bit' part, in reality it's pretty important and you'll micromanage your crew in practically every battle. Your crew will have to repair important parts of your ship and setting them up correctly might make them reload your weapons faster, or recharge your shields faster. They'll even have to engage enemies in combat from time to time.
Killed enemies will give you resources to upgrade your ship and buy stuff in shops. Stuff you desperately need in order to advance. In fact, soms of us might never even be able to complete the game, considering the fact that things are entirely random and it's also based on lots of luck. But it will never stop you from quitting the game. It's always fun, no matter what happens to your ship. You'll keep telling yourself; 'just one more game'. And isn't that what a game's supposed to do?
FTL is a great game and anyone who gives it a try will absolutely learn to appreciate it. Maybe not instantly, but after a few games ? Absolutely !
[Rating: 87/100]

As you jump into each new sector, the difficulty will ramp up considerably, meaning if you are unlucky or adopt poor tactics, you will quickly die. This can and usually does result in frustration and may put some off from playing the game. Keep in mind there are no retries in this game, so each death means you start over from scratch.
If you like a very challenging strategy game, you might try this, but dont expect any huge fleet type battles. This is strictly a one on one fight kind of game.

This game is well crafted enough in the horror genre to keep you enthralled (and scared) through a mix of jump scares, and natural dread settling in as you explore the various areas of the ship, all alone and most of the times, armed with less ammo than you'd have liked. And would you believe it, the story is actually decent and makes you care for the characters and the endgame.
There are also collectibles to be found like data tapes and text logs, which aren't a chore to collect and supplement the story very well. It's Dungeons Of Dredmor and The Binding Of Isaac but  in space. Faster Than Light is a roguelike game, meaning that if you die, it's truly game over. There's no reloading savegames, checkpoints, anything. You have to start all over again, except for a few things (like new ships or layouts) that you'll unlock during your games.
The whole game is randomly created so you'll never play the same game twice. There's also a bit of micromanaging. Scrap the 'bit' part, in reality it's pretty important and you'll micromanage your crew in practically every battle. Your crew will have to repair important parts of your ship and setting them up correctly might make them reload your weapons faster, or recharge your shields faster. They'll even have to engage enemies in combat from time to time.
Killed enemies will give you resources to upgrade your ship and buy stuff in shops. Stuff you desperately need in order to advance. In fact, soms of us might never even be able to complete the game, considering the fact that things are entirely random and it's also based on lots of luck. But it will never stop you from quitting the game. It's always fun, no matter what happens to your ship. You'll keep telling yourself; 'just one more game'. And isn't that what a game's supposed to do?
FTL is a great game and anyone who gives it a try will absolutely learn to appreciate it. Maybe not instantly, but after a few games ? Absolutely !

No doubt, Antichamber is a hard game. It's not so much that it challenges the skill of a player, his reaction times, his ability to multi-task or, as you might think from the screenshots with the gun, his precision with a crosshair. Antichamber throws the player into a labyrinth of wisdom for life, one that will sometimes force you to take a step back and see the greater scheme of things, one that will throw you back for you to start over again and make you learn from unforeseeable mistakes. It's what makes this game immersive. You don't know what to expect, what you'll encounter around the next corner or even better, what you will encounter after an endless set of corners. What is the sense of this? There might be no answer to that question. This is Antichamber, a metaphor for life.

Been a while since I completed this game, but I would definitely recommend this to anyone looking for a Sci-fi Horror game with Survival elements. At its core, it's a third-person shooter that has you playing as Isaac Clarke, an engineer stuck on a doomed mining ship, struggling to find a way out while uncovering the secrets of the former crew and the cause of the outbreak. The backstory is the real star here. It's told through audio recordings, notes and letters by former crew members and survivors. The main story itself is serviceable, but has quite a few horror film clichés and tropes. Lots of plot devices are often recycled to keep the game going. For example, half the chapters consist of fixing something that has broken down somewhere in the ship for whatever reason.
The gameplay itself is quite satisfying and provides a fair challenge that rarely feels frustrating or unfair. All weapons function differently from each other and give certain advantages and disadvantages. The crafting system isn't anything special, but it's not bad at all. As far being "scary", it's a pretty mixed bag. If predictable jump scares are your thing, then you will be scared most of the time. However, there is a psychological horror aspect to this game that the sequels never quite replicated. A lot of events are never actually seen or experienced, but rather heard or found after they've taken place. Some of them are quite startling and adds a sense of impending doom to your journey. Disembodied voices (if listened to carefully, may imply it's actually just Issac going insane) also add to this layer of fear. My biggest problem with the gameplay is that the mouse controls are unresponsive or too sensitive at times, but there are several   community guides to fixing this. Overall a solid 8/10 game for me.

Risk of Rain is an enjoyable platformer which offers familiar yet fun gameplay in a platformer. The goal of the game is to find the teleporter in each floor, survive and move to the next level. It features a colourful cast of characters to play from, each offering their own skills and perks which change gameplay according to each character. Each level has 2-3 variants in its type and offers some variety in the levels but limited.
The game offers a huge variety of items to be picked up in the game with varying effects and boons. The game's difficulty increases with the time spent on each run as well the fun of the game. When I first started the game, I found the game extremely difficult and the bosses if not familiar can rip you apart. However, once you get better in the game, the game becomes a joy to play especially when overloading runs (Going back to the first level before the final level with all items intact as well as difficulty).
The game gives some more variety in its gameplay as well through the use of unlockables called artifacts and different artifacts can alter the gameplay slightly to drastically. This game also offers online multiplayer so going online with your friends and playing with them adds to the fun in the game. Just join in a game altogether, skype between all of your and you will have a blast.
Overall, this game is a great platformer with its familiar yet fun gameplay. It has unique gameplay elements and enemies that give the game its enjoyment and with friends it is even more fun. I recommend this game if you're looking for a classic level platformer with unique twists.

A great Solitare game. There's upgrades to buy, and many pets to collect and grow. Collecting all the pets can be a chore though, since the eggs they hatch from are randomly spawned from game to game, so sometimes you can go dozens of games without seeing an egg. Well, towards the end of the pet collecting anyway. At the beginning you get them at a decent rate, but around the halfway mark it starts to slow down. Also, it takes 'time' to hatch and then mature. Each card you click will tick down it's 'hatching' and/or 'growing timer, so it can take a while.
However, the pet feature is completely optional. This is the kinda game people buy when they either want a coffee break game, or they're a huge fan of solitaire games. Either way, you'll be playing this game a lot normally and the pet feature is a nice thing to do on the side, which for long term players is the only thing left on the side.
There's an upgrade system which will make playing more convieniet, however it doesn't take too long to max those out and afterwards the only thing left is the pet feature and solitaire... which is great too.
Overall, this is just a great game and the devs are great people. Back when this game was first released, the devs were generous enough to host many giveaways in various communities, giving away quite a few copies, which is how I got mine.
As for the current price point, I feel $10 is a good price considering that this game has given me more hours than an uncomfortable number of AAA.

Risk of Rain is an indie platformer with a strong focus on fighting against large mobs of enemies, and some rouge-like elements such as unlockable characters and items. It's unique characteristic is that difficulty isn't tied with level progression, as the game allways becomes harder and harder as the clock ticks away.
Art, soundtrack, hard difficulty and different playstyles for different characters are it's strong points. Perhaps you will enjoy being swarmed and being forced into kiting tactics rather than brute force or skill upgrades (there aren't any), perhaps not.
Despite not being story-rich, the world is memorable, the soundtrack is one of the better ones (and one of my favourites), and the pace and progression is spot on for my tastes.
The game is highly recommended if you're on the fence. If you dislike platrofmers or rage easily, probably avoid. Looking at the game on Twitch and YouTube, it's not easy to see what's so good about it. I had a *very* poor opinion about it, until i was convinced to try it. Immediately, my opinion went from utter dislike to surprised enjoyment.
You kinda have to love games where you gotta move fast and react to chaotic swarms of enemies and projectiles rather than stalk things quietly and plan ahead (for most characters anyway, Sniper does it sligthly differently). If you enjoy very difficult, breakneck speed gameplay then this will satisfy you thoroughly. The game is very easy to play and very hard to beat. Beating it feels tremendously satisfying.
The style, soundtrack and overall mood is somber rather than guts n' gore or slapstick. Like a weeping willow with a minigun, things get very violent but rather than being a hero or villian you're forced to fight as hard as you can just to survive.
The story is largely ambiguous, told in bits and pieces of journal entries or item logs. Whatever the reasons brought you there, it's going to end in a lot of death.
Items are numerous, humorous and range between very mildly useful and overpowered. With items and command artifacts it's possible to tweak gameplay difficulty and make the game nigh-on-impossible to beat. If you're into that sort of thing.
The main gimmick of increasing difficulty as time goes by is executed very well and it's possible to win either by taking your sweet time and hoping to acquire as many useful doodads as possible or by rushing as fast as possible in order to clear later stages before the difficulty increases. It will make the first few attempts pretty hard but the game stays challenging longer that way. And as i've mentioned before, beating the game is an acomplishment!
I've also mentioned the soundtrack being excellent but i'll mention it again!
There's some bugs. The game engine was upgraded post release and as a results some old bugs were fixed and some new ones appeared. The level generation can occasionaly bug out and co-op play can suffer from port-forwarding problems or disconnects. Other bugs are pretty rare and minor but they get patched out occasionally.
As a single player game Risk of Rain is almost a classic. As for multiplayer, well it's got a few problems and it's difficult to get it working until the bugs get fixed.

Batman Arkham Knight: PC review
Warning: This review has full spoilers. There will be breaks in between the video to skip spoilers. Also this Review is a candid opinon of a longtime Batman Fan and a Batman Arkham Fan.
Preface:
The Arkham Series reached its cult status after It's first iteration: Batman Arkham Asylum. Asylum Offered Batman fans to actually BE the Batman. Using batarangs, Grapple gun and His Martial arts expertise was an immersice and memorable experience and even changed the modern combat system that we all see from various titles such as Assasin's creed, Shadow of Morder, Remember Me . The succsess of Asylum set a bar for future Arkham Games to surpass and utimately led Arkham Knight to its lackluster release on the PC.
In early 2014 I had built my Pc enough to actually stop using my onboard graphics from my motherboard and I had actually saved enough to get that sweet sweet GTX980. It was a no-brainer I would recieve My card and get The Witcher 3 and Batman Arkham Knight codes In no time. but I waited and Waited, and after both delays I convinced myself that they were improving the game and perfecting its details but in reality it seemed that everything was rushed, ports were rushed, missions were nutured. Suddenly Batman had become a rushed triple A title that failed to capture the essance of what made the Original trilogy great. The high bar that was set by both games had somehow tainted the third from being the Batman game that every 12 year old kid wanted.
Story:
Arkham Knight isn't without it's merits though, what it does great it does Phenomenal. Events throughout the story make you FEEL like the batman as you endure the struggle of fighting to get your city back.
After the events of City "spoiler alert" We know Joker is definately dead. DEAD. Batman is then shown watching as a gaurdian as his city is being usurped by its evil denizens. Scarecrow is back with a vengeance with a little dose of his new fear toxin and looking menacing as ever. His presence gives a sense of dread and seriousness, his threats that makes anyone think "Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥..Well here we go" You're not alone though, Oracle, Jim Gordon, Tim and Alfred make it clear they are willing to help and it's nice to see their presence (clip) but we all know what makes Batman tick is willingness to sacrifice himself to be the savior of gotham.
As we enter gotham we find Scarecrow's warehouse. We "save" poison Ivy as a clever foreshadowing and get aquainted with the batmobile.
Fast forward and we finally see The Arkham Knight Staring straight at us. We come to find out The Knight is mobilizing his forces getting ready to strike, meanwhile this part of the game shows us the basics of our core gadgetry, combat, Batmobile mechanics and predator in a seemless manner without holding your hand. (although certain in certain  moments, button prompts do seem excessive but are inherently a double edged sword in games these days)
The Ace Chemicals segment perfectly what you're getting yourself into and offer a little taste as to what is to come. We fight through various tank battles, ninjas and puzzles to reach the Ace Chemicals workers and finally Scarecrow. We enter the chemical mixing room and find scarecrow, at this point I was on the edge of my seat and when he says this:(clip)  I was like
but then we smash his face in so its all good. We find out that Oracle is in some deep trouble and that scarecrow trapped you inside. My heart at this point is about to burst through my chest. We know now that we have to stop this bomb but at this point my mind was racing with thoughts like "WHAT is going on" "is this the end of that game?" All this tensions accumulates to the big twist that I didn't see coming.
Joker is back.
We come to find out that Joker's blood has affected 5 people and is actually mutating their cells and taking over. It's obvious that Batman is one of the carriers, and we get to see his ailment visually with hallucinations. The attention to detail is astounding, you see building take the shape of the clown prince of crime and you get to hear his humourous views about what's goling on. You start realizing though that the gas is excacerbating batman's condition and can see it getting worse.
While your infection is getting worse other villians pop in making breif appearances to introduce them and side quest villians. At this point you realize that most of these villains are not going to be shown extensively or actually see them trying to take down Batman which is a real dissapointment. Other villians thought get completely shafted and get lame boss battles which left me with a sour taste in my mouth.we come to find out The real hard hitters in the story line are scarecrow and The arkham Knight.

Pros:
atmopshere-
techland finally achieved the atmospheric vibe the dead island games never quite delivered on. There's a healthy amount of fear in every combat situation. you know 2 zombies is a challenge, 4 is an issue and 8 is overwhelming. Then when night falls bravery is for fools. I never really felt the need to get to a safe place after the first hour of any dead island playthrough, The ones that come out at night in this are.no.joke. you will die.
Looks quite nice-
when (and i stress when)you're not thermal throttling down to 17 fps, its quite decent looking. the enviroment is beautiful yet rough around the edges in a positive way.(at the time of this amd platforms are not playing super smooth but im sure it will be patched and i can crank back up to high visuals)
The Drop kicks-
Yea. If you've played it. you get what i mean by this. the first time you drop kick a zombie off a building.... kool-aid man
Cons:
free running system-
After being delayed almost a year, the free running works, but it still feels sloppy at times. in such a hostile game,turns into a real big issue.
Level bars-
yes the strength of the atmosphere is also a weakness. yes i think from a visual prespective of removing the arcade-like level bars that were in the dead island games does A-LOT for immersion, but as you play deeper into the game is causes great confusion. you go from weapons that do 20 damage to 200 damage and you can't in your heart of hearts always admit you can tell the difference. there's maybe 6-8 zombie templates you see most often. on the off chance you'll get two side by side. one takes one hit to the head and dies. the other one takes 14 hits and keeps getting up. there's no visual que as to why. and when youre making fast twitch descions like do i climb this or that? do i fight or run? it really makes you feel cheated when damage seems to be so randomized.
The Haystack Jump-
the blue trash bags you jump into. yes it's a cool idea as far as fitting into the way the game plays with the free running. but they're a mess. i get it not locking into them like in assassin's creed makes it more threatening and dangerous but also it makes it hard to trust and/or use. sometimes you see two dumpsters.the blue bags dont appear from the certain angle you happen to be at so you have to guess (once again after some perfomance patches i exspect this will be mostly cleared up from a visual settings stand point) which almost always results in death. worse yet often, and yes 4 players in one game and it's happened to all of us many times, you land on the bags but they don't cushion your fall and you die. so yes atmospherically not locking you into a dive is cool. but the execution is so untrustable that you're better off not risking it
losing xp-
when you die you lose survivor points.that sucks but once again it lends to the atmopshere of the game by making you actually fear death. unfortunately you're going to die alot from clunky game actions. i dare say equal or more often than playing flat out irresponible. for example in co-op we were spawned in a bad area of the game after dying.somehow it had shift a few hours to total darkness,we got murdered. respawned in safe zone across the map, but the night zombies were sitting at the door so we couldn't leave without dying. so we broke up the co-op game.spawned me in my single player game, at night, and you guessed it! surrounded by zombies. died. it's frustrating system when the game has the table on tilt. also why does it takes xp instead of currency? becuase the currency system is pretty much useless after $2000. all you need to buy is medkits.
no fast travel or vehicles-
sometimes you die  at night just meters away from a mission objective and it sends you across the map.like...great....thanks....let's try that again in 15 minutes
gameplay in general-
at first i was like wow! this game. but each hour has shown cracks and leaks and fractures. and to be honest the story is tacky. Your character volunteers for everything. the man can't say no! he's lifeless. there's a tower with the last 30 people left alive in it and they didn't notice a guy on the roof was selling drugs!!! the loot is unrewarding and shallow. and the combat just goes AWOL at times. you can't hit a zombie with a baseball bat but it has enough reach to smack you. it's repetitive. very. but worst of all the game just seems to turn on you at times. with everything i listed above all at once. even weirder the game plays fine untill you just hit a 20 minute skid where the game just goes from difficulty and skill to being flat out against you.
final answer:
All in all the art, world, and feel of this game is worth the ticket of admission. There's alot to like. but it's frustrating at times. not in a ninja guidan or megaman way. but in a flat out "why can i suddenly not hit anything/ why does a 10 foot drop take all my health/ why does hitting the slide button stop me dead/ why does everything i normally do suddenly not work" kind of way, and the worst sin of all....it's a little boring. beautiful, dangerous, but boring. and its because of this i can't recommend this game. maybe with some a.i. tweaks and some patches that i know will be coming in the following weeks and months it will be much less frustrating. but i've went to bed unhappy two nights in a row now. this game was so close to great, really. there's alot of talent put into this game.

This is a neat little game with some very big frustration.
The premise is simple, you command the crew of a small starship who must escape from an ever advancing enemy armada in a desperate attempt to reach safety with your own fleet. Along the way you'll find yourself fighting other ships in individual combat and engaging in random events whose outcomes are decided primarily on random chance, crew selection, and equipment selection.
As you jump into each new sector, the difficulty will ramp up considerably, meaning if you are unlucky or adopt poor tactics, you will quickly die. This can and usually does result in frustration and may put some off from playing the game. Keep in mind there are no retries in this game, so each death means you start over from scratch.
If you like a very challenging strategy game, you might try this, but dont expect any huge fleet type battles. This is strictly a one on one fight kind of game.

It's Dungeons Of Dredmor and The Binding Of Isaac but  in space. Faster Than Light is a roguelike game, meaning that if you die, it's truly game over. There's no reloading savegames, checkpoints, anything. You have to start all over again, except for a few things (like new ships or layouts) that you'll unlock during your games.
The whole game is randomly created so you'll never play the same game twice. There's also a bit of micromanaging. Scrap the 'bit' part, in reality it's pretty important and you'll micromanage your crew in practically every battle. Your crew will have to repair important parts of your ship and setting them up correctly might make them reload your weapons faster, or recharge your shields faster. They'll even have to engage enemies in combat from time to time.
Killed enemies will give you resources to upgrade your ship and buy stuff in shops. Stuff you desperately need in order to advance. ——————————————————————————————————————
发觉自己之前卡得不能自理的原因是N卡的程序不认识启示录2需要手动设置 = = 设置好就不卡了……
这下二逼得有点过了……于是回来重新写评论……而且之前那篇百感交集实在太混乱了233
如果觉得太长 =。= 那么可以拉到最后看总结233
首先，优化的问题的确是存在的，表现于某些时候突然的瞬间顿卡，就是那种突然画面定格然后半秒/一秒后全局瞬移……不过数量不多，可以接受；相比于光影，雾气/颗粒等效果对于帧数的影响要更为明显（比如突击模式里6代雪地那张图）
游戏目前打了两章（目前也就两章Orz）
Ep1的流程比较短，相比较而言Ep2感觉上要长不少；不过从两个章节的流程上来看，克莱尔阿姨这边在游戏性和多样性上都要略逊于巴瑞大叔那边，至少我是这么感觉的——主要原因有二：C&M线的流程变化不够，有点大同小异的感觉，而B&N线这边，敌人变化多不说，娜塔莉这个角色用法上的设定也增加了B&N线的趣味，相比之下那边黑丝妹就有些鸡肋了 = =
总体来说，两条线是两种风格较为不同的玩法，C&M那边比较紧张（剧情主要是逃亡与探究，动不动就是守卫战和逃亡桥段），而B&N线那边比较有趣（以追寻C&M线的轨迹为主，场景/敌人设定多变，两位主角能力各异且契合度很高）
这次启示录2有一个优点，恰恰是拜章节式所赐，两条线交叉进行，虽然C&M线多样性比较差，但是和B&N线穿插在一起，节奏上的感觉还是不错的，不像6代4个主线如果选一个一路到底多少会有些审美疲劳。
整体系统，与1代相比，武器与插件系统没有什么实质变化；主要变化在于 1）角色特长：每个角色能干的事情不一样，主要是为双角色服务，体现角色区分度，并且增加合作的必要性（然后卡婊华丽丽地COOP跳票也是醉了……），其中道具搜索也改进了，不是用探测器，而是靠特定角色的能力（和探测器一样，一开始很新鲜，后来就越来越烦了……）　２）角色技能通过评分所得ＢＰ来解锁技能……我不太喜欢在一个所谓的恐怖生存游戏中看到这种设定……不过有就有呗，技能大体上和图集模式中的差不多　３）潜行／暗杀 并不是大多数场景都能依靠潜行灭敌（拜娜塔莉所赐，B&N线机会很多……），不过这个也的确为某些场景提供了另一种选择（不过说实话，多少给人那么些跟风的感觉 ←_← 不过吧6代就已经有类似系统了，
突击模式这次搞得有些复杂，角色等级分开算，还有每日任务刷，每个人都有自己的技能池来组合……实际上氪金的存在，完全不影响你好好刷突击←_←玩极限的还是玩极限，搞TA的还是搞TA，研究组合的依然研究组合……卡婊就是想赚一点脑门发热的玩家的钱而已←_←
不过说实话你已经卖出那么多DLC的还要氪金的确有些那啥……不得不说学样学得还真快……虽然不影响我们玩游戏但是印象分会大打折扣←_←
（话说拜这次优化所赐，突击模式有两张掉帧神图←_←6代武器店和6代雪地，配置将将达标的筒子遇到这两张图绝对会哭的……
剧情目前不好说……
之前也提过了，C&M线逃啊逃，顺带在顺藤摸瓜；B&N线追寻C&M轨迹。至于这剧情到底好不好，我觉得挺好，虽然还没大量的悬疑来扣住我的心悬，也没有神展开，也没有史诗般地叙事（……），启示录2的故事我感觉，大体上更像是在服务游戏性，配合着游戏场景的切换、玩法的变化……
话说这次“Evil is Watching”这个主题我觉得选得不好，虽然把也算是适时地点了题 = = 我玩了两章以后倒是觉得那句“Fear what you will become, and become what you fear”倒是意外地带感……反正不管哪一个本身都与游戏流程、系统设定没有关系 = =
最后总结下吧：
+游戏节奏掌控地很不错，另外B&N线趣味性十足
+相对于1代在系统上做了一定地升级和扩成，让玩家除了武器以外在其他方面也有了一定的选择
+打击感虽然不及正传5、6，不过相比于1代已经有了质的飞跃
+升级后的突击模式，与剧情那边相似，在角色定制方面增加了一定的自由度
-优化不完善，在CPU和显卡方面的要求并不如将配置要求中所写的那么友好
-故事被章节式的发售形式切割成4块，但是剧情推进略缓慢
-DLC卖成这样还氪金，卡婊你快醒醒！

Get ready for the longest 6 minutes of your life.
The rules of Super Hexagon are incredibly simple: Don't hit the walls.
You control a miniscule triangle with that one purpose. But as the field tilts and rotates to the amazing chiptune soundtrack, this becomes much easier said than done. Your first time playing, it is entirely possible you will not survive more than 3 seconds. But the real brilliance of Super Hexagon is the way it makes failure just another part of the game. It doesn't rub in the fact that you lost; There's no sad music, no slow fade out, no "would you like to try again?" prompt. Just a stern "Game Over" and a one-button restart option. This means you never lose your groove, and you always want to just try again.
This is the kind of game you'll want to show to your friends every time they come over, just to see how well they do, and Arcade Mode makes it perfect to break out at parties.

It's Dungeons Of Dredmor and The Binding Of Isaac but  in space. Faster Than Light is a roguelike game, meaning that if you die, it's truly game over. There's no reloading savegames, checkpoints, anything. You have to start all over again, except for a few things (like new ships or layouts) that you'll unlock during your games.
The whole game is randomly created so you'll never play the same game twice. There's also a bit of micromanaging. Scrap the 'bit' part, in reality it's pretty important and you'll micromanage your crew in practically every battle. Your crew will have to repair important parts of your ship and setting them up correctly might make them reload your weapons faster, or recharge your shields faster. They'll even have to engage enemies in combat from time to time.
Killed enemies will give you resources to upgrade your ship and buy stuff in shops. Stuff you desperately need in order to advance. In fact, soms of us might never even be able to complete the game, considering the fact that things are entirely random and it's also based on lots of luck. But it will never stop you from quitting the game. It's always fun, no matter what happens to your ship. You'll keep telling yourself; 'just one more game'. And isn't that what a game's supposed to do?
FTL is a great game and anyone who gives it a try will absolutely learn to appreciate it. Maybe not instantly, but after a few games ? Absolutely !

Confusing and tricky, but more of a traditional puzzle game than you might think at first. Much of the fun of Antichamber comes from figuring out the strange logic that governs things, and using it to make sense out of situations that wouldn't make sense in any other game. It rewards exploration and experimenting more than it does logically deducing the answer on the spot, and fairly often the solution to something can come about by accident while you try everything you can imagine.
Having a mostly non-linear map that opens up more as you collect new abilities makes it much more fun to progress through than a straight, linear sequence of puzzles and for the most part there is enough direction that the temptation to look at a guide is rarely there. It's an unusual sort of puzzle game that plays smoothly and maintains a certain level of immersion instead of just leaving you wandering in circles in frustration. It can trick you and mess with you, and it is very satisfying to overcome its illusions and quirks.
On the negative side, your results may vary, but I did find it very hard on the eyes with all the glaring white backgrounds. You may want to turn down your brightness and play in a well-lit room.

After just completing the story I recommend this game for many reasons but here are a few.  First off is the parkour, it is a very sort of playground type parkour with a good skill tree to further enhance your fun such as dropkicks, rolls, and the good ole shoulder bash from Sam B himself.  Melee combat in Dying Light has been revamped since their release of Dead Island.  A whole new physics remake makes it feel satisfying when you get that hit on a zombie that pops the skull.  However, if your fighting humans the melee system can be a lot trickier.  They can block your attacks often (sometimes even throwables!) they can dodge kick etc.  Now onto my favorite part, the story of this game.  I will be sure to include no spoilers as I have just completed the game.  It is a very well done story that can keep you captivated.  I often found myself being drawn to story missions rather then as something I had to do to progress.  The people you meet, tasks done are interesting and overall fun.  There are even some humorous spots around.  Now the heart and soul of Dying Light, the zombies.  No one is quite sure where it came from but some interesting side quests do have theories.  Dying Light got their zombies right the first time you see a new zombie it should really make you jump.  Take the volatiles for example my first glance at one scared me real bad.  Like heart pounding.  I was terrified to be out at night alone.  Eventually I had to and I was still scared.  The zombies can be quite entertaining during the day however, watching them flop around.  But just remember this game is entitled Dying Light.  Which brings me whimpering to the next topic, coop.  Coop is a fun thing to me, I have and always will love coop in free roam games.  Coop can be used as a therapy for fear.  Grab a couple of buddies and from a raiding group to travel at night.  Raiding not your thing?  Try challenges to add to the mix to keep the competition up.  When you've experienced the fear from first seeing a zombie that is probably gonna make you scream and cry.Repeatedly.  Coop will help you overcome that fear.  Dying Light for me is a fun game, it can keep you entertained with it's rapid parkour and combat while keeping you intertwined with the story and many fun side quests which includes fetching coffee, crayons, and even gathering stuff at night.  Don't forget Jeff's crazy idea "The Apocalypse Wall."  I like Dying Light it brings to light some new and interesting mechanics (see what i did there) and a great storyline.  Definitely worth a try to pick up and play if you get the chance.

Tl;dr: Poor pc port of a reasonably good game.  Recommended because problems are mostly fixed now, and totally playable.
So this game was a disappointment for many when it came out, not least for me, waiting until midnight with the game pre loaded, prepared to immerse myself in rocksteady's masterpiece franchise for the final time.  An fps cap and numerous graphical problems were the first things i faced, and summarily shot my plans of marathoning the game right then and there.  Rocksteady's use of a poor third party pc port made the game's textures and highly-vaunted graphical prowess abysmal, but that's certainly covered in the other reviews.  In time, patches helped, but did not fix entirely, these issues, and i returned to the game ready to play it completely.
If you haven't played the other arkham games, stop reading this and play them.  I won't have spoilers, but the first two games are too good to skip over.
As the finale in the arkham series, and rocksteady's grand return to the cowl, expectations for this game were high, beyond the technical stuff.  The previous games were excellent combinations of gripping sorry and fun gameplay, a balance of two gold standards not really found elsewhere.  So I'll discuss this game as a sequel to them.
The ideal sequel should be, i think, what arkham city was to asylum at the time.  A straight improvement on mechanics, continuity in voice acting and theme, and a story building on that of the last.  Knight succeeds at many of these things, streamlining the mechanics quite well, keeping up the same va art from city/asylum, putting forth a superb story, and still coming through on what made these games so fun for me: they make you feel like Batman.  Where knight fell short was in its reaches, where it looked to make itself not just a sequel, but a finale.
CONS
-The batmobile is impressive, as a game mechanic, but is, to put it lightly, poorly implemented.  The open world can now be explored from the air/rooftops and the street, butthegamewouldreallypreferitifyouusedthestreetthanks.  Too many story missions and side quests required extensive time in the seat of the batmobile, not always in full on battle mode, or in high speed chases, but utilizing winches and levers to enable travel.  The batmobile starts to feel less like a feature and more like a chore.  Don't get me wrong, there's still plenty of gliding/grappling, and i enjoyed both methods of transportation, but the constant switching to the car-remote gadget to turn things on, and raise/lower platforms made me really search for other ways to do things, which were rarely available in the main missions.
-Combat in the batmobile is fun, and not easy, but feels like a mini game.  In direct contrast to the highly-creative predator encounters that made me love the series, fighting behind the wheel feels simplistic, and boring.  This would be fine if so many boss fights did not stick you in these situations, preventing the game from shining at its franchise's greatest moments.
-You may notice the game is rated M, a first for the series.  The games, in story and content, were never light hearted, but as far as Batman goes, there have been many far grittier interpretations, so this isn't entirely out of left field.  However, the story is hurt by a few more hamfisted dark moments, which, while acted beautifully, make this Batman feel very different from the rest of the franchise, or even the rest of the game, for that matter.
The issues above, for me, kept this game from being all i expected in the arkham finale.  But hell, i expected a lot, in retrospect.  The game, in all respects belongs in the series because of what it does well:
PROS
-God, the mechanics are fun.  When you don't have the manacle of the main questline on your feet, the batmobile and gliding combination of movement works perfectly, doing exactly what open world games need to do: make travelling the map fun.  Combat on foot and in predator encounters is redesigned, and simplified, and while it isn't perfect, it still allows for a lot of flexible play, and opens up a ton of new doors in level design and strategy.
-The map itself is grand in scope and perfectionistic in detail.  There's something to see everywhere, and something to do with it.
-The story is edge-of-your-seat action and cliffhanging, all the way through.  Respectful of the comics, and, at the same time, successful in its own creative liberties.
-The voice acting that brings this story to life is, as is to be expected, top notch. It made city and asylum what they were, and does the same here. Nothing else to say about it.
-The side quests here are much better designed and presented than the previous games, making 100% completion a more achievable goal.
-The best of the old gadgets remain, and the new are all useful, and feel like worthy additions to the belt.
-The score is quite good, and will stick with you.
Really, the bottom line for me was that knight is not the paragon of gaming city and asylum were.  Are there flaws?  Yes.  Is it as shining an example of games at their finest as city and asylum were? No.  Is it as fun as city and asylum? Absolutely.

This was a great survival-horror experience.  I have completed the story to its fullest; here's my opinion.
The graphics were a marvel if you have the system to run it at higher settings but the optimization quality here is sadly subpar as the "View Distance" slider was the only true catalyst for a better or worse framerate.  Even with the view distance set at just below the halfway mark, there would be a rare occurence of HORRENDOUS frame drops.  I have no idea why these occured as I have been in rooms with about 40 zombies in this game without an issue and has about 4 occasions where the game dipped to about 10fps during a grapple sequence.  Yes, 10fps.  Really took me out of the experience.  Besides these issues, the city is gorgeous.  The world is littered with cars, debris, gore, the undead, and still manages to look beautiful (especially in "Old Town," unlocked about halfway through the story) with its tall buildings  and the sense that this was once a thriving, elegant city.  The voice acting was pretty good all around but it had its weak moments with a couple of side characters.  And the sound.  The sound in this game is sure to immerse you as the undead growl from a distance, each melee connects with a satisfying crunch, the slight sound of wind as you parkour your way up rooftops and through safe zones, and quite frankly I enjoyed the sound immensely.  This is all backed up with a pretty good story.  I actually had a motivation to continue with the story and did very few side quests throughout my time with it.  I only really developed a slight connection with one character besides the protagonist but I wasn't fond of the villian.  There are a couple of boss fights.  They give you a good arena to battle and offer a good challenge, but one of them feels unfair when the enemy is able to throw axes THROUGH walls.  Luckily, it wasnt enough to kill me, but it was mildly infuriating that he was able to defy the laws of physics to damage me.  The conclusion to the game was more or less satisfying, as what you expected to be an epic boss battle turned out to be a quick time event.  As to avoid spoilers, thats all I have to say about that.  Now the gameplay.  This game has extremely addicting melee combat.  It does start off slow with the weak weapons and the whole take-8-hits-to-take-out-a-single-zombie-for-the-first-4-hours bit, but once you get going the game gives you a great sense of progression.  You'll start seeing zombies being dispatched more quickly, an abundance of arms flying to your left and right, and finish each fight off with a well-placed swing to the neck and watch the heads roll.  There's a variety of weapons, whether your busting heads into pieces with pipes or sledgehammers or simply decapitating the undead with a sickle or a machete.  The ragdoll physics are quite entertaining, too.  I found myself dropkicking a LOT of zombies off of rooftops because its just so enjoyable to watch them spin and distort themselves before inevitably landing headfirst into the concrete 50 feet below, leaving chunks of brain spewing all around them.  Another core element of gameplay is the parkour.  People have referred to this game as Mirror's Edge+ Dead Island, and for good reason.  Navigating the rooftops is a breeze and I've only had a few moments where I couldn't climb a wall I previously thought was possible to scale.  You can jump quite far, too.  I kept asking "Can I actually make that jump?"  Yes, I could make that jump.  The last major element to the gameplay is the day and night cycle.  During the day, the zombies are really just wandering the streets with no real goal in mind until you confront them.  Still, they can overwhelm you in numbers, especially when a viral is among their ranks.  A viral is just a fresh infected-you'll hear a human voice go "Please" or "Stop" as you bash their heads in.  It adds a layer of humanity to the game, and you almost feel bad for having to put them down.  It is a necessity to as virals run at a faster speed than even you and can climb buildings.  They also appear during the night.  The night is absolutely terrifying in my opinion.  I have the sense that every zombie is looking for me and only me.  The elite zombies, or Volatiles, are a higher mutation of the normal zombies and essentially cant be killed unless you have an ultraviolet flashlight on hand, which really only stuns them.  The night almost completely switches all of your gears to stealth.  You do not want to be caught in the line of sight of a Volatile or a Viral, and even a normal zombie is tougher during these hours.  Unless you have a mission, your best bet is to flip on that flashlight and navigate your way to the nearest safezone; most of which have to be liberated, so make sure you are close to one or you'll have an experience like me where I cleared a safe zone as the night began.  What a terror-ensuing experience.  This game is quite punishing, also.  This is a good thing as most modern games are an actual walk in the park.  I enjoyed its difficulty, but I do wish there was a slider.  The game takes away experience points for dying, which I felt was a little much especially when I died from those Exploders.  Almost every single exploder I've come across, undead with inflated guts that explode when they're close enough, has killed me.  I'll just be doing a story mission and open up a door and OH GOD ITS ONE OF THOSE RUN AWA-...You are Dead.  I felt they could have limited its power as it doesn't even take out zombies as often as they take me out. There's a reason LEGO Marvel Super Heroes is one of the highest-selling LEGO video games of all time; actually, three reasons.
First, the characters. The game features not only the existing Avengers, X-Men and Ultimate Spider-Man LEGOs on the market, but a legion of characters and vehicles either only recently released in 2014 or not even created yet. From the Fantastic Four to the Sinister Six, this game includes the majority of Marvel's well-known characters along with a handful of lesser-known ones. Plus they've included the legendary Stan Lee himself as a playable character possessing multiple superpowers. What more do you need from this game?
Speaking of characters, the next reason is what the minifigures take part in: the story. You can tell the writers and game designers had fun trying to combine a coherent Marvel storyline with the quirky humor found in every other LEGO game. And you know what? They did it. The story features the Avengers, Fantastic Four and X-Men teaming up against villains like Magneto, Doc Ock, Doctor Doom, Loki, Abomination and Sandman, in an epic quest filled with crazy left turns that only a LEGO video game could have. And it all leads up to a stunning twist you'll never expect (so I won't ruin it for those who haven't played yet).
Finally, the gameplay. I was very pleasantly surprised just from playing a free PC demo of the game which was released online early last year, featuring the game's very first level, Sand Central Station. This level features Iron Man (Mark 6), the Hulk and Spider-Man taking on Abomination and Sandman in New York's Grand Central Station. But what blew me away the most during the level was the sheer number of abilities each character had, from Hulk's famous Puny God move from The Avengers, to Spider-Man's ability to actually swing around on a web. When I finally bought the actual game, I was thrilled to discover that the rest of the characters in the game were just as incredible.
So, if you're skeptical about buying this game, I suggest you try out the demo featured on
first, and if you still don't feel like buying the game, then at least you technically tried it for free. But based on my personal experience, I think all of your doubts will go away and you'll want to buy LEGO Marvel Super Heroes right away.

Back when I first played Dead Space on the Xbox 360 it was the game which scared me; now it's the controls.
I feel as if I should get this aspect cleared out first. The controls kinda suck and even on the highest sensitivity the clunkiness what still there to a certain extent though you'll be surprised when you get used to it looking back. It's more like that kind of game where you have to take a couple minutes to get used to them each time you start it up but then master them with ease.
The weapons are great. There's something for each when it comes to a form of dismemberment but while I think you're not really dependant on any there's still the same 4 weapons you'll stick to every time you play. Considering that later on you'll probably upgrade them only strengthens the point further.
The story seemed to have a much faster pacing than before though that could be said of many replays of different games. Nothing felt rushed and the story manages to captivate you no matter how much but overall it tends to be cliche. Without spoiling anything back in 2008 there was still a lot of unexplored ground but even then I wouldn't have considered it an original idea aside from the iconic, industrial aesthetic Dead Space has.
As far as chapters or levels go you have 12 of them, each "moduled" into contained segments. While this kind of design is almost a synonim to linearity it makes up for when taken apart. You'd have a  friend come over and play a chapter from the middle of the game without necessarily needing to fill in what happened. Tight animations, "resource management" type of combat - that's what this game is.
Overall Dead Space is a fun adventure for those who wish to play a horror game or shoot Necromorphs (or "alien zombies", whatever you wanna call 'em) in a manner similar to Doom 3. I had a pretty solid, almost "cinematic" experience with it and for the price it gets when on sale it's a nice offer. Dead Space is clearly a classic of the horror genre.

*IF YOU ARE ON THE FENCE ABOUT PLAYING SHADOWVERSE*
The Take Two (arena-style draft) mode played against a friend is COMPLETELY free, and you can play it as much as you want. This is the best way to play with some of the neat legendary cards and to get a diverse feel for some of the classes with the least amount of investment. If you at least have a little cardgame knowledge (enough to draft with a friend and have fun), then this part is at least worth every bit of your time to download it and try it out.
Anyways, Shadowverse is neat little collectible card game with a few unique mechanics, low RNG variance, and easy to learn cards that aren't written in Lawyer's Prose but have a layer of finesse to them, on top of a very, erm, deliberate choice of artstyle. You start with a rather generous amount of free card packs at the start, and is riddled with ways to earn packs/arena vouchers/gold/dust through the achievements system. Each of the classes feels very distinct from one another, and have rather strong identities, along with at least 1 mechanic many class cards are tied to. As an example, bloodcraft's minions are often tied to Vengence, which activates when a player hovers at 10 health or lower, making health management very important to that class. One of the most interesting aspects to Shadowverse is its Evolve mechanic which serves to make the midgame rather vibrant and adds a lot of extra decisions to consider, even when you may have few cards in your hand.
If you're at all interested in playing, I'd recommend giving it a shot and, at the very least, dicking around in the Take Two mode.
The PC port is better than the phone/emulator, but is little lacking in some ways; the interface is largely the same as the phone one, but the art on the cards looks much crisper and clearer. It's a lot better than on an emulator, but could be improved upon. Make sure if you're playing for the first time to fix your resolution and you toggle the option for 60fps instead of 30fps.
