It's hard to review a game that hasn't been fully released but having played two chapters I can at least write my first impressions.
--There are plenty of angry people who were raging about not having offline co-op and to be honest I don't care. Having said that I am angry because Capcom falsely advertised it on Steam ( That's a bad practise If I ever seen one ).  However I do care about ONLINE co-op especially in Raid Mode which If i'm not mistaken will be added later. --
What I don't understand is why people are not getting angry on micro-transactions and a "chapter-y" nature of the game. Add to the fact that they have released second chapter and FRAME RATE ISSUES are still there! Which to me is more infuriating because I actually died couple of times thanks to the FPS drops and stutters. Luckily it doesn't happen everywhere but in certain areas ( it goes between 60 then it drops to 30 and then its all over the place... ).
Since we are talking about the negatives let me add few more things :
- support characters ( especially Moira ) are out of place in Resident Evil universe ( at least in my opinion ). Japanese voice over doesn't seem to have swearing and yet English dub or even subtitles have swearing which feels like cheap horror movie. Moira is rarely helpful and she doesn't add much to immersion, she is rather irritating and sometimes you wish she could just shut up.
- It's not SCARY. Most of the time you are accompanied by the support characters and it dampens the feeling of being alone and facing the horror by yourself. There are some jump scares here and there but most of them are predictible.
You fight, move through quiet area/safe zone then music comes in you fight or sneak again ( rinse n repeat ).
It could have been scarier if they added flickering lights for example in some of the areas ( you move in the house doors locks, move to the center then lights flicker, boom darkness, growling ,red eyes lights come back and you have to fight for your life ). *not in this game though*
I remember going through the forest with Barry and this could have been made into scary part but it just ins't, audio is not there music is a dead giveaway and it's not dark/dynamic enough. It's rather average horror experience.
- microtransactions. WE DON'T WANT THEM CAPCOM! It feels like free to play game which I HAVE ALREADY PAID FOR! Just to limit my STORAGE in Raid Mode? You want 72 more space slots for guns BUY DLC. Stupid.
I can understand characters or maps heck EVEN extra weapons but storage space? What the hell Capcom? Just NO.
- Story although immersive it doesn't feel like Resident Evil anymore. It feels like the Movie "Saw" with "Overseer" lady messing around with the people on the island  ( which *spoilers* will turn against you because they can't take the pressure ). I felt dissapointed that this is not your Resident experience but it feels like a cheap horror movie scenario, like they just needed an excuse to shoot those "infected". Barry and Claire are probably the only things that gives me the "feeling" of Resident Evil.
Ok those are basically the bad points ( there are others like grindy Raid Mode, Gestures ( blatantly borrowed from LOST PLANET 2 ) that dumbens the RE characters, reused textures in some areas,  but I'm not going to go there ) let me talk about the good points :
- Combat have been improved and now you can perform dodge more easily ! There is also stealth mechanic which albeit being simple it gets the job done and the animations are satysfying.
- A lot of skills and guns ( especially in Raid Mode ).
It's fun at times?
Less of a horror game or a Resident Evil game for me but above average third person shooter that can be enjoyable ( lot's of replay value for the price, If you like Raid Mode that is ). Once the issues with the FRAME RATE have been sorted and WHEN they add ONLINE co op, then I can recommend this game.

A long time fan of Resident Evil since the playstation, and even a long time horror fan I have to admit that there are a few gripes with Revelations 2. Since we are in the mood for sandwiches, a la Claire and the infamous Jill sandwich, I'm gonna do a negative sandwich bunned with positives.
It was too early to judge a game by the first episode, but by the second episode it was redeemed. Each episode is about 2 to 4 hours worth of gameplay, which does include both Claires and Barrys paths. Graphics are okay, nothing to much too behold. It is comparable to the graphics of Resident Evil 6. Gameplay is what you would expect from third person shooter and a Resident Evil game, nothing groundbreaking. Each characters non-combatant "co-op" partner provides some skills that compliment the combabatants characters abilities. Moiras flashlight than can blind foes, and Natalias enemy sensing ability.
However, despite having Resident Evil 6 graphics, the game at times does have a slow down of FPS. Most notably in areas with high amounts of effects. It does question why it's happening since the graphics themselves aren't groundbreaking. Speaking of which, a lot of the assets are ripped from Resident Evil 4, 5, and 6; to be more specific the breakable crates and barrels. The inventory system isn't the greatest, nor is it the worst, but it is something. RAID overall is horrible; understanding that it's suppose to be based on an RPG, leveling up and what not, Resident Evil Mercenaries mode is a better alternative. Co-Op in RAID will probably be implemented later, but is not available upon release. There copius amounts of DLC, most of which are extra inventory space for RAID, and alternative costumes for the campaign characters, and characters for RAID(mind you that the characters in RAID are only skins, and have such minor differences that they are not different at all). Episodic releases seems redundant if each episode is going to get released every week.
One of the things that I do enjoy, is that each campaign has a different gameplay aesthetic. Borrowed from Resident Evil 6 on how each campaign plays different, Revelations 2 does the same. Claires campaign is more action oriented, due to enemies being more mobile; whilst in Barrys there are slower, zombie-esque enemies with a touch of enemies similar to those found in Revelations one. The story should not but put aside from only one episode. As a long time fan, the second episode got me hyped for the next release. The general story isn't profound, and employs a past and present narrative. Claires being in the past, and Barrys in the future. While it is cheap to reuse the some of the environments, you do get different scenarios and go to side areas.
In closing, the game is worth the price of $24 or so dollars. From the looks of it, you get about 8-12 hours of gameplay. It is worth buying, right now, or when it's on sale. If you are a long time fan of Resident Evil, and have kept track of the minor details will be rewarded. Heres a hint
If you know what I meant, you are in for a treat, if not, well reconsider if you really ARE a fan of Resident Evil since this isn't really explored in the main games,since it was referred only in a small memo. Regardless, it is more of a side story and not really necessary if you don't want to know what has happened to Claire and Barry.

Tl;dr: Poor pc port of a reasonably good game.  Recommended because problems are mostly fixed now, and totally playable.
So this game was a disappointment for many when it came out, not least for me, waiting until midnight with the game pre loaded, prepared to immerse myself in rocksteady's masterpiece franchise for the final time.  An fps cap and numerous graphical problems were the first things i faced, and summarily shot my plans of marathoning the game right then and there.  Rocksteady's use of a poor third party pc port made the game's textures and highly-vaunted graphical prowess abysmal, but that's certainly covered in the other reviews.  In time, patches helped, but did not fix entirely, these issues, and i returned to the game ready to play it completely.
If you haven't played the other arkham games, stop reading this and play them.  I won't have spoilers, but the first two games are too good to skip over.
As the finale in the arkham series, and rocksteady's grand return to the cowl, expectations for this game were high, beyond the technical stuff.  The previous games were excellent combinations of gripping sorry and fun gameplay, a balance of two gold standards not really found elsewhere.  So I'll discuss this game as a sequel to them.
The ideal sequel should be, i think, what arkham city was to asylum at the time.  A straight improvement on mechanics, continuity in voice acting and theme, and a story building on that of the last.  Knight succeeds at many of these things, streamlining the mechanics quite well, keeping up the same va art from city/asylum, putting forth a superb story, and still coming through on what made these games so fun for me: they make you feel like Batman.  Where knight fell short was in its reaches, where it looked to make itself not just a sequel, but a finale.
CONS
-The batmobile is impressive, as a game mechanic, but is, to put it lightly, poorly implemented.  The open world can now be explored from the air/rooftops and the street, butthegamewouldreallypreferitifyouusedthestreetthanks.  Too many story missions and side quests required extensive time in the seat of the batmobile, not always in full on battle mode, or in high speed chases, but utilizing winches and levers to enable travel.  The batmobile starts to feel less like a feature and more like a chore.  Don't get me wrong, there's still plenty of gliding/grappling, and i enjoyed both methods of transportation, but the constant switching to the car-remote gadget to turn things on, and raise/lower platforms made me really search for other ways to do things, which were rarely available in the main missions.
-Combat in the batmobile is fun, and not easy, but feels like a mini game.  In direct contrast to the highly-creative predator encounters that made me love the series, fighting behind the wheel feels simplistic, and boring.  This would be fine if so many boss fights did not stick you in these situations, preventing the game from shining at its franchise's greatest moments.
-You may notice the game is rated M, a first for the series.  The games, in story and content, were never light hearted, but as far as Batman goes, there have been many far grittier interpretations, so this isn't entirely out of left field.  However, the story is hurt by a few more hamfisted dark moments, which, while acted beautifully, make this Batman feel very different from the rest of the franchise, or even the rest of the game, for that matter.
The issues above, for me, kept this game from being all i expected in the arkham finale.  But hell, i expected a lot, in retrospect.  The game, in all respects belongs in the series because of what it does well:
PROS
-God, the mechanics are fun.  When you don't have the manacle of the main questline on your feet, the batmobile and gliding combination of movement works perfectly, doing exactly what open world games need to do: make travelling the map fun.  Combat on foot and in predator encounters is redesigned, and simplified, and while it isn't perfect, it still allows for a lot of flexible play, and opens up a ton of new doors in level design and strategy.
-The map itself is grand in scope and perfectionistic in detail.  There's something to see everywhere, and something to do with it.
-The story is edge-of-your-seat action and cliffhanging, all the way through.  Respectful of the comics, and, at the same time, successful in its own creative liberties.
-The voice acting that brings this story to life is, as is to be expected, top notch. It made city and asylum what they were, and does the same here. Nothing else to say about it.
-The side quests here are much better designed and presented than the previous games, making 100% completion a more achievable goal.
-The best of the old gadgets remain, and the new are all useful, and feel like worthy additions to the belt.
-The score is quite good, and will stick with you.
Really, the bottom line for me was that knight is not the paragon of gaming city and asylum were.  Are there flaws?  Yes.  Is it as shining an example of games at their finest as city and asylum were? No.  Is it as fun as city and asylum? Absolutely.

After just completing the story I recommend this game for many reasons but here are a few.  First off is the parkour, it is a very sort of playground type parkour with a good skill tree to further enhance your fun such as dropkicks, rolls, and the good ole shoulder bash from Sam B himself.  Melee combat in Dying Light has been revamped since their release of Dead Island.  A whole new physics remake makes it feel satisfying when you get that hit on a zombie that pops the skull.  However, if your fighting humans the melee system can be a lot trickier.  They can block your attacks often (sometimes even throwables!) they can dodge kick etc.  Now onto my favorite part, the story of this game.  I will be sure to include no spoilers as I have just completed the game.  It is a very well done story that can keep you captivated.  I often found myself being drawn to story missions rather then as something I had to do to progress.  The people you meet, tasks done are interesting and overall fun.  There are even some humorous spots around.  Now the heart and soul of Dying Light, the zombies.  No one is quite sure where it came from but some interesting side quests do have theories.  Dying Light got their zombies right the first time you see a new zombie it should really make you jump.  Take the volatiles for example my first glance at one scared me real bad.  Like heart pounding.  I was terrified to be out at night alone.  Eventually I had to and I was still scared.  The zombies can be quite entertaining during the day however, watching them flop around.  But just remember this game is entitled Dying Light.  Which brings me whimpering to the next topic, coop.  Coop is a fun thing to me, I have and always will love coop in free roam games.  Coop can be used as a therapy for fear.  Grab a couple of buddies and from a raiding group to travel at night.  Raiding not your thing?  Try challenges to add to the mix to keep the competition up.  When you've experienced the fear from first seeing a zombie that is probably gonna make you scream and cry.Repeatedly.  Coop will help you overcome that fear.  Dying Light for me is a fun game, it can keep you entertained with it's rapid parkour and combat while keeping you intertwined with the story and many fun side quests which includes fetching coffee, crayons, and even gathering stuff at night.  Don't forget Jeff's crazy idea "The Apocalypse Wall."  I like Dying Light it brings to light some new and interesting mechanics (see what i did there) and a great storyline.  Definitely worth a try to pick up and play if you get the chance.

ENGLISH REVIEW:
Dnd is a game about four friends mistakenly summoned in a world of magic and believed
to be heroes. In reality they're a bunch of nerds trying to return to their homes while they
enjoy a wonderful adventure in a fantasy land filled with treasures, castles, dragons, orcs,
elves and... Santa Claus.
The first thing I thought about Doom and Destiny was "here's another rpg maker game that
is trying to be a parody of other famous rpgs like final fantasy"... And I was right, the
game is just this, but done well... very well.
The humor is very captivating and the jokes will make you laugh in more than one occasion. And don't think the story doesn't take itself seriously at all, because it does, delivering a fascinating story without "plot holes" even though it's a parody.
I dare to say Doom and Destiny is a perfect blend of storytelling and great humor, with a gameplay on par with titles from the final fantasy series and the possibility of exploring the world, which is something that similar games don't do anymore. And secrets, lots of secrets scattered through the map and in the numerous locations of the game.
Also the game has 3 difficulty settings so it can be played by everyone.
Both the music and the graphics are licensed contents, they weren't made by the developers but bought from third parties and put into the game. I don't consider this a real flaw, but I know some people stay away from games with rpg maker graphics because they think they're not worth it... Well, if you can get over the fact that the graphics is standard rpg maker, I assure you'll find a real gem.
If you played "the Bridge", a very good puzzle game here on Steam, you'll notice that the game opening music is the same of Doom and Destiny, but does this make The Bridge a bad game only because they share the same opening song? no, so don't be discouraged by these things someone could call "flaws" and give this game a chance. You'll not regret it.
RECENSIONE ITA:
Dnd è un gioco che racconta di quattro amici evocati per sbaglio in una terra magica e scambiati per eroi. In realtà sono quattro nerdacci della peggior specie che cercano un modo per tornare a casa, ma non prima di essersi gustati una fantastica avventura in un mondo pieno di tesori, castelli, draghi, orchi, elfi e... Babbo Natale.
La prima cosa che ho pensato di Dnd è stata "ecco un altro gioco fatto con Rpg Maker che cerca di fare la parodia di altri famosi rpg come Final Fantasy"... e avevo ragione, il gioco è essenzialmente questo, ma fatto bene... davvero bene.
L'humor è accattivante e le battute ti faranno ridere in più di un'occasione. E non pensiate che la storia non si prende sul serio nemmeno un po', perché lo fa, regalando una trama affascinante senza "plot holes", e questo è già tanto essendo una parodia.
Mi permetto di affermare che Dnd è una perfetta miscela di storia e umorismo, con un gameplay al pari di titoli della serie Final Fantasy e la possibilità di esplorare il mondo di gioco, qualcosa che non si vede più tanto spesso in questo tipo di giochi... e segreti, tantissimi segreti sparsi per la mappa e nelle numerose aree del gioco. Inoltre il gioco ha 3 livelli di difficoltà, così da poter essere giocato da tutti.
Sia la musica che la grafica sono contenuti acquistati da terze parti e concesse dietro licenza. Personalmente non considero questo un vero difetto, ma so che molta gente si tiene alla larga dai giochi con grafica Rpg maker perchè pensa manchino di originalità... ebbene, se riuscirete a guardare oltre le grafiche di rpg maker vi assicuro che vi ritroverete di fronte ad una vera perla del genere ricolmo di originalità ed estro creativo.
Se avete giocato "The Bridge", un buon puzzle game qui su Steam, noterete che la musica di apertura è la stessa di Dnd, perché acquistata dallo stesso musicista; ma questo rende forse "The Bridge" un brutto gioco? non credo, quindi non fatevi scoraggiare da queste limitazioni del titolo e date una chance ad un grande gioco; non ve ne pentirete.

This was a great survival-horror experience.  I have completed the story to its fullest; here's my opinion.
The graphics were a marvel if you have the system to run it at higher settings but the optimization quality here is sadly subpar as the "View Distance" slider was the only true catalyst for a better or worse framerate.  Even with the view distance set at just below the halfway mark, there would be a rare occurence of HORRENDOUS frame drops.  I have no idea why these occured as I have been in rooms with about 40 zombies in this game without an issue and has about 4 occasions where the game dipped to about 10fps during a grapple sequence.  Yes, 10fps.  Really took me out of the experience.  Besides these issues, the city is gorgeous.  The world is littered with cars, debris, gore, the undead, and still manages to look beautiful (especially in "Old Town," unlocked about halfway through the story) with its tall buildings  and the sense that this was once a thriving, elegant city.  The voice acting was pretty good all around but it had its weak moments with a couple of side characters.  And the sound.  The sound in this game is sure to immerse you as the undead growl from a distance, each melee connects with a satisfying crunch, the slight sound of wind as you parkour your way up rooftops and through safe zones, and quite frankly I enjoyed the sound immensely.  This is all backed up with a pretty good story.  I actually had a motivation to continue with the story and did very few side quests throughout my time with it.  I only really developed a slight connection with one character besides the protagonist but I wasn't fond of the villian.  There are a couple of boss fights.  They give you a good arena to battle and offer a good challenge, but one of them feels unfair when the enemy is able to throw axes THROUGH walls.  Luckily, it wasnt enough to kill me, but it was mildly infuriating that he was able to defy the laws of physics to damage me.  The conclusion to the game was more or less satisfying, as what you expected to be an epic boss battle turned out to be a quick time event.  As to avoid spoilers, thats all I have to say about that.  Now the gameplay.  This game has extremely addicting melee combat.  It does start off slow with the weak weapons and the whole take-8-hits-to-take-out-a-single-zombie-for-the-first-4-hours bit, but once you get going the game gives you a great sense of progression.  You'll start seeing zombies being dispatched more quickly, an abundance of arms flying to your left and right, and finish each fight off with a well-placed swing to the neck and watch the heads roll.  There's a variety of weapons, whether your busting heads into pieces with pipes or sledgehammers or simply decapitating the undead with a sickle or a machete.  The ragdoll physics are quite entertaining, too.  I found myself dropkicking a LOT of zombies off of rooftops because its just so enjoyable to watch them spin and distort themselves before inevitably landing headfirst into the concrete 50 feet below, leaving chunks of brain spewing all around them.  Another core element of gameplay is the parkour.  People have referred to this game as Mirror's Edge+ Dead Island, and for good reason.  Navigating the rooftops is a breeze and I've only had a few moments where I couldn't climb a wall I previously thought was possible to scale.  You can jump quite far, too.  I kept asking "Can I actually make that jump?"  Yes, I could make that jump.  The last major element to the gameplay is the day and night cycle.  During the day, the zombies are really just wandering the streets with no real goal in mind until you confront them.  Still, they can overwhelm you in numbers, especially when a viral is among their ranks.  A viral is just a fresh infected-you'll hear a human voice go "Please" or "Stop" as you bash their heads in.  It adds a layer of humanity to the game, and you almost feel bad for having to put them down.  It is a necessity to as virals run at a faster speed than even you and can climb buildings.  They also appear during the night.  The night is absolutely terrifying in my opinion.  I have the sense that every zombie is looking for me and only me.  The elite zombies, or Volatiles, are a higher mutation of the normal zombies and essentially cant be killed unless you have an ultraviolet flashlight on hand, which really only stuns them.  The night almost completely switches all of your gears to stealth.  You do not want to be caught in the line of sight of a Volatile or a Viral, and even a normal zombie is tougher during these hours.  Unless you have a mission, your best bet is to flip on that flashlight and navigate your way to the nearest safezone; most of which have to be liberated, so make sure you are close to one or you'll have an experience like me where I cleared a safe zone as the night began.  What a terror-ensuing experience.  This game is quite punishing, also.  This is a good thing as most modern games are an actual walk in the park.  I enjoyed its difficulty, but I do wish there was a slider.  The game takes away experience points for dying, which I felt was a little much especially when I died from those Exploders.  Almost every single exploder I've come across, undead with inflated guts that explode when they're close enough, has killed me.  I'll just be doing a story mission and open up a door and OH GOD ITS ONE OF THOSE RUN AWA-...You are Dead.  I felt they could have limited its power as it doesn't even take out zombies as often as they take me out.  Overall, this game is a great experience because of its great visuals, though with its problems, amazing sound design, and fluid, tense, and satisfying gameplay, though unfair at times.  Smaller breakdown -
Graphics - 8/10  (+Beautiful,-Frame Drops)
Story - 7/10 (+Pretty Interesting,-Not much connection with cast)
Sound - 10/10 (+Immersive)
Gameplay - 8.5/10 (+Satisfying and Brutal and Tense,-Unfair at times)
In my opinion, Dying Light is an 8/10.

This game might as well be fantasy because it can very easily cast a binding spell on the player, forcing him to play until he can no longer stand grasping at the air around the tantalizing key to his chains called victory. One can potentially play for days and still never see the final boss in all its... uh, majesty? There isn't much I can say here, except it's a roguelike with an incredible combat system and an almost text-based exploratory system. You have your visuals, but you never truly see what happens outside of combat, and you must use your imagination to enhance the experience here. If you're lucky, all you'll ever see of the Rebellion is that large expanding wave from the left side of your map, and that is all the game needs to push you in the direction of the exit.
It's easy to see why this game can sometimes make the player feel as though he has been cheated out of a run; sometimes, early one, just the right combination of guns on an automated Rebel scout ship can smash your ship apart in seconds flat. The same can happen in the final throes of the game, or the final boss, whose fighting style and weapon combinations seem like a sensei to your grasshopper no matter how much you've put into your shield strength. (can anyone say "drone army?") This game on the misnomered "Normal" difficulty asks perfection from a constant struggle to make it through the end, and it is never an easy task to perform.
There is no other game out there that proves the existence of game compulsion quite like this one. For days I felt like I had to complete it, I had to play through at least once, to see if I could make it. I think I've forced my handcuffs off, at least long enough to write this review, by reaching the final boss once. I thought I had it in my grasp, my powerful weapons charged but missing ammo, my shields holding as I beamed my crew into their various weapons bays (what a structural weakness, separating those rooms from the rest of the ship and manning them with but one helpless human... so very susceptible to mantis venom) and destroying them slowly but surely. Who knew they'd come back with a functioning drone control augmentation and a few seconds that redefined the word "hopeless?"
If you want to feel as though you've been chained to your computer for weeks trying to beat this game into submission, or you want to experience an effective simulation of the struggle of a lonely mission through space, where supplies are short and hope is shorter (for a TV example, look no further than Firefly or Battlestar Galactica), delivered through mechanics alone, $10 does not do this game justice. It is too good, but almost too arresting. Buy it... if you dare.

Shadowrun Returns is a throwback to the days of old, which feels absolutely fresh in this modern era. This takes me back to the golden era of RPG's in the mid-to-late 1990's - which was back when RPG's were often isometric; turn-based; party-based; and used a mixture of both 2D + 3D environments + character models. If this sounds like something that would be up your alley - you likely have already have purchased SrR (Shadowrun Returns) or should buy this game ASAP. Shadowrun Returns is simply nothing short of fantastic.
Shadowrun Returns (base-game) comes equipped with "Dead Man's Switch" for its base-game's single-player campaign. You play a runner (whose class, if you want to pick one; race, class, skills, etc can be determined by you) whose friend recently died. Actually, he was murdered. Your job is to find who is responsible, why, and decide what to do about the matter. It seems that our friend is linked to a bunch of strange murders that have being happening in this futuristic mix of both a cyberpunk setting (futuristic world where corporations, computers, hacking + whatnot are all par for the course) + fantasy elements (elves + dwarves are here; and magic can all take place in this game-world here). And that's just the start of things - so, that I don't spoil everything.
One thing that absolutely sets SrR apart from many other modern-day games - there is just no voice-acting. It's not that this game needs voice-acting, either. This is one of the best written games I've seen in years, feeling like a throwback to the days of Planescape: Torment (late 90's). This game is not just a great game, but it also so happens to be a great book to read. You'll be doing plenty of reading here. The prose, dialogue & characters are absolutely excellent - littered with tons of description + is extremely verbose. If you've been missing games to be littered w/ tons of description when characters actually do things, since graphics do plenty of the talking these days - you're in for a treat here with SrR, since the writing here is excellent.
While the graphical quality will certainly not top the technical aspect of the most recent hardware-pushing graphical show - the direction of the graphics are excellent. The artistic direction game is loaded with tons of style + substance - with its excellent 2D + 3D mixture of graphics. This feels like a modern-day revival of games from the Infinity Engine.
Combat feels very similar to the classic Fallout 1 + 2. You have a limited number Action Points that you can use spend to do attacks or moves. The combat of this game is quite tactical + turn-based. It always feels great, sounds great, and is a lot of fun to take on. Some of the most interesting + fun battles take place when some of your party members are in the literal game-world, while other party members might be in the computer-world matrix - where you'll be balancing doing combat on two different fronts. Nothing short of awesome.
Most of this game's campaign is a linear affair, where you also might have a few side-quests here and there on your way. This is not an open-world game, by any means. Not that it needs to be, either - as the game often stays very focused on its excellent story, game-world, settings, and characters. Here and there, you'll be given a few different ways to solve quests - which can be be done or result differently, all based on your stats, skills & whatnot.
Shadowrun Returns is a fantastic throwback to the 1990's era of RPG's, if it was just made with modern graphics + high-resolution support. Gamers that have been wanting a high-quality turn-based RPG where you control an entire party entirely - look no further. If you've wanted superb prose, dialogue, and writing - look no further than SrR. If having this great "Dead Man's Switch" campaign (which took me around 16 hours or so to finish) wasn't enough - this game has the Editor come with it. SrR is on the Steam WorkShop and there are a good deal of mods + campaigns made by gamers out there. Being given such a great campaign + an editor here - is there more that old-school RPG gamers can really ask for here?
Grade = A.

Faerie Solitaire is an average Solitaire game and lacking in the "neat things we added that make it different" department. There's a story mode that throw objectives like "create a 5 combo" or "clear a stage in less than a minute" or "get x number of perfect clears" at you and you can't progress until you clear all of the objectives and pass/fail all 9 stages. It gets incredibly repetitive. Between stages you get some exposition that tells you about the backstory and why you're playing Solitaire to rescue fairies and stuff but it has absolutely no effect on the gameplay and it is there just to look nice.
Sometimes when you clear cards you find either materials or a creature egg that you can hatch and equip. After you've equipped the pet for long enough time you can evolve it, provided that you've obtained enough of the aforementioned materials. There are over 30 pets to collect and evolve and not a single one of the pets do a damn thing for the game overall. They're just there to look nice and provide fake replay value.
Since this is a card game there has to be some degree of randomness to it. The objectives for each stage are fixed, but everything else is random. Whether you get eggs or materials behind cards is random. Whether your pet evolves or not is probably random too. The game tells you that it evolves after you get enough EXP but that's just as good as saying "your pet will randomly evolve as you play." Clearing a stage is pretty much random too. Which is great for the challenge modes where you often have to win at least 3+ times to pass that challenge mode. I spent 5 hours trying to clear Stone Temple and you need 6 perfects to pass it, and the most I ever got was 5. Completely arbitrary and random. Casual, sure, but to the point of frustration.

Pros:
Lots of replay value with multiple things to do and find, and numerous achievements to get (some Steam achievements, others in-game ones).  At the time of writing I've played over 100 hours and still have plenty to do, and I am still enjoying the game.
Great atmosphere, engaging characters, excellent voice acting, decent graphics which at times look quite impressive (though probably still not as good as the much older RE5 but that was a much bigger budget release), excellent music and sound effects, decent story, controls generally decent (for an RE game), combat feels very satisfying.
Raid mode is a lot of fun although the difficulty level is more casual than its predecessor which may disappoint some.  At first I was underwhelmed but I came to find it addictive and rewarding.
Cons:
Some framerate issues even though I have a powerful i7 system, at times the framerate will dive to the single figures for a few seconds before suddenly going back to a solid 60 (I have it capped at 60 and vsync turned on).  This isn't a frequent or major issue and most of the time the framerate is perfect though.
Some cutscenes can't be skipped, and those that can sometimes make you wait a few seconds before the skip button will work which is a little thing but it can be annoying.
The game contains numerous 'cutscene like' moments where you still have control of your character but the game forces you to walk slowly, or snatches the camera view and makes you look somewhere else, which can be jarring and irritating especially in the timed modes.
Sometimes the partner AI is frustrating, I've had my partner refuse to follow me, and I have to take manual control of them.  Or they walk into danger (such as spinning blades) and get killed.  This isn't a major problem but it could have used a bit of tweaking.
Controls can be a bit fussy at times - you may be standing in front of a lever to pull, or a ladder to climb, and press A to do it, but the game insists you move another few pixels, or sometimes you may have to walk away from it and then back again - these are rough edges which could have been smoothed out.

I cannot think of enough praise for South Park: Stick of Truth. In my opinion this is a nearly flawless game.
I am speechless at the faithfulness to the South Park brand; from the voices and animation, to the dead-on satirical humor and a strong fan service of reference after glorious reference this game is everything one could ever want from a South Park game. From start to finish I felt like I got to direct and enjoy my very own 20 hour South Park marathon. It was absolute joy! And the detail put in the game is astounding as well. Every item you pick up has a hilarious description and a majority are key props from some of the best episodes of the TV series.
Oh the game? Yeah it’s alright.. turn based party RPG combat, some little timed elements here and there. But did I mention the best trip to Canada ever taken and one of the funniest moments I’ve ever experienced in gaming?!
Needless to say South Park: Stick of Truth has a particular audience. I think it’s nearly flawless, but if you’re not a South Park fan then there’s nothing to see here. I’m fully aware that the combat is not exactly complicated or strategic, and the game on anything but Hard difficulty is a cake walk. But those elements aren’t the point; you don’t watch an episode of South Park for the state of the art CGI and you don’t play a South Park game for the revolutionary gameplay.

This game might as well be fantasy because it can very easily cast a binding spell on the player, forcing him to play until he can no longer stand grasping at the air around the tantalizing key to his chains called victory. One can potentially play for days and still never see the final boss in all its... uh, majesty? There isn't much I can say here, except it's a roguelike with an incredible combat system and an almost text-based exploratory system. You have your visuals, but you never truly see what happens outside of combat, and you must use your imagination to enhance the experience here. If you're lucky, all you'll ever see of the Rebellion is that large expanding wave from the left side of your map, and that is all the game needs to push you in the direction of the exit.
It's easy to see why this game can sometimes make the player feel as though he has been cheated out of a run; sometimes, early one, just the right combination of guns on an automated Rebel scout ship can smash your ship apart in seconds flat. The same can happen in the final throes of the game, or the final boss, whose fighting style and weapon combinations seem like a sensei to your grasshopper no matter how much you've put into your shield strength. (can anyone say "drone army?") This game on the misnomered "Normal" difficulty asks perfection from a constant struggle to make it through the end, and it is never an easy task to perform.
There is no other game out there that proves the existence of game compulsion quite like this one. For days I felt like I had to complete it, I had to play through at least once, to see if I could make it. I think I've forced my handcuffs off, at least long enough to write this review, by reaching the final boss once. I thought I had it in my grasp, my powerful weapons charged but missing ammo, my shields holding as I beamed my crew into their various weapons bays (what a structural weakness, separating those rooms from the rest of the ship and manning them with but one helpless human... so very susceptible to mantis venom) and destroying them slowly but surely. Who knew they'd come back with a functioning drone control augmentation and a few seconds that redefined the word "hopeless?"
If you want to feel as though you've been chained to your computer for weeks trying to beat this game into submission, or you want to experience an effective simulation of the struggle of a lonely mission through space, where supplies are short and hope is shorter (for a TV example, look no further than Firefly or Battlestar Galactica), delivered through mechanics alone, $10 does not do this game justice. It is too good, but almost too arresting. Buy it... if you dare.

Dying Light is an enjoyable experience co-op wise (with friends at least), and a somewhat lacklustre experience singleplayer wise. It's not a great game if your looking to play this on your own, it just isn't strong enough to hold up to a satisfying singleplayer experience.
Having played this from start to finish co-op with 2 other mates of mine, I can safely say it's a good fresh outing into the craze that is Zombiemania that seems to have taken the video gaming market these days. It's also got staying power despite the limited amount of quests. The devs have said that the game holds around 50 hours, but I've exactly completed this game at 26.8 hours. So your looking at around 20 hours of story (assuming you do just the story) and about 10 hours of side quests. So roughly around the 30 hour mark to get everything done, which you could push it to say 35 hours.
It's got just about enough meat on it to keep you occupied beyond that mark if your playing with friends. There is some replayability to the game but it depends on how high your tolerance level is for doing the same stuff over again. Dying Light does feature a New Game+ so there's always that.
Storywise the game is so-so. There is nothing remarkable about the story, and I didn't buy Dying Light for its story, so I didn't expect to be wowed by it. The main villian in the game is your typical traditional over-the-top video game baddy who has no depth, no complexity to him and is just there for you to pile your hatred onto him. Which is perfectly fine for a game like this.
The games protagonist is also lacking in that department. While the voice actor portraying him is pretty good, everything else about the character comes across as dull and just not interesting. This Crane fellow you play as comes across as a bit of a push-over who is caught between a morality fence and doesn't seem to know what he is even doing. There are also some very frustrating parts in some of the quests, mainly the side quests. For example; in one particular quest, Crane gets insulted quite a lot by a pair of what I would assume to be brothers. Lets just say that words like 'ape-like cranium' and 'de-evolved specimen' get thrown at you while they subsquently ask for your help.
There's a certain lesson that developers tend to forget in games like these: If your going to insult the player character, you better give a god damn good response in return or at least provide some option to deal with it. But what we do get instead is a silent Crane. It's situations like these that make the character your playing as come across as frustratingly weak and without substance.
Combat wise, its very similar to Dead Island. I've personally not noticed much improvement other than of course the parkour type moveset you get to employ against the walking dead. Aiming can be somewhat clunky with melee weapons and feels stiff. Wielding an axe you could find yourself chopping the mid-section when you've meant to strike for the head, and it can be frustrating to deal with. But regardless the combat is humourus and does its job just well enough to be liked.
I've often seen Dying Light parkour get compared to say Mirrors Edge by some reviewers and I have to disagree. Dying Light parkour is a poor mans Mirrors Edge. Dying Light parkour is again, like its combat, stiff and sometimes simply does not work right. You could jump and reach a ledge that you would grab 99 times out of a hundred, only to end up getting that 1% more often than not and end up plummeting to your death. However the parkour element is still excellent. It may not be Mirrors Edge quality but it definitely is fun and despite the occasional hiccups from the game, rather than player input, its of course one of Dying Light's strongest aspects.
There are a few other gripes but they are minor at best. The grappling hook you get later on in the game, is far far too powerful and kinda ruins the parkour element so if your like me, you'll end up trying to force yourself not to use it all the time. The writing is also not the best, but again, this isn't the sort of game you come into expecting a AAA story to be told.
I can definitely recommend Dying Light if your planning on playing this with friends. And I can only say get it on a hefty discount if your planning to play the singleplayer only part of it.
Minor Edit: While I did say I played this from Start to Finish co-op, I forgot to add that this excludes the starting tutorial mission and the ending mission. The devs have publicly stated that you can play Dying Light from start to finish co-op and this is simply not true. The ending mission does NOT let you play with friends, and that was a major disappointment for me.

If you missed the description, Shadowrun Returns is an isometric tactical turn-based RPG. Think XCOM: Enemy Unknown's battle system simplified a bit. I recommend Shadowrun Returns, but with the caveats that it's under $15 and you go in knowing you'll have to play workshop content to get your money's worth.

Excellent story.  Very interesting campaigns.
Gameplay is a little wanting.
Graphics aren't the best, but they could be worse.  A lot of animations are reused and somewhat boring.
Access to steam workshop so there is replayability and extra gameplay.
Story:
The original campaign "Dead Man's Switch" is relatively well written with an interesting plot which morphs and changes the further you go starting with something mundane and ending with bizarre.  It is extremely linear with very little in the way of optional quests not related to the story.  The ones that do exist often times are just there for flavor giving no benefit to the player.  However the finale to the campaign was very entertaining, though the ending was somewhat of a let down compared to the build up.
The DLC campaign "Dragonfall" was a surprisingly well written story.  It ties together a number of different plots in such a way as to make the whole much greater than the sum.  There is a lot more in the way of optional quests compared to "Dead Man's Switch", but the story is still pretty linear since your likely going to have to do most of those "optional" quests in order to advance the story anyway.  This isn't to say that it's a bad thing.  Like I said, the plot for Dragonfall is very satisfying with excellent pacing, a surprising amount of flavor, and a number of plot twists which send a shiver down your spine including an ending with interesting ramifications for the world.  As a side note, the game played excellently in hard mode, though there are two sections in the game which I know a lot of people had trouble on.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is shallow compared to more familiar RPGs.  The selection of skills is rather small and the abilities associated with the skills are very basic.  Magic is a little more interesting, but for the most part many spells are very similar with many offensive spells having little variation between them.
Fighting in Shadowrun can be satisfying, but what really detracts from it is the way your character gains experience.  Instead of the basic XP system your character gains a resource called "Karma" as you complete quests, optional objectives, and other events.  The problem I have is that fights give you virtually nothing in terms of Karma.  This makes a number of fights just something to get through knowing that your likely not to get a reward.  I assume it has something to do with the nature of the resource in the game.
Issues:
There are a number of gameplay mechanics that are either under utilized, not working, or simply missing.  Etiquettes are a way of slightly customizing your character giving you access to some player decisions and conversation topics which almost always gives you either some sort of advantage or extra flavor to the game.  However in both campaigns, certain etiquettes are virtually ignored throughout the entire story making its choice a complete waste to the player.
For some reason some abilities available to a player are not shown in the character skill progression.  An example is all of the throwing skills you can use despite nothing indicating that they are available when increasing your throw skill.
Another thing I found issue with is the complete inability to decide which of my characters would pick up an item when out of combat.  That's right, your able to manually get your individual characters to pick up items in combat, but as soon as your out of it those items may as well be useless if your main character has a full inventory while your partners sit there with empty slots.  Which also brings up the topic of why aren't you able to enter the combat phase at will?  This would let you set up for fights such as getting in position, setting up buffs, and being able to get your partners to do things that you can't such as pick up an item or using their character skills.  The game gets around some of this by forcing the combat phase, but it would be better if you could manually enter combat phase yourself.
Despite these issues which make the game seem as if it was left undone in some areas the story is, again, excellent.  It may not be worth the current full price to some, but if it's on sale I would recommend trying it out.  This is especially true in the case of Dragonfall, which will require the base game.  It should also be noted that you will also have access to the steam workshop which has a number of community made campaigns and scenarios available as well as the ability to make your own campaign should you so wish it.

I'm proud to say that I contributed to this game's initial Kickstarter campaign.  It delivers a solid turn-based-tactical-RPG experience, and it paints a beautiful-if-grim-and-gritty image of the Shadowrun setting, and it tells a solid story in the process.
For the uninitiated, the setting of Shadowrun is a dystopian future in which corporations rule the world and governments are beholden to the whim of these international corportations.  Magic, and all the fantastic creatures that come with it, reentered the world in the early 2000s.  And in all of this, a 'shadowrunner' is a mercenary who is hired to use their guns, magic, muscle, computer hacking, or remote-controlled drones on a job-by-job basis.
One of the neat tricks that this game pulls is that different types of character literally see the world differently.  A mage can see ley lines on the ground that can bolster their magic (or that of their enemies!) if they stand on them.  A shaman can see spirits lingering in the world, ready to be called into battle.  A decker (read: hacker, who have neural interfaces in this world) can see hackable computers.  Okay, I think that anyone can see hackable computers, but you need a decker to get into them.
Without revealing any spolers, I'd like to say that the story in the original game is solid.  It's nothing to write home about, but it makes for a great introduction to the setting, and fans of Shadowrun video games will see a familiar face.  The story in the expansion - which, by the way, was at least as long as the original campaign, and I've sunk 82 hours between the two of them - is, on the other hand, phenomenal.  Both games have great characters, although be warned that there's no voice-acting - if you demand that from your stories you should be aware of its absence.  The dialogue is similar to Baldur's Gate or Neverwinter Nights - style, although if your character doesn't have the skills needed to engage in a particular line of dialogue, that line and its requirement show up, greyed out, so you know how to build your character next time.
Of course, the game also comes with a level editor, and Steam Workshop support.  This was one of the big features touted during its Kickstarter.  I'm not immediately seeing a link to the editor from Steam but it's in the same folder as the game files.  I have not put this to the test but I'm told that it's a very powerful toolset.
The combat system is interesting.  The greatest depth can be found in building your main character and selecting a squad for each mission as there is quite a bit of variety available in a character's skill-set.  Once you're on the ground there's still quite a few decisions to make, from where to take cover, to how tightly to pack your squad, to when and where to expend your consumable resources.  Personally, I found the game to be a smidge too easy on Normal difficulty, even when I realized that my character concept wasn't a particularly strong one in this universe.  There were two harder (and one easier) difficulties that I didn't try.
Visually, the game performs solidly.  It's a nice, clean (well, grimy) - looking game, but it won't turn any heads for reasons other than the unusual setting.  The developers had other priorities, and they're priorities that I happen to agree with.
Shadowrun Returns delivers a passable audio experience.  The game sounds great, all of the effects sound like I imagine they should...but there could really, really be more variety in background music.  What is there sounds wonderful, but I for one was tired of hearing the same music for every battle by the end of it.  Again, if you can't stand reading text, pass this one up, because it has no voice-overs whatsoever.
All in all, I would heartily recommend this game to RPG fans, turn-based strategy fans, and Shadowrun fans alike.

The most memorable and stand-out aspect of this game surely has to be the visual styling.  That, of course, is something you can partially see on the store page, so I'll spare you the run-through, save for stating that I really liked how this game looks.
The puzzling nature of Antichamber is what I found to be the most enjoyable part.  I can play with any variety of rubiks cubes and chain-puzzles all day and never get a really good variety of spatial reasoning exercise compared to what this game offers as the player progresses.  Your gun/tool thing evolves as the game goes on and allows you to manipulate the puzzles in different manners, which will cause a change in just how things can be solved.
The non-euclidian coding that may cause you to be running in circles without realizing is really a fun experience to play through the first few times, but once you get the gist of it, you may predict things of the sort to happen.
Throw in a handful of optional "Gotta catch 'em all" goosechases, some neat development rooms, and hidden puzzles, and you've got a pretty solid game that'll keep you thinking right up until the straaaange conclusion.

It was one of those troublesome weeks for finding something to review, the habitual drunkard that is the release schedule: belched up the last of its’ latest round of rancid gut butter and has rolled over and gone back to sleep as we awkwardly hold the bucket and wait for the next tremulous stomach gurgle like a nest of baby birds.
I was gonna do Pillars of Eternity, but after I rolled a character and went through the prologue, I walked out into a meadow and was immediately slaughtered by a small group of wild piglets, I’m not sure I’m on the right wavelength for that kind of game, although I did start enjoying myself later when I was reading through some conversational text and was suddenly magically transported to a dark thorny forest, full of gigantic monster crabs. But then I realised that I’d actually fallen asleep from boredom and my face was resting on a 1970’s issue of Mayfair.
So instead, let’s do what I usually do when current releases are letting me down Let’s Get Ret...Ro. After all you can’t polish a turd but you can at least reminisce about the lovely pie and chips it used to be. It’s not hard to find relevant retro games since remakes, remasters and updates are constantly raining down upon us like someone planted landmines in the graveyard.
Half Life 2 was recently updated with the imaginatively-titled Half Life 2: Update, a community-made mod that improves the graphics in such a way that you probably wouldn't notice without a side-by-side comparison. But hey, graphics are like public toilet cleaners: you know they’re doing their job properly if you never notice or think about them. The update also adds commentary not by the original developers but by quote, "members of the Half Life community". And forgive me if that feels a little presumptuous. Bob the stinky tramp is technically a member of the community, but I wouldn't ask him his opinions on local government. The thing about fan commentary is that it’s pretty-much always going to be cheer-leading 'cause that’s what defines a fan, whereas the developer ten years down the line might actually have some self-criticism with the benefit of hindsight. 99% of creators claim to loathe everything they made more than five years ago and the remaining 1% are liars.
So with the occasion of the update,let’s see if Half Life 2 still holds up, Half Life one did the last time we rode the retro metro, but Half Life 2 isn't quite the same vent full of Space Crabs.
After escaping the research facility and after defeating the leader of the alien invasion in Half Life one, Gordon Freeman has a well-deserved lie-in for the next twenty years before finding the earth he fought so hard to save double-backsy reconquered by an even WORSE alien race, and the struggling human resistance now considers him to be speccy Jesus. God knows why, when none of them actually saw him blow up the alien leader and most of the rest of Half Life one was spent gunning down American serviceman and failing to rescue scientists. Also, the leaders of the Earth resistance all used to work with Gordon at Black Mesa, as did the human overseer of the occupying aliens, which is the kind of extraordinary coincidence that could only be explained by writers trying to force continuity between what could have easily been two completely unconnected plots. But I suppose it wouldn't have been the same without Gordon Freeman, it’s not like players would have accepted any other mute personality-deficient goof, allegedly lurking behind the first-person camera.
Old games that in their day sold themselves on ground-breaking tech usually now come across as kind of quaint at best. Kind of Quake II at worst. Half Life 2 (Surely it would be a Full Life, then?) was most noticeable for its ground breaking physics engine, and if there’s a single word that summarizes its approach to physics it would be “Tadaaaa!”
In this day and age when physics engines are just another old toy cluttering up the playroom of the most hideously-spoiled child to have ever existed, improved physics engines are that where everything doesn't feel like it’s made of vulcanized rubber and characters don’t ragdollise like their bodies  have spontaneously transformed into over-cooked pasta. One might reasonably wonder why we have to pause in the middle of a daring escape through enemy-infested tunnels to pile some bricks onto a see-saw and jump off it onto a ledge when we could just do a single pull-up. The exciting airboat chase has to break flow three or four times because we have to disembark and figure out a Rube-Goldberg machine someone set up to activate a ramp, that could've quite easily been constructed by two planks and a fat person. And the other new tech the game is very keen to showcase like a weirdly chippy roommate humming and skipping round the house desperately hoping you’ll ask how his date went last night is facial animation. To that end we’re occasionally locked in a room for lengthy story sessions that just barely escape being tarred with the cutscene brush ‘cause we’re still free to climb on the furniture and jump on people. Certainly the facial animation is good, the characters are well-rounded but there’s something kind of off about them, maybe it’s the way they remain so weirdly chipper, while the oppressive regime is murdering people next door, or how their enthusiasm never wavers no matter how many times Gordon never speaks or visibly reacts.
This was fine in Half Life one when the cast consisted of ninety-thousand clones of the same five guys, but when there’s an emphasis on individual characters and their interactions, the silent protagonist feels weirdly out of place in the middle of it. It feels like everyone’s acting at him y’know what I mean? Like he’s a casting director at a restaurant and they’re a waiter with big ambitions. But now that faces rarely need to animate much beyond a grim, determined-frown and physics engines are largely used to make bits of grit realistically fly off of chest-high walls, don’t you think the wonder and creative spirit that tech was intended to provoke has been lost? It wasn't just that Half Life: 2 Episode: 0 had physics it was that the gameplay made it work! The whole game is a series of showcase set-pieces linearly strung together, but at least it had something to showcase. Most action games have physics engines now but precious few have a mechanic as simple and gratifying as the Gravity Gun to use the physics to its’ full potential and give the world a sense of true interactivity. Many admittedly have better endings where the story doesn't just screech abruptly to a halt because its run out of set-pieces, with two more episodes bolted on after the facts that end on a cliffhanger that goes unresolved forever, thus earning a permanent benefit of the doubt. Well ♥♥♥♥ing played Valve.

If you're a fan of South Park, you will love this game.  If you are also a fan of RPGs, you will love this game even more.  The story is 100% South Park.  It feels like I'm watching a Lord of the Rings length episode of South Park.  The RPG element, though, is what really makes this game shine.  The world is just the right size (large enough to explore, but not so large that it feels overwhelming like a lot of current RPG titles).  The leveling system is solid and really does take you the whole game to get to 100%.  There is a weapon/armor crafting system in the form of augmentations that you can add to compliment your play-style.  The combat system is solid turn-based style combat with the ability to counter enemy attacks in a way that requires you to be engaged throughout the battle.  Even the length of the game feels just right.  It's not a game like Portal that you can blast through in an afternoon, but it's not XCOM: Long War where you spend months on a campaign.
In short, this game sits comfortably in the "Goldilocks Zone" in just about every category.  Perfectly balanced between storytelling, exploration, customization, and combat.  Nothing ever gets old.  Basically, if you're the type of person who would click on a South Park game in the first place, you're going to love this game.

7/10: Engrossing tactical RPG in the cyberpunk-fantasy future, but hampered by so-so mechanics
Shadowrun Returns, along with the Dragonfall expansion, are good tactical RPG's with interesting stories to keep you going. Taking place on Earth in the 2050's, it combines cyberpunk with fantasy and comes up with Elven hackers and multinational corporations owned by dragons.
Returns takes place in Seattle, while Dragonfall takes place in Berlin. While purely single player experiences, I still found myself enjoying the intrigue as it inevitably escalated to apocalyptic proportions. Lacking any cinematics, this is all conveyed via text, though at least this is accompanied by the portrait of the speaker.
The biggest drawback for me was the degree of specialization that it required to be effective. Even the game itself warns against multiclassing and only provides enough time per campaign to really max out one approach. This really railroads a lot of the choice, and in my opinion fun, of character building and leveling. Outside of yourself, you don't get any say in how your party members level.
The inventory system also irked me. I can bear that on a mission the inventory should be limited, but being unable to transfer things to other party members and drones with ease limited my effectiveness in battle quite a bit. Not only that, but if you did give something to a party member and they didn't use it in that mission, it would simply disappear from their inventory next time you checked.
It's nice that it comes with its own editor so anyone can make their own campaign, especially since you can use the assets of the campaigns you own. Still, the aforementioned annoyances with the mechanics kept me from investing more than an hour experimenting with it.
Overall, it's an engrossing story with a good setting, but the graphics, mechanics, and gameplay are middling at best.

EDIT: After actually beating the game, my point stands. The frustrating inconsistency in platforming and really poor job of indicating where you need to go, added to the fact you are constantly under fire in a game where combat is absolute trash, make Mirror's Edge a missed opportunity that is brilliant in some areas and unbearable in others. Also, story takes the triple crown of bad, cliched and forgettable.

I haven't played Dragonfall and can't judge on that account, but Dead Man's Switch is a bad campaign, simple as that. Dialogues are, simply put, meaningless, the options lead to the same result without actually provoking different responses or influencing your karma, reputation or whatnot. The game is extremely linear, and most of it is filled with rather repetitive and easy battles (since developers didn't bother with tweaking AI), so there is a sensation of playing a visual novel with occasional fighting scenes. AI won't do a single smart thing - too often have I seen the enemies just skip their turn entirely and run around in full circles, doing nothing. And bear in mind, I played the game on the highest difficulty level. Fights are boring, and writing won't surprise or delight you in any way if you are used to reading good books. Animation of the characters also looks pretty ridiculous, it's as if they are not real living beings, but rather figures made of clay, animated by motions of an awkward puppeteer. The player is limited in all choices, there isn't much in the area of customization, there aren't that many usable items or skills, and most of the companions you can hire are mute, only serving as meat shields.
And if you are used to reading decent books and novels, the writing will strike you as mediocre. The only thing the developers succeeded in is the atmosphere, since it's so close to Wil Gibson's books. It's as if you're playing as one of the characters of his novels. But, naturally, the game's plot doesn't come even close to the maestro's writing.
Overall this was a huge disappointment. I consider myself lucky I bought this game on sale, since I had much higher hopes for it.

I didn't expect much from this one, and yet I got much more out of it than from lots of other, far better reviewed games of recent memory.
First of all, the (first episode) of the story campaign is a well done mix of the old and new Resident Evil styles with room for bizarre body horror mutants and slow walking zombies as well. The pacing is really good and fun, violent action as well as slower moments of exploring the creepy hallways both coexist. The game is often surprisingly scary, especially in the second act where you control Barry.
And that's just the first two hours of the game: After that, there's the Raid Mode which turns out to be a completely different game in and of itself. It contains of a bunch of unique levels (not just recycled ones from the single player campaign). You have to shoot your way through them, earn points, purchase new skills and weapons, earn trophies, unlock new levels and then do it all again with another character. It unfolds an incredibly depths and enables a variety of completely different play styles and I'll probably sink many hours into it.
That's what I got for just 6€. It's an incredibly good value for a well produced and polished game (especially the game play). After all the discussions of The Order: 1886 I hope this game might serve as an example of how smaller AAA games can succeed with a more humble pricing and a high focus on gameplay. Resident Evil Revelations 2 has one priority: offering an enjoyable and fun time.

There are a couple of interesting game mechanics, especially the way necros need to be killed (won't spoil it), and the Zero-G sequences. Interaction with the environment is also pretty ok, and player conomy is something that the player cannot overlook (especially ammo conservation).
The game's difficulty is actually heightened by the deadly combo of clunky camera+controls, but on the other hand, if this game had pixel-precise controls like CSGO or Gears of War, it would be WAY too easy.
A very bitter note in conclusion: the PC port policy is really unfair, since PC owners of Dead Space don't get any of the many DLCs available on the console version, nor the achievements (which, again, both console versions have...). The Rebellion knows you've got the information and they're right on your tail, so gather what allies and equipment you can on the way to strength your recon ship and if your FTL drive dies; so do you.
Picked up this game on the cheap after hearing the gaming magazines and internet rave about it (and meme galore about how brutal it can be). It's fiendishly addictive: you can name the ship, give your starting crew their identities and customize your ship to buggery; then zoom off into your own little space drama where you hope you'll lose no one and save the day.
It rarely happens like that (at the time of writing I only just completed Easy for the first time with one of the hardest starting ship types) and just like the game Cannon Fodder from the 1990s, you'll probably get really ticked when one of your crew members that you've lead through the entire campaign (and grown fond of) suddenly gets cut in half by an alien insect or dies of suffocation while repairing the FTL drive to save the crew. Or if they're unlucky, killed by giant spiders, some unknown plague or blown to pieces by a cunningly teleported bomb.
Buy this game if you're into space strategies or even just jump-in/jump-out fun gaming. It's not a long game (approx. four hours on a single run IF you make it to the home system and survive), but it has heaps of replay value due to the random system/encounter generator programmed into it. And the music is a treat.
Doesn't scare me, I'm to manly. But it was fun.

As someone going into these games with *zero* experience with the Shadowrun universe beforehand, I was pretty overwhelmed with the notion of a setting that essentially exists at the intersection of BLADE RUNNER, NEUROMANCER, and THE LORD OF THE RINGS. Where one can meet a street-wise elven bartender, turn around, and project your consciousness into cyberspace -- all done in the shadows of massive mega-corporations that happen to run most of the world. Also, there are dragons.
And seeing how this game is based on a pen and paper campaign setting that has been expanding and refining itself over the course of 25 years, the depth and breadth of the universe can most definitely be felt as you walk the streets of Seattle and Berlin. This is an outstandingly versatile and exciting setting, and the two campaigns currently available to a fantastic job of exploiting it to its fullest.
SHADOWRUN RETURNS: DEAD MAN'S SWITCH - (8/10 Stars)
Campaign Length: Approx. 12 Hours
When you purchase the base game, SHADOWRUN RETURNS, you'll be purchasing a campaign titled DEAD MAN'S SWITCH, which has you tracking down a murderer in Seattle after an old acquaintance of yours turns up dead. The story takes a lot of twists and turns, as getting closer to the truth seems to be hazardous for your health. Along the way, you'll run into a number of very interesting characters (albeit, sometimes for far too short a time), including a few that fans of the SNES/Genesis/Pen and Paper games will find familiar.
As others have pointed out since launch, DMS is a tad linear compared to most other RPGs on the market. There will be dialogue options aplenty, allowing you to play your character the way you want, but ultimately there are few choices that make a real impact on the story, and you'll feel the invisible hand of the narrative tugging you along without much room for sidequests or exploration.
Regardless, the story of DMS is *more* than worth the price of admission. The writing and attention to detail do the setting a great service and it acts as a great introduction to the Shadowrun universe.
DRAGONFALL - (9/10 Stars)
Campaign Length: Approx. 18 - 20 Hours
That being said, it's a shame that most people have been judging the overall package on the weaknesses of DMS, because DRAGONFALL really is the definitive Shadowrun experience so far, and more than worthy of being counted among the best RPGs to be released in recent years.
This time around, you play as a citizen of the Berlin Flux-State, where anarchy reigns (or doesn't reign?) and the nation's stability waxes and wanes as gangs, corporations, and political clubs fight for controlling interest in the chaos. As a shadowrunner, your latest mission goes horribly wrong, leaving you and your team kicked to the curb with no explanation as to what just happened. As you start peeling back the layers, you uncover conspiracy after conspiracy, and find yourself getting caught up in an F-State conflict that may very well lead to disaster for Berlin.
As I said, many of the "weaknesses" of DMS have been rectified this time around. The linearity is not completely gone, but it's certainly well hidden, providing plenty of sidequests with multiple ways of accomplishing each, a more permanent group of companions with rich backstories, and a greater emphasis on choice. And, like DMS, DRAGONFALL does a fantastic job of playing up its setting, and making Berlin feel suitably unique in comparison to Seattle. There is just a greater sense of effort all around, including a more engaging story on top of it all.
The base game and the expansion are presented anthology-style, with individual sets of characters and stand-alone stories, so if one hold more appeal than the other, feel free to play DRAGONFALL first. (Though, you will still need to purchase the SHADOWRUN RETURNS base game.)
In the last few years, we've been seeing an RPG renaissance by way of Kickstarter, and SHADOWRUN RETURNS was among the first out of the gate. Neither game is completely perfect, but there's an attention to detail and a reverence for the source material -- not to mention some fantastic writing -- that makes the game and its expansion an absolutely immersive experience. I sincerely hope we get to see more of this universe, and judging by the dramatic leap in quality between DEAD MAN'S SWITCH and DRAGONFALL, the next game will surely be something to keep a close eye on.

Short of it: I loved this game - right up until the cliffhanger ending and trying to find the last two eggs.  I got this game for $1 and had a lot of fun with it, but the ending and the egg drop rate left me not with warm fuzzy feelings but feelings leaning more toward annoyance and anger.  Part 2 has become a huge project with 15 parts and last I checked part 4 wasn't even done.  A remastered version of the original is in the works to fix the egg drop problem, but it means starting the game over.
Long of it: I enjoy solitaire games anyway, but thought the fairy theme was really fun.  I was enjoying the story and the sense that something wasn't quite right and I really wanted to know what happened next.  I felt like I was finding pets on pace to maybe unlock them all by the time I finished story mode.  I really liked that the pets had baby and adult forms, but I felt like the evolving process was too slow.  Then I got to the end of the game and after my initial shock upon realizing that really was the ending, I told myself surely they must have released the second part by now since this game is over three years old.  After some research, I discover that not only have they not released part two, they have turned it into this huge project of 15 parts and they haven't even completed part 4.  However, the really frustrating thing is trying to get the last two pet eggs.  After you clear all the cards in a stack there is a chance that a material will drop (used to evolve your pets), nothing will drop, or an egg will drop.  Then IF it is an egg drop, it is a random drop of an egg from any level and if you already have all the eggs in that level you get no drop.  I'm not big on the math but that means your odds of dropping that last egg or two are ridiculously low.  Check out the forums and read the many frustrated posts of people who have spent 100+ hours on this game and still have not found the last eggs.  The developers have responded and said that instead of patching the game, they will be releasing a remastered version that addresses this issue and removes the randomness from the drops after so long.  However, that was announced in 2012 and whenever it is released it means starting over.
I've put 16 hours into this game and I still have 9 pets to evolve and 2 to find. Like I said, I really enjoyed the story and I like the idea of the pets, but I find the replayability of this game to be really low - aside from the forced replayability of trying to find the last two pet eggs and evolve the pets.
I absolutely recommend this game if you can find it for $1 like I did, if not unlocking all the achievements is ok with you, and if you go in eyes wide open that the ending is a cliffhanger.
Edit - Since writing this review, the developer has decided to release a game called FaeVerse Alchemy which is in early access (still in development).  I have no idea why they would choose to push this in front of Faerie Solitaire 2 (which they agree is overdue).  I understand them pushing it in front of the remaster of the original Faerie Solitaire because they have promised the remastered version as a free update.  Still it's lame.
