- Great game, some flaws, a game no South Park or RPG fan should miss.
Taking place immediately after the Game of Thrones inspired 244th through 247th episodes of the series in which the town's population have gone through the Blackest of Black Fridays, fighting to the death over random stuff on sale and in which game console the Boys should stake their futures.  The Stick of Truth is the Boys playing a full blown Live Action Role Playing Game in South Park even as sinister forces work against the unsuspecting town.  In comes the New Kid, and in keeping with the tropes set down by the genre, this silent protagonist must navigate the conflict between two warring factions as they seek to save the day.
Unfortunately the game feels like a bunch of it hit the cutting room floor, not for lack of inspiration, but for lack of funds.  The Stick of Truth suffers from being made by Obsidian and originally set to be published by the defunct THQ - this defuncting having occurred during the game's development and risking the fate of the game.  Obsidian representatives have on more than one occasion said their company nearly ran out of funds entirely while making this game.
Allow me to explain my gripes, and I apologize for the minor spoilers, I will try to keep it minimal.
Literally nothing you do will impact the game.  The two factions at war serve no purpose, they are a choice with no consequence.  You can obtain costumes which would imply allegiance to one or the other faction, but it has zero impact on the game.  You don't get a different power, you don't get a different weapon, you don't get a different hair cut even, you get sweet♥♥♥♥♥♥all for siding with either.
In most similarly designed games - the Fallout, Elder Scrolls, and Forgotten Realms series in particular, you will find that wearing the clothes of a faction impacts that faction's opinion of you and what you do and how you do it also factors into their responses.  Not so much here, again, nothing you do matters.  No quest will ensure the 5th graders will attack your enemy, reducing their combat effectiveness later in the game.  No dialogue will allow you to unlock a special companion.  Stealing from someone will not make people think less of you.
The game zips through story at a rather high speed, you go from arc to arc with little time to engage in what is happening.  Had the player a little more engagement with the events and characters, a branching story, this would not be a problem.  As it is however, you end up with a game that is boring to replay, most games of this type are awesome for replayability.
There are bugs, you will find yourself disappearing for no reason, and the camera focus moving off to the wrong part of the map.  You will need to restart the game to fix these sadly, but luckily they are not very common.
Oh lord, loading screens.  The game is not a graphically intense thing, it should not need so many.
Do not take these complaints as hate for the game, this is disappointment.  There could have been more to this, it could have been a clear Game of the Year, instead of just being one of the better games.
Combat is that of Super Mario RPG and it's kin, a very forgiving QTE-ish element is present to improve your attacks' and abilities' power.  Except for a lack in variety of combat, this is great.  And there are a few little full blown QTEs in game, but they also give plenty of reaction time and are clear with what to do.  This is easy enough that a child can play through the whole game without needing a hand.
The graphics are great, everything feels natural and looks like it belongs.  The art team should be given high jobs and blow fives.  The setting is wonderful, the town of South Park feels smaller than it should be, but what is there is alive and interesting.  I wish it was bigger to match the portrayal of the town from television, but we got a good chunk to play with.  The music, the voice acting, these are completely flawless.  They match the show in every way.  This all because the game was developed with close ties to South Park Studios who make the show.
If this game were not a South Park game, I would recommend it for everyone.  As it is however, anyone who is into RPGs and legally old enough to have a Steam account will have to do.

I see a lot of the reviews for "Dying Light" on Steam praising the multitudes of monsters, or the fluidity and realism of the parkour or even the graphics but honestly? These aren't all that great. They're good, don't get me wrong. Just not great,
For the monsters there's maybe about nine different things to kill. There's your run-of-the-mill zombies, slightly faster run-of-the-mill zombies, exploding things that can kill you in one hit, spitting things (because we can't have a zombie game without something spitting some noxious green goop at us), big guys with concrete clubs, bigger guys that like to throw rocks at you, screaming children (zombified of course) and faster, stronger run-of-the-mill zombies that only appear during the night time. On top of that there's also desperate survivors that you're supposed to feel bad about carving up (but I didn't) and about an entire national army's worth of armed thugs for you to kill. Maybe with my lack of remorse when carving up other humans I'm supposed to feel like I'm the monster? I dunno.
The parkour is what most people were looking forward to this game for and honestly? It's good. You're able to make your way across the city any way you want to. On foot of course as Crane seems to be the only person in the city that doesn't hold a valid driver's licence. I did have a few minor problems where I couldn't grab a ledge similar to others I had grabbed hundreds of times because I was looking a millimetre more downwards than what was considered by the game to be acceptable. Then the game suffers from a virus (Haha, get it?) that I like to call Assassin's Creed Virus (I'm not great with names) where I can leap off as tall a building as I like so long as I land in something considered to be soft. In♥♥♥♥♥Creed this would be the wagons of hay, in this it would be a pile of trash bags that could be full of dirty, hepatitis-infested needles for all I know. These things are rather minor I admit, but it does break the flow of the game a bit I feel.
Graphically the game is sound... At bits. I've seen a few things in game that would have been embarresed to be seen in even a PlayStation 2 game (Take a look at the crate of... onions? I guess? When you're in The Tower.) It seems designed for consoles too I feel. The menus have a nasty habit of returning to the very top after you press enter or click on something which caused me to craft the wrong thing a few times and it also seems to be poorly optimised for PC. I bought my computer back in September 2014 and it was top of the line at the time and I had to lower the graphics and view distance just to play the game.
Night Time was hyped up to be some sort of terrifying ordeal that you'd be extremely lucky to be able to survive if you decided to ignore the screaming voices of protest in your head and venture outside in the dark but from the moment you get the grappling hook night time just isn't scary. It's like when you were afraid of the monsters under your bed as a child but when you finally get brave enough to look you find that it's just an old T-shirt, a dinosaur toy and your mum's old vibrator that had been left on the "on" position. Okay, that metaphor wasn't clear. Night starts off as being genuinely scary, not as terrifying as other reviews say or as terrifying as it was hyped up to be, but that was only because these scary old T-shirt, dinosaur, mum's old vibrator monsters seemed to have no weakness. By about mid-game night is no scarier than day time. You can have strong weapons to fight if you need to and the grappling hook lets you escape from most chases with ease.
That's another part where the game breaks down a bit. When you unlock the grappling hook. Most of the enjoyment in the game is deciding which route you should take to get from point A, through point B, up point C and to point D. But with the grappling hook you pretty much just zip from A to B with no real thought or sense of danger and as said before it lets you break pursuit with ease. The grappling hook also takes away from the satisfaction of solving a climbing puzzle by yourself because you can just skip most of them. (Puzzle is used very loosely there!)
Combat seems to be another huge sticking point in other reviews. People keep mentioning how most fights are better avoided or how it's dangerous to fight your way through to a different area but to be honest it's really not. There's this massive bridge swarming with infected and I was able to clear the entire thing using a few molotoves, a handful of home-made exploding shuriken and a couple of machetes, and then there was enough loot left lying around afterwards for me to enjoy being king of the dirty survivors for a few weeks.
My review does seem to be very negative, and that's because it is mostly. The developers really let themselves down in certain aspects but at the same time I can't help but enjoy myself while playing. Despite the flow sometimes being broken, the sense of real freedom you get while running from A to D is something that I've never experienced before in any other video game. The combat is fun at times and honestly pretty funny at others. The graphical issues were sorted by just changing my settings a bit and night time was genuinely scary. But only for the first few nights.
"Dying Light" is a fun enough game to play on your own but I feel that the game really comes into it's own when you play co-operatively with some friends. My friends and I were able to pull off some amazing team-work that just wouldn't be possible during single player. Everyone you play with has a slightly different play style, you might be working with someone who likes to stealthily sneak past all of the infected, or you could be playing with a gung-ho gun-nut who shoots everything that moves and then some things that don't move just for good measure. One of the coolest parts of the multiplayer is just watching your friends get from point A to point D. While running you could see one of your friends on the streets below you sliding into an impossibly small gap to evade a fast zombie while at the same time you could say a black rope appear just above you and see another friend use it to grapple their way to the next building.
I've given the game a lot of flack and deservedly so, it is the game we all expected it to be, just not as good as we had hoped. Given time I hope they update the game to iron out some of the more minor inconveniences.
Maybe I've been overly harsh? Maybe not. Overall I'd give it 7/10. 7.5 at a push. It's a really fun game, just don't go into it thinking that it's going to be the best game you've ever played.

My rating: 8.5 / 10
Mirror's Edge is an innovative game that will leave you looking at things a little differently.
Pros:
- Unique gameplay: Less gunning, more running leads to some fast-paced sequences.
- Fun combat system oriented around disarming enemies hand-to-hand.
- Amazing visuals. This game is gorgeous.
- Great atmosphere. The visuals and soundtrack blend well into an immersive experience.
- Strong female lead that depicts the female game character in a less sexual, more powerful way.
Cons:
- Collision glitches. Some areas will not always register your grabbing on to them, leading you to plummet to your death.
- Frequent death, can be frustrating for some.
- Sometimes combat can be glitched; disarms may not register properly.
Mirror's Edge isn't a traditional first person shooter, and that difference may be hated by some and loved by others. This game however, happens to be one of my personal favorites.

Shadowrun.
A cyberpunk world heavily inspired by William Gibson's "Nuromancer."
In fact, so heavily inspired much of the early lore and "techno-speak" with in the table-top RPG was taken straight from his 1984 novel and pasted.
When I was 14 years old, I mingled with a small herd of nerds who held Shadowrun as some sort of Holy Grail amongst table-top games. I played it once, and hated all 30 minutes of it. Needless to say, my friendship with them didn't last much longer there after, but my interest was stoked a little.
In my late teens and very early twenties, I read a trilogy of Shadowrun novels. My intrest went from mere intrest to a desire to gather more Shadowrun knowledge.
I later acquired a battered and torn copy of 2nd edition.
Again, my first game- this time Gm'd by me, did not bode well and was a complete failure, lasting just about as long.
I have now however, acquired 4th edition- hopefully that will work better.
But onto this game it's self.
When my brother In-Law (soon to be) told me of a Shadowrun game on Steam, I was very excited and very jelous he had it too!
Having been bought it by my wife during the summer sale, this has been one of the best buys I've gotten for any game.
What has led to to write this though, isn't the core game it's self, but the ingenous user made content.
The core game made, gives a good story an awesome over view of the Shadowrun world with a cool RPG element.
The user content I has sampled thus far though, brings this game to a whole new kind of awesome.
Users have spent their (probaly what little of it they have) spare free time to craft gems of gaming story with layers of Shadowrun lore, politics, intrigue and magic threaded within it. These aren't just "I made this for a laugh (guff)!!!" These are stories. Character driven and user defined.
So why get this game?
Get this game to find others who want to share a dark magical future with you.

I am finding that I can only play this in small bursts. Not because it's bad in any way, but rather that the atmosphere it creates is frantic and stressful. There is a distinct juxtaposition between my desire to move slowly in order to feel a measure of control over the premise and the nagging impression that I have no control whatsoever. The game pushes the player forward with clear goals and even has a pathfinding feature in order to make getting to those goals simple; the problem lies in the fact that one begins to suspect (reasonably) that the monster will be around every single corner. The horror is unique in the genre in the way that other horror games inspire fear through the use of jump scares, dark environments, maybe some type of entity following the player, and while Dead Space certainly makes use of these tropes the fear is very visceral. It often feels as though the player is being hunted and the sense of impending predation is palpable. I often find myself backing into corners after completing actions related to an objective because my faith in quiet moments has disintigrated rather quickly. While this game does feature a share of what could be considered jump-style scares, they are done in a way that forces the player to engage and overcome the threat, thus increasing the adrenaline of the original scare, rather than sink into his seat and curse at the screen like in many other popular horror games available currently. Overall I find Dead Space to be an exciting and fresh approach to the horror genre despite its growing age, and it is certainly worth picking up at the relatively low price of $20. Getting it on sale for any cheaper would be a steal.

Replayed this in 2016 after being reminded by it in the ‘EDGE special edition – the 100 greatest video games’, not having touched it since release.
Incredibly it stands up enormously today, both in terms of gameplay, graphics, and story. The integration with the game world is complete, focusing on survival, exploration, and tightly choreographed bouts of intense combat. In particular, the sound and monster design is out of this world, making it just as creepy and unsettling as it was back in 2008.

Of the material that inspired it, Alien I strongly prefer, and if like me, you enjoy being sucked into a realistic world of terror in space, this is the one for you.

Short of it: I loved this game - right up until the cliffhanger ending and trying to find the last two eggs.  I got this game for $1 and had a lot of fun with it, but the ending and the egg drop rate left me not with warm fuzzy feelings but feelings leaning more toward annoyance and anger.  Part 2 has become a huge project with 15 parts and last I checked part 4 wasn't even done.  A remastered version of the original is in the works to fix the egg drop problem, but it means starting the game over.
Long of it: I enjoy solitaire games anyway, but thought the fairy theme was really fun.  I was enjoying the story and the sense that something wasn't quite right and I really wanted to know what happened next.  I felt like I was finding pets on pace to maybe unlock them all by the time I finished story mode.  I really liked that the pets had baby and adult forms, but I felt like the evolving process was too slow.  Then I got to the end of the game and after my initial shock upon realizing that really was the ending, I told myself surely they must have released the second part by now since this game is over three years old.  After some research, I discover that not only have they not released part two, they have turned it into this huge project of 15 parts and they haven't even completed part 4.  However, the really frustrating thing is trying to get the last two pet eggs.  After you clear all the cards in a stack there is a chance that a material will drop (used to evolve your pets), nothing will drop, or an egg will drop.  Then IF it is an egg drop, it is a random drop of an egg from any level and if you already have all the eggs in that level you get no drop.  I'm not big on the math but that means your odds of dropping that last egg or two are ridiculously low.  Check out the forums and read the many frustrated posts of people who have spent 100+ hours on this game and still have not found the last eggs.  The developers have responded and said that instead of patching the game, they will be releasing a remastered version that addresses this issue and removes the randomness from the drops after so long.  However, that was announced in 2012 and whenever it is released it means starting over.
I've put 16 hours into this game and I still have 9 pets to evolve and 2 to find. Like I said, I really enjoyed the story and I like the idea of the pets, but I find the replayability of this game to be really low - aside from the forced replayability of trying to find the last two pet eggs and evolve the pets.
I absolutely recommend this game if you can find it for $1 like I did, if not unlocking all the achievements is ok with you, and if you go in eyes wide open that the ending is a cliffhanger.
Edit - Since writing this review, the developer has decided to release a game called FaeVerse Alchemy which is in early access (still in development).  I have no idea why they would choose to push this in front of Faerie Solitaire 2 (which they agree is overdue).  I understand them pushing it in front of the remaster of the original Faerie Solitaire because they have promised the remastered version as a free update.  Still it's lame.

For any of my friends considering purchasing this game I say do it. This is a First Person Shooter/Puzzle game set in the future dystopian universe of the Half Life series.
Half Life 1 saw the series protagonist Gordon Freeman, survive an industrial accident and then work his way through an extra dimensional adventure that was part survival, part horror, part military shooter and part 3D platform puzzler to escape the facility known as Black Mesa. Black Mesa was a secret U.S. Government research facility.
In Half Life 2 Gordon Freeman begins the game with a cryptic message from the mystery G-man and then wakes up on a train entering City 17. The military villain faction is suppressing the civilian population who are rebelling against them. Gordon meets other scientists who are trying to survive and escape as well as work out who or what is behind the evil experiments. Gordon faces enemy soldiers, vile mutants, zombies and a traitor to finally thwart the plans of the villains.
The aspects of this game that keep me coming back are the masterfully created dystopian atmosphere, the attention to detail in the weapons, the fluidity of combat, the perfectly suited sound track and the lore of the Half Life series. Puzzle problem solving could be more flexible and there is usually only one solution to find in order to move on. This is an older game but it stands the test of time.

Vice City was one of the expanded entries of the GTA franchise which you can already tell why there's no roman numerial in the title. The game isn't intended to be GTA4 but a side story set in the GTA universe focused on characters who have connections to the main entries of the franchise. There are certain characters, products, and businesses from GTA3 that reappear in this installment which helps connect it better. Letting you know that it's the same universe only a different city. With that explaination put up front, now for the review. Vice City is a prequal to GTA3 set in the year 1986 putting the event at about 15 years prior to the events of GTA3. The story is focused on a parolee criminal named Tommy Vercetti who is a cross between Tony Montana & Henry Hill(hence Ray Liotta voicing the character) after being released from prison Tommy is given a task that involves taking a trip to Vice City, Florida. Vice City is a parody of Miami and is like heaven compared to Liberty City. Upon Tommy's arrival to the beach side city he is to partake in a drug money trade in with the Vance Brothers. When the deal all the sudden went south, one of the Vance brothers is killed and both the drugs and money are gone leaving Tommy with nothing. Leaving Tommy to no other choice than to hunt down the responsible party by taking on odd jobs and gaining trust from a cast of crooked characters. Vice City is a big improvement over GTA3 in both story and gameplay wise. The graphics are improved a notch  as the characters are a little more loose and flexable. The options of how to succeed in the missions are also an improvement as there are more weapons to choose from and more forms of vehicles to actually control in like helicopters, motorcycles, and scooters. Outfits are avalible from certain areas in case you get tired of the default clothes Tommy wears. There is now an option to buy out new safe houses including certain businesses that serve as a daily income and safe house. And best of all, you now have the option to look at the entire city map while the GPA system is more improved! The plot is more in depth when the main protagonist speaks a first in the GTA series believe it or not. I did enjoy Claude from the previous game, but Tommy was more likable because of how his ambitions in getting back in his enemies results in him gaining access to new businesses and properties making him a well earned boss. This game like its predessor has its own cons. The fighting mechanics are a little improved, but its not recommended to fight on a group of enemies bare handed as you get easily locked in the group until you are beaten up to death. As before melee weapons and guns are a best course of action in taking down enemies. While this con is minor but every time you die with a new outfit, Tommy is reverted back to his default outfit. The outfits are scattered throughout the city so unless you memorized the map, it's often not worth the time to change into something else. Most of the safe houses store the higher level weapons but not the clothes, which the safe houses only supply the default set of clothes. With those issues aside, this game is loads of fun and I found the satisfatory level for this game to be higher than the level for GTA3. The art style is very colorful matching the 80's with the sceneary, clothes, and music making this game look as retro as its suppose to. The voice acting is as good as the cast from GTA3 which like that game a cast of high profile actors are casted like Ray Liotta, Burt Reynolds, Danny Trejo, Dennis Hopper, William Fitchner, and many others. If you like GTA3, you will immediately fall in love with Vice City it is an instant masterpiece and proves that later titles of a franchise can improve along the way.

Alright folks. This is an interesting one for me. Buckle up.
Risk of Rain, as most of you are propably well aware, is a game that falls into the category of roguelike (or rather roguelites). You are, most of the time at least, supposed to die at some point. Although there is a clear end to a run. A run will take you on average something from 10 to 60 minutes, depending on your ability to survive. Each run is gonna be different, based on the following factors: Your starting character, the selection of levels you are gonna get, the equipment you'll receive and the bosses you encounter along the way. I say "selection" of levels, because in contrast to a lot of other roguelites there is no random level generator. The game has a set of different levels within a set of various settings. The selection and order of those will be random each playthrough though.
Each character comes with different skills and attacks, which helps the replayability a ton. The characters feel unique and distinguished enough from each other, that you want to unlock them and try them and roll with them.
Anyway, although the characters feel different from each other, the development within a run seems very limited. As per genre your run and character will develop with the items you'll receive and most of the items don't really make you adjust your strategy all that much.

You get what I mean. But to be fair - there are active items which add to your strategic decisions and there are some passive items that will make you think.
Still, often times to me it feels, that from stage 2 onwards you'll be doing the same routine for most of the remaining run - the most effective strategy based on your characters skillset. It's still fun and I adore the endgame (including the final boss), but I feel like there was more potential.
I don't wanna elaborate to much on the presentation, because this kind of style is something you love or you hate. I love pixelart, I love the simplicity and the soundtrack to my ears is gorgeous. From a presentation standpoint I got nothing to complain about.
Let's put this together and clear up why this game is a special one to me.
The flaws of the game are obvious and I know which parts and designchoices I don't agree with, but I still keep coming back. Give it a month or two, but I'll be back - and I'll be enjoying it as much as I ever did. I get curious, I get excited, I get a bit frustrated at times. And although I unlocked most of the game - there is still this sense of mystery for me. There are still riddles within the levels of which I know (or seen parts of) but haven't solved yet. There are still characters I haven't quite mastered and items I haven't seen. I still feel this sense of complete accomplishment, everytime I beat the final boss. No matter how often I come back - the game, so far, did not get stale for me.
There is just something in this game that caters to my gaming-needs in a special way. The genremix of platformer and roguelite, the fireworks on the screen, the art design, the difficulty. Something in between all those qualities just gets me everytime - and propably will as well in the far future.

Batman Arkham Knight has come a long way since the first port made its way over from console to the PC. From a muddled mess to a now very refined and polished version, the game has more than made up for what was done in the past. Does that change the past? No, but it does mean that they made right on their promise to fix it.
Arkham Knight is an amazing game that will last you as long as you really want it to last. Overall though I would say this is atleast a 20+ hour game to 100% and about 12-15 hours for basic story completion. The amount of side missions, collectibles, and riddles to all complete will make you appreciate the amount of detail and work that went into creating the last iteration of Batman from Rocksteady. Everything from flying through the city to driving through it is fun, fast, and exciting. The tools add another layer of complexity to combos and solving riddles while the fighting is still very fluid and not too challegning to beat. The added vehicle truly made me feel like batman and the added tank fights were a welcome addition to the difficulty the game presented.
Overall, I can't recommend the game more than in it's current forms. The DLC may not be all that worth it, (Except the "Most Wanted" mission pack, that is!) but for what you're getting at this price, the game will satisfy you greatly. Please buy this game and experience the knight.

Build a character into a close quarters shotgun specialist and use them on maps with tight quarters and narrow hallways.  Give Barry his magnum and have a great one shot one kill all around character.  Or just have fun equipping Gina with a bunch of dance emotes and have her do the robot until everything around her is dead.
The story is fine for a resident evil game, and I look forward to the next episodes.  If you play RE games for the story, God help you, but you'd probably be happier waiting for all the episodes to come out next month.  Moira is annoying and dumb, but all teenagers are.  I'm more looking forward to future episodes because they'll unlock more gear, upgrades and levels for the raid mode.
Overall, great game, great value, ignore the cash shop completely, and don't buy any DLC until there's a huge sale.

Antichamber is a very good puzzle game, which uses the first-person perspective like a lot of shooter games. It is very ground-breaking in the sense that a lot of the game mechanics are completely new. So as far as originality is concerned, Antichamber scores big. Unfortunately, the actually game playing experience does not quite live up to the originality of the design. The puzzles all involve progress from one room to another. There is no storyline to speak of other than "inspirational posters" that you encounter at each puzzle. For me the satisfaction of solving the puzzles would have been greater if there was an overall story. Also, it would have been better if some of the puzzles had been of a type where you do more than just figure out how to move from point A to point B. There are a few cases where it is hard to tell if you have really solved the puzzle. If there had been a kind of running score, or a little "happy music" when you solved a puzzle, this would have enhanced the game experience. There is no tutorial at all as to the rules and mechanics of the game, you figure this all out during the game. In some cases this makes the game more fun, since figuring out the game mechanics is part of the puzzle. In other cases, it is just plain frustrating, since there is a lot of trial and error to figure out how the game works. One big problem is the color coding system. There are parts of the game that you will encounter early on that are impossible to solve before you progress in other areas. You can waste a lot of time and become very frustrated before you figure this out. I still think this is a very good game and well worth your money. I would recommend starting with a strategy guide that explains the basics of the game mechanics and the color coding system, and how to use the map in the starting area. Don't spend too much time in any one puzzle, use the esc key to go back to the starting area and choose a new puzzle (color appropriate) before spending too much time on any one puzzle.
Not recommending this game till everyone puts the brightness on 0 and difficulty on hard. ;p

Well, where do I begin? I'll start by saying the developers really did the Shadowrun name a lot of justice with this release. Basically a party-based tactical RPG set in the cyberpunk world of Shadowrun. It really nails that futuristic, dystopian vibe I look for in this type of story. The gameplay is very enjoyable and you'll have a lot of fun leveling up your character in the main campaign. The options for character development and customization are pretty solid.
My only complaint is - the main campaign is too short. Sure, you can get Dragonfall (the expansion) for another $15, and that is much bigger than the original campaign... but the stock capaign just sort of disappointed me. I also felt like it was a bit too linear. I was expecting a LOT more side-missions and stuff like that to help me develop my character before the endgame. I wouldn't let that deter you from buying the game, but I would set aside a little extra money for that expansion - first.
Some would argue that the Workshop has player-made campaigns in case you get bored with the one that comes with the game, but I find it tedious sifting through mountains of crap to find a decent player-made campaign. Most of them suffer from the "Oh here's part 1....part 2.... part 3... And you have to download them all seperately.. oh but im not done with part 4, and I quit working on it cause I got bored.." It's just annoying. Same thing as most any game that comes with a toolkit... most of the player developed content is half-arsed.
Anyway, I don't want the review to sound too negative because I actually did really enjoy the 20+ hours I've spent with Shadowrun Returns, and I'd recommend it to my friends - As long as they can afford to buy Dragonfall with it.

As far as the game goes, it's a satisfying action/horror game. Graphics aren't the best you'll see on pure technical aspect, but there is a style to it, and a good use of lighting, blur and filters. It looks dirty, a bit noisy. The artwork is a step in the good direction after the terrible character design from the first Revelations (I mean, that was god awful...). The enemies aren't the most original, but the protagonists are really well designed, and modeled; they look next-door and at the same time, they have character. The gameplay is more in the steps of Revelations than RE6, which is a good thing. Not that RE6 wasn't good in terms of possibilities (people who REALLY played it knows how much thought went into the mechanics and the overall challenge) but it feels more natural and less super-heroic/block-busterish. And it still gives a great Arcade feel to the Raid Mode which gives the player a way to play the game while waiting for the next episode: nicely done. It's fluid, and the fact that you have to use partner swapping (in story mode) often, is a good addition, though it clearly let that idea go away by the third episode. Overall, I enjoyed the ride, especially for a price so low and that much fun content (the Raid mode is still really enjoyable and that's where I spent most of my time).
BUT...japanese developers don't love the PC too much, do they. The game is weirdly un-optimized. Sometimes, it's fluid 60FPS on highest settings, than BAM 15FPS, and getting to the lower options doesn't help. I had a couple of freeze while trying to load a Raid Mode Lvl too, and the game doesn't feel stable in a general sense. Sometimes, it works perfectly, then you have annoying FPS issues. That's not even talking about the local-coop mode which isn't in the game, but is in the game, but not really, oh but wait you need a mod, but maybe they'll release it with an update.
TL;DR
Fairly good game (I enjoy it much more than the first Revelations, that I already quite liked), with a good money/time ratio (if it's what you are interested in) but poorly executed on PC...

Alright folks. This is an interesting one for me. Buckle up.
Risk of Rain, as most of you are propably well aware, is a game that falls into the category of roguelike (or rather roguelites). You are, most of the time at least, supposed to die at some point. Although there is a clear end to a run. A run will take you on average something from 10 to 60 minutes, depending on your ability to survive. Each run is gonna be different, based on the following factors: Your starting character, the selection of levels you are gonna get, the equipment you'll receive and the bosses you encounter along the way. I say "selection" of levels, because in contrast to a lot of other roguelites there is no random level generator. The game has a set of different levels within a set of various settings. The selection and order of those will be random each playthrough though.
Each character comes with different skills and attacks, which helps the replayability a ton. The characters feel unique and distinguished enough from each other, that you want to unlock them and try them and roll with them.
Anyway, although the characters feel different from each other, the development within a run seems very limited. As per genre your run and character will develop with the items you'll receive and most of the items don't really make you adjust your strategy all that much.

You get what I mean. But to be fair - there are active items which add to your strategic decisions and there are some passive items that will make you think.
Still, often times to me it feels, that from stage 2 onwards you'll be doing the same routine for most of the remaining run - the most effective strategy based on your characters skillset. It's still fun and I adore the endgame (including the final boss), but I feel like there was more potential.
I don't wanna elaborate to much on the presentation, because this kind of style is something you love or you hate. I love pixelart, I love the simplicity and the soundtrack to my ears is gorgeous. From a presentation standpoint I got nothing to complain about.
Let's put this together and clear up why this game is a special one to me.
The flaws of the game are obvious and I know which parts and designchoices I don't agree with, but I still keep coming back. Give it a month or two, but I'll be back - and I'll be enjoying it as much as I ever did. I get curious, I get excited, I get a bit frustrated at times. And although I unlocked most of the game - there is still this sense of mystery for me. There are still riddles within the levels of which I know (or seen parts of) but haven't solved yet. There are still characters I haven't quite mastered and items I haven't seen. I still feel this sense of complete accomplishment, everytime I beat the final boss. No matter how often I come back - the game, so far, did not get stale for me.
There is just something in this game that caters to my gaming-needs in a special way. The genremix of platformer and roguelite, the fireworks on the screen, the art design, the difficulty. Something in between all those qualities just gets me everytime - and propably will as well in the far future.

Batman Arkham Knight has come a long way since the first port made its way over from console to the PC. From a muddled mess to a now very refined and polished version, the game has more than made up for what was done in the past. Does that change the past? No, but it does mean that they made right on their promise to fix it.
Arkham Knight is an amazing game that will last you as long as you really want it to last. Overall though I would say this is atleast a 20+ hour game to 100% and about 12-15 hours for basic story completion. The amount of side missions, collectibles, and riddles to all complete will make you appreciate the amount of detail and work that went into creating the last iteration of Batman from Rocksteady. Everything from flying through the city to driving through it is fun, fast, and exciting. The tools add another layer of complexity to combos and solving riddles while the fighting is still very fluid and not too challegning to beat. The added vehicle truly made me feel like batman and the added tank fights were a welcome addition to the difficulty the game presented.
Overall, I can't recommend the game more than in it's current forms. The DLC may not be all that worth it, (Except the "Most Wanted" mission pack, that is!) but for what you're getting at this price, the game will satisfy you greatly. Please buy this game and experience the knight.

- Great game, some flaws, a game no South Park or RPG fan should miss.
Taking place immediately after the Game of Thrones inspired 244th through 247th episodes of the series in which the town's population have gone through the Blackest of Black Fridays, fighting to the death over random stuff on sale and in which game console the Boys should stake their futures.  The Stick of Truth is the Boys playing a full blown Live Action Role Playing Game in South Park even as sinister forces work against the unsuspecting town.  In comes the New Kid, and in keeping with the tropes set down by the genre, this silent protagonist must navigate the conflict between two warring factions as they seek to save the day.
Unfortunately the game feels like a bunch of it hit the cutting room floor, not for lack of inspiration, but for lack of funds.  The Stick of Truth suffers from being made by Obsidian and originally set to be published by the defunct THQ - this defuncting having occurred during the game's development and risking the fate of the game.  Obsidian representatives have on more than one occasion said their company nearly ran out of funds entirely while making this game.
Allow me to explain my gripes, and I apologize for the minor spoilers, I will try to keep it minimal.
Literally nothing you do will impact the game.  The two factions at war serve no purpose, they are a choice with no consequence.  You can obtain costumes which would imply allegiance to one or the other faction, but it has zero impact on the game.  You don't get a different power, you don't get a different weapon, you don't get a different hair cut even, you get sweet♥♥♥♥♥♥all for siding with either.
In most similarly designed games - the Fallout, Elder Scrolls, and Forgotten Realms series in particular, you will find that wearing the clothes of a faction impacts that faction's opinion of you and what you do and how you do it also factors into their responses.  Not so much here, again, nothing you do matters.  No quest will ensure the 5th graders will attack your enemy, reducing their combat effectiveness later in the game.  No dialogue will allow you to unlock a special companion.  Stealing from someone will not make people think less of you.
The game zips through story at a rather high speed, you go from arc to arc with little time to engage in what is happening.  Had the player a little more engagement with the events and characters, a branching story, this would not be a problem.  As it is however, you end up with a game that is boring to replay, most games of this type are awesome for replayability.
There are bugs, you will find yourself disappearing for no reason, and the camera focus moving off to the wrong part of the map.  You will need to restart the game to fix these sadly, but luckily they are not very common.
Oh lord, loading screens.  The game is not a graphically intense thing, it should not need so many.
Do not take these complaints as hate for the game, this is disappointment.  There could have been more to this, it could have been a clear Game of the Year, instead of just being one of the better games.
Combat is that of Super Mario RPG and it's kin, a very forgiving QTE-ish element is present to improve your attacks' and abilities' power.  Except for a lack in variety of combat, this is great.  And there are a few little full blown QTEs in game, but they also give plenty of reaction time and are clear with what to do.  This is easy enough that a child can play through the whole game without needing a hand.
The graphics are great, everything feels natural and looks like it belongs.  The art team should be given high jobs and blow fives.  The setting is wonderful, the town of South Park feels smaller than it should be, but what is there is alive and interesting.  I wish it was bigger to match the portrayal of the town from television, but we got a good chunk to play with.  The music, the voice acting, these are completely flawless.  They match the show in every way.  This all because the game was developed with close ties to South Park Studios who make the show.
If this game were not a South Park game, I would recommend it for everyone.  As it is however, anyone who is into RPGs and legally old enough to have a Steam account will have to do.

Two years ago I played Mirror's Edge on the Xbox 360 and, although it was a visually stunning game and a distinct, novel premise; Its gameplay was an unmedigated nightmare. A janky, almost broken mess that stripped away every redeeming quality this game offered. But because it was such an individual among the countless other FPS games out their, I felt it deserved a second chance on the PC.
Not to play favorites or anything, but what a difference a keyboard and mice makes!
It still has some of the issues that plagued the console versions, but on this platform tranversing the roof tops and alley ways of this crisp, carefully constructed skyline is no longer an agonising labour. And because you're not constantly fighting with the controls, you'll actually be allowed to partake in the scenery and bask in the clean aesthetics around you.
If I had to give a criticism, its that the fighting in Mirror's Edge is difficult in the wrong ways. Naturally, the protangonist, Fiath; has to be as flesh and bone are her adversaries, but it is not a fair fight confronting several heavyly armed guards without nothing but you bare hands, and the exit behind them. When you do disarm one and seize the gun your obliged to hold on to it for as long as you are able. And in tense moments that does break the flow of the gameplay, going from elegantly dancing through the map too menandering around corner with a heavy machine gun, determined not to be gunned down again.
But in the end, if Mirror's Edge was a PC only game, I suspect it would have been better received by the public. If you're burnt out on your typical brown shooter, try this one.

Mirror's Edge is more of a first person platformer or action/adventure game than a FPS.  The parkour mechanics are very fluid and the actions are representative of what you would find in a Prince of Persia game (climbing walls, wall running, leaps, slides, zip lines).  There are no iron sights or ADS except for the sniper rifle, but you will spend more time running away or beating down your foes than shooting at them.  While it is not technically the best looking game on PC, it is the most beautiful game due to varied and stark color usage combined with some excellent lighting.  However, some people will be put off by the bloom.  The story is neither bad or necessarily good, but just there.

Update 3/5/15: Episode 2 (hard difficulty).
Well, it was pretty good IMO. I won't spoil anything, but I just want to touch upon it. Creepy atmosphere was definitely still there, still prefer Claire and Moira's campaign, as there were much more tense moments. There's a similar scene to RE4 and RE5 where you basically have to hold your ground in a house while enemies are trying to break in. That was great. And in both campaigns you get to meet your first boss fights. Claire's campaign's boss fight is much more dynamic if you will, lots of things going on, granted I am playing on hard difficulty. I don't know how many times I died. Barry's boss fight was more of a rinse and repeat type of thing, at least to me,  it was alright.. But outcome was pretty much the same, I came out of both boss fights with either little ammo (I'm talking like 10 rounds left or less) or none at all with one to no herbs left. That feeling of initial helplessness when you see what you have to overcome with what little you have left is just great, does really bring back old RE memories of resource management. But I did find myself thinking "whhhyyyyy" or "NOOOOooooooooooooo" when I see what I have to face with such little ammunition left, but it's good. That's what survival horror is about. I'm really liking Revelations 2 at the moment. The game isn't completely patched up well yet though, raid mode is definitely still has issues. Campaign for me seems to be working quite well, except for areas where I have to restart b/c I died, I have stuttering and fps issues for the first 30 seconds or so. Partner AI can be pretty dumb at times too, more times than not they kind of just stand there and get whacked.
I'm writing this review soley based on the game itself, not based on the PC co-op blunder, because honestly I feel like not enough people are giving credit to where it's due, and also, I'm not that big on co-op either in the main story, but I would definitely like to see co-op in raid mode.
Anyway, on to the review.
So far, Revelations 2 has a great atmosphere. Pretty creepy at times, and it does definitely bring back memories of old RE titles because there are areas of back tracking, such a refreshment from the linear RE6 campaign. Revelations 2 plays a bit like The Last of Us, which is a good thing. I love the new implementation of being able to crouch. And the afflicted that come running at you is pretty nerve racking, which is similar to the runners in TLoU. Also similar to TLoU is the crafting system, although not as robust, but just reminded me of it. The ability to swap characters anytime you wish is something I really like too, more so in Claire and Moira's campaign than Barry's, but nonetheless, I'm liking this new gameplay addition. Does certainly give the player more freedom.   I am also quite fond of the new dodge mechanic. Much better than the dodge mechanic from the first revelations, and isn't over the top like in RE6  (jumping to the side and rolling and getting up again). I do feel like Revelations 2 strikes a nice balance in terms of being not too action-y and not too tank control like. However, I would like slightly tighter controls during sprinting. One thing I LOVE is that enemies do not have health or ammo drops. YES. This is what I'm talking about. I legitimately was running out of ammo on my play through as Claire (hard difficulty) and it was glorious. Me likey. Production value is definitely up from the first Revelations title, but still a step away from the main AAA RE installments, but it still looks and feels great. However, I wish that there were more melee options. If only it had RE5's melee gameplay, where there's different melee animations depending on how the enemy is staggered.
So far, I am impressed with the first episode, hopefully, I will continue to be with the other subsequent episodes to come. I just hope the story doesn't turn out to be some crazy plot like Revelations 1...
Raid Mode
If you were like I, and wasn't much fond of Raid Mode in Revelations 1, I think you'll really like this new Raid Mode in Revelations 2. Now it doesn't seem like a chore to play. Matches are just right in length, much more customization options to make you come back for more. It seems like the roster is going to be quite robust. It would be nice if pretty much all the RE characters were to be included. We already know Leon, Chris will be. I'm hoping for at least Sherry, Ada, Rebecca, and Jessica. They have to include Sherry because Claire is there...wouldn't it be nice?
Cons
-Bug, bugs everywhere! Campaign seems to be alright, for the most part. but there are instances of really bad stuttering and frame rate drops, and lip sync issues (most notably the first real time cutscene in Barry's campaign). After the first patch, it has gotten slightly better for me, but definitely still there. I am running an i7-3770K, 16GB ram, R9 290, and I get areas of 30~ish fps especially when there are effects on the screen (snow, fire, hard lighting). Most I've seen come from raid mode, possibly because of the variations in environment/stages that bring these issues up.
-Slow mo. I feel like my character seems to be running in slow mo at times, especially during reloads animations. I'm not sure if it's due to the stuttering/fps issue.
-When aiming, sometimes the thing that you're aiming at is slightly out of focus, and also the laser sight as well. Other times it's fine. Also not liking how the character is also out of focus/slightly fuzzy when aiming as well. Really reminds me of RE6 when it first came out too. If they fixed it for RE6, why implement it in Revelations 2?
-Enemy AI can be really stupid sometimes. They can get stuck in doorways or window sills or run in circles trying to get to you on another level but have no idea that the stairs is just behind them (experienced in raid mode). Had an enemy just turn around and walk into those spinning spike traps during the campaign when Claire was at the door way, crouched and slightly out of view from it. It kept on walking into the wall next to the door way, gave up and committed suicide.
Even with these cons, it doesn't render the game unplayable. Yes, I know there's those out there where the bugs do render the game unplayable for them, and that's quite unfortunate. But for me, it's just something I'll have to live with until a patch comes out that fixes everything, which I'm pretty confident that Capcom will do, since the first patch rolled out two days after release. However, it does leave a sour taste in one's mouth, especially for PC gamers when the game is not properly ported/optimized.

I am very happy with Shadowrun Returns. I think the game lives up to the hype. I am a passionate fan of the Super Nintendo Shadowrun game (which I've been playing for over twenty years!) and playing Shadowrun Returns feels like a homecoming. It is very reminiscent of the SNES game, but very contemporary and modern, of course.
The combat and puzzles are of medium challenge (just right for me when I played on the game's easy level of difficulty) and the storytelling is good. The visual design and music are extremely well done. There is a well-balanced blend of exploring and fighting. I finished the game in about twenty-four hours of playing time, with only a couple of mission "do overs." A quicker and more skilled player might take about twenty hours to finish. I’d like the game to be longer, but that is hardly a legitimate complaint, merely a fond wish and a desire for more of a good thing. I noticed no flaws in the game other than a rash of minor typos about halfway through, mostly in dialogue windows. The only real problem I had was some serious lag in combat scenarios featuring about eight or more characters on screen, but my system, while of good quality, is not a gaming rig, and I'm running only the minimum 2GB of RAM the game recommends. The turn-based system employed in Shadowrun Returns made the lag easily tolerable.
In my first play-through I found that playing my character with thoughtfulness and manners gained me lots of karma. The option to be a hardcore, coldblooded merc is always there, but I can't say how taking that tack affects the gameplay. My key to success in combat was always being smart with in-combat strategy. No matter what mistakes I made with equipping or tactics, or how my luck went when the fighting began, I was always able to overcome by making good strategic decisions.
Thanks to everyone involved in making the game. Great job!

I began playing post-2015 release meltdown. From what I can tell, the vast majority of the issues have been resolved. Some people are still having problems. As it is, I am reviewing the gameplay and story rather than the technical pains that may or may not exist.
Overall, this title wraps up the Arkham story arc in good fashion. A few minor characters are shoehorned into the story for the sake of busywork for the player. This isn't bad, per se. The main story is engaging and provides an interesting perspective into Batman's pysche as he battles his foes and inner demons. The lore of Batman is held up well, which is this game's greatest accolade.
The gameplay is fluid and as familiar as ever. Players of past Arkham titles will hit the ground running, while newcomers will have no problem blending into the gameplay. In regards to the batmobile, you will either enjoy it or you will hate it. Why would you hate it? Because while the batmobile is seemlessly integrated into the game both as a character and as a weapon, the battles are excess and repetitive. I don't mind this, but many will and do.
I highly recommend you play this game. It is vengence. It is the night. It is Batman.

South Park: The Stick of Truth is a role-playing adventure game.
The game starts with the mute protagonist being ordered to leave the house and make friends in his new home town of South Park. Immediately you become a friend of Butters and he gets you into the Human clan of a Dungeon & Dragons-esque group ruled by the Grand Wizard Cartman. You are given the choice between four character classes. You can be a Fighter, a Mage, a Thief, or a Jew.
At the first part of South Park: The Stick of Truth you spend your time recruiting factions and battling elves to reclaim the stick. In true South Park fashion the story escalates out of control leading to being abducted by aliens, shrank by underpants gnomes and travelling to 8-bit Canada to translate abortion documents written in French. The story makes sense in the context of South Park and it was genuinely a lot of fun to play through.
Between collecting Chinpokomon, completing all the side quests and levelling up this game will take up close to 20 hours to complete.
The game looks exactly like the show.
The voice acting is very good, all known voices from the television show are there. The music is also very good. Besides of epic middle-earth music playing in the town, you can listen to songs from the television show in stores.
Overall South Park: The Stick of Truth is absolutely epic! It literally feels like the show. If you are a fan of South Park you will love it.

I see a lot of the reviews for "Dying Light" on Steam praising the multitudes of monsters, or the fluidity and realism of the parkour or even the graphics but honestly? These aren't all that great. They're good, don't get me wrong. Just not great,
For the monsters there's maybe about nine different things to kill. There's your run-of-the-mill zombies, slightly faster run-of-the-mill zombies, exploding things that can kill you in one hit, spitting things (because we can't have a zombie game without something spitting some noxious green goop at us), big guys with concrete clubs, bigger guys that like to throw rocks at you, screaming children (zombified of course) and faster, stronger run-of-the-mill zombies that only appear during the night time. On top of that there's also desperate survivors that you're supposed to feel bad about carving up (but I didn't) and about an entire national army's worth of armed thugs for you to kill. Maybe with my lack of remorse when carving up other humans I'm supposed to feel like I'm the monster? I dunno.
The parkour is what most people were looking forward to this game for and honestly? It's good. You're able to make your way across the city any way you want to. On foot of course as Crane seems to be the only person in the city that doesn't hold a valid driver's licence. I did have a few minor problems where I couldn't grab a ledge similar to others I had grabbed hundreds of times because I was looking a millimetre more downwards than what was considered by the game to be acceptable. Then the game suffers from a virus (Haha, get it?) that I like to call Assassin's Creed Virus (I'm not great with names) where I can leap off as tall a building as I like so long as I land in something considered to be soft. In♥♥♥♥♥Creed this would be the wagons of hay, in this it would be a pile of trash bags that could be full of dirty, hepatitis-infested needles for all I know. These things are rather minor I admit, but it does break the flow of the game a bit I feel.
Graphically the game is sound... At bits. I've seen a few things in game that would have been embarresed to be seen in even a PlayStation 2 game (Take a look at the crate of... onions? I guess? When you're in The Tower.) It seems designed for consoles too I feel. The menus have a nasty habit of returning to the very top after you press enter or click on something which caused me to craft the wrong thing a few times and it also seems to be poorly optimised for PC. I bought my computer back in September 2014 and it was top of the line at the time and I had to lower the graphics and view distance just to play the game.
Night Time was hyped up to be some sort of terrifying ordeal that you'd be extremely lucky to be able to survive if you decided to ignore the screaming voices of protest in your head and venture outside in the dark but from the moment you get the grappling hook night time just isn't scary. It's like when you were afraid of the monsters under your bed as a child but when you finally get brave enough to look you find that it's just an old T-shirt, a dinosaur toy and your mum's old vibrator that had been left on the "on" position. Okay, that metaphor wasn't clear. Night starts off as being genuinely scary, not as terrifying as other reviews say or as terrifying as it was hyped up to be, but that was only because these scary old T-shirt, dinosaur, mum's old vibrator monsters seemed to have no weakness. By about mid-game night is no scarier than day time. You can have strong weapons to fight if you need to and the grappling hook lets you escape from most chases with ease.
That's another part where the game breaks down a bit. When you unlock the grappling hook. Most of the enjoyment in the game is deciding which route you should take to get from point A, through point B, up point C and to point D. But with the grappling hook you pretty much just zip from A to B with no real thought or sense of danger and as said before it lets you break pursuit with ease. The grappling hook also takes away from the satisfaction of solving a climbing puzzle by yourself because you can just skip most of them. (Puzzle is used very loosely there!)
Combat seems to be another huge sticking point in other reviews. People keep mentioning how most fights are better avoided or how it's dangerous to fight your way through to a different area but to be honest it's really not. There's this massive bridge swarming with infected and I was able to clear the entire thing using a few molotoves, a handful of home-made exploding shuriken and a couple of machetes, and then there was enough loot left lying around afterwards for me to enjoy being king of the dirty survivors for a few weeks.
My review does seem to be very negative, and that's because it is mostly. The developers really let themselves down in certain aspects but at the same time I can't help but enjoy myself while playing. Despite the flow sometimes being broken, the sense of real freedom you get while running from A to D is something that I've never experienced before in any other video game. The combat is fun at times and honestly pretty funny at others. The graphical issues were sorted by just changing my settings a bit and night time was genuinely scary. But only for the first few nights.
"Dying Light" is a fun enough game to play on your own but I feel that the game really comes into it's own when you play co-operatively with some friends. My friends and I were able to pull off some amazing team-work that just wouldn't be possible during single player. Everyone you play with has a slightly different play style, you might be working with someone who likes to stealthily sneak past all of the infected, or you could be playing with a gung-ho gun-nut who shoots everything that moves and then some things that don't move just for good measure. One of the coolest parts of the multiplayer is just watching your friends get from point A to point D. While running you could see one of your friends on the streets below you sliding into an impossibly small gap to evade a fast zombie while at the same time you could say a black rope appear just above you and see another friend use it to grapple their way to the next building.
I've given the game a lot of flack and deservedly so, it is the game we all expected it to be, just not as good as we had hoped. Given time I hope they update the game to iron out some of the more minor inconveniences.
Maybe I've been overly harsh? Maybe not. Overall I'd give it 7/10. 7.5 at a push. It's a really fun game, just don't go into it thinking that it's going to be the best game you've ever played.

If you are tired of the usual genres and gameplay styles and want something new give this a go.  Yes, parkour is sooooo 2005, but it's really well done here: it's fast, fluid, and fun with just the right balance in player control required to keep the game from turning into ether a cumbersome and overcomplicated mess or an over simplified and tedious push-a-button-and-mindlessly-jump-from-roof-to-roof "Assassain's Creed" type experience. A fantastic game that is enormously long on real world believability and atmospheric observation. Every detail is carefully crafted to put you in the shoes of a real person running about in a real environment: your screen is constantly bobbing a pair of human eyes instead of a floating camera, enemies are normal people and not hulked out sci-fi body armor, and above all else, the enironment is pulled directly from the real world.  You'll see birds fly away on rooftops, typical walkways, folliage, the sounds of the street below, wind, and the beauty of an urban city. I play the game like I'm on a site-seeing tour.
Problems only creep when you consider the story, which is 1980's paranoia cliche, and the human obstacles you face. "Boss" battles last only seconds and gun combat is pathetic. ME really rewards when you understand the controls, but that's a steep learning curve. Game length is also very short, but full of entertainment. I REALLY want a sequel.

Before I carry on with the review, let me post my computer's specifications:
i7 4770k @ 4.5 Ghz
GTX 780 x 2 (SLI)
32Gb Corsair Vengeance @ 1866Mhz
500Gb Samsung 840 Evo (SSD)
1Tb HDD
I've had EVGA Precision X track the framerate, GPU usage, and VRAM usage for this game.  I never saw RER2 use more than 1Gb of VRAM... not even with ever setting set as high as it could go with the FXAAHQ3; hell, I even enabled 8 CSAA in nVidia's control panel (didn't really need to).  My system never used more than 1Gb of VRAM and GPU usage stayed under 40% for each card.
With my beefy system I still encountered massive framerate drops (as low as 20fps) without any corresponding spike in VRAM/GPU usage... no CPU bottleneck either.  Lowering the settings does not yield a descernible benefit or increase in fps.
---
Putting the technical issues aside, I'm enjoying this game immensely.  I do miss Claire's original VA and her character model from previous games, but its been about time for Claire to redebut in another installment.
Raid mode is fun (lvl 50 w/Claire).  The main story (Episode 1) was good - albeit short; that is ok considering the Episodic release.
Even with the fps dilemma, if you're a fan of RE and have a soft spot in your heart for Claire Redfield, you will enjoy this game (story pending).  Once Capcom optimizes/fixes RER2, it'll be a great installment in the series.

As a fan of all things zombie, I’ve been looking forward to Dying Light for a while now. Overall, it’s a great game, and it has much going for it, but there are some odd design issues, a serious case of couriering (is that a word?) and just some attention-to-detail features that make me go, what?
I’ve played for about 28 hours, I’m at 70% story completion, I’ve finished 39 side missions, and I’ve done six of the quarantine zones, as of the time of this review.
Great game with great mechanics, a story that slowly devolves into a clichéd mess, with some technical issues that shouldn’t really exist, and a few questionable design choices spread throughout. Still a great game. If I were to put it on a numbered scale, it’d get a seven out of ten.
+ Visuals are astounding, great atmospheric effects (such as debris floating around), explosions look terrific, zombies have great models. One touch I quite like is if a viral is in front of you and screams, their mouth actually opens and closes as it screams. Not a big deal, but adds a touch of realism.
+ Sound is also great, be it the music or effects. Connecting with a melee weapon gives a satisfying crunch, and guns sound like how guns should; firing off a shotgun blast results in a roar, not a pathetic tinny sound many games use for gun sounds.
+ The story, at least at the beginning. Sure, it’s rehashed (something happens, people become zombies), but it’s presented differently and keeps you intrigued for a bit, drawing you into wondering what happened.
+ The main mission. The primary goal of the game changes a few hours into the story, but the missions that you undertake for the main story are great, and they aren’t recycled very much.
+ Parkour. If Dying Light didn’t have a parkour element, it would definitely be your standard zombie exploration game. Not only does the parkour add an extra dimension, but it’s also done right; it doesn’t feel tacky or sloppy.
+ Progression and perks. There are three categories you improve in: Survivor, Agility, Power. Survivor points are gained by completing quests and quarantine zones, as well as challenges. Agility points are gained by just playing the game; climbing, jumping, strafing. Power points are gained by killing; melee, firearms, explosions, traps. There are 25 levels of each, and the perks are pretty nice. They act as a tree, and to unlock one, you’ll have to unlock the first tier and go from there. It’s not too in-depth, but adds a nice touch.
+ Night mode. Nighttime adds an extra layer of trouble for you; it’s pitch black, and there are more dangerous zombies with heightened senses. It’s basically a stealth mode. However, completing quests, exploring or just being outside doubles what you earn for the period.
+ Random events. There are many random events. Air drops, which contain relief packages and some other goodies, are the big one for the first little bit. Get there quick enough, it’ll be yours. Take your time, you may have to fight off some other humans for it. Take too long, and you’ll lose the drop completely. There will be random survivors under attack who will reward you for helping them. Some people may turn into shopkeepers when you save them, giving you another location to buy and sell from. Some people might only be there to give some background on life in Harran before the outbreak. Maybe you’ll help a group of survivors fight off some zombies, only to have them attack you afterwards. Lots can happen!
- The story. As I said, the story starts off great, but after a couple of hours, it devolves into what has been seen hundreds of times before. I won’t give it away, but you can likely figure out what your goal changes to.
- Hit detection/clipping. I’ve mainly seen this on the bigger guys with the huge rebars, but the hit detection is atrocious. He’ll begin swinging, I’ll dodge backwards completely out of range (even of the shockwave), yet I’ll still get hit by it. Same for clipping. I might run behind a truck, yet the attack still manages to get me.
- First aid. To make a medkit, you need alcohol and gauze. Pretty realistic, as that will actually tend to wounds, although not restore you fully. Yet every single first aid/medical box you open will have gauze. Just gauze. No alcohol. A few hours in, I had maybe nine bottles of alcohol, yet I was up to 50 or so gauze. Just seems weird.
- Night mode. Yes, night mode is good (see The Good). But it’s not really that much more difficult. Your survivor sense will show an outline of the dangerous ones, and the minimap always shows their vision cone, so it’s not at all challenging to avoid them. You’ll likely only run into them if you mistime a jump and fall hard and one’s nearby, or if you kill an enemy that makes a loud noise (hazmat guy by attacking the air compressor, or have one of the bloaters blow up).
- Technical issues. Even after the 1.2.1 patch, there are a few technical issues. While they obviously won’t apply to everyone, every few times I quit the game, it doesn’t exit properly. It drops me to the desktop, but the game is still running in task manager. I then have to end the task, and upon restarting the game, it begins in windowed mode, and I have to set it to full screen.
Aside from the odd exit issue, cutscenes sometimes freezes for a few seconds while the audio plays. If I wind up getting hit directly by the belching zombie’s green blob thing, the game freezes for a few seconds. Lowering view distance seems to help, but I shouldn’t have to lower that to compensate for poor optimization.
+ Zombie models are pretty varied, with lots of different combinations. While you will run into reused models, they’ll be few and far between.
- Godlike human enemies. Zombies, sure, they might take a little to knock down. But the humans are definitely of a godlike stature. There is no reason why, after burning for ten seconds from a Molotov cocktail, that they should survive a shot to the head from a pistol, and still require a few whacks to put down for good. That’s just ridiculous.
- Not much variation in the boxes or crates you run across. If you see a green, white or yellow box that looks dirty or rusty, it’ll never require a lockpick. Likewise, if you come across a box that looks nice, or adorned with something, even if it’s in the dirtiest part of the slums, it’ll require lockpicking.
- Most of the side quests are typical courier fare. Go talk to person, get item for them, return, get reward. This is a good 90% of the side quests, not including the quarantine missions. It’s like an MMO in the way they’ve handled Crane being a courier.
- Protected survivors. Every now and then, you’ll see a shield icon on your map; these are survivors who need escorting. They are all annoying, they don’t shut up, it’s never A to B, and they all run headfirst into every zombie without waiting for an escort. For example, a fisherman wants you to escort him to his secret fishing spot. But before that, you’ll need to escort him to his rod. And listen to him talk about what a good deal it was. There’s also the American guy. I wanted to shoot his legs out and leave him for the zombies.

Finally a worthy next installment in the series of researching and defending against unknown invaders. This is the modern interpretation of the all time classic UFO: Enemy Unknown done right. While staying true to its roots it still manages to iterate on those mechanics and show of some of its own. This is a game you'd want to come back to find out what tech you're gonna find and what comes up next.
After the horrible first expansion, Firaxis has finally understood what the term "added gameplay value means". The expansion, Enemy Within, is as close to a perfect add-on as you can get which harkens back to how expansions were in the past - content mastodonts. In fact, it adds so much new content it's hard to go back and play it without. From gene modification of your soldiers, to new enemies and research trees it's a absolutely stunning addition to an already stellar game.
The mission variety is also greater than ever and it the "classic" difficulty seems even harder now than it was before - that's a good thing. You're gonna feel constantly underpowered, outgunned and outmanned for a long time. Nations will panic and leave the XCOM project and you have to balance the small amount of spending power you have. Thankfully, much thanks to all the new "must see" technology and functions they've added to the game, it's well worth getting some beatings before you get the bearing straight. Did I mention you get MECs (Mechanically Enhanced Commanders) here? Those are almost worth the admission price alone.
All in all, a fantastic addition to the game that is what I personally was just waiting to arrive. 2k and Firaxis have outdone themselves again, and that my friend, is no easy task.
