Traveler's Tales LEGO Marvel Super Heroes is so much disappointment.
The controls are kludgy as ♥♥♥♥.  I am playing on PC, so this may be due to the port.  However, I use WASD for movement of my character as well as selection in SOME menus, while I can only use the arrow keys for selection in other menus.  Sometimes the key to press to make a selection is Enter, other times it's U, J, or H with apparently no governing rules regarding why ONE KEY ISN'T ALWAYS ACCEPTABLE.
Speaking of one key, the U key is used to switch between characters so you can use various powers to progress in puzzles and advance the story. In free play, an extended pres of the U key brings up your character menu so you can access areas or items unavailable to the characters allowed during story play.  Unfortunately, with characters that have a second identify (last I checked, that's literally all of them, though this doesn't happen with every single character) such as Spiderman's Peter Parker or Bruce Banner's Hulk,  you have to wait for a three to five second animation  while they change identities because you can press the U key again to bring up the character selection menu.
Regarding the character selection menu: there are 155 playable characters in this game.   While this sounds cool on it's face, it gets to be somewhat annoying in practice.  Instead of having 155 individual selections in the character menu, versions are grouped into one selection which cycles.  Iron Man is a prime example as to why this bogs down the game.  There are 5 or 6 versions one can play, some with different abilities.  One of Iron Man's abilities is an energy ray with is used to cut or destroy gold objects (Mark 42).  If you want to select this from the character menu, you have to highlight the selection and wait for it to cycle through.  Not every version has this ability, meaning that if you want a specific one, you have to time your selection properly or wait for it to cycle through again.  This may appear to be a small gripe, but having to wait every single time you wish to select this character for that ability adds up quickly.
There are no controls governing camera direction while in the game.  If a character has an ability to aim, one can use this to somewhat direct the camera, but it's still time consuming and not always easily accessible.  If something ends up behind the 4th wall of your screen, you have to move towards the camera long enough for the games to spin it around to your character's back.  Adding this to the lack of finesse in moving a character adds more headache to the game.
Vehicle movement is even worse than character movement.  In a game where a large portion of side missions require racing to acquire an object, hard turning becomes your enemy.  The challenge becomes not hanging one's self up on the sides of the track instead of getting to the goal in the allotted time.
Other issues with the side missions are that most are fetch mission where in you have to go somewhere, usually across town, acquire an item or find an individual, and return to the NPC which started the mission.  This means you may swing halfway across the city as Spiderman or fly quick as Thor, Iron Man, or anyone else with the ability, find your target, and then WALK this secondary NPC back to the starting point.  If you move too quickly, you have to turn around to get them to follow again.  Not every side mission is like this, but other issues regarding the camera or character movement suck most of the fun out of these.
While a tutorial level isn't necessary for every game, most controls are only mentioned at random during loading screens.  Given the immense size of the game world, it would seem that a quick run through could have been included without sacrificing any of the overall game play.
This game is not as much fun as it should be, given how many fun LEGO games are in existence.  I picked this up during a sale for 4.99 and I still feel as if I over paid for it.  The initial excitement of getting to play as my favorite Marvel characters has quickly diminshed and I may finish this game at some point.  Right now, it's run through part of a mission, save (assuming it doesn't lock up, though I accept that may be a lacking machine as opposed to poor programming), and then come back for another small snippet at a later time.  It's difficult to get into this game for longer than 20 minutes in that the 2 second wait here and difficult controls make that feel like a drudgingly long time.

Almost a perfect title.
First off, the focus on the editor and the "module" approach to the campaign made me think of neverwinter nights (the first one). The fact that the game focused on being highly expandable and customizable made me more forgiving of the campaign's shortcomings.
That being said, the game's pretty good, but still lacking. Some of it in terms of interface, some in terms of design (gameplay). Please note, I played on normal difficulty. The storyline is quaint, the visuals are detailed, and flow overall is smooth and enjoyable.
1) With all the awesome artwork, the protagonist visuals were extremely boring, whatever look I had in mind for my hero was nowhere to be found in the portrait collection. I just gave up in the end and went with a whatever-approach.
2) The chapter oriented campaign moves the story along nicely, but the linearity(sp?) of the game was disappointing, if you didn't manage your resources well, it's gone. This includes karma (xp).
3) Moving around when there's no (immediate) combat in combat mode is a chore.
4) Too many illusionary dialogue choices. Great, but acknowledging it was also an acknowledgement of it's extremely linear gameplay design (like combat, progression, resource allocation and game balance).
Ultimately, I think if they fixed a few things, this title would have a been a true A+, and fans would be clamoring for a sequel like crazy. Unfortunately, in it's current state, it's a great experiment to the throwback that is the shadowrun RPG, but that's all.
Maybe some mods would've helped, but the online presence for the game wasn't really there like other games neither. Hopefully they'll come out with some improvements in due time, if not a sequel.

Where to begin?
I guess the best place to start would be in saying that this game and its original version are two different experiences. While the first one would emphasize on optimizing your Time Units during battlescape phase (that's when you shoot aliens directly) and preparing you for a job as an acquisition/warehouse management specialist during geoscape phase (that's when you're uh.. not shooting aliens directly), the second iteration has a lot more to do with choice, and the rewards/penalties emanating from your decision-making process. In other words, the core mechanic of the old classic went along the line of maintaining efficient chains of supply in order to drive progress (with little to no indication as to what constituted progress, besides the technological) and this new classic elevates cost/benefit analysis and risk-management to blown out proportions (and does a nice job at guiding you toward the path of where you need to go, without too much hand-holding).
As a matter of fact, I do believe option two to present a more mature, nerve-racking challenge; there are times you will literraly stop and ponder your decision, because even when it's the best one, you will likely live to regret it at some point in some way (spending the resources on sattelite surveillance OR body armors OR Interceptors OR laser weaponry is always a really though call). On its own, Xcom 2012 presents a really good graphic engine that sucks you right into the action, and the class specialization brings new and fascinating tactical depth, both serving to heighten the tension at the core.
As you could guess, the graphics and sounds are amazing. More importantly, they also serve ambiance quite well, driving in this sense of epic/climactic showdown where you must win; and the stakes are huge indeed. Losing a soldier on the field (and you will) is a terrible experience you do not want to see again (but you will). The game is undoubtedly tough, but still fair, although it does become somewhat easier toward the end (if you make it there). Despite this, the game always keeps you on yours toes and the feeling of loss is well felt and emotionally discouraged; and there is always something to be said about games that can create genuine emotions in the player.
While the endgame is perhaps not as epic as the original, and the replayability may be somewhat compromised by asset-recycling, have no doubt that this title will bring you considerable pleasure - even if that pleasure should take the form of some twisted, perverse agony.
For the best Xcom experience in that regard, switch it to "Ironman": you can thank me later.

Designed for online cooperative play, the game also supports less desirable offline play. A nice selection of twelve fairly large, detailed levels is available; enemies spawn near the team during each wave, and chokepoints are present to funnel the enemy threat. Each of the ten classes has a selection of different starting weapons, preferred weapons to upgrade to during the match, and passive perks to help out the team. The classes include melee-focused, support, area attack, and ranged options, giving all types of players something to choose. Ten enemies, some with special abilities must be dispatched of during each wave. Doors may be welded to hold back the horde, while healing syringes can stave off untimely death. Each map has preferred, more easily defensible locations, and while the quantity and specific arrangement of enemies is different every playthrough, you still encounter the same types each game. That said, the chaos of combat is confusing and exciting. Killing Floor 2 is an enjoyable, albeit repetitive, gore-filled cooperative first-person shooter.

A truly enjoyable game with a few problematic elements.
Best of all: it has a strong story (both Returns and Dragonfall) with interesting NPCs you can build relationships with. It reminded me quite a bit of the Baldurs Gate games in that (and to some extent, visually as well). The NPCs have distinct personalities and voices, and while the game is pretty linear, it is written in such a way that your choices feel meaningful and contribute to the story.
In terms of mechanics, I would add that I'm not a fan of turned based play in general, but I thought it suited the game, and also found it to be not particularly onerous. (What was annoying was the to-hit rate, which seemed to me to be both low and incorrectly reported.)
Also: the paperdoll options could have been better, but the portraits were gorgeous.
On a more serious note, the game does have a few issues. Like the pen-and-paper version, it uses the term "shaman" and incorporates Native American spiritualism in ways that are culturally appropriative. There is also a section in dragonfall where one of the conversations with an NPC make some statements about modern paganism that at best could be described as inaccurate. Hard limits on stats (especially intelligence) depending on race also comes across as less of a critique of racism than the opposite.
All of that said, it's also clear that the writers of the story are interested in grappling with these issues, even though they don't entirely succeed. There are reasonably complex philosophical and moral conversations to be had and choices to be made in the game, and overall I would recommend the game.
On final note: the games are quite short. Each game took about 24 hours to play (steam doesn't seem to have counted dragonfall towards the total, so I can't be sure).

My experience with this game has been extremely positive, though it must be said that I'm writing this review from the perspective of an old school RPG gamer to whom some trappings of modern-RPGS, while not unwelcome, aren't considered necessary.
So, some things that might annoy a younger gamer didn't even register with me, such as the lack of voice acting for dialogue, the lack of vehicle-use and other fast-travel options.
High points:  The atmosphere is very, very nice in the stock campaign, with a very similar 'feel' to the old SNES Shadowrun game.  Lots of neon and cyberpunk-flavored urban squalor, with the nuances reinforced by the type of storyline and characters involved.  The way missions are setup eventually does a very good job of making ever familiar Shadowrun character type useful.  And the game is very, very easy to get into as far as controls, etc.  The setup is quite intuitive.
Low points:  The stock campaign is pretty linear and doesn't take advantage of how well a more sandbox-style environment would suit the Shadowrun universe.  I realize that there may be all kinds of mods to fix that now or eventually, but I'm reviewing the game I bought, not the game fans will help it become.  Also, while the availability of mercs for your runner team is sufficient, there's no real personality programmed into any of the 'for hire' guys -- yes, there are NPCs that'll come along with you who are more fleshed out, but for a better example of what can be done, character wise, with a bunch of killers for hire, see Jagged Alliance 1 and 2, which have been out for a long, long, long time.
Overall:  I am having a great deal of fun with this game without any mods or user-created campaigns installed and feel purchasing the game was a good use of some 'fun money'.  I am not a mod creator, so I can't speak in an educated fashion about how easy it is to produce mods and campaigns, but if the ease the designers were apparently hoping for is there, I'm excited about seeing what the community has already and will later come up with.

I got this game with minimal expectations, yet Capcom still very nearly managed to disappoint me. This game on release was, without a doubt, just not properly play-tested for the PC.
The performance issues have been fixed. Thank you, Capcom.
Fixed, but I gather some people still suffer frame stutter.
I often hear sounds coming from right beside me. Actually the foe giggling maniacally is indeed right beside me, just a floor up.
Very wonky. I've got a controller, but I prefer keyboard and mouse. Often the camera tilts in the exact opposite direction to my mouse movements, presumably because it's expecting the motion of an analog stick.
Rewards (both Campaign and Raid) place a lot of emphasis on takedowns, yet there's a snag.
As you come out of a finisher, you are instantly vulnerable. It's annoying, because the camera angles so you can't see much during the kill, and leaves you completely unprepared. Coming out of it I wish there'd be a reprieve, like momentary invulnerability. This is just a quirk I have, so feel free to dismiss it.
Mouseclicks are interchangeable with the pick up and climb keys for... some... reason. So if there happens to be a ledge or ammo nearby, be prepared to see your character climb up a ledge or vault instead of performing a finisher/melee to conserve ammo.
Raid Mode:
Hunk's Stealth skill looks to be bugged. There are times when a Revenant was still able to track me under cloak. It seems to be an AI issue, since the same happens with a decoy bottle, but it's a nice way to muck up a DLC character right off the bat. You should've tested this thoroughly, Capcom.
Campaign:
I am absolutely convinced they did not do
playtesting on release.
Objective markers will overlay anything, so you've got a giant icon hovering over the middle of your screen.
They've made an attempt at moving item icons to the side, which is a start. No idea why all the other UI elements (like the exit icon) are still completely opaque. Try shooting anything when half your screen is filled with "Elite" icons.
On top of that, Raid Mode
feels unfinished. None of the missions have level descriptions/pictures to jog your memory; just a one-line objective. You're stuck memorizing which mission number corresponds to which arena.
The folks at Capcom are releasing additional... weapon space? For a price.
I understand that there ought to be a limit on the number of weapons/parts, but paying for more storage is an odd way to conduct business. I think somewhere down the line Capcom thought RE turned into an MMO or something.
Raid Mode now has online co-op support, but you're in for long waits. Luckily, you can invite friends who own the game.
You'll only unlock all four weapon slots at higher levels, meaning you're restricted to one or two firearms until you unlock the other slots. This messes up my innate weapon-mapping. So instead of thinking that I've got my shotgun bound to a certain key, I now have to remember weapon-bindings for each and every character in Raid Mode.
It looks like this was an attempt at balancing characters' strengths, but there are better ways.
... doesn't disappoint. There are very witty jabs that tie into RE/Biohazard history. And frankly, the scripts in the RE universe are not known for wit.
I was genuinely creeped out by the endgame boss, and despite each being a single episode-long, the bonus episodes were very well done.
I'm a huge fan of this franchise, and I half-expected that Capcom botched up Moira to be yet another token throwaway character, or one that swears every five seconds. She still cusses, but her personality is likeable and there are some strong attempts at character development throughout the main campaign and bonus episodes.
I went into this game thinking that I shouldn't expect a resurgence of "old school" survival horror, that those days were long past. Yet this game does do a good job of reliving the "feel", I guess. It isn't true Survival Horror where you attempt to run by foes, and avoid fights as much as possible, but there is a pleasing homage to it.
There are definite attempts to utilize stealth and environmental hazards to minimize ammo usage. A key mechanic throughout the game requires you to focus and scavenge items you'd otherwise miss.
The powers that be have decided to be very merciful. There is limited space and an abundance of everything, so it helps that you can combine items even if the components are on different characters.
Same as the first RE:Revelations. ThankyouThankyouThankyou.

My internet was fine, but an in-game notification stating "network connection was lost" paused my game, and I feared the worst. Luckily, the game still allows you to play on after dismissing the warning. Aw, Capcom, you're so considerate (Now please stop charging for extra parts' space).

Casual player review follows...
Length of gameplay in this game is somewhere around ~15 hours and in addition to that, it is not difficult game to beat at all. That doesn't sound like positive introduction, but don't get me wrong and continue reading. Because these two facts are very positive in this case.
I have been waiting for this game to release since first announcement. I was very excited as I am fan of south park series since it's early seasons. My expectations were set very high. I was wondering and thinking if and how the developers will be able to fill the game with the feeling we have when watching TV series. After some time and some more announcements game was released with price set to 50 USD price level. I was convinced to buy the game just after the release - but I did some research about game performance, because I have been using mainly my notebook (with integrated graphic and i5 processor), and other users' experience was rather discouraging. I cowardly stepped back and waited for sale. And I was wrong - the game worked really flawlessly on my notebook (i5, 4gb ram, 7200rpm hdd). Now I think it was mistake.
The game is basically adventure with RPG elements and turn-based battle. At beginning you would be surprised by easy difficulty, especially in battles, and you would expect to rise during gameplay. You would be surprised how horribly wrong you were. The game is piece of cake, I would say that even 5 y/o child would beat the game without *cereal* problems. But I suspect that it was originally meant to be that way. As the south park graphic design invokes, that series are for child, game feels the same way. It's just feeling again, the story in the game is twisting like roller coaster from start to end. And it is vulgar and explicit, I don't want to spoiler too much, so just few examples -> hailing nazi zombies, explicit sexual scene (very very great idea in that particular case), abortions and of course alien abduction with everything what it means. As Randy would say - "That's the price for living in mountain village, but traffic is good".
The game is simple and amazing. It has just one little flaw - battles. Battles with new enemies are entertaining, but if you do few encounters with same types of enemies, you will be flustrated a bit. If game would contain half the battles it would be 10/10. It is not, still it is one of the best south park episodes and in fact it is probably the first south park movie.
Recommended if you are any kind of player and if you like south park.

Duck. Did I say duck ? Yeah, because that's what the game feels like. Wibbly wobbly duckin' duck. Whoever enters this place, leave here all your preconceived ideas about what games are, along with your definition of logic. Might as well put your sanity in a box and kick it goodbye until you finish Antichamber.  That's what I did after 10 minutes, and it felt great. For the 5 hours it lasted, I enjoyed being toyed around by an unending flow of pseudo-philosophical panels, a weird mix of portal-like puzzles and weird thingies, made of cubes, eyes and colors. I came sceptical, I shouldn't have. I came thinking forward is forward, that up is up, and that I was smart.
Turns out I was wrong.
So, what is Antichamber ? Definitely not a game that'll make you laugh. Definitely not a game that'll make you feel accomplished. Hell, I don't even know if I can call it a game. But if you are willing to
try something new, something that will challenge everything you know, then go forward. You won't understand everything. You won't like everything. You probably won't play more than 30mn at a time. But this is probably one of the only game I've ever played that I will remember, not because of it's gameplay, but because of it's meaning and contents.
What are you waiting for ?

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is without question one of the best turn-based tactical games I have played.  It blurs the genres of strategy games and tactical role playing games beautifully.  I like to think of it as a modern, sci-fi counterpart to such turn based classics like Final Fantasy Tactics, Jagged Alliance, and even the earlier XCOM games.
What makes this game work for me is the feel, and polish, along with great combat design.  Sure the actual story is kinda goofy, but the game never takes itself seriously, except when it comes down to combat.  The turn-based system is good, the cover system is excellent, and the class diversification allows you to play a given mission your own way.
Permadeath is glorious in this game, as you become attached to your assaults, supports, heavies, snipers (and psionics).  When one of them gets critically hit and killed, they are gone forever - at least there is an in game memorial for your fallen soldiers.  The reasearch and technology upgrades are wonderful, and the worldwide panic increases will keep YOU in a constant state of panic.

This game is too good. The developers really thought of everything.
Items are easy to find, crafting is a simple system which only requires finding the plethora of materials around the city, and zombies actually take some time and thought to kill (good luck if you get stuck in a group of them). The quests are fun but you can spend hours just running around and never do them, finding plenty of other stuff to open, save, or scavenge.
Co-op is very smooth with drop in/drop out features. When you're in a game hosted by your friend and he/she leaves the game never ends, continuing your missions exactly where you're at. You can join a game in which players are farther behind you and your inventory stays updated regardless of the game you're in. IMO one of the best game mechanics is the instant, fast travel that is optional whenever someone activates a quest or elevator, making it easy to move on without having to run all the way to your coop buddy.
Get this game and get it now.

Shadowrun Returns is a decent CRPG that has definite bona fides back to the isometric giants of ages past.  The content is well written and fits the universe it's set in.  The combat is fun, if a bit less than challenging and less common then you'd hope.
The game does feel a bit "on rails", however, especially when compared to the games it harkens back to.  This isn't the utter gigantism of something like Baldur's Gate.  The game is pretty small, the party options are limited (you only get to allocate stats and alter the inventory of the main character, for example).
I bought SRR during the steam summer sale.  It was worth the $3.50, easily.  I'm hoping to discover a lot of additional content in the workshop.

Look, the game is a great re-do walk down memory lane...  I haven't purchased it yet but there is some DLC which is supposed to be incredible.  I will likely pick that up soon enough.
Until then, I will play through Enemy Unknown a few times to find out if I can pull it off with more efficiency.  What becomes apparent though is the game is pretty linear.
There are two types of gameplay; tactical turn based and a roleplaying base building portion.  Within the tactical I found a couple issues right off the bat that, while not a real detriment to gameplay, which annoyed me.  The aliens a set and stationary until you stumble upon them.  There is no feeling that they are running around causing a ruckus.  You move your units up far enough and the aliens were standing there in a group of three.  They scatter behind cover and you kill them, that’s it.  Be patient and you can easily clear a map.  The other issue I have is the old XCOM gave you additional options while in tactical combat.  Specifically a stance choice (stand, kneel, and prone) which offered bonuses of one sort or another.  In Enemy Unknown unless you end your turn with all of your squad behind cover you can find that one unit not fast enough is dead before your next turn.
Within the roleplaying base build portion there are some cool ideas in place.  Those become apparent quickly with some research and power resources.   My only gripe is you can’t zoom into specific departments to watch what the people are doing in there.  This is minor but I was curious.  I wanted to look into the barracks and see my solders pumping iron or see my scientists screwing around with beakers or something.  Again, not a serious point to take into consideration.
Overall I enjoy this game.  For how long will I continue to play though would be a good question.  If you played the original and would like to reminisce with a good attempt this game is not a bad purchase.  Buy it on sale though so you feel like you’re getting deal.

Faerie Solitaire is an excellent card game.  It is played much like the traditional game TriPeaks but with the added excitement of a story line.  The other big difference between TriPeaks and Faerie Solitaire is that Faerie Solitaire has different card layouts for each hand and level.  as the player progresses through the game there are different kinds of challenge cards that require special cards to be used before other cards are revealed.  This adds a fun challenge to the upper levels.  In addition to the clearing of the cards, to progress though the story line the player must also meet certain  goals such as, get an 8 card streak and earn $2000, these goals must be met during one or more hands in a level to release the faerie at the end of the level.  There are also fun upgrades and pets you can earn and level up.
This is also an excellent starter game for Steam, a player new to Steam is quickly introduced to achievements and playing cards.

Edit: Alright so having finished all four episodes now, I can safely say I wouldn't recommend this game. A lot of people have been hailing this as a return to for for Resident Evil...as the best title since 4. I....do not see that at all. While not as action heavy as 5 and 6, it still is a far cry from the "heavy on the atmosphere and tension" days of old.
-As I mention above, this game has some really terrible dialog. Some have defended it, saying that the series has always had terrible writing, which I still say is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t claim. While the dialog in the series has never been award winning by any means, the only game to truely have god awful dialog was the very first Resident Evil. 20 years ago. Even then, characters weren't acting like they were straight out of Lethal Weapon, Die Hard or some other ish. They constantly (and I do mean constantly) crack wise about their circumstances, spouting horrible one liners and psuedo-badass quips every few feet. This might not have been THAT bad if the story didn't try to make you take it seriously. They'll act one way in in cutscenes, then in-game act the complete opposite. I feel there's no real consistency to any of them. There's one point where one particular character receives what should be devastating news, soul crushing stuff and they don't even really react accordingly. Hell, not even two minutes later they're back to yelling B-movie action hero lines. It doesn't mesh at all.
-As for the story....It rips so much from Code Veronica yet still ends up being nowhere near as interesting. Characters are half baked (if even that much), the antagonist is boring compared to the Ashfords (really compared to almost anything), and the 'twist' in the final episode seems to set up yet another horrific story failure in later installments.
-Enemy design I found to be really bland, save for the final boss, who looked truly disturbing.
-Environments too felt bland. Nothing stood out at all. Well, nothing outside of the overwhelming amounts of brown and grey
So uh...yeah that's it. Another bad Resident Evil. Yay!

I love scary, intriguing innovative FPS/TPS games. Of course, it's not that easy to get spooked for me.

If you like games that have great story, very innovative and non-linearly behaving enemies that will surprise you sneaking around to get to you. When you like shooting scary, disgusting, mutated monstrosities coming at you and not being able to just "shoot them up" in a blind rage - but having to precisely target them. And each enemy needs a different tactic + you need to utilize your choice of 4 guns throughout the game to the fullest - then this is a game for you. It also has some really cool - and usually interrupted by tons of enemies... logical puzzles to solve tho most of them aren't that tough to crack.
I rarely have time to play these days. But this game was a beautiful - PTSD inducing experience to me, so I consider it time well spent. Yes, it was so good I was ending some sessions of it in sweat and tired as after a workout. It was soo scary that at times I was just telling myself "It's ok... just skip it for tonight... will help you sleep better".
I repeat - this is a great game!
Tip:
Two things you might want to keep in mind, since I realized them very late in the game and wish someone told me.
1 - Telekinesis... you can not only pull and swing and hold objects. But if you press fire button while holding something - you can shoot it forward.
2 - Green item boxes - YES you CAN open those. By stomping on them (sometimes there's enemy inside, but rare). So keep that in mind esp when you're playing on Hard. I did and realized it only at second to last chapter...

I am not normally a big fan of puzzle games, but Antichamber has a rightful spot among the few that I enjoy.
It starts off with challenging preconceived notions of how a 3D game in the ego perspective works, and continues to exercise your brain with unusual problem solving. There are often multiple ways to go about solving something, and only later will you realize how easy something could have been if you had thought of it. While there is SOME timed jumping to test your reflexes, it's a very minor aspect of the game. Often the game will surprise you with unexpected behaviour like falling because you looked downwards, or falling off a platform being the actual way to progress, but there are always rules behind everything.
The stylized graphics might be minimalistic and have some occasional black jitter where there should be only a white wall, but they serve to not distract you from the puzzles.
If you ever liked any 3D puzzle game and have some hours to spare, give this game a try.

Pretty fun game!  It is a very basic RPG style turn based gameplay.  You level up, collect gear, and modify the gear.  Use misc power up items through the game to heal status/health/mana/pp.
The bad guys and bosses level up as you level up.  So you cannot over level up... or at least I think you cannot.
You get "special magic" attacks and special upgrades that unlock previous unreachable areas.  The game rewards you with humor or items for being curious.
That being said... its all in the Southpark Universe.   So the story goes through some of the memorable and strange places from the Cartoon Series, but not the favs... just the memorable.
I did however find it quite easy... the only time I died was on Al Gore and it was because I thought I was doing something wrong and trying to "save" him; but that was because the dialog was odd and made it seem like there might be a secret way to do it.
Anyway ~ I totally recommend it if you like old school turn based RPG's and South Park.

On the surface, this game doesn't have much to boast: it's mostly in black and white, and the graphics are far from optimized, which can actually cause motion sickness. However, once you get into the game you're in for hours of entertainment and mind-bending puzzles. You'll encounter situations that would otherwise occur only in an M. C. Escher painting, and the first casualty of the game will be your basic sense of geometric logic. Your mind will twist in a way that puts even Portal to shame, that you can't help but wonder in amazement how the developers even got the engine to behave like they wanted it to. And when you do finally end up solving the puzzles, the sense of accomplishment you get from it is like almost nothing else.
If you don't have this game in your Steam Library, you should fix that problem ASAP, because this game really is that fun. It has an extremely simple control scheme, but the game is so complex and deep that it definitely beats many other titles out there.

Every game is its own world, with its own laws and rules which you, the gamer, must abide by. These are programmed into the code. Things like the direction and strength of gravity, how fast you can move, what sort of interactions you can have with the environment. Often, these rules are made to be as close to reality as possible. This allows the developers to avoid having to teach you how to play in their game, it comes naturally. Most games do not need to spell out these rules, they are implicit.
Antichamber does not play by our rules. Space can change and warp, object can be perceived differently depending on how you look at them. The game does a great job of introducing you to each of its new mind-bending rules, but never explicitly. The map is open for you to explore, gently guided by new knowledge of the quirks of this alternate reality.
Some of the puzzles are tough, especially if you just don't "get it". This wasn't a game I could just sit down and play for hours. I often got stuck and had to wait for inspiration to strike. Don't use a guide though, that feeling of solving each puzzle is great.
A game for fans of Portal or Quantum Conundrum, where the rules are made to be broken. Except this game takes it to a different level. No rule is safe, no law is true, and you can’t always trust what you see...

Look, the game is a great re-do walk down memory lane...  I haven't purchased it yet but there is some DLC which is supposed to be incredible.  I will likely pick that up soon enough.
Until then, I will play through Enemy Unknown a few times to find out if I can pull it off with more efficiency.  What becomes apparent though is the game is pretty linear.
There are two types of gameplay; tactical turn based and a roleplaying base building portion.  Within the tactical I found a couple issues right off the bat that, while not a real detriment to gameplay, which annoyed me.  The aliens a set and stationary until you stumble upon them.  There is no feeling that they are running around causing a ruckus.  You move your units up far enough and the aliens were standing there in a group of three.  They scatter behind cover and you kill them, that’s it.  Be patient and you can easily clear a map.  The other issue I have is the old XCOM gave you additional options while in tactical combat.  Specifically a stance choice (stand, kneel, and prone) which offered bonuses of one sort or another.  In Enemy Unknown unless you end your turn with all of your squad behind cover you can find that one unit not fast enough is dead before your next turn.
Within the roleplaying base build portion there are some cool ideas in place.  Those become apparent quickly with some research and power resources.   My only gripe is you can’t zoom into specific departments to watch what the people are doing in there.  This is minor but I was curious.  I wanted to look into the barracks and see my solders pumping iron or see my scientists screwing around with beakers or something.  Again, not a serious point to take into consideration.
Overall I enjoy this game.  For how long will I continue to play though would be a good question.  If you played the original and would like to reminisce with a good attempt this game is not a bad purchase.  Buy it on sale though so you feel like you’re getting deal.

I'll start out by saying that I have a very limited experience with Turn Based games, and had absolutely no experience with Shadowrun before Shadowrun Returns.
With that in mind, I may overlook lots of aspects that you find very important if you're more experienced than I am. Here are my thoughts nonetheless.
The whole world of Shadowrun Returns sounded really interesting to me, as I like futuristic societies in general, and I don't think it's been done a whole lot in videogames, lately. And having heard good things about the game, I decided to give it a go.
This is almost an RPG engine, in the world of Shadowrun. You'll have a short and very linear campaign, with a lot of dialogue, decent amount of combat, but not a lot of depth, mechanically. The depth is there, certainly, but I don't feel like it was explored at all with the main campaign. However, it comes with Steam Workshop and a level editor! Which means that user generated content will keep coming, and I have no doubt some talented people will manage to create much more interesting stories than the one told here, and even explore the mechanics far better.
Let's talk about presentation.
The
look awesome, in my opinion! And it's one of the aspects that pushed me to buy the game. Everything is
. I made the mistake of not using AA (I don't know why) and the characters looked a bit too bad to me, but I later saw my mistake, and they actually look much better, and certainly fit with the scenery.
In addition to the hand-drawn style, there are shadows and lightning, that complement it pretty well, and give it a more modern feel.
It reminded me of a more modern Bastion, actually, which is always good. Not much to complain here, I'd say, it looks great!
The
was pretty good as well! It changed seemlessly, and had a good futuristic, oppressive feel to it. Nothing groundbreaking, but I liked it.
The
was a bit clunky, probably because the game was on iOS as well. More clicks than it needed, and too few hotkeys.
Regarding the main campaign, the story was good enough, in my opinion, but a bit too limited. It was very narrow, with no significant choices at all, and barely any sidequests. Besides being very linear, it was also much shorter than I expected, and left much to be desired. half of the game's mechanics were left on the side.
It was mostly story-combat-story-combat-etc. Between each mission, you're sent into your Hub area, a bar, and you can buy new equipment there, buy spells, consumables, etc. And also learn more about the world and the characters by talking to them, and learning more about their purpose and role in Shadowrun. Before going into a mission, you also had the choice of choosing 2-3 partners to help you in battle, for a price. These had very varied classes to choose from, each with its uses, but overall, I didn't feel like I needed most of them. And some were really useless... didn't feel very well balanced.
Its purpose was mainly to give you more freedom regarding your own character progression, by giving you a chance of having every skill that you needed. For that, I think it worked well.
The
was enjoyable, overall, but I don't think it was very unique. You had action points to spend with movement, skills and attacks, of which you gained more with time. It's turn based, with a cover system, and also a hit/miss chance. Which was what I found pretty bad, to be honest.
It was everything but reliable, and it screwed me over more times than I felt like it should. It also helped me, but overall, it was not satisfying at all. This problem can be sort of avoided by using buffs regarding accuracy, but it still felt a bit cheap, at times. I would have liked the game to be harder, but more strategic and reliable. It's not like it only screwed me once or twice, it happened way too often. I didn't like the
of it, but overall, it was good.
The characters' synergies were good, I liked that aspect regarding the combat.
The inventory system was also a bit too limited. You could only manage it before each mission, without an opportunity of trading with other team members, or looting corpses. The rooms in the levels seemed fairly open, but there was very little to it, actually. Barely anything to collect, and not much backstory spread out.
Another aspect that isn't very good, but can most likely be solved by the community!
Now, with my biggest problem with the game. The character progression, classes, and the lack of information.
Right from the beginning, you choose a few traits and a class, of which you know absolutely nothing about. You are free to choose whatever you want (including a classless option, if you know what you're doing), but it's also very easy to screw it up.
The games does no effort at all in teaching you about each class, and how you should build one. You're simply thrown into the wolves, and have to deal with it the best way you can.
I'll admit that my character was probably useless. I focused my attention in two things at once, one of which was pretty much useless, leaving the other one half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I can tell you that it didn't feel satisfying at all. There was also no respecialization that I've heard of, so I had to stick with it.
There was also an aspect of choosing cybernetics, or magic, which was barely mentioned, and didn't feel in any way relevant.
Equipment followed the same path, being very limited, and having almost no variation. No interesting side-grades, or anything.
Consumables and drugs were also present in the game, but I had absolutely no need to use them, except for grenades (for AOE) and healing.
And I was playing on Hard Mode. It was challenging at the beginning (due to bad character progression, and choosing the wrong support team mates), but it was overcome after a few hours, and experimenting with the different setups.
It did a really bad way of teaching the mechanics to the player, and an even worse job at taking advantage of them. But I feel like much better campaigns can be done with the engine, and I'll probably spend a lot more time browsing through the UGContent, and maybe even try my luck with it.

Well, what can I really say that hasn't already been said by numerous critics and player reviews?  I'm not sure I'll break any new ground here, but this game deserves every word of praise it's received, so I have no qualms adding to it.
In a nutshell, graphics are perfect to the intent, the music is well constructed and implemented, voice acting is spot on, and combat is fun, but easy to exploit so could become repetitive.
It's the script and execution though, that really bring it all together.  If anyone were to ask me to point to a game that exemplified the right way to make a show or movie into a game, I would point to this as the ultimate.  I won't go into the story, but this game not only felt completely true to the series, but playing was almost totally immersive, with the town of South Park truly feeling like a living, breathing entity you were visiting.  Granted, some of the "random dialoge" people around town would throw out would become old, but within the scope of the universe they were creating, it wasn't a detractor.  Even the moments where characters would breach the 4th wall served more to involve me further in the world  than remind me I was playing a game.
If you are a fan of South Park in any capacity, I can almost guarantee you'll like this game.  If you hate all things RPG-related, it may not be your deal, but I'd venture to say that if you enjoy the former but not the latter, you'll still be wildly entertained by the content, if not the play style.
The only caveat which I think deserves some mention in any review here, is that they definitely go above and beyond in terms of trying to offend or create uncomfortable situations.  I loved every moment, but I do know a few fans of the show who thought one or two scenarios were "a bit much".
Finally, it's a little shorter than many contemporary, big-budget RPG's out there - I took 20 hours to beat it, and a majority of the side-quests.  That said, I would still say it's worth every penny of it's price tag even at full price.  The care taken by Tray and Matt to ensure that this was a faithful, and enjoyable representation of their intellectual property, deserves reward if we want to see more of this type of quality material.
At the end, I was satisfied, but definitely left with a strong desire for the experience and fun to continue.  When it comes down to it though, isn't that the way any great story should leave you?

Game: Faerie Solitaire
Genre: Puzzle
Developer: Subsoap
System: Steam (PC)
Total Score: 76/100
Value Score: 7.6/10
• Story: 7/10
o Basically a story involving a character who goes on a journey in a mysterious world. The game continues the storyline as you go through the levels in a artistic view of the surrounding world of the game.
• Characters: 5/10
o Basically there are a few characters, your character whose identity isnt even known or a focal point, a bunch of faeries who play different roles and make an appearance in the storyline and your pets you can collect and grow.
• GamePlay: 8/10
o Basically the game is like Solitaire except you can do all sorts of tricks and be encountering certain obstacles which can be destroyed by attempting certain combos. Each level and stage has a unique goal or requirement such as completing a level in a amount of time, having a certain number of combos or making enough money. At the end of each stage you gain a bit of money from you gained during gameplay and as a extra bonus. You can use these extra amounts of money to purchase different abilities and locations - along with the money you also receive or find items during the gameplay which you can use to feed your pet and thus make them stronger.
• Graphics: 7/10
o The game has a unique art style but pretty much any PC should be able to run this game. Very basic visual design more like a art book. The storyline is depicted through the fancy artwork and the animations within the gameplay and the menus are well done.
• Sound: 8/10
o The sound effects are like what you would expect in a fairy tale type of setting of a story. The usual magical incantation sound effects and etc. The sounds are actually well done.
• Music: 7/10
o For each level there's a different track used which plays a soothing calm song representing the stage's environment. The game's menu music is well done, nothing special with the entire OST but it is a nice departure from what you would hear from the usual games as this game's OST fits well with its casual feel.
• Length: 8/10
o There are several levels and stages with about over 8 chapters with several stages. Going through them and playing the game of solitaire may take you a while - each play should take you about anywhere between 5-10 minutes depending on the number of cards and obstacles.
• Replay Value: 9/10
o Although there are specific obstacles in each stage the number of cards and which cards are stacked are always different so each time you play any level in any stage it is always different. Along with that even after you finish the game's main storyline there may be some extra items you can purchase or train more pets which will add a few more hours overall to your game time.
• Player Value: 7/10
o If you are looking for a casual game that doesnt require a lot of PC power - something to get your time by and something that is actually quite simple and can be as fun as a casual game such as regular solitaire - then this is the game for you because it adds more than regular solitaire - a unique way to play the game along with a storyline to boot along with a well fantasy like OST and overall visual design.

I am not normally a big fan of puzzle games, but Antichamber has a rightful spot among the few that I enjoy.
It starts off with challenging preconceived notions of how a 3D game in the ego perspective works, and continues to exercise your brain with unusual problem solving. There are often multiple ways to go about solving something, and only later will you realize how easy something could have been if you had thought of it. While there is SOME timed jumping to test your reflexes, it's a very minor aspect of the game. Often the game will surprise you with unexpected behaviour like falling because you looked downwards, or falling off a platform being the actual way to progress, but there are always rules behind everything.
The stylized graphics might be minimalistic and have some occasional black jitter where there should be only a white wall, but they serve to not distract you from the puzzles.
If you ever liked any 3D puzzle game and have some hours to spare, give this game a try.

On the surface, this game doesn't have much to boast: it's mostly in black and white, and the graphics are far from optimized, which can actually cause motion sickness. However, once you get into the game you're in for hours of entertainment and mind-bending puzzles. You'll encounter situations that would otherwise occur only in an M. C. Escher painting, and the first casualty of the game will be your basic sense of geometric logic. Your mind will twist in a way that puts even Portal to shame, that you can't help but wonder in amazement how the developers even got the engine to behave like they wanted it to. And when you do finally end up solving the puzzles, the sense of accomplishment you get from it is like almost nothing else.
If you don't have this game in your Steam Library, you should fix that problem ASAP, because this game really is that fun. It has an extremely simple control scheme, but the game is so complex and deep that it definitely beats many other titles out there.

It might not sound like much, but I felt it kept things interesting over playing standard solitaire. You can unlock a few power ups along the way also, which evolve the gameplay as you progress. Again, nothing drastic, but they do impact the way you play just enough. This is a casual game, so it won't provide any particularly strong challenge.
There are little objectives for each level and 30 reasonably obtainable Steam achievements, though the pet collecting ones will take a bit of time. Achievements are really the only reason to raise pets. There's really not much story to it. I can't even recall the story at the time of this writing.
Not much more to say about this. It's a fun game. A nice relaxing way to pass the time. If you like casual games and/or card games, there's plenty to like in Faerie Solitaire.

Every game is its own world, with its own laws and rules which you, the gamer, must abide by. These are programmed into the code. Things like the direction and strength of gravity, how fast you can move, what sort of interactions you can have with the environment. Often, these rules are made to be as close to reality as possible. This allows the developers to avoid having to teach you how to play in their game, it comes naturally. Most games do not need to spell out these rules, they are implicit.
Antichamber does not play by our rules. Space can change and warp, object can be perceived differently depending on how you look at them. The game does a great job of introducing you to each of its new mind-bending rules, but never explicitly. The map is open for you to explore, gently guided by new knowledge of the quirks of this alternate reality.
Some of the puzzles are tough, especially if you just don't "get it". This wasn't a game I could just sit down and play for hours. I often got stuck and had to wait for inspiration to strike. Don't use a guide though, that feeling of solving each puzzle is great.
A game for fans of Portal or Quantum Conundrum, where the rules are made to be broken. Except this game takes it to a different level. No rule is safe, no law is true, and you can’t always trust what you see...

Launch woes and potential performance problems aside, this is another excellent entry in the Arkham series by Rocksteady.
When I bought the game at launch it would not run smoothly on my dated gaming rig. Since then I have bought a new PC, and the game has been patched up a bit, so it was running at a smooth 60fps throughout with all settings maxed. Be warned, you will still need a beefy PC to pull this off.
As far as gameplay goes, it's much of the same from the previous Arkham games. Except for the Batmobile, which is foisted upon you regularly - dare I say I enjoyed the Batmobile bits for what they were worth.
The storyline certainly goes through peaks and troughs but overall it sets a captivating backdrop for all of the Bat-shenanigans and keeps you driving forward to the conclusion.
Visually, the Arkham universe has never looked better, and there's plenty to do to help you explore every nook and cranny.
Overall, the general criticisms you will read levelled toward the game itself (forgetting the technical issues) are warranted. If you consume the game in bursts you will likely not grow weary of the myriad gameplay beats and eke out many hours of Bat-joy.
Definitely a must-play for fans of the Arkham series.

Mirror's Edge is fairly maligned for it's terible shooting mechanics, bad plot and design discontinuity. Middle item aside, I think these criticisms are unfair. Where Mirror's Edge succeeds is in visual design, first-person animation, and in creating an incredible sense of momentum. You will feel it when you leap off a building, and when you crash back to earth.
The incredible sense of motion is, to me, worth all the trouble. When you get distracted, the keys can seem unresponsive and the first person camera unfair. But if you take the time to get used to the mechanics of Mirror's Edge it starts to click. You start to see the world in terms of speed, efficiency, path lengths. You don't need to use the clunky combat system anymore--you've become the ultimate running machine. It's a tough sell, for a game with this many surface flaws. And, much as I love it, I feel that a game should be better than this on is at the base of its learning curve. But once you work your way up there, the view is spectacular.
Gunplay is not a requirement. Picking up a gun and firing it a few times before dropping it to carry on running can make your life a lot easier, though, in certain levels and the shooting mechanics are designed with precisely that kind of use in mind. Further, first person platforming is Mirror's Edge's great success. There is nothing fundamentally discontinuous in that goal. It works and it works beautifully; there's just a fairly steep learning curve before the game really starts to shine. This is nothing like those awful jumping puzzles every shooter in the early 'aughts thought it needed. This is a beautiful digital encapsulation of the joy of movement.
Definitely worth a redesign/sequel and, in my view, a chance.

As of 2/27/2015, the game is mostly playable save some raid maps which slow down to a slideshow. I'm running an X4 860k paired up with a 750ti. It's really not that bad, I can usually keep 60fps running at max. I don't think the issue deserves a negative rating as I'm sure it will get patched sooner or later (optimistic). Edit: It's fixed.
The game itself is solid. However, coming from the prespective of someone who played RE6 a lot, the mechanics are a step down. I'm not sure if it's the game or just the port, but the controls seem a little rigid, especially the running and aiming. It has nuances that you have to keep in mind. Specifically, while your character is in a sprint, you have to only press forward and change direction with the mouse. If you try to move left or right with the keyboard, it will shift the camera in that direction. This wouldn't be a problem normally, but the speed it changes the view is too fast. It's minor, but having the reverse controls would have made more sense (ala RE6).
The story is typical. It has a much more "horror" feel (still not very scary, but it does get tense). The first episode is laughably short. Anybody can go through it in 3 hours at most. It almost felt like a tutorial. I'm really hoping the next episodes will be much longer.
Partner switching is back! This is the best addition, in my opinion I feel like this is neglected a lot. Claire gets Moira while Barry gets Natalia. Moira initially gets to use the flashlight which can stun enemies which allows you to either melee them, or switch to Claire to follow up with a ranged attack, you can then switch again to keep stunning the enemy. Switching back and forth is very fun, and finding ways to circumvent enemies with both characters is satisfying. Barry's Natalia takes more planning as she can throw a brick once before having to retreive another. This makes sense as the enemies you encounter in Barry's story are slower while they are faster in Claire's. This great design in play, and Capcom is not getting any recognition for it.
Raid mode, what can I say. It's fun. It's no mercenaries, though. Progress by beating missions and upgrade your skills and weapons. I'm not a fan of the weapon upgrade system, a lot of the time it feels like RNG, but at least you're never totally underpowered and having to keep up with new weapons does mix things up a bit.
I recommend the game to the Resident Evil fans. For everyone else, please know what you are getting. A solid game with a few hiccups. It's not broken like some others are making it out to be.

So I'm about 50% of the way through this game so far. Antichamber is a really good puzzle game similar to Portal, but it's definitely not for the faint-hearted. While Portal gets you to solve physics problems (e.g. ballistics, momentum and line-of-site) Antichamber breaks a lot of rules. It totes itself as a game about solving logic problems, but it really isn't because a lot of the chambers are impossible shapes (the trailer video explains better). If you walk through one door, it'll lead somewhere different if you immediately turn back. There are invisible entrances to rooms and things hidden in the dark you must find in order to progress. My first impression was "Is this acid?" The answer is no... it's meth. Digital Meth. The game is mind-melting.
It can be frustrating. There are some things that you would NEVER find unless you did a Google search. One example is a small portal hidden in a pitch black hallway (a hallway that I already found going through
hidden door i found in the dark). And what makes it worse are these teasing little sayings on the wall:
"Sometimes we find things in the place we least expect" Mmm cryptic... any chance you can shine some more light on that buddy? It's like playing canasta with the the Wachowski brothers (sorry, siblings).
"But G00CH, why would you torture yourself like that?" Because I'm an IDIOT that's why!!!
That said, Antichamber is fun to play. Would recommend for people that like really testing puzzle games. The sense of reward you get when you actually solve a chamber is great, probably because it is so difficult.

Dead Space is one of those horror games that EVERYONE should own. The entire trilogy is worth every penny spent. The first game isn't perfect. It's flawed, it has issues, it's not really scary - but it's a damn good game.
GRAPHICS: Visually, the game has aged quite a bit, but the graphics do their job. The game is every much as visceral and gory and disgusting as you could want, filled with Saw-like moments that leave you wanting to throw up.
SOUND/MUSIC: The musical score isn't too special, but it does its job. Most of the soundtrack is composed of typical horror themes that play during jump scare moments. The sound design, however, is fantastic - every monster, gun, creak and groan of the ship; all of them set you on edge. There's never a moment where you feel safe, even on the easiest difficulty with the most maxed out character you could ever create. It's simply a wonder for horror fans.
STORY: Story-wise, Dead Space is possibly one of the most unoriginal pieces ever conceived. If Ridley Scott's Alien was merely Jaws in space, then Dead Space is just Ridley Scott's Alien but with zombies. The plot is predictable, the characters on-dimensional and unlikable in every conceivable way, and the twists and turns so dull and emotionless that it makes M. Night Shyamalan look good by comparison. This game isn't really going to satisfy people searching for deep, interesting, unique lore by any stretch, but it's good enough to compel you to complete the game.
GAMEPLAY: This is where the game flops - or at least, the PC version does. I played Dead Space on the Xbox 360 long before I had a functioning PC that could run anything more demanding than Solitare, and even then, the gameplay was clunky, but it at least worked. The PC version seems like it wasn't tested at all. The mouse and keyboard controls are abysmal and practically broken. The aiming in particular is so bugged that it's nearly impossible to hit your targets without wasting half of your ammo, and when it comes to the Dead Space formula (shoot off the limbs) that requires precision, it's absolutely ludicrous that the developers would skimp out on testing the most important part of the game. The Dead Space franchise has always had stellar gameplay: there's no hud, leaving you to see your health meter, ammo, and other such important pieces of information on your guns or armour. The gameplay consists of strategically shooting the limbs off of your opponents, and it's a blast to play, but even when I plug my Xbox controller into my PC, the port simply barely works. I've played this game for years, and can't even begin to count the amount of unnecessary deaths I've experienced on the PC port due to bad controls that hindered my ability to aim. The sad part is, I TRULY love this game, but with controls that are so dysfunctional, I doubt that I'll ever pick it up on my PC again.
I wish there was an in-between rating, because the game is DEFINITELY worth playing, but people should be warned about the bad controls. Overall, if you can find a series of mods that will keep you from destroying your PC from the rage that this game will put you through due to the devs refusing to test it out, then you should DEFINITELY buy it.

One of the best sci-fi horror games out there. Amazing ambience, story and gameplay. This is the game equivalent of the first Alien movie.
The story puts you on a mining station "Ishimura" after responding to a distress call. On arrival you and your two crew mates crash land on the station and find out that the station is overrun by creatures called necromorhps. It is up to you to figure out what's exactly going on at the station, find your girlfriend who was stationed there and get out.
The story is quite interesting and takes through the different parts of the ships where you gather bits and pieces to solving the mystery of what exactly happened. Takes quite a while to go thrugh all the chapters but it's engaging, interesting and at no point repetitive.
Graphics still hold up very nicely - the level design is very nice and there are just a few areas you will re-visit. The audio layer is amazing and gives a lot to the ambience. The thumps in the air ducts, the humming of machines and the echo of your footsteps. Makes your hair stand up.
As far as mechanics go - this is somewhat of a 3rd person shooter but the array of weapons and the way you fight the enemies is not from a standard shooter. Most of the weapons are energy weapons each with its own distinguish ammunition. The way you use them against the necromorphs is you need to cut off their limbs rather than going for the classical headshots. This makes for a very interesting mechanic where the first thing you aim at are the legs - at least for the most enemies.
Additionally you get a stasis power which lets you slow down the enemies affected by the stasis field which comes in handy with a bigger amount of enemies. There is a couple of different enemy types and most of them differ significantly from each other requiring a bit different approach which is really nice.
The only problem I've had is that you can tell that the game was designed for console. And the sensitivity on the mouse changes when you go into aim mode and feels a bit sluggish. But its not very hard to get used to it and enjoy this great game.

HL2 has been in my Queue for a long, long time. And, after playing through it I have two things to say: "What a ride," and "Why did I wait so long to play this game?" I now understand the hype. I get it. People talk about it all of the time even more than 10 years after its initial release for one simple reason:
It's a
good game.
I'm not usually not into Shooters, First Person or otherwise. But something about this game is just so... thrilling. It's not quite a horror shooter by today's standards (though, I'm sure when it was released, it had people screaming and flailing), but there are so many pulse pounding, heart racing, gut wrenching moments that it cannot be ignored. The artistry and, often times, very subtle ways of making the player feel exactly what the game wants him to feel. Spoiler:

Everything about this game is perfect. Well… Almost.
I found myself backtracking out of desperation. Almost constantly. I was never entirely sure of where I was going a good 70-75% of the time. I would be fine with this, if the NPCs didn’t all believe that I had an extensive knowledge of a place (well, many places) that I had never seen before. Sure, at checkpoints, there are sometimes maps on the wall, but they are poorly done and show no real indication of where you are actually going. Now, I’m not a big fan of the Fable 3 glowing-trail-that-shows-you-right-where-you-are-supposed-to-go method of leading a player, or even a compass on the HUD that points you in the right direction. But, I mean, come on, how many more lines of code would it have taken to give me a map I could access on the fly? I didn’t really need a “you are here” button on it, and it didn’t need to be interactive. Just a little something to keep me sane.
But, even the sometimes confusing level design can be forgiven. It’s just another way of making the player feel hopeless and helpless. Most games take too kindly to funneling players along the story so much that it feels like the gameplay is interfering with the game. I’m looking at you Final Hallway 13. But that is something that HL2 just doesn’t do. It makes the player, once the actually accomplish something, feel like they did something meaningful.
One last thing and I swear I’ll shut up. How great is the way HL2 introduces you to new enemies? I’ll tell ya how great! It introduces enemies in a very “Mega Man” way. You almost always can see what new enemy you will be fighting before you actually have to engage that enemy. And, sometimes, you can actually SEE its attack patterns. This is done with
and almost every single concept of gameplay. It’s CRAZY! Crazy like a
fox. This is how games
be designed. As a player, I never once felt overwhelmed by a new concept or enemy. Sure I had a lot of “OMG, that guy is spooky,” or “That was a lot tougher than expected,” or “I’m supposed to
that jump?!” and, let’s not forget all of the “Gosh Dang-oh-Darn, that puzzle was the most convoluted thing I have ever seen,” moments. But I never once got overwhelmed by something. Stuck a few times, yes, but never felt like I COULDN’T progress.
The main takeaway is this: If Half-Life 2 isn’t already in your inventory, you should fix that. It really is a problem. But, if you are going to go ahead and get it,
just shell out the ten extra bucks for the Orange Box. Because you WILL want Episode One and Episode Two. And also Portal. ^_^ Basically, you’ll get HL2 and HL2:E1 and get HL2:E2, Portal, and TF2,
free. It’s a great deal.
Tl;dr—8.5/10, Want map, crazy awesome game design in general, Orange Box get.
Thanks for your time and buckle up for the ride that is HL2.

Launch woes and potential performance problems aside, this is another excellent entry in the Arkham series by Rocksteady.
When I bought the game at launch it would not run smoothly on my dated gaming rig. Since then I have bought a new PC, and the game has been patched up a bit, so it was running at a smooth 60fps throughout with all settings maxed. Be warned, you will still need a beefy PC to pull this off.
As far as gameplay goes, it's much of the same from the previous Arkham games. Except for the Batmobile, which is foisted upon you regularly - dare I say I enjoyed the Batmobile bits for what they were worth.
The storyline certainly goes through peaks and troughs but overall it sets a captivating backdrop for all of the Bat-shenanigans and keeps you driving forward to the conclusion.
Visually, the Arkham universe has never looked better, and there's plenty to do to help you explore every nook and cranny.
Overall, the general criticisms you will read levelled toward the game itself (forgetting the technical issues) are warranted. If you consume the game in bursts you will likely not grow weary of the myriad gameplay beats and eke out many hours of Bat-joy.
Definitely a must-play for fans of the Arkham series.

Liked: - Raid Mode is still fun!

Disliked: - WAY TOO MANY BUGS!!!!!!!!
- No offline coop for the PC version.
- It's an episodic game (seriously whoever thought that was a good idea for Resident Evil should think twice before making another game).
- Claire is....different somehow.  She's still a bad♥♥♥♥♥but her attitude and personality is different (also the new voice aint bad but I realy wish the Degeneration voice actor was her voice actor in this game).
- Game is WAY TOO ACTION ORIENTED.  Not once did I fear I was gonna run out of ammunition and the stealth gameplay should not of been there.  The stealth on its own is fine but it makes the game far too easy and helps in saving ammo that you already have too much of to begin with.

I purchased this on Saturday November 19th, 2016.
Not sure why everyone is complaining about the game honestly. It's a sequel, not a reskin of the original.
While I do have fond memories and many hours in the original I'm expecting new things from this game. And from what I've seen they've been delivered. I'm only really disappointed about the map variety and would personally love reskins of all of the old maps. I would also love to be able to transfer my rare costumes from KF1 that I achieved through doing Halloween Achievements.
Pros:
- Great Graphics
- Excellent Gameplay
- Guns feel great
- Medic has been improved
- Kiting Patty around the entire map is still possible
- The gore is superb
- New character skins
- Added vanity skins
Cons:
- Soundtrack isn't as good as KF1
- Zed spawn locations seem a little weird (spawning only where the large group of players are)
- Old maps were better
- I actually miss the old trader
- KF1 medic weapons were better
A lot of people are saying that there aren't enough maps. The bulk of the KF1 maps were added over time. They didn't just appear there over night. I'd expect more maps to be added in the future through events. That said I would love to see all of the old KF1 maps redone and re-released. I know there are a few mods for maps like offices or west london, but I'd like to see them all. Maps like Foundry (my favourite), Mountain Pass, Biotic Labs, Abusement Park, etc.
People are complaining about a cash shop. I hate to break your bubble but KF1 had numerous items that were available through dlc. These were mostly weapon skins and character skins. i.e. News flash this isn't anything new. A snazzy character skin or a sleek weapon skin isn't going to change how you experience the game.
Do I like Killing Floor 1 more? Yes, without a doubt it is one of my favourite games.
Does that mean that this game isn't good? No, of course not.
I think a lot of people are complaining just to complain. At least this isn't NMS.

RER2 is a terrible port. It's poorly optimized to the extent that I doubt the "minimum requirements" are truly enough to run it, and the coop doesn't work. HOWEVER, as a game, RER2 is everything I wanted it to be. Hell, it's everything I wanted Resident Evil 5 & 6 to be; genuinely atmospheric in single-player, with companions that don't waste ammo by default and who won't need you to save them every ten seconds. I've yet to encounter any QTE sections, and as I only play keyboard this is a huge plus. I even like that you can switch between your useful (carries gun) and not-so useful (uses melee weapon/carries flashlight/fits in tight spaces) characters at will, and that anyone who plays single-player is forced to do so if you want to find half the ammo in a level. For the first time in a Resident Evil game I found myself genuinely desperate for more bullets, and it's actually kinda fun (anyone who struggled to keep enough ammo in RE4 may have less fun).
Raid mode, the thing you do after you beat story mode, has been giving some people problems. However, aside from the occasional frame drop, I've found Raid mode to be a highly playable variation on the hoard mode formula. You'll encounter specialized/modified monsters, unlock weapons, and earn cash and experience to put toward a character upgrade system (there's a similar skill system in single-player, but there doesn't seem to be any overlap between the two).
RAID MODE FEATURES MICROTRANSACTIONS, but the things you can buy appear to be mostly meaningless: gems that allow you to continue a Raid mission without losing any found items or progress, and extra guns and parts. RAID MODE LOCKS ELEMENTS OF GUN/UPGRADE STORAGE AS DLC, which is sad, but you are free to sell any weapons/upgrades you don't want/need.
Does releasing a bad port and sticking in microtransactions make Capcom a huge corporate ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥? Yes. Do I regret my purchase? Not at all.
Buy if you like Resident Evil.

GTA Vice City takes place in in Vice city, in the year of 1986, and we Play as a mob named Tommy Vercetti, that just after getting out of prison, got in a drug deal for his crime family that goes wrong, and now he owes them lots of money.
+ Vice city is a great, beautiful city to get lost in, the sun, beaches, bikinis, roller blades, neon lights, everything just screams the 80's.
+ Good graphics for the time (looks dated now, but tolerable)
+ Great gameplay for the time
+ Good arcade driving physics
+ Different outfits were introduced
+ Has Cars, bikes, boats, helicopters and a plane
+ Motorbikes, Helicopters and a Plane (1 sea plane ) were introduced and are very fun to use
+ Great story, with many references to 80's movies, with a heavy influence from Miami vice and Scarface.
+ Tommy Vercetti is badass
+ The open world, now considered small, felt very big at the time, with around twice the area of GTA III
+ Good selection of weapons
+ One of the best soundtracks of the whole series, with MANY awesome 80's hits
+ Huge mod community

Everyone should have a puzzle game like this in their library. One of the best puzzlers I've ever played, up there with Fez and Braid. This one hits a far different note though, as it is a wide open world with little to no explanation of anything. It truly captures the essence of puzzling around, trying to find out what does what on your own, while still keeping a great pace. The game quickly breaks the illusion of logic physical space, which results in a world bound together in a weird and intriguing fashion. Falling down this pit might send you to this place, while going down the stairs in the next room sends you somewhere completely different. At first it's confusing, but once you start to accept the idea, it makes the world far more interconnected and ensures that you don't feel stuck nearly as often. Once you start learning the different mechanics, you can suddenly figure out the puzzles that had you stuck earlier, which gives a great sense of accomplishment, proving that you don't need achievements to reward the player! Each time you get a new tool, you suddenly get flashbacks to the annoying places you couldn't get pass, and you instantly want to go back and destroy that puzzle with your new best (and only) friend. A game with great exploration AND superb puzzles; it's really a no-brainer.
Anyone who haven't played this and have even the slightest interest in puzzles ought to buy this as soon as possible. The price might be a bit steep for a 5-10 hour puzzler, but it's a great experience, and you could always pick it up during a sale ;)

Risk of Rain... This is one of my favorite games, it has tons of replayability through its many completly different characters, different difficulties, and unlockable gamplay tweaks.
