HL2 has been in my Queue for a long, long time. And, after playing through it I have two things to say: "What a ride," and "Why did I wait so long to play this game?" I now understand the hype. I get it. People talk about it all of the time even more than 10 years after its initial release for one simple reason:
It's a
good game.
I'm not usually not into Shooters, First Person or otherwise. But something about this game is just so... thrilling. It's not quite a horror shooter by today's standards (though, I'm sure when it was released, it had people screaming and flailing), but there are so many pulse pounding, heart racing, gut wrenching moments that it cannot be ignored. The artistry and, often times, very subtle ways of making the player feel exactly what the game wants him to feel. Spoiler:

Everything about this game is perfect. Well… Almost.
I found myself backtracking out of desperation. Almost constantly. I was never entirely sure of where I was going a good 70-75% of the time. I would be fine with this, if the NPCs didn’t all believe that I had an extensive knowledge of a place (well, many places) that I had never seen before. Sure, at checkpoints, there are sometimes maps on the wall, but they are poorly done and show no real indication of where you are actually going. Now, I’m not a big fan of the Fable 3 glowing-trail-that-shows-you-right-where-you-are-supposed-to-go method of leading a player, or even a compass on the HUD that points you in the right direction. But, I mean, come on, how many more lines of code would it have taken to give me a map I could access on the fly? I didn’t really need a “you are here” button on it, and it didn’t need to be interactive. Just a little something to keep me sane.
But, even the sometimes confusing level design can be forgiven. It’s just another way of making the player feel hopeless and helpless. Most games take too kindly to funneling players along the story so much that it feels like the gameplay is interfering with the game. I’m looking at you Final Hallway 13. But that is something that HL2 just doesn’t do. It makes the player, once the actually accomplish something, feel like they did something meaningful.
One last thing and I swear I’ll shut up. How great is the way HL2 introduces you to new enemies? I’ll tell ya how great! It introduces enemies in a very “Mega Man” way. You almost always can see what new enemy you will be fighting before you actually have to engage that enemy. And, sometimes, you can actually SEE its attack patterns. This is done with
and almost every single concept of gameplay. It’s CRAZY! Crazy like a
fox. This is how games
be designed. As a player, I never once felt overwhelmed by a new concept or enemy. Sure I had a lot of “OMG, that guy is spooky,” or “That was a lot tougher than expected,” or “I’m supposed to
that jump?!” and, let’s not forget all of the “Gosh Dang-oh-Darn, that puzzle was the most convoluted thing I have ever seen,” moments. But I never once got overwhelmed by something. Stuck a few times, yes, but never felt like I COULDN’T progress.
The main takeaway is this: If Half-Life 2 isn’t already in your inventory, you should fix that. It really is a problem. But, if you are going to go ahead and get it,
just shell out the ten extra bucks for the Orange Box. Because you WILL want Episode One and Episode Two. And also Portal. ^_^ Basically, you’ll get HL2 and HL2:E1 and get HL2:E2, Portal, and TF2,
free. It’s a great deal.
Tl;dr—8.5/10, Want map, crazy awesome game design in general, Orange Box get.
Thanks for your time and buckle up for the ride that is HL2.

It's not a surprise to see my "thumbs up" conclusion to Rocksteady's latest, the series finale Arkham Knight. Although in my humble opinion this was the best time to put an end to the adventure of the caped crusader, because the gameplay couldn't handle another episode without feeling a little bit tired. All in all, Arkham Knight is the most polished member of the Arkham family in gameplay terms. Batman and his allies have a wide variety of gadgets and combat/stealth moves, not to mention the debuting Batmobile, which is also great to drive around. On the other hand I feel obliged to mention the repetitiveness of the possible side missions. Capturing control points, disarming landmines over and over is a chore and I couldn't feel but disappointed to see that aside the great settings the villains side quests were not able to produce interesting and varied gameplay mechanics. I spent a significant amount of time with the challanges as well, which require you to improve your skills to complete them flawlessly. And in order to finish my review with a boom, the story is first class, a real rollercoaster to every Batman fan out there. Arkham Knight is a worthy conclusion to the Arkham series, which wasn't as much a pinnacle as Arkham City, but a highly recommended action game nonetheless.

TWI has no transparency and never listened to the community except for that one time the reviews tanked and they got desperate.
SWAT: The 9th perk that was meant to be a tanky commando with smg's is actually squishier, requires more ammo to kill trash, and instead of the commando's ability to extend Zed time and reveal stalkers to the team, he gets to stun large zeds with his grenades. A really crappy clone. At least he can kill large zeds with the kriss if he has a flashbang. Lots of people really wanted a swat shield. Nope, that ♥♥♥♥ will got to zerk.
Survivalist: A literal clone of the other 9 perks. It does not have its own weapons and its skills are taken from other perks (in other words: no unique skills). The community had so many amazing ideas for a 10th perk, and TWI went with this trash.
Zedconomy aka microtransactions: I recently thought that the zedconomy was meant to fuel the development process even further, resulting in great new content. Alas, since TWI took the easy way out and neglected the community, the only purpose the zedconomy accomplished was wasting valuable development time to tweak it, time that could have been spent on a real 10th perk, bugfixes, ect.
This is the best the game will get: The reason TWI wanted KF2 rather than updating KF1 and slapping microtransactions on it was because of a change in the game engine. The problem was that TWI did want to update KF1, but couldn't add new content without amping system requirements. Now that they have switched engines, they can load up assets when they are needed instead of at the beginning of the game, allowing them to potentially add new content forever. Unfortunately, updates have been getting worse until they added literally nothing with the release of the survivalist. Any new updates they put out for KF2 now will most likely be half-♥♥♥♥♥ and add nothing to the game, unless Swift Brutal Death adds new maps [grats on making the dev team btw ;) ].
Teasing the community: TWI showcased the fire axe, M32, and have released a workshop mod where you can use the husk cannon with the use of in-game cheats several months ago. These weapons still have not made it into the game, and probably never will.
Casualized as hell: The crap that you get away with on HoE are things that you cannmot do on KF1 on hard mode. Ever try running up to a siren? You survive that ♥♥♥♥. Want to outrun a raging scrake as a demo? No problem, he slows down a bunch when he attacks. Fleshpounds no longer deal a ton of damage when they are enraged, but breaking LOS will no longer reset his timer. The zeds hit like wet noodles; armor has become useless as a result. What did you expect? This game is going to be available for PS4 users. Gotta make this playable on controller.
Never EVER invest in early access. That is a critical lesson that TWI has taught me.
If you enjoyed KF2, then KF1 would make you question why you ever got KF2. Download ScrN as well for a ton of extra content.

Shadowrun Returns is an adaptation of the classic cyberpunk tabletop pen and paper RPG. Set in an alternative history future where magic has returned to the world, elves, dwarves, trolls, and orks live side by side with humans in dense urban cities, and corporations are a law unto themselves; the game centers around the segment of humanity who makes their living in the shadows, the runners. Hacker, mercenary, detective, sorcerer, where there is a job that needs doing, there will be someone willing to get paid to do it.
The game itself is a single player, turn-based strategy RPG, utilizing 3/4 isometric perspective with 3D character models set against sprite based backgrounds. The sprite backgrounds are static and well done, while the character designs are somewhat poorly textured with resolution below that which the majority of modern systems could easily handle; belying the limited budget the company had to work with. Gameplay takes the form of point and click interaction with the world map and carries over directly into combat, utilizing the same environments. Combat is somewhat klunky, as there are problems with the interaction of the courser and corners of the movement field.
The game itself is, however, merely a platform. It is in reality intended for players to build and share their own Shadowrun campaigns, and the full game editor comes included with the base game as well as a professionally developed campaign. Thanks to Steam Works, player campaigns are free, though professionally developed campaigns will be sold as DLC as they become available. Sadly there is no multiplayer option what-so-ever, crippling one of the intregral elements of the pen-and-paper game.
Overall, the game's campaign will run you around 12 hours, and is a good buy if you can get it on sale, for any enthusiast of turn-based strategy RPGs.

Apparently it's sin to enjoy KF2 if you had previously played KF1 and enjoyed that. Golly gee i wonder why someone would like a sequel that has slightly different gameplay to that of a UT2K4 mod-turned-buyable but looks gorgeous and plays significantly less clunky. What's the importance of people saying "thx 4 refund Tripwire" like they won some sort of giant battle of sarcasm and "who's the bigger snobbish twit?"
KF1 and KF2 both encompass the same general wave survival, buying weapons, using perks, and all that other stuff. The difference is that perks in KF2 use a general xp system (and neat skill system) over a number of dumb challenges of how many nuts you can shoot off fleshpounds to level your sharpshooter. Weapons, graphics and the sort are all beautiful and updated; blood everywhere, guts flying, and extremely detailed weapon animations when in Zed Time. The game plays faster, encouraging cycling through the map over holding a single room constantly with C4 at the ready. Difficulties aren't as bullet spongey as they are in KF1, favoring new movesets and faster zeds over zeds made of diamond.
The biggest sin is that of microtransactions. Oh dear god, with Tripwire saying that they hope to give out free content over DLCs, it's doubly a sin for them to add in microtransactions to make some extra cash from cosmetic items over forcing people to buy, say, steampunk weapons, zed killer weapons, and other stuff that those damn POOR people can't get.
The people complaining about the game just want KF1 but prettier, and that's about it. They like their paid DLCs over dumb, pointless cosmetics that don't give you new weapons, but only prettier weapons only you will see most of the time. They enjoy sitting in a room with C4. They don't like nerfs and buffs and changes. After all, they love KF1 too much to enjoy something even remotely different under the same name, but with a '2' slapped on.
The only major issue I have with the game is that the fleshpound is no longer as terrifying as I feel he once was. Once a tall, marching hulk with a distorted and creepy voice, getting ever closer to you at a steady pace until he can shove those mallets in your face to let them spin. Now a walk-until-he-mad actual Hulk who makes his presense known with a yell and smash of his spinning mallets, ready to hop and twirl until you die, probably flinging bits of your intestine around like confetti.
Overall: Great game, gets boring pretty fast just like KF1 does, but those dailies to sell make me put a little bit of time per day into KF2.

Story
Sci-fi horror with RPG elements, Dead Space provides a graphic experience aimed to induce fear as you make your way through hellish sections of a broken mining ship. Set on what's left of a large 'planet-cracker' ship named USG Ishamura. You play as Isaac Clarke, an engineer assigned to perform routine repairs of the Ishamura. Upon arrival you and your team soon learn there are much more concerning matters than rebooting engines and repairing downed communications. By working together with your remaining crew, you will uncover the truth behind the Ishamura's downfall and it's now necromorph staff, and struggle to avoid sharing the same fate.
Gameplay
Movement and aiming controls felt cumbersome and clunky, like two bad dancers stepping on each others toes. Enemy AI behaved intelligently when ambushing and cornering, despite their predictable appearances and entrances. Dead Space's minimal HUD helps bring about a more immersive experience and interaction with objects and environments felt fluid. Abundance of items and gear dampens the horror aspect, but creates an enjoyable amount of gear customization and weapon variety. (For a more intense experience I'd recommend a harder difficulty) Nicely paced story and chapters that introduce new obstacles and enemy variants as the game progresses. Challenging yet rewarding.
Sound
Eerie and grim, the music works well in adding to the gruesome nature of the game. Sound effects and necromorph screams/grunts are hair-raising, despite feeling amplified for cheap jump scares. Quality voice acting, though it's worth mentioning you (Isaac) play as a silent protagonist.
Graphics
Playing 8 years later it's impressive that these graphics don't show their age. Necromorphs are horrifically stunning in detail, as well as the games gorey environment. Lighting and textures appear believable and fitting for both the horror genre and sci-fi. Unlike movement and aiming, the graphics and sounds come together in a beautifully orchestrated ensemble of fear and sweet, sweet necromorph dismemberment.
Replay Value
Offering NG+ it's hard to not revisit Ishamura for a round 2. Even after much exploring there still feels like Dead Space has a lot more to offer and likely grows in enjoyment each playthrough, giving it a strong replay value which I feel we can all agree on is a wonderful feature for any game.
Wrapping Up
Overall Dead Space offers a quality gaming experience, interesting story, detailed atmosphere, and nicely implemented scares. What few flaws you can find in the game are outshined by everything it does right.

One of the best puzzlers I've ever played, up there with Fez and Braid. This one hits a far different note though, as it is a wide open world with little to no explanation of anything. It truly captures the essence of puzzling around, trying to find out what does what on your own, while still keeping a great pace. The game quickly breaks the illusion of logic physical space, which results in a world bound together in a weird and intriguing fashion. Falling down this pit might send you to this place, while going down the stairs in the next room sends you somewhere completely different. At first it's confusing, but once you start to accept the idea, it makes the world far more interconnected and ensures that you don't feel stuck nearly as often. Once you start learning the different mechanics, you can suddenly figure out the puzzles that had you stuck earlier, which gives a great sense of accomplishment, proving that you don't need achievements to reward the player! Each time you get a new tool, you suddenly get flashbacks to the annoying places you couldn't get pass, and you instantly want to go back and destroy that puzzle with your new best (and only) friend. A game with great exploration AND superb puzzles; it's really a no-brainer.
Anyone who haven't played this and have even the slightest interest in puzzles ought to buy this as soon as possible. The price might be a bit steep for a 5-10 hour puzzler, but it's a great experience, and you could always pick it up during a sale ;)

I find games like this to be disturbingly intuitive, so the general mindf*ck aspect doesn't get to me as much as it might some people.  That said, I do tend to reach a point where I know I am missing _something_, but not what, and at that point I frequently resort to grabbing a walktthrough so that I can move on.  If it turns out I was lacking some basic comprehension of a game mechanic, that can result in my losing the enjoyment of the remainder of the game, simply because I wasn't willing to do a general hunt through the whole game to figure out where I should be looking for the missing piece.
This game avoids that "brick wall" kind of aggravation. I have made it halfway through the game, and while I can tell I am missing something, and the difficulty of the puzzles is increasing, I have no urge to grab a guide. I know I will figure it out, and that I will feel like a rock star when I do.
If you want something along the lines of Portal, but without the sadistic-computer plot to distract you from the awesome puzzle mechanics, I couldn't recommend this more.

It's not a surprise to see my "thumbs up" conclusion to Rocksteady's latest, the series finale Arkham Knight. Although in my humble opinion this was the best time to put an end to the adventure of the caped crusader, because the gameplay couldn't handle another episode without feeling a little bit tired. All in all, Arkham Knight is the most polished member of the Arkham family in gameplay terms. Batman and his allies have a wide variety of gadgets and combat/stealth moves, not to mention the debuting Batmobile, which is also great to drive around. On the other hand I feel obliged to mention the repetitiveness of the possible side missions. Capturing control points, disarming landmines over and over is a chore and I couldn't feel but disappointed to see that aside the great settings the villains side quests were not able to produce interesting and varied gameplay mechanics. I spent a significant amount of time with the challanges as well, which require you to improve your skills to complete them flawlessly. And in order to finish my review with a boom, the story is first class, a real rollercoaster to every Batman fan out there. Arkham Knight is a worthy conclusion to the Arkham series, which wasn't as much a pinnacle as Arkham City, but a highly recommended action game nonetheless.

Risk of rain is fantastic!
The game has a very simple yet detailed pixel art style, and interesting monster, weapon, and character designs, each masterfully animated.
The music seems to be inspired by retro game beats, yet feels fresh, and oscillates from being adreniline pumping, to calm and relaxing, it's a good, fun, varied sountrack.
The simple yet deep gameplay, offers various characters to unlock, each offering very unique movesets that all have been perfectly balanced, so one should be able to find one character that fits their playstyle. While the game is hard, it never feels so due to monsters having an unfair advantage, however several artifacts can also be unlocked to alter gameplay so it either ends up easier, or more difficult.
Additionally three difficulty levels can be selected, so you can cater the challenge to your own tastes.
The gist of the game is to fight off a neverending wave of enemies, that become progressively more difficult the longer the game is in play, over the course of 6 levels. Each level is completed by first finding a teleporter, then fighting off against a boss, and surviving a time limit wherein serveral enemies will spawn to attack the player, after successfully doing so the player will be transported to the next level.
A lot of work went into the design of the game, from the easy to navigate menu's, to the environments available, and amount of enemies you can come across, to the games ostensibly simple story that reveals more depth as you dig into the lore.
Along with the many secrets, hidden areas, and unlockables to discover.
Multiplayer is a blast, but unfortunately very difficult to set up with others...
Risk of rain is fun on all levels, and an excellent addition to the indie genre, that should keep one entertained for hours!

I just finished "Dead Man's Switch" of Shadowrun Returns and I really enjoyed it.
Just a heads up before my review, the main reason I purchased this game is because I used to play the table top version of Shadowrun back in highschool. Just the product's name brings back great memories and my review (and enjoyment of the game) of course is partially biased due to this background.
Here is a quick review for those interested in the title:
What is "Dead Man's Switch"?
Think of Shadowrun Returns as the client, and DMS as the story you plug into it. There is also a DLC that I've purchased but not started yet that is another story for Shadowrun Returns. I'm hoping they will continue to support this product!
Game Mechanics:
Smooth, easy to learn, and well done. The game plays like the first Fallouts or the Baldur's Gate series as an overhead tactical turn-based gameplay. With that said you do not need any prior experience with this type of game to enjoy Shadowrun Returns. The menu, UI, and rpg elements are all straight forward. The only thing that bothered me about the combat UI was reloading my rifle, however I'm sure there was a hotkey I could've used.
Story vs. Action:
The biggest compliant I saw on my own research of this game prior to purchase was the amount of dialog. The team that created this game obviously aimed to reproduce a table-top setting that focused primarily on storytelling, not combat. There are plently of short engagements throughout this product and I felt the combat was very satisifying. However, if you are the type that clicks quickly though dialog in other games you won't be impressed with this title.
The best part of this game is the story and for those don't care about that and just want an action / adventure title should look elsewhere.
If you have any direct questions please comment below! I just wanted to hit those two points since they I felt they were not communicated well in other reviews.

I bought this game during the summer sale a few days ago and paid $3.74 for it. It's easily worth 10 bucks to me. Having just finished my first play through on normal difficulty as an Elf Decker of the base game (Dead Man's Switch), I figured I'd share my thoughts on it:

The cityscape looked how i envisioned it would.  The Matrix, magic, cyberware, and other things were there as well. It was missing the shadowrunning feel to it though honestly.  Instead of it being a single Johnson or a series of Johnsons giving you missions, it focused on a single mission which kept getting more complex as it went along until it was concluded... which leads to one of the things I was not impressed with (mentioned below).
It's a Turn based Action Point system alternating between you/your team and enemies going.  This is a deviation from the combat system of the Shadowrun Tabletop, but was still solid and required some strategy.
I played 6 straight hours my first time sitting down with it and the only reason I stopped is because I realized I had fallen asleep in my chair for 4 hours and had to get up to go to work.  It wasn't a thrill a minute action story, but it was a good solid line that progressed evenly and kept me interested ehough to see what happened next. It didn't feel like it was too long, but didn't feel like it was quite long enough. Maybe 1 more scene to the game would have been perfect for length.
The implementation of the matrix was close to how I'd envisioned it from the 3rd and 4th edition Shadowrun game books. It was fast and sleek looking, although I wish there were more of it and a little more customization capability of your Avatar in it. (It would have been nice to have the genesis version with random systems and a Johnson that could give side quests?... which would also fix one of my  previously alluded to complaints about the game.)
My cons:
The maps were small and basically there was nowhere to go outside of your target destination. You entered and moved from insertion point to objective building. Everything else was blocked off.
Outside of the main story line which basically rewarded you for clicking on/finding everything or metered infusions of money as the story line progressed... there was no way to earn money to upgrade your gear.  Through most of the game it felt like I was being forced to pick having a team to run with and mediocre gear and little to no cyberware upgrades or get the cyberware and best gear to go it alone.
The fact that there were no Johnsons to take runs from in the game was frustrating as it is a big part of being a shadowrunner.  Although when you look at the storyline of the game, it is more of a single run  instead of living the full life of a shadowrunner so maybe the lack of Johnsons and side runs isn’t actually missing from the game, but it would have helped to make some money to buy better tech.
Overall, I’d say the game is a gem for anyone who likes the shadowrun universe but would fall flat for anyone that’s just a gamer.

Resident Evil has always been a sort of guilty pleasure for me after Resident Evil 4, and after the less enjoyable Resident Evil 5 & 6 it feels nice that Revelations 2 is going back to a more calmer narrative and a more creepy atmosphere. (Have not played Revelations 1 so can't compare to it.)
I enjoyed the combat a lot in this game. I played on hardest difficulty which made it hard but fair. Although if you're not familiar with the combat in previous games I would say go for normal.  Switching between guns and melee attacks is smooth and as intensive at it should be. And with a decent amount of variations to the enemy all the action scenarios feelt intensive and creative the entire first episode.
The controls are decent, it's clearly designed for a controller, but works good enough with mouse and keyboard.
Not really much to say about the story within the first episode, but I really liked the setting and Barrys and Natalias part of the game has some enjoyable dialogs. Clearly the best part of  the plot so far. And as I said, I liked that the narrative is much slower compared to the newer Resident Evil games and it doesn't try to give a bunch of details of what happened in the previous games. So far you can get into it without any experience with Resident Evil games.
It's just such a shame it's such a bad version of the game. I didn't encounter much issue with the frame during the main campaign and so that part was really enjoyable, and made me look forward to the next episode. But it really shows in raid mode when the game throws as many enemys as possible. At times the enemys would start move in slowmotion, and one snow level in raid mode was next to unplayable because the frame rate went from 60 to 7-10.
The graphics quality is so so, its some great design and the main campaign there are parts that looks really nice. But when they show you more larger open areas in raid mode it can become really butt-ugly.
And the there is the absent of coop, which should be there.
I really hope they fix the frame rate issues, because overall this was a step in the right direction for the franchise. It had a great atmosphere and gameplay, and I want to play the next episode. But if you have a nextgen consol, you might wanna buy this for that instead. And if you don't well, it is 7 euros/dollars, if you find the trailers appealing and can forgive it's issues than step right ahead and give it a shoot. Otherwise......Umm yeah, I kinda liked it.

Dead Space - Pros and Cons.
+ Haunting design
+ Thrilling sound design both in musical cues and sound effects ranging from snapping bone the ripping flesh, gore is all the more chilling.
+ Controls, coming from console the management of Isaac is much better with the mouse and keyboard.
+ Graphics don't make the game but the art direction compliments the theme of the game making the experience immersive and hard to pull back from.
+ Horror is the intended genre and mixed with the beforementioned this game makes for some decent scares and a constant feeling of dread.
- It relies mostly on jumpscares for a cheap scare which might be a turn off for some players.
- Tank controls, it works well with the atmosphere but some might find it frustrating to navigate with.
- As gore is used often and nothing new other than enemy types so the creatures aren't as creepy or scary past a couple hours.
- Ammo and health is distributed from every enemy making challenge somewhat existant.
Overall, a glorious price and an overall excellent addition worthy of the Horror tag, my personal recommendation is to play on the harder difficulty to keep the tension high.

Antechamber is an original and fun game. The game mechanics and particle gun (if that's what it's called) are very clever and well exposed. It feels as though the gun modes were made first, then the puzzles were arranged to demonstrate the capabilities of each mechanic. There are some great 'click' moments when the solution requires you to use the gun in a new way. A great balance of difficulty, chore-factor, and frustration.
The first puzzle in the game asks you to choose one of two hallways, and each one leads back to the original choice. To progress, you have to turn around half way through one hall and go back. The game is introducing itself as a 'think outside the square' puzzler. The problem is, you can't actually 'think' about a puzzle like that, it's like searching an invisible door. To solve it, you have to systematically try everything, which is not fun. To me, that first puzzle undersold the rest of the game. There is much more to Antechamber than rooms that sneakily change behind your back. Picking up the first gun made me keep playing and with the first gun upgrade I knew why this game had succeeded.
The map and progression sequence are also very original. I'm not sure that this works well. You keep walking around the amorphous main level and access new areas as you gain abilities. Each main room can be accessed from the 'menu screen' (which is actually an area with a clickable wall). There are also linear sequences of rooms where you puzzle through to a dead end, to be rewarded with some extras, development screenshots, concepts and the like. You only really know you've moved forward when you upgrade the gun. It's often hard to tell whether you've missed something without endlessly crawling through the whole map one square at a time.
For full completion, you have to find about 100 wall panels. They have a 'the oatmeal' style cartoon with a saying such as 'try try again'. I like the game, but the panels are terrible and I hate them. They look hideous; white lines on black. More importantly, the game and puzzle style is extremely eldritch and mysterious. These cutesy little cartoons are way out of place and almost ruin the theme. It would have been far better to lose them and have the slogans by themselves. Maybe in a creepy font.
Final gripe, in the hardest linear sequence the devs 'forgot' to put anything at the end. I spent minutes on end in a featureless room, that locks when you enter, looking for another ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t invisible door or anything. It was a lame laugh for the devs at my expense and I'm still mad almost a year later.
In summary, I am very much a fan of this game and would recommend to others. The minimal white-on-white graphics style is striking. It is very long and intricate for an indie-release, and much more cerebral and original than most blockbuster games. I think the fact that I have so many memories (fond and otherwise) shows how deeply I was engaged.

Antichamber is one of those weird puzzle games where most of the solutions require odd leaps in logic, but is so far removed from reality that it works in it's favor. The game has no narration, no plot, and no real reason to be there, it just kind of exists. I never found any solution to be unfair, and the game never really goes out of it's way to be difficult. It's an interesting experiment, that can probably only be called a game in that there was always some way to press forward.
The lack of any plot or story in the world works mostly in it's favor. Unlike other puzzle games, such as Portal, there isn't any antagonist, or a "right way" to go through the motions. If your solution is to ignore a puzzle entirely and spam cubes (the games primary solution device), that works too. Ultimately though it does mean that some puzzles have no reason to exist other than to be solved, despite the existence of an endgame. I managed to see the credits roll without getting the last upgrade, as well as several unsolved rooms. And there isn't much in the way of replayability. Unless you're interested in challenging yourself in some way, once a solution is found you're likely not going to go back and try again.
The most interesting bit is it's use (and abuse) of non-natural space. Often times you will be navigating puzzles only to find that they take up space that they shouldn't. Infinite loops, teleporting rooms, all a part of the game's main draw: puzzles that have rational solutions if you only listen to the rules the game gives you.
Realistically, it's a fun little game that doesn't go out of it's way to be entertaining, and instead makes the most out of it's own mechanics to create a unique experience.

Dying Light is a fantastic game in so many respects, hence why I rate it positive. It's a great effort towards the holy grail of the 'perfect' zombie game. It is however let down by soooooooo many mistakes by its dev team. Ignoring the game wrecking day one instability and FPS issues that are becoming a sad staple of AAA games on release and the fact that my particular copy REALLY doesn't cooperate when I press 'quit', there are still some pretty clear issues. Free running is touch and go in some cases, but on the whole, pretty great. Weapons have an annoying tendency to miss occasionally, even when swinging a huge axe at a zombie three feet away. Human enemies are annoying to face without a gun, melee weapons are a bit UP against them, though catching one unaware and decapitating him is AWESOME.
Those aren't really massive issues though. My bone lies with the design choices. Missions are constrictive in many regards, and too linear for an open world game like this. Missions like the one that sees you escorting an annoying american to pick up some worthless♥♥♥♥♥♥ listening to him bleet on are pointless. In reality, any normal person in a zombie apocalypse would just bash the annoying sod on the head and rob his corpse. Sewer missions and 'clear the tower' missions are super linear and pretty predictable. Traps basically don't feature at all. I'm completed and used them about 3 times. Having to unlock them with skill points is stupid. Loads of stuff is plaigarised from the Far Cry series. Climbing towers to switch them on. Trippy drug induced 'follow the woman' playable cutscenes, picking up flowers to make 'booster' drugs, the yellow and black clad enemies (late game FC3) and more besides. And they are all annoying and not done in the same style or flair as FC. The final mission is an insult. Another linear mission in a tower. But this time you get to run away from infinite amounts of enemies somehow occupying the boss' main base and somehow attracted by his disembodied supervoice towards you. As soon as I [SPOILERS] started the run away 'challenge' I was bored. When I fell into a sewer and predictably had my weapons made useless by a screamer whilst attacked by stupid amounts of night hunters I yawned and switched off for the day. Level design like that is no better than a QTE. No fun, just boredom.
That seems like a lot of negatives xD Really though I love the game, and there are too many great features to write about. It's mission level design may be boring, predictable and uninspiring, it may have simply plaigarised a bunch of other games and tacked them onto Dead island, it may have recycled most of Riptide's story and it may have been a day one FPS/stability disaster, but it is still a hugely enjoyable free-roam game. Play it the right way. Block the painful story memories and just free run across the map killing sh*t.

I was rather skeptical about this game, even though I've been waiting for its release since I've first heard about it (which was probably the very first announcement). I got especially suspicious when it turned out that they didn't give away keys to reviewers, which supposed to mean that it's gonna be another broken release. I am happy to tell you that it is not the case.
It is quite alike Dead Island, but with parkour and better graphics and improved combat. Speaking of combat, it didn't feel that good at the start, but once you get a few skill points and fun weapons it's going to satisfy your thirst for blood. It is definitely much better than Dead Island's combat, even though mechanics are very similar. The gore level is high, you can cut off limbs or even cut zombies into two pieces, blood is going to be everywhere (sometimes it would be even hard to see, because it covers the entire screen at times). The variety that comes at the latter stage of the game is just amazing. And it's both variety in weapons+modifications and in the killing skills. For example, this game has a Whirlwind ability. It's not entirely as in Diablo, you can only make one 360 degrees swing at time (which mostly cuts everything around you in 2 pieces), but damn it's fun!
Parkour is not as fluent as in Mirror's Edge, but it's above my expectations: you can climb pretty much everywhere. At night, you often have to run for your life and this is one of the most thrilling experiences that I've had in the last year of gaming (excluding Alien: Isolation, I guess, but it's a different type of thrill). The nights are really dark and zombies get deadly (rarely the case during the daytime).
Storyline is mediocre (often close to stupid), but it manages not to annoy me that much (I guess the standard is lowered these days anyway). At its worst moments it’s getting rather silly (that kind of silly that makes you smile or even laugh) than annoying. There are plenty of side quests that rarely make much sense, but are quite fun, especially if you’re playing in Co-op.
Speaking of Co-op: it’s just amazing. I just can’t describe how awesome it is to swing through hordes of zombies during the day and to run in panic during the night together. It’s a pity that players are just clones of each other, meaning there’re no additional characters for co-op, but you can change your outfit (which you unlock with progression), so it’s not that bad. Animations are great (there are some flaws, of course, but overall it’s a well-made mode).
However PVP system could be improved. It’s not the focus of the game, so it’s actually great as it is already, but it would be nice to have more variety in modes, other than simply defending/destroying nests which gets repetitive very fast. But the main issue for me is that it’s really hard to join someone’s game as a zombie. In average it takes above 20 tries and then people often leave afterwards or stay in the safe zone. I was really lucky with my first round though, the other guy was playing fair and good and it was a lot of fun. In short, don’t consider multiplayer as a big part of the game, but definitely give it a try if you decide to buy the game.
If you wonder how open the world is, just remember Dead Island to get the idea. It’s a big (or, by some measures, huge) map filled with quests, side quests, houses/shops/cars/chests to loot and, of course, hordes of zombies of different types. You probably would explore all of it if you finish all the quests (which are many), so there’s not much to poke around after you’re done with quests. I’m not sure though, since I haven’t finished the game yet.
So, in short, if your expectations aren’t too high, grab it and you won’t regret it. However it’s not a revolutionary game.
PS: I’m really curious now what new Dead Island 2 is going to bring in terms of gameplay. Because this game feels like this is what Dead Island 2 supposed to be.

First off, lemme say that I think the game is an overall enjoyable experience considering the budget. I don't regret my purchase and will definitely play all the future episodes. But the game certainly has many problems, and I honestly don't really expect them to fix any of these as more episodes are released.
The biggest thing about Revelations 2 is the overhaul to the partners system. Rather than simply having an incompetent AI who won't kill anything and might as well not be there at all, each partner now actually feels valuable. I had my concerns when I saw the trailer and discovered I had to switch control to a second character just so I can shine a flashlight at stuff, but after playing, I realized playing as the "utility character" can actually be pretty fun.
However...
While the partner actions are well designed, they're very poorly implemented. The AI is still as dumb as ever, and the fact that more is now expected from your partner only makes it worse. During a fight, you can't even predict if your partner will follow you as you run down a corridor... some times they just stand still and get hit!
There are some fun partner-melee combos in Revelations 2, but you simply cannot expect the AI to properly do their part, so if you want to perform them, it's usually best that you switch back-and-forth and perform both roles by yourself.
In Revelations 2 you have one "weapons" character who carries all the firearms, and an "utility" character who doesn't really have any weapons at all. Now get this: if you're in control of the utility character, the AI in control of the weapons character WON'T FIRE THE GUNS AT ALL until you've beaten the story and unlocked a perk on the post-game screen, said perk will actually allow them to fire guns and not consume any bullets at all, but at a drastically reduced damage (hint: just have the AI use a weapon with high knock-back power).
And while the utility character can indeed do many cool tricks, the game likes to keep those a secret from you until it's too late. There are many moments where you will have barely survived an onslaught, and the game will tell you, "BY THE WAY, YOU COULD'VE DONE THIS AND AVOIDED ALL THAT TROUBLE ALTOGETHER." Come on, seriously?
Gameplay complaints aside, I did enjoy the story. The decision to do episodic releases is kind of weird - I guess they wanted a share of The Walking Dead's success. But the first episode did end on an interesting cliffhanger, and I'm curious to find out what happens next.
Raid Mode is mostly the same as it was Revelations 1. It's very grindy and not quite as fun as Mercenaries. It's enjoyable though. If you have the patience to get through the boring early levels, you'll find yourself pleasantly surprised at the variety of enemies this mode offers.
I'm not sure if this is exclusive to the Throwback Map pack, but I've played through quite a few stages taken from RE6. It's fun to start a mission and be thrown into a familiar setting. The downside is that revisiting these levels will really make you realize how inferior the graphics are in this game.

Antechamber is an original and fun game. The game mechanics and particle gun (if that's what it's called) are very clever and well exposed. It feels as though the gun modes were made first, then the puzzles were arranged to demonstrate the capabilities of each mechanic. There are some great 'click' moments when the solution requires you to use the gun in a new way. A great balance of difficulty, chore-factor, and frustration.
The first puzzle in the game asks you to choose one of two hallways, and each one leads back to the original choice. To progress, you have to turn around half way through one hall and go back. The game is introducing itself as a 'think outside the square' puzzler. The problem is, you can't actually 'think' about a puzzle like that, it's like searching an invisible door. To solve it, you have to systematically try everything, which is not fun. To me, that first puzzle undersold the rest of the game. There is much more to Antechamber than rooms that sneakily change behind your back. Picking up the first gun made me keep playing and with the first gun upgrade I knew why this game had succeeded.
The map and progression sequence are also very original. I'm not sure that this works well. You keep walking around the amorphous main level and access new areas as you gain abilities. Each main room can be accessed from the 'menu screen' (which is actually an area with a clickable wall). There are also linear sequences of rooms where you puzzle through to a dead end, to be rewarded with some extras, development screenshots, concepts and the like. You only really know you've moved forward when you upgrade the gun. It's often hard to tell whether you've missed something without endlessly crawling through the whole map one square at a time.
For full completion, you have to find about 100 wall panels. They have a 'the oatmeal' style cartoon with a saying such as 'try try again'. I like the game, but the panels are terrible and I hate them. They look hideous; white lines on black. More importantly, the game and puzzle style is extremely eldritch and mysterious. These cutesy little cartoons are way out of place and almost ruin the theme. It would have been far better to lose them and have the slogans by themselves. Maybe in a creepy font.
Final gripe, in the hardest linear sequence the devs 'forgot' to put anything at the end. I spent minutes on end in a featureless room, that locks when you enter, looking for another ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t invisible door or anything. It was a lame laugh for the devs at my expense and I'm still mad almost a year later.
In summary, I am very much a fan of this game and would recommend to others. The minimal white-on-white graphics style is striking. It is very long and intricate for an indie-release, and much more cerebral and original than most blockbuster games. I think the fact that I have so many memories (fond and otherwise) shows how deeply I was engaged.

*** - 3/5

Antichamber is one of those weird puzzle games where most of the solutions require odd leaps in logic, but is so far removed from reality that it works in it's favor. The game has no narration, no plot, and no real reason to be there, it just kind of exists. I never found any solution to be unfair, and the game never really goes out of it's way to be difficult. It's an interesting experiment, that can probably only be called a game in that there was always some way to press forward.
The lack of any plot or story in the world works mostly in it's favor. Unlike other puzzle games, such as Portal, there isn't any antagonist, or a "right way" to go through the motions. If your solution is to ignore a puzzle entirely and spam cubes (the games primary solution device), that works too. Ultimately though it does mean that some puzzles have no reason to exist other than to be solved, despite the existence of an endgame. I managed to see the credits roll without getting the last upgrade, as well as several unsolved rooms. And there isn't much in the way of replayability. Unless you're interested in challenging yourself in some way, once a solution is found you're likely not going to go back and try again.
The most interesting bit is it's use (and abuse) of non-natural space. Often times you will be navigating puzzles only to find that they take up space that they shouldn't. Infinite loops, teleporting rooms, all a part of the game's main draw: puzzles that have rational solutions if you only listen to the rules the game gives you.
Realistically, it's a fun little game that doesn't go out of it's way to be entertaining, and instead makes the most out of it's own mechanics to create a unique experience.

This is an enjoyable game which at its core involves directing a group of soldiers on turn-based missions defending Earth against an alien invasion.  The turn-based gameplay is easy to pick up but still offers a challenge in that your soldiers must maintain cover to have a chance at mission survival.
Ultimately your core choices for each soldier will be to advance forward, shoot at an enemy (if one is in range), weapon reload, overwatch (shoot at an enemy if one comes into range during the aliens' turn), or hunker down (improve defense throughout aliens' turn).  As your soldiers rack up kills and become promoted, they will be assigned to one of four classes and will need to be assigned abilities at every new rank.  Each class has unique abilities that can be used on the battlefield during the turn-based missions.
As the game progresses it introduces other elements such as the construction of a satellite network to help track UFOs, the maintenance and upgrade of aircraft to attack UFOs when detected, and
research (which allows you to develop new armor, weapons, and equipment for your soldiers and aircraft).  But ultimately all of these elements are secondary to the core, turn-based gameplay.
And finally, even after completing the game for the first time, there are additional difficulty options which help with replayability, including an Ironman mode, which means there is no loading of a saved game file allowed throughout the entire campaign (game is saved frequently and automatically, no going back to undo bad decisions).
Even after all the hours I've invested in this game I continue to come back to it from time to time and would highly recommend it to anyone.

So there has been a lot of negativity surrounding this game, mostly due to the lack of "co-op" that was mentioned on the Steam store page prior to launch, so let me throw my hat into the ring;
First of all; Capcom have apologised due to any misunderstandings caused by the way the game was listed on Steam, The have also stated that they are looking into ways of re-implementing the missing split-screen mode.
With that said, the only co-op in the original Revelations was raid mode, and that game is, and has always been, listed as having 'co-op' on it's Steam store page - I have no idea why some people expected there to be online campaign co-op in Revelations 2 or are annoyed that it doesn't exist.
I'd also like to point out that, as mentioned by Capcom (and as was always intended) "Raid mode will support online co-op shortly after launch when a free patch is available for players to download which adds this feature" - So technically, just like the original Revelations, the game will have a co-op feature. There's no 'scam' or 'false advertising' like some of the wild claims other people have been making; This is how the game was intended to be. If you thought differently, you should have done your homework (or played the first Resident Evil Revelations, which would have told you exactly how co-op in this game was going to work).
With that addressed, I'll move on to the actual game itself:
Having completed the the first episode of the story, I can say that, so far, the atmosphere is fantastic. The way the game is being released episodically isn't a bad thing, instead of burning through the game in just a couple of days, like a favourite TV series, you have to wait to find out what happens, which aids in building the suspense factor nicely. Can't wait for next week.
The characters feel like they have been properly worked on rather than just 'copy paste name from RE game here'. I was super excited as a long time RE fan to finally see Barry Burton back, and for the first time (not including that awful gameboy outing) as a playable character, I can say that I'm not disappointed. The scripting and voice acting work is great and goes a long way to making the characters feel 'real' - Moira in particular acts just like you'd expect your typical teenager to.
Gameplay is solid. The two-character system is a fantastic feature, instead of just having an AI partner following you around, getting to instantly switch between and fully use both characters is brilliant and helps in just about every situation in the game. Raid mode is fun, and feels like a combination of both old and new "Mercenaries" modes, time attack style gameplay, but with a goal and the ability to kill all enemies in the stage.
Graphically the game looks nice, the character models in particular are very nicely detailed and the environments do their jobs well. Like some other people, I had some performance issues until I tweaked the settings and capped the frame rate, it doesn't run brilliantly by any means, but I wasn't expecting it to on my now outdated 560ti, (I imagine it will run a little better after a couple of patches and a game-ready graphics driver.) No game-breaking bugs or crashing, nothing major on that front.
The micro-transactions in raid mode aren't anything I would spend my money on, though it seems like all of the stuff in there is completely unnecessary (extra continues should you run out; I've not used a single one yet, extra item storage, items you can get just by playing for the ultra-lazy). It kind of feels like an obvious cash grab attempt and in my opinion, the game would be better off without it... That said, it can be completely ignored and doesn't detract from the gameplay in any way, so it's not a big deal.
So far, my considered opinion, I'd give this a solid 7/10, stand out point being one of the few games recently that has instantly grabbed my attention and made me care about the story, biggest negatives being the sub-optimal performance and those annoying micro-transactions.
If you're a fan of Resident Evil, the campaign makes it worth getting now, if you're not that interested in the series and are looking at it from the point of view as it just being a game to play, I'd say stick it on your wish list and wait for the next sale.

If you thought Portal was fun, and you're up for a bit more of a challenge, try Antichamber.
I don't play a lot of puzzle games because I usually find them either trite or frustrating. The idea of completing puzzles just to complete puzzles is a little off-putting to me. However, this game got great reviews from ArsTechnica and other places I had seen, and the idea of a first-person puzzle game with "puzzling game mechanics" sounded very intriguing, so I checked it out.
Absolutely worth it (I paid around $8).
I was worried when the game mostly started out with "impossible structure" puzzles, a la Stanley Parable and others that it was going to be overly simple and silly, but the game was quite challenging indeed. Some of the game mechanics took a fair amount of time and experimentation to fully understand, making the puzzles using them all that more rewarding. Doing a 100% (full map + panels) took me around 7 hours with no looking at outside resources, but your time will probably vary based on which puzzles you encounter in which order (I have a feeling some paths will be much quicker).
Pros:
- Lots of intriguing game mechanics to puzzle over and use
- Doesn't take too much time to 100%
- Any% finish doesn't take forever
- Learning game mechanics and meta mechanics (map, 'achievement' wall) is very rewarding.
Cons:
- When completing the post-end-game stuff (going for 100% completion), puzzles become much less rewarding
- A number of unfinished areas and activities (disappointing in retrospect)
- Some of the hardest puzzles to solve include no tangible reward whatsoever
- No achievements when the game honestly seems ripe for achievements
Overall... If you thought Portal was fun, and you're up for a bit more of a challenge, try Antichamber. I spent about $1 per hour I played on it, and that seems reasonable to me. Don't look at any guides/gameplay before playing, though, if you really want to get the most time out of it.

Batman: Arkham Knight is the finale to the Arkham franchise of videogames, concluding the story that started with Batman: Arkham Asylum. Set ten years after Batman: Arkham Origins, the titular comic-book hero must save Gotham once again when Scarecrow threatens to release a chemical weapon that will devastate the city, with the help of a mysterious newcomer called the Arkham Knight.
Story: Batman: Arkham Knight has the best story of the series, and a more original one at that. While elements of Batman: Arkham Origins, Batman: Arkham Asylum, and Batman: Arkham City all shared comic-book similarities, this game is completely original, and what little they do borrow from the comics is heavily changed. It is impossible to continue on with praise of the plot without spoiling it, so this section ends here.
Graphics: At launch, this game featured many, many issues. But as of 2016, almost all of them have been resolved. My PC specifications are: CPU: Intel Core i5 4460; GPU: Nvidia GeForce GTX 970 4GB; 8GB RAM. I had this game running at a solid, steady 60fps at maximum settings at 1080p resolution, which is quite good. The game looks absolutely stunning, but it is not issue free. When in the open world of Gotham, I sometimes encounter audio lags, but none of them last for too long. This is the extent of graphical issues I experience.
Experience: This game is fun. It features an updated combat system which still tops any other game available, and the Batmbobile can get repetitive at times, but is usually a blast to control. This is a game that I would play over and over again, having beat it four times (the reason the recorded hours at the top may be lower is because for 2015 I played this on Microsoft Xbox One before buying it on PC).
Overall, I definitely recommend this game, and I promise you will enjoy it too.
EDIT: Since the review was written, a number of updates have completely fixed the audio lag issue.

Resident Evil Revelations 2 is the best thing to happen to Resident Evil since Resident Evil Revelations. The controls are tight, the graphics are good, and the plot is more compelling than any RE game in the last 5 years.
PROS:
A unique soundtrack.
A surprisingly functional partner system. Both Moira and Natalia have logical, well-implemented functionality.
More "classic" looking zombies.
A lot of eastereggs/in-jokes for long time fans
Fantastic dialogue.
Limited ammo drops.
The island has a fitting atmosphere that actually makes you fear the next group of enemies.
The graphics are good, but clearly not the biggest concern of the developer.
There's an interesting plot that compels me to play more.
Co-Op! Finally!
A lot of throwbacks to the older games in terms of level design towards the end.
They finally patched the framerate issues.
CONS:
Over-expensive, unnecessary, day one DLC (such as sexy costumes and storage space for Raid Mode weapons/items).
Health bars on the zombies in raid mode feel out of place in a Resident Evil title.
The twists in the plot are pretty predictable. They're still fun and entertaining, but they're not as surprising as they could have been, and in some cases the plot spoils itself with heavy handed foreshadowing. For example:
On the subject of Raid Mode:  If you liked the previous incarnations of Raid Mode or Mercanaries Mode, then you're going to like this. If you didn't like the other ones, then this one won't sway you.
For $24 you can't go wrong.

The good:
Perhaps this game's most innovative aspect is
. You fight your way with Clair and Moira through one place, and then Barry and Natalia show up in the same place later. Whichever way you affect the environment with the first duo, the second will be there to witness it (or fight it). It makes you plan ahead and think twice as hard for both pairs of characters.
Many of its qualities so far, from the almost intentionally
and golden continuity nods, to the airtight
and neatly hidden objects, feel like a true service to the fans of survival horror genre, and classical RE games specifically.

they've added lends you specific secondary abilities that you can do without if you so please, but they can certainly help a lot, especially ones that have to do with healing or dealing damage. It's more of a flavor addition than a mandatory component.

you in combat is not a good idea, though the fact that he/she won't spend any ammo by doing so kind of balances it out.

Lets get a couple things straight. This is a good game, i'm enjoying it more than RE6. Definately worth the money.
First things first, Splitscreen coop, guys, this is PC how often do you all REALLY play local coop on your computers? Let alone a RE game? Remember all of us used to ♥♥♥♥♥ about RE being coop with partners? And now all you want is coop. Yes it was misleading but it's still a good game solo, the way RE is meant to be. Online coop would be nice but don't let no coop stop you from playing this, it didn't stop you from playing RE4 I bet.
Second, DLC. For those of you who know capcom, this game has microtransactions and other minor DLC. Lots of you complained without thinking saying they cut things out of the game to sell seperately. This game is only $25, it comes with the maps and characters and all episodes for $40, Revalations 1 is $50... the dlc that isn't included isn't necessary, storage space, currency and weapons. All not needed and the guns can be bought in game with in game money. No one is being ripped of here... yet. So DLC is fine. They pulled things out to make the base game cheaper, you want more then pay for the full game at $40. All they did is give you options to pay less for the game if you don't want those extra things, that's pretty cool.
Third, Optimization. The game runs decent, it's very playable. The game was clearly made to run at 60. Dark Souls had problems forced past 30fps. Until patches come though to optimize the frame dips and stutters here's all you have to do to play it smooth as butter. Turn Vsync on and turn framerate to 60. Variable is what makes the character stutter and Vsync off will make the framerate drop occassionally. Change those two options for now and it's highly playable at a slight trade off of responsiveness.
My only complaint with this game is the Online Raid matchmaking is delayed until around the time the final episode releases about a month from now, that is going to hurt Raid as it sucks only playing solo.
Is this game worth the $25 price? So far yes, the game looks to be picking up speed and I like where the campaign is headed. Raid is fun and the first episode took me 2 1/2 hours on survival. If you want a taste, do what I did and buy the first episode, totally worth $6 as a RE fan.

Dead Space
You've probably heard the name before, on TV, from a friend, or maybe even your favorite Youtuber. The name has become synonmyous with horror, atmosphere, and gore. Breaking it down into its separate parts we can see the ingredients that make this game up.
Dead:
Yep, there is quite a lot of death here. Maybe from the thousands of ungodly abominations you are forced to kill to survive,  disgustingly mutated humans, torn apart and rebuilt into hungry beasts; or maybe from the weapons you use to do the job: a slowly acquired arsenal of death dealing mining equipment, from Plasma Cutters, to Flamethrowers, to Explosive Charge Laying behemoths. It could also be what awaits you if you fail, ever unique death animations filled with unchecked brutality, and beautifully rendered blood and gore. Dead silence maybe? The calm before the storm you know is coming; an eerie peace that you know can't last long. Maybe even worse than the horrors themselves is the horrors you imagine. The visceral anticipation for the monstrosities, are they lurking in the shadows, or haunting your steps?
Space:
In space, no one can hear you scream. It's cheesy, but the feeling of helplessness is very real. You're stuck on a rustbucket of a mining vessel in the middle of nowhere, and you're supposed to be the rescue mission; hanging in the black of void of nothingness, with millions of miles of absolutely nothing. Perhaps the space is actually the lack of it?; a vast majority of the game is spent in dark, shut-in hallways. Feelings of claustrophobia are sure to set in after only a short time playing through cramped metallic rooms, strewn with the leftoevers of whatever horror begot the ship beforehand. Maybe it's the suit you're wearing, a dated set of engineer's protection; heavy, uncomfortable, and too tight to breathe.
We are empty, we are forsaken, and nothing that happens here truly matters. We are but ants poking for food in the land of sleeping gods. What revelations we make are ours, and the atonement for our sins is ours, and pyre that impales us is ours and only ours.

When I was a younger and more ignorant person, I looked on the advertisements for Dead Space with holy disdain, distancing myself far away from the gory, horror-filled secular content that I was not accustomed to.
My, my. How the times have changed for me.
Dead Space is a game in which you play as Isaac Clarke: an engineer who was assigned with a small crew to investigate the mysterious mining freight, the USG Ishimura. While onboard, they discover the disturbing necromorph creatures have made a new home amidst the dead bodies and decrepit machinery and have also graciously trapped you onboard to endure with their delightful company.
Let me say, the manners of these creatures are atrocious. They don't invite you tea (they don't even have a daily tea), they don't acknowledge you verbally, and most of all they get incredibly intimate with you far too soon to begin any intimate relations in the first place. My stay with them at the Ishimura was atrocious. I'm definitely not going back anytime soon.
All bad jokes aside, Dead Space is a damn good looking game. The presentation through the graphical and sound design is fantastic, especially on PC. The ship feels dead, alone, but at the same time writhing with disgusting alien growth always off somewhere in the distance. If it were for the atmosphere and presentation alone, I'd be giving this game a high recommendation.
But, alas, far more problems hinder Dead Space from being a fantastic horror experience. For one, the writing's pretty stale. It's not bad. But not really that good either. The majority of the speaking characters are all pretty one-dimensional and not that interesting to talk to. And the story tries to tie such emotional weight for Isaac and his wife, Nicole, but it just isn't there. The main reason behind this failure to feel any emotion with Isaac is that he's a silent protagonist.
"But, Double Uppercut, that's a strange criticism for you to make! You like Half-Life and Portal, don't you? They have silent protagonists and they're the best games ever. Why are you hating on Dead Space for having the same thing they have?"
Well, you can enjoy cheese but it doens't go good on everything, does it? I dare you to smother some melted cheese all over some ice cream and tell me it's delicious.
See, a silent protagonist is supposed to be used purely for player-immersion. If you want to create a character the player can empathize with, they have to speak. I relate to the struggles of Kratos (only in the first God of War) and Joel from the Last of Us, because they're given enough time to have their characters fleshed-out and distinct enough for you to learn who they reall are, as well as care for them. Do I think Gordon Freeman, Chell, or Link are fantastically-written characters? Of course not! They're merely vehicles for the player to immerse themselves in the larger game world. They don't have backstories, and if they do you personally experience it because they ARE you. Isaac feels like a player-driven vehicle, but whenever his wife is thrown into the picture or the question of his insanity is brought up, I feel nothing. I don't know who Isaac is, and I honestly don't care.
The gameplay, while pretty fun, is a little clunky too. I'm not a huge fan of how Isaac controls. He tends to walk around a little too awkwardly and the looking around with the mouse is a little too slow. Even when the sensitivity was bumped up, Isaac just wouldn't look around right.
On top of that, the game has a weird upgrade-system bolted on that seems to cater more towards an action-focused style of gameplay rather than a horror-focused gameplay. Silent Hill gave you weapons but you didn't have to worry about upgrading them or upgrading your health. It was purely focused on you surviving. While playing Dead Space, I was always thinking about saving money or extra supplies to buy stuff and make Isaac more powerful, which doesn't feed well into that isolated-horror game vibe. It's more of a mechanic for action-focused shooters and fighting games. By the end, I didn't have my metaphorical pants scared off, I felt like a bada**.
That's f***ing terrible. EA, you should be ashamed of yourselves.
That's just the problem that lies at the heart of Dead Space. It's not that scary. Sure, the monsters are pretty freaky and jump out at inopportune times, but they don't have a lot of presence- ESPECIALLY towards the end of the game when you mow through hordes of necromorphs by the dozens. It's not like Silent Hill where each fight with one of the monsters you'd encounter felt as intimidating as the last, because you never upgraded your character. You always had the same gear and the same health bar. Maybe the designers of Dead Space should have focused on limiting your supplies and making the creatures much tougher to reinforce that horror vibe.
And maybe I should stop talking about how much I love Silent Hill during every god**** horror review I write.
For what it's worth, Dead Space is a fine game. I think it's pros outweight its cons. The visuals and atmosphere and inventive anti-gravity and space segments really make up for what is otherwise another bland science-fiction horror story. It feels like so many ideas were taken from other horror stories like Alien, The Thing, and even The Shining to some extent. It just doesn't have much to it to really stick with you after you've finished the game. If EA really fleshed out the game by making it more of a horror game than an action game with little horror elements thrown in, this could've been a lot better. But I'm sure people can find some enjoyment in what terror this game provides.
However, I think you could play Close Your Eyes for free and it's a much better horror experience than Dead Space. I'm giving it a 5/10. It's a pretty solid game without any defining features to make it fantastically memorable- either as terrible or wonderful. If it intrigues you, go buy it. But if you're looking for something truly frightening, I'd recommend you try out something else.

Anti-chamber is an abstract puzzle game played from the first person perspective that features alternating pathways between puzzle areas. For example, there is a coridoor in the game that you will be seeing a lot of because after walking down other coridoors and looking back, you will be in a different area. The area you explore is fairly large and has lots of puzzles and secrets, and everywhere seems to be connected.  There isn't really a story to this game at all, infact there isn't even a main character. You might aswell assume yourself to be a floating gun! But that doesnt detract from the overall experiance of the game, especially in an industry that is over-saturated with pointless cliché stories that are shoved down your throat.
The game is essentially made up of different puzzle areas that require different techniqes to get past them.The puzzles consist of laser beams that open or close doors, platfoms that you have to jump on in order to get higher or lower, platforms and walls that can appear or dissapear deppending on whether or not you are jumping or moving fast, and special 'guns' that can absorb and shoot out cubes. The cubes can be used as platforms, but there main purpose is to block or triger beams to hold open doors.
while there is no drive or goal to the game other than to explore and get to the next puzzle, there is an 'endgame' of sorts and replay value can be found in the nature of speedruns. some people have got to the endgame in under 3 minutes! It is very interesting to go back after you have finneshed and see pathways that you didnt before.It took me nearly 12 hours to beat Anti-chamber, and i enjoyed every minute of it.
:Anti-chamber uses the Unreal Engine and has a clean graphic style. Some people have criticised the game for its simplistic graphics, but i felt the game worked better for it. The white coriddors can lead you to all kinds of different places and the game wouldnt really work if every area had its own unique graphics or style. The colors used also give you hints to where you are and you can easily find your way around after getting used to the mind bending nature of the game. Anti-chamber doesnt have a main menu or a pause menu, but instead boots into a closed room with clickable options on the wall and a map, which you can use to travel to places you have visited. This map also shows how all the rooms are linked to each other.
The only problem or issue with this game is probably the performance.The cubes used in the puzzles can be placed in an open square shape to generate more cubes inside it. but if you place to many cubes down and leave a big gap, the game will sometimes crash becasue it cant handle that many operations at once. It is only a very minor concearn though because the game has no loading screens what so ever and you can quickly get back to the puzzle after booting the game up again. This might be more of a problem on lower end machines though.
If you like puzzle games that make you think outside the box and explore then you will love this game, but if you like a story driven experiance or an action oriented experiance then you might not like this game as much. If you see this game on sale, and you are curious about it, then i would fully reccomend that you buy it just to try it out. it is different enough that you probably won't regret buying it, unless you hate puzzle games and exploring everywhere.

However, even if tactical parts are stripped down to a certain extent, this remake isn't anymore a simple remake. It's a remaster or a reboot; it has a rather good story line, it adds tons of gameplay features to consider being really good design choices, it got rid of bothering features like the air combat system (which had an awesome music track in the original nonetheless) and of course it has considerable visual/audio overhauls. This game stays true to its root(s) in a degree that it indeed is comparable to the original game (which is a really rare achievement for reboots) but, in my opinion, blows it away with so many additions that it beats the classic masterpiece.
