What an absolutely wonderful game. For anyone who has ever played the Lego games before, this is a giant step up, particularly if you haven't played since the early games like I have.  They added voice acting, open world, more detail, just everything.
The amount of characters you can unlock is staggering, and they even group characters that are the same. So the variants of Iron Man are all in one rotating selection rather than separate characters themselves to pad out the character list that's already enormous. The open world of New York is amazingly fun to go through, and the game gives you many ways to go about it. The voice acting is top notch, they even managed to get Clark Gregg to reprise his role as Coulson, although having James Arnold Taylor as Spiderman was a bit offputting at first, kept seeing Ratchet instead of Spiderman.
New York has many side-quests for you to do to unlock new characters, vehicles, and Gold Bricks, many of which require you to get new powers to obtain them so you can't get them all in one go. The streets are littered with attention, constant amounts of Studs placed around for you to pick up, with each area having completely different patterns and placements so no two buildings are the same. Really appreciate the time the folks who placed those put into it. You can hijack cars, although they're much slower than any form of transportation you already have, and drive into other cars, drive like a maniac, etc. But since it's a Lego game the characters don't break apart, they mainly just fall down and yell at you to watch where you're going.
Side-quests by themselves are pretty standard, either you go pick something up, fight a wave of enemies, escort someone through the open streets, or race someone. The best part of them is honestly the starting and ending comments the characters make, and that makes up for the monotony of the whole thing.
The writing is great, tons of jokes for kids, tons of jokes for comic fans, tons of jokes for adults, tons of everything for everyone to enjoy. The writing is also really aided by the silly things characters do in the background, like The Hulk sweeping things, or Coulson making jumps to save things Fury threw away, etc. SDeadpool can get to be pretty annoying, but I understand that's his entire thing, so I can deal with it, while Spiderman can be annoying at the start but ends up being enjoyable. Iron Man/Tony Stark is by far my favorite character along with The Thing, they both were great.
The story levels are very enjoyable from a writing standpoint. It's really nice to hear the silly banter between characters and see them in the cutscenes. The levels feel alright, they're basically just "Find a way to get this guy over here so you can get him to open something up for the other guy to open up" over and over without much change throughout the entire game.
Regarding gameplay, the fighting is the same as it always has been, mashing X to win, although the bosses seem to be way draw out this time. All bosses amount to spending ages waiting to hit them for one damage on their 3-6 heart health bar and then they fly away for a while and taunt you while sending a bunch of mooks your way. There's really no penalty at all for dying, you basically just lose 1,000 Studs which is absolutely nothing even from the start, and there's Extras to increase your four hearts to five as well. The actual use of the characters is fantastic though, any characters with flight, particularly Iron Man, are a joy to use pretty much anywhere and especially in the overworld. You get to go super fast and doing things like falling to the ground and boosting straight through the street never gets old.
Now, the game does have its own share of problems. The draw distance is very poor, you will see stuff in terribly low resolutions on anything pretty much two buildings away even on high. The top of the Empire State Building has its spire and the "fins"(Pardon me, don't know the exact name of those things) in some horribly low quality even when you're standing right next to it. In certain Free Play levels(5 for me) you can get stuck in elevators during area transitions, so you can't progress anymore because one character gets stuck in an infinite death loop and you can't switch or get them out in any way. Save and Quit sometimes fixes it, but not guaranteed. Help messages are a constant if you put subtitles on. They will never go away, they will always show up, even when you've beaten the game unless you turn off the subtitles. Getting stuck in items is very common, I would get stuck in boxes, walls, or sink into the floor at times which would require to either switch to another character and then wait a few seconds for the AI to teleport to me, or save and quit to fix it. The driving is completely awful, you turn so sharply that it's hard to control things and get caught up on the slightest of ledges in certain vehicles which makes the racing missing just that much harder. The AI pathing is awful. If you don't give the character an Iron Man(Or sometimes, even when you do) they will end up running into a corner for eternity because they can't get out. This is especially bad when they're Spiderman-type characters because they will get in a "Jump on wall --> Fall down --> Run at wall --> Repeat" pattern.
All in all, this is a wonderful game. It's extremely charming, appeals to pretty much everyone, and even though it's quite easy and repetitive it knows how to hit all the sweet spots, whether you're a comic book fan or not. You also owe it to yourself to try out Iron Man at least once, flying as him is amazing and done perfectly.

FIrst - the misleading bit about local coop is unfortunate and is certainly a strike against Capcom.  I'm hoping they rectify this issue for those who bought the game solely for this. But....
I wasn't planning on trying any sort of coop with this game so luckily I wasn't affected.  Res Evil has always been a single player experience for me, and to that end I found the first chapter of this iteration to be a lot of fun.  It keeps the structure of the first Revelations intact, but adds something new into the mix with a light crafting feature and an AI partner that is actually somewhat helpful.  If you've played any RE since the fourth one, you're fairly familiar with the gameplay from the start; and I'm glad to say it's just as tight a third person shooter you could ask for.  There are bits of exploration and action which are fed to the player at a good pace.  It's not quite the backtrack-fest of the earlier RE's, but it's also not the Michael Bay-fest of the 6th game.  It's a good balance and I appreciate the thought put into both the creepy atmosphere and the enemy encounters.  That said, the setting is a little ho hum so far (act 1), and I'm hoping to see some diverse environments as it continues.  Also of note is the performance - I had some stuttering issues, but when setting the framerate limit to 60fps this dropped dramatically, though not completely.  So I am hoping for a patch to address this.  Lastly I'd like to bring up Barry's daughter.  We're supposed to like her, and hope for her well being through Barry's sections; but she's far from agreeable.  With all her f-bombs and angsty complaining, I kind of wish Claire would accidentally shoot her - I've tried believe me!
All in all, a good start to what I'm hoping is a great game.  I give it a hesitant recommendation only because of it's performance issues.

Every once in a blue moon, a new game comes out that actually delivers on it's promises.  A game that feels next gen not only graphicaly but also mechanically.
Dying Light is that game.
Pros:
Absolutely Gorgeous.  Detailed character models, environments, weapons, ect.  Pretty much everything you look at is filled with artistic subtelty and gives a sense of craftsmenship.  I think it's great that variety throughout the game was not sacrificed in any way.  Everything looks good.
Viceral combat.  I can't even begin to describe how good the combat feels in this game.  You smack a zombie in the legs, it topples over.  Hit it in the head? It recoils and crys out in pain.  Every aspect of combat feels realistic and satisfying.
Cons:
Graphical requirements.  Pretty much the only con I can think of is how difficult it has been for some people to enjoy this game at a stable frame rate.  I wouldn't recommend playing this game unless your machine is up to spec.  You could probably run this game on an older machine but you wouldn't get to enjoy that "nextgen" graphical feel.  If that doesn't phase you, go for it.

I had heard lots of bad things about this game before trying it, but the truth is that this game is really fun. It's like a game of old-school Sonic: if you're skilled at using the environment to your advantage, the reward is incredible speed and grace. The plot, sadly, is terrible, and sometimes the level design can get in the way (stupid obligatory gunfights), but the basic parkour mechanics are a blast, and they control very smoothly. The first person camera can be troublesome at times, but it's really cool at others, and again, I blame the level design for that.
This game may have disappointed people at its original price tag, but I got this for peanuts when it was on sale. I finished the campaign in about 10 hours, though. Due to the short campaign, I couldn't recommend it at its current price tag of $20, but pick it up if it goes on sale.

Bottom line: I love this game!
It has everything a turn-based strategy game should have: great back story, addictive gameplay and highly replayable maps. Plus the new expansion, Enemy Within, adds a new element to the game, a rogue enemy organization which is not working directly with the aliens but is in fact working very much to undremine the XCOM project and your efforts to stop the alien invasion.
Finances and research play a huge role in this game and a careful balance is the key since the aliens will always have much better weaponry than you do until you reach the endgame. So, gradually increasing your tech knowledge in the game needs to also be balanced with funding for troop enhancements, new weapon/armor purchases and building new expansions of the XCOM facility. Additionally, as a tip you should ALWAYS be building satellites and lauching them ASAP in order to prevent countries from potentially abandoning the XCOM project altogether from increasing nationwide panic. The 'panic' level of a country can be increased from alien terror missions (which are the hardest of all mission types) and from not taking a XCOM mission in a particular country. But then again, you can only send your team members to one hotspot at a time so pay attention to the world panic levels carefully.
In the end, this is a fantastic and well-thought out game that is just a hellava lot of fun to play. Recommended for all fans of strategy turn based games.

Batman: Arkham Knight is the final entry in Rocksteady's Arkham Triology (Arkham Origins being deveolped by Warner Bros Montreal (I think)), and is a suitably epic conclusion to an amazing series.
The Arkham series' free-flow combat system returns and is once again improved on, feeling much more natural and smooth than it ever has, and it felt damn smooth and natural already. Rocksteady have added so many different enemy types and ways to take down your opponents (be that in combat or stealth), it's actually kind of daunting how much choice you have.  Relating to that is also the much-requested inclusion of the Batmobile, which seems to have the community divided. Going into this game, you will need to be prepared for the fact that you will be required to use the Batmobile, a lot. There is less puzzle solving in detective mode and combinations of gadgets this time around, instead there is more focus on traversing buildings and pulling switches/triggers with the aid of Batmans tricked-out car.
In-keeping with the arkham formula, the main story is always there, but there are also a multitude of side-quests for you to complete around Gotham city, which will feature quite a sizeable roster of villains from Batmans past, some we've seen before, like Firefly, Penguin and Killer Croc, but we'll get treated to some new baddies too, including
The main story is plenty meaty enough, but this just adds to it. By the time I had completed the story and all of the side quests (bar collecting the last of Riddler's Riddles, which yes, there's still fecking' loads of em), I had clocked in just over 40 hours of gameplay, which, for a single player AAA game, is pretty impressive these days (this also includes the DLC missions, but they only contribute about 1 and a half hours of that playtime).
Even then thats not it, as challenge maps also return. I'll admit I was fairly dissapointed at all of the predator challenge maps, but the combat ones are great, and at 54 hours in-game I've yet to complete even half of the total, which includes combat, predator, batmobile racing and batmobile combat challenges.
This game all-and-all has really impressed me, not only with its story, gameplay and graphics, but also in how they took the devastating mess of a port from release and have transformed it into one of the best-running games I've played, up there with ALIEN: Isolation (system specs can be found on my profile). I fully recommend picking up this game as soon as possible!

My machine did struggle at times and there were a few instances where it wasn't clear what i was supposed to do next.

+ Story mode:  Good survival horror atmosphere and is overall interesting so far.  There is a good balance of action and survival/puzzle mechanics.
+ Raid mode:  Greatly expanded upon compared to Revelations 1.  I can already tell that this will be where the majority of my playtime will come from.
- Graphics:  Texture quality is far inferior to RE6 and even RE5 (a game that was released in 2009).  It looks like an upscaled game that was originally designed for a handheld, similar to the Revelations 1 port.  Revelations 2 was designed for consoles and PCs though so there is no excuse for this.  The contrast is also bad.  Dark areas are overly dark, and bright areas are overly bright no matter how you adjust the settings.  There are no proper Anti Aliasing options, the only choice is blurry post processing FXAA.  There is also a constant grain filter applied that can not be disabled.
- Game stability:  I have had a couple of freezes when exiting the game that forced a shut down (couldn't even get the task manager to come up).  Others are reporting huge dips in FPS, I have had no problems myself after the second patch.
- Lack of co-op:  As of release there is no story mode or raid mode co-op (online or offline).  They are planning to add online raid mode co-op eventually but there is no reason this shouldn't have been included out of the box.  This is a feature that Capcom outright lied about.  They advertised offline and online co-op up until the day before release and then changed the store page description once everyone started complaining.  This sort of false advertising is unacceptable business practice.
- Microtransactions:  Want extra storage space for your raid mode gear?  That'll be $1.99.  This isn't an MMO, save files are stored locally so there is no reason for this.  This is just a cheap cash grab attempt.
Overall the core gameplay experience of both Story and Raid mode are dank.  However, the lack of polish, false advertising, and microtransactions feel like a slap in the face and hinder the experience quite a bit.  I'm sure I will put a good amount of time into RE Revelations 2 mostly thanks to the raid mode but I can not recommend it at this time due to the glaring faults.  I will update this review if Capcom addresses these outstanding issues in a future patch.  Until then, this stank turd isn't worth the asking price.

So as of late I've been pretty bored with games. I've played Mass Effect and found that fun, have been mulling around on Ori  and the Blind Forrest, and have even bought and dowloaded other games that just don't seem to hold my attention. Well, I got some news for you, because I literally have played this game over a four day period from start to finish and loved every minute of it. Dead Space brought horror and dread back into my gaming library like no other game has in a long time. I'm not one for horror games, but if you enjoy sci-fi/action/horror and games like Mass Effect I HIGHLY reccomened you try this game!
Pros:
- Great use of multiple weapons and different functions for each weapon
- Unique grotesque monsters designed off of actual dead and multilated corpses for extra dramatic effect
- Enemies are difficult to kill in the sense that they have their own mechanics as in how to kill them all (cutting off limbs etc)
- The character Issac may be a silent hero, but certainly a badass for going through some f@$ked up sh#t.
- Unique Horror and jump scares
- Sound design is wonderful, and you'll learn to hate violin after this game. (Lol)
- Good use of starvation on items in certain sections of the game to make you feel like you're at impossible odds until you win.
Cons:
- Controls are odd and clunky at first, and melee animations and usage is nearly pointless and difficult to actually use
- A maze like game where scenery stays stagnent for most of the game and can be boring at times when you enter a room designed like previous ones to know what lies ahead (obviously some baddies from a vent or from a wall)
- The game can be very easily manipulated by the player after understanding all monster mechanics, and cheese strating enemies by knowing they cannot enter certain rooms or hallways. (By this I mean using a hallway with a door to protect you, running up so the door opens and popping shots to kill some baddies, then backing away from the door to stay shielded in your safe room)
- Ammo clutter for weapons you didn't purchase because the only two weapons you'll ever need is the assult rifle and the pizza cutter (If you play the game, you'll undertsand why i call it the pizza cutter lol.)
- underwhelming mini bosses and boss fights using the same mechanics as mobs, or using the same enemy as a boss multiple times.
All in all, Dead Space was awesome and I thouroughly enjoyed it! It has its ups and downs with boss battles or mechanics when in Zero gravity and more. But over all it was a fun theatrical experience with many scares. I had blood rushing through my body most of the game. It is loaded with creepy errie sounds coming from vents, objects in the world, dead boddies, and whispers and cries coming from the distance. I can't wait to start playing Dead Space 2! And that's exactly what I intend to do after giving my thoughts on the first one. :)

This is a game that is not deserving of the praise that it receives.  On the one hand, it has an interesting and unique graphical style and (for the first part of the game at least) has an entertaining way of undermining your expectations.  For example, you may walk down a cooridor and find that it never ends, and the only exit is to turn around and go back the way you came and you discover that the door you came in, actually leads out to a new location.
The game is filled with puzzles like this that defy your expectations.  Where things in the world change and your perspective and location play a key role in discovery of the solution.
That's the good, but the game is horribly flawed in several ways.
The first is that all the puzzles are presented without explanation or hint at their solution.  Because the world is horribly inconsistent, the only real way to solve a puzzle is brute force--to try everything you can think of.  As the game goes on and on, the things you can think of grow and grow and eventually even a simple puzzle can have dozens of time-consuming possible solutions.
Sometimes the solutions are clever and interesting, but often they're just not obvious.  It's like if I had hidden the key to a door behind a rock next to the door and you spent forever trying to open the door only to finally realize the key was there the whole time.  It's not a satisfying solution to the problem, it's just obscured.
Often the solutions aren't that easy.  They sometimes consist of building difficult bridges out of blocks or dragging blocks through hard-to-control keyholes.  If you are doing things right, this wouldn't seem like much of a problem, but when you are doing the wrong thing it just wastes your time.  Often, once you realize you have gone down the wrong path the only way back is to return to the start, which resets your progress in every puzzle.  Much  time can be spent unrewardingly as you try and fail different solutions.
The game also introduces tools but doesn't explain how they work.  I got one of the guns only to find that holding CTRL does something critical to solving puzzles.  There is nowhere in the game they suggest that CTRL does ANYTHING.  The menu which at first I felt was clever, doesn't adequately explain all the buttons that the game utilizes.  Eventually I accidentally discovered this additional control and that made me more frustrated than satisfied (Turns out CTRL is a replacement for the middle mouse button, and the middle mouse button isn't mentioned in the controls either.)
The puzzles are presented in a non-linear fashion so you can go to an area and spend time trying to solve puzzles you aren't equipped for.  It's hard to tell when you're inept at a puzzle and when you're not prepared to defeat it.  It's not like you go somewhere and the keyhole is triangular but you only have square keys.  Instead everywhere the game deceives you so you spend time exploring, only to often discover that there is nothing to find--you are just in the wrong place at the wrong time.
Ultimately, the reason this game is getting such praise is that the things the puzzles do are very interesting and surprising.  The puzzles toy with your expectations the way an M.C. Escher drawing is engaging to look at.  But what a player does to discover these solutions is just brute force trial and error.  There is little smarts to solving the puzzles and so it's not a rewarding endeavour to attempt to solve them.
Seeing all the puzzles solved in a video would be way more engaging than playing this game, and ultimately games should be fun to play.  When gameplay fails, the game fails.

When this game was first released I was excited. It felt fleshed, it felt as if they had taken care to revive my childhood and introduce it to a new audience. It looks good, sounds well, and has a repetoire of tactics you can perform with your sense of play. It all felt so good, at first. Then the game fell to complete and total♥♥♥♥♥♥
At first it was nausiating that I couldn't tab out without the fear of the game unexpectedly crashing; this meant I couldn't reply to instant messages from friends, or see how a download was coming as I passed time. Fine, I can deal with this. I learned to play Xcom in an enviroment where I didn't require the need to respond to anyone. Had that been the only bug, I would have been fine. But of course it isn't.
Then another game breaker approached. This one involved an issue with the game locking itself on a character if you had chosen to reload a gun after you had selected over watch and not confirmed the overwatch. There's a work around for it (though there shouldn't even NEED to be a work around for it) whereby you switch to your soldier's other weapon. However if you're like me you'll have two heavies on your team. They can't switch weapons, they can't alter anything. The only thing you can do is close the game down and lose your progress, then try and stomach the desire to play to that point again.
However the number one breaker for me is the infinite animation loop. Every so often you'll move a unit into place. Nothing will happen. You won't be forced to sit through the annoying animation of the startled motion where the aliens scurry in a panic to take cover. That's fine. But as it turns out the aliens should have panicked when that unit came into sight; so they skitter and panic in an infinite loop where they go no where, but are shown to run in place. This goes on forever. There are no options to select, the HUD is gone, and you can't even escape the game by normal means. You have to tab out (maybe that will crash it automatically!) and either force the program to exit with a right click, or control+alt+delete and close it out.
There are numerous other bugs in this game that makes it feel like they had shoveled it out in a hurry. To what hurry, exactly? I wasn't expecting an Xcom game to ever be re-introduced to the market since the last game fumbled into existence in 2001. It would be 11 years before another one would see the light of day, and it barely works. If you even get into a groove and forget to save, it will put you off the game for an extensive amount of time. You don't want to waste hours of play and lose it all to some bug they have yet to polish it out of the system.
If you want this game, pirate it. Don't bother paying for a malformed product; encourage the developers to take their job seriously and make them pay through the nose. Had I paid full price for this, I would be hosed in anger and fought violently to get my money back. But it was part of a humble bundle. So it was nice to get it for the $5.50 I paid.

As someone that grew up playing the original UFO and TFTD games (alongside other Turn-Based classics like the Jagged Alliance franchise), the genre will always have a special place in my little gaming heart. I was both optimistic and hesitant when I heard about a franchise reboot for XCOM-- excited, of course, but would it live up to the gold standard already carved out by its predecessors?
Make no mistake, the core gameplay *concepts* are all present and accounted for, but the mechanics have changed. XCOM now concerns itself with one central HQ, removing the need to micromanage several different bases. Radar coverage is replaced with remote satellites, and each continent is nice enough to allow you some hangar slots to police the airspace. Within the battlescape, your squaddies now perform two 'actions' per turn, as opposed to the traditional TU system. Move, fire, sprint and a handful of unique abilities replace the classic system I grew up with, and it's... different. Admittedly, I had a little culture shock when I first jumped in, but I feel like it's a case where change really can be a positive thing. My hesitation about the new system faded even within my first session-- it's a genuinely intuitive set of mechanics that very quickly grew on me.
All things considered, my optimism paid off. If you're like me and harbor a classical love of the genre, don't miss out. It's a different game, but I can't put it any more simply than this: The game is a legitimate credit to the franchise, and with the flair of a more modern look and feel, it truly lives up to the XCOM name.
The game still holds up in 2015.

Not a very complicated game.  While many other games have exciting engines and flashy graphics, this game harkens back to the '90s style of turn based action.  The interface is basic and easy to use.  There are plenty of Workshop quests to go on if you complete the main story line and want to keep playing.  Try your hand at GMing and craft a plotline for your fellow shadowrunners.  This reimagining does the tabletop RPG justice.

Good News:
This game stays extremely close to the feel of the core game of Shadowrun, so much so it feels like it's been released by FASA during the 90's in tone and theme,  It also tries very hard to give you customization of the shadowrunner classes or lets you make your own main character to get through the plot the way you want to.  The story is engaging and the characters are deep.
Bad News:
The core mechanic of combat feels simple.  It uses a turn based, seek cover mechanic which feels a bit like a slower version of Dawn of War II.  Combat starts abruptly and you can be left in the lurch.  There's also no way to end combat which makes some parts just a little bit of a slog once you kill all of your enemies and have to traverse the map taking turns.   I played a mage and feel like I got a little shafted because you don't get to play in the Matrix unless you want to split your skills, you can't assense, go astral, or summon elementals.  You're just a better, more versatible combat monster.
However:
The Good outweighs the bad.  If you were a fan of the tabletop RPG or like the theme of technology mixed with magic, it's definitely worth a playthrough.  If you don't like story or you expect more tactics in your combat, skip it.

I hesitated in picking up this game after reading a lot about how terrible the original campaign was and how the game was dull and boring. It also didn't help that I didn't really know anything about the Shadowrun universe. During the Summer Sale though, I was in the mood for something new, and picked it up. I just finished playing through the original campaign (Dead Man's Switch - DMS) and have to say, I'm glad I bought the game.
Getting the basics out of the way, I admit that DMS is very linear. There is a lot of reading involved. And besides combat, there's not a lot of interaction with the world. Still, as someone who knew next to nothing about Shadowrun before I started, I think DMS does a very good job of introducing the player to the world and the mythos surrounding it. The reading will probably be boring to someone who is deeply familiar with the setting, but I found it very useful. Gameplay is likewise straightforward which allows a new player to dive in without fear of messing up. I played a Street Samurai / Decker and had no trouble. I did find myself wishing I could build a party and level them up, outfitting them and whatnot ala Baldur's Gate, but perhaps that will happen in an expansion.
All in all, this game was well worth the $4 I paid. I also picked up the DLC, which I read is much better - I look forward to trying that next.

This is a very good game that begins decent and then improves with each episode to become a creepy, fun, action-horror experience. Although the graphics are not astounding, the atmosphere is suitably creepy with varied environments (including a nice homage to the past...). There are creepy enemy encounters, some great tension filled battles in which character switching is very useful, a few shock scares, and one shock scare in particular that *almost* made me scream, haha. There is varied gameplay between the Claire/Moira episodes and the Barry/Natalia episodes. While I generally enjoy stealthy games, I did find myself feeling that Natalia's ability was a bit to powerful and made the stealth component a bit easy. Overall, on Normal the game isn't too difficult, and I was a little surprised that most of the boss battles weren't very tough...I am eager to try the game on hard to see if this changes! Raid mode, although I have only played it for a couple hours, is very fun in an arcade-y, addictive, pick up and play sort of way. Combining this with the multiple difficulty levels, all of the things to search for and find, and all of the medals to attempt to acquire means that you are getting a substantive game for $25. Highly recommended!

There has been very little development in terms of mechanics, and the controls feel a little clunky and unpolished, particularly with mouse and keyboard. The same goes for the graphics. This game could have easily been made several years back from the way it looks and feels. The story so far is typical RE fare and I am having trouble getting invested in it. A successful start to the first episodic Resident Evil all while taking the elements that are in place for a traditional and memorable Resident Evil experience with the most effective scares the series has seen in years.
But thats not to say Resident Evil Revelations 2 dont have its problems with weird frame drops/stuttering and occasional crashes outside story mode (while connected to the online service), but the sheer amount of content you get for such a small price make these easy to overlook.
And while you wait for a new episode each week, go play the Raid mode (Hordemode with a few twists) for some more awesome zombie slaying fun. (Raidmode will have Online mode via a patch.)

I've played the first episode and have done just about all the gauntlets/maps in raid mode so I feel confident enough to write a review for this.
Story- It's pretty meh, but it's just the beginning so I'd imagine it picks up and gets better with further episodes.
Raid Mode- Fantastic as ever. I like most of the changes they made, though some are rather annoying and degrade the experience. There's plenty of levels to play through currently and you got enough characters to progress with. Overall good times.
Pros- Good bit of content for $6 if you buy the episode individually or $25 if you get the complete season. I managed to get 2 copies at a discount and it is plenty worf so far. Raid mode is the main course while the Story mode is like an appetizer at the current moment.
Cons- FPS drops harder that the bass in all dem fancy kazoo songs. Lack of offline co-op for story mode might bother some people, not me really. 2nd player would really only be either holding a flashlight or pointing and throwing bricks. Not too much fun. The real main problem is lack of offline and online co-op for Raid mode. What's the point of fighting off hordes of cancerous infected with the downs if you can't do so with a buddy? Fix the FPS drop and add Raid mode Co-op and I'm a happy camper. Also, the limit of weapons, parts, and discs you can store is terrible. In that regards, it's blantant cash grab with their expansion packs for storage. Bad Capcom, bad.
Bottomline- If you enjoyed the first Revelation's Raid mode, then get this game. Best would be getting the complete season as it's cheaper alternative than each individual episode or the retail copy that comes out in March. Unless your internet is bad, then well get the retail. If you're just looking for a quick bit of fun, just buy the episode and play Raid Mode. If you are all enamored with the offline Story Mode Co-op, get the console versions. If you don't like Raid mode then you're just outta luck.

A top-down, indie, roguelike spaceship simulator.
A particularly good example of a game with has a handful of basic concepts, which can be fleshed out to have an elaborate plethora of tactics.  For example, will you play a ship that focuses on weapons, if so, beams, missiles, lasers, or something else?  Will you play a ship that focuses on boarding parties, and teleports hand-to-hand specialists to kill the enemy crew?  Will you make a ship that revolves around the use of drones that attack the enemy or protect your own?  Will you do a mix of everything mentioned?  Do you upgrade your engines for more avoidance, or your shields to soak more hits?  Do you want better blast doors to protect your crew from boarders and isolate fires, or do you upgrade your sensors to see what your foe is up to?
My tip to you, do not feel bad for having to look up how to go about unlocking the other type of ships, as some of them have rather convoluted requirements that do not occur in every playthrough.
Speaking of playthroughs, the game was developed with a 10% win rate in mind, even on “easy,” and since the sectors are procedurally generated, it is possible that even through you did everything right, you can still get WTFROFLStomped.
You cannot do worse then -my- first playthrough, I can guarantee that.

First off, a thank you to Techland.
I'm a gamer who never falls for the trailer hype. Ever. Why? Because they're made to sell the game. Wait! Before you say "well duh, of course it's made to sell the game", just let me explain... Even the worst game ever made can have a badass trailer. It doesn't matter how big of a turd a game is, it can still look like the shiniest diamond with the help of a good trailer.
This is why I decided that before I bought this game I should probably check out some game play footage. This is where I throw out a HUGE thank you to Techland/WB for deciding to give select Youtubers exclusive access to this game before release. It really payed off for me, and probably for Techland as well.
On to the review!
I loved Dead Island and Dead Island Riptide (again, because I didn't fall for the trailer hype), and one of my favorite games of all time is Mirror's Edge. Therefore this game fits me like a glove. It has the braindead slaughter of zombies plus awesome free-running all wrapped up in a stunningly beautiful package.
Sufficed to say, this is a pretty solid game. However, not without its flaws and optimization was one of very few. My FPS dips to 45 at certain points, but most of the time it's a solid 75-ish. Good thing I'm not an obsessed performance freak, or I would've found that annoying and ripped this game a new a-hole just based on that. Yeah... I'm looking at you, fools. You know who you are.
Anyway...
I think Techland did the right thing when they decided to make this game (which was obviously meant to be Dead Island 2) and dump the semi-bad reputation of Dead Island in someone else's lap. It has the exact same mechanics of Dead Island and it plays exactly like a Dead Island game. Now this is not something bad. On the contrary. Techland learned from their mistakes with Dead Island - and obviously wanted to start over with a fresh franchise and thus a better reputation - and they managed to fix everything that was wrong with the Dead Island games.
I only experienced two bugs in the first 30 hours of playing the game; one where a zombie clipped through the hood of a car (happened 3 times) and me falling through the world when climbing a com tower (happened once and never again). That is not bad at all by any video game standard.
The crafting system is exactly the same as in Dead Island with one exception: you can't upgrade guns. This is neither a good nor bad thing. They are guns. Shoot a zombie in the head and it'll die wether you do 500 extra electrocute damage to it or not. Gun modifications could have been helpful when trying to take down some of the bigger brutes in the game, but it's not a big deal since you can avoid 99.9% of them anyway. Dying Light is not a gun-heavy game and you will not miss these upgrades.
I have one main rule when it comes to buying games; get roughly 1 hour of gameplay per euro payed. If you are like me you will not be disappointed. Granted I did get my game cheaper than on Steam at another retailer, so I was quite happy since it has already pretty much payed off, with me having played just about 50% of the main story in almost 31 hours.
And no in-game shop for micro-transactions! Thank you!
I've been thinking hard about the negative aspects of this game and I can't really think of anything. I haven't experienced anything bad or game breaking at all. The climbing is solid as a rock - no Assassin's Creed BS where your character jumps opposite of where you wanted him to go half the time - and the game's mechanics work well. The skill trees are helpful and actually do make the game a tiny bit easier for you, but not so easy as to you just running through the game without even trying. It really feels as if Crane has become more skilled at what he does and it's the perfect feeling for a game like this. The skills do exactly what they should. You are not a god, you are just a man who, as time goes by, learns how to take care of himself in a zombie infested world.
And of course, night missions are scary as hell. +1!
This game gets a solid 10 out of 10 from me. It's a breath of fresh air in an otherwise over-saturated market filled to the brim with rehashes, micro-transactions and badly optimized games with huge day one patches. Thank you, Techland. You did extremely well.

Who is this Game For?
==================
Fans of Horror, puzzling stories and third person shooting will find a lot to like about Dead Space. The story in Dead Space is one of its strong points. It tells a great cinematic sci-fi action horror tale. You can definitely see the inspiration from films such as Event Horizon, Aliens and The Thing.
Is it good?
=================
A lot of this atmosphere is due to the brilliant sound effects. The voice acting is good, but it's the background noise that really gets to you. Hearing monsters crawling around the air vents, or the growling of something possibly watching you, all adds to the level of tension and fear - especially during the quieter moments in the game, or outside the ship in the emptiness of space. The graphics help, too - this is a very impressive looking game with excellent lighting.
Does it have any problems?
========================
Another thing that starts to kill the scare factor is the few times when you run into other people still alive (usually not for long) on the ship. These are always scripted sequences where you find someone and almost at that exact moment they either kill themselves (they've clearly gone nuts) or get killed by something else. This is fine a few times, but after a while, it's just a bit much and starts feeling too convenient and a little bit fake.
As for PC ports go, it’s not the worst, but it does have its problems. There are problems with mouse lag, and running the game at higher frame rates. A lot of people still report audio shudder and crashing at desktop. All these problems can be fixed with a bit of tinkering
but I would still recommend playing the game with a controller.
Final Thoughts!
====================
Dead Space is one of best Survival Horror releases in years. Tense, violent and incredibly aggressive; playing it at night with a loud 5.1 sound system can provide you the most spectacular scare moments of your life. It is a potentially great game that's hamstrung by an attempt to completely ape a console controller with a mouse and keyboard.

This game is the best of both the horror and action genre. It mixes so many good elements to scare you through suspense, jump scares, gore, fear and the big broader threat that everyone could die if you aren’t successful. Dead Space has set the standard for Sci-Fi Survival/Horror and its name stills sends shivers down the backs of gamers almost a decade later. The game starts with you, Isaac Clark, with a maintenance crew attending to the distress call on the U.S.G. Ishimura; a massive mining ship. Things go south quickly as the ship crashed into the main hanger and the crew is nowhere to be found. Throughout your struggle to restore functions to the ship and find out what happened you have constant deadly problems to deal with. This game is very original in the way the threats develop and you deal with them. There are sequences where you have to solve zero-g puzzles, mazes in zero-g, fight enemies with unique abilities, time very careful threats from the decaying ship and use the full range of your abilities. The game has 12 chapters, which you can finish in about an hour each making it great to set down with natural pauses. The game has upgrades from the stores found around the ships and you need to balance your credits and upgrade pick-ups with your need for ammunition and health throughout the game. One of my personal favorite mechanics in this game has to do with the soundtrack changing from the ambience to combat music. Most games start combat music when you enter a room or an enemy spawns. In Dead Space, with the exception of cut scenes, the combat music doesn’t start until you almost make eye contact with an enemy. This makes it terrifying when that one enemy that you missed comes up behind you and grabs you suddenly out of the nice ambient space music. There are also many sequences when you are in the vacuum of space and the game lets you only hear one sound, Isaac’s breathing. Unless you see the enemy coming, he’ll be behind you. The most immersive aspect of the game is the face that there is really no HUD. Your health is displayed as a series of bars on the back of Isaac’s armor and when looking at your inventory he projects the screen from his armor rather than the game opening a menu. Overall, the game is a wonderful, immersive sci-fi survival/horror game that has really set the bar for its unique niche. I would highly recommend it and play it in a dark room with headphones all the way up in the dead of night.

When i first bought this game, i really loved everything about the game. The matchmaking and the server is really stable and smooth, something that rarely happens when you play a Co-op game from unpopular region, the gameplay is fun and challenging, the graphics is somewhat better than most of my games (at that point of time), and the soundtrack is badass.
The grinding of the game might be an issue to some, as it is to me, since you need to reach a certain level of perks to be useful, but it's otherwise can be ignored, since not all difficulty requires that high level.
And it was just that, a fun co-op zombie survival with great characters and gameplay. Fun to be played in a short burst, or when you're feeling like slaughtering a bunch of zombies.
Then development went a bit stale. Nothing really changed, nothing was really added, nothing much was new. It wasn't long until the whole game went stale as well, because there's so much you can do in a game until you get bored of it. With the slow grinding, several complex mechanism, and unchanging gameplay, i soon dropped KF2 and went back to other co-op games. There's a few gameplay spikes though, since after a while, Tripwire releases a new perk and new weapons. This doesn't really last long either, because again, slow grinding, several complex mechanism, and still unchanging gameplay.
Then the microtransaction hits. I don't know what Tripwire executives was smoking, releasing a microtransaction and cosmetic crates and keys, in the wake of Payday 2's microtransaction bomb. It was later revealed that Payday 2's microtransaction was due to their superior's demand, but in KF2's case, it wasn't about the superiors or stuff, it's their own decision to implement microtransaction, and it's there to stay. On that note, Tripwire added microtransaction, in an early-access game.
This sparked an outrage, and some players are abandoning ships. Everything since that point has been a wreck. The developer not hearing what the playerbase has to say, the playerbase getting frustrated, and then Tripwire started rolling out updates that doesn't sit well with the playerbase.
Up to this point of release, there's not really much to say, other than that some sacrifices was made to make this game exit early-access, and some portion of the playerbase is not pleased with the sacrifices made.
TL;DR If you ignore all those problem aboves, it's a great game by itself

For having a good amount of time on this game, i must say this game is pretty impressive. Despite this game being sitting in my library collecting dust me and a few friends decided to pick up and play it again. This game has a lot of variety and no game play will ever be the same! With randomly generated "worlds" being created every time it really creates different tactics and functions available for your Civilization every time. This strategy game is like no other...
You start anywhere in a "world" with a warrior unit and settler unit in the year 2000BC, from here you must thrive into the-brave new world (DlC reference) and start your civilization. You go through science and technology all the way to future tech from the wheel, to coal, to electricity and to spaceships. Throughout this course you are tasked to make your civilization the best!
Despite the game being slow at the start with limited choice, doors start opening up after every turn indulging you more into the game. This game is not to have superiority over "the world" but there are infact multiple ways of winning:Culturally, scientifically, total annihalation,win the UN vote or be the player with the highest amount of points at the set date victory . This game brings great challenge and you cannot pick it up for 30 minutes and leave, its a game that you will need to devote time and effort into in order to accomplish. So far i have only played the "fast" worlds where the years go quicker but "marathon" game modes can last up to days or even a week/s (i have not yet played this). Overall i think this game is a must play for those who love stratergy games and have ALOT of time on their hands. This game is surprising for a relic from 2010!

This game totally rocks!!  It's a little old, and if you're looking for graphics and cosmetics, go elsewhere, cause those are things you won't find here.  But it has everything else.  Lots of interactivity, like you just don't find:  a lot of the decisions you make for how you say things are just your own flair, don't make a difference, but decisions you make in game impact things early on and forward.  Some of these decisions, naturally, Shadowrun being a logical universe, require you to be able to do it-- so if you don't have the skill in question high enough, it's not an option-- but not to worry, there are more than two ways to skin a cat sometimes, and there's pretty much always going to be more than one.  Sometimes, that involves creativity- like buying coffee if you figure out a solution for a street junkie who wants more money than you (may) have, even if you talk him down in price (though you might have enough) but is too out of it to be able to get down to the cafe for himself, so, insert errand, you pay less than you would have doing it straightforwardly-- though it's the future, and real coffee is still pretty pricey (for coffee).
You get money multiple ways for different things, including of course selling loot-- but so far in my playing the game there's more of an emphasis on selling mission items, specifically software you stole, and by completing jobs and/or tasks.
Tasks:  this is also how you level up.  In this game, trust me from the start, you *really* want to explore the world around you.  There are people to interact with you, and as often as not, the things they want from you can give you a karma point.  You don't know what will give you karma points, but it's not hard enough to figure out looking around and seeing things you can help people with helps.  Karma would seem an odd name for the resource for levelling, but it's actually not, because you can do things like get a junkie help-- which you hear more about later if you do.  Again, you can pick how you go about getting her to get help, too:   do you play it higher-than-thou, at least that's how I see it, do you talk logic to her, do you scare her-- you might have to do two of those at least, actually, but I only played through once.  Just on the earlier point.
But back to karma.  You get karma for beating mission objectives, which again do not just come up without chatting, looking into things and such, clicking on things to figure out what's going on in the world around you-- if interactivity does not appeal to you, this is not the game for you; it is not simply fighting.  If it does, it's more complicated than I make it sound in experience, because there are so many different things to interact with... it would be hard to categorize.  *Ahem!*  You explore, you complete tasks, you get karma....
... and you level up!!  Leveling up takes up a lot of karma, and there's a whole lot to level up, so you have to pick and choose, but a lot of it you're just going to forget about anyway, because your character isn't specialized in hacking- oh you included that?  S/he is a super crappy fighter then, at least as far as I've gotten, but okay, that's what you get when you want to hack computers instead of being a gunslinger.
I kinda didn't like the extensive use of spell-like systems in this game to start with, but now that I've gotten more used to it, I just want to go all out when I have the credits and buy like everything and use it all.   The spell-systems are different, though they don't all get called that (there are three of them) and they're not as out of place as you may be thinking.  If you read about the game, bear in mind, there are guns and computers and hackers, but there are also trolls and ogres and dragons.  Just sayin'.
Oh.... the dragons are bad*** and you literally don't mess with them.  Taking down a dragon takes an army, not a small unit, generally speaking, and in this futuristic society the dragons wiped out large bodies of people before getting taken out... not all of them have been.   All of this is in the lifetime-recent past of the living, some of it having started *it's true* since after the game came out, presumably, but at any rate also before 2014, which is when I'm writing this.
Man, I've spent a fortune it seems on MMOs that I got sick of.... this game cost me under $5 while on sale and I can't get enough of it so far.  I'll get tired of it, too, but I'm definitely looking for another game for nothing again when I get tired of it... graphics aren't bad for being old and cheap budget, and I like reading the text better than listening, but oh, there is a lot of reading, did I say that?  lol... you have to read the conversations, no voice acting... it's all low-budget... just straight-up good creativity is what makes it such an awesome game.  Modding community too, though I haven't tried their work yet, no reason-- still playing through my first campaign.
So I highly recommend this game.... it should run on your computer if it's not a fossil, though I could be wrong, and I apologize if so.... this is the first review I've written for Steam, and the game definitely deserved some "credits."
Universe is scifi, if you missed that part, looks a lot cheesier than it is.  Lots of effects and ways to acheive them, grenades for instance that do different things, robots that do different things-- you have seriously limitied inventory, but you've got a killer size stash, so the limit is on missions (you can keep as much as you like, there's nothing there specifiying an inventory limit on your stash.)
To tell the truth, there are still things I haven't figured out how to do in game yet, or if there's a way to do them (I'm pretty sure I level my own team too, but I don't know how-- or even how to switch out their gear) but there's a help me section I've been having way too much of a blast to wade through lmao.... I don't have the credits right now to buy Igger a new gun anyway lol.
You have time after every mission involving fighting to wander around town and do more missives that are just interaction and figuring stuff out (nothing requiring a high IQ, don't worry-- just be curious, that'll get you more than far enough), during which time you can stock up on supplies, sell stuff, tip a dancer, that kind of thing... have a cup of soykaf!  Woo-hoo! lololol....
World:  Well-drawn.  It's like reading a good book, really.  There's stuff happening, nothing boring, lots, and I mean lots, of drama, nevermind you're a cold-hearted professional cutthroat, you care about sentiment because everybody does in reality and so therefore do you.  You may be bad***, and your team too, but you all care.... I'm only a little way in but I play this game for interacting with a world in more ways than one, with real results (albeit it's a game xD), and not so much so for adrenaline rushes or combat.  Gear is great-- not just armor and weapons, but lots of other stuff too.  You can replace limbs with robotic parts, use different-purpose grenades (including shrapnel xD), use medkits and trauma kits (the latter bring you back to life from a near-death encounter, but you don't have much inventory-- just 7 slots-- so it's not like this makes everything peachy.).. lots else
Anyway, the characters are all different, it's not like your team consists of the same 5 people, per se, though your party expands in time- they all have personalities, and they don't all feel exactly the same toward you, and while most of them follow your leadership as far as I've gotten, there are differences that come up-- after something adverse, one of them wants to share alcohol with you (which gives you a choice-- do I drink in this game?  there are more than just two answers).  Naturally there are limits to how much impact you have on storlyine six times in a single conversation, don't get me wrong-- but usually, if I think about it, so's life.  -noroom

Whatever your opinion of this whole PC same-screen co-op “scandal”, as some people say, the game itself is still fun to play. It’s Resident Evil, and comes with all the quirks and issues that have plagued the other titles, but is still a fun game to play.
As only one episode has been released, the story is still somewhat unknown. The events of episode one take place many years after those of the original game. You begin as Claire, waking up in a prison cell, with no clue as to where you are or how you got there. You soon meet up with Moira, Barry’s daughter, and adventure together. You do eventually leave the prison itself, only to discover where you are.
The second part of episode one has you playing as Barry, who received a distress call from Moira, and has come to the prison to investigate (how he tracked the location down we’ll either find out later, or may never know). He meets a young girl named Natalie, who winds up accompanying him in his search, because why not take a little girl into a monster infested location while you search for your daughter who sent out a distress call from a monster infested location.
The story isn’t too convoluted, yet, but that will surely change. Capcom is known for throwing twists and turns at every corner.
Once you find out where you are, you’ll come to appreciate the location. Capcom has done a great job rendering the prison and its surroundings, and you’ll get to see many parts of it, from both Claire and Barry’s perspective.
Gameplay is almost similar to the Outbreak games, where you control multiple people. As Claire, you’ll be accompanied by Moria, who holds a flashlight while you hold the gun. Why Claire is incapable of holding both a gun and a flashlight I don’t know, but that would throw off the whole mechanics of the game, I guess. After a certain point, you can freely switch between both characters, and you will need to do that for certain parts of the story. Moira can also find collectibles, or ammo, or other items by seeing a glint, then shining the light at the glint to make it interactive, allowing her (or Claire) to pick it up. If the AI is controlling Moira, you can’t do this.
The same goes for Barry and Natalie. Natalie can crawl through small spaces to open the way for Barry, while also being able to point at glinting objects (literally, you point), which allows her or Barry to then pick up that object.
Like the first Revelations, you can dodge enemy attacks, but the dodge seems far superior and actually works, compared to the first game. You have the quick turn (180), and can walk while firing.
The game looks good. Characters are well detailed, except for their faces. Claire quite often looks like she’s constipated. Environments are dark, disturbing, moody, dank, etc. I find the enemy models to be terrific.
The environment is done well, too. Trees cast an eerie glow from the sky, bushes and leaves rustle. Is it your AI partner running through that bush, or something else?
There isn’t a lot of graphical options to set in-game, and are pretty much standard fare.
And while the game does look good, it doesn’t look fantastic. But, such is life when it comes to what is essentially a straight port. Resident Evil games have always been developed with a console first attitude, and that’s fine. But Capcom is especially lazy and/or incompetent when it comes to porting games. Resident Evil HD Remaster is the exception to this rule, and is actually a very well done port.
The music, as usual for Resident Evil games, is great. If you pre-ordered it, you get some soundtrack selections. My game only has four music files, but I don’t know if more will be released with each episode, or if that is the extent of it.
Sound effects are great, and really lead to some tense moments. The acting, while passable, is like all Resident Evil games, and occasionally sounds forced while always sounding cheesy. The characters even poke fun at certain things, such as Claire exclaiming how she didn’t become a Claire sandwich, and Barry making fun of his master of unlocking comment from 1996.
And this is where Resident Evil Revelations 2 falters. The performance is spotty. Often times, when readying your gun to aim, there’s some slight lag as the game zooms in to your character’s head. There are lots of moments where the framerate stutters for no apparent reason. It’s a completely unoptimized product. Which is also evident when the game tells you not to turn off your console while its saving. Yes, the PC version tells you not to shut off your CONSOLE. If that isn’t incompetent “optimizing”, I don’t know what is.
I didn’t experience any crashes or startup issues.
So this is what’s causing an uproar by a lot of fans. The PC version of Revelations 2 is the only version not to have local, offline co-op. Not that it’ll be patched in later, but it just doesn’t have it to begin with. I don’t get the big deal myself, but I can understand how people feel deceived by Capcom, as this information was not originally in the game description, so people who pre-ordered or bought it thinking they’d be able to play locally with a friend are annoyed, and for good reason.
Online co-op for Raid mode (not the campaign) is to come in a later patch. If I remember, I’ll update my review accordingly whenever that happens.
The game is short. I completed both acts of the first episode in about three hours. Let’s assume each episode is about that time, you’re looking at twelve hours of a story once all episodes are out (four episodes at three hours each). It’s not horrible that it’s short, and it’s not a full priced game either, so value for money is pretty on par.
Raid mode, while fun, is somewhat boring at the moment, as you’re limited to playing yourself. Once co-op is patched in, I’m sure it’ll get better.
Don't judge the game based on Capcom's multiplayer issue. Judge the game on what it is; a game. Don't give it a bad review because you're ticked off with them, give it a bad review if it's actually a bad game.
It’s Resident Evil, and you either love or hate them. I, personally, have hated the fact that the games have taken an action-heavy stance, and I loved the slow and methodical pace of the first three games. However, it’s still a fun title, with what little time you’ll need to invest into it. And the story is always worth seeing.

Dead Space hooked me early and then went approximately nowhere.
(spoilers below)
I'm attracted to story-driven games.  And when innovative or otherwise interesting mechanics advance that story, so much the better.  Dead Space wasn't quite the opposite, but it was close.  Severing limbs was a little different, and it caused an impressively tense first encounter, but the practice quickly became rote.  The kinesis and especially stasis modules were fun to play with but really only amounted to toys - except when they were blatantly obviously required to pass an obstacle.
The story in Dead Space had a lot of potential, but very little of it was tapped into.  The marker was interesting, but it was barely touched upon until the game's conclusion.  Nicole is in the same boat, even though she played a minor role on and off earlier in the game.  Toying with whether she exists or not could have been far creepier and more engaging than it was.
I guess I went into this game expecting story-driven horror, and what I really got was mediocre action.  Irrelevant bonus: the map of the ship shown between chapters was a great throwback.

Plot Synopsis
Dying light is an open-world survival-like fps-rpg set in a fictional city. After a recent outbreak of a zombie virus you are sent in to the slums to recover a stolen document of the utmost importance to your employers, the only conditions is to not blow your cover. After a failed attempt at infiltrating via air-drop you are forced into helping your rescuers survive the virus in any way they need.
Positives: (no particular order)
+ Looks stunning
+ Combat system provides a fluid experience
+ Satisfyingly realistic freerunning ( - bar the 20ft falls broken by bags of rubbish)
+ Array of weaponry ranging from chair legs to automatic rifles.
+ Engaging Story
+ Night is terrifying
Negatives: (no particular order)
-  Optimisation needs work (60fps when looking one way, under 30 when looking another)
- May become repetitive
- Though fluid, parkour can occasionally stop abruptly due to grab detection not working properly
Overall, I do recommend this game to those who wanted more from dead island, and those who enjoy the FPS/melee genre in general

After 100+ hours on this game, I feel I have played enough to write a solid review. I preordered this game about 3 months prior to release and was able to play the game on day 1. After watching trailers and gameplay I was super hyped for this game (I am a huge zombies fan in general).  On day 1 as you can probably imagine the game had some optimization issues and ran very poorly for all the people using AMD hardware. These issues were resolved about 3 weeks later and as of right now this game runs very smoothly and consistently if you have a GTX 960 or higher. Visually this game looks amazing and the developers did a fantastic job with the graphics (the Chrome Engine 6 is stunningly beautiful if your hardware can drive it), something I always appreciate being a graphics fanatic. I played around 60 hours in the month of January, finished the game, and absolutley loved it. Not every game keeps me interested from start to finish the way this game did.
Now for those of you wanting a comparison between this game and Dead Island. This game is a HUGE improvement. The 4 player co-op is perfectly done and actually allows you to play through every mission (INCLUDING THE MAIN STORY), together with your friends. Another awesome addition is the Terrifying Day/Night cycle where the deadly volatiles come out and make even the best weapons seem like plastic. At some point you will find yourself outside as the sun goes down and the city becomes completely dark. then all you are left with is your flashlight and however far you have to run to get to a safehouse. The thrill of getting chased by Volatiles in the dark while running for your life is quite exhilarating. If you are looking for the best co-op zombie game to play with your friends, this is it, Period.
Although the storyline is quite predictable and ends with a somewhat displeasing boss fight at the end; it is pretty irrelevant in the grand scheme of this game, the game has Tons of other side quests for you to complete, most are rewarding and enable you to get some kick *** weapon upgrade or blueprint. The game is extrememely fun to just mess around in and have fun with your friends and there are many easter eggs and craftable items which enable you to keep making your character more and more OP and awesome. After 60 hours in January I have recently Racked up another 40 in the past 2 weeks after I found out about all the blueprints and easter eggs there are to complete (all 40 hours spent playing with friends and people I met playing Dying Light).
I must take a quick moment to mention how gratifying it is for me to kill a zombie in this game. Not even Dead Island has as good animations as this game does for executing zombies. I can literally drop kick a zombie to the ground, run at it, cut its arms off, throw a knife in its head, cut its head off, knock it to the ground again, cut its arms and legs off, kick the body away leaving the body parts scattered 10 feet from each other, and then burn the remains. Now that might have sounded gory to some of you...but for those of you sick of playing COD zombies and only being able to shoot a zombie in the head...well..you can probably guess why killing zombies in this game is Nothing short of amazing.
Lastly I have to mention the Parkour and open world of this game. I have never played a game with such a fun parkour system as this. I can literally entertain myself for hours just having races from one side of the city to the other with friends; Jumping over rooftops and getting creeped by those moments when your "Not sure if your gonna be able to make the jump to the other building". The parkour system in this game is designed perfectly and surprisingly I can say that I have never encountered any glitches when jumping around and climbing walls where I fall unexpectedly.
Bottom line, it's the best zombie game out there and the best game of the year for me. It will be interesting to see how Dead Island 2 compares to this game when its released.
Very good and exciting game, I recommend to everyone!

This is literally an incredibly extended episode of the show, and because of that it has to be extremely streamlined for fans of the show as well as casual gamers. So think of it as a "beginners RPG" where you have 1 main quest which is esentially the meat and potatoes of an episode of the show, and the side quests which don't branch off into extended side plots or have any effect on the main story, they are mearly there to serve as fanservice for die hards of the show. When i first bought this game, i really loved everything about the game. The matchmaking and the server is really stable and smooth, something that rarely happens when you play a Co-op game from unpopular region, the gameplay is fun and challenging, the graphics is somewhat better than most of my games (at that point of time), and the soundtrack is badass.
The grinding of the game might be an issue to some, as it is to me, since you need to reach a certain level of perks to be useful, but it's otherwise can be ignored, since not all difficulty requires that high level.
And it was just that, a fun co-op zombie survival with great characters and gameplay. Fun to be played in a short burst, or when you're feeling like slaughtering a bunch of zombies.
Then development went a bit stale. Nothing really changed, nothing was really added, nothing much was new. It wasn't long until the whole game went stale as well, because there's so much you can do in a game until you get bored of it. With the slow grinding, several complex mechanism, and unchanging gameplay, i soon dropped KF2 and went back to other co-op games. There's a few gameplay spikes though, since after a while, Tripwire releases a new perk and new weapons. This doesn't really last long either, because again, slow grinding, several complex mechanism, and still unchanging gameplay.
Then the microtransaction hits. I don't know what Tripwire executives was smoking, releasing a microtransaction and cosmetic crates and keys, in the wake of Payday 2's microtransaction bomb. It was later revealed that Payday 2's microtransaction was due to their superior's demand, but in KF2's case, it wasn't about the superiors or stuff, it's their own decision to implement microtransaction, and it's there to stay. On that note, Tripwire added microtransaction, in an early-access game.
This sparked an outrage, and some players are abandoning ships. Everything since that point has been a wreck. The developer not hearing what the playerbase has to say, the playerbase getting frustrated, and then Tripwire started rolling out updates that doesn't sit well with the playerbase.
Up to this point of release, there's not really much to say, other than that some sacrifices was made to make this game exit early-access, and some portion of the playerbase is not pleased with the sacrifices made.
TL;DR If you ignore all those problem aboves, it's a great game by itself

One of the most bemusing first person puzzlers I've ever experienced. To succeed, you must banish all notions of how standard 3D space works and learn the rules of the game to beat it (The Matrix!). Below are some positives and negatives:
Positives:
Art style: a beautiful minimalist's dream, taking the Mirror's edge style to extremes. Unambiguous objects ensure you can always see every part of the puzzle.
Intuitive mechanics: Once you understand a puzzle, completing it is easy: the mechanics are tight and easy to control.
Not frustrating: a puzzle may force you to quit, but curiosity brings you back, wiser than before and filled with awe when you complete each puzzle.
Non-linear level design: the path frequently splits and allows you freedom to take whichever path you want.
Story: subtle, no cutscenes, all mechanically driven.
Negatives:
Art style may not appeal to everyone.
Level design: while non linear (good), some paths are impossible to complete without completing other paths first.
A great game exploring how the 3D world is boring, and always impressing you with new gimmicks and challenges, no two puzzles are identical.
A solid puzzler that succeeds to throw you off, and throw you into little lessons and thoughts about life. Simple, by nature, and by visuals, yet deeply complex and enthralling. Get it.

***A lot of people are still complaining about the PC port being underwhelming, despite having been patched into March of this year. Let me make something clear: in my 74 hours of playing this and getting 120% completion, the game only crashed twice for me. Once during the Batgirl story DLC, and another during one of the late-game side missions. Another late-game side mission had a pretty glaring glitch, but this is also in the console versions and it doesn't look like that's ever going to be patched. It's nothing game-breaking though. Aside from that, the game ran fairly smoothly, and I have a pretty decent rig with a GTX 780. The only times it dipped significantly for me were in extreme PhysX scenarios, and that was only in two areas. At max settings, I got an average of 50fps.***
You use the Batmobile a LOT in this game. However, to me that's only an issue if it's not fun. And most of the time, it is. Using it to take out mooks and chase down APC's, the Riddler racetracks, and general usage in conjunction with Batman's other abilities using it with the remote control, all of that is fun and I don't mind it at all. The Batmobile is also a much faster way of getting around the city.
It's just that you're in it way, way more often than you are on foot in this game. Remember how in Arkham City there were a lot of indoor areas? The steel mill, the museum, the GCPD, the subway? You didn't spend a huge amount of time outside unless it was doing side missions or getting to your next objective. Here, you're almost always outside. There are only three sizeable indoor areas to explore: the movie studio, the airship, and the shopping mall. There's one other, but it's navigated almost entirely with the batmobile, even the boss. There's not a lot of atmosphere in this game compared to City, and especially not Asylum.
The tank battles are fun at first, but they get old pretty quickly. The biggest problem is that they take forever. It feels like they just keep spawning endlessly with no end in sight, and shooting them down is monotonous and doesn't take any skill or strategy like with combat and stealth. It can get pretty intense and engaging, but often it feels like you're fighting an armada of tanks just because the game feels like it.
***Tips from me: upgrade the Batmobile ASAP if you want to get as much enjoyment out of these as possible. Every point you ever make should be put into the Batmobile until it's fully upgraded. Trust me. Also, in the options, set the tank mode to Toggle, not Hold. This makes the controls much more like traditional driving games, and more comfortable. I don't get why this wasn't the default.***
The combat and stealth are better than they've ever been, especially the stealth. Enemy variety is through the roof and the AI is much smarter than before, and you have to be on your toes this time around. Everything you do has been streamlined to a point where it's going to feel weird going back to previous games after this. The music is also fantastic. It has more strong, emotional melodies rather than the Hans Zimmer-esque cinematic stuff they were going with before. Definitely my favorite OST in the series.
And the plot? I won't spoil it, but I will say it's pretty weak with several things that are either unnecessary, don't make sense, or do make sense, but are still being explained and referenced several hours after we get the picture. The ending was especially egregious, and a poor excuse for not making any more Arkham games. There are a lot of great little moments though that tugged at my emotions more than the previous games ever did, and also a lot more Scarecrow hallucinations to spice things up. It's almost like a horror game sometimes.
The Riddler stuff is back, but unlike City which had over 400 trophies to collect (ugh) this time there's only 243. Still over half, but there's a LOT more variety this time. Racetracks, robots to either beat up or order around to press switches, a Simon Says minigame, following a trail of question marks with your car, and a lot of trophies just sit there without you having to solve a puzzle to grab them. No need to backtrack to every area with Catwoman either. That being said, the riddles are much, much harder than before. There were several I gave up on and looked at a walkthrough for because the solutions were so obscure.
The DLC is overall pretty nice, but not worth the $40 it originally cost. I got the Premium edition with all the DLC for $17 as part of the Halloween 2016 sale, so I'm satisfied, but I understand if some people aren't. The story packs aren't much, they're just a series of stealth/combat challenges with no exploration, and there's barely any "story" at all to them. The Batgirl story pack is great though, because you get your own HUB world to explore with multiple areas to go to, plus a sidequest and Riddler-esque minigames. As far as everything else, the challenges are back with a bunch of racetracks based on the 60s show, and the Burton/Nolan movies. You even get to hear the 60s show theme song and the Danny Elfman theme play as you drive. No Hans Zimmer music though. It's great how you can use the alternate skins in the story mode too, since the cutscenes are rendered in real time.
There's a lot of stuff exclusive to the PS4 version though. The Scarecrow Nightmare missions for example, which are almost like a cut final boss to the game, and the 60s Batman skin, despite every other version having 60s Robin, Catwoman and Batmobile. Even in the Batmobile DLC tracks, you're driving in the suit, so there was no reason to cut that out. Thankfully, you can mod it back in with no issues, but every other DLC thing isn't available. If that stuff matters to you, then you want that particular version because it will never be modded.
Despite everything, I consider this game the best in the series. There's just so much content and streamlined gameplay that I can't not recommend it.

Let's start with bad sides of the game. At first, this game DOESN'T have co-op scenario! It's not a big problem for me cause i love the times game leaves me all alone but for those wants to play with a friend, it's a stupid thing.
