I don't know if I really need to review this...I mean, its Half-Life 2! EVERYONE should play it! But, anyways, let's get to it.
Half-Life 2 dumps you into a dystopian society under the rule of a mysterious alien force known as the Combine. As it turns out, your character (the now-legendary HEV suit-wearing Ph.D Dr. Gordon Freeman) indirectly caused this to happen (see events of Half-Life 1 for details :).
Gameplay: 10/10 The game is extremely well designed, and though the graphics look a touch dated by today's standards, it is still a fantastic experience. The chase scenes where you are escaping a city via airboat through abandoned canals gets your heart racing, and while you're in the city, there are many small touches that help to emphasize the depressed nature of the beginning of the game. It was one of the most immersive gaming experiences I've had.
Story: 9/10 To top off having good gameplay, the storyline is fantastic. While not the best I've ever seen (that title goes to The Ur-Quan Masters, aka Star Control II), it is still quite good. The dialogue is reasonably good, the voice acting is quite well done, and the animations to go along with it really make the story hit home. When a character is talking to you, they actually make eye contact with you. The lack of cutscenes helps a lot, as well, keeping you "in your role" throughout the storyline.
Characters: 9/10 The characters in the game are well-designed, with your companions having distinct personalities and behaviors. The only main character that I feel is the exception to this rule is Dr. Judith Mossman. I'm not entirely sure what to make of her, to be honest, not to mention that it's never really made clear why she's in the game in the first place.
I also need to take a moment here to give one of the main reasons for my love of this game: Gordon Freeman is one of the most awesome ideas for a main character ever! Instead of choosing a soldier or ex-soldier (or perhaps a hired gun of some kind), Valve elected to go with a theoretical physicist with a Ph.D from MIT. The other bit of genius is this: since Dr. Freeman doesn't say anything, it allows the player to "tailor" his actions to create their own personal version of the protagonist. For example, in my playthrough, becuase of my playing style, Gordon Freeman is a calm, reserved, cautious man, always on alert for things to jump out at him and always trying to keep as many allies alive as possible, whereas when my friend plays as him, he's a maniac with a death wish who rushes into things and sprays bullets everywhere, lol.
Weapons/In-Game Items: 7.5/10 This is really the only category in which the game comes a bit short in my opinion. Don't get me wrong, there's still plenty of weapons to choose from, ranging from pistols to assault rifles to RPG's, but I still feel like some more diversity would have been nice. The original Half-Life did an excellent job of this, giving you everything from experimental energy-based weapons to classic assault rifles to exotic alien weapons. Still, its not enough to really hold back the game. As far as other items go, there's not a whole lot to say. The Gravity Gun makes up quite a bit of diversity in and of itself, allowing you to make kills with various props within the game. I mean, okay, there's no fancy laser cannons or anything, but I killed a Combine soldier with a toilet, so that counts for something, right?
All in all, I give this game a very solid 9/10. This game is probably one of the most complete packages around in term of overall quality. It may not win in any one category over other games, but it does a good enough job with everything that it doesn't matter. As you might be able to tell by my profile pic, I reallly, really like this game :) So, stop reading this review and go get the Half-Life Complete pack right now, because once you play one, you'll want to play them all!

About game:
Half-Life 2 (stylized as HλLF-LIFE2) is a first-person shooter video game and the sequel to Half-Life
Gameplay:Like its predecessor, Half-Life 2 is a single-player first-person shooter broken into several chapters, permanently casting the player as the protagonist Gordon Freeman. The sequel has nearly the same mechanics as Half-Life, including health-and-weapon systems and periodic physics puzzles, except with the newer Source Engine and improved graphics. The player also starts without items, slowly building up an arsenal over the course of the game. Despite the game's mainly linear nature, much effort was put into making exploration rewarding and interesting; many optional areas can be missed or avoided.A diverse set of enemies are present, which usually require being approached with different tactics: some coordinate in groups to out-maneuver or out-position the player; others, like the Manhack, fly directly at the player through small openings and tight corridors; some use predictable but powerful attacks, while others hide before swiftly attacking the player. Gordon can kill most enemies with his weapons, or make use of indirect means, exploiting environmental hazards such as explosive pressurized canisters, gas fires or improvised traps. At one point in the game, Gordon can be joined by up to four armed Resistance soldiers, and can send his team further from him or call them back; however, they can still die easily due to lack of damage protection. Squad members are indicated on the HUD (squad member icons with a cross sign are field medics).Many of the game's new features utilize its detailed physics simulation. Two sections of the game involve driving vehicles. Instead of button-based puzzles from Half-Life, environmental puzzles are also introduced with makeshift mechanical systems, revolving around the player's new ability to pick up, move, and place objects. Solutions involve objects' physical properties, such as shape, weight, and buoyancy. For example, in Chapter 3, Route Kanal, the player is required to stack cinder blocks on a makeshift see-saw ramp to proceed over a wall. Alternatively, the player can use these to build a crude staircase, so sometimes, multiple approaches lead to the desired outcome.Part-way through the game, Gordon acquires the Gravity Gun, which allows him to draw distant objects towards himself or forcefully push them away, as well as to manipulate larger and heavier objects than he is able to alone. These abilities are required to solve puzzles later in the game, and can also be used to great effect in combat, as any non-static object within proximity to the player has the potential to be used as a makeshift defense (e.g. a file cabinet) or a deadly projectile (e.g. a gasoline can or a buzzsaw blade).The game never separates the player with pre-rendered cutscenes or events; the story proceeds via exposition from other characters and in-world events, and ensures that the player controls Gordon for the entirety of the game. Much of the backstory to the game is simply alluded to, or told through the environment.
Setting:
Half-Life 2 presents a dystopian alternate history of Earth, where the resources of the planet, including the human race itself, are being harvested by an oppressive multidimensional empire, known as the Combine. The game is set around the fictitious City 17, roughly 20 years after the events of its predecessor Half-Life.During Half-Life, the scientists, including Gordon Freeman, at the Black Mesa Research Facility, accidentally caused an inter-dimensional instability known as a resonance cascade and later as the "Black Mesa Incident", when an experiment on an alien crystal sample went wrong. Alien creatures, such as the Vortigaunts and headcrabs, from the borderworld of Xen, flooded into the facility. Gordon fought his way through them and the government cover-up response combat units, making it to the Facility's Lambda Complex. There, the Lambda scientists helped Gordon teleport to Xen, where Gordon destroyed a large alien entity keeping the rift open. Gordon was then suddenly extracted by the mysterious G-Man, who had been watching Gordon over the course of the game. Impressed with his ability to survive against all odds, the G-Man offered him a job before placing him into stasis, which Gordon had no option but to accept.Some time after the ending of Half-Life, the instability at Black Mesa had attracted the attention of the Combine empire, and they invaded Earth. Humanity surrendered at the conclusion of the resulting "Seven Hour War". City 17 became the home of the gigantic Combine Citadel, and Dr. Wallace Breen, the Administrator of Black Mesa who had negotiated the surrender, was appointed representative and Administrator to supervise the survivors on behalf of the Combine. Unable to breed due to a Combine suppression field, humanity matured. The Combine implemented a brutal police state of Civil Protection officers and Overwatch soldiers by recruiting and biologically assimilating humans and other species. Meanwhile an underground "Lambda Resistance" of humans and Vortigaunts, now working together, was formed, and saw Freeman as a savior who would lead them to freedom.
Plot:
Gordon Freeman is brought out of stasis by the G-Man, who inserts him into a train arriving at City 17. After arriving at the station and eluding Combine forces, Gordon joins Lambda resistance members including Barney Calhoun, a former Black Mesa security guard now working undercover as a Combine CP officer, and Alyx Vance, the daughter of one of Gordon's former colleagues, Dr. Eli Vance. After a failed attempt to teleport to Eli's resistance base known as Black Mesa East from Dr. Kleiner's makeshift laboratory in City 17, Gordon, re-equipped with the HEV suit and a crowbar, is forced to progress on foot through the city's old canal system. After obtaining an airboat, he battles his way to Black Mesa East, several miles from the city.Gordon is reintroduced to Eli and meets another resistance scientist, Dr. Judith Mossman. Alyx introduces Gordon to her pet robot D0g and gives him a "gravity gun", an instrument which allows Gordon to pick up and move large objects with ease. Black Mesa East comes under Combine attack, and Eli and Mossman are taken to a Combine prison, Nova Prospekt. Separated from Alyx, Gordon takes a detour through the zombie-infested town of Ravenholm with help from its last survivor, Father Grigori. After making his way through the town and a mine, Gordon arrives at a Resistance outpost. He uses a customized dune buggy to travel a crumbling coastal road to Nova Prospekt, encountering Combine patrols and assisting the Resistance in fending off raids.Gordon lays siege to Nova Prospekt by using alien "pheropods" to command the hordes of antlions that infest the coast. He reunites with Alyx in the prison and they locate Eli, but discover that Mossman is a Combine informant. Before they can stop her, she teleports herself and Eli back to City 17's Citadel. The Combine teleporter explodes as Gordon and Alyx use it to escape Nova Prospekt.Reaching Kleiner's lab, Gordon and Alyx learn that they were caught in a "slow teleport", during which a week has passed. In their absence, the Resistance has mobilized against the Combine, turning City 17 into a battleground. During the fighting, Alyx is captured by the Combine and taken to the Citadel, as Gordon fights through the city with the aid of D0g and Barney to reach it. Inside the Citadel, he is caught in a Combine "confiscation chamber" that destroys all of his weapons except for the gravity gun, the energy enhancing its capabilities and turning it into a superior weapon.Eventually, Gordon is captured riding in a Combine transport pod and is taken to Dr. Breen's office, where he and Dr. Mossman are waiting with Eli and Alyx in captivity. I don't write reviews very often but this game is so amazing I just have to.  This game is a total trip, I've been co-op'ing with a friend of mine since the beginning and we were so scared of the regular zombies at first, then we would unlock a skill or a weapon and we'd get a little braver. The game has a leveling system where you level up your skills by using them, so you are rewarded for doing things like killing zombies and running on rooftops. Then as we practiced and got better skills, it wasn't so bad, but the night hunters were still terrifying.  Then came the grappling hook - and that changed everything.  I feel like batman but with super badass weapons that have tons of customizable options.  The game rewards exploring and doing sidequest, and even doubles your xp for parkour'ing at night.  I often just log on and go from one side of the map to another.  The combat is hilarious and there are tons of ways to kill zombies thanks to the diverse weapons and tons of environmental kills you can get.  My favorite by far is the drop kick, I recommend everyone get it as soon as possible.  I have over 20 hours with this game and have still not beaten it, I'm in no hurry, due to the random events that happen and tons of sidequest and loot you can find.  I think if you combine Mirrors Edge + Borderlands + Assassins Creed you would somewhat have this game.  It's awesome and you should get it.

As many avid fans of Resident Evil will tell you; before you read on, curb your enthuiasm and leave it at the door because 'This game contains scenes of explicit gobshite and poor quality.'
By now, the Resident Evil franchise is becoming a fossilised shadow of its former self and is desperately trying to recapture the essence of its glory days with all of the budgeting and none of its soul and that is exactly what it feels like, a budget rendition of the far more successfully acclaimed Resident Evil: Revelations which was a remarkable step in the right direction; but as they say, one step forward and two steps back.
RE:R2 is in some dire trouble right out of the gate for as soon as you boot the game up, you are whisked into watching the opening cutscenes in forced 720x480 quality. No time for the main menu then? I suppose you want this♥♥♥♥♥♥over as fast as possible? Fair enough given the drunken state you are in, Capcom.
An immediate escape as soon as I have skipped the cutscenes and I am on the main menu, sorting out what I assumed at the time was just a small misfire on its own part, no big deal but as soon as I am back in the game restarting; more warning bells begin to kick in, the screen tearing is real but what becomes worse is the absolute diabolical level of voice acting and audio work, a party thrown in the honour of TerraSave, that feels completely devoid of life and any enthusiasm, quiping awful lines of dialogue such as "terr... doesn't have to end with ...rist" .... What.. Resident Evil was founded on cheesy dialogue but it had a sense of class and elegance beneathe the full plates of cheese, it was down right campy and we loved it for that but then, enter Claire Redfield.
Addressing the fan-boyism so we can move past this, I just want to say; Alyson Court (The true 'Voice' of Claire Redfield) I am so, so sorry for the complete butchering of a character you made your own, one that you have dedicated your voice talent, heart and soul, to bring to so many gamers over the span of the last eighteen years.
Claire Redifeld, now, has no passion, no character and no interest in her own voice work to even be compared. This voice actress sounds how wet cardboard looks and is completely devoid of emotion, taking the term 'B-Movie' to new lows.
On the opposite end of the spectrum however, is the newly introduced, Moira Burton and daughter of "What IS this?" Barry Burton. Two individual voice actors who have all the spark and interest of wanting to get involved with the franchises colourful past and give it their all. Barry & Moira are both well written, brash, spunky, relatable and moreover, an interesting pair of characters to want to get to know. Of the current roster, Moira & Barry Burton are the most grounded and well realised of the plot so far.
EPISODE 1:
The presentation and graphics, though appearing dated by todays standards, hold up well once you are in the game and you take control of the characters. Animations are fluid for the most part such as when your character takes heavy damage, they do become visibly more stressed and tired as they will hunch over and clamber for dear life, using a tourniquet if they begin to bleedout all over the screen will ensure survival just long enough for you to see the next green herb, lip syncing however is one major factor that is so HORRIBLY off, they may as well be 5000 yards from one another and hearing distant echos long after the talking stops, much like radio signals travelling through our cosmos.
The detail of the environments is just the right level of grimey without becoming imposing or vulgar. Environments are generally well rendered, appropriately dim and equally unnerving, allowing RE fans to settle right in based solely on the visual aesthetics that have come to be expected of a Resident Evil title. It begins typically linear as you move through tight, narrow hallways filled with prison cells, medical bays, antiseptic batheing rooms and large trash compactors full of large insects and all kinds of nasty; with some bewildering environmental traps, it is clear to see that architect George Trevor, has had an obvious admirer here at the prison, which clearly is not a redressed Rockfort Island (anyone?). Once the Prison opens up to some exterior locations, the quality in presentation jumps up higher as light shafts and dynamic looking fog set in that gives the environment itself some real character. It is beautiful, mysterious and has a few vistas to really breathe in and appreciate. The simulacrum of a sprawling Island is a gorgeous thing to behold, even if the grass tends to wave a little preternatural.
The story moves at a rather steady pace based on higher difficulties although I wished your antagonists would have done the same as many of those enemies you will fight appear to be stuck in a strange time warp and while running look like they are doing their best impressions to avoid conflict altogether. They are slow, cumbersome and awkward yet they can leap through the air with all the grace and agility of a cat. Very peculiar.
You can switch between partner characters to solve puzzles and each come loaded with their own inventory and play style, complete with a basic crafting system that allows the player to juryrig their own survival tools out of certain objects found throughout the world, such as molotovs, explosive bombs or herb combinations, with it only being the first episode, this may grow over time as I also found gunpowder, hinting at a more robust crafting system to come as the episodes are released. Claire will use sheer firepower and brute force to smash through resistance you find along the way whilst Moira opts to wield only a flashlight and crowbar which comes with its own game mechanics, she can blind enemies with her flashlight and follow up with a devestating strike from her crowbar, guns are out for her by pacifists choice, but give her an item she can do blunt force trauma with; wind her up and watch her go (makes sense right?). The controls are really what you would expect, they are digital, best with controller and appropriately tanky, but you wont find yourself hard up for maneuvering and traversing the environment nor is there any grievances with aiming. For the most part though this all feels believeably justified with each characters background story and offers a unique and indepth combat system which offers itself well to cooperative play which brings me to our highlight.
MULTIPLAYER:
This is probably going to be the clincher for many of those looking to buy this game on the PC as Co-op is UTTERLY abscent, assumed dead. Now, reports were initially that multiplayer will have an eventual release after all the episodes for Raid Mode, at least online it will (or as supposedly promised, now who really knows or can trust?) but PC gamers have been completely lied to and decieved when Capcom initially stated that Revelations 2 would come packaged with a cooperative campaign, which not even twenty-four hours after release did they turn around and say that they have stripped this feature out to "ensure a stable user experience across a variety of different PC settings and devices." This is totally unfounded and COMPLETELY unnacceptable. Outright lying to consumers is bad business practice by anybodies standards and shame on us for being so privvy to their obvious and blatent disregard for our respect. Aside from the fact that we can choose to knock down our graphics on lower end machines if we were to have trouble, but the console ports offer the very same with further reports coming through about it being a far less stable product than even our own!
Very soon it is going to take more than a solid dose of herbs to bring Resident Evil back from the dead because its veins are beginning to flow with far too much 'poison' and we know who is ultimately responsible.
SCORE:
[35/100]

Now that the game is fully out, I feel like I can finally write a review of it. I absolutely loved every moment I had in Killing Floor 1, and I feel this is a worthy successor of it. To a certain point. The game isn't perfect, that's for goddamn sure. So, let's start with the pros.
<Pros>
- Game looks absolutely beautiful on max settings, runs smoothy, and the gibbing. Oh man do I love a good gibbing.
- Steam Workshop support. Community maps have become official maps, and player creation of guns skins and customization itmes being welcomed is a nice touch (but I'll talk more about that later.)
-Character customization. Not only can you pick your own character (again), but you can customize them with different glasses, maks, and helmets/hats. (Like the community creations, I will touch base later).
-New perks and ability choices! Not only did they add new perks such as Gunslinger and Survivalist, but you can pick side abilities within the perks to give you more of an edge.
-The soundtrack. Call me Mr. EdgeLord666, because I think the soundtrack to this is pretty damn good, and fits the game really well, just like the first game. And of course, they had to bring back the memorable Disunion Reconstructed song. Both with and without vocals.
-Modded servers. I still love these things, a great place to go if you just wanna♥♥♥♥♥♥around or feel like you're playing good ol Killing Floor 1 again.
<Middle>
-Steam Marketplace. This is where all those boxes and community creations go. I've never been a fan of games taking this direction, but I will admit I have purchased a few things from there for this game.
-The survivalist perk. It's... meh. It's really only good if you're a solo player, which is a minority in this game.
<Cons>
- Startup Time. Oh my ♥♥♥♥ing god it takes for-♥♥♥♥ing-ever to start up. Before you say anything, no, it's not my specs.
- Perk balance. Berzerker, the one supposed to be tank, is now outclassed by Medic and Swat for tank. Firebug is now a gimmick. And survivalist, as I said earlier, is really just for solo players and doesn't work in multiplayer at all.
- Lack of weapons. Compared to Killing Floor 1, the weapon variety is very lack luster. Hopefully Tripwire will add more weapons soon.
Overall, I'd say this is one hell of a game. Better than Killing Floor one? Debateable. I'd give this an 7.5/10. GG, Tripwire.

There is so many details and methods of strategy in this game. Guides alone for Civ have so many pages from basic to advance plays, that listing everything here would be impossible. And that fact alone is just amazing. The fun about this game is not to do with the graphics or the music – but the sheer amount of strategy and planning that goes in with building up your nation, and adapting against other nations, depending on how they choose to play – and whether you want to back-stab your friends or not in multiplayer games.
Before I start with anything else, I would recommend for those planning to try Civ for the first time to get the expansion packs. Without them, the game simply doesn't have its full potential. This is one of the most negative things I can probably say about it. You can wait for a sale, but I would not play this game without them. After you have them, you'll find your time well spent, as you can commit hundreds of hours through everything it has to offer. As a note, I have played this game for hundreds of hours in offline mode, so what you see is not the true amount of hours I've put into it.
So I would … prepare some time for this game. A lot of time. And possibly marathon runs.
First off, Civ 5 is turn based, and the campaigns and difficulties are adjustable. There are eight altogether, from really easy to insanely hard. If you feel particularly brave you can choose the hardest difficulty: Deity. And then weep. Unless of course, you are fabulous and have that rare ability to be able to wipe out most of the world's nations before 100 turns have even passed. You can choose single player campaign mode, customise your own game, or play against friends and opponents online. You can also choose if you want battles animated and your movements animated. I would personally, for a smoother gaming experience, select everything as fast – so it's more like board piece placement, rather than watching them move. Why? Because Civ games can take ages. And with the animations, they take even longer. Also as well, you can choose what “era” your civilisation starts in. The longest games come from starting from the ancient era.
And you'll be wanting to spend a lot of time on this game. Single player will go a lot faster since you're not waiting around for other people's choices. The only problem is being able to check yourself before your whole night has gone on that turn you were so convinced was going to be the last turn before saving and going to bed.
So, lets say you chose to play a custom game. Here, you select your nation. Each nation has different strengths for different play-styles. Some are built for war. Some are built for sea travel and trade, others are for advancing technology and culture, and others again for promoting faith and religion. Lets say you have one opponent, and you chose to start in the ancient era.
When your game starts, you'll have two units. You'll have “Settlers” and “Warriors”. Your “Settlers” are what you use to found cities. Each Settler unit you obtain is the chance for another city that you can place down.  Once you make a city, you then have options to produce something from a city. Now this can be another unit, or a building. And depending on how built up your city is, depends on how many turns it will take before something is produced. The more resources you have in your city/cities and around it/them, the better off you will be – if you produce Workers to extract them, and research the necessary Technology needed to extract the resource. Your Warriors in the meanwhile will be exploring the land nearby, to see if there is any enemies or potential allies and resources.
From here on, it all boils down to finding your own play style, and working with or against the opponents you find on board. You can research technologies to become better at war or better at producing food. You can see that maybe there are Barbarian encampments near you, so you produce military units early on to contest them. You can choose “Policies” that your nation follows to focus on the play style that you want. If you like having lots of cities, then choosing the Liberty Policy tree is your best bet. If you like killing everything, then choosing the Honour Policy will be your best friend, and so on.
Above all, you need to make sure your people are “happy”, throughout whatever path you choose. Since an unhappy nation means little production, and happy means more production in less turns. There are many different ways to do that – but hopefully you get the gist. Found city. Produce stuff. Harvest stuff. Explore stuff. Trade stuff. Adopt Policy stuff. Research Stuff. Fight stuff. And let people be happy and stuff. Eventually you will advance to a point where World Congresses will happen, or you'll be building super Death Robots, nuking cities, and exploring space.
The sheer amount of thought that can go into one game is great, which is why I find this game so addictive. You will have to do research, and spend time coming up with good strategies if you want to succeed well at this game.
The historical accuracy in this game is slightly questionable, but it does make for some hilarious games in context. Although the actual information given with the objects, wonders, and civilisations in this game is great – you will have some moments where you sit back and think: Well. So I built the Great wall of China in Germany. And I started a world war in 1150 AD … with tanks. And my allies at this time are Alexander the Great and ... Queen Elizabeth.
Still pretty fun.
Last but not least, the community have done some great mods in the Steam Workshop to help enhance your playing experience. People like to play as their own nations in the game, and not every nation is represented. The Workshop helps resolves those with some clever creations by the community – so once you're off your training wheels, it's well worth a browse around to see what extra things are there to be offered.

First thing is to adress the elephant in the room. Yes the performance is awful, yes it was inexcusable for them to release it in this condition, and yes it still is far from perfect. However, there's a far more pressing issue with the game. It's not very good.
The best parts about Asylum and City(Origins as well, though that was by someone else), was how it captured Batman and his rogues gallery like no one had since the Animated Series in a non comic medium. So naturally, for their grand finale I was expecting the world. And I got a Batmobile Tank game with one of the laziest stories I've come across.
First thing is the batmobile.
The freeflow combat, predator system is all perfection, honed after 3 games to be the best it could be. However, you'll never get to use it as you won't be able to go three feet without running into huge tank fight. one after the other, and soon what seemed like a cool gimmick, quickly becomes a repetive nightmare. And it's not just the regular fights that are effected.
Remember those legendary boss fights from Asylum, City, and especially Origins? ALL GONE. Instead take a tank fight. Expecting an epic final battle? How about a series of ridiculous tank fights instead? And if it's nota tank fight, it's a one hit QTE, and it's over.
But that would be okay, if the story was as legendary as the other. Unfortunatly dear readers that's not the case.
Rocksteasy made a big deal about two things. 1. That the Arkham Knight was a brand new character that would blow gamers minds, and 2. Scarecrow was going to be given his chance to shine. Both were outright lies.
Not to get into spoilers, but as for the Arkham Knight's identity, not onlyis it not original, but unless this is your first Batman story you'll known who he is first encounter, making the twist worthless. To make matters worse, he's never used any way creativly, and his story just fizzes away.
Then their's Scarecrow. Often maligned, he's one of Batman's most intersting villians as he too uses fear as a weapon. And at the start they seem to do well, show him to be the threat he always culd have been. Then(again avoiding spoilers), someone else appears to completely overshadow him and the plot quickly forgets he exists. Until the hastily tossed together ending of course, that feels like they did it becasue they were told they needed to make and ending.

I like games that have tons of items and abilities, but I don't really enjoy roguelike games in general. After looking at people's recommendations, I decided to give
a try (shoutout to Humble Bundle!). Things didn't go well at the beginning. I couldn't survive for more than 10 minutes. Needless to say, it was not fun. But after figuring out how things work, the game suddenly became so addictive.

Two points above combined with randomness make the game challenging and highly replayable. Another factor is that not all the items and characters are playable at first. So you have to play more and get achievements in order to unlock them. The gameplay itself is great. It's all about killing minions, upgrading your character, and making explosions. Clearly it is not a game for everyone.
It has good graphics, the type of pixel art that I don't hate. I personally like the colors. They give soothing feeling to your eyes, considering the battle can be chaotic. It also has nice visual and sound effects. But the most endearing part of the game is the soundtrack, I give it 10 out of 10! They're all amazing!
I don't know how good the multiplayer feature is because I haven't tried it yet.
The in-game achievements failed to synchronize with the Steam achievements, so I hope the devs fix it asap.

CAPCOM use to be such an upstanding company with a wide diverse catalog of games that while not all award winners were, in fact, rather fun and varied. The Resident Evil series has been wildly skewed since its humble, campy beginnings but it built a lucrative franchise for CAPCOM so it's not surprising that they've been milking this particular cash cow for close to two decades. Unfortunately, their last few additions to the RE series have been ludicrous rather than lucrative, some so terrible that they've become the insult to the injury that the movie adaptations scored in the franchise.
RER2 EP 1 plays absolutely horrendously. The frequent frame rate drops, terrible mouse and keyboard controls, the frankly dated environment graphics, the terrible integration of standing graphics verses interactive graphics, the too short episode (which played like a prolog to the episode rather than an episode), and the blatant lies and hamfisted attempts to cover up those lies about features that were advertised since day 1 of the preorder cycle lead me to conclude that this game was never intended for a PC audience. CAPCOM yet again just wanted to cash in on the PC market money without actually committing effort to adapt to the needs and requirements of the market. It's clear that there was little to no testing for this badly ported title and in how quickly the company was to blame the consumers as well as some unknown copy-editor or intern for the misrepresentation of their product which didn't seem to bother them until the consumers started to complain about missing and/or misrepresented features promised to them.
The cons outweigh the pros thus far in this disastrous addition to the RE series and not even the absolute nostalgic novelty of playing Barry Burton can or ever could take the sting of betrayal, shady business practices, and simply bad ports that CAPCOM continues to employ when it comes to their offerings to the PC market.
TL;DR: This game might look good at first but it pretty much takes a dive within the first few seconds of gaining control of your character(s) and plays like an absolute brick. The story is paper thin, the "zombies/monsters" are laughable, and the dialog, while well acted, is typical RE♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ My suggestion is to give this game a pass until at least two more episodes and a veritable crap ton of updates and optimization fixes are released because otherwise you're paying for a terrible gaming experience. Save your money for now, my friends.

Essentially this game is just Dead Island 2.0. Anyone who has played dead island basically knows how this works out. What is different here is the quests and storyline in general is much more fleshed out and the loot is a bit more liberal. The combat flows smoother and the free running style of movement adds alot of depth to the game play making it fun to just get around.
In my opinion though the best addition to this game is the "be the zombie" mode. Anyone who has played dark souls will understand how it works. A player who chooses to be a super zombie will "invade" your game (if you allow them to via your multiplayer settings) what follows is a rather intense fight between the survivors and the zombie. The zombie plays basically like the alien from the alien vs predator games with stealth and quick kills being its strong point but if it is to brash and just charges in the survivors will burn it down with the UV light and then run up to it and easily kill it.
I have seen some people pull off some amazing triple and quad kills as the zombie but I have also seen alot of really bad ones as well.
Either way I would say if you enjoyed dead island and or mirror's edge and are sorta disappointed with the current zombie titles out there then this one will serve you pretty well. The story line isnt all that indepth and is pretty predictable but it is much better then the previous dead island story lines. Id say give it a go or if you arnt sure when it goes on sale probably in the near future it should be picked up.
also as a side note.. the 4 player cooperative mode is really seamless and adds alot of fun to the game even if it does triviliaze some of the more difficult areas when you can just get four guys loaded up with assault rifles taking down wave upon wave of zombies while parkouring their way across the landscape.. but that doesnt make it any less fun.

Fans of the original game be warned, This is a Resident Evil title in name only. There are absolutely no elements of survival horror to be found here.
1. The entire game is basically The Evil Within staring Resident Evil characters.
2. There's no Co-op  offline or otherwise. Major deal killer for me and my lady as we had planned on buying this for the RAID online mode to enjoy together.
3. More action oriented, no puzzles or thinking to complete the game required. First episode is a gear cog "fetch" quest. Fetch quests belong in WoW and other pay to win subsctiption  based games. Not RE.
4. Episodic. Thank you Tale tale for bringing this horrible idea to market. Thank you for indirectly ruining Resident Evil and putting ideas into countless other developer's heads.
5. Pay to win. Raid  mode includes a store where you may purchase weapons and gear with real life money. Another greedy move by Capcom. I find this trend in video gaming to be very sad, as I grew up in a time when  you received all of the content on the disc on day 1 and there was no such thing as "DLC". Games used to be sold based on their content. Not the after party.  Hell, it was a HUGE selling point if they added a couple of levels and advertised it on the jewel case.
This game could have been so much more had the developers stuck to the original formula instead of dumbing it all down to appease the CoD and BF kiddies that have ran rampant in the gaming community lately. As a life long fan of the franchise I was excited to see Barry Burton finally featured in his own game and extremely disappointed in the final product.

FTL is a great game, especially if you like games you always lose at. FTL is a great roguelike, with a strange almost strategy aspect to it. Its nice to be able to command your crew around your ship, strengthening or repairing different parts. However, its extremely difficult to manage a crew while fighting another ship and being boarded by enemy crewmen. Thank god for autofire, right? On one hand, I really love this game. On the other hand, I'm disappointed. While it is really fun, it could've been made on a low budget, but instead the developers (a two man team) asked for $10,000 on Kickstarter. They got much more than they asked, and ended up with over $200,000. That's great, right? I mean surely this means they can hire more people, or spend more time working on features and things. WRONG. They continued to work on it as they had, and ultimately made a game that while great, could be a lot better. Luckily, that's my only real complaint about FTL. It's still amazing, and hopefully they will release add on content in the future. The game is all random, so you really have no idea what will happen next. As you plot your jumps running from the rebel fleet, you will be constantly attacked by pirates, rebels, and confused 'allies'. You will find burning space stations, and have the options of trying to put out the fire, dock to rescue survivors, or leave them to their unfortunate fate. But you don't know what will happen when you choose one. If you dock for survivors one time, maybe you save them and bring them home, and gain another crew mate. You do the same random event later, and fail to rescue the people, and end up losing a crew member to the fires. You never know what will happen next, and that is a truly great feeling.
Overall, the graphics aren't much (but they aren't bad either), the gameplay is incredible, the story is generic (but the species and relations are interesting), and the game is very easy to run.

KIlling Floor 2 is a masterpiece of a wave based co-op shooter. It has a difficulty for everyone, perks (classes) with customization of the skills for each playstyle, a new added plethora of aethstetic customization options, and a good amount of weapons to start (If the first Killing Floor was an example, we will get many, many more). The weapons all feel, and handle very nicely, while all being satisfying to use + all with their own ups and downs. The melee is where the games combat gets even more impressive, with directional combat, parrying, and many limbs to cut off.
If you enjoy wave based shooters and co-op games, I would HIGHLY recommend this game.
Killing Floor brought me and my close friends a great amount of good times and fun. Between the endless amount of maps, weapons, and characters (all over time) - mixed with the holiday events, made this game fun and excited everytime you booted it up.
When we heard that Killing Floor 2 was comming out on early access, we jumped right on it. I grabbed us a 6 pack of the game and handed it out to my close buds, as well as my wife. It started slow but every single update seemed to bring more and more to the game. It was almost a direct copy of KF1 as far as game play. Mixed in with the newest verion of Unreal and  a new feature of liquids, visceral gore etc., KF2s gore was the most noticeable difference. The music was spot on with the same band, and some songs as the first (not sure why the music isnt synced across all players like it was in KF1. It was great to all be slaughtering to the same great song).
By the time release came, we had played so much and had so much fun that we forgot it was in early access, because the game was always in a far better state than most games that are sold as "finished".
KF2 has become a daily play for my wife, my close friends, and of course myself.
We are eagerly waiting for more weapons, maps, and most importantly HOLIDAY EVENTs!
Again, I would HIGHLY recommend this game.

Killing Floor 2. Where to begin.. Well first things first I should give a little background. I currently have roughly 250 hours played in this game, I purchased it during Early Access prior to the release of the Firebug and Demolitionist perks, roughly a year ago. I've played every perk in the game on every main map and tried innumerable custom maps, I'm sure there are those with far more time invested than me but I'd say I'm pretty up there considering.
I love solid horde mode shooters, I know many find them stale or repetitive but I could play a good one ad nauseum and never get bored. Even if it has no "progression treadmill" or loot rewards, if the game play is fun I will keep comming back. As such Killing Floor 2 should be right up my alley.. and it is.. for the most part.
The animations are spot on, with multiple bits of flare for each gun that really add personality and charm to the game. Hitting the Reload button when full will queue up idle animations for your weapon that range from checking the magazine to tweaking gas bottles or charging slides. This dedication to detail is commendable and gives the game a great sense of weight. Enemies also benefit from this level of polish, each with their own unique animation quirks and well designed organic looking attacks that all flow very well. From the agile stalkers to the creepy crawlers, to the shuffling clots and waddling bloats.. it all comes together to present a solid audio-visual experience.
system in the game takes this one step further and adds a real.. meat.. to the game play (couldn't resist). Zed's heads explode in satisfying pops of blood, bodies get cut in half as their viscera and fluids paint the level red and burning corpses stumble about with some of the best fire effects to be seen in a non-tripple-A title.
Couple this with a cheese-metal sound track (which, admittedly, your mileage may very on. As a metalhead, much of it sounds like generic metal to me and I turned it off after a couple play throughs) and you have a game that is dripping with a grindhouse horror aesthetic. It's pure fun that doesn't take itself too seriously (or at least, in this sense it doesn't). Really isn't much to complain about when it comes to the visual and audio presentation of the game. As a bonus it's always ran well for me on my mid-level rigs.
is, at it's core, another win. KF2 has responsive gunplay with most weapons feeling quite powerful and enjoyable to use. The sound assets are generally good and few things are more satisfying than chaining head-exploding shots in the games signiture slo-mo as you line up zeds and knock them down. Most Perks (aka, classes) are capable of handling themselves well enough, but teamwork is very important. You abslutely will get overrun on harder difficulties if you try lone-wolfing. Things can quickly get chaotic which lends the game a high energy charm.
Most styles of play are reasonably represented. You have Perks that focus on acurracy, rewarding consistant head shots or targeted limb takedowns. You have Perks that focus on mass destruction, killing large amounts of fodder Zeds so the heavy hitters can down the big threats. There's even a melee brawler if you want to get in close and chop Zeds to Shreds with a claymore or an explosive sledge hammer.
You only really have one option if you want Support (which, ironically is not the Perk named support but rather the Medic) which focuses on healing the team. The actual Support Perk is more accurately described as a CQB specialist with a selection of shotguns at its disposal, it's "Support" aspect is mostly limited to a once-per-round ammo refill for a teammate (if you take the skill that allows it).
All in all there's a decent variety of play styles available. The usefulness of each varies from patch to patch as Tripwire balances the game, but they tend to cycle around on the blancing-merry-go-round. Ultimately the game play experience is an enjoyable one that rewards dipping in and out of from time to time. It's not a bad looking game certainly and it's very well presented. Still, things aren't all sunshine and rainbows..
So, after such a glowing first half what could possibly be wrong with the game? Well..
To start with you should know what you are getting here; KF2 seems to offer a great deal of potential but a key thing to keep in mind is simply.. Tripwire was not that ambitious. They set out to a make a solid core experience and they've, generally, succeeded. The end result is, however, fairly rudimentary.
There is only one (PVE) game mode available right now. Every match consists of 4/7/10 waves (depending on which length you choose) and your only goal each time is just to survive. There are no objectives to complete or bonus tasks to accomplish. Your goal is to kill as many zeds with as little ammo as possible so you can buy your next weapon ASAP. This can lead to the gameplay getting rather stale. I mentioned at the start of this review that I personally enjoy repetitive gameplay loops and that's true, but I need some level of depth to exist in them to maintain that enjoyment. KF2 simply doesn't have this. Generally speaking every game plays out the same, the only variable being whether your teammates get luckier on the Zed spawns and rack up kills faster than you (thus slowing down how quickly you can get your weapons, refill your ammo, or aquire armor/grenades).
Each wave is always the same. Even without certain more dangerous enemies announcing their spawns with level-shaking roars, you'd still quickly figure out when they are comming. X number of Y baddies always show up on wave four, wave five  (in a ten wave match) always has the first big bruiser while wave seven will frequently be the fail point for a bad PuG.  There's an element of variation to this from the games "Director" AI, true. If you've ever played Left4Dead then you know what that Director
be capable of. Unfortunately KF2's version of this is a pale immitation and, unless you know to look for the differences it's possible you wouldn't even realize its there.
Perks have only the most basic level of inter-team synergy. There are no "powers" in KF2, just guns, and while that's not neccisarily a bad thing it does mean that there's not neccisarily much you can do beyond shoot the same targets. There aren't any combos to pull off or bonuses beneath the surface. Team synergy really just consists of "shoot the same thing" with the occasional stun tossed in.
Weapon variety is also a bit on the bland side. Tripwire themselves are self-declared gunnuts which is easily seen in the attention to detail they've given both the guns and the gunplay. While that's commendable, they also haven't really put much creativity into the weapon list. Most guns are based on real world, functioning fire arms which feels more than a little at odds with the rest of the games shlocky B movie vibe. There are a couple outliers; Berserkers can carry a giant buzzsaw that can shred enemies like a chainsaw or fire buzzsaw blades like bouncing frisbees of death. Firebugs get a Microwave gun that cooks enemies from the inside out causing them to explode in showers of blood. Unfortunately these are the only two really outlandish guns in the game.
There are other issues as well. Tripwire conducted a community poll to see if we wanted PVP, it was overwhelmingly against the idea but they added it anyway instead of improving the PVE. The game notoriously recieved a microtransaction system mid-EA, your mileage may vary on what to make of that. Ultimately KF2 feels like a solid basis for a game, crippled mostly by an unambitious dev team. There's not much content in the game but what is there is solid enough. I really wouldn't reccomend it at full price, but on sale? Sure.

Possibly one of the best games I've played in a very long time and for good reasons.
Without playing any of the classics I had a reasonably nieve look at it and went in not expecting a lot. The combat mechanics was a new twist strategy games and appealed to my logical thinking over fast reactions. My main criticism was the unpredictablility of the battles as one turn there will be no aliens then the next you would be flanked as if they "knew" you were there. I also hated not being able to position my snipers into high spots without activating 6 squads of aliens. Seriously, my sniper isn't dressed in a neon suit.
Right off the bat the story opens strongly and draws you into the world they have created. The graphics, the additional dialogue from the Chief Engineer and Scientist and permadeath soldiers do a great job in turning something that should be dull and repetitive into exciting and fresh. Too bad the story line dies off and becomes not really aparent because it had some good ideas. There are some bugs which annoyed but while ironman is disabled it wasn't much of an issue as I could just reload the last save.
I enjoyed the design of the X-COM base with the ant farm style look at the base and being able to name each of the soldiers after my friends, especially giving them nicknames when they ranked. The basic customisation sucked (only loadouts with no extra colourings etc) and the skill tree was very basic, requiring no specialisation in anyway. Sure, you're a grenadier by role-play but you can also be a medic if you want.
All in all these were minor issues and I still enjoyed wasting hours of my days playing X-COM. Reccomended to anyone! 9/10

About game:
Half-Life 2 (stylized as HλLF-LIFE2) is a first-person shooter video game and the sequel to Half-Life
Gameplay:Like its predecessor, Half-Life 2 is a single-player first-person shooter broken into several chapters, permanently casting the player as the protagonist Gordon Freeman. The sequel has nearly the same mechanics as Half-Life, including health-and-weapon systems and periodic physics puzzles, except with the newer Source Engine and improved graphics. The player also starts without items, slowly building up an arsenal over the course of the game. Despite the game's mainly linear nature, much effort was put into making exploration rewarding and interesting; many optional areas can be missed or avoided.A diverse set of enemies are present, which usually require being approached with different tactics: some coordinate in groups to out-maneuver or out-position the player; others, like the Manhack, fly directly at the player through small openings and tight corridors; some use predictable but powerful attacks, while others hide before swiftly attacking the player. Gordon can kill most enemies with his weapons, or make use of indirect means, exploiting environmental hazards such as explosive pressurized canisters, gas fires or improvised traps. At one point in the game, Gordon can be joined by up to four armed Resistance soldiers, and can send his team further from him or call them back; however, they can still die easily due to lack of damage protection. Squad members are indicated on the HUD (squad member icons with a cross sign are field medics).Many of the game's new features utilize its detailed physics simulation. Two sections of the game involve driving vehicles. Instead of button-based puzzles from Half-Life, environmental puzzles are also introduced with makeshift mechanical systems, revolving around the player's new ability to pick up, move, and place objects. Solutions involve objects' physical properties, such as shape, weight, and buoyancy. For example, in Chapter 3, Route Kanal, the player is required to stack cinder blocks on a makeshift see-saw ramp to proceed over a wall. Alternatively, the player can use these to build a crude staircase, so sometimes, multiple approaches lead to the desired outcome.Part-way through the game, Gordon acquires the Gravity Gun, which allows him to draw distant objects towards himself or forcefully push them away, as well as to manipulate larger and heavier objects than he is able to alone. These abilities are required to solve puzzles later in the game, and can also be used to great effect in combat, as any non-static object within proximity to the player has the potential to be used as a makeshift defense (e.g. a file cabinet) or a deadly projectile (e.g. a gasoline can or a buzzsaw blade).The game never separates the player with pre-rendered cutscenes or events; the story proceeds via exposition from other characters and in-world events, and ensures that the player controls Gordon for the entirety of the game. Much of the backstory to the game is simply alluded to, or told through the environment.
Setting:
Half-Life 2 presents a dystopian alternate history of Earth, where the resources of the planet, including the human race itself, are being harvested by an oppressive multidimensional empire, known as the Combine. The game is set around the fictitious City 17, roughly 20 years after the events of its predecessor Half-Life.During Half-Life, the scientists, including Gordon Freeman, at the Black Mesa Research Facility, accidentally caused an inter-dimensional instability known as a resonance cascade and later as the "Black Mesa Incident", when an experiment on an alien crystal sample went wrong. Alien creatures, such as the Vortigaunts and headcrabs, from the borderworld of Xen, flooded into the facility. Gordon fought his way through them and the government cover-up response combat units, making it to the Facility's Lambda Complex. There, the Lambda scientists helped Gordon teleport to Xen, where Gordon destroyed a large alien entity keeping the rift open. Gordon was then suddenly extracted by the mysterious G-Man, who had been watching Gordon over the course of the game. Impressed with his ability to survive against all odds, the G-Man offered him a job before placing him into stasis, which Gordon had no option but to accept.Some time after the ending of Half-Life, the instability at Black Mesa had attracted the attention of the Combine empire, and they invaded Earth. Humanity surrendered at the conclusion of the resulting "Seven Hour War". City 17 became the home of the gigantic Combine Citadel, and Dr. Wallace Breen, the Administrator of Black Mesa who had negotiated the surrender, was appointed representative and Administrator to supervise the survivors on behalf of the Combine. Unable to breed due to a Combine suppression field, humanity matured. The Combine implemented a brutal police state of Civil Protection officers and Overwatch soldiers by recruiting and biologically assimilating humans and other species. Meanwhile an underground "Lambda Resistance" of humans and Vortigaunts, now working together, was formed, and saw Freeman as a savior who would lead them to freedom.
Plot:
Gordon Freeman is brought out of stasis by the G-Man, who inserts him into a train arriving at City 17. After arriving at the station and eluding Combine forces, Gordon joins Lambda resistance members including Barney Calhoun, a former Black Mesa security guard now working undercover as a Combine CP officer, and Alyx Vance, the daughter of one of Gordon's former colleagues, Dr. Eli Vance. After a failed attempt to teleport to Eli's resistance base known as Black Mesa East from Dr. Kleiner's makeshift laboratory in City 17, Gordon, re-equipped with the HEV suit and a crowbar, is forced to progress on foot through the city's old canal system. After obtaining an airboat, he battles his way to Black Mesa East, several miles from the city.Gordon is reintroduced to Eli and meets another resistance scientist, Dr. Judith Mossman. Alyx introduces Gordon to her pet robot D0g and gives him a "gravity gun", an instrument which allows Gordon to pick up and move large objects with ease. Black Mesa East comes under Combine attack, and Eli and Mossman are taken to a Combine prison, Nova Prospekt. Separated from Alyx, Gordon takes a detour through the zombie-infested town of Ravenholm with help from its last survivor, Father Grigori. After making his way through the town and a mine, Gordon arrives at a Resistance outpost. He uses a customized dune buggy to travel a crumbling coastal road to Nova Prospekt, encountering Combine patrols and assisting the Resistance in fending off raids.Gordon lays siege to Nova Prospekt by using alien "pheropods" to command the hordes of antlions that infest the coast. He reunites with Alyx in the prison and they locate Eli, but discover that Mossman is a Combine informant. Before they can stop her, she teleports herself and Eli back to City 17's Citadel. The Combine teleporter explodes as Gordon and Alyx use it to escape Nova Prospekt.Reaching Kleiner's lab, Gordon and Alyx learn that they were caught in a "slow teleport", during which a week has passed. In their absence, the Resistance has mobilized against the Combine, turning City 17 into a battleground. During the fighting, Alyx is captured by the Combine and taken to the Citadel, as Gordon fights through the city with the aid of D0g and Barney to reach it. Inside the Citadel, he is caught in a Combine "confiscation chamber" that destroys all of his weapons except for the gravity gun, the energy enhancing its capabilities and turning it into a superior weapon.Eventually, Gordon is captured riding in a Combine transport pod and is taken to Dr. Breen's office, where he and Dr. Mossman are waiting with Eli and Alyx in captivity. So basically I recommend this game in every way, even at full price.

After playing the first episode of Resident Evil: Revelations 2, I was happily surprised. I've never played the original Revelations, but I had heard good things about it. The thing that drew me to this one was the episodic release and the characters. The game being episodic and having a weekly release date instead of monthly like certain other episodic game series brings an interest to me. It's keeping me engaged in the story. The twists and turns of the story are really what's keeping me interested in playing the game. And the fact the rest of the game is being released over the coming month makes me feel as if I'm getting my moneys worth instead of spending the first two days playing the story all the way through and then never playing it again. I actually don't mind having to wait, and I'm happy the waits arent as long as The Walking Dead or Game of Thrones. The characters are where the game falls a little bit short in my opinion. Claire has her history, but unless you know it, I don't think she would gain any sympathy for the situation she's in. Moira is made out to be the steriotypical rebelious teenager who HATES HER DAD and wears a t shirt that says THE WORLD BURNS and says things like OMIGOD and THAT BLOWS. Too much, Moira. However, Barry and Natalia definitely make for an interesting duo. Barry on this quest to save his lost daughter and Natalia who apparently has no parents but has a strange power that complements the gameplay in their story well. My favorite part of the first episode was actually Barry and Natalia's half because of the stealth based combat and the exploration. As far as the scares go, there are one or two good jumps, and atmoshpere is definitely there, it just doesn't bring that feeling of WHAT THE ♥♥♥♥ WAS THAT SOUND I WANT TO RUN AWAY BUT I CAN'T CAUSE THERE WAS ANOTHER SCARY SOUND OVER THERE TOO AND OMIGOD ARE THOSE PEOPLE HANGING FROM THE CEILING WITH MILLIONS OF HOOKS SKEWERED THROUGH THEM HOW EVIL WITHIN OF YOU GAME.
All in all, I'm very much enjoying the game so far. The characters aren't the best, but they are what's driving the story, and the story is, in my opinion, well worth the ride.

I think people may have been expecting too much from this. Having played through nearly the entire series (aside from RE Survivor and RE Dead Aim), I'm impressed with the story progression (not sure what it says about me that I can follow the convoluted, contrived and swiss cheesed plot strung together by the series [live-action movies not included], but I stand by my enjoyment of its evolution). Capcom's had hiccups, and no franchise can last forever, but they've definitely made a decent effort here. I also can't say I've had the technical problems that others have had, as far as frame drops or game crashes. In fact, the only technical problem I had was a lapse in borrowed internet connection; the reliability of which I have no control over.
As far as the co-op debacle, Capcom does shady crap like that all the time...no surprises. And although I didn't buy for the co-op, it would definitely be a nice addition for Raid mode. As far as the campaign, whether or not they add it later, I like the way it is. Resident Evil campaigns are best when the solo player is ambling through the dark and solving puzzles. I can't get into the story if I have some whelp yelling in my ear to hand him herbs all the time. All in all, no game is without sin; and I'm certainly enjoying this one, sins and all.
Now for those that enjoy them, a list:
Pros:
- Callbacks to the '90s games through dialogue and characters. (lol, 'Clair Sandwich')
- Adequate, yet still below average, puzzles. (finally, problem solving is back)
- Incredible atmosphere and well-paced plotline, complete with cliffhanging plot twist.
- Replayability, especially in Raid, which will assist in waiting for the rest of the episodes to drop.
- Cost less than every other game I've ever pre-ordered in my life.
Cons:
- No option for co-op after co-op was offered. (not an issue for me, but still wrong)
- What the hell happened to the RE6 control scheme? Would have loved making Gina roll with a sniper rifle in Raid.
- Episodes not all available on release. (Though with the possibility that they'll make patches based on customer feedback [co-op option/optimization for unusual setups, I suppose waiting won't be all that bad.)
- Microtransactions (I knew there was a reason it wasn't $50-$60, but really Capcom? If you even halfway tolerate the fans of the games you release, don't follow EA's example. Costume DLC is one thing, but drop the penny pinch scheme.)

Now there is no mistake about it I am a massive Resident Evil fan and rank some of the earlier titles as my favourite games of all time. Unfortunately some of the more recent titles have lost a little bit of what made the earlier games special. The original Resident Evil Revelations changed this when it was released on 3DS a few years ago.
Set on an abandoned ship it provided an experience much more akin to what made the original games in the series so good.
Needless to say I rank Revelations as one of my favourite games of all time and was very excited when I heard they were making a sequal. Now unlike the previous this game is made in episodes that are each being released one week apart to make the whole game. Normally I am not a fan of episodes as they come miles apart and I lose interest but the fact they are 1 week apart and the “Next time on Revelations 2” that is presented to you upon completion of the first episode really dragged me in to its world.
Episode 1: Penal Colony see Resident Evil Alumni Claire Redfield and Barry Burton’s daughter Moira Burton taken by a military group and imprisoned apparently as test subjects in a SAW like game. You play as these character trying to escape and find help. The second half of the game sees you playa s Barry Burton trying to rescue his daughter along with Natalia a young child he meets upon arrival who seemingly has some kind of abnormal powers. The pairing of these 2 is very akin to the relationship between Joel and Ellie in The Last of Us.
These pairings work well and as a solo player the switching between the characters is handled perfectly with little mess. There were a few times when evading monsters the ai character seemed determined to hump the thing we were running away from’s leg but generally this was a small thing. Now there has been some controversy recently that the Steam version does not support local co-op but the PS4 and XB1 versions do. Personally I am not overly fussed by this but if this is something that will factor into your decision to buy this game please bear it in mind.
The relationship between the characters in excellent and unlike normal Resident Evil games the voice acting is pretty decent. A personal favourite of mine sees Barry making a quick remark about “Now whose the master of unpicking locks” right after using a crane to destroy a door.
Gameplay wise this builds well on the previous game but as this time it was not designed for DS it controls a lot better. I played with a 360 pad but equally my short time playing with a mouse and keyboard seemed pretty good to.
Graphically the game is a mixed bag. Visually pretty decent but the locations themselves while atmospheric are rather dull and could have done with a little more intrigue… but this is Resident Evil after all.
The raid mode again a decent diversions once you have finished the main game but this section allows the creep of one of the game’s biggest annoyances… micro transactions.
There is no need to have this in a single player game but you can use it to buy weapons and health and hearts for use in RAID mode which is totally unnecessary and leave a bit of a sour taste. Coupled with the local co-op that was removed from advertised on the steam release right before sale and Capcom aren’t trying to win any PR competitions.
But overall I must say I really enjoyed episode 1 of Resident Evil Revelations 2. Its well made its engaging and I cannot wait to tune in to episode 2 next week.

Besides Mass Effect, its been a very long time since I've found a roleplaying game that I've really enjoyed.
Honestly, Shadowrun Returns blew away my expectations, especially since I didn't really have any going into it. I knew that it was based off a classic sci-fi tabletop RPG, but that was about it.
The first campaign, The Deadman's Switch, draws you into the world of Shadowrun very well, introduces you to some characters, and generally how the game works and feels. It's a nice introduction to the game, but it does have a few things that annoyed and irked me. Especially the linearity of it all. It was one story the whole way through, with not many different ways to approach things, or side quests to take up your time.
That's why I recommend getting the Dragonfall expansion with it. I've played the expansion for three or four hours at this point, and all of my problems with the original game have been taken care of, as far as I can tell. There are a lot more things put in place to sidetrack you, and I really like that.
But, there's also the horde of player created content that the game allows access to, and that could provide a lot more gameplay than the original campaign allows for, therefore not necessarily making the Dragonfall expansion worth it, but I recommend it none-the-less.

First off, I am an AMD user.
Second, this game is AWESOME. Yes my game freezes up sometimes and I have to press the "oh♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; button, but guess what? I don't care. That will be fixed in the future. It's a minor issue that they are working on and are addressing. I've noticed the freeze ups ONLY happen during a cutscene, I have had no freeze ups outside of them.
The parkour in this game is VERY fun. The fighting is like dead island, so if you are a fan of that you will probably like this. Easiest example is Skyrim with zombies.
I have only been through one night, and it wasn't bad, but I feel my heart beat pick up. Night time isn't just some low light but it gets VERY dark. Without your flash light, you really can't see anything.
There are a vast number of skills you can upgrade with separated into 3 different trees.
Survivor: This is where normal experience goes.
Agility: Experience for jumping around and running basically. Example, I jump off a building and land on an enemy.
Power: Experience for fighting. The more you fight, the more you rank this up.
I don't know if there is a level limit but you progress at a steady pace. At least right now I have been.
You can press "Q" to activate survivor instincts. Think Tomb Raider for this one. It highlights any items and chests you can find. Use this often and you will never have to buy a weapon, though the weapons you find are usually pretty weak. So don't waste your money buying weak weapons.
There are A LOT of zombies. Loads in the street and sometimes there are some in buildings, so watch where you jump or a zombie might break through a broken down door to get you.
You don't have to stay out at night, you can and activate safe zones which let you skip the night cycle.  But as far as I know, you get bonuses for fighting and exploring at night. I will update this more when I have hit the night cycle again, though I may wait for a patch for AMD users. Hopefully in the next patch! *fingers crossed*
The menu is very nice in my opinion. Very easy to use and organized. You can craft things like lockpicks, medkits, and other items. I don't know all the items so I can't really list anything other than what I've found.
Only have encountered one "boss" zombie, but I didn't kill him. He was a giant zombie carrying around a sledge hammer. Pretty much just♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at the world.
Aside from the freeze ups, I would easily give the game an 7.5/8 out of 10.

If you loved or even liked Killing Floor 1 then you will this one.
Everything about it is just the first game but improved or with added features, the exception being weapons since not all of the ones from the first game made it into this. Overall the game is absolutely amazing, if you love the first game or games like Left 4 Dead then I highly suggest buying this. For me it's worth the price but hey if you want to get it on sale then go ahead.
Also I recommend playing with some friends for better teamwork.

So, I got gifted this game by a buddy in the early days of.. Well, early access!
This game has had a rough ride, and for a while, like just after the trashy microtransactions got added, I thought the game would be lost beyond repair. They stopped listening to the community, and they added a terrible, unbalanced "Versus" mode, that the first game didn't have, and god knows why they did, what a waste of time that was. The martial artist even got scrapped and replaced with survivalist, who is arguably the most generic class in the game, and I'd have been fine without him there.
This game reminds me of the Zombies installments from the earlier Call of Duty games, being round based, buying the weapons etc., but there're a lot of good spins on it, and a cool class system that you can level up each perk individually to access new abilities every five levels!
On the plus side, this game has been great fun even through the tough times, and there is still work to be done here, but the game is in a pretty good shape as it is, and the devs seem to be listening to the community again.
I do recommend this game! It's great fun, and it's only £20 max, £15 on this launch day sale. So if you're looking for a "zombie" styled, first person shooter, gore filled fun-time, this is the game for you.

My favorite game in the franchise. Instead of silent protagonist Claude, you are now playing as Tommy Vercetti, charismatic member of Italian Mafia, who gets out of prison after serving 15 years for multiple killings. Soon enough he gets involved in a drug deal gone wrong and determines to find out who was behind it while building his own criminal empire.
Setting is moved from cold streets of Liberty City to more relaxed Vice City which is based on Miami. References to 80's culture are numerous - disco music, pastel suits, styled cars. The American crack epidemic, drug trafficking and organized crime that followed it are heavily represented in the game, which also draws inspiration from many movies and tv series such as Miami Vice, Scarface, Carlito's Way, Godfather and many others. I will mention some examples:
Retired colonel from Central America and drug trafficker Juan Cortez - parody of Manuel Noriega, Panama dictator and major player in drug trafficking during 80's.
Drug baron Ricardo Diaz may be influenced by Frank Lopez, character from Scarface who happens to be played by late Robert Loggia who did voice acting for Ray Machowski, corrupt police officer in GTA 3. Diaz's mansion is very similar to Montana's from the same movie. Betrayal and the same clothes also add to the full picture. Interesting thing is that he is voiced by Luis Guzmán who played Gonzalo Rodríguez Gacha, drug trafficker and one of the leaders of the notorious Medellín Cartel in Netflix original series Narcos. Diaz's physical resemblance and temper to him are rather substantial.
Ken Rosenberg's appearance and behaviour are nearly identical to David Kleinfeld, who was played by Sean Penn in Carlito's Way.
Lance Vance is voiced by Philip Michael Thomas who played Ricardo Tubbs in Miami Vice, which heavily influenced Vice City.
Tommy Vercetti was inspired by Tony Montana from Scarface. Memorable shootout scene was also incorporated.
Last but not least there is Escobar International Airport, no need to say anything about that one.
Game introduces bikes which are way more fun to drive than standard cars and will probably become your first choice in exploring the city. Later you get access to helicopters which are easy to control and are much better solution when you need a quick way to certain place, or you just want better view of the city. Those who prefer adventures on the sea are not forgotten, you can also drive boats.
Major gangs in VC are Cubans, Haitians, Vice City Bikers and members of Forelli Crime Family. All of side activites from GTA 3 are also present here. Newly introduced are assets purchases. They include strip club, taxi company, film studio, dance club, printing works, car showroom, ice cream factory and boatyard. Each of them has a number of missions attached, and once all of them are complete a given property will begin generating an ongoing income.
There is nine radio stations in the game - on seven of them you will listen great collection of licensed music, while talk shows that contain lots of satire are on remaining two. Big step was made compared to previous title in quantity of material - there is over 10 hours of it compared to 3.5h in GTA 3.
Voice actors lineup and their performance is phenomenal; Ray Liotta, Tom Sizemore, Burt Reynolds, William Fichtner, Dennis Hopper and Danny Trejo are present among many others. One person that you certainly don't expect is porn actress Jenna Jameson, who gives voice to appropriately named character Candy Suxxx.
Like its predecessor, Vice City was given a lot of GOTY awards and achieved huge commercial success, over 20 million sold copies speaks for itself. I really liked main character, and hope that Rockstar will bring him and Vice City setting back in the future.
