If it's lying on the ground, kill it. Don't matter if it looks mangled beyond recognition; if it's lying on the ground, you kill it with everything that you've got.
That's the first and basic rule of Dead Space: a game that's full of horrifying surprises around every corner. This game is so scary, you'll feel relieved upon meeting that one random guy, banging his battered head against the wall. Everything that moves either wants to decapitate you, or make you one of their own - and those resilient beings will stop at nothing to get to you, unless you tear off their pointy limbs apart from their fast-moving bodies. The Necromorphs can crawl through the vents, and appear out of the blue - ready to pounce at a moment's notice. And what better man to face them than a hardened engineer who fights these abominations with space shop tools? Isaac Clarke acts like a desentisized shell for the player, lacking emotions and words to speak, with only one goal in mind: to find his girlfriend. In short, he's the perfect horror everyman - and he's too in love to let the undead freaks get in the way to his sweetheart.
And there you have it.

FTL Faster Than Light is a rogue-like with the added twist of being set in space and based around ship management. The gameplay involves you mainly micromanaging your spaceship and crew as you travel through a number of random encounters trying to reach the other side of the map so you can deliver a warning to your rebel headquarters and defeat the final boss.
FTL is a game that relies heavily on it's difficulty, being much shorter than your average rouge-like. You manage a number of fairly limited resources as you slowly improve your ship and crew. You gather fuel, missiles and money and hope for new and better weapons and drones as your crew members gain experience in whatever field they are working.
It is a well made game and one I'm happily recommending but it's also a game that has some rather annoying limitations.
Your ship has very little customization options which makes repeat playthroughs somewhat dull, an unusual trait for a rouge-like. Choosing a different ship often yields much the same gameplay as even though your starting position changes a little, the only real change longterm is the configuration of the various rooms on your ship.
Another problem is the relatively short campaign you will begin to take note of once you've learned the basics and only the unforgiving higher difficulty gives it any sort of longevity.
All in all FTL: Faster Than Light is a nice little game, but it is also a game that needs something more before I'll agree with the underdog hype that seems to be going around everywhere these days. Perhaps strong developer support and a growing modding community will one day make this into the game it could be but as it sits now it is nothing special.

There's a reason LEGO Marvel Super Heroes is one of the highest-selling LEGO video games of all time; actually, three reasons.
First, the characters. The game features not only the existing Avengers, X-Men and Ultimate Spider-Man LEGOs on the market, but a legion of characters and vehicles either only recently released in 2014 or not even created yet. From the Fantastic Four to the Sinister Six, this game includes the majority of Marvel's well-known characters along with a handful of lesser-known ones. Plus they've included the legendary Stan Lee himself as a playable character possessing multiple superpowers. What more do you need from this game?
Speaking of characters, the next reason is what the minifigures take part in: the story. You can tell the writers and game designers had fun trying to combine a coherent Marvel storyline with the quirky humor found in every other LEGO game. And you know what? They did it. The story features the Avengers, Fantastic Four and X-Men teaming up against villains like Magneto, Doc Ock, Doctor Doom, Loki, Abomination and Sandman, in an epic quest filled with crazy left turns that only a LEGO video game could have. And it all leads up to a stunning twist you'll never expect (so I won't ruin it for those who haven't played yet).
Finally, the gameplay. I was very pleasantly surprised just from playing a free PC demo of the game which was released online early last year, featuring the game's very first level, Sand Central Station. This level features Iron Man (Mark 6), the Hulk and Spider-Man taking on Abomination and Sandman in New York's Grand Central Station. But what blew me away the most during the level was the sheer number of abilities each character had, from Hulk's famous Puny God move from The Avengers, to Spider-Man's ability to actually swing around on a web. When I finally bought the actual game, I was thrilled to discover that the rest of the characters in the game were just as incredible.
So, if you're skeptical about buying this game, I suggest you try out the demo featured on
first, and if you still don't feel like buying the game, then at least you technically tried it for free. But based on my personal experience, I think all of your doubts will go away and you'll want to buy LEGO Marvel Super Heroes right away.

Dead Space is essentially a 3rd-person-shooter set in a haunted house in space. As Isaac Clarke you spend the vast majority of the game on the USG Ishimura, a mining ship with technical difficulties. However, you soon find out that technical defects are the least of your worries on this ship, as the reanimated remains of the crew chase you down while you're doing your best trying to get out of this predicament alive. Interestingly, Isaac is not military personnel, but rather an engineer, so instead of shredding aliens with assault rifles and shotguns you slice them to pieces with your power tools. During combat you'll mostly be dismembering different types of the so-called Necromorph to incapacitate and ultimately kill them, and even though Isaac moves rather slowly and heavily the fights are very gratifying, not least because of ample (and very gory) visual feedback.
Dead Space liberally uses and mixes elements from other established horror and sci-fi franchises and manages to concoct something that's interesting and fun to play. Everything, from the clean visuals to the simple but good enough story is tight and to the point, and there are rarely sections where you feel like you're just wasting your time. Even though the story backdrop is rather thin and won't win many prizes, it works well, gives you clear goals and enough context to know what you're doing. The atmosphere is tense throughout and some of the imagery is rather creative and maybe even a bit disturbing.
In summary: I can very easily recommend Dead Space if you're looking for a solid horror game set in a sci-fi universe. It's an interesting spin on many ideas and tropes you'll have seen somewhere else already and never outstays its welcome.

First off, My RIG:
ECS A960m-m3 Motherboard
AMD Fx-6350 3.9ghz/4.2ghz with CoolerMaster Hyper 212+evo
Asus Strix GTX 970 4gb oc
16 GB Geil Dragon 1333 Ram
1TB HDD (game on this one) 256GB SSD (os on this one) - irrelevant -
First Impressions: The game is fun! As you may have heard, it is a mash up of a 'good' dead island, mirrors edge, a bit of assassins creed (securing safe zones - like in creed claiming borgia towers), fallout (looting and lock picking) and the movie I am Legend ( night time play ).  Parkouring around the map is fun because it feels natural at times.  Sometimes you will struggle to climb a ledge and sometimes you will flow across rooftops as if you were Aladdin!  Almost everything seems scalable/climbable!  The first part of the game actually reminds me of Metro where characters are talking amongst each other and you can just listen in.  You get a slight sense of character understanding, but am sure that you do more so along the campaign.  At times your main character sounds like Nathan Drake from Uncharted and at times he sounds like Rick from PawnStars.
Graphics:  This game demands graphics AND cpu performance!  Off the bat, I notice as you may have read elsewhere, the god awful fiiiillllmmmm graaaiiinnnn effect (film grain, noise).  You can disable this, which I highly recommend. Just google it. I have done this and set my graphics to high and get between 35 and 50 fps in the outside world and a solid 60 inside buildings.  Here is the kicker - I have the draw distance set to zero. I've noticed only a few trees have popped in and out from zero setting to full setting. I advise setting to zero because you really only need to see in your viscidity anyway, which is a good (simulated) 300 feet, don't get me wrong, you can still see across the map, and i bet you won't notice much change between the settings.  You may read in threads to set sun shadowing to 0, but when i did that, it looked really bad, certain inside areas and face shading got muddy and dark, but frame did jump like 15-20.  I'd leave this on for the sake of playing a pretty game.  The one thing I really enjoy about games like this is the level of detail in the environment. Random real pictures of things like people and animals and little note, the knobs on a radio,  the crusting on a picture frame.  This kind of stuff makes the world feel more real and less game like. Besides that, lighting and shadowing are great, some textures look real, some look fake, i'd say its pretty, but not really ground breaking.  This is one of those games that looks good, and gets better along the way, because your mind is creating what the world is to you ...
Story:  You get dropped in this town called Harran, which has been affected by the infection, and you are part of what is called the GRE ... some government cleanup crew maybe... isn't that always the case. Anyway, along the way you seem to question your morals on who you really want to help, the GRE or the citizens trying to survive. Only a few hours in, so not really deep into the story, but seems interesting enough to keep playing.  Oh and your name is Crane.
Gameplay: Ragdoll Ragdoll Ragdoll! Gotta love rag doll effects!  Killing zombie and then kicking it around...that can be a game in itself! oh wait, look at that, it is now! :)  Besides that, melee is near identical to dead island, you may get frustrated trying to bash a zombies head in about 10 times before it dies, but its surprisingly satisfying. Searching for items is kind of silly, you just feel the air when prompted to search.  Also opening doors, you have the hand of god which magically opens and closes doors! Silly, but meh, negligible. When running and parkouring, you have to look at the ledge or area you are jumping to, this makes for more realism and excitement, especially at night when "they" come out to get you. Everyone rants about this game, and I decided to give it a go. At the time of this review, I'm very near the end (I think).
Unfortunately, Antichamber failed to impress me. The environment looks unfinished, the philosophical hindsight wall panels are boringly cliche and the game has no story and almost zero ambience. The only interesting things about the environment are the "Three Paths in Sight" museum room (which had some creatures I hoped I might encounter) and that black Macguffin block that's always floating out of sight and whispering.
The audio was just confusing in places. What's with all the sounds of nature? Most of the time, it seems to serve no purpose.
This game is supposed to "mess with my head", which it did for about two minutes. The non-Euclidean geometry that Antichamber employs would probably have been a lot more effective at messing with me if there was any narrative at all to hook me in. But there isn't, so it isn't very impressive. Once you realize that this is all possible because it's a computer game and can have all the wacky spatial physics that it wants, it sort of takes the fun away. To make up for the lack of plot, I imagined that this game is like a benign version of the movie Cube; where you can't die, and if you just persevere, you will eventually complete it. And there are a lot of cubes.
That being said, Antichamber does have some redeeming features. Being able to try any chamber from the start of the game saves you the endless frustration of having to go back through all the other puzzles should you get stuck or fail a section. The game relies quite a bit on a "learn as you go" approach, which I appreciate, and the help tools were limited, forcing the player to work out the "Cube Gun" and the different color cube functions on their own. Some of the puzzles were actually quite fun to solve.
One of the problems with puzzle games is that they have little replay value. However, you may want to play them as a quick run-through for nostalgia's sake (Portal series). But for that to happen, the game has to provide you with some desire to play it. As I went further and further into Antichamber and realized that there was no story at all, it robbed me of my motivation and turned the game into just something to complete, which is a disappointment. I feel like it could have been more, but it seems more like a beta build than a finished game that sells for twenty dollars. I'm glad I bought it on sale, because if I had bought it full price, I would be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Likely as not, I'll uninstall Antichamber once I've completed it and not play it again.
Imagine Portal 2 without GLADOS, Wheatley, Cave Johnson, physics gel, Aerial Faith Plates, cake and only six colors. You've just played Antichamber, and I've just saved you twenty dollars.

Dead Space is essentially a 3rd-person-shooter set in a haunted house in space. As Isaac Clarke you spend the vast majority of the game on the USG Ishimura, a mining ship with technical difficulties. However, you soon find out that technical defects are the least of your worries on this ship, as the reanimated remains of the crew chase you down while you're doing your best trying to get out of this predicament alive. Interestingly, Isaac is not military personnel, but rather an engineer, so instead of shredding aliens with assault rifles and shotguns you slice them to pieces with your power tools. During combat you'll mostly be dismembering different types of the so-called Necromorph to incapacitate and ultimately kill them, and even though Isaac moves rather slowly and heavily the fights are very gratifying, not least because of ample (and very gory) visual feedback.
Dead Space liberally uses and mixes elements from other established horror and sci-fi franchises and manages to concoct something that's interesting and fun to play. Everything, from the clean visuals to the simple but good enough story is tight and to the point, and there are rarely sections where you feel like you're just wasting your time. Even though the story backdrop is rather thin and won't win many prizes, it works well, gives you clear goals and enough context to know what you're doing. The atmosphere is tense throughout and some of the imagery is rather creative and maybe even a bit disturbing.
In summary: I can very easily recommend Dead Space if you're looking for a solid horror game set in a sci-fi universe. It's an interesting spin on many ideas and tropes you'll have seen somewhere else already and never outstays its welcome.

First, an explaination: When you buy SHADOWRUN RETURNS, you get one campaign - "Deadman's Trigger." It's a solid introduction to the gameplay and story world. There's one additional campaign for sale from the studio - "Dragonfall," which also adds some new items and gameplay functionality. Additionally, the game comes with a campaign editor, allowing you to create your own or download campaigns from others on Steam Workshop.
In terms of gameplay, SR is basically a glorified point-and-click adventure, with XCOM-style turn-based combat added in. TL,DR: The port is awful. If you really need to play this game, do it on console. The game is just worse than RE:4, which also has a better PC port (They’ve updated it).
First, I’ll talk about the port, then I’ll talk about the game.
The port is awful. With vsync on, the input delay is hilariously bad. With vsync off, the game is extremely unstable. Critical characters will fall through the ground, and you’ll have to reload over and over until you get lucky. Sometimes, especially in the zero G sections, the game gets confused about where you should be, or how you should be standing, and then just gives you and kills you. I’ll falling through the ground multiple times, and there was one section near the end of the game the froze over and over. The mouse support is terrible. The acceleration feels very odd, and even at max sensitivity, I needed to pick up the mouse and swipe several times just to turn 180. I don’t think there have been any graphical improvements over the console version, so you might as well just play that version.
The game isn’t great. If you need to scratch that 3rd person “horror” shooter itch, just play RE:4 again. Yeah, the controls are kinda odd, but the mouse actually works properly. Once you get used to the RE:4 controls, they feel much smoother and more responsive than Dead Space’s. Prepare for more unfavorable RE:4 comparisons by the way. The gameplay in RE:4 rarely stops. Yes, there are traditional cutscenes, but they aren’t too frequent. Dead Space doesn’t have traditional cutscenes, but you do get talked at by “support” characters almost constantly, and when you’re being talked at, you can’t run, or open doors, or use save stations. I feel that the game will drop inputs fairly regularly, and movement is annoyingly slow. Dead Space introduces a mechanic in which you can dismember various enemies, but there’s always one correct choice per enemy. For example, a standard zombie is running towards you, cut off the legs, then cut off the arms. It gets quite repetitive. In RE:4, there are time when you might want to go for headshots, or legs shots.
Dead Space tries be scary at all times, and I suppose it has a more consistent tone, but I was actually scared less often in this game. It can get scary at a couple moments, in fact, precisely two moments in my opinion, largely owing to the sound design, which is usually good. Most of the enemy design is just a worse version of The Thing (John Carpenter, no one cares about the 50’s version). It’s actually quite odd how inconsistent the quality of the scares are. Sometimes, you hear a terrible sound of anguish, and an odd, strained breath, followed by a vision of a shadow of a strange, once human creature slowly walking around a corner, backlit by a cold, fluorescent light. At other times, you’re locked in some airport terminal waiting room until you kill X number of lame zombie men. There’s an enemy that can regenerate, and you can never kill it, but there very first time it’s introduced, you’re locked in a small room with it, and can get used to how amazingly slow it is. They try to hype up the same monster later on, but you already know just how small of a threat it poses.
The world of the game feels like it was design to be open from the beginning, but then some cooperate suit decided that that might confuse people, so they made it linear. Not only is it linear, you have a magic line on the ground that makes sure you never get lost, because it’s not like being lost can be an effective aspect of fear. RE:4 is linear as well, but it feels like it was designed to be linear from the beginning, and it just seems to flow better.
Most survival horror games build tension by limiting your ammo and health supplies, but Dead Space doesn’t do that. Instead, your inventory is always full, and you will often need to backtrack to the nearest store to empty it out. You get upgrade materials to improve your armor and weapons, but you get so much cash from selling all that health and ammo you aren’t using that you’ll have everything leveled all the way up by the end. RE:4 gave you too much ammo as well, but cash was limited, and you needed to save up for the guns and upgrade you actually wanted.
The story is pretty straight forward, and none of the characters are interesting. RE:4 has a basic story as well, but all the characters are so strong, and the entire narrative is delivered with such camp, that it’s always entertaining. Dead Space treats its story much more seriously, which was a bad idea, because the story is lame and predictable.
Story spoilers:
It was so obvious that I didn’t even realize it was supposed to be a mystery, but they treat the revelation as a grand, Earth shacking reveal.
This review is obviously very negative, but the game is more disappointing than really bad. It isn’t as good as RE:4, but the zero G areas are fun (if glitchy). Cutting off limbs is fun at first, and deciding what to upgrade first can be interesting. The scenery changes often enough to stay interesting, even if most of it really doesn’t make sense to be on a space ship.  A couple of the monster designs are quite good. But overall, I would tell you to skip this game unless you are massively into action horror, and have already played RE:4, and F.E.A.R. (the first two), and Condemned (the first one), and Fatal Frame (the first two), and Metro 2033, and a few others that I’m sure I’m, forgetting.

"Why would you put online coop in a survival horror game? That's terrible! - 2/10
Why isn't the online coop in this survival horror game working yet? That's terrible! - 2/10"
Gotta love hypocrisy... Oh and, about coop: This might be the first horror game to use coop, and still manage to feel tense and (dare I say) scary. Why? Because only one of the characters has weapons. The other player/AI is used as either a spotters, and/or to finish enemies while they're down.
It works beautifully, and the ability (and necessity) to switch between both characters keeps it tense. You never feel like the other character is just there for the sole purpose of making the game easier and less fun. They actually complement each other's abilities perfectly (ex: one knocks it down the other uses its heavier melee weapon to finish it off. One shows the weak point, the other attacks it)... You know, kinda like they're cooperating.
As far as the whole Resident Evil thing is concerned, this is the purest RE experience since... Perhaps RE4? It's definitely more "classic RE" than 5 or 6. Not sure how it compares to Revelations 1, since I haven't played that one. I know it also has all the traditional back-traking and map exploring Rev1 had. You know? The one that's at the core of every good Resident Evil game.
On the hardest difficulty, it will mess you up. Ammo is scarce and enemies are brutal. Barry's portion is much easier (and linear), but he can still die rather easily.
The story is pretty good. Nothing like the convoluted, bombastic, over-the-top bulls**t of RE6. It doesn't have the campy tone of RE4. I'd say the tone and story are closer to the gamecube Resident Evil Remake, for lack of a better example. Only, with more humanity. It almost feels like a Final Fantasy game, at times.
Production value is the only real setback. It's clear this game was made on a much smaller budget than a major Capcom game. Environments, animations and overall setpieces aren't very complex. As a whole, it feels less like a AAA game and more like a... Like a Telltale game, I guess? It's doing the absolute best it can with what little it has. And, much like a Telltale Game, its "absolute best" is great enough to ignore its rougher aspects.
Anyway, great game! Pleasently surprised. I give it 2/10 because Leon isn't in it.

TL:DR Bottom Line you have a fun open world RPG zombie game with great graphics, a good story an amazing freerunning mechanic, really poor optimization, dry color pallate and a difficulty level based off the time of day (in game day). Also this game hates AMD users so don't get it if that describes you.
INTRO: Yet another zombie game. However, if your going to be another one of thousands than you might as well be good at it. Dying Light sets out to achieve that and, in my own opinion, does a great job. Many people have said it mixes the ideas of Far Cry, Dead Island and Mirrors Edge.
OVERVIEW: It's Far Cryish in the survival sense. You can find plants and supplies then use them to craft yourself a new weapon or maybe some medicine. It also has neat little first person animations for healing yourself or messing with a power box. Dead Island brings zombies to the table and the skill trees (yes Far Cry has those too) it also brings it's diabloish loot system. What it DOESN'T bring however is a♥♥♥♥♥♥story line, an unplayable launch (unless you run AMD) crap AI and queastionable at best gameplay. Mirrors Edge comes into this and brings my favorite part. The freerunning.
FREERUNING AND THE WORLD: It feels smooth yet challenging. Some games would have you just hold LT to start climbing walls. This game uses right bumper (I used a controller) to jump and to grab onto ledges and stuff. The small bit of challenge and interaction comes in how you might go about climbing that building over there. Theres a telephone pole do you want to use that? Should you just try to climb strait up it? Oh maybe you can use that new wallrun ability you got somehow! Or you could climb to the building next to it! It's this type of thinking that made it really fun. The game also constantly rewards you for just freeruning around for the fun of it with xp. The levels are huge and being an open world game it gives you plenty to do. More sidequests than I can even imagine completing and lots of little things to get distracted with like airdrops and people to save talk to or buy things from.
LEVELING AND DIFFICULTY: The powers you get from Leveling up are fun. My favorite was probably the drop kick. Using it on a zombie that is at the edge of a building will never get old. The game at no point felt unfair but it was pretty difficult. I suppose it might feel hard as most the time I tried to do the missions and stuff at night because you get double xp from it. You also most likely get dead. Night time brings a whole slew of problems. Zombies become more aggresive, you can be invaded (if you have online turned on that is) and the most stressful part is that you have nigh invicinble hunter killer zombies that will chase you down like you told them that you lactate weakness.
STORY: The story itself was actually pretty good! I got quite immersed and loved the attitude of the main character. I won't say too much for fear of spoiling anything but the gameplay portion in the end was an excelently well done and the story left me feeling satisfied. Like the end of a good book or movie.
BAD STUFF: Now to get to the rough stuff. What I hated about this game. Not disliked. Things I hated. First off was optimization. The game might as well not have it. It's quite glitchy at times and the story while overall good took some turns where it felt like the developers wanted a whole new story. The enviroment is colored with browns and greys although I should say it still looks pretty stunning. The "Be the Zombie" mode that everyone and they're mum were flipping out about doesn't work due to connection issues. Everytime I start it up I begin joining someone it says the connection couldn't be done and to try again later. Also the game does this wierd thing where everytime I load it up it's saved all my options except full screen. So every time I have to open it up I'm forced to go to the options menu first thing. Last thing and this♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off the most. ANYONE WITH AMD the game won't work for you right now. Although to give the game developers some credit they have recognized the problem and are claiming that they are trying to fix it.
Dispite all these rough edges though this game will go down as one of my new favorites.

The main detractor of this game (at least on PC) is the lack of both online and offline co-op. I feel like the game needs at least one of these to truly shine.
That being said, RE: Revelations 2 is an enjoyable experience both in Campaign and Raid mode. It was fun playing as the different characters+also switching between them in order to find items, get attack combos, or for exploration in general. I particularly thought it was ingenious the way the partners complemented each other. Moira can blind enemies for Claire and Natalie can point out enemy weaknesses for Barry to exploit. Switching back and forth to create these effects felt really cool in terms of strategizing and dealing with enemies in the most efficient fashion.
The campaign is indeed very actiony, but I was glad that it included horror elements. Barry's and Natalie's storyline, in particular, had some really intense scary moments that put me on edge. This was compunded by the fact that I was playing in hard mode, which made it very friggin' difficult for me to manage my ammo and health item usage efficiently. It truly did feel like Survival Horror despite the fact that its style is more similar to a third person shooter rather than a classic horror game.
Raid mode is a lot of fun and I haven't grown tired of it yet, nor do I think I will for a while; the level and skill progression system ensures this. There's always something to look forward to after each level up, whether its by using skill points to level up skills or by finding out that you've unlocked a new active or passive skill slot to use. It's also fun to mess around with all the different characters available, given that each has his/her own skillsets and level progression. It's definitely a great mode to have fun with. It really is a shame there is no online co-op, though.
The game does have its downsides, too. Like DLC. It is indeed annoying that there is so much day-one DLC when it feels like there really shouldn't be. Thankfully the DLC doesn't include anything that's truly crucial, most of it is just bonus stuff that just makes the game easier. It does suck that we have to pay for costumes though. I wish they could have just been unlockables like they've been on previous games. Why Capcom? Why?
All in all, though, I was pretty satisfied with the game. Despite its issues I still think it is a worthy addition to the Resident Evil series.

Alright, follow suite of the majority of my fellow gamers who purchased this game under the guise that it would have co-op play.... No.  It does not.  Nor did it mention the lack of such literally until just as the game released.
However, unlike the majority of the gamers, I've experienced no visual lag or frame drops, and the input lag mentioned was fixed simply by turning "Fast Mouse" on in the options....  My mouse was no longer 'smoothed' out, causing me to look past what I was attempting to look at.
The first episode, however, was upsettingly short, leaving me, of course, wanting a bit more out of my game, and, yes, I know that more is coming, however... Raid mode, should... I hope, keep me interested in this game, except... oh wait... I'm still all alone, aren't I?  -sigh-
Aside from that, the game actually plays relatively well, and, it has it's few surprises here, or there....  But from the standpoint of someone who followed the series from the first released back on the PSX.... yeah... nothing surprising.
I've already found an annoying unlock glitch, as in, the final character I have to unlock in Raid mode specifies I must have 90 or more Completion Medallions... I have 100... still haven't unlocked that final character....
Can I recommend the game in it's current state... well... honestly...?  I could... yes.  If you're interested in playing the game specifically for continuation of the series, or scratching some completion itch... sure.  If you want the game to go crazy with a friend... no, I can't....
But, in a nutshell:
-     No co-op, yet.  Of any kind.  Despite any description above, none.
-     First episode is disappointingly short.  Comparable to one chapter in RE5.
-     Survivalist difficulty actually does offer some challenge.
-     Raid mode, as well, can offer challenge, but is mostly the same rinse and repeat kill everything and leave.
-     Personal experience was, no video issues whatsoever, but... according to others?  Maybe?
-     Personal experience; ?Bug? preventing me from unlocking final character in Raid mode?
-     All things considered, it's not bad, nor is it something I'd straight up tell everyone to buy.
Side note, to those claiming the game has crazy amounts of DLC already... I dunno... I bought the complete season in advance and... it came with the first 23 dollars worth of DLC.... so... uh... sure.  The others, as in, the weapon/parts/album slots... seem relatively unnecessary....  So, if you have the complete season, you really don't have any DLC to download as of this time....
Anyway, just my outlook.

Risk of Rain is one of the perfect games to play when you have a good hour or so to breeze through. It is a roguelike where the longer you are alive the harder the game becomes. Each stage has chests and a portal to the next stage. You earn money by killing things and when you are done with a stage you have to survive for 90 seconds as an increased number of enemies spawn. Once you've killed everything in the level you progress to the next stage and do it all over again until the fourth stage, at which point you have the choice to go back through the stages to gain more items or to progress to the final stage. The game has a number of varied characters, my personal favorite being the huntress, that you unlock by fighting specific bosses or doing challenges. The items you pick up throughout the game come in a number of varieties, white, green, yellow, red, orange, and purple. White, green, and red are normal items going up in rarity that can be bought or found in chests, yellow items are boss items that you have a chance of getting from bosses bestowing a power that the boss used, orange are usable items that can be found similarly to regular items, and purple items are hidden relics that change the base stats of the player and monsters around them as well as other effects that can make the game harder or easier. Each stage is varied and have unique designs that are beautiful to look at while not being distracting from the action. The final stage has many different side paths to take that can unlock different items and some machines that can be used against the final boss to make it an easier battle. The final boss goes through many different stages and it is a steady challenge, especially towards the 50 minute mark. The only real negatives I can think of from the game is that the multiplayer never really worked well for me and despite having gotten all the achievements in the game some of them did not unlock on my steam profile.
TL;DR Excellent Roguelike with a lot of different characters, enemies, and items.

People might think Half Life 2 is over-rated, but it isn't. This game is literally the pinnacle of FPS gaming, and deserves all the praise it has received.
Despite being over a decade old, HL2 delivers stunning visuals and excellent graphics quality even today. The fact it's old enough to run at max settings even on weak machines makes it even better, and almost anyone with a half-decent rig should be able to play it without any issues.
The gameplay is simple to control, but level design makes the game a complex puzzle in addition to its excellent shooting mechanics. You won't receive any hints, tips, prompts, or waypoints. You'll have to rely on your own ability to observe and navigate your environment, and solve carefully engineered puzzles using Source's physics engine. Observing and understanding what's happening around you is vital to HL2's gameplay, and puts it miles ahead of the simple linear shooters that are common today. The atmosphere is brilliant too, and captures elements of both action and horror.
The game's characters are fantastic as well; each one is unique and memorable. This is one of the few games where I've been seriously worried when any of the main characters were in danger.
Finally, the story is one of the best out there. You'll always want to know what happens next, and it's nearly impossible to walk away. Replaying the game to catch subtle snippets you missed on your first runthrough guarantees hours of gameplay, on top of an already multi-hour game.
Half Life 2 (along with its sequels) is easily the best shooter I've had the opportunity to play. It has visual excellence, mind-blowing level design, unique enemies, and a fantastic story that leaves you wanting more. No game library is complete without it.

The nail in the coffin is the story (SPOILER ALERT). RE Revelations 2 as the potenial to be an amazing title, however there are glaring problems:
1. Frame Rate drops, like most reviews before mine I have experienced drops and freezes. I managed to make them less frequent by lowering my settings a bit, but they are still incredibly noticable. ***Patched***
2. Co-op functionality, while I personally don't play Resident Evil as a co-op game anyway, we were promised co-op for this version of the game and I expected the option to be available as most others did.***There's a local co-op mod being released/worked on if it's that serious??***
3. Window settings, there doesn't seem to be a Fullscreen (windowed) option and the Windowed view made the game sluggish. ***No lionger an issue.***
While these things take a fair amount out of the submersion of the game, they don't make it unplayable.

1. Atmosphere, I'm not too far into Episode 1 but I personally think the Horror aspect is definitely there within the prison setting so far. Had a few jump scares even when I knew that something was going to jump out.

The very short and simple version is this: If you didn't like the previous Arkham games, you won't like this one.
That said, this game seems to have had a shoddy release on PC. Not that I'd know, I only recently upgraded to a point of being able to play the game. And 48 hours later after 100%ing the story (not newgame+ or DLC or whatever), I'd say this is a damn fine game. There's one specific factor that keeps it from surpassing Arkham City as my favourite Arkham game, but it is a very solid second.
Performance-wise, I was expecting this to have some issues. I didn't expect that the game had been fixed entirely. I
be right with that. Three specific areas in the game caused the game to freeze and practically crash multiple times. Made the Riddler challenges within them annoying because they froze, they wouldn't have saved and I'd have to do them again. Made me paranoid about hunting them in big rooms.
The areas were {SPOILERS}
When I say "might", I mean that I'm also running the Windows 10 Anniversary version, notorious for messing with a hell of a lot of programs, and I hear Arkham Knight has issues in this version of Windows 10. So whether it is to blame, or the game itself, I don't know. It seems strange that some sections of the game within enclosed buildings would crash instead of the big open world where everything is happening.
Besides those, I had no issues with the game at all. No glitches, no defomities, no frame drops, no blurry textures... The weirdest thing I saw was probably just a physics issue in which Batman dropped from the sky and beat up a Riddler informant, all with his cape stuff over his head covering his face. Everything besides that seems to work as it should.
But onto gameplay. Loved it. I was practically prepared for some poor showings, like say any and all the sections with the Batmobil. I continuously see how that got a lot of complaints. But honestly, I thought those were fine. The controls were easy enough, they weren't terribly difficult or annoying (and I played the game on Hard first go), there's DEFINITELY been far worse driving controls/mechanics in AAA titles, and there's something I found enjoyable about driving in a sneaky way around the streets to take out the larger tank drones.
I guess the only downside I have for it is just how many missions needed the Batmobil. Plenty of which just take the bad guy back to the GCPD.
But besides that, I spent majority of the game just grappling and gliding around everywhere. That was the thing I originally saw with the game that got me hyped. I ran everything on the highest settings I could get it and it was smooth, 60+ frames at all times. It made Gotham look gorgeous to fly around in. All I wanted to do since that first trailer was just fly around for a while. I got plenty of that and not once did I get tired of it.
Everything else with the gameplay is pretty much what you'd expect. More of the same, but improved in some areas. Still plenty of gadgets to use, more combo options, more takedown options. Plenty to learn, difficult to master.
The one thing I see as the annoying factor for people are the Riddler stuff to hunt around for. It's no better or worse in this game than the previous ones. If you liked it then, you'll like it now. Some are stupidly easy, some are hard enough that you'll look them up on how to do. The bottom line with it is I personally enjoy things that make me go out and explore this open world, particularly in places I probably wouldn't go otherwise. The only thing that stops this game from being my favourite is the lack of boss fights.
boss fights. Remember Mr. Freeze in Arkham City? Or Deathstroke in Arkham Origins? None of those here. Some of them turn into almost standard Predator challenges with one of the bad guys in the mix as well, hardly doing anything to make them significant, or they'll just be there after beating down many of their thugs. Or be reduced to Batmobil tank battles. Either way, majority of the time it boiled down to "Press Button to Win". Two characters got a semi reasonable encounter, but they somewhat blended in with the multiple minions around them. They stood out and had special attacks needed for them, but they ultimately still flowed in the same combat and combos and such. Nothing felt terrifically epic as previous game encounters, sadly.
All in all, solid 8/10. I enjoyed it, will replay it several times. Hell, I still got New Game + and DLC stuff to sift through, but as of this, I thought the main game was fantastic.

A good open world game as far as mechanics and execution go, AK does many things right. The Gotham City is probably the best crafted one in the series, allowing for convenient exploration both on foot and inside of the Batmobile. The side missions are fed to the player at a great pace, allowing for logical and nearly seamless dipping between the side stuff and the main story. What enhances this quality is the fact that many of the side missions require the player to wait. The antagonists leave trails or establish their positions as the story progresses, some objectives are impossible to achieve until Batman can bring in his car to a specific island of the city and, probably my favourite part, many of the missions require you to notice sound cues and follow them. This is quite brilliant, making some of the side-stories to appear more naturally, instead of magical markers showing you everything you need to know. Overall, the open world aspect is fantastic with the exception of Riddler trophies, which are probably the most tedious one in the entire series; a surprise, given that a fair few of them were unexpectedly clever. Sadly, the majority is just an annoying busywork and locking a side-mission conclusion beyond getting 100% of them, while traditional for the series, pains me so much more this time. Needless to say, I lacked the patience to do this.
The gameplay lives up to the high standard set by the design: combat is the smoothest, most dynamic yet, not afraid to throw tonnes of enemies that require old and loved tactics to overcome; but also introducing a few new ways of dealing with the peskiest of adversaries. While the combat received slight polish when compared to the older games, the stealth is where the true revolution happened. Fear Takedowns are a fantastic and satisfying tool, with an interesting balancing mechanic of recharging after stealth takedowns, an action much harder to perform after inciting panic among the enemies. Several gadgets received new functions, uniquely tuned against the new opposing forces, broadening the possibilities of the player. Mobility in stealth sections was improved as well, opening the areas for a much more interesting design.
The variety is further built upon with the most notable toy of them all: the Batmobile. I didn't find myself hating it, personally. It makes exploration faster and brings player's attention to the ground level, which holds some of the surprises, and the usual combat feels good. Not as great as the on-foot fighting, but the hordes of enemy drones do introduce a proper combat dynamic. Car chases, however, get old after just a few of them, and it doesn't help that one of the classic enemies was included for a little bit of a different flavour in a few chases. They just got barely anything going for them, boiling down to a long drive and waiting for when you can hit the attack button again. Once. The boss fights, when in the car, have a similar problem: they are either an exercise in frustration, dragging for far too long or both. I much preferred Riddler racing tracks which, despite requiring a lot of repetition to get them damn perfect for the challenges, served their purpose well and actually amused. Similarly, the new traversal options and weapons contained within the Batmobile breathed some fresh air into the "riddles". Overall, a great addition.
Now, just like the open world was great, the story is... well. Forgettable might not even cut it. It has some moments that surprise, but over the course of the hours, it becomes blatantly obvious that the person in charge of writing the story had no idea what to do with it. Scarecrow is completely wasted, coming off as a weaker, bland and lacking villain who basically just rambles on about everything. His appearance in Asylum was more impactful than the leading role, that is how bad it is. The trend of bad storytelling is taken further with the titular Arkham Knight. While an expected nod to the comics, he comes and goes without much of an impact. Definitely a missed opportunity there. Shockingly, the side missions are written much better, at least some of them. For every intriguing, emotional little bit, there is an episode that is short, unengaging and its absence wouldn't hurt the game one bit. And that is on top of half the rogue's gallery having "revenge" as the sole reason for being in the game. I expected better of these characters, and the game has some of them taken to proper depth. We are even given unexpected and daring conclusions to two of the well-established villain's stories, something I enjoyed seeing and continues the tradition introduced by the ending of Arkham City. Overall, writing is mixed, but the main plot disappoints severely.
And yes, even on a decent setup the game still has hiccups during Batmobile sections, but it is nowhere near unplayable. GTX 970 kept me on 60 FPS most of the times with driving stages dropping, at worst, to 45 FPS.

This game can be mentally exhausting. For me it is a very advanced chess game. My favorite option within XCOM is the ability to play on "Ironman" meaning permanent death and no returning to previous saves. Depending on the difficulty, a few missions will be unbeatable, and you have to have the tenacity to fall back to base. As a turn based game there will be many moments where you calculate all your avaliable options, bringing such a depth of strategy. This game utilizes percentage and statistics. When you shoot at an alien you have a % to hit and crit, based on position, gun used, type of enemy, rank of soldier, etc. Some people do not like the though of basing shots on percents, but in real life the cummalitive shots by any soldier can be shown as a percentage.
The main base is another core feature of the game. It allows a lot of customization and hard choices to best adapt to your situation. You build up different facilities for enineering and science related projects, as well as other buildings to improve and add gameplay features. You have to mange money and items, and choose between items and research that benefits you. You develop relationshops with the soldiers in the barracks, because you can customize their names, armor, race, voice. You can look around and zoom in at different locations to see your base that you have created. It really makes you feel like the "Commander", making the big decisions.
This is a very balanced game for me. Playing on Classic Ironman, I have very few mistakes I can make, making decisions tough and challenging. Good soldiers die, I lose some missions, but that was makes it so interesting. Online is addicting, and now with the Enemy Within expansion, you have a ton of customization to use online. This game will make you pound your table, it will make you throw your hands up in excitement, but isnt how real life works? Try the demo, and even without Enemy Within, this is a very complete game in itself.

Update for final episode release.
It was really good, all of the episodes were a joy to play through, fans of earlier games will definitely like this game, has some neat references. To be honest its the best Campaign/story in a Resident Evil game since the series changed to 3rd person "shoulder" view, atleast i think so. big step in the right direction.

There are multiple endings aswell, without spoiling i can say that the differences were quite huge so it is worth playing both.
I also highly recommend picking up the bonus episode "The Struggle" aswell. It added alot of story and filled some points.
oh and the stuttering issues was hotfixed :)
------------------------------------------------------------
The campaign is not as fast paced and explosive as most of the recent games in the series, its more of an atmospheric horror shooter (would ya look at that). And you dont get cabin fever from the level design either :) The first "episode" set up the story nicely and was interesting, especially at the end.
The game plays alot like Resident Evil 6, and if you havent played that game it is the least clunky game in the series control wise, you can still move and shoot at the same time and melee is still fun (while not as dynamic as RE6) but its satisfying enough to make you wanna kick and hit things. And you dont have to stop jogging for turning etc. Oh and the evade system from Revs 1 is back and works much Much better this time.
Graphics are very good too, feels really next-gen ish, with clothes having their own physics and all that.
Raid mode is just as fun this time aswell, still a ton of weapons and modifications to unlock, and individual levels for different characters. And the dreadful bonus for not taking damage during a map is replaced with a "dont use a herb" medal, this saves alot of frustration, atleast for me lol. Nothing but improvements in this mode.
There was also some negativity around the game lagging and stuff and people being unable to fix it. I have an average PC and i had a few lagspikes in the first bit of playing.
What i did was set Framerate to "Variable" and lowering the Effects quality, the blood splashes and gunfire sometimes made me lag if there was alot of them at once, dont know why.
TL:DR_
Better raid mode.
Smoother non-clunky gameplay.
Old school campaign, more slow paced.
Awesome graphics.
Good characters.

First Impressions: The game is fun! As you may have heard, it is a mash up of a 'good' dead island, mirrors edge, a bit of assassins creed (securing safe zones - like in creed claiming borgia towers), fallout (looting and lock picking) and the movie I am Legend ( night time play ).  Parkouring around the map is fun because it feels natural at times.  Sometimes you will struggle to climb a ledge and sometimes you will flow across rooftops as if you were Aladdin!  Almost everything seems scalable/climbable!  The first part of the game actually reminds me of Metro where characters are talking amongst each other and you can just listen in.  You get a slight sense of character understanding, but am sure that you do more so along the campaign.  At times your main character sounds like Nathan Drake from Uncharted and at times he sounds like Rick from PawnStars.
Graphics:  This game demands graphics AND cpu performance!  Off the bat, I notice as you may have read elsewhere, the god awful fiiiillllmmmm graaaiiinnnn effect (film grain, noise).  You can disable this, which I highly recommend. Just google it. I have done this and set my graphics to high and get between 35 and 50 fps in the outside world and a solid 60 inside buildings.  Here is the kicker - I have the draw distance set to zero. I've noticed only a few trees have popped in and out from zero setting to full setting. I advise setting to zero because you really only need to see in your viscidity anyway, which is a good (simulated) 300 feet, don't get me wrong, you can still see across the map, and i bet you won't notice much change between the settings.  You may read in threads to set sun shadowing to 0, but when i did that, it looked really bad, certain inside areas and face shading got muddy and dark, but frame did jump like 15-20.  I'd leave this on for the sake of playing a pretty game.  The one thing I really enjoy about games like this is the level of detail in the environment. Random real pictures of things like people and animals and little note, the knobs on a radio,  the crusting on a picture frame.  This kind of stuff makes the world feel more real and less game like. Besides that, lighting and shadowing are great, some textures look real, some look fake, i'd say its pretty, but not really ground breaking.  This is one of those games that looks good, and gets better along the way, because your mind is creating what the world is to you ...
Story:  You get dropped in this town called Harran, which has been affected by the infection, and you are part of what is called the GRE ... some government cleanup crew maybe... isn't that always the case. Anyway, along the way you seem to question your morals on who you really want to help, the GRE or the citizens trying to survive. Only a few hours in, so not really deep into the story, but seems interesting enough to keep playing.  Oh and your name is Crane.
Gameplay: Ragdoll Ragdoll Ragdoll! Gotta love rag doll effects!  Killing zombie and then kicking it around...that can be a game in itself! oh wait, look at that, it is now! :)  Besides that, melee is near identical to dead island, you may get frustrated trying to bash a zombies head in about 10 times before it dies, but its surprisingly satisfying. Searching for items is kind of silly, you just feel the air when prompted to search.  Also opening doors, you have the hand of god which magically opens and closes doors! Silly, but meh, negligible. When running and parkouring, you have to look at the ledge or area you are jumping to, this makes for more realism and excitement, especially at night when "they" come out to get you.  As far as quest, this is like dead island too, but seems less annoying, sometimes things are hard, but everything seems manageable.  Some areas you will think with you head more than your brawn. The lock picking seems straight out of fallout, which is cool, cuz that was fun. Crafting is simple and easy, just find blueprints, find the items and craft. There is also a simple skill tree which you can level up with skill points and branch out the skill tree. There is also a level up bar for running and melee at the top of your hud in game. Stamina comes in to effect when running and melee, but its actually not annoying, its done very well. I have not played multiplayer, but would imagine it is awesome... i mean come on.. you can be a zombie!
Overall:
Pros+
+Pretty Graphics
+Fun Gameplay
+Easy crafting/skill tree level up
+Parkour is fun and real-ish
+Level of detail is nice
+Not annoying like Dead Island gameplay
+Ragdoll and melee is satisfying
+Movement is fluid
Cons-
-Weapons kind of degrade quickly ... but you're not always bashing things, you are running too.
-Apparently use of on core on whole game seems to create performance issues, but plays good still depending on rig.
-film grain ( you can fix )
-lip movement when characters speak ( not synced correctly - negligible to gameplay )
Last Words:
Get rid of film grain in game files, set your draw distance to zero, but them graphics up and enjoy the island of Harran!
Oh and when nightfall hits ... Run to the Hills!!! (Iron Maiden reference) ... or just run like hell to a safe zone, because it is scary and you may pee your jammies...

South Park: The Stick of Truth is a must own for anybody who even moderately enjoys watching the show. The Story, Graphic style, and Voice Acting are all spot on and, you can easily tell that Obsidian poured their heart and soul into crafting this faithful adaptation of the satirical cartoon. The story flows well and fits into the bizarre universe that is Southpark. It is like watching a long episode of the show that you happen to be a part of. The weapon and armor modification is one of the better systems that i've seen, with Armor patches and Weapon strap-ons (yes they are called weapon strap-ons but hey its a southpark game what exactly did you expect) you can create devastating synergies of one or more DOTs (Damage over time) and/or modifiers that increase Damage/DOT Durations/Life Steal/ETC. and you can use Armor patches to increase your Defense/Health/Regeneration/Mana (which in Southpark is called PP and yes the obvious joke is make). You aquire Class abilties, Magic abilites, and Traits as you level up and make new friends you also aquire out of combat abilities that help you get around as you progress through the story, the ranged weapon being the only of which that can be use both in and out of combat. One of my personal favorite mechanics of the game is that you can somethime use the enviroment to eliminate/thin out groups which in turn makes combat far easier. The game plays a bit like Paper Mario in that it is turn based and you time your attacks by pressing the corresponding button at the correct time to maximize the damage done.  As someone who enjoys watching Southpark I love this game.
I give Southpark: The Stick of Truth a solid 8/10 and, I recomend it to anyone who isn't Grossed Out/Offended Easily

In Antichamber, you wind your way through a massive maze of puzzles and challenges that often defy physical logic. Despite that, there is a logic to the world; you just have to learn to understand the odd logic. As the game progresses, you also gain the use of a gun that can absorb and spray cubes that may be used to help solve puzzles and reach otherwise inaccessable areas.
If you like to be challenged and enjoy having to think outside of the box, I highly recommend Antichamber. However, the learning curve in the game is very high, so this game isn't for everyone.

I've been thinking about this review for a while.
Arkham Knight is the most uneven game in the series. Some of the story beats are the best the Arkham games have to offer. Together with the once again top-notch soundtrack, its hard not to get emotionally involved in what's playing out in front of you. Characters are well voiced and their (one in particular) interactions with Batman are a highlight.
However, this is let down by the large amount of repetitive objectives in some of the side missions, and in the end, a rather uninteresting main antagonist. Gameplay is as tight as ever with combat maintaining the flow all Arkham games are famous for.
The batmobile is great, but overused. I understand Batman is powerful, but after you have shot literally HUNDREDS of tanks in similar battles for both story and side missions, it becomes a bit monotonous. I also missed the martial art specialists from Arkham Origins, they were the most interesting type of 'normal' enemy in the series.
Having purchased the season pass, the most wanted missions for Mr. Freeze and Ra's Al Ghul are great. The rest are only worth a purchase if you really want to experience some small extra story content or gameplay with other characters.
From a technical standpoint, don't bother unless you have at least a GTX 970.
Overall, I enjoyed Batman's final outing and the game is an essential purchase for any Arkham fan.

Video games, comic books and LEGO bricks.
is an incredible game for both LEGO- and comicfans.
The Good:
· A fun story that stays true to the Marvel universe.
· Countless characters like Spider-Man, the Hulk, Thor, Captain America... Basically any Marvel character you can or can't think of. (Even Stan Lee. Hell yes.)
· An open world with tons of side activities, collectable Bricks and breakable LEGO constructions.
· A wide variety of character types that offer for great replayability. Sometimes you will need to replay a level with heroes you have unlocked later on to reach secret areas and so on. For example: Captain America's shield to walk over flames, the Hulk's force to break weak walls, moving metal object with Magneto, and so on.
· Plenty of fun references to the Marvel movies.
The Bad:
· No online co-op, only a local split screen option (that doesn't always respond all to well, unfortunately).
· The game basically requires a controller to play. You can play with the keyboard just fine but there are no mouse controls, which takes away some of the experience. It's not especially a downside, but I thought I'd list it so you know what you're up against if you don't have a controller.
The Ugly:
· For a LEGO game it's absolutely stunning. Gorgeous lighting effects, fun animations, amazing voice-actors... It's a LEGO game to be proud of.
Final Verdict:
An amazing game for both casual gamers, LEGO-lovers and comicbook fanatics like myself. A game every Marvel fan has to own. 9/10

TL;DR Not at all like Shadowrun on 360, great text-based story, must get
I played the Shadowrun deathmatch spinoff for Xbox 360 years ago and it has always had a special place in my heart.  The combat was refreshing and very fun.  It had fleeting little story but I was intrigued by it nonetheless.
It's funny how much of a 180 this game is compared to the spinoff.
The combat is an ersatz XCOM and not really satisfying.  I played on normal so of course I wasn't playing the game to its full potential.  The combat was pretty boring and felt like an afterthought.
BUT WAIT!  This game doesn't suck!  In huge contrast to the only other Shadowrun game I have played this game has a story!  And what a story it is.  The plot is positively enthralling (hehe).  Sorry you'll get it when you buy this magnificent game.    The plot is split into two acts, of which the first I believe is stronger.  The first act is a pretty standard whodunit and the second is... I don't know if I missed out on some backstory from the tabletop game, but it's a lot to take in.  But sometimes it's nice to be overwhelmed by a story, you know?  The characters, dialogue and text descriptions (setting, items, etc.) is really where the game shines.  The characters are interesting (I found myself talking to every single one at every opportunity) and feel real.  Their personalities don't feel fake and nobody does a complete character change halfway through as an excuse for a plot twist which is common in games.  The dialogue is witty and enjoyable.  Sadly there are no voice actors, but it doesn't take away too much from the immersion.
There's just something special about the written word and its power to completely immerse you in a story.  The writers for this game are truly skilled, as the settings described are so much more than what I could ever gain from just seeing it.  There's such a huge emphasis on graphics these days that I think people get caught up in it and forget that sight is only one of many senses.  The written word describes all of them.  Sight, smell, sound, touch, you name it and it can be described.  I hope this game succeeds and more developers join this niche of text-based RPG, as there is truly no better way to immerse the player than to write down what you want them to know.
I give this game a 7/10 but it is really a must buy for me.  The story itself makes the game well worth the price when it's on sale.

Both chapters are fitting conclusions to this game, although the bad ending (although great) is VERY short and unsatisfing. The good ending is as cheesy, as over the top, as bazooka and as chopper as every other REsi game. In the end I would say this was the best game in the franchise since "the over the shoulder camera" revolutions.
I like it more than RE4 because of the story and characters, I like it more than RE5 because it has less action set pieces and I like it more than Revolutions 1 because it is not bound by the restrictions of a hand held system. BUT it is a truly shame, that there is no online Co-Op...
Still this is one of the greatest REsi games!
The Claire/Moire chapter not only is again very strong in survivor mode, which is amazing, considering the evolution of RE games, but also boosts amazing textures and lightning to generate a very creepy atmosphere full of tension and terror. The biggest new (old) addition are the classic RE-puzzles... they might not be to everyone's taste, but they are very classic and fun for those who solved those back in the day. I love how the game solves single player co-op, but still, not featuring online co-op in this game is disappointing, because it would make strategic stealth and survival even more complex and fun. This is THE major downside: Lack of online co-op!
One thing that deserves a mention are the boss fights... they are really REALLY tough...
The Barry chapter is no pick-nick, but is much shorter, but still great, with lots of opportunities for co-op kills and stealth.
While the first one, was really just a teaser, this one changes things up a bit... both, the Claire and Barry parts get more interesting, with interesting enemy types and great level design. Also, while in Ep.1 Barry played more like a shooter, here we are truly and always down to just one more round, one more bullet and survival is tough, therefore the welcome addition of stealth, which can instant-kill enemies normally able to swallow a buttload of bullets.
One downside is again the attack of the frame drop. After so many patches, it still is frustrating, especially on the boss fights, but with nerves of steel it is manageable... But this REALLY requires ANOTHER performance patch. I am truly having doubts at this point if going forward with episode 3 makes sense at this point.
Another great pro... the ending... so cheesy... so cliche... perfectly right for a Resident Evil game :D
Claire chapter is great, the atmosphere is superb, THIS is the RE game I want! The Barry chapter kinda dragged but also was really fun. The story is intriguing. I still experienced SOME frame rate drops, but these were minor. Also, the game seems to load heavily after each death and this causes frame rate drops, which go away after a few seconds, so if you experience this, simply wait before starting to play after death.

It's unfortunate, but, before I was able to really play this game, the option of giving it a positive review went right out the window. Yet again, a publisher treated the PC version of a title like an afterthought and gave us a slapped together copy/paste P.O.S. console port that
. The vsync is broken and locks the game at 30 fps, and if you turn it off (assuming you can get past the screen tearing) it actually
quite a few problems with the game. I can only assume that the movement and camera controls are in some way dependent on polling the framerate because it actually causes the mouse to have major problems and creates an invisible wall in a doorway very early on in the game. This can be fixed, but not without disabling the in-game vsync and forcing it through 3rd party software - in fact, the forced vsync option in AMD's Crimson control panel can't even get it to work (and from what I read, this is the same with the default control panel for NVIDIA cards) so you have to use a program like RadeonPro to get it to work properly.
If that wasn't bad enough, the controller support is terrible. First, there are no separate controller / keyboard & mouse settings - this is an all-too-common problem with PC games and it really shouldn't be; I often like to switch between the two (and I know I'm not alone), but, without separate settings for a controller, I have to pause the game, go into the control settings and properly invert the Y-axis every time I want to use the controller and then disable it every time I want to use the keyboard & mouse -
. And just in case that wasn't aggravating enough, you actually have to enable/disable the controller entirely, adding an additional, tedious step to an already tedious process.  Even if you decide to just commit to the controller entirely (and let's face it, unless you want to be constantly bouncing in and out of the settings window, you kind of have to), the deadzones on the control-sticks are HUGE so moving the camera with any kind of precision is out of the question, and precision aiming is a KEY game mechanic in Dead Space - you're supposed to slice apart the enemies limb-by-limb. They don't even offer a camera sensitivity slider for the controller - just the mouse - so to use a controller you have to use something like Durazno - an Xinput modification program - and bump up the anti-deadzone to 45%-50%.
I hate leaving a bad review for this game because, so far, the game itself seems great, and if you're someone who is willing to take the time and effort to get it working, you'll probably really enjoy it (just make sure you get it on sale). But when a publisher refuses to put the time and money into making a true PC version of thier game and instead just s*** out some console-to-PC-port garbage that won't even run without putting in hours of time troubleshooting issues that should have been ironed out before the game was ever released, I can't and won't give it anything less than a scathing review.

Update:  3/30/2015
So, it's been over a month since this game came out, and while updates have improved things, the game still suffers from frame rate issues and stuttering.  In the campaign it isn't as bad as it used to be, and seems to level out save for changing areas (the PS4 version has a similar issue but not as bad).  Raid mode is a crapshoot and typically the framerate is still jerking and stuttering for seemingly no reason.  Some missions it's less, some it's more.  The game is playable in the campaign with this, Raid mode less so.  And yes, I updated my drivers, messed with my settings, re-installed the game, and it's STILL having these issues.
What's pitiful is that this is marring what is otherwise a damned good game.  On the PS4 I actually enjoyed this game much more than I expected to.  Bu tas it stands I still can't recommend this game with the performance issues it has.  It's playable, but I feel ripped off that this game came out in such a state.  I stand what I said before, and I will not be pre-buying another game for a LOOOONG time from Capcom, or Steam for that matter.

In Antichamber, you wind your way through a massive maze of puzzles and challenges that often defy physical logic. Despite that, there is a logic to the world; you just have to learn to understand the odd logic. As the game progresses, you also gain the use of a gun that can absorb and spray cubes that may be used to help solve puzzles and reach otherwise inaccessable areas.
If you like to be challenged and enjoy having to think outside of the box, I highly recommend Antichamber. However, the learning curve in the game is very high, so this game isn't for everyone.

This game really is not anywhere near as good as people think it is. I would promise you that at least 90% of the people who have praised this game have not actually played it in a true Ironman and Classic playthrough. And I want to make two poiints here: Why the game fails as a game, and why it fails as an XCOM game.
Why it isnt an XCOM game:
This game is simple, and by that I mean REALLY simple. Xcom enemy Unkown plays like a really old board game(think Monopoly/Risk), the ruleset is extremely simplistic and leave such a large gab to chance that almost all decisions you make are irelevant.
Most people(even those who dislike this game) do not seem to understand this as they complain about 'bugs' that cause shooting through walls, floors, and other things. If you actually play this game and look at the ruleset applied it becomes clear that those were never bugs or oversights, this is simply how this game works. 'Props/Cover/objects/ground' never exists in this game, it all applies a very Warhamer/LOTR/40k logic, but simplified: If you have line of sight on an enemy you can shoot at it, only you and the object matter, the hit calculation is PURELY created by the different effects on a unit.(aka, if he is in cover you get -40% on the hit chance. What is the cover and how is it actually position and what about the 5 other things obscuring the view? Like I said, board game logic.
As such the shooting through a wall was never a bug, it simply is that the ruleset has no consideration for anything but the 3 or so objects used in the calculation.(That is why there is no free shooting, 'bullets' do not exist, that is why explosions always do the same damage, through walls or not through walls. That is why all cover works in a very binary state of existing or not existing.)
Why am I rambling on this? The people who played the old Xcoms and say this has the spirit of xcom are utterly wrong, Xcom (as silly as it sometimes was) was in a way  a simulation. It tried to "simulate" squad combat, based on a ruleset that was as 'reaslitic' as would be possible while being fun. If you looked at something and thought about how it would work based on your reasoning then most of the time  it would react the way you expected it to. Bullets would travel, if they missed or were shot at a bad angle they would travel in an angle away from where it meant to go, if the bullet hit an object it would damage or destroy the object, an explosion would damage objects, if the bullet can travel the path and is shot in the correct angle it WILL travel the path. Expectations were formed on your understanding of how things would interact, not simply by the very (often binnary) ruleset given to you.
This game has nothing to do with XCOM besides the skin and that both are a Turned based strategy, their fundemantal game design is different and as such it fails to be an XCOM game.
Why is it a bad game even on its own terms?
As said, it plays like a board game would, which can be fine, I like board games...
It plays like a bad board game.
A board game will give the player a defined set of rules the player has to adapt to in order to overcome a certain problem. Almost any board game ever will be forced to fall back to the concept of luck as certainty on everything will become boring.
But the job of any good game is to give the player a multitude of meaningful obtions for allow him to minize the randomness of the dicethrow to such a level that he can confidently predict the outcome based on the rulest the game uses.
This game fails to do that across the board.
Why?
Because just about every single thing you can do has simply has far too little actual impact on the game. Cover can either lower your chance to be hit by 20%, or 40%. Which might not sound like so little but considering that the whole game is cenetered around the concept of cover and by extension of it flanking, it means that flanking is not a nessesary move, cover simply isnt reliable as it is. Compared to other such games(Warhamer/LOTR/40k) where a wall would be a wall and it would give you 100% cover, and flanking it would give you 100% more of a chance to hit.(small cover would amount to something akin to 50%)
Add to it that just about every unit in this game has 60 to 75% aim, and the fact that the 20% and 40% is a simple reduction(not a multiplcation or such, simply: 75% is your aim, -40% is cover, 35% chance to hit. And 1 hit mostlikely means dead) and you quickly find out that hiding behind a wall has very little actual power, at which point it becomes clear that  the direction of engagment is rather a minor detail.
What about height?
Well, the game gives you a set boon for being 'above' an enemy, but do to its very simplistic nature that 'Above' is often rather wonky.
An enemy can be in 'high' cover, getting a 40% defense boon while being two floors below you(meaning you could easily shoot over their 'high' cover as it is not as tall as the object you are standing on) While you are in 'low' cover, still two floors higher.
In the end you will both have the same odds of hitting each other and even if you have 'high' cover while being on a roof, all you got is an extra 20% hit chance.
Do you see the general theme? Anything and everything you do moves the hit chances up or down by such minute amounts that they really have very little impact. Throw a smoke granade(of which you got 1 per mission in early game) and you get 20% more cover for two turns. In what sitersations is a 20% shift really that important?
Because often those 20% is all you can change when it comes to winning or losing your 10 hour long campaign.
The dice throwing is also made much worse by the fact that all engagments are very small scale, while in a game like Warhamer you would throw 30 dice and 30 units, you throw 5 or 6 here, of which any can decide the whole game. The more dice the more likely things will even out to be reasonable odds, here they never do.
So, playing this game pretty much amounts to playing a extremely simple(to the extent of being almost completely binary in logic) board game that doesnt even have the curtesy to let you infulence it. It gives you a lot of strategic options but most of them will have such minor impacts on the dicethrows that the most important strategic advice for this game is 'never trigger more then one group at a time'(As implied by that, the game is also full of really bad design decisions which I won't even touch on as those are commenly complained about)
Besides that it is worthy to note that big oversights were never fixed in this game even though the expansion 'fixes' it. The example being that there is no button to easily disarm all your troops so you can re-equipt things.(Which is a UI oversight and should have been patched, not an expansion feature).
Look at Xenonauts, look at this and give it some thought, you'll figure out why I called this game 'simple' and a 'bad board game'.

A complete experience at playing as Batman, marred by some flaws.  I recommend picking up at $30 or below.
Pros
- Great graphics
- I liked the story.  It felt immersive and had some good twists (and some bad twists).  Some unique storytelling elements, such as camera tricks to reveal essential elements
- Predator missions are fun with smart AI who have good technology to try to stop you.
- Brawling is fun with simple controls
- Flying around and exploring the city is a good experience, with a variety of smaller side missions you can work on.
Cons
- TOO MUCH BATMOBILE.  Half the game revolves around using the batmobile.  Worst in protracted battle missions.
- Game ends in a very long cutscene that doesn't really resolve anything.  You are expected to collect 293 riddler secrets to see the "true ending". No thanks.
- Some frame drops, graphical glitches and I encountered a couple soft locks that forced me to reload the game.
