I absolutely love the rogue-style gameplay; the basic rules are simple enough to learn, but what makes this game are the decisions you make. You save all your scrap up and then decide that at the next station to spend it all on a new crew member, only to find out at the next station that you could have spent the same scrap on a ultra-powerful weapon that makes your latest addition look shameful; that's when you feel that pang of "what could have been" that forces you to keep playing, your mind gets focused on the "mabye next time I'll get an even better choice"  and for that reason you play on. Even if you beat the game, it teases you with the possibility of having an even faster more successful run with a new shiny ship. This coupled with emotionally written randomized events which often put you in charge of making life-or-death choices really pluck the heart strings of what amazing gameplay should be. ... one minute you are flying brazenly across the galaxy and then you come to a fork in the road, one of the beacons is unknown, while the other is a distress beacon - after a quick thought you decide,  against your better judgement, that you'll risk your damaged hull and exhausted hand-picked crew to be those peoples hero in their time of need. You click jump and launch faster than light to the distress signal only to find that it was a trap set up by a group of pirates! After less than a minute of heavy laser fire the pirate ship hails you, "Please! Take everything we have, just don't kill us...please" they  beg over the intercom. Mabye its just you and your over active imagination, but you SEE those pirates in your mind...cold, scared and alone they were most likely cast out of their home worlds and told to fend for themselves, driven to piracy out of despiration and probably not much older than yourself, its time for you to be the hero you came here to be; You hover over "accept surrender" and then mis-click by a fraction of a milimeter. You watch with mouth slightly agape in dis-belief as a heavy laser mark II soars accross your  screen, breaks through the enemy's weak shields and then smashes full-force into the flimsy hull of the pirate ship. In shock you imagine the vacuum of space robbing the young bandits of everything they had, even the right to one last scream as it  instantly tears them into impossibly small shreds leaving only 14 meager pieces of scrap drifting in the black void of space as a remebrance of the hard and troubled lives those murauders led before they were smeared from the pages of history. Your ships crew retrieves the scrap with a robotic arm and then returns to their posts and awaits your orders. Within a matter of seconds everything had changed and it could never be taken back; you click jump, find the nearest beacon and take off with a heavy heart.

My favorite childhood pastime toy combined with my favorite reading adventures leads to a nerdgasm of enjoyment. I mean really who doesn’t love LEGO or super heroes? Playing with many of my favorite heroes in LEGO form to battle it out with many great supervillains and lead to a giant battle with Galactus is just a dream come true.
LEGO Marvel is another great addition to the LEGO game franchise that deserves its recognition. The game features 155 different characters to unlock, 26 levels to play through, and a huge New York City to wonder around in. You also have the standard gold bricks and red bricks to find too. There’s plenty here to take up many hours of your time to complete 100%.
The story is about Galactus coming to Earth to devour it like in the old Fantastic Four story. Silver Surfer is shot down when he was scouting the planet and the supervillains are trying to use his cosmic power to take over. You’ll battle through 15 different levels for the main campaign which will take place in places like the Baxter Building, Latveria, and the Savage Island just to name a few. There are 11 levels you can access after collecting the right amount of gold bricks to unlock them. These are mini missions to play where you find the red bricks and some of the characters to unlock. Voice acting wasn’t too bad in the game and it also had plenty of goofy LEGO humor to go along with it.
The gameplay is pretty much the same as other LEGO games but the characters are pretty good with using their abilities and fighting skills each in their own unique way. Thor fights with his hammer for melee and calls down lighting to power up certain objects or even shoot enemies or Spiderman who shoots his webbing, has a spider sense for hidden objects, and swings around on his webs. I really enjoyed playing through the levels and playing in the open world of NYC but it did become a chore finding everything. Especially the races you had to do to get some of the gold bricks which would become frustrating and annoying.
Most of the game ran fine but I did run into a few bugs. Sometimes I couldn’t pick up objects I needed, I’d get stuck on stuff, or couldn’t get NPC’s to do what they were supposed to do. I even had the game crash on me a couple times. Even with these items I still had a great time playing and they never really took away from the experience.
If you have enjoyed playing the previous LEGO games and enjoy Marvel comics this is a great game to play. It did feel a little more refreshing and not like every other LEGO game before but it is still a LEGO game so don’t expect a world changing game. Just enjoy it for what it does and have fun. It may bring back childhood memories and can even be fun playing with the kids if you have any.

If you like South Park, get this game.
If you have never watched South Park then do you have a sense of humour?
It is hard to put into words why South Park is something to be loved, the humour spans many categories from light to dark, clean to disgustingly vile and edgy to as some would put it 'unforgivably racist'. Forget political correctness when you are in the realms of South Park.
The best description I can come up with is: South Park makes fun of all groups, topics and denominations. Is that not equality?
That said, I would wholly recommend watching a few episodes of the show before buying this game. The humour and content will definitely spoil this game for you if you are of a 'more reserved standing'.
On to the actual game,
The game takes its main theme from the Black Friday/Game Of Thrones trilogy from Season 17, the game was named at the end of the final episode.
The children are playing their fantasy RPG around South Park which consists of two factions battling over ‘The Stick of Truth’.
You are the new kid in town; as such your goal is to make friends with the local population (the menu interface takes on the form of Facebook, hence the emphasis on making friends).
As a kid, you join the children in their RPG taking on one of four roles: Fighter, Mage, Thief and Jew (see where I was going about the humour? :D).
Things quickly spiral out of control, what with every adult in South Park’s universe being a complete imbecile, leaving the children’s game free to run wild across the whole town.
New factions emerge and your loyalties are tested. Soon great battles are fought, fortresses are constructed and conquered, buildings ransacked and houses obliterated.
Pure lunacy follows as the children’s fantasy world spirals out of control. Everyone - child and adult fighting over ‘The Stick of Truth’ and bringing the entire town to the brink of destruction.
Every part of the story felt faithful to the source material, every plot device or sub-plot felt like it belonged. In my honest opinion, this felt like playing an episode of the show. This is how well the story has been constructed.
The combat system isn’t too hard to pick up; different enemies are weak to different moves depending on what they are and what buffs they currently have etc. The challenging element is the blocking and attacking system which could catch out some people who have trouble with responding to timed prompts/quicktime events. In order to successfully land or block an attack the player must press the prompted key/combination with correct timing, it isn’t a hard concept to master and it does shake things up a little and keep combat fresh in my opinion.
The combat moves are brilliantly done, as in any RPG there is an array of equipment and weapons you can obtain – As the children are playing a fantasy RPG around town they are using old clothes and such with their imagination doing the rest – That’s not a stick, it’s a level 4 club of smiting.
Each friend-follower/enemy comes with their own personality, equipment and moves. Once again their moves are all imagined and completely absurd – Want to cast a fire spell at your opponent? Light a firework and shoot them in the face! Or fire your dreidel of doom at the enemy :D!
As the plot accelerates and things dive down the rabbit hole of absurdity so does the equipment, initially innocent weapons like sticks and rubber arrows devolve into swords, darts and 'pleasure devices' (yes you heard me) as the children’s game escalates into all-out war for the stick.
In your quest for the stick you encounter most of South Parks cast, from Kyle’s mum to Jesus. There are many collectibles (yes friends are a commodity! Gotta find em all), Easter eggs and mini-quests to complete. Spoiler:
No part of this game felt like a grind to me, the levelling didn’t require grinding and I was always strong enough to continue to the next stage. Yet, it didn’t feel too easy - the combat system while easy to master can enable your rapid defeat if you lose focus.
Overall I thoroughly enjoyed this game, I still have 2 classes to play through (Completed Mage and have nearly finished Jew) and am not yet bored of it… Did I mention right click is fart? Farting is an entire combat mechanic… obviously!

The Good, the Gore, and the…I need ammo. Killing Floor 2 is an awesome Early Access sequel to Killing Floor 1 brought to you by the Tripwire team. This game combines squad based combat like the Left for Dead series with the leveling up system of Borderlands. It’s starts out with you at level 1 having to kill waves and waves of monsters to earn money to buy new guns, Armor, and better items. You get to choose from one of 2 different perks for each level, plus you can change you perk after the wave. As you keep killing to level up your Perks you gain more special abilities for each different class starting at 5 then at 10 with you finally maxing out at 25. This can help you team out in a pinch.
The “Good”
This game is pretty solid, the game play runs like silk, it’s a beautiful and yes gory as hell game. Let’s start with looks, Graphically Stunning run on the Unreal Engine 3, do turn on your particle effects on High and watch the Blood hit the floor with some sick wetness and Michael Bay explosions as you fire off your RPG into a group on big nasties. The music is METAL…This is the type of music you need to be listening to as your killing hordes of the undead mutant monsters trying to eat your face. If you played KF1 the team did do some epic remixes of your favorites from the first game. As for gun play, the sights work and you do hit your target I haven’t had any LAG problems. Speaking of sight, you can look down the barrel of some guns and have an ALT fire and sights mode. Let’s talk level design- they are stunningly gorgeous this world really works for this type of game, you feel like you are there. As for right now only having 8 official maps, I can’t wait for more levels to come out soon. Partying up with people is really quick nowadays there matchmaking system helps players party up with friends and join games with easy.
Some of the ”I need Ammo”
This is an Early Access game so it is lacking in a few places. Yes only 8 maps is a little hard to deal with right now, but more coming soon and the modders are hard at work making more. The weapons options are a little slim, each character only has about 6 or 7 guns to choose from. The first KF had a lot more choices.  The characters look great but they sound like really bad C movie characters. You play them all the time and I only like 3 or 4 of the voices and quotes. A re-dubbing might be a good idea for some of the characters. They have also now added microtransaction system to me- this is weird because the game is still in Early Access. I know it’s for weapon and character skins but please finish the game first! Complete the entire list of items you said it was going to have before you add microtransaction.
The Ending
This is a great game and I highly recommend it, if you’re an old school FK1 fan or enjoy a team shooters. The $30 price tag is a deal for what you are really getting, so go grab your friends get your game on, start the killing field of a bloody sea of undead monsters. Kill to wave 10 and now meet the BOSS. Good luck and enjoy the slaughterfest and welcome to Killing Floor 2.

I'm having a hell of a lot of fun with this game.
Whatever problems Arkham Knight had at launch (and I understand they were signfiicant), it's fixed now, the game runs beautifully, and I'm glad I was able to pick it up. For people wondering if they can play it, all I can say is that plays flawlessly on my rig with a GTX 970, an i5 processor, and 8gb of RAM on Win7.
Pros:
- Incredible graphics. The rain, the lighting effects, Gotham's visual atmosphere, little details like wrought iron fences on train platforms and gargoyles on Art Deco buildings...all of it's exceptional. Character models are first-rate as well, and Batman has never looked so good.
- The Batmobile is awesome, and while it's true that you have to use it in certain situations, it isn't forced on you half as much as some people seem to think. There's plenty of time to glide across Gotham and swing between rooftops, and there are long sequences (like a mission involving a pair of airships) during which there's no Batmobile play at all.
- Combat in the Batmobile is also fun. There are upgrades you can buy with experience points -- like harder-hitting weapons, faster reload times, heavier armor -- and there are also upgrades from Wayne Tower that allow you to do things like hack enemy tanks so they attack friendlies. It's fun rampaging through Gotham's streets in Battle Mode, hearing thugs scream and run at the sight of your car.
- The audio design is awesome and contributes heavily to Gotham's atmosphere. All the thugs you hear on local surveillance still sound like they're from Staten Island, and some voice performances are over the top, but that's what you get with Batman. He may have the wackiest cast of allies and enemies of any comic book character.
- The game flawlessly incorporates cutscenes so they don't even feel like cutscenes. There are no loading screens or delays in between gameplay and the cutscenes -- in fact, it looks like all the cutscenes are in-engine, with filters making them look more cinematic and allowing for a greater level of detail.
- Most of the gameplay is fun, especially gliding across Gotham when you've got some of the Batsuit upgrades and can fly higher and faster.
Cons:
- There are way too many combinations to remember between "regular" special combat moves and the various upgrades you can purchase, and some of them are just akward. (Like pressing Alt+2 in the middle of a fight that requires you to juggle three mouse buttons, the space bar, the control key and the number keys.) Between that, and the fact that some moves can only be performed at certain times, it feels like there could have been a better way to implement special movies.
- Some moves don't reliably work, and there's no indication why. I freely admit some of this may be my own noobishness, but things like the shockwave drop, Batmobile-assisted takedowns, etc., seem to be temperamental.
- There were times during the story quests that I was annoyed to be stuck in a linear section of gameplay for too long. A good example is the abovementioned airships.
- Sometimes the game doesn't make it clear that you have to actively have a certain mission for an action to happen. For example, in one mission I did everything I needed to do for Alfred to lower a bridge so I could get the Batmobile to another island...but I could only trigger that action if I went back and re-selected that mission in my log, which then prompted Alfred's dialog and the bridge opening.

This game really is not anywhere near as good as people think it is. I would promise you that at least 90% of the people who have praised this game have not actually played it in a true Ironman and Classic playthrough. And I want to make two poiints here: Why the game fails as a game, and why it fails as an XCOM game.
Why it isnt an XCOM game:
This game is simple, and by that I mean REALLY simple. Xcom enemy Unkown plays like a really old board game(think Monopoly/Risk), the ruleset is extremely simplistic and leave such a large gab to chance that almost all decisions you make are irelevant.
Most people(even those who dislike this game) do not seem to understand this as they complain about 'bugs' that cause shooting through walls, floors, and other things. If you actually play this game and look at the ruleset applied it becomes clear that those were never bugs or oversights, this is simply how this game works. 'Props/Cover/objects/ground' never exists in this game, it all applies a very Warhamer/LOTR/40k logic, but simplified: If you have line of sight on an enemy you can shoot at it, only you and the object matter, the hit calculation is PURELY created by the different effects on a unit.(aka, if he is in cover you get -40% on the hit chance. What is the cover and how is it actually position and what about the 5 other things obscuring the view? Like I said, board game logic.
As such the shooting through a wall was never a bug, it simply is that the ruleset has no consideration for anything but the 3 or so objects used in the calculation.(That is why there is no free shooting, 'bullets' do not exist, that is why explosions always do the same damage, through walls or not through walls. That is why all cover works in a very binary state of existing or not existing.)
Why am I rambling on this? The people who played the old Xcoms and say this has the spirit of xcom are utterly wrong, Xcom (as silly as it sometimes was) was in a way  a simulation. It tried to "simulate" squad combat, based on a ruleset that was as 'reaslitic' as would be possible while being fun. If you looked at something and thought about how it would work based on your reasoning then most of the time  it would react the way you expected it to. Bullets would travel, if they missed or were shot at a bad angle they would travel in an angle away from where it meant to go, if the bullet hit an object it would damage or destroy the object, an explosion would damage objects, if the bullet can travel the path and is shot in the correct angle it WILL travel the path. Expectations were formed on your understanding of how things would interact, not simply by the very (often binnary) ruleset given to you.
This game has nothing to do with XCOM besides the skin and that both are a Turned based strategy, their fundemantal game design is different and as such it fails to be an XCOM game.
Why is it a bad game even on its own terms?
As said, it plays like a board game would, which can be fine, I like board games...
It plays like a bad board game.
A board game will give the player a defined set of rules the player has to adapt to in order to overcome a certain problem. Almost any board game ever will be forced to fall back to the concept of luck as certainty on everything will become boring.
But the job of any good game is to give the player a multitude of meaningful obtions for allow him to minize the randomness of the dicethrow to such a level that he can confidently predict the outcome based on the rulest the game uses.
This game fails to do that across the board.
Why?
Because just about every single thing you can do has simply has far too little actual impact on the game. Cover can either lower your chance to be hit by 20%, or 40%. Which might not sound like so little but considering that the whole game is cenetered around the concept of cover and by extension of it flanking, it means that flanking is not a nessesary move, cover simply isnt reliable as it is. Compared to other such games(Warhamer/LOTR/40k) where a wall would be a wall and it would give you 100% cover, and flanking it would give you 100% more of a chance to hit.(small cover would amount to something akin to 50%)
Add to it that just about every unit in this game has 60 to 75% aim, and the fact that the 20% and 40% is a simple reduction(not a multiplcation or such, simply: 75% is your aim, -40% is cover, 35% chance to hit. And 1 hit mostlikely means dead) and you quickly find out that hiding behind a wall has very little actual power, at which point it becomes clear that  the direction of engagment is rather a minor detail.
What about height?
Well, the game gives you a set boon for being 'above' an enemy, but do to its very simplistic nature that 'Above' is often rather wonky.
An enemy can be in 'high' cover, getting a 40% defense boon while being two floors below you(meaning you could easily shoot over their 'high' cover as it is not as tall as the object you are standing on) While you are in 'low' cover, still two floors higher.
In the end you will both have the same odds of hitting each other and even if you have 'high' cover while being on a roof, all you got is an extra 20% hit chance.
Do you see the general theme? Anything and everything you do moves the hit chances up or down by such minute amounts that they really have very little impact. Throw a smoke granade(of which you got 1 per mission in early game) and you get 20% more cover for two turns. In what sitersations is a 20% shift really that important?
Because often those 20% is all you can change when it comes to winning or losing your 10 hour long campaign.
The dice throwing is also made much worse by the fact that all engagments are very small scale, while in a game like Warhamer you would throw 30 dice and 30 units, you throw 5 or 6 here, of which any can decide the whole game. The more dice the more likely things will even out to be reasonable odds, here they never do.
So, playing this game pretty much amounts to playing a extremely simple(to the extent of being almost completely binary in logic) board game that doesnt even have the curtesy to let you infulence it. It gives you a lot of strategic options but most of them will have such minor impacts on the dicethrows that the most important strategic advice for this game is 'never trigger more then one group at a time'(As implied by that, the game is also full of really bad design decisions which I won't even touch on as those are commenly complained about)
Besides that it is worthy to note that big oversights were never fixed in this game even though the expansion 'fixes' it. The example being that there is no button to easily disarm all your troops so you can re-equipt things.(Which is a UI oversight and should have been patched, not an expansion feature).
Look at Xenonauts, look at this and give it some thought, you'll figure out why I called this game 'simple' and a 'bad board game'.

So it was on sale and I bought it because I wanted to try one of the Batman: Arkham games. I know it got a lot of negative press for its terrible performance on PC, but it ran quite well for me, even if I didn't have enough ram when I bought it.
The only video issues I had were the occasional stutter, but that was fixed once I installed more memory, which I really needed to do anyway. It also really likes the number 40, because that was about my framerate for much of the game (and I'm running an i5-4690k and a GTX 1070), but it was an impressively smooth 40 fps. Then again, I did drag the video settings past the preset maximums, so the 40 fps may be partly my fault...
But, video performance aside, this game is great. An excellent movement system, combined with a large and varied city to explore, combined with a great soundtrack and a mind-blowing story add up to a game that I will remember for a long time.
Yes, the Batmobile is a bit overused by various missions and the Riddler's stupid trophies are a pain in the rear to collect, but I don't feel like this game's cons outweigh its pros.
In short:

When I played Arkham Origins, I thought it was a fine game with some notable flaws that made it inferior to Arkham City, but all would be made right with the release of Arkham Knight. But that's not exactly what happened -- instead, I think Arkham Knight is a fine game with some notable flaws that make it inferior to Arkham City.
Let's tackle the first elephant in the room: the botched port and initial release. It stank up Steam so bad that it single-handedly
popularized the refund policy (
), and it was the reason I held off on actually buying it until a good long while had passed, despite being a massive fan of the series. I can be brief about this: my brand new rig has 16 GB of memory and a GTX 1070, and the game runs at a near-constant 70 FPS at 1440p maxed settings while looking absolutely gorgeous. Now, I get that not everyone has had that experience, or will have that experience, but I can only judge the game on how it plays for me at this point in time, and I have no reason to complain. That's not to say I tihnk that putting out a release as broken as this one is in any way acceptable or excusable -- it's not -- but I'm not going to count it against the game in its current state.
The same can't be said for elephant number two, which is the Batmobile. The Dynamic Duo in this game isn't Batman and Robin, but Batman and his amazing rooftop-hopping car. It quickly veers from cool into silly and contrived, and about the only thing missing is the Batmobile doing inverted takedowns (it
hang upside down a few times, so that's not as implausible as it sounds...). They made sure you can't miss out on the experience by putting in vehicular combat and puzzles that require the Batmobile, but I found myself more frustrated than entertained by these sections. Despite what the game designers thought, it would have been completely fine if the Batmobile had just been there as a cooler way of getting you from A to B. Throw in the optional racetracks for the people who like that sort of thing, I'm fine with that. Have maybe
sequence where the Batmobile gets to slug it out with a tank or helicopter, sure. But repeated vehicular combat sequences and painfully forced puzzle sequences just detract from the experience. While you can avoid almost all racing and puzzles if you just don't go after the Riddler (as if!) the tank battles are there to stay. It's as if someone baked you a delicious, velvety smooth chocolate cake, except that they mixed in crunchy peanuts to chip your teeth on, because they read somewhere that chocolate and peanuts go well together.
There are a lot of things Arkham Knight gets right, too. The meat and potatoes of the game, combat and predator encounters, work as smooth as ever, and there are the requisite tweaks and new moves to keep things interesting without completely unbalancing things like the shock gloves in Origins did. There's a smorgasbord of villains on the loose in Gotham waiting for you to arrest them, and they all involve different gameplay, so you can easily mix things up without getting bored. The voice acting is top notch, both from the regulars and the guest villains (special tip of the hat to Dwight Schultz, who plays a terrifying Professor Pyg -- I was surprised to find out it was him when I looked it up). The story is engaging, and I'm happy to say that's still the case even if you had the identity of the Arkham Knight spoiled before you picked up the game, like I did. I especially like the way the writers justified the issue of Batman suddenly deciding to stick massive guns on his Batmobile (even if they do conveniently fire "non-lethal rounds" when targeting humans). If this sounds a bit out of character for Batman, it's because it is... and you'll find out why as you play the game. Having said that, I'm definitely not a fan of the ending (the true ending you get with 100% completion), which is deliberately ambiguous on the ultimate fate of Batman and Gotham. It's not terrible, I can live with it, but it still feels like a cop-out and something the writers could absolutely have avoided in favor of a stronger statement. As a cap to the whole series, it's a bit underwhelming.
Arkham Knight gets an easy "recommended" from me, but it's not as great as the final installment could have been.

*This is a review for Dragonfall, the DLC to Shadowrun and not the original campaign*
An absoulute gripping look into the cyberpunk universe and one of the most mesmorizing narratives I've seen this year. Everything Shadowrun's original campaign does, Dragonfall does it three times better. This is a case where you should buy the game, just for the dlc. Your party members (which you don't have in the original shadowrun campaign, thanks) all have a plethora of fascinating backstories and dialogue choices. The game takes place in Berlin which uses a completely unique politcal structure for government combined with beautiful enviroments that just make the game feel real, even though it's such a stylized version of a mystical future.
The decsions you make later in the game are excruciatingly hard. Dragonfall doesn't treat you like an omnipotent god that makes all the right choices. This is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ world with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ choices to make and if you mess up too bad, everyone suffers for it. There was one choice in particular I had to stop playing for about 20 minutes to decide what I should even do. The gameplay is exactly the same as the original campaign or Xcom unknown so no real changes there. This is a game you need to play if your into old RPGs, well constructed plotlines and characters, and if your a fan of sci fi or cyberpunk, no exceptions if you meet any of these guide lines -Enjoy

My review of the first Revelations can be seen here:
The serious performance issues mentioned by others in older reviews have been dealt with although thats not to say minor niggles don't remain. Negative reviews were and very well may still be just. Features that were in the console version were only added after MASSIVE player outrage and review bombing hit the game. Not to mention that before the patches the unimpressive graphics didn't run properly which made them looking shoddy worse where as now it at least makes up for it's ugliness with performance. With that out of the way Revelations 2 is an addictive well designed and very replayable game that was constantly being patched and updated with free DLC for Raid mode (Which is honestly an excellent game even if it were by it's self.).
The atmosphere could be great at times and the game expands greatly upon the originals design (key word design) with memorable boss fights and locations although it never once tops the ship location. It's a shame that the graphical fidelity is not up to par with the decent level and art design (Some creatures are really generic looking.). While the textures are generally better than RE6's that really doesn't say much as RE6 wasn't much of a looker either. While shadows are better than they were in RE6 (No longer blotchy and  pixelated.) the general lighting falls flat particularly when playing on a stage ported from RE6 in Raid mode. RE6 had large flat, ugly environments so the tradeoff in RER2 is the the environments are smaller and more densly detailed. It's got a bit of an ugly duckling thing going on but it doesn't make me sick looking it.
In short, a decent sequel with great moments that make it worth the price of admission and that doesn't just rehash the first game but rather improves upon certain aspects of it and tries new things that work for the most part in addition to bringing back elements from Resident Evil Zero, Nemesis and Code Veronica to name a few. Personally, It's not as replayable as the first but there's certainly been worse. You also don't need to wait for the AI to touch a door to open it any more and when they do lag behind they only need to be within a certain radius for it to be opened. One thing that's a little worse then Revelations is the fact that I can't think of a single moment in the core game where it let's you explore an area alone whilst an AI waits for you or takes an alternate route. There ALWAYS being a buddy nearby AND you need to take care of them unlike the first Revelations where their survival was their own problem.
My biggest gripe is something thats no surprise to anyone that has played Resident Evil. And thats the story. The scenarios like a zombie infested mansion, city, rural town or cruise ship have always been interesting but the stories that take place in them are usually messy at best or trite at worst. As is the usual the story both annoys you and doesn't surprise you all whilst trying to be Metal Gear in terms of preachiness but being without any substance or awareness of it's unironically convoluted nature. The quality of the writing, dialogue and characterization are also at an all time low with Barry "Ho my Cawd" Burtons daughter Moira attempting to mimic his accidental legendary memetic quality with constant attempts to reach his level of ludicrous lines failing. They are forced and unfunny where as Barrys were unintentionally funny.
Making a useless character who swears and complains a lot is waste. Not to mention Moira's a very one note character who's only personality trait other than swearing is complaining about Barry. The rest of the cast is alright. Call me biased but the best character and parts of the game involve you playing as a more Liam Neeson esque Barry Burton which is surprisingly awesome. You'll find yourself exploring the aftermath of Claires carnage while on the hunt for his daugter and that can make for tense stuff crappy crate puzzle aside.
I think I'm getting of track. I definitley reccomend it and mechanically it's leagues above the first but the setting isn't quite as good as the first Revelations and it doesn't do much more than that. For the price it's a good buy and with all the chapters it's pretty solid. The Raid mode is the real selling point.

As per usual, Capcom have completely disappointed their fanbase. What kind of company sells a game based on its co-op features, promises offline co-op in the store description, and then doesn't deliver ANY kind of co-op on launch?

It's a shame because the dialogue is a decent peg above standard Resident Evil fare, and the plot is genuinely interesting for once with a wonderfully fresh SAW-esque vibe to it. You know a series is stagnating when borrowing from SAW makes it feel fresh.
Do NOT waste your money in this game until co-op is patched in. Although knowing Capcom, they're probably lying about that too.

If you like South Park, get this game.
If you have never watched South Park then do you have a sense of humour?
It is hard to put into words why South Park is something to be loved, the humour spans many categories from light to dark, clean to disgustingly vile and edgy to as some would put it 'unforgivably racist'. Forget political correctness when you are in the realms of South Park.
The best description I can come up with is: South Park makes fun of all groups, topics and denominations. Is that not equality?
That said, I would wholly recommend watching a few episodes of the show before buying this game. The humour and content will definitely spoil this game for you if you are of a 'more reserved standing'.
On to the actual game,
The game takes its main theme from the Black Friday/Game Of Thrones trilogy from Season 17, the game was named at the end of the final episode.
The children are playing their fantasy RPG around South Park which consists of two factions battling over ‘The Stick of Truth’.
You are the new kid in town; as such your goal is to make friends with the local population (the menu interface takes on the form of Facebook, hence the emphasis on making friends).
As a kid, you join the children in their RPG taking on one of four roles: Fighter, Mage, Thief and Jew (see where I was going about the humour? :D).
Things quickly spiral out of control, what with every adult in South Park’s universe being a complete imbecile, leaving the children’s game free to run wild across the whole town.
New factions emerge and your loyalties are tested. Soon great battles are fought, fortresses are constructed and conquered, buildings ransacked and houses obliterated.
Pure lunacy follows as the children’s fantasy world spirals out of control. Everyone - child and adult fighting over ‘The Stick of Truth’ and bringing the entire town to the brink of destruction.
Every part of the story felt faithful to the source material, every plot device or sub-plot felt like it belonged. In my honest opinion, this felt like playing an episode of the show. This is how well the story has been constructed.
The combat system isn’t too hard to pick up; different enemies are weak to different moves depending on what they are and what buffs they currently have etc. The challenging element is the blocking and attacking system which could catch out some people who have trouble with responding to timed prompts/quicktime events. In order to successfully land or block an attack the player must press the prompted key/combination with correct timing, it isn’t a hard concept to master and it does shake things up a little and keep combat fresh in my opinion.
The combat moves are brilliantly done, as in any RPG there is an array of equipment and weapons you can obtain – As the children are playing a fantasy RPG around town they are using old clothes and such with their imagination doing the rest – That’s not a stick, it’s a level 4 club of smiting.
Each friend-follower/enemy comes with their own personality, equipment and moves. Once again their moves are all imagined and completely absurd – Want to cast a fire spell at your opponent? Light a firework and shoot them in the face! Or fire your dreidel of doom at the enemy :D!
As the plot accelerates and things dive down the rabbit hole of absurdity so does the equipment, initially innocent weapons like sticks and rubber arrows devolve into swords, darts and 'pleasure devices' (yes you heard me) as the children’s game escalates into all-out war for the stick.
In your quest for the stick you encounter most of South Parks cast, from Kyle’s mum to Jesus. There are many collectibles (yes friends are a commodity! Gotta find em all), Easter eggs and mini-quests to complete. Spoiler:
No part of this game felt like a grind to me, the levelling didn’t require grinding and I was always strong enough to continue to the next stage. Yet, it didn’t feel too easy - the combat system while easy to master can enable your rapid defeat if you lose focus.
Overall I thoroughly enjoyed this game, I still have 2 classes to play through (Completed Mage and have nearly finished Jew) and am not yet bored of it… Did I mention right click is fart? Farting is an entire combat mechanic… obviously!
10/10

After completing the story, it's safe to say. Dying Light is worth the 60$.
The story is guided along nicely with some decent pathing, while combat feels rewarding. Bone breaking is a fun aspect, but it's so miniscule in terms of just hacking off limbs. Blunt weapons become weaker at later phases of the game because everything is moving quickly.
Weapons feel rewarding but at a cost, dealing with constant swarms of viral. Not too fun except against other ranged.
Some zombies feel outrageously strong for a lot of the phases of the game and helping survivors at a certain point in the game
is unrewarding for the effort taken.
Night remains a problem through the entire game, but it feels certainly less fun in the later phases, where you can take a volatile out easily without much threat other than other virals.
The ranking system feels fleshed out without one being completely pointless, while I thought some traits were personally pointless to grab, it works well with how you play and depends on your type of style completely.
PvP feels tacked on at last second for a more thrilling experience and to urge people to preorder, which isn't fun. Monster feels like it should be totally powerful, but in reality feels too weak compared to humans due to UV. Which is disappointing.
There are a few bugs here and there, taking random damage from unexplained sources and sometimes I couldn't be prompted to open a door. A close game and re-entering from menu seemed to fix that.

When I played Arkham Origins, I thought it was a fine game with some notable flaws that made it inferior to Arkham City, but all would be made right with the release of Arkham Knight. But that's not exactly what happened -- instead, I think Arkham Knight is a fine game with some notable flaws that make it inferior to Arkham City.
Let's tackle the first elephant in the room: the botched port and initial release. It stank up Steam so bad that it single-handedly
popularized the refund policy (
), and it was the reason I held off on actually buying it until a good long while had passed, despite being a massive fan of the series. I can be brief about this: my brand new rig has 16 GB of memory and a GTX 1070, and the game runs at a near-constant 70 FPS at 1440p maxed settings while looking absolutely gorgeous. Now, I get that not everyone has had that experience, or will have that experience, but I can only judge the game on how it plays for me at this point in time, and I have no reason to complain. That's not to say I tihnk that putting out a release as broken as this one is in any way acceptable or excusable -- it's not -- but I'm not going to count it against the game in its current state.
The same can't be said for elephant number two, which is the Batmobile. The Dynamic Duo in this game isn't Batman and Robin, but Batman and his amazing rooftop-hopping car. It quickly veers from cool into silly and contrived, and about the only thing missing is the Batmobile doing inverted takedowns (it
hang upside down a few times, so that's not as implausible as it sounds...). They made sure you can't miss out on the experience by putting in vehicular combat and puzzles that require the Batmobile, but I found myself more frustrated than entertained by these sections. Despite what the game designers thought, it would have been completely fine if the Batmobile had just been there as a cooler way of getting you from A to B. Throw in the optional racetracks for the people who like that sort of thing, I'm fine with that. Have maybe
sequence where the Batmobile gets to slug it out with a tank or helicopter, sure. But repeated vehicular combat sequences and painfully forced puzzle sequences just detract from the experience. While you can avoid almost all racing and puzzles if you just don't go after the Riddler (as if!) the tank battles are there to stay. It's as if someone baked you a delicious, velvety smooth chocolate cake, except that they mixed in crunchy peanuts to chip your teeth on, because they read somewhere that chocolate and peanuts go well together.
There are a lot of things Arkham Knight gets right, too. The meat and potatoes of the game, combat and predator encounters, work as smooth as ever, and there are the requisite tweaks and new moves to keep things interesting without completely unbalancing things like the shock gloves in Origins did. There's a smorgasbord of villains on the loose in Gotham waiting for you to arrest them, and they all involve different gameplay, so you can easily mix things up without getting bored. The voice acting is top notch, both from the regulars and the guest villains (special tip of the hat to Dwight Schultz, who plays a terrifying Professor Pyg -- I was surprised to find out it was him when I looked it up). The story is engaging, and I'm happy to say that's still the case even if you had the identity of the Arkham Knight spoiled before you picked up the game, like I did. I especially like the way the writers justified the issue of Batman suddenly deciding to stick massive guns on his Batmobile (even if they do conveniently fire "non-lethal rounds" when targeting humans). If this sounds a bit out of character for Batman, it's because it is... and you'll find out why as you play the game. Having said that, I'm definitely not a fan of the ending (the true ending you get with 100% completion), which is deliberately ambiguous on the ultimate fate of Batman and Gotham. It's not terrible, I can live with it, but it still feels like a cop-out and something the writers could absolutely have avoided in favor of a stronger statement. As a cap to the whole series, it's a bit underwhelming.
Arkham Knight gets an easy "recommended" from me, but it's not as great as the final installment could have been.

I'll just say right now, this game has taken 60+ hours of my life. It is super fun, quick paced, run and gun, rogue style, artistic gloriousness. The art is amazing and gives a sense of wonder and solitude, and the music drives the point home with melancholy and futuristic sounds. You start off at the first level and the point of you being alone and needing to survive is driven almost immediately. You need to grab some items and get to the teleporter, however when you do you have to fight a wave of enemies and a boss. This is where the difficulty comes into play, it's a fun challenge. Every death is caused by your own mistakes. Each enemy has a fair warning for when they go to attack and if you don't take heed of that warning you will pay. I never got mad at the game, whenever I died I'd just hit retry and go again. It's forgiving to the point of making each new run in the game more fun than the last.
Now the game will eventually get a bit boring, that's where artifacts come into play. You can make yourself have only 15% of your original health, but do 500% damage, making you a glass cannon. The artifacts add some spice to the game and aren't tooo difficult to find. With a bit of determination and some exploration you can find these artifacts with ease. The only real complaint i have is that multiplayer is a bit of a pain to set up. It involves some port forwarding and tunneling, but it took me less than 30 minutes to set up. Overall Risk of rain is an awesome game and if you can get it on it's usual sale price of $2.50-$5, it is more than worth it. It's the best 2 bucks I've spent in a long, long time. The game is fun, challenging and a great time if you can get some friends to join in. I strongly recommend Risk of rain to anyone remotely thinking of buying it.

Game is fun and has good replay value. better with friends if you get the multiplayer working. Worth it's price.

Dead Space is probably one of the best scifi action-horror games I've played. It has amazing atmosphere, visuals that still hold up, art design and interface design that blends awesomely and some of the best sound design ever.
Firstly, if you get this game turn the music off. Yes, off. It has musical ques that while cool, give away there are enemies around/alive. If there's still some kind of music playing, you have a monster about. It ruins the atmosphere as great as the music is.
You get a number of weapons that have alternate firing modes that make the game pretty damn replayable. All function differently and offer different pluses and minuses.
Some people write this off as jumpscare the game, I say ...well yeah kinda. But that's fine since the tension matches the jumpscare. Stand idle in any area and listen. The sounds you hear, the creaking of the ship, the buzzing of electronics and the rustling of monsters really sets the mood.
This game is the scifi-version of Resident Evil. You're trapped in a large place and have to deal with the hell onboard while dealing with limited supplies. You'll be running all over the ship doing tasks but things change as you go along, it's never dull. They keep things interesting.
The interface is as I said, brilliant. There's no hud. All of Issac's gauges are on the back of his suit, or project from them, including the menus. It's really really well thought out and it keeps you focused on what's important, the center of the screen.
Now on to the problems. This is a old PC game indeed, right when PC games were getting back on track with decent ports. This game is pretty good but I'm going to say some things that may break this game for you.
Unless you change the game to have vsync every time you enter it, the game will lock at 30 if booted with vsync on. If you put vsync on after the game is on it'll lock to 60.
However blasphemous as it sounds, you may prefer 30FPS since if you leave the framerate unlocked the mouse controls even at wildly high sensitivity levels are too slow to use. Also, the physics go haywire at above 30, killed enemies will bounce up and zero G bodies will start spinning like tornadoes.
The crap mouse controls can be countered by using ....I'm gonna say it, a controller. Works perfectly with a XB360 or XB1 controller straight away. Which may not be ideal but it works. There could be a mod to fix this as well, I'm not sure. But I've played it with a controller and it's nice. Then again I've used controllers a bunch back in the PS2 days so I'm familiar with them.
The last thing I noticed is if you jump in zero G at too narrow an angle, the game can bug out. <-this is avoidable.
Even with these problems I still recommend it. You may have to use a controller or use a mouse at 30fps but it's still a fun game. I kinda link it with you're not supposed to be a badass shot, you're supposed to unused to shooting people/creatures.
The sequel fared much better in terms of porting and is also a great game.

UPDATE:
Now that this game is playable with splitscreen, and after playing through the main campaign,  extra episodes, and quite a bit of raid mode, I can say that this game is worth a buy. I still do not appreciate all of the mistakes Capcom made near the game's launch, which should not have happened in the first place, but I do appreciate how fast they responded after their customers called them out.
STORY:
The campaign is overall pretty decent and has a genuinely creepy setting and atmosphere. A secluded island is a good follow-up to the Queen Zenobia from RE: Revelations 1, and it makes for tense moments. The story, while not the most compelling in the world, is interesting enough to keep you hooked through the entire game. It also hearkens back to plot points from previous games: obviously Revelations 1, but also RE1 and RE5. The playable characters are well developed, but the most of the rest of the cast is pretty generic. Most of the monster designs, barring a few cool bosses, are also pretty generic (one is pretty much pyramid head from Silent Hill). But despite all of the generic stuff, the game is still a fun and creepy adventure.
It is also important to know that the plot/location is more focused than Revelations 1. It takes place solely on the island, rather than being split up between multiple locations.
GAMEPLAY:
I'll start off by saying I played through the entire game using splitscreen multiplayer with a friend. The co-op in this game is a lot better than in previous RE titles. It shines especially during Claire's campaign, as using Moira's flashlight along with Claire's fighting ability can help save ammo or your life. The co-op aspect in Barry's campaign was not bad, but also not quite as balanced as Claire's. Instead of both players being able to defend themselves (Claire=guns, Moira=flashlight/crowbar), Natalia is left with nothing overly useful, and is left to pointing out enemies and their weak points and running around while Barry cgets to do all of the zombie killing. Some of the earlier stages (the forest) were built very well around Natalia's mechanics, but some of the later stages like the hospital and the mines left us wishing that Natalia could do something more useful than throw bricks.
Also, Glasps are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Sure, they give Natalia's sense more use, but any monster that can kill you automatically in one hit leads to stress and annoyance rather than tension and fear. (I'm looking at you, hospital basement....)
The controls are a mixture of the ones from RE6 and Revelations 1, and it works very well; it lets the player move at their own pace, whether that means taking it slow or dashing through like a madman. Luckily, there isn't any RE6 kung-fu garbage; the melee system is straight from Revelations 1.
The inventory/crafting/upgrade system is also simple, yet good. I like it.
RAID MODE:
Raid mode was one of my favorite pieces from the first Revelations, separating the game into stage missions and making the game more "arcade-y". The enemies had life bars and you could level up your weapons while unlocking different characters to play as. It was pretty sweet, especially the last level that encompassed the entire ghost ship, filled with branching pathways and hoards of enemies.
Revelations 2's Raid mode is also very fun, but also a little bit disappointing. It gives a larger cast of characters to unlock and play as, not only from Revelations 2, but from previous RE games. Each character also has a set of skills that you can level up, which makes each character feel different. You can also upgrade your weapons in a similar way to the first Revelations. The way this mode handles the characters/upgrades is fantastic.
The stages on the other hand, are the disappointing part. One point that I was very excited about prior to this game's launch was the variety of stages in Raid mode; there would not be just stages from Revelations 2, but from previous RE games as well. Would we get some cool maps, like the castle or village from RE4? The ghost ship from Revelations 1? The mansion from RE1? Raccoon City? Some other stuff from RE5? I was pretty bummed to find out (through experience) that around 75% of the stages are from RE6, 23% or so are from Revelations 2, and maybe 3 or 4 of the 52 stages are from the first Revelations. Some more variety would have been nice, or even more stages from Revelations 2. To top it all off, there is no stage that captured the same fun and majesty of the ghost ship stage from Revelations 1. They missed an opportunity to have a stage that encompassed the entire island, and it makes me shake my head.
Despite the over-representation of RE6, raid mode is still fun to play and I would recommend it.
EXTRA EPISODES:
This game features two extra episodes, The Struggle and Little Miss.
The Struggle is a fun, short, and brutal chapter that details events that happen between the two campaigns.
Little Miss is a stupid forced stealth mission that insta-kills you if you get seen. Not fun.
That is all.
TL;DR:
This game is pretty good, and I would recommend it if you like horror games/Resident Evil games, especially for the price. The only part that I absolutely hated was the extra chapter, titled "Little Miss". The rest was fun.

This game is doing it's best to be Baldur's Gate II, BUT TOTALLY DIFFERENT (read: exactly the same but somehow not as good), and it comes closer than most who've tried and failed to ape that landmark gaming style. Having played both the 2007 FPS and the actual tabletop roleplaying game, I'd have to say this one is most similar to the later. Brace yourself for lots of reading quest text, dialogue options of questionable significance, unexplained slang, and an overwhelming amount of options that may or may not actually affect anything at all.
If you like playing tabletop games but don't have enough interested friends to scrape a real Shadowrun campaign together or would rather settle for a generic cookie-cutter adventure set in a diverse and interesting world that you can see just enough of to get the feeling that you're not quite experiencing it to its full potential, then boy howdy, chummer, have I got a game for you!
All in all, it's really not that bad, it's just trying *so fragging hard* to replicate something that really wasn't meant for a videogame, and I guess I can't fault it for that. But I can still regret wasting my nuyen on this piece of drek instead of just buying a book.

I'm changing my review for 3 reasons, 1st, I finally finished the first episode and have played the raid mode, 2nd, I finally came off the anger of the controversy from Capcom, especially after they apologized, 3rd, It's unfair to soley base my recommendation on the mistakes of the company rather than what the actual game has to offer. The delay of online gameplay and lack of offline co op is certainly very disappointing, but not reasons to hate on the game.
I'm recommending this game because it is very fun, and the way they finish the episode on a cliffhanger is just tantalizing; this, along with the short wait time of only a week for the next episode, makes the anticipation for the next episode that much better.
Gameplay: I played on a mouse and keyboard, and frankly, had very little to no issues at all. A little tweaking of the sensitivity and mappings and bam, I have the controls to my liking. The features are intuitive and easy to use. If you've played RE6 then you will feel at home. The only real difference is the dodging mechanic, it's not like the dives of RE6, it's more akin to Lara's scramble from Tomb Raider. Personally, I didn't use it much, so I'm not sure how vital of a mechanic it is, but that could just be my play style.
The charchater switching mechanic can be a nice touch. I say "can" be because with Moira, it feels very lazy and quite frankly, uselss.  She hates guns, so she only attacks through melee and she uses a flashlight to "reveal" items  so Claire can pick them up. The only time she feels useful is to blind enemies with her flashlight. It's only the first episode so he abilities can be developed later and che can become more useful. Natalia on the other hand, she can sense enemies and some enemie's weak points, so I found myself constantly switching to her when using Barry.
All in all, the gameplay is fun, sprinkled in with just the right amount of action.
The Raid/Mercenaries mode is better this time around. There are different types of missions to engage on, so far I've gotten 'clear this area of enemies' and 'defend this object'. I'm sure there's more, but what really surprised me was that some enemies have properties like freezing. For example, there was the blue glowing enemy that when I got too close or meleed it, I slowed me down or froze me. I'm guessing there are more types as I'll keep playing, but that certainly adds a nice twist. You get to customize your character with different guns and abilities, you also get to sell and upgrade your guns. It makes it feel very RPG-ish.
Graphics: Not much to speak of here. It seems they reused the same engine as RE6 and I believe RE5. Althrough the characters themslevs look great, the environmental textuers are pretty average, even less than average since we're moving to a more technologically capable generation. Still, the game looks overall adequate and sometimes decent.
Story: I like that they don't reveal everything at once, or that you can see things coming from a mile away. The cliffhanger at the end of the episode was great and had one, maybe two, twists that I did not see coming. If they keep this up, they have a quality story on their hands, the best probably since Code Veronica.
Bugs: The only bugs I experienced were the FPS dips (no matter whether on my laptop or desktop) and a really bad game freeze on my desktop PC. The game certainly needs optimization, but nothing was game breaking in my expereince.
All in all, this is a step in the right direction. The story is good, pacing is good, gameplay is great. If Capcom can build on this, then I look forward to Revelations 3 or RE7

Maxed cloak and the ability to fire while cloaked. 2 Drones. 6 crew members. And still on the second stage of the boss I absolutely get my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me. On easy difficulty. Antichamber is definitely one of the most intriguing puzzle games I have played. It takes all you believe to know about how puzzle games work, and turns it upside-down. There will be a lot of moments when you are so confused that you will need to take a break from the game, just to suddenly notice the solution to a puzzle come up in your mind without you even thinking about it.
The game is logical, yet messes with your logic in a way that will leave you in awe, slowly realizing the scale of the entire thing.
As you progress, you will unlock more and more powerful tools, allowing you to solve more complex puzzles, but also backtrack and find alternate paths and solutions to previous puzzles. But only a portion of these tools will be actual in-game upgrades, while the rest is simply knowledge you gain while solving the puzzles. Seriously, this game can be beaten in about 20 minutes, but it took me more than 10 hours, and might take you even longer, because I had some puzzles spoiled for me.
Oh, and regarding spoilers: Don't watch any videos, except for the trailer on the Steam store page. Every bit of every video might possibly spoil something so important it can cut your game time in half and leave you wishing you never found out about it.
To decide if you want the game, ask yourself the following:
Does the trailer look interesting, even if it's just a tiny bit?
Are you fine with the game's visual style? (personally, I love it, it's simplistic and effective, but some people seem to be feeling nauseous after playing the game for a bit, so you might want to watch out for that... again, the trailer should be enough to figure that out)
Are you interested in puzzle games?
If you answered yes to those questions, definitely get the game.

Risk Of Rain is without a doubt one of my favorite rogue likes. It really has the feel of an old shcool Super Nintendo or Genesis game and is brutally difficult to boot. This game will make you tear your hair out sometimes, its unforgiving and hard to be good at let alone master. Every character plays differently, very differently and its always interesting trying a new one. They all have fun skills and abilities and all of them seem viable with enough practice. When you finally get into the grove with a certain class you'll really feel like badass as you fight for minutes on end with the same 3x or 4x over leveled enemies in massive swarms. The aesthetic is really fun to watch in motion and is really quite pretty in action. Seeing your enemies keel over after being riddled with bullets and fall into a pile of bits and blood is always satsifying. Adding to that satisfaction is the sound of the weapons, explosions and monsters in this game, great sound design.
When I bought Risk of Rain I kind of expected a game more in line with mobile games and cheap games that you might put a few hours in once in a while. It took those expectations and ripped them a new ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, just like the game did to me on my first playthrough. The combat is so engaging, and the rogue-like elements are so solid in this game that I personally have almost no complaints in regards to gameplay or visuals. And again, the sound in this game, the music is fantastic and if you're the kind of person who likes video game soundtracks then you'll probably like it too. Every track is a winner and pairs so well with the environment its being played on. The visual style, levels and back drops in this game blend so well with the music and with engaging combat it can be mesmerizing. Everything adds to the other worldly feel of this game and that feeling of imminent death. Something about this game, inspite of its difficulty, keeps me coming back for more time and time again like a masochist. Possibly the most organic dual-mode game that has come out in the past few years.  The strategic mode leaves you researching and contructing a bunch of toys to use and looking forward to the missions where you'll get new resources and things to research, and the tactical missions leave you with new enemy after new enemy and all sorts of items to bring back.  It evokes the feel of the original very well.  I'm not the biggest fan of the change to a much more colourful and Fisher-Price type look of the tech and in particular the weapons, which all look like childrens toys, but otherwise the visual look and feel is implemented very well and perhaps just as importantly consistently.  The game just gels very well together in terms of gameplay, visual design, and sound design.  The production values are high and so is the fun.  The only real thing I felt was a misstep other than some elements of the visual design is the difficulty.  While the original could be tortuous sometimes and some scaling back was probably neccesary in today's gaming market, the game is actually pretty easy on all but the highest difficulty, as long as you stick with troops with good stats and stay on top of research and production of new weapons.  One of the disappointing things for me in that regards was the chrysallids.  In the original they were Aliens-inspired creatures that would zombify your men or civillians, and when you killed the zombie a new chrysallid would emerge.  It made things very frantic when you saw one.  Comparatively, the new chrysallids look and feel very different.  While they do have an instant-kill melee attack (the originals actually didnt, except insofar as they hit like a brick s**thouse), the zombies are mostly unthreatening enemies and there's no extra chrysallid when you kill them.  It effective neuters what was one of the original games greatest threats, because of how quickly a chrysallid could ambush and spawn more chrysallids.
Those gripes aside, its an engaging and well-done game which remains a time sink for me to this day.  The only turn-based strategy game in the last decade which has had me going "just one more turn"

You looking for a challenging game that can be played from either the most advanced pc in the world or a potato. Then this game is for you. Even if you didn't want a game that can run on just about anything, this game has lots of variety and varying levels of difficulty. It's not enough that you have an initial difficulty (there are only 3), but the longer you play the game, the more the difficulty gets ramped up. There are a decent amount of stages, and bosses, to encounter, as well as variations of these monsters. Throughout all the stages, depending on the variation of the stage, there are relics that can either hurt, or help your gameplay.
You start with one character and have to perform certain tasks to unlock them; some are stage based and others require you to do something special or meet a certain criteria. Each character has their own, four special abilities that are unique to them alone. Hell, I've played this game a decent amount of time and have still to unlock the Mercenary.
Now, this game does have its faults. A couple of the relics, while they are helpful, make it way too easy to earn achievements and blaze through this game even on it's most difficult level. Luckily (sarcasm), there's been a bug in the recent update that seems to be preventing some players from actually unlocking achievements on their profile. I have pretty much unlocked all but one achievement in-game, but only a few of them have unlocked on Steam, and they were before the update/patch.
Overall, I give this game about an 8/10. I would give it a 9 if the bug gets fixed and they add in a fourth difficulty.

To start with I'm relatively new to the resident evil series, having only played 4-6 and, now, both Revelations.  I found both 4 and Revelations to be the most fun by far.
Currently revelations 2 feels like a mix of RE4 and Revelations with a small bit of 5/6.  The basic controls are the same as revelations, but there is a true inventory system like the one in RE5.
A feature that I am currently ambivalent towards is the partner swapping feature.  While the support character has useful abilities, they cannot use guns and as such their ability to fight is severely limited.  Additionally the hidden items in the area can only be seen at all with the support character.
I did have framerate dips here and there, but nothing to bad.
As for the co-op features, I didn't get the game for co-op, but fully understand the issues with no offline co-op on the PC version when it was advertised as having it.
Currently I would recommend it if you are OK with the lack of co-op and enjoyed RE Revelations and RE4.
Edit: As for the day one DLC, it's raid mod characters, costumes, and inventory slots.  If you REALLY need those extra inventory slots, then it's a microtransaction.  Personally I never even came close to running out of inventory slots in revelations 1, so there might be no issue here.
Edit 2:  A couple of new things now that episode 2 is out.  It's telling me to purchase the next episode, despite my having bought the complete season.  So, that needs to be fixed ASAP or I'll be droping this to not recommended.
Second, having played more raid mode I've noticed a lot more issues with frame rate drops in certain maps.  Particuarly defense and timed maps.  As for the new features and changes to raid mode, there don't seem to be any real hidden things in the maps (or at least I havn't found them) like the BSAA medallions in revelations 1 raid mode.  Additionally there are basically 3-4 ammo boxes in each map, and at most 3 weapon or part boxes.
The combining weapon mods to level them up is a feature I like, since it does make it far easier to get  better mods that you want, and I feel that the mods being locked to the weapon they're installed on until you either destroy a part to free a slot or destroy the weapon to free the parts makes it a bit more challenging to decide on a loadout.
The character options also allow for much more customization, similar to the RE6 skill loadouts.  Each character has a different set of skills, which are unlocked as that character levels up.   You use skill points to upgrade the skills that you want, to match your playstyle.  This includes the secondary grenades, which are limited use per mission skills.

Shadowrun Returns is fun, has great writing, and is a good match for any classic CRPG fan. If you liked Baldur's Gate, Planescape: Torment, or any other similar game, you'll probably like this.
That being said, don't expect too much from this game. When compared to the classics, Shadowrun Returns isn't just short - it's light. VERY light. Expect to solve puzzles quickly and easily. Choosing gear doesn't involve much more than buying the most expensive gun. Combat is actually quite dull. Speccing out your character is kind of fun, but I was left wishing I had more options. It's a surprisingly simple game overall.
I played as a Decker, which was great for the story but left me relying on the tried-and-true (and boring) combat tactic known as "shoot things with guns a lot." Mages seem a bit more interesting, since placement in battles was somewhat more important, but since you can't use hired Deckers to interact with objects outside of combat you're somewhat hamstringed if you go with a non-Decker class. Each area could have definitely used a LOT more alternative solutions.
I've only played the basic campaign so far, and I will probably pick up the DLC, but the fact is that most of these problems are with mechanics and game design, not with the campaign itself. Still, the writing is good - really good. Combined with the rich built-in lore, it makes an otherwise mediocore game a fun experience worth your time and money.

The game features pretty much all the Marvel characters you can think of, and is fairly tongue-in-cheek. Mr Fantastic at one point deploys himself as a parachute to save The Thing and The Invisible Woman, looking to the camera and saying "I saw this in a movie once...".
As the story progresses, more and more characters, vehicles and locations are unlocked, and the story culminates in the heroes and villains joining forces to defeat Galactus (not a spoiler, since Galactus is in the intro cinematic and in the trailer).
The story mode is pretty straightforward (it is a game designed for kids after all...) but completing that only gets you 20% of the way to completely completing the game. Once you complete the story mode, you switch to the Free Play mode, which lets you go over the game again, this time with all of the characters you've unlocked (so you can access additional bits of the level you've just played through to unlock extras). This becomes one of the more frustrating bits of any Lego game, the grind needed to feel like you've actually managed to make reasonable headway to complete the game.
This version at least tries to open things up by creating a "Mission Hub" modelled on New York. You wander along the streets of the City, tackling side missions on your way (including saving Stan Lee from an increasingly bewildering array of situations). This addition (compared to the Mos Eisley Cantina hub from the Star Wars version) at the very least gives you some diversion from having to run through each of the 15 levels twice, but you still end up performing variations on the same side-quest a dozen or so times on your way to unlocking everything. 
Overall, it's a fun game (it's rather funny being able to re-stage your own version of the Hulk Vs Abomination fight from The Incredible Hulk in a Lego Harlem and have a load of Lego characters simultaneously cheer and tell you to "watch it, buddy!") and if you're a Marvel fan, you're going to get a kick out of it. 100% completion is a long slog, and if you're not a fan of open world sandbox games, you're likely to drive yourself a bit mad trying to finish it.

Best movie license game I've ever played. I love it. The turn based RPG system fits so well with the animation. This is the game that south park fans deserve. I'll go over the positive aspects and the negative aspects.
Positive:
-This game is incredibly funny. It's raunchy and dirty sense of humor fits me so well. I love it. However, if you are not into that kind of humor, this game will not appeal to you.
-The turned based combat would sound bad, and boring... But it actually has you involved. You don't just choose a move and then watch it play out. It's kind of like the Mario rpg games, where you have to put in some sort of actions to make a "Perfect" hit. The combat is also fairly fleshed out. There are status effects that can be inflicted on enemies. Also the unique ways each buddy can be used to suit your play style. You can even use the enviroment outside of combat using your abilities you get, such as your fart magic, and an anal alien probe. Skipping combat completely, but getting the experience.
-Plenty to explore, and has some replayability. Although I never completed it after doing it twice.
-It is creatively written. The story line is fantastic. Which it should be, being written by the developers of the show themself.
-Due to the kids larping, it makes some creative items. You can literally take a crap in a toilet, and throw it at an enemy to gross them out.
-The story line and all side missions can give you around... 20 hours, even more if you want to replay it.
Negative:
The negative aspects are just me nit picking a bit, but some of these can be an issue for others.
-This game is for south park fans, and for people who are not easily offended. If you are not a south park fan? You might not enjoy this game, and not get most of the jokes.
-The game is too easy on the default difficulty, and even on hard mode, it can be easy. I've found myself never losing a single battle when you follow the story line.
-20 hours is a VERY short rpg game, when it ends, you just want more!!

GTA Vice City is a great game and maybe you've played it before on the PS2 or Xbox. This is less of a review and more of a, "here's what you need to get it running perfectly on PC." Because, by default, it doesn't support widescreen resolutions, you need to force v-sync, it has a number of bugs that can be fixed using a patch,
Let's start with the controller. This modder, Silent, is a diety. They've done so much for the classic GTA games. They modded the GInput inputs for 360 controllers so that the 360 controller button will actually appear on screen, not to mention function since Rockstar really didn't bother with controller support for the PC versions. Also, the controllers can be set to the style of GTA IV gameplay. This mod has full support of other controllers as well, such as the Dualshock and most certainly Logitech controllers. I haven't tried the Steam controller on it though. Download it here:
, you'll be able to pick out Vice City from the options given. Once download, just unzip and follow the instructions.
To get GTA Vice City working in widescreen, you will need to download a fix from ThirteenAG. It's extremely simple. Just download, unzip, and read the instructions.
You'll also see widescreen fixes for GTA III and San Andreas if you haven't gotten to those.
To force v-sync, it's going to depend on whether or not you're using an AMD or Nvidia card. I have an AMD R9 280, so if you have an AMD card, you're going to want to access the Radeon settings, go to the gaming tab, find Vice City, click it, find a tab that says "Wait for Vertical Refresh", hit the drop down arrow, you want it set to always on. On an Nvidia card, you want to open the Nvidia control panel, go to 3D settings, find Vice City from the drop down bar, select it, scroll down til you find v-sync, and same thing, set it to always on.
The SilentPatch is necessary if you want good lighting and shadowing.
, you have your options to choose from the classic GTA games, but be sure to also download the DDraw patch from the same set of downloads. It improves the draw distance. Download both files, extract, and read the instructions.
That should be about it. I hope you enjoy the game as it is quite a lot of fun. Brilliant soundtrack. Good story. Fun side missions (asset missions). Doesn't take itself too seriously. It's a solid 9.0/10
