is a horror game. In where you play as our reluctant and intrepid hero Issac Clarke, a technician. Sent to the USG Ishimura, a Planet-Cracker class ship designed for mining. Upon arrival, Issac and friends have a bit of a tift actually docking with the Ishimura. After avoiding near death almost immediately upon introduction. We find ourselves upon the ship ready to get to work; Only no one is responding to our radio hails. Entrance into the first room, we are attacked by monsters later given the name Necromorphs and being the consummate professional that Issac is we decide to continue to repair the ship regardless of it's now infested alien presence.
And so it begins...
It's not a terribly in depth game. It is indeed your basic walk through hallways and shoot anything that moves sort of affair. But it's an effective and atmospheric one even still today. Is it contrived that in a world that requires you to dismember enemies you're given a plasma cutter that is effective at range and presumably your character would know not only how to use  it but an expert in his field? Yes, it is.
The story is more in depth, I feel, than most horror. Creating a universe rather than “an experience”. Without saying anything specific, the game makes commentary on the frivolity of desperation in the creation of a new religion based almost exclusively on not knowing something. The game does feature what I'd consider “insanity effects” but they are more scripted than ambient.
Throughout the game Issac does not speak. Sometimes awkwardly not saying anything but mostly this is reminiscent of the Gordon Freeman effect wherein it allows the player to place themselves more into the role. Now, at this point I should mention this is my 3rd play-through of this game and that I have also completed the rest of the trilogy. The series takes a direction that I am both happy with and thought could have been better. But that is neither here nor there. This is the beginning of that adventure.
, it's a shooter with a camera made popular by Gears of War and Resident Evil 4. It was also made in a time that “immersion” was all the rage. The HUD appears entirely “in-game” meaning that all feedback normally given to the player (Health, power for abilities, ammo count, inventory) are all made visible in-world to the characters themselves. You collect power nodes used for upgrading either your suit or weapons.
The big mechanically unique thing regarding this game is the Zero-gravity areas. They are interesting, at the time they may have been more impressive but they stand to be a pretty standard element.
Sound design is excellent, walking into the vacuum of space is always an incredible feeling hearing only the muffled shuffles within your own suit.
Now, there is a section of this game that is borderline game breaking. It's one of the more egregiously needless frustrating sections of a game I've ever seen. Which incidentally speaks volumes to the rest of the game. I don't want to say exactly what it is, I get that it's supposed to be a stressful situation but I know a number of people that actually stopped playing the game because of that section.
, the game has full gamepad support and there is no issue with this. However, if you desire to use mouse and keyboard you'll notice that even at max sensitivity the controls are as though they are stuck in quickly hardening mud. (I used a 1600DPI mouse at max sensitivity and moved the mouse roughly 1ft actual space and turned about 90° in game) However, there is a simple solution to these issues. For whatever reason EA forgot to and didn't patch the fact the game V-sync doesn't include the mouse (console ports huh), so you'll have to force enable it through the video card control panel. The v-sync works as expected otherwise.

Dead Space is a third person, linear story-drivien, single player horror game. Gameplay focuses on third person shooting with some light puzzel solving.
Oh, Dead Space, why did I wait so long to play you? This title has been in my backlog since 2010. I can't believe it took this long for me to play it, but I'm glad I finally did. The graphics hold up and in many cases still look amazing, but the real draw here is the ambiance. EA redwood Shores completely nails the derelict spaceship atmosphere. I'd like to put the sound design on a pedestal here as well. The 5.1 surround sound mix will instill a deep paranoia within you, making your walks through the ship extremely tense. Another stand out here is the HUD, or lack thereof. All the elements of a traditional HUD you would find in another game are here, but they are cleverly presented in a fashion (mostly through holograms) that fits the game world. You're left with a third person perspective that feels incredibly immersive and cinematic.
I liked how most of the weapons had a utilitarian use (cutting, mining, torching, etc) that fit within the game world rather than just being military in design. The zero-g sections of the game did a good job of distorting your perspective and in a couple cases gave me that weird feeling in your gut like you're falling. It reminded me of Prey (2006). There's some solid Sci-Fi elements to be found here too.
If there's a weak point, it comes from the story. It's not bad, but certainly not great. It doesn't bring anything new to the table and that's not necessarily a bad thing, just a little disappointing. What it does bring though, comes with competence, at least at first. The setup is perfect. You're there to investigate a communications black out. It was intriguing to unravel the mystery of what happened on the USG Ishimura. But near the end of the game, all the typical tropes and cliches of the genre surface and you're left scratching your head as to some character motivations and the would-be twists that you saw coming a mile away. Had the story been less typical and more interesting, I would call this a must play title. But it misses that mark for me.
Near the end of the game I grew weary of the tasks and the "but first you need to do this" missions. I spent about fifteen hours for my play-through on normal difficulty and around hour ten I seemed to have built up a tolerance for the jump scares. My fear dropped a couple notches down to anxiety, but I'd say that's probably normal for most people and just the nature of repetition.
Still, it's easy to forgive any negative points when you're having such a great time. The game lives up to the atmosphere of titles like BioShock and Resident Evil: Remastered. It's one of those games I'll buy the art book for. It's scary and well crafted throughout.
TL;DR: Play this game.

So, Killing Floor 2 has finally left Early Access after about a year and a half with what I think is a huge improvement over the first Killing Floor. There has been a few bumps here and there with the whole microtransaction thing during early access and the somewhat slow update speed, but what we got here is something that is worth your $30-$40 USD depending on if you want to buy the digital deluxe edition. If you're somehow new to Killing Floor, I'll give you a breakdown of the main gameplay loop: shoot zeds, earn money, buy guns, throw dosh, back to shooting zeds, rinse and repeat, then boss. I gotta tell you, I have played this game ever since Early Access launch on April 21, 2015 watching it slowly grow as the days go by, but like I said before, the whole Early Access process wasn't perfect.
In terms of gunplay and melee combat, this is a huge improvement with smooth animations and good sound assets making you feel like you are actually playing with real guns instead of what I think most shooters do is make them sound and feel indistinguishable from one another (I'm looking at Left 4 Dead). What most developers do when handling melee combat in a first person shooter is mostly made as a last resort with janky animations and sometimes dodgey hit detection similar to how melee was handled in the first Killing Floor despite having a class that purely focuses on melee weapons. All of the melee weapons here have a feeling of weight behind those swings. I like how they handled the difficulty this time around as they decided to add additional abilities for all zeds with some of them being more agile and harder to hit and perhaps my favorite change is the husk who gets a new flamethrower attack and if near death, it will try to take your life by suiciding. The main thing I did not enjoy from the first Killing Floor was how long it took to level up your perks and with that, if I wanted to play on the higher difficulties due to boredom, most servers that play hell on earth have a plugin that autokicks players who joins with a perk lower than level 5 and even if you do play it with 5 other people, the enemies are so bullet spongey that it makes all the weapons feel weak on top of the price of weapons if you're not max level. At least in Killing Floor 2, if you have enough experience with the game then you can certainly attempt to play hell on earth at low levels, although people tend to kick low levels off of hell on earth games with a certain degree of understanding.
The game now has 10 perks for you to pick from with a certain set of weapons in that they specialize in, but that doesn't stop you from taking off perk weapons if you'd like just like in the first Killing Floor, only except it's more viable because in the first game, the weapons were so ridiculously expensive and did so little damage on the higher difficulties, especially hell on earth, it was almost never worth considering. Going into the whole Survivalist perk that was added on release, a lot of people were disappointed with it only because at a glance there were no new toys for us to play with. Now for those of you who do not know what I'm talking about, the perk is a jack of all trades kind of perk that utilizes every weapon in the game to the best of its ability while not really exceling at anything at the same time, meaning the perk does not get their own unique set of weapons. I get it. It's always nice to have more toys to play with, but this whole thing reminded me on what the culture of Early Access is like in general. Some people feel entitled to have anything they want thinking that they and they alone have influence of the entire development process and that is annoying to see that constantly flooding the Steam forums. While people do have genuine criticism for certain things and that's a good thing to see, but then you have other people who leave nothing of value for Tripwire to consider and instead just insult them just for adding microtansactions and perhaps a few other things that are maybe out of Tripwire's control or perhaps something better for the game in the long run. Call me a fanboy all you want, but I'm just trying to have a better understanding of the whole development cycle. They never had any set promises, but people just started to fill in the blanks on their own, just like what people did with No Man's Sky only to a lesser extent.
As of launch, there are only two game modes to consider, but looking at which is more popular, it almost feels like there's only one and that's kind of sad to see that. There is coop survival mode where you have up to 6 players fighting against waves of zeds up to the boss round where they will not hesitate to turn you into their next science experiment. Versus Survival is a player vs player version of the regular coop mode and while it does have a few balancing issues, it's still fun to play every once in a while, but unfortunately it's not a very popular mode.
I have to say, this game made me into a Demon Hunter fan. Roughly about half of the soundtrack is originally composed by a guy who goes by zynthetic who also did the soundtrack for the first Killing Floor and the other half is licenced music from various artists, most of them are from Demon Hunter.
To keep it simple, all of the items in the game are purely cosmetic that offers no statistical advantage whatsoever and you don't need to buy them if you don't want to.
This is a purely subjective opinion, but now every single character has their own unique voice lines instead of recycling the same 3 sets of dialogue for every character that gets released. I know some people miss the cheesy voice acting from the first game, but they do make a return here, it's just that some people are not 100% satisfied just because it's not exactly the same, but again it's purely subjective. Some voice commands are missing from the first game like a command for thank you or the insult players command.
Currently there are 12 official maps at the time of release both from Tripwire themselves and a few community made maps becoming official similar to what they did with the first Killing Floor. If you are ever bored with those maps, there are other community made maps on the workshop for everyone to enjoy.
Even after almost 800 hours at the time of this review, I still enjoy Killing Floor 2 as I think there is enough content for first timers to jump in and have a blast with your friends shooting zeds and chucking dosh at each other. How Killing Floor 2 manages to keep you in the core gameplay loop is entirely dependent on how much you like the weapons and how much you like playing horde mode. In my opinion this is 100x better than Call of Duty Zombies.

In this genius game of puzzles, the laws of nature take a back seat. Forget everything you ever learned in puzzle games. Trust nothing. Not what you see... not what you hear. Take nothing for granted. The hall you just walked may not be the same hall you remember when you take a second look. This game really forces you to think outside of the box on so many levels. It is deep, engrossing, challenging, and absolutely mind blowing. Walls vanish when you try to walk through them... floors appear when you try to walk over them... and sometimes and endless loop isn't quite so endless at all. Perspective is everything in this game, and looking at the same thing from a different view can render completely unexpected results. Nothing is impossible in this strange yet beautiful world. My word of advice? When you think you are stuck... take a second look. As one of the signs states... just because you fail does not mean you fail to make progress.

Civilization V is an interesting game to me.
I was interested in it to due enjoying RTS games, but never really playing a turn-based version of them, so I didn't know what to expect.
I was disappointed... at first. It wasn't quite what I was thinking it could possibly be, and played a quick match against AI on an easier difficulty, and got bored very quickly. It's slow at the start, but as time goes on it gets overwhelming managing so many units, wars, deals, economy, science, tech, etc. I played for about 5 hours total without having any idea on what I was doing, so I was doing basic stuff and not advancing properly.
I was extremely bored one day and gave it another chance, in which I have a game that's still ongoing at the point of typing this review (20+ hours total) and I'm having a blast. I understand the whole "one more turn" thing now.
It takes some getting used to if you come from RTS games (I played Age of Empires mainly, and they do share some common things, so I slightly had an idea of what I was doing), however if you're used to, and like turn based strategy games this is a must have. Even if you're not fond of the genre, it wouldn't hurt to give it a try when it's on sale since we have refunds now.

X-com is a game you will love and hate in almost equal measure, the single player campaign does a really good job of teaching new players how the game mechanics work if you have the teutorials on. I expecially love the detail in regards to research of new technology & the biology of the aliens you autopsy/interrogate, going from simple frag/bullet weapons to having a awsome heavy plasma gun melting terrain and enemies alike is awsome.
The tactical battles are really cool too, pretty much all buildings are scalable or you can enter and the environment is destructable. An alien bunkered down in a building suppressing your guys with no real way to hit him? No problem just get a heavy trooper to launch a rocket and blow it up along with most the building, but you can get punished in the long run for ecessive use of expolsives :P. This game will never go easy on you & is very unforgiving for moving or attacking without planning, one wrong move & your soldier or team could get killed. That being said the tactical battles can be really frustrating the % to hit calculations can really screw you over, one I was about 5 feet away from an alien in minor cover & had on 37% chance to hit ..... really & these guys are supposed to be the best soldiers from all nations in the world?
I haven't played the multiplayer so can't say anything about it, but at the end of the day X-Com is a really fun game with a good story, in-depth lore & campaign, difficult decisions & a challenging combat system. I would reccomend anyone new play to X-Com is to pick up the expansion enemy within as it does add a ton of really cool stuff to the game.

I took advantage of Steam Holiday Sale and bought LEGO Marvel Superheros. It took me a while, but I managed to finish this game in 100%. It wasn't a walk in the Central Park, though.
I really enjoyed the main storyline and Deadpool stories and even going back through all levels with different mix of heroes and villains to get every possible collectible was quite fun. Especially when some characters have very unique special attacks, which keeps things interesting.
On the other hand, the free roam on the streets of Manhattan felt more like a chore. The sub-quests for citizens and heroes quickly become repetitive. I suppose the racing quests were supposed to keep things fresh, but, because of dreadful controls, those were an utter failure. Driving races are just so-so, you can do them when you accustom yourself with how the vehicle reacts to a controller. The flying is just frustrating. The idea of using acceleration and free-fall buttons to adjust height must have come from a mind of a sadist.
Let me explain how flying (not) works: to fly upwards, you press A button, but if you double tap it, the flying hero goes into hyper-fast flight (usually in the wrong direction). Similarly, to fly downwards you press B button, but if you double tap it, you loose all speed and just drop to the ground (dragging the camera with you).
Overall it's a good game, but it has it's flaws. Because of it's flawed controls, I enjoyed only main missions part of this game, so I don't think it's really worth full retail price. It's best to wait for some kind of sale or a price drop.

A fairly good computer interpretation of the shadowrun table top roleplaying game for the computer. Character creation is more or less identical to what I remember of the table top RPG. The game has no voice overs throughout the campaign so it does involve a lot of reading of dialogue. The dialogue is well written and funny in places but the sheer amount of dialogue might make you feel like you are reading a graphic novel, perhaps a throwback to pre-CD gaming days when voice overs were not used as frequently.
Game is a little unresponsive at times and controls can be a little cluncky and inprecise. The supplied campaign isn't very long and can be completed in a couple of hours. That said there is content you can download from the community to extend your game time. Some are quite good but unfortuantely there isn't that many currently available.
Probably a game I would more recommend to a Shadowrun fan than a generic computer gamer. That's not to say I didn't enjoy the game, that I did, but the flaws present in the game hold me back from recommending it to anyone but shadowrun fans.

Note: I have played about 14 hours in total (about 64% through the game on my playthrough) however I played it mostly in Offline mode due to internet connection problems.
First of all: This game is remarkable; the graphics look stunning and the gameplay feels fluid and most of the times not staggered. The Parkour is alright to say the least, it isn't Mirror's Edge but it is tied in well enough to be fun most of the time - I have seen many people have problems with the port but I have to say that I have found no problems with any lag (Running on a GTX 760 4gb) and because I do not have an AMD card or any GTX 900 series cards - the main cause for concern with this title, I can only state that it should work fine with the 700 series.
The story is lackluster at best and leaves alot to be desired; it starts to pick up pace from about half way onwards but it still is nothing to write home about. The voice acting of Crane is monotone and at times obnoxious and later on he begins to put in more emphasis when more dramatic plot points come up but equally can't save it.
The combat is basically a more refined version of Dead Island's with more fluid animations and better feeling weapons that actually have a sort of weight behind them, when you decapitate a zombie with a knife or bash its head in with a pipe the Sound, Slow-Mo and X-Ray compliment it without it being in the way of actual combat.
Atmospherically this game has nailed it - being out at night is tense, especially at the start of the game when you have barely any decent weapons, and at day when you can see everything the city is eerie yet beautiful, nothing really seems out of place. I get a sort of Resident Evil 1 vibe from it at some points where I know something will happen, but I don't know when. The horror in the game is purely atmospheric, nothing will jump out at you and scream but the enviroments and lighting (or lack there-of) can be intimidating at times.
Finally, the tone is a massive contrast to Dead Island. Where Dead Island was colourful and vibrant, this game was dark and gritty; we talk about the infamous Dead Island trailer but at times I think that the trailer for that would fit this game better - still not perfect but much better because of the tone of the game.
In Conclusion; this game is incredible - it has it's flaws, as does everything, but it is already one of the best modern games that I have played and it will take alot to top it.

Dead Space is one of my all-time favorites, and in a true sense a masterpiece. I bought and played it upon its original release, and it was pretty much bug free and stable out of the box, even if it pushed my trusty old Core2Duo I had then pretty hard.
The design choices, story line (augmented by a couple of animated movies ,"Dead Space: Downfall" and "Dead Space: Aftermath"), atmosphere, and gritty industrial Sci-Fi environment, make this a memorable, terrifying, and unique experience. Think of it as an amalgamation of Aliens, Event Horizon, The Thing, and Pandorum. It does have some jump scares, but mainly all the adversaries are manageable, especially since you get to upgrade your gear throughout.
You definitely get the feeling of being in space, in particularly due to the very, very awesome Zero-G sequences, and your requirement for Oxygen and the ability to magnetize your boots. This is pretty unique in games, and certainly was a novelty back when Dead Space was released. This is probably the fourth time I've bought the game, for one due to DRM-freeness, and because it's worth it. Of all the games published by EA over the years, the Dead Space (and Mass Effect) franchises are certainly one of the best games ever made.
In fact, the only negative I have to say about Dead Space is the ridiculous control/button assignments. Being left handed I do not use WASD, I use the cursor, and surrounding keys, and Dead Space isn't very helpful there. I had to get a program called GlovePIE which I've had to use a few times since. Once setup though, everything works just fine.
In conclusion, if you are a Sci-Fi/Horror fan, enjoy a good third person shooter style experience, and enjoy roaming around in beautiful, atmospheric environments, then this is for you! And remember: In space, no one can hear you scream!

I expecially love the detail in regards to research of new technology & the biology of the aliens you autopsy/interrogate, going from simple frag/bullet weapons to having a awsome heavy plasma gun melting terrain and enemies alike is awsome.

An alien bunkered down in a building suppressing your guys with no real way to hit him? No problem just get a heavy trooper to launch a rocket and blow it up along with most the building, but you can get punished in the long run for ecessive use of expolsives :P. This game will never go easy on you & is very unforgiving for moving or attacking without planning, one wrong move & your soldier or team could get killed. That being said the tactical battles can be really frustrating the % to hit calculations can really screw you over, one I was about 5 feet away from an alien in minor cover & had on 37% chance to hit ..... really & these guys are supposed to be the best soldiers from all nations in the world?
I haven't played the multiplayer so can't say anything about it, but at the end of the day X-Com is a really fun game with a good story, in-depth lore & campaign, difficult decisions & a challenging combat system. I'm very impressed.
It goes without saying this is a South Park game for South Park fans. I've had people ask me if this game was any good but they're not a South Park fan and as a game, it's alright. It's an RPG with gameplay along the lines of Costume Quest or the Paper Mario series, but if you don't like or never seen South Park, 80-90% of the game will be lost on you.
The humor is left intact; from the common juvinile tastes (farts, poop, other childish stuff), to other cleverness and character quirks. Heck the entire plot is believable from the show perspective. This game could pass as a multipart episode or a movie in it's own right.
The game is somewhat easy for veteran RPG players, I say somewhat cause there's many battles where you need to be on your toes or things get pretty hairy, but other than that it's a nice pace. There's 4 classes to choose from (Fighter, Mage, Thief and Jew, which is pretty much a paladin) with their own unique skills and the standard friends (Stan, Kyle, Cartman, Kenny, Butters & Jimmy; all bringing RPG class tropes, flairs and their character personalities) as party members. There's a lot of customization that can be done which is pretty good.
All in all I don't have much negative thoughts towards this game. It's the right length, there's a ton of side stuff, there's a ton of South Park fanservice. This is the first South Park game that's actually good and not licensed mediocrity. Not bad for being in development forever.

It's okay. If you're kind of expecting technomancy fallout, this isn't it.
Pros:
It looks good
It plays good - it's a very smooth isometric feel. The mapping isn't the best though, and more than once I've wondered why I was in combat when all I neede to do was move to the next area.
Its stable - no crashes, no bugs that I noticed.
Cons
Its short. 5.8 hrs and I've already beaten main antagonist number 1. And now there's a mystery second antagonist because oh no, we've only got 6 hours of content.
It's linear - Wow. No side quests, no interesting lore, no interesting characters just to talk to. It's the opposite of Skyrim.
It's very cliched (it's like your otaku friend vomited all the cool japanese words he knew into this game somewhere).
The RPG elements aren't quite there
It's not really an RPG - The item/armour choices are ridiculous. I bought armour in the first 20 minutes of the game, and haven't changed it since, as I was never offered better options. Same with guns. The spells aren't that interesting, they seem to be heavily geared towards support magic (reducing enemy armour, etc) so any mages I have are usually spamming one or two spells all the time. They're pretty though.
It's not written very well - It's okay, but again, it's cliched. You're gonna roll your eyes a bit, and you never really do get too invested in the characters. You get maybe one or two side missions with each character, maybe, and then not even so much as an option to converse in hub worlds.
It's repetitive - I'm probably not going to play the main campaign again, ever.
Most of the enjoyable content of this game will be made by players, not devs. I feel like the devs gave us an amazing tool to craft isometric stories, but that it's not really their job to build a sprawling fallout-esque world. Maybe it isn't. But I'm glad I didn't pay full price for it, then.
In short, it looks nice but there's no life to this world. Skip it, or pick it up at bargain bin prices, and get some of the player made content. Or buy Fallout 1 or 2.

There isn't much time! You have to deliver these important schematics, all the while racing across the galaxy to escape the Rebel wave of forces pursuing you! Jump from FTL Beacon to FTL Beacon, running into space pirates, Rebel forces, aliens [some friendly, some not so friendly] and whatever else is floating around out there.
Very much in the vein of rogue-likes, this game takes it and does it in a slightly different direction with various gameplay assets and such, but the rules are the same: Play the game, try and progress. With a little bit of skill and a LOT a bit of luck, you should be able to complete your mission. [Count on failing often, though. And when you do, be prepared to start from scratch.]
An excellent thing about this game is that you really feel like a small crew on a nigh-impossible mission, trying to overcome tremendous odds. You get attached to your crew. You get attached to your ship. Watching your crew members die [or worse yet, having them killed by an insane space-hobo] really gets to you for some odd reason. When you're doing well, though, it's just so damn satisfying. Just imagine it:
You're under heavy fire, and there's a fire in the engine room! "PLOTSKY, AMY, GET INTO THE ENGINE ROOM. The captain will manage the shields while you guys get that ready, because IF WE DON'T GET THAT ENGINE ROOM UP AND RUNNING, WE CAN'T JUMP AND WE'LL BE SCRAPPED!" This is just one of the many experiences you might have playing this game.
Now, do you like micromanagement? This game has it. Shields, weapons systems, engines, oxygen, medi-bay; almost everything [or at least everything important] about your ship can be managed. Say you're fighting a guy who's beating the crap out of you and your ship. Divert your power from your weapons and into your engines, and get the F[TL] outta there. While we're on the subject of combat, the game's combat system is deceptively simple at first, but turns into a completely different animal once you start picking up Ion weapons, or get blasted by a beam that does nothing but set your ship on fire. Better get your crew on that [even more micromanagement!]. It seems like with so much you're able to control that things might get really confusing really quickly, but it flows so smoothly, you hardly realize that you've fallen into the routines that almost popped out of nowhere.
If you don't mind the brutality that is a hard reboot every time you fail, and have a love for space and space-travelly sci-fi, I would HIGHLY recommend this game. It's good! It's so good. The music's awesome, the graphics are crisp and beautiful, and I love a game that makes you work hard to get some EXCELLENT satisfaction from it.
Oh, and go ahead.
Call your ship "Serenity".

nVidia Control Panel > Advanced > Manage 3D Settings > Software settings

Story completion takes about 7 hours on your first run with all 4 Episodes for those curious.
Graphically the game looks great, the sound and music are solid, and my opinion of the over-the-top b-movie emulation of the story is something I adore. I have no complaints here whatsoever.
Resident Evil Revelations 2 is a solid entry on a budget so far to the Resident Evil franchise. The locales aren't quite as iconic as the mansion from the original RE1, but they certainly convey the proper sense of doom and gloom that the game was going for.
Mechanically the game has shifted quite a bit even from it's predecessor Revelations 1 overall the combat itself feels much smoother than the first. Over the span of the more action oriented RE games they've made overhauls to the dodging mechanics in each game. In RE4/5 dodging was a QTE, in 6 it was more or less a dive or a roll in one direction or the other, Revelations 1 changed this to a timing mechanic where you would either push forward or quick turn before you were hit where the enemies telegraphed their abilities.
I would have to say that in this game so far they've really hit the mark with the dodging mechanics. A skillful dodge to the left or right feels solid when faced with a charging enemy.
Capcom has also taken the best of several other series when it comes to the weapons and skills. You can carry 4 weapons at a time and switch them out at will with any other weapons you come across similar to Revelations 1. The Weapon parts system hasn't changed much. On top of that they've added skills using RE6's BP system which augment your characters. Some are shared/Some are specific to either Barry or Claire adding another layer of depth and customization to the campaign.
Decapitations are gone, and it's somewhat of a letdown because the enemies don't react much to anything but leg and headshots, but the contextual melee attacks on stunned enemies will feel familiar to anyone who's played any of the games past 4.
Switching between the two characters is actually a rather fluid process but disorienting at first until you get used to it. Looking in one direction and then switching into a character who's staring in another can cause some mistakes in combat especially when the game encourages you to do so. One of the newer tricks in the game is to have Moira shine her flashlight on an enemy for a stun so Claire can kick it and then Moira can stab it with a crowbar all without using any ammo.
Overall shooting, dodging, and combat are solid and quickly becoming my favorite in any RE game even over RE4 because of the at-will dodging mechanics.
Actual exploration of the levels is done somewhat similarly in both Barry and Claire's parts of the story. In general you want to use Barry/Claire for combat and Moira/Natalia for exploration and collectibles as both can point out shining object that are generally ammo or BP used for skills.
Extras have generally been a staple for the series and Revelations doesn't shy away from them at all there's an invisible enemy mode as a nod to the original RE along with other fun goodies.
Raid mode is probably the meat of this series and what'll keep it going however. You play a single character of your choosing, level them up, buy/unlock/upgrade weapons and take on increasingly harder stages of enemies with different prefixes and modifiers. Somewhat in a similar way that you'd play a Diablo game where you fight enemies, level up, and get more loot to fight even more powerful enemies.
As a side note there are now gestures taken from Lost Planet 2 that bring back fond memories and it makes me happy to see them again.
If you're an active part of
Capcom always hosts events for these modes that unlock extra things and challenges to the community.
Raid mode in Revelations 2 I would say is hands down 'the' best extra mode in any RE game from mercenaries to raid in revelations 1 they put most of their polish into this mode and it shows. This is most certainly where the game will shine and have people sink most of their time into.
Overall this is one of the better games in the series, and I think it has a lot of potential in both the story and raid mode.

Dead Space is a fun horror survival game I have owned numours times and enjoyed replaying. I first bought this game on the PS3 and put almost 2 days worth into playing it both for achievements and the experience. Dead Space's atmosphere is great and does a beautiful job of creating a spooky sci-fi horror on top of third person survival shooting. The game's story starts off as players playing as an engineer named Isac Clark who knows how to fix
and his team who were sent to fix a planet cracker ship called the Ishimurra. Clark's wife named Nicole was working on the Ishimurra untill something went wrong with their dig site and sent out a distress call for help. As Clark's team enters the Ishimurra they uncover the horrorfying necromorphs in the ship and try to desperatly escape. This game offers hours of fun from straight replayability to the experimenting with gear and tactics used to help you survive. The equipment in Dead Space is upgradable consisting of your suit (RIG), Stasis, Kenisis Module, and a total of 6 guns to use; 5 of them purchasable in game. These upgrades require nodes found in game or purchased at the store to upgrade their arsenal. In order to kill these necromorphs players are forced to shoot/cut thier limbs off instead of just shooting their head or torso bringing a new formula to survival shooting. Shooting thier legs off will only make them crawl towards players and shooting their heads off will make them swing wildly and aimlessly. The horror in this game is good and provides good jump scares even to people who replay the game. There are small mini games in Dead Space both rewarding prizes that aid the player in upgrading equipment or selling to the store. Dead Space is a great horror survival shooter with replayability both for higher difficulty and new game + to experiment with new weapons or simply play again with current equipment. I would not recommend purchasing this game on its own purchasing the Dead Space 1 & 2 bundle is a better price and more bang for your buck as the sequel is equally if not better than the original Dead Space.

I have almost nothing but praise for this game. Damn is it good. The parkour is amazing, fast, fluid and sometimes dangerous. The day night cycle has been perfectly balanced, and you won't be getting♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at how often night comes around. The combat is satisfying as all hell and brutal. Some people believe it to be exactly like Dead Island combat, but I was not fond of that combat at all.
The story was a surprise. I thought this was gonna be a great♥♥♥♥♥♥around game, yet I started to care about what happens to the characters, and was affected by the plot throughout the entire thing. This game is a bit strange when it comes to performance though. The View Distance bar is the only thing that really effects performance, so if you do get this game, set that to about a quarter of the way or half way, that should do fine with BARELY any difference at all. These issues are said to be getting fixed by Techland in the near future. (They did, but in a way that didn't make much sense)
There are plenty of weapons, side quests, and a massive open world to play in. The one HUGE problem I have with this game is something that happens ONCE, and that is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and annoying QTE boss fight. The entire game doesn't have them except when zombies bite you for about 3 seconds, so why the developers put a rather long one randomly in a boss makes little sense. No one likes QTEs.
The night time is... intense. I have experienced it quite a bit now and I still panic. My heart rate rises whenever I go out at night. Sometimes terrifying things will happen, and escaping with your life in those situations is a different kind of rush I haven't felt in a game before.
Other than that, I can't think of any bad things about this game. I don't want to give scores anymore since I feel its a bit unfair to the developers to just assign their game a number, so I will sum it up. The world is gorgeous, the combat is great, parkour is fantastic and I hope one day there is a sequel to expand upon the parkour and maybe a different setting with a new city. I haven't had this much fun with a game in a long time, and have played it nonstop for 2 days whenever I got the chance.
(Side Note: There is a Be The Zombie mode in this game, which is a pvp 1v4, 1v3, 1v2 or 1v1 gamemode that pitches a powered zombie up against the survivors. I have only played this once, playing against the lead game designer of this game, and all I can say is that both sides have OP abilities, all of which will be annoying for the opposing side, but I have not played it enough, or even want to, to write about it here. Its fun, but the singleplayer is better.)

What a gem of a game. This is a 3rd person horror/action game set in a sci-fi setting. I happen to like horror games, action and sci-fi, so this is right up my alley. The programming on this 2008 eclipses that of several crappy so-called AAA releases of 2016. The game works flawlessly on my 21:9 monitor on its full native resolution and full refresh rate. You can't say the same of Fallout 4..
The audiovisuals on this game are brilliant. You really do feel like you are on a massive space station with different locales for different needs. The ambient sounds really add to the atmosphere, sometimes you hear roars, clangs, echos which do not directly affect your gameplay but add to the atmosphere. Occasionally you may have a breather with almost a full quiet, and the next moment you are fighting the enemies again with all the sound stage that is required. The graphics, effects and textures still hold up to this day, no complaints on my end. I wish all AAA games looked this good and especially, ran this well.
The story is well told from several viewpoints: the video feed from your colleagues, from tense audio and text logs which open the past events for the player.
The weapons and other equipment can be upgraded through nodes that you can collect from the station and buy from the store. I always enjoy upgradeable weapons and equipment in games and this one doesn't disappoint. It adds to the experience and allows you to fight/play the way you want.
All in all it's a solid 10/10 from me. I've played this one through before on retail, and am doing it now again on Steam. Great game for fans of this genre.
Just beware, there is plenty of gore, violence and horror, so if you don't enjoy those, this game is not for you. The game is very violent and the enemies grotesque.

Top Things to DO in order to have a good experience playing this game:
1. V-Sync :
Disable it withing the games VISUALS menu, enable it in you graphics card options  (NVidia Control Panel or Radeon Control Panel). This will allow the game to run at 60 FPS rather than 30 FPS, it will also fix the invisible wall problem on the door to proceed, in the room you aquire the plasma cutter.
2. Mouse Sensitivity:
Now this one is a bit more tricky, first and for most let me say that if you choose to play this game with a controller then more power to you as I believe that's the intended main input method the developers had in mind for this game.  Even with the hightest sensitivity the mouse aiming in the game is pretty awful, that's where a gaming mouse saves the day.
If you want to use M&K for the best experience you should use a mouse that allows you to change it's DPI (Dots Per Inch) as noted above gaming mouses are perfect for this. Go to the software (SteelSeries Engine, Corsair Utility Engine etc.) for your mouse and adjust the DPI to the hightest possible.  Now start the game and adjust the mouse sensitivity within the games menu to a level you feel confortable with.
3. Put headphones on, turn off the lights and wear a diaper. Enjoy.

This game takes a well known PC series and consolifies it, dumbing down the base building to a single base, dumbing down the soldier customization into locked equipment slots with a shallow skill tree, and dumbing down the combat into praying you don't get flanked by enemies who get free turns and stat bonuses. Ah XCOM, where to start. This game is quite well done and visually pleasing, but very unforgiving because if you mess up, the game will not hold back at all. If you're looking for an unforgiving turn-based strategy, this is for you.
The story as you might have guessed, involves you as the faceless, nameless commander of the worlds earth defense force repelling an alien invasion. You are tasking with managing and building a base, sending out interceptors to take down UFOs, and sending in ground squads to either clean up the downed UFO or repel an invasion.
Missions vary a little with escort missions, bomb defusal, and what are known as "panic missions" where the goal is to evacuate as many civilians as you can before the aliens kill them, or simply kill all aliens on the map. Some of the story missions do introduce base invasion missions, but those are the only time these can be done.
On to the gameplay. The movement and combat are controlled by an action point system. Each unit has 2 action points, and the usage of these action points varies a little per unit. For example, the sniper uses 2 action points to fire their sniper rifle, although, this requirement can be removed later using a promotion perk.
With the movement, I have run into a few issues where my zone of movement disappearing so that I couldn't tell whether I was simply using 1 action point to move into cover or dashing because the game doesn't tell you outside of those onscreen prompts when you mouse over a location, this was fixed a couple of times when I switched to another soldier, but there were a couple times which it never came back until I moved someone. There was also a fair share of times when the isometric view messed with my perception, especially when moving to higher ground, resulting in some misplaced movements and some starry eyed rookies standing blatantly out of cover because there is no way to undo a move.
The combat is all percentage based, resulting in some rage moments where your soldier is 4 spaces away from an alien, in a flanking position, with a 90% hit chance, and STILL MISSING THE SHOT!! It's functional, but it feels unfair at times when your rifle shot can do "up to 3 damage" and only hits for 2. Cover plays a big part in the game, because if you ever leave a soldier out of it, they will be shot dead so make your moves wisely.
This game is very good at what it does in making a challenging, unforgiving game with a constant sense of vulnerability, but sometimes it felt cheap, like when you move in contact range of an alien, they immediately detect you and basically get a free move into cover, effectively gaining the upper hand before shots were even fired. In too many cases though, I have resulted to save-scumming because if your super star team gets taken down, there is no way to get back to that point because you can't send your troops back at the base through "marksman training" or anything like that, so the meta-game is limited to base building, research, and arms manufacturing. There is a new element with psychic training for soldiers later, but this is limited to the combatants that come back positive from that testing, so again, it's rather limited.
I would reccomend this to anyone who played the original or is familiar to turn-based games, because this is very good at what it does. To anyone that is new to turn-based strategy, buy this game, play it on easy, and save after every single encounter because otherwise this game will eat you alive.

So, my only complaints are the difficulty and the length.  Even with the game set on the hardest difficulty, the battles are a joke because you're just so strong. Additionally, you're healed after every battle and can save anywhere, so there's never any threat of dying and losing progress.
Second is the length.  You'd think a show that spans more than 15 years can have enough content to make a game that's longer than 10 hours (15 if you take your time and do all the side quests and collection.)  So many characters and locations are just given a tiny cameo or mention.
Still though, I hope this is a the start of a beautiful journey of quality SP games.  I would love to explore its world with a full 4-5 man party with an actual challenge.

Top Things to DO in order to have a good experience playing this game:
1. V-Sync :
Disable it withing the games VISUALS menu, enable it in you graphics card options  (NVidia Control Panel or Radeon Control Panel). This will allow the game to run at 60 FPS rather than 30 FPS, it will also fix the invisible wall problem on the door to proceed, in the room you aquire the plasma cutter.
2. Mouse Sensitivity:
Now this one is a bit more tricky, first and for most let me say that if you choose to play this game with a controller then more power to you as I believe that's the intended main input method the developers had in mind for this game.  Even with the hightest sensitivity the mouse aiming in the game is pretty awful, that's where a gaming mouse saves the day.
If you want to use M&K for the best experience you should use a mouse that allows you to change it's DPI (Dots Per Inch) as noted above gaming mouses are perfect for this. Go to the software (SteelSeries Engine, Corsair Utility Engine etc.) for your mouse and adjust the DPI to the hightest possible.  Now start the game and adjust the mouse sensitivity within the games menu to a level you feel confortable with.
3. Put headphones on, turn off the lights and wear a diaper. Enjoy.

Your weapons arent't as powerful and they can/will break permanently.  During the day it's all good.  You can outrun the zombies and as long you're not going head to head with a zombie pack you'll be fine.  But this all changes when night falls in...  My first night encounter almost left me♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥my pants.  I've made it to a drop when suddenly it got all dark.  And I mean really dark...  I knew I didn't have much time.  I had to get to a safe house.  Then it spots me.  This big ugly crazy zombie beast.  I start running, but I can't see where I'm going.  I run and jump and I hear the creature right behind me.  I'm afraid to look back and keep going, completely disorientated.  Then I try to climb on a rooftop when it bites me...  I still manage to get on the rooftop and turn around.  I'm surrounded...  A pack of menacing zombies approach and climb on the rooftop.  I swing at them with my electrical pipe and sparks fly all over the place.  But I knew a was in real trouble... The kindest thing I can say about Faerie Solitaire is that it's designed to let you bite off very small servings. From the time when you start the game, you can be playing a hand in about 15 seconds, and each hand takes just 90-120 seconds to complete. So if you need to kill 5 minutes but don't feel like waiting a full minute or two to fire up a larger game, this is a fine time waster, right here.
Having said that, it's not a particularly good solitaire game. It's basically TriPeaks with some variation to the layouts. It adds in grind features to compel you to continue playing, but these features aren't very well designed. Some of these features, in fact, add strategic elements to the game that actually make it less enjoyable, for me.
I'm prying myself away after about 4 hours. Friends who have finished it tell me it takes 12-15 hours. Can't do it.

Ah XCOM, where to start. This game is quite well done and visually pleasing, but very unforgiving because if you mess up, the game will not hold back at all. If you're looking for an unforgiving turn-based strategy, this is for you.
The story as you might have guessed, involves you as the faceless, nameless commander of the worlds earth defense force repelling an alien invasion. You are tasking with managing and building a base, sending out interceptors to take down UFOs, and sending in ground squads to either clean up the downed UFO or repel an invasion.
Missions vary a little with escort missions, bomb defusal, and what are known as "panic missions" where the goal is to evacuate as many civilians as you can before the aliens kill them, or simply kill all aliens on the map. Some of the story missions do introduce base invasion missions, but those are the only time these can be done.
On to the gameplay. The movement and combat are controlled by an action point system. Each unit has 2 action points, and the usage of these action points varies a little per unit. For example, the sniper uses 2 action points to fire their sniper rifle, although, this requirement can be removed later using a promotion perk.
With the movement, I have run into a few issues where my zone of movement disappearing so that I couldn't tell whether I was simply using 1 action point to move into cover or dashing because the game doesn't tell you outside of those onscreen prompts when you mouse over a location, this was fixed a couple of times when I switched to another soldier, but there were a couple times which it never came back until I moved someone. There was also a fair share of times when the isometric view messed with my perception, especially when moving to higher ground, resulting in some misplaced movements and some starry eyed rookies standing blatantly out of cover because there is no way to undo a move.
The combat is all percentage based, resulting in some rage moments where your soldier is 4 spaces away from an alien, in a flanking position, with a 90% hit chance, and STILL MISSING THE SHOT!! It's functional, but it feels unfair at times when your rifle shot can do "up to 3 damage" and only hits for 2. Cover plays a big part in the game, because if you ever leave a soldier out of it, they will be shot dead so make your moves wisely.
This game is very good at what it does in making a challenging, unforgiving game with a constant sense of vulnerability, but sometimes it felt cheap, like when you move in contact range of an alien, they immediately detect you and basically get a free move into cover, effectively gaining the upper hand before shots were even fired. In too many cases though, I have resulted to save-scumming because if your super star team gets taken down, there is no way to get back to that point because you can't send your troops back at the base through "marksman training" or anything like that, so the meta-game is limited to base building, research, and arms manufacturing. There is a new element with psychic training for soldiers later, but this is limited to the combatants that come back positive from that testing, so again, it's rather limited.
I would reccomend this to anyone who played the original or is familiar to turn-based games, because this is very good at what it does. To anyone that is new to turn-based strategy, buy this game, play it on easy, and save after every single encounter because otherwise this game will eat you alive.

This one-trick pony of a game uses a poor control paradigm and distracting visuals to create artificial difficulty by making the game harder to play - rather than a proper simple-challenge game, which is easy to play, but hard to do well at. Imagine if Pacman had only two ghosts, but was just as hard because it had no power pellets and the board had fewer branches. And also you can't see the entire board at once. Are you starting to see what I'm getting at?
This is a perfect case study of how not to design a game; right off the bat it's painfully obvious that it's designed to create as large a barrier as possible to the player's state of flow and feeling of tense, ongoing accomplishment. I can't briefly express just how immensely the control scheme and visual style completely undermine and anti-pattern with the core gameplay. This game doesn't just not want to be beaten; it doesn't want to be PLAYED.
I would have quit at 2 minutes, but Steam doesn't let you review until you've played for 5; let me tell you that the next 6 minutes were far, far worse than I anticipated. The longer you play this, the more subtle design flaws you discover. If only the game weren't so abstract I could tell myself it was a satire. If I could remember who gifted this to me, it would put our steam friendship in jeopardy.
If you want a simple, challenging game, almost any option you could possibly choose would be better than this, including just about any popular free flash game on the internet. One Finger Death Punch is good, try that one instead.
UPDATE: I haven't played it but Boson X looks like a much, MUCH better attempt at basically the same game. It looks like it actually wants you to play it and have fun, so try that instead.

This game started out as being excellent. I've now bought it on a console and on Steam (for the Enemy Within content), and have been happy (excited even), by each addition to the game that has been put out. In my opinion, each additional piece of content has all added to the game's overall allure. I have to admit that I've always loved turn-based gameplay, and resource management, so it was going to be hard for a game like this not to make me happy, but I think that the creators have outdone themselves with this mixture of those two game types.
The latest addition-Enemy Within-is a little pricey, but if you are a big fan of the game, you are likely to find that content worthwhile. You can now further enhance your squad-members with genetic and cybernetic enhancement, there is an interesting added side story, with good battles, and tough new enemies to fight. I know that it will have me playing through the entire game at least several more times, and I haven't played more than about three or four games through to the end over the last decade.
The only real downside that I've seen is on the multiplayer-side of the game, which I wish had been geared towards cooperative play, and which is simplistic when compared to the expansiveness of the campaign mode. That being said, the game is worth it without any kind of multiplayer option, so I don't mind seeing it as a minor addition, for when I just don't feel like playing the main game.

One of my favorite indie games.
Pros:
-The combat system is surprisingly deep. You have 4 basic attacks for each character but learning when to perform each of them takes practice.
-I find the music in this game great. It has a futuristic/space-like style into it and it really suits the game.
-The game also has tremendous replay value. There are many characters and items to unlock and also it feels like playing a Pac-Man/Tetris like game, it just never gets old. In fact I think if they ever release a sequel they should add a high score feature similar to Super House of Dead Ninjas.
Cons:
-The game has some bugs that will ruin many perfectly good runs. Updates have solved many of them but they also created new ones.
-The multiplayer is pretty basic. You either have to install third-party software or go to some websites where you can post your server’s IP or connect to another player’s server. For people that are not familiar with router setting and IP forwarding it might be difficult to play multiplayer.
-Not really a negative in my book but the high difficulty (at least initially) might put some people off.

Do you like space?  Do you like zombies?  Do you like fighting through wave after wave of faceless, terrifying enemies?  If so, this game is a must!
Story:  9/10  As Isaac Clark, you get plunged into a desperate struggle for survival as you try to find a way off of the USG Ishimura, a deep-space mining ship that becomes infected with an alien parasite that turns corpses into vicious, mindless zombie things called Necromorphs.  You must fight your way through the ship, repairing key systems and unravelling the mysteries of the ship's mission.  The tory does a great job of keeping the tone of the game consistent throughout.  The whole time, you are seemingly one step behind, as you desperatley try to repair life support systems, engines, etc.  The problem I have with the story is the plot twist at the end, which I won't spoil.
Gameplay:  9/10  This game has one of the most creative combat systems I've come across in my many years of gaming.  It is, at its core, a third-person shooter, but not like the Mass Effect series where you run around guns ablaze.  To kill the necromorph enemies, you have to dismember them with your improvised weapons made from engineering tools.  You have to use your environment to your advantage.  The weapon upgrade system is very simple, yet rewarding.  As the game progresses, the enemies become more challenging to defeat, and require different strategies and weapons to beat.  Also, this game does a great job, in my opinion, of making boss battles.  They are simple and not too challenging (at least at easy difficulties), but I can't think of many modern games with actual boss battles.  Pretty much every level ends with one.  You also have at your disposal a stasis tool that sets anything it hits, wether it's an enemy or malfuntioning door, into slow-motion.  You also have a kinesis tool that allows you to grab things from afar and throw them.  You will have to use these things in conjunction to solve puzzles.
Setting:  9/10  The USG Ishimura gets a little boring after a few levels, as everything kind of looks the same.  That being said, I'm a sucker for scientifically accurate space games.  Upon entering the vaccuum of space, you loose sound for the most part.  There are many places of zero-gravity, where you get to float around in dissorienting fashion.  The ship is creepy and almost archaic-looking, which fits the tone of the game very well.  The game has a few moments of horror, especially at the begining.  You pick up voice and text logs throughout the game, which add depth to the story.
Overall, I really enjoy this game.  It also has some nice replay value as it allows you to keep all of your weapons, with their upgrades, and your suit when you start a new game.  The story is also pretty fun the second time around because of the several plot twists you know about from the first play through.  The best thing about this game is the atmosphere it creates when you play it.  If you aren't playing with all of the lights turned off with sound-cancelling headphones, you aren't playing it right!

A game that borrows a little bit of something from others, like parkour, lockpicking from Skyrim, melee, crafting, open world and does it all very-very well.
- Parkour actually requiress a bit of skill. Just going forward while pushing down a button is not enough, which is good, as it makes you feel as you actually are in control of the movement. The movement itself is dynamic: as you gain speed, you start to run and climb a bit faster. If you fall a lot - don't complain, as it's mostly your fault. Unlockable agility skills also don't hurt.
- Melee combat is heavy and you can feel the contact. You might appear underpowered at first, but with new toys you will discover a whole different flow of combat, when you can slice through multiple enemies at once, or crush them with one blow.
- Discovery is interesting, with different places and tone variation to them. The vistas are spectacular. The game also somehow manages to make you feel a bit scared of heights.
- The game, despite it's predictably boring story, has great atmosphere to it.
- The game is also quite beautiful, just be sure to tweak the options (especially the texture quality), as the default ones are often wrong for your system, and you will end up with massive stutter and freezing. One of the system I had to install it on has a fx6300 CPU and a gtx670, whith horrendous freezes and hickups once you get into the world - turns out I had to reduce the viewing distance to 0 (which still rpvides a very goo viewing distance with lots of detail), and textures to medium and it runs very well now, mostly in 38-45 range, with other setting on and medium, inculding the NVIDIA-specific ones.
- It's so rare to have a game with open world traversal and main campaign coop, not just some tack-on coop missions ( like in Far Cry 3 or4, etc...)
- There's some challenge in the game, which is a nice change from Dead Island.
As I go along, I doubt my opinion will change much, as Dying Light is almost exactly what I wanted it to be.

After hearing so much praise for this game, i'm rather surprised it was incredibly lackluster experience for me. I don't think it's because of having good expectations going in and them not living up to them. It was actually just not that good of a game to me.
Dead Space is a game with very cliche story-telling and boring, uninteresting characters who have rather immature fights with each other, and you pretty much just have you shoulder the responsibilites of... everything really. They ask you to do just about everything and spit really menial boring "story dialouge" at you that I found myself almost passively ignoring because it was just so bland and uninsprired and typical/predictable. Even then, there was hardly a story to really follow, in the sense of, it was really laid out for you. Incredibly simple.
There's a church, they have the ishimura on a illegal planet cracking trip to uncover the marker. Then psychotic "the church" people believe the coming of gods new children are here (the necromorphs) and it's time for humanity to die out and be replaced by the necromorphs which are 'better' than humans. It's just so simple and boring and like, it really only took a couple of logs you pick up in the game mid-to-late game to really just lay out the entire story for you in a nutshell. Everything else is focused on 'survival'. Which is really just an extremely unncessary amount of fetch quests, because apparently, for the most part, not a damn thing in the ship almost the entire game takes place works. Every single new chapter is really just these really baseboards characters whining and crying about how nothing works and nothing is simple and how spooked and scared of the necromorphs they are and how they think (x) is dead.
I ended up just getting infuriated and annoyed by the story design of essentially doing nothing but fetch quests with no new interesting developments or changes to the story. Like yeah they added new characters, but it was just a guy who was like "The marker is bad, lets' destroy it or give it back." and then the crazy church guy who was like "Humans are weak, necromorphs are gods new children, let them take over."
Woah, totally interesting not cliche boring characters.
Then we get to the gameplay. It was easy, very easy. Too much money floating around, the beginning guns are really good (except the assault rifle) and there's no need to change them. There's no tension or fear I felt fighting the enemies. The atmosphere was boring because you quickly just got used to gore and blood be splattered everywhere and seeing nothing but metal walls, the entire atmosphere just got incredibly tasteless and bland. Rarely did a set do anything to set itself apart from other rooms, and I don't count things like the hospital either, that's just a metal room with medical equipment and tools in it.
Anyways, how was the gameplay easy? The very first gun you get is basically just god-like and really, really good. Not in the sense from the get-go, but giving it mods and developing the thing just turns it into a killing machine. With plentiful of ammo for it always around, I never felt tension or fear cause bullets for the gun that just quickly kills everything was everywhere. And if it wasn't everywhere? ...you buy it! There's so much money in this game and excess of items, I don't think I used one large medpack in this entire game, I just sold them for credits, and ammo for the line gun (one of the first new guns you can acquire) is quite easy to find and I rarely ever used it. So I could sell off the ammo for it for loads of cash, which in turn can be used to buy modules that allow you to mod you guns and make them EVEN MORE POWERFUL! :D
And with that, you can increase your health, increase your air-time in space, increase your guns powers, your power to slow-down enemies.
You can also buy new suits that allow you to carry more stuff, aka more stuff to sell. There's a lot of money lying around in this game, there's lots of items WORTH a lot of money just lying around. Medpacks are in ample supply. I beat this game using nothing but the first two guns you can acquire and the flame thrower to clean up some of the smaller more simple monsters that I don't want to waste ammo on.
And then we get into bad game design. It's incredibly hard not to compare this to resident evil 4 and think about how much wrong there is in this game.
The lack of variety in enemies, how easy it is to dispatch them, how the game constantly spams them at you whenever they can.
Now, first off. When I say lack of variety in enemies. They really all just look the same, except some of them have tougher skin. The game showed off new enemy types WAY too far late into the game, and by then, they're very easy to kill, and not very interesting either. Really all the enemies are, are just tentacle babies, and floor crawlers, and then your standard guy standing in their legs and with sycthe arms. To kill enemies in this game, you kill them by cutting off their extremities. I just cut off their legs first and then their arms, to basically immobilize them and then easily cut off their arms.
I don't care to get too much into that, cause it's really just that. Easily lopping off limbs without much of a sweat. Nothing changed to make it more difficult or interesting or dynamic. It was almost... generic. It like just easy enemies lining up for the headshot except their head is their limbs.
The pacing is awful, this game spams enemies at you at every given turn, it's becomes an annoyance. I actually yelled at game game for putting just even more enemies in needless locations. Constantly in tiny rooms, never can go down a big room without some alien attack. It was aggravating and annoying, I couldn't do anything without monsters being there. There's ways to build tension and fear without having boring insessant conflicts all the time. You can't even do the no-gravity space puzzles without being attacked. It's incredibly tiring and annoying.
I don't know, this entire game was a disppointment to me. Most of what I did felt like a chore, combat was easy, I felt no fear or tension, the story was elementary, and the characters were faceless contructs that had relatively nothing to contribute to the "story" and had I want to say no personality to speak of.
Some people may find enjoyment in this game, because they will perhaps just simply enjoy gunning down zombie-like monsters and exploring the (woefully unexciting) ship and space, and that's fine. Plenty of people enjoyed this game clearly. However I found the experience to be a complete letdown and i'm just voicing why I think that it was not good.
Regardless, thanks for reading my review. I hope it helped you in your decision to get this game or not. Have a good one.
Edit: Also I played this game in its enterity on my xbox 360 controller.

Vice City is, perhaps, not the most notable game in the GTA franchise. It could've been a DLC for GTA 3, but content-wise it's a full game of its own. It puts you in a world oozing of 80s pop culture, and you would have to be crazy not to love that. The game has some small improvements over GTA 3, and features some new stuff that vary from good to less good. It's easy to see that things started leaning toward a less arcade-like experience than GTA 3, which continued later in the series. For instance, the protagonist now has a voice and personality. The series gains some new grounds with Vice City, but it's pretty much on-par with GTA 3. It's not as revolutionary as GTA 3, but it's definitely a good game, and shows the direction the franchise later took. A positive recommendation from me.

This game started out as being excellent. I've now bought it on a console and on Steam (for the Enemy Within content), and have been happy (excited even), by each addition to the game that has been put out. In my opinion, each additional piece of content has all added to the game's overall allure. I have to admit that I've always loved turn-based gameplay, and resource management, so it was going to be hard for a game like this not to make me happy, but I think that the creators have outdone themselves with this mixture of those two game types.
The latest addition-Enemy Within-is a little pricey, but if you are a big fan of the game, you are likely to find that content worthwhile. You can now further enhance your squad-members with genetic and cybernetic enhancement, there is an interesting added side story, with good battles, and tough new enemies to fight. I know that it will have me playing through the entire game at least several more times, and I haven't played more than about three or four games through to the end over the last decade.
The only real downside that I've seen is on the multiplayer-side of the game, which I wish had been geared towards cooperative play, and which is simplistic when compared to the expansiveness of the campaign mode. That being said, the game is worth it without any kind of multiplayer option, so I don't mind seeing it as a minor addition, for when I just don't feel like playing the main game.

At first i was sceptical at the release of a new X-Com title after almost 15 years (X-Com Appocalypse was already quite a dissapointment compared to X-Com 1 & 2). The most noticable difference is that you don't build your base like you would in the former X-Com. Instead of managing eight different bases all around the globe, you just take care of one using some kind of ant-farm side-view. The platoon phases use a slightly different turn-based mechanic which offer an alternative to the good old time-unit system without differing much.
It's interesting. Different, but interesting. The graphics are very nice. The levels have a decent variety. But for some reason it doesn't feel like the old X-Com. It's a reduced scale of the classic X-Com. 8 times less bases to manage. 8 times less soldier to take care of (max 6 soldiers in your squad, here). 3 times faster to complete...
It's a modern X-Com which tries (reasonably well) to keep all the features of its ancestor. While it benefits from the quality level of curent technologies, it also suffers the same issues that plague any other resurected franchises today: Visually and technically improved... but also shorter, less challenging or involving than its predecessors.
So my verdict is that i liked that new X-Com very much for long awaited sequel. But i was expecting much more. I'd still give it 7/10 even as the old classic X-Com fan i am.

It's been a hectic ride, and the game is finally out. The development has had its ups and downs, often with the developers bringing in an update every now and then that screwed things up for many loyal fans of the original game.
As it stands now, the game is pretty much in its prime. 10 unique Perks, 1 of which is a "do anything" versatile one, plenty of maps, and a full integration with steam workshop if you wanted more.
Visually, the game never ceases to amaze. Even on mid-range pc's, it functions well, and doesn't lose too much quality as you bring the settings down. AI is smart, dodging attacks, swerving while dishing out their own to avoid even point blank shots, and a crazy variety that keeps the flow tense and varied. If you can handle it, the Flex system adds a level of gore that feels really brutal.
With almost 500 hours in, I can vouch that both solo and online modes provide hectic gameplay. On solo, which makes up most my hours, the game can be relaxing on normal and hard, tense on suicidal, and absolutedly nightmarish on hell on earth. On higher difficulties, every mistake you make the game will punish you. Every accomplishment you make will just feel like normal as you continue on. Or you can keep the difficulty limited and enjoy some blaring metal as you bring death and destruction on everything in your way. That works too.
Online, the challenge is less about surviving and more about communicating. Bigger zeds will pummel you down if you don't focus on them, while smaller zeds will swarm you if not everyone keeps the pressure off each other.
As for your bosses, you currently have volter, a gas obssessed German with an exo-suit, dual rifles, grenades, gas grenades, and a rage mode that has him spamming gas grenades while running at mach speed and rip you apart. Did I mention the gas grenades?
The Patriarch is a different story. A hulking wall of flesh from the original, his attacks are easier to dodge (probably because he warns you about what he's about to use), including a minigun, rocket launcher, invisibility, and his stomach-arm-thing.
A perfect transition for old-school fans? Probably not. A reason to transition from L4D and other horde games? Most definitely.

A classic horror game that I played back on the 360 in 2008 and replayed on Steam in  2016.
Pros:
-Good atmosphere made by the music and gory environment.
-Plenty of well placed jumpscares along with spooky stuff that isn't necessarily a jumpscare but raises the tension.
-A small but unique array of weapons to blast apart the baddies (although I'm a plasma cutter for life).
-Interesting narrative with plenty of backstory and notes to add more.
Cons:
-Controls are pretty crap. Isaac controls like an old 8-bit tank where you could only turn and move, not both simultaneously. Makes him feel really clunky, especially when you need to be desperately running and gunning to survive. Looking around also has an acceleration to it, so you cannot snap to your target. Instead it feels like you're dragging your reticle through molasses.
-Load times are pretty long, whether its a screen or a door that blocks you while spawning the next room. Even on a powerful rig load times are frustratingly long.
Overall:
Even with the two gripes, this game is a solid 9/10. I would recommend it to anyone looking for an action-y shooter game while have that layer of horror strapped on top. Definitely recommend it for anyone who hasn't played it before or those looking for a nostalgia trip if you have. Darkness and Headphones are a must while playing!

FTL is a gem of a game. Originally one of the early Kickstarter video game projects, FTL managed to raise over $200,000 of it's meager $10,000 goal. With the expanded budget, Subset Games was able to improve upon the alpha build that made it's way through Onlive and has become what you see now.
Based off of "rogue-like" titles, where dying is commonplace and failure is merely a tool to learn how to do better, FTL has you captaining a vessel and crew trying to outrun a hostile fleet with vital information about an ongoing war effort. As you race through sectors of friendly, neutral, and hostile space, you work your way up to improving your ship and crew.
Fight off enemy boarders, fires, hull breaches, and repair damaged subsystems. Deal with things in a diplomatic manner as best you can, or just make for that beeline to friendly forces.
FTL is an absolute steal, and it's great to have it here on Steam.

To sum up, If you liked or loved Dead Island you will enjoy this game, if you enjoyed Dead Island for only a bit and found it to be not good but rather barely ok you may still enjoy this game because the parkour makes a big difference, and if you absolutly hated Dead Island you will probably not like this game either.
